paper_profiles.title: Impact of AI-Blended Learning and AI-Personalized Learning on Undergraduate Biology Students' Attitude and Performance in Climate Change Education
paper_profiles.venue: Anchor University Journal of Science and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-enhanced instructional approaches improve undergraduate biology students’ attitudes toward climate change and their academic performance in climate change education better than traditional classroom teaching. The study is motivated by the concern that conventional instruction may not sufficiently engage students or address diverse learning needs when teaching complex environmental topics.

The intervention compared three instructional conditions: AI-Blended Learning, AI-Personalized Learning, and Traditional Classroom Instruction. In the AI-Blended Learning condition, students used ChatGPT-3.5 alongside face-to-face teaching. In the AI-Personalized Learning condition, students relied on ChatGPT-3.5 as the primary instructional support in a fully AI-driven personalized environment. The comparison group received conventional face-to-face instruction without the AI intervention. Outcomes were measured using a Climate Change Attitude Assessment (CCAA) and a Climate Change Achievement Test (CCAT), with pretest and posttest scores analyzed using ANCOVA.

The study involved 70 300-level undergraduate biology students at Federal University Gusau in Nigeria. Students were drawn from existing classes and assigned into three groups: AI-Blended Learning (20), AI-Personalized Learning (20), and Traditional Classroom Instruction (30). The intervention lasted four weeks and covered climate change topics such as causes, impacts, mitigation strategies, and policy actions.

The main finding is that AI-Blended Learning produced substantially stronger gains in both attitude and performance than either AI-Personalized Learning or Traditional Classroom Instruction. Post hoc analyses showed that the blended approach significantly outperformed both alternatives, while AI-Personalized Learning did not significantly differ from traditional instruction on the reported comparisons. The paper concludes that integrating ChatGPT-3.5 with teacher-led classroom instruction is more effective than relying on AI alone, and recommends that higher education lecturers adopt AI-blended approaches to improve engagement and learning outcomes in environmental education.

paper_profiles.title: Studying the effect of AI Code Generators on Supporting Novice Learners in Introductory Programming
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI code generators such as OpenAI Codex help or hinder novice learners who are first learning introductory text-based programming. The authors focus on a key educational concern: although AI-generated code may improve immediate task performance, it could also create over-reliance and weaken learners’ ability to understand, modify, or retain programming knowledge. The study addresses whether novices can effectively use AI code generation, how it changes task performance, and whether prior access to such tools affects later independent coding and retention.

To study this, the researchers built a web-based Python learning environment called Coding Steps. Learners completed a three-week, 10-session remote program consisting of a Scratch-based introduction and pre-test, seven Python training sessions, and two evaluation sessions (an immediate post-test and a one-week retention test). During training, one group had access to an AI code generator powered by OpenAI Codex, while a comparison group did not. Participants worked through 45 code-authoring tasks, each followed by a code-modification task, plus multiple-choice questions on core introductory Python topics such as variables, conditionals, loops, and arrays. The system logged code edits, documentation use, errors, submissions, and AI prompt/code-generation behavior.

The population consisted of 69 novice learners aged 10-17 recruited through coding camps in two major North American cities. All reported no prior text-based programming experience, though many had experience with block-based programming environments such as Scratch. Participants were assigned to conditions using a matched-groups design based on Scratch pre-test scores to balance prior programming knowledge. The study was conducted remotely via Google Meet, with instructors available to provide support and personalized feedback during training.

The main findings were that access to Codex substantially improved performance on training-phase code-authoring tasks: learners completed more tasks, achieved higher correctness, made fewer errors, and finished faster. Importantly, prior use of the AI tool did not reduce performance on subsequent manual code-modification tasks, and learners in the Codex group performed similarly to the baseline group on the immediate post-test without access to the tool. On the one-week retention test, the Codex group showed slightly better performance, though differences were not statistically significant overall. The authors conclude that AI code generators can support novice programming learning without clear evidence of harming short-term retention, and that learners with stronger prior programming competency may benefit the most.

paper_profiles.title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-generated feedback on student writing can be used effectively in higher education language learning, and whether students prefer it to feedback from human tutors. The authors focus on the emerging use of generative AI, specifically ChatGPT/GPT-4, as an automated writing evaluation tool for English as a new language (ENL) learners. The study addresses two core questions: whether AI feedback produces stronger writing gains than human feedback, and whether students prefer AI-generated or tutor-generated feedback.

The paper reports two longitudinal studies conducted over six weeks. In Study 1, the intervention compared GPT-4-generated writing feedback with feedback from human tutors in a repeated-measures quasi-experimental design. ENL students completed weekly 300-word academic writing tasks, received either AI or human feedback, revised their work, and were assessed through pre- and post-writing tests scored with an analytic rubric. In Study 2, a separate group of students received both AI-generated and human tutor feedback on weekly assignments, then completed weekly surveys with Likert-scale and open-ended items about satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and overall preference.

The population consisted of 91 ENL university students enrolled in an academic reading and writing course at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region. Study 1 included 48 students, and Study 2 included 43 different students. Human tutors were trained English language tutors from the university’s ENL Tutor Program, while GPT-4 feedback was generated using an iteratively developed prompt designed by experienced language educators. The intervention occurred in the context of regular course writing assignments during a shortened Spring 2023 semester.

The main conclusion is that AI-generated feedback did not produce significantly different writing gains compared with human tutor feedback. Students in both conditions improved similarly over the six-week period. Preference data showed an almost even split between AI and human feedback. Students who preferred human tutors valued face-to-face interaction, engagement, and the ability to ask immediate follow-up questions, while those preferring AI valued clarity, specificity, consistency, and detailed academic language suggestions. The authors conclude that AI-generated feedback can likely be incorporated into ENL writing instruction without harming learning outcomes, and they recommend a blended approach that combines the efficiency and specificity of AI with the interpersonal benefits of human tutoring.

paper_profiles.title: Examining Faculty and Student Perceptions of Generative AI in University Courses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students and faculty perceive generative AI tools such as ChatGPT in higher education, with particular attention to perceived ease of use, ethical concerns, intentions to use, and views about impacts on learning. The study addresses a gap in empirical evidence about how attitudes toward generative AI differ across university roles and across student subgroups defined by gender and STEM versus non-STEM disciplines.

The study used an anonymous online survey grounded in a modified UTAUT framework and supplemented with items about perceived effects on learning competencies and ethics. The survey measured constructs such as performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, hedonic motivation, habit, personal innovativeness, and behavioral intention, along with views about academic integrity, policy needs, and the frequency of generative AI use. The approach was descriptive and comparative rather than experimental.

Participants were 982 students and 76 faculty members at a single large land-grant public university in the southeastern United States during the Fall 2023 semester. The student sample included both undergraduate and other university students, and analyses compared students with faculty as well as four student subgroups: STEM male, STEM female, non-STEM male, and non-STEM female. Data were collected between December 2023 and January 2024 through voluntary online survey distribution.

The authors conclude that students and faculty were broadly similar in their attitudes toward generative AI, though students reported higher ease of use, hedonic motivation, and personal innovativeness, while faculty reported more habitual use. Both groups used generative AI at similarly low rates overall and shared concerns about negative effects on learning competencies and academic dishonesty, while also supporting the development of institutional policies. Within the student sample, male STEM students tended to express the most positive attitudes and non-STEM female students the least positive, suggesting that gender and disciplinary context shape how generative AI is received in higher education.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Students’ Multimodal Representations of Ideas About Epistemic Reading of Scientific Texts in Generative AI Tools
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students represent their ideas about reading scientific texts generated by generative AI tools, a process the authors call GenAI-science epistemic reading. The problem addressed is that students need to draw on both their understanding of science and their understanding of GenAI in order to critically interpret AI-generated scientific information, yet existing measures in this area are often limited to Likert-scale surveys. The study asks what students’ multimodal representations of these ideas look like in terms of presentational, organisational, and orientational meanings.

The study uses a qualitative collective case study approach and develops a multimodal instrument in which students draw and write short explanations about (1) how ChatGPT/Poe generates scientific texts and (2) how they themselves read scientific texts in these tools. The authors analyze 44 students’ drawings and written responses using Lemke’s framework of presentational, organisational, and orientational meaning, and from these data they construct an analytical framework with categories such as epistemic trust, epistemic knowledge, organisational form, and representations of the nature of science and GenAI. Although the responses were collected before an explicit-reflective instructional activity that was part of a larger project, this paper focuses on the pre-instruction representations rather than testing intervention effects.

Participants were 44 Grade 8 and Grade 9 students in Hong Kong participating in extracurricular lessons. The instructional context involved a bilingual teacher who had prior online training workshops on implementing the teaching approach. Students completed the multimodal task in two classrooms before instruction, and the broader project centered on improving students’ understanding of epistemic reading of scientific texts from sources including GenAI and online media.

The main conclusion is that a multimodal approach is useful for characterising students’ ideas about GenAI-science epistemic reading in ways that standard survey instruments may miss. Students expressed a range of epistemic trust positions, including trust, critical thinking, confusion, and non-evaluation, and used different semiotic modes to express these ideas. The paper’s core contribution is an analytical framework teachers and researchers can use to diagnose and discuss students’ epistemic understanding of AI-generated scientific texts. The authors argue that such multimodal representations can serve as a richer diagnostic and instructional tool for future intervention studies on GenAI in science education.

paper_profiles.title: AI Responses to Challenging Problems and Educator Responses to AI Availability
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI tools, specifically ChatGPT and Gemini, respond to cognitively demanding secondary mathematics tasks and what educators should do in response to increasing AI availability. The authors are concerned not only with whether GenAI can produce mathematical answers, but also with the pedagogical implications of tools that can engage in open-ended reasoning, generate explanations, and revise responses after prompting. The article situates this issue within secondary mathematics education and argues that educators should move beyond a ban-oriented stance toward instructional uses that preserve student thinking and reasoning.

The approach is a conceptual and illustrative analysis rather than an empirical intervention study. The authors posed three mathematics tasks spanning middle and high school content areas—rates and proportional reasoning, geometric proof, and quadratic interpretation—to ChatGPT 3.5, ChatGPT 4.0, and Gemini 1.0 during March–April 2024. They then analyzed the quality, strengths, and errors in the AI responses and derived two instructional strategies for educators: having students interact with GenAI to explore, clarify, and extend mathematical ideas, and having students critique AI-generated solutions and arguments. The paper includes concrete examples of prompts teachers could use to support these strategies.

The population and context are secondary mathematics education in the United States, with examples drawn from US middle school and high school mathematics curricula. However, no human participants were recruited and no classroom implementation data were collected. Instead, the article focuses on hypothetical and proposed uses of GenAI by students and educators in classroom mathematics settings.

The main conclusions are that current GenAI systems can engage with cognitively demanding mathematics tasks in ways that exceed traditional calculators or step-solving apps, but they also make substantial mathematical and logical errors. The authors therefore recommend that teachers use GenAI as a conversational and critical-thinking tool rather than as an answer engine. They argue that student learning can be supported when students are asked to interrogate, extend, and evaluate AI responses, especially in ways that preserve mathematical communication, reasoning, and proof-oriented thinking.

paper_profiles.title: Secondary school teachers’ perspectives on GenAI proliferation: generating advanced insights
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how the rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is affecting secondary education, with a particular focus on academic integrity, teaching practices, assessment, and teacher support needs. The central research question asks what significant challenges and opportunities Ontario secondary school teachers perceive as GenAI becomes more common in schools. The authors position the study as addressing a gap in the literature, noting that most prior discussion has centered on postsecondary education rather than secondary schools.

The study uses a qualitative interview design grounded in invitational education as a theoretical framework. Seventeen practising Ontario secondary school teachers from five publicly funded school boards were recruited and interviewed in semi-structured sessions lasting about 60 minutes. Data were collected between November 2023 and January 2024, transcribed, member-checked, and coded in Atlas.ti. The analysis produced three main themes: generating people, generating programs, and generating policies. These themes capture teachers’ calls for professional development and expertise-building, structured and transparent school programs for GenAI integration, and clear policies to govern acceptable use, academic integrity, and institutional expectations.

The population studied was high school teachers in southern Ontario, Canada, rather than students directly. Participants represented a range of teaching experience levels and subjects, but all were secondary educators working in public school boards. The study context is school-based secondary education, though the data come from interviews rather than classroom implementation of a specific AI tool or intervention.

The paper concludes that teachers see GenAI as both a disruptive challenge and a potentially valuable educational tool, but they feel underprepared and under-supported. The authors argue that effective GenAI integration requires coordinated action across three areas: teacher capacity-building through professional development, purposeful programs and practices for assessment and instruction, and adaptable policy frameworks that support ethical and equitable use. They emphasize collaboration among teachers, administrators, policymakers, parents, and other stakeholders, and propose a train-the-trainer style model using teacher champions to support scalable GenAI integration while preserving academic integrity.

paper_profiles.title: Suitability of Chinese GenAI platforms for early childhood education: A multifaceted evaluation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether currently available Chinese generative AI platforms are suitable for use in early childhood education (ECE), a context in which young children’s developmental needs, age-appropriate content, and ethical protections are especially important. The authors argue that existing AI evaluation frameworks do not adequately capture ECE-specific requirements, so they develop and apply a Chinese evaluation framework organized around three dimensions: technical performance, pedagogical adaptability, and ethical and safety considerations.

The study evaluates 10 freely accessible Chinese GenAI platforms using a mixed-methods design that combines quantitative scoring with qualitative content analysis. Platforms were assessed on multimodal support, response speed, lesson-plan generation, activity organization, personalization for different age groups, ethical compliance, content appropriateness, and algorithmic fairness. Testing was conducted under standardized hardware, network, and prompt conditions over a two-week period in February 2025, and scoring was completed through expert review and consensus. Rather than testing learning outcomes in classrooms, the study evaluates the capabilities and risks of AI tools that might be used by early childhood educators.

The context is Chinese early childhood education, especially preschool-aged children and the educators selecting tools for them. The platforms were not necessarily designed specifically for ECE, but were chosen because they are prominent, open-access Chinese GenAI systems with potential relevance to education. The paper also discusses implications for other stakeholders, including parents, developers, and policymakers concerned with AI use in early learning environments.

The main conclusions are that the proposed framework can differentiate among Chinese GenAI platforms and identify meaningful strengths and weaknesses. Doubao and iFlytek Spark showed particularly strong overall performance, with Doubao excelling broadly and Spark performing especially well in pedagogical adaptability; DeepSeek stood out for pedagogical adaptability but performed poorly technically. Across platforms, the authors conclude that improvements are still needed in multimodal support, transparency of privacy and recommendation policies, ECE-specific datasets, personalization, and ethical safeguards before GenAI can be considered fully suitable for early childhood education.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the potential of LLM to enhance teaching plans through teaching simulation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can support teachers—not students—by improving lesson planning before instruction takes place. The authors focus on a common challenge in teaching preparation: novice teachers often struggle to anticipate students’ misconceptions, learning difficulties, and the kinds of classroom interactions that reveal whether a lesson plan is effective. The study asks whether an LLM can improve teaching plans by simulating teacher–student interactions, generating teaching reflections, and then revising the original plan accordingly.

The intervention is a prompt-based workflow using GPT-4 (and, in one comparison condition, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) to enhance high school mathematics teaching plans. Starting from existing lesson plans, the model first simulates classroom dialogue involving students with varying ability levels and typical errors, then produces teaching reflections based on those simulated interactions, and finally refines the lesson plan using those reflections. The authors evaluate eight datasets of lesson plans, including LLM-generated plans, human expert-written plans, and plans written by pre-service teachers, with improvements produced through one or two rounds of LLM-based refinement. Human raters scored plans on a detailed framework covering problem chains, teaching activities, knowledge content, teaching methods, evaluation, interdisciplinarity, practical value, scope, and overall quality.

The context is high school mathematics in China. The evaluation corpus included 480 teaching plans drawn from 60 lessons across four knowledge modules: Algebra, Functions, Geometry, and Statistics. Human evaluation was carried out by mathematics teachers with teaching experience, and the paper compares baseline lesson plans against LLM-enhanced versions rather than measuring direct student learning outcomes. The workflow was implemented through web-based LLM interfaces rather than custom-coded systems, with the aim of keeping the approach accessible to ordinary teachers.

The main conclusion is that LLM-based simulation and reflection substantially improved the quality of teaching plans. In many dimensions, the refined plans matched or exceeded the quality of high-quality human-written plans, and plans originally written by pre-service teachers also improved notably after LLM enhancement. Performance varied by content area, with the strongest results in statistics and weaker performance in geometry, where visual reasoning is harder to support through text alone. Overall, the paper argues that LLMs can serve as useful pre-class rehearsal and lesson refinement tools for teachers, especially for instructional preparation, though further work is needed on challenging question design, disciplinary depth, and broader validation in authentic teaching settings.

paper_profiles.title: Reinforcing L2 reading comprehension through artificial intelligence intervention: refining engagement to foster self-regulated learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether an artificial-intelligence-supported reading environment can improve second-language (L2) reading comprehension, learner engagement, and self-regulated learning. The study addresses a gap in the literature on AI for reading instruction, especially for language learners, by asking whether AI-enhanced classrooms can outperform conventional instruction and how learners perceive such an environment.

The intervention centered on the ReadToMe (RTM) platform, an AI-based, multi-sensory reading system that converts curricular text into text-to-speech, synchronized highlighting, pronunciation support, concept images, dictionary support, and knowledge-graph-based scaffolds. In the experimental condition, students used RTM for homework and reading practice, while the control group received conventional reading instruction and feedback from the teacher or peers. The study used a mixed-methods design with pre/post quantitative measures and follow-up semi-structured interviews.

Participants were 60 Iranian female EFL students from two intact classes at a language institute, with 30 students in the experimental group and 30 in the control group. They were upper-intermediate/C1 learners with a mean age of 21, attending in-person classes twice weekly for about 12 weeks. Both groups used the same reading textbook, and the same instructor taught both groups to reduce teacher effects. Outcomes included an objective reading comprehension test plus self-report scales for engagement and self-regulation.

The main findings indicate that the AI-supported group significantly outperformed the control group on reading comprehension, self-regulation, and engagement. Qualitative data also suggested that most students viewed the AI platform as motivating, engaging, and helpful for personalized feedback and comprehension support, though some reported usability problems such as slow loading and navigation issues. Overall, the paper concludes that AI-enhanced reading instruction can be an effective approach for improving L2 reading outcomes and supporting learner engagement and self-regulated learning, while also noting the importance of addressing technical usability barriers.

paper_profiles.title: How do generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools and large language models (LLMs) influence language learners’ critical thinking in EFL education? A systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a timely question in education: whether generative AI tools and large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT support or undermine critical thinking in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education. The authors note that prior work has focused mainly on technical benefits like grammar correction, vocabulary development, and writing support, while giving less attention to higher-order thinking. To address this gap, they conduct a systematic review focused specifically on critical thinking in EFL contexts.

Using the PRISMA framework, the authors searched Web of Science, Scopus, ProQuest, ERIC, and Google Scholar for studies published from 2022 to February 2025. After screening 3,243 records plus 4 additional sources, they included 15 studies. The review synthesizes evidence on the dual nature of generative AI and LLMs, the research methods used, the main thematic focuses, the theories and models applied, and the limitations and future directions in this research area. The reviewed studies concern EFL learners and teachers, with contexts including classroom teaching and language learning activities such as writing, speaking, argumentation, and literature learning.

The main conclusion is that generative AI and LLMs have both promise and risk for critical thinking in EFL education. Ten of the 15 studies (66.67%) reported positive effects, including improved argumentative writing and speaking, stronger analytical reasoning, better evaluation and problem-solving, increased engagement and confidence, and support for self-directed learning. At the same time, five studies (33.33%) warned that overreliance on AI could reduce analytical depth, creativity, autonomy, and independent reasoning. The authors conclude that AI can nurture critical thinking when used with guidance, critical evaluation, and pedagogical structure, but may hinder it when learners passively accept AI-generated content.

paper_profiles.title: Reading differently with ChatGPT: EFL learners’ use of Question-Answer Relationship strategy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how university English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners developed reading comprehension when using ChatGPT together with the Question-Answer Relationship (QAR) strategy. The core research question was how learners’ reading comprehension changed through this integration, especially across different QAR levels: locating explicit information, synthesizing across text segments, and making inferences about tone and author intent. The study addresses a practical problem in EFL reading instruction: students often need individualized support with vocabulary, sentence structure, and higher-order comprehension, but traditional instruction may not provide timely, adaptive scaffolding.

The intervention combined structured reading strategy instruction through QAR with guided use of ChatGPT. Students completed five weekly guided reading sessions in which they read texts, answered TOEFL-style comprehension questions, generated their own QAR questions and answers, asked ChatGPT to generate questions, and then compared, revised, and discussed responses through free-form interaction. The study used three rounds of semi-structured interviews across five weeks and analyzed 105 interviews thematically using the QAR framework categories (Right There, Think and Search, Author and You) alongside inductive coding.

Participants were 35 first-year undergraduate students in an academic English program at a university in northern China. They were enrolled in two EFL classes per week and also completed one guided ChatGPT-supported reading practice session per week. Most participants self-identified as low-intermediate in TOEFL-related reading proficiency and had limited prior experience with generative AI. Interviews were conducted in Chinese, transcribed, translated, and coded in NVivo.

The main conclusion is that learners described a developmental progression in comprehension: ChatGPT first helped them identify explicit information and understand vocabulary and sentence structure, then supported summarizing and synthesizing across paragraphs, and finally helped them engage in inferential and interpretive reading about tone, stance, and author intention. Students did not simply accept ChatGPT outputs passively; many used it dialogically to compare reasoning and refine their own understanding. At the same time, participants identified limitations in ChatGPT, including weak handling of polysemous vocabulary, unclear parsing of long sentences, overlong summaries, and sometimes inaccurate inferential explanations. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can be a useful reading partner when paired with structured strategy instruction, but its value depends on critical, strategic use and AI literacy.

paper_profiles.title: Lecturers’ perceptions of the influence of AI on a blended learning approach in a South African higher education institution
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how lecturers perceive the influence of artificial intelligence on blended learning in a South African higher education institution. The central problem is the limited understanding of lecturers’ views on how AI can enhance blended teaching and learning, what challenges arise during implementation, and what kinds of support are needed for successful integration. The study is framed by the SAMR model (Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, Redefinition) to interpret different levels of AI integration in teaching practice.

The researchers conducted a qualitative single-case study using semi-structured focus group interviews and document analysis. The approach focused on how lecturers were already using AI within blended learning rather than testing a controlled intervention. Reported uses of AI included answering student queries, generating customized learning materials and assessments, enabling translation across languages, providing real-time feedback, supporting interactive activities, and automating some administrative tasks. The document analysis was used to corroborate lecturers’ descriptions with examples from module sites, such as adaptive quizzes, AI-generated case studies, automated feedback, and translation tools.

The study involved 15 lecturers from the College of Education at one South African higher education institution. Although the direct participants were lecturers, the educational context included their students in blended courses, and the paper discusses perceived effects on student engagement, communication, personalization, and learning support. The setting was a blended higher education environment combining face-to-face and online instruction.

The main conclusions are that lecturers generally viewed AI as beneficial for blended learning, especially for personalization, communication, quick feedback, adaptive assessment, and broader access to learning materials. At the same time, they identified substantial barriers, including resistance to change, time constraints, uneven student access to technology, ethical and privacy concerns, limited infrastructure, and the need to balance AI with traditional pedagogy. The paper concludes that successful AI-enabled blended learning requires strong institutional support, professional development, management backing, reliable internet and technological infrastructure, technical support, and dedicated time for lecturers to learn and implement AI effectively.

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ perceptions and uses of generative artificial intelligence in Moroccan schools: Evidence from the Fez–Meknès region
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines teachers’ awareness, perceptions, and actual use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in schools, addressing a gap in empirical evidence from Morocco. The authors focus on how in-service teachers understand generative AI, what they think it can do for teaching and learning, what barriers limit use, and what kinds of professional development they want.

The study uses a descriptive cross-sectional survey of 420 primary and secondary school teachers in Morocco’s Fez–Meknès region. Participants came from multiple subject areas and completed an online questionnaire covering general understanding of generative AI, current use, perceived contributions, useful applications, challenges, and training preferences. Data were analyzed descriptively using frequencies and percentages.

Findings show that most teachers had heard of generative AI and generally viewed it positively, especially for content creation, personalization, engagement, and support for lesson design. However, regular classroom use was much lower than perceived usefulness, largely because of limited training, weak infrastructure, and privacy concerns. Teachers also preferred hands-on workshops, live classroom applications, and coaching, and many saw generative AI as a complementary tool rather than a replacement for teachers. The paper concludes that targeted professional development, better infrastructure, and clear ethical guidelines are needed to translate interest into effective and responsible use.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model tools that can create text and other content, support personalized learning, and assist with feedback or assessment tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed primary and secondary teachers’ awareness, perceived usefulness, actual use, perceived contributions, challenges, and training preferences regarding generative AI in teaching and lesson design.

findings.finding_summary: Among 420 primary and secondary teachers in Morocco’s Fez–Meknès region, 68.9% reported having heard of generative AI and 64.4% accurately defined it as a content-generation technology. Teachers’ perceptions were generally favorable, with 72.5% saying it is useful for improving education and 81.1% viewing it as an essential part of the educational process.
findings.measure: Teacher awareness, definition accuracy, perceived usefulness, future outlook

findings.finding_summary: Only 21.5% reported frequent use, while 18.8% used generative AI occasionally and 37.6% had not yet tried it. The most valued applications were creating educational materials (36.4%), customizing teaching methods (20.5%), and creating personalized assessments (17.9%).
findings.measure: Frequency of actual use; preferred/useful applications for teaching

findings.finding_summary: Teachers most often reported that generative AI could customize educational content (23.4%), provide innovative and dynamic content (22.5%), enhance student engagement (21.4%), and support interactive motivation tools (21.1%).
findings.measure: Perceived contributions to education

findings.finding_summary: The leading barriers were lack of training and knowledge (27.3%) and lack of technical resources and infrastructure (25.7%), followed by privacy and data security concerns (15.2%). Despite this, 82.6% expressed interest in additional training, and 34.2% preferred workshops/training sessions while 29.2% preferred hands-on/live classroom applications.
findings.measure: Challenges, training interest, preferred professional development methods

findings.finding_summary: Regarding role concerns, 45.6% did not fear generative AI would reduce their role, 24.8% expressed concern, and 29.5% were unsure. For equity, 52.0% believed generative AI could foster educational equity, while 40.5% were unsure and 7.4% disagreed.
findings.measure: Fear of role reduction; perception of educational equity

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive cross-sectional survey with self-reported perceptions and usage data, not an experimental or quasi-experimental impact study. Evidence is informative for needs assessment but is correlational and context-specific.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong perceived value and training demand, but no causal effect sizes or learning outcomes are measured. Observed impacts are therefore unclear rather than demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: Redefining Teacher Leadership in the Age of ChatGPT: Instructional Practices, Ethical Challenges, and Professional Agency in Moroccan High Schools
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Language and Literary Studies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, is being used by high school teachers in Morocco and how that use is reshaping teacher leadership and professional agency. The study is framed by instructional leadership theory and asks how teachers use ChatGPT in lesson planning, activity design, and feedback, what motivates those uses, and how AI affects their classroom leadership roles.

The researchers used a mixed-methods design. Quantitative data came from an online survey of 87 high school teachers in the Casablanca-Settat region, and qualitative data came from semi-structured interviews with 12 teachers plus analysis of ChatGPT-assisted lesson plans. Teachers reported using ChatGPT most often for lesson planning and activity generation, and less often for drafting feedback. The paper argues that teachers are not simply adopting AI passively; they are selectively integrating it where it saves time and supports creativity while retaining human control over evaluative and ethically sensitive tasks.

The findings show three main themes: pedagogical efficiency and creativity, ethical and pedagogical concerns, and leadership/professional agency. Teachers saw ChatGPT as helpful for reducing workload and generating ideas, but they also worried about plagiarism, student overreliance, and occasional inaccuracies in AI outputs. Overall, the study concludes that ChatGPT is reshaping teachers into instructional leaders and ethical gatekeepers who filter AI-generated content through professional judgment. It calls for AI literacy professional development and clearer policy guidance for responsible AI use in Moroccan high schools.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/large language model system used for conversational text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by Moroccan high school teachers for lesson planning, classroom activity generation, and drafting feedback on student work; lesson plans developed with ChatGPT were also analyzed.

findings.finding_summary: Among 87 Moroccan high school teachers, 64.4% reported using ChatGPT for lesson planning, 51.7% for activity generation, and 41.4% for drafting feedback. The mixed-methods results indicated teachers viewed ChatGPT as saving time and supporting pedagogical creativity, but they used it more cautiously for evaluative tasks like feedback.
findings.measure: Self-reported ChatGPT use for lesson planning, activity generation, and feedback drafting; interview/document themes on efficiency and creativity

findings.finding_summary: Qualitative findings from 12 interviews and lesson-plan analysis showed ChatGPT supported creativity and differentiated activity design, but teachers also raised concerns about plagiarism, student overreliance, and occasional inaccuracies. Teachers positioned themselves as ethical gatekeepers who filtered outputs before use, indicating selective rather than wholesale adoption.
findings.measure: Interview themes and document analysis of ChatGPT-assisted lesson plans
findings.sample_size: n=12 interviews; lesson plans analyzed from interviewees

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods observational study with survey, interviews, and document analysis rather than an experiment. The evidence is informative but not causal, so it fits the yellow tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial usage and perceived workflow benefits, but it does not provide effect sizes or outcome gains on student learning. Impact is therefore suggestive but unclear at the evidence level.

paper_profiles.title: Using Generative AI to Evaluate Pre-Service Teachers’ Project-Based Learning Designs
paper_profiles.venue: RE-Source. Journal of the Centre for Didactics of Technical and Vocational Education and Training, Special Issue 1: Engineering Pedagogy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can be used to evaluate pre-service teachers’ project-based learning (PBL) lesson plans and provide useful formative feedback. The central question is not only whether AI can score PBL designs against an established framework, but also how its judgments compare with expert teacher evaluations and how different chatbots vary in the feedback they generate.

The intervention is a system prompt built around the Gold Standard PBL criteria from Larmer, Mergendoller, and Boss (2015). The prompt instructs chatbots to evaluate seven dimensions of project quality, provide criterion-based commentary, identify strengths and weaknesses, and recommend improvements. The study tested this prompt on 10 PBL teaching preparations created by students in vocational teacher education. Five genAI tools were used (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, and Perplexity), and two vocational education teachers independently evaluated the same materials in parallel.

The paper reports both quantitative scoring of the seven PBL criteria and qualitative analysis of verbal comments. The findings suggest that GenAI can produce structured, reasonably consistent first-pass evaluations and that its average ratings were similar to those of the teachers overall. The strongest criterion across evaluators was authenticity, while reflection, critique and revision, and sustained inquiry were the weakest areas. The authors conclude that GenAI is useful for rapid, criteria-based feedback, but teachers remain essential for deeper pedagogical interpretation and for judging the educational significance of the designs.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based conversational AI chatbot used to generate and evaluate text based on prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of five GenAI chatbots to evaluate 10 pre-service teachers’ project-based learning lesson designs against the Gold Standard PBL criteria and to provide strengths, weaknesses, and recommendations.

findings.finding_summary: In the 10 PBL plans, ChatGPT’s average rating was 1.88 on the 1–4 Gold Standard PBL scale. Across all criteria, it was generally less positive than Gemini and Perplexity, but the paper reports that the average overall AI rating matched the teachers’ average overall rating of 1.79.
findings.measure: Average Gold Standard PBL criterion ratings and overall rating for 10 lesson designs

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic’s conversational AI chatbot used for text generation and analysis.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of five GenAI chatbots to evaluate 10 pre-service teachers’ PBL lesson designs and provide criterion-based feedback.

findings.finding_summary: Claude had the most critical average rating among the chatbots, with a mean of 2.50 on the 1–4 Gold Standard PBL scale. The paper notes that Claude evaluated all criteria with reservation and was especially critical of Reflection and Critique & Revision.
findings.measure: Average Gold Standard PBL criterion ratings and overall rating for 10 lesson designs

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s conversational AI chatbot used for generating and evaluating text.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of five GenAI chatbots to evaluate 10 pre-service teachers’ PBL lesson designs and provide structured feedback.

findings.finding_summary: Gemini received the most positive average evaluation among the tools, with a mean score of 1.36 on the 1–4 Gold Standard PBL scale. The paper reports that it was the most generous evaluator overall, while still identifying weaknesses in Reflection and Critique & Revision.
findings.measure: Average Gold Standard PBL criterion ratings and overall rating for 10 lesson designs

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI chatbot(s) used for producing criterion-based written feedback from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper compares multiple unnamed GenAI chatbots as a category, alongside teacher expert evaluations, for assessing PBL lesson preparations using the same system prompt.

findings.finding_summary: Across the five chatbots, the average AI evaluation was 1.79, which matched the teachers’ average overall rating of 1.79. The paper concludes that GenAI can serve as a valid first stage of evaluation, offering rapid and structured assessment, while teachers remain essential for deeper pedagogical interpretation.
findings.measure: Average Gold Standard PBL rating and verbal strength/weakness descriptions for 10 lesson designs

identified_tools.name: Copilot
identified_tools.description: Microsoft’s conversational AI assistant used for text generation and analysis.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of five GenAI chatbots to evaluate 10 pre-service teachers’ PBL lesson designs and generate feedback.

findings.finding_summary: Copilot’s mean rating was 1.75 on the 1–4 Gold Standard PBL scale, placing it between ChatGPT and Gemini/Perplexity. The paper describes its feedback as concise and clear, with a brief final overview and relatively few recommendations.
findings.measure: Average Gold Standard PBL criterion ratings and overall rating for 10 lesson designs

identified_tools.name: Perplexity
identified_tools.description: Perplexity AI chatbot used for prompt-based question answering and text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of five GenAI chatbots to evaluate 10 pre-service teachers’ PBL lesson designs and provide constructive feedback.

findings.finding_summary: Perplexity’s mean rating was 1.46 on the 1–4 Gold Standard PBL scale, making it one of the most positive evaluators. The paper reports that its outputs were compact, included strengths, weaknesses, and recommendations, and ended with a brief summary and Gold Standard level.
findings.measure: Average Gold Standard PBL criterion ratings and overall rating for 10 lesson designs

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small empirical study with 10 lesson-design cases and qualitative/quantitative descriptive comparison across chatbots and teachers. It is not a randomized trial and provides no inferential statistics or effect sizes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports useful practical differences in feedback style and average ratings, but no effect sizes are given and the measured differences are modest and descriptive. The main conclusion is about feasibility and usefulness for teacher support rather than demonstrated large outcome gains.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI as a partner for teachers in building personalised learning paths for students with ease in Tanzania
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can help secondary school teachers create personalised learning paths more efficiently and effectively. The author frames the problem around overcrowded classrooms, limited teaching resources, and the difficulty of providing differentiated instruction and feedback at scale, especially in low-resource settings.

The study evaluates generative AI tools, including ChatGPT and Grok, as teacher supports for lesson planning, assessment creation, adaptive content delivery, and feedback generation. Teachers used these tools to generate personalised quizzes, lesson plans, and tailored materials aligned to student profiles and syllabus objectives. The study uses a mixed-methods design, combining teacher surveys, thematic analysis of teacher feedback, and pre/post comparisons of student engagement and academic outcomes.

Participants were 120 secondary school teachers from public schools in Dar es Salaam and Dodoma, Tanzania, with some attention to urban and rural differences. The paper reports that teachers perceived the tools as easy to use and helpful for reducing workload and adapting content to learner needs. It also reports improved student engagement, homework completion, attendance, and test scores after AI integration. The main conclusion is that generative AI can serve as a supportive partner for teachers in personalised learning, but its impact depends on better professional development, infrastructure, and attention to equity gaps, particularly in rural schools.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM system used for text generation and interactive assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by secondary school teachers in Tanzania for lesson planning, quizzes, student feedback, and generating personalized learning materials and adaptive content.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers using generative AI tools reported significantly higher ease of use than teachers without experience (M = 4.3, SD = 0.6 vs M = 3.1, SD = 0.9; t(118) = 4.62, p < 0.001). The paper attributes this to user-friendly interfaces and notes improved usability after exposure to ChatGPT.
findings.measure: Teacher-perceived ease of use

findings.finding_summary: Teachers with AI experience reported greater workload reduction than non-experienced teachers (M = 4.1 vs M = 2.9; t(118) = 5.13, p < 0.001). The study states that ChatGPT-supported lesson preparation, feedback, and grading helped reduce routine teacher tasks.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported workload reduction

findings.finding_summary: Teachers using generative AI rated the ability to adapt content to learner needs more highly than teachers without experience (M = 4.5 vs M = 3.0; t(118) = 6.02, p < 0.001). The paper reports that ChatGPT helped tailor content to learning styles and support differentiated learning.
findings.measure: Teacher-perceived ability to tailor content to learner needs

findings.finding_summary: Across the pre/post comparison of AI integration, the study reports improved student engagement, homework completion, mean test scores, and attendance after generative AI use. For the broader AI-assisted condition (including ChatGPT), student engagement increased from 2.8 to 4.3 and mean test scores from 61% to 75%.
findings.measure: Student engagement, homework completion, test scores, attendance (pre/post comparison)

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI tools/large language model chatbots used to generate instructional content, assessments, and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper frames generative AI broadly as a collaborative partner for teachers in personalized learning, with examples including ChatGPT, Grok, Curipod, and MagicSchool.ai.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that generative AI-supported personalized learning improved student engagement, participation, and academic performance, particularly for low-performing learners. The paper also reports average test scores increasing from 61% to 75% and student engagement from 2.8 to 4.3 after AI integration, based on the study's pre/post comparisons.
findings.measure: Student engagement and academic performance in AI-supported personalized learning

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that generative AI reduced lesson preparation and grading time, allowing more time for individual student support and innovative teaching strategies. The paper describes this as a shift from manual workload to AI-assisted efficiency.
findings.measure: Teacher workload reduction / time saved in lesson preparation and grading

identified_tools.name: Grok
identified_tools.description: xAI's generative AI chatbot designed to provide real-time assistance and reasoning-based responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Used alongside ChatGPT by Tanzanian secondary school teachers for lesson planning, assessments, adaptive content delivery, and creating problem-solving activities tailored to student needs.

findings.finding_summary: The paper groups Grok with other generative AI tools used by teachers and reports that AI-enhanced instruction improved adaptability to individual learning needs, timely feedback, and student engagement. However, no tool-specific outcome separate from ChatGPT is reported.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported perceived benefits of Grok within AI-assisted instruction

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods study with surveys, pre/post comparisons, and teacher perceptions, which places it in the yellow tier rather than an experimental blue/green tier. It provides empirical evidence, but the paper does not report a tightly controlled design or full causal identification for the tool-specific effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive pre/post changes in engagement and test scores, but effect sizes are not reported and the tool-specific impacts are not cleanly isolated. Because the magnitude is promising but not quantified in a way that supports a precise impact classification, the overall impact is best treated as yellow.

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ perceptions of generative ai integration: A qualitative case study at a university in Baluchistan
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines university educators’ perceptions of integrating generative artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education, with a focus on how such tools affect teaching practices in a resource-constrained context. The authors frame the study using the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework to understand how technology, pedagogy, and content knowledge interact when educators adopt generative AI for instructional work.

The study is a qualitative case study conducted at a university in Baluchistan, Pakistan, with 25 faculty members from multiple departments. Data were gathered through semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions, then analyzed thematically. Participants discussed generative AI as a tool that can streamline lesson planning, improve access to resources, support differentiated and personalized instruction, and provide data-driven insights into student engagement and performance.

At the same time, educators expressed concerns about academic integrity, data privacy, unequal access to devices and internet, and insufficient institutional support. Many participants also emphasized the need for sustained professional development, mentorship, and clear policy guidance to use AI effectively and ethically. The paper concludes that generative AI has strong potential to improve teaching in higher education, but successful adoption depends on robust training, supportive infrastructure, and explicit ethical and institutional frameworks.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI tools that can create content, support instructional tasks, personalize learning, and provide feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: A qualitative case study examined university educators’ perceptions of generative AI integration in higher education, with emphasis on lesson planning, personalized instruction, resource access, and engagement; no specific product was named.

findings.finding_summary: Educators generally viewed generative AI positively for streamlining lesson planning, improving resource accessibility, and saving time. The paper reports that 80% of participants (20/25) highlighted these benefits, but no effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Participant perceptions of lesson planning efficiency and resource accessibility

findings.finding_summary: Participants reported that generative AI supported personalized instruction and differentiation, with 68% of educators noting improved ability to tailor materials to diverse student needs. The study is qualitative and reports participant perceptions rather than a quantitative effect size.
findings.measure: Perceived ability to differentiate instruction and personalize materials

findings.finding_summary: Educators stated that generative AI helped provide real-time feedback and analyze student performance data, supporting earlier intervention and student monitoring. The paper reports these as perceived benefits from interviews and focus groups, with no effect size provided.
findings.measure: Perceived real-time feedback and student performance analytics

findings.finding_summary: The study found strong demand for professional development: 70% of participants emphasized ongoing training needs, and 65% wanted mentorship or communities of practice. This indicates that effective adoption depended on institutional support and teacher capacity building rather than tool performance metrics.
findings.measure: Perceived professional development needs for AI integration

findings.finding_summary: Educators expressed concerns about academic integrity, data privacy, limited institutional support, and unequal student access to technology. Approximately 60% raised ethical concerns and 40% raised access concerns, indicating barriers to implementation in this context.
findings.measure: Perceived ethical, privacy, support, and access barriers to AI integration

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative case study using interviews and focus groups, which provides contextual insight but not causal evidence. The methodology is appropriate for perceptions research, but it does not support strong effect estimation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports broadly positive perceived benefits for instructional planning, personalization, and feedback, but these are self-reported and not quantified with effect sizes. The practical impact appears promising yet unclear because implementation barriers and institutional constraints are substantial.

paper_profiles.title: Systematic Review on Teacher Education and the Integration of Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Cultural Analysis and Social Change
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapid but fragmented growth of generative AI, AIGC tools, and digital simulations in teacher education. The authors ask how these technologies are being integrated into pre-service and in-service teacher training, and what effects they have on pedagogical competence, digital readiness, professional identity, and related professional outcomes. Because the literature is scattered across pedagogical, psychological, and institutional perspectives, the review aims to synthesize empirical evidence and identify the major themes, barriers, and theoretical frameworks shaping this emerging field.

The approach is a systematic review of 32 empirical studies published between 2024 and 2026, retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, and ERIC. The included studies span pre-service teachers, in-service teachers, teacher educators, and university professors across multiple regions, with most work located in Europe and East Asia. Methods across the primary studies include surveys, interviews, mixed-methods designs, quasi-experiments, and simulation-based training studies, examining tools such as ChatGPT, AI co-teachers, VR/AR systems, avatar-based simulations, 3D modeling, and AI-supported internships.

The review concludes that GenAI and digital simulations can support lesson planning, differentiation, feedback, self-directed professional development, communication skills, and scenario-based decision-making. However, adoption is constrained by uneven AI literacy, limited infrastructure, short interventions, and heavy reliance on self-report outcomes. The authors argue that teacher education programmes should embed structured AI literacy, model AI-rich teaching, strengthen policy and institutional support, and ensure equitable access to technology. Overall, the paper frames AI as a promising but still early-stage component of teacher professional support, whose impact depends on long-term, rigorous, and context-sensitive implementation.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General generative AI/large language model tools used for content generation, instructional support, feedback, and adaptation in educational contexts.
identified_tools.use_case: This systematic review synthesized empirical studies on generative AI, AIGC tools, and related general AI chatbots used in pre-service and in-service teacher education, including lesson planning, lesson-plan critique, self-directed professional development, and teacher support.

findings.finding_summary: Across the included studies, GenAI emerged as a pedagogical partner that enhanced lesson planning, differentiation, feedback, and teacher self-directed professional development. The review also notes that teachers generally reported curiosity and optimism, but actual pedagogical integration remained uneven and constrained by limited AI literacy, training, and institutional support.
findings.measure: Synthesis of reported effects across included empirical studies on lesson planning, feedback, differentiation, and professional development

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that ChatGPT-supported lesson-plan critiques improved pre-service teachers' cognitive and affective critiques of lesson plans, though effects were weaker for metacognitive feedback. In the same synthesis, GenAI-supported bilingual instruction and self-directed professional development were described as supporting adaptive tasks, personalized instruction, brainstorming, and goal-setting.
findings.measure: Lesson plan critique quality, professional development behaviors, and pedagogical adaptation

findings.finding_summary: The review found that teachers appreciated GenAI's time-saving and personalization potential, but also expressed concerns about plagiarism, reliability, trustworthiness, and possible erosion of students' critical thinking. It further notes that advanced pedagogical uses were rare in some teacher samples, with many teachers limiting use to information search and translation.
findings.measure: Teacher perceptions, adoption patterns, and concerns about GenAI use

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review synthesizing mostly survey, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies rather than a single controlled intervention. The evidence base is informative but heterogeneous and relies heavily on self-report, with limited objective performance data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests meaningful promise for GenAI in lesson planning, feedback, and professional development, but it does not report pooled effect sizes and notes that actual use remains limited and uneven. Overall impact appears promising but still uncertain and context-dependent.

paper_profiles.title: Code of Ethics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents the American Educational Research Association’s Code of Ethics, a formal statement of principles and ethical standards intended to guide education researchers in research, teaching, practice, and service. Rather than addressing a specific empirical problem, it provides a normative framework for professional conduct, emphasizing competence, integrity, responsibility, respect for rights and diversity, and social responsibility.

The document lays out detailed standards across areas such as scientific and scholarly practice, conflicts of interest, confidentiality, informed consent, data sharing, authorship credit, publication processes, reviewing, teaching, mentoring, and supervision. It also highlights obligations related to avoiding harm, nondiscrimination, and proper handling of data and communications in professional settings.

Because this is a policy and ethics framework rather than a study, it does not report a sample, intervention, or educational setting. Its main conclusion is that education researchers should adhere to high ethical standards and use the code as a guide for daily professional decision-making, with violations potentially leading to sanctions within AERA.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / LLM chatbot system used to generate and provide feedback or support for instructional and professional tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The provided paper text is the AERA Code of Ethics and does not study any AI tool; it is a framework for ethical conduct in education research.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an ethics/code-of-conduct document rather than an empirical study of an AI tool. No research design, sample, intervention, or outcome evaluation is reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not evaluate any AI system or report outcomes, so there is no measurable educational impact to assess.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Integration of ChatGPT for Teaching English in a Malaysian Primary School
paper_profiles.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF RESEARCH AND INNOVATION IN SOCIAL SCIENCE (IJRISS)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers in a Malaysian primary school integrated ChatGPT into English language teaching and what they perceived as its effects on instruction and pupil engagement. The study is motivated by growing interest in generative AI for education, alongside questions about whether such tools can meaningfully support classroom practice in a way that is pedagogically appropriate for young learners.

The intervention/approach studied was teacher use of ChatGPT for lesson planning, grammar explanations, generating teaching materials, differentiated tasks, and collaborative activities. The authors framed the study using TPACK, SAMR, and THUMB to interpret how AI supported instruction while still requiring human pedagogical judgment. Data came from semi-structured interviews, classroom observations, and document analysis in one Malaysian primary school in Puchong, Selangor, with 10 English teachers who had prior technology exposure.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT can reduce lesson-preparation time, support grammar instruction, and help teachers personalize activities, but its outputs are often too formal, generic, or culturally disconnected for young pupils. Teachers therefore had to adapt AI-generated materials to local context, age level, and curriculum goals. The study argues that ChatGPT should be treated as a complementary tool rather than a replacement for teacher expertise, and that successful implementation depends on training, contextual adaptation, and maintaining human interaction in teaching.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/language model for natural-language generation, question answering, and content drafting.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by teachers for lesson planning, generating teaching materials, grammar explanations, instant answers, differentiated tasks, and feedback support in Malaysian primary English teaching.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative case study with 10 English teachers, ChatGPT was perceived as helpful for grammar explanations, instant answers, lesson planning, and generating creative teaching materials. Teachers also reported using it to support differentiated instruction and personalize tasks, but repeatedly noted that outputs required adaptation for younger pupils and local context.
findings.measure: Teacher perceptions/interviews, classroom observations, and document analysis of lesson plans/materials

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/language model for natural-language generation, question answering, and content drafting.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a classroom support tool for English teaching, including lesson planning, grammar support, collaboration tasks, and pupil engagement in a Malaysian primary school.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that ChatGPT improved efficiency in lesson preparation and provided quick grammar support, but its responses were often too formal, generic, or complex for young learners. Engagement and learning depended on teacher mediation: unmodified AI content was less engaging, while adapted and interactive use improved participation.
findings.measure: Teacher perceptions, classroom engagement observations, and lesson/document review

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative case study with 10 teachers, using interviews, observations, and document analysis. It provides contextual insights but no experimental control, randomization, or effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports practical benefits such as faster lesson planning and improved engagement when adapted by teachers, but no effect sizes are reported and the impacts are descriptive rather than quantified.

paper_profiles.title: Teaching with Analytics: Towards a Situated Model of Instructional Decision-Making
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how instructors use learning analytics dashboards to inform instructional decision-making in authentic teaching settings. The authors note that prior work had documented the existence and usage of instructor-facing analytics tools, but had not fully unpacked how instructors actually interpret data, decide whether to act, and consider the impact of their actions. To address this gap, the paper synthesizes prior literature into a template for inquiry and then uses it to analyze instructors’ analytics use across questions, interpretation, response, and checking impact.

The intervention/approach studied was a learning analytics dashboard developed through a university pilot project. The dashboard drew on multiple institutional data sources, including the registrar, the LMS, streaming video, quizzes, and surveys. Before and during a semester, five faculty members at a large U.S. private university were introduced to the tool, developed use cases with the instructional technology team, and then used the dashboard in their courses. After the semester, the researchers conducted one-hour retrospective semi-structured interviews and analyzed transcripts qualitatively using constant comparative methods.

The study found that instructors often began with broad curiosities rather than precise questions, and new questions emerged during interaction with the data. Interpretation involved both reading patterns in the analytics and explaining them using contextual knowledge, with triangulation to other information sources and affective reactions such as surprise or frustration. Responses included whole-class scaffolding, targeted scaffolding, course design revision, waiting to see more data, and deeper reflection on pedagogy. The authors conclude by proposing a situated model of instructional decision-making and argue that analytics tools should better support question generation, relevant reference points, collaborative interpretation, and the translation of data into actionable pedagogical support.

identified_tools.name: Adaptive Feedback System (General)
identified_tools.description: A learning analytics dashboard or feedback system that aggregates student activity and performance data to support instructor decision-making.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by five university instructors to review student engagement, quiz results, and course activity in order to inform teaching decisions during a semester.

findings.finding_summary: This qualitative study of five university instructors found that the dashboard supported sense-making and some pedagogical responses, including whole-class scaffolding, targeted scaffolding, course revision, and deeper reflection. However, instructors often adopted a wait-and-see stance, rarely checked impact, and reported barriers such as lack of clear reference points, transparency concerns, and misalignment with teaching concerns.
findings.measure: Retrospective semi-structured interviews about dashboard use; themes from qualitative analysis of asking questions, interpreting analytics, taking action, and checking impact

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative mixed-methods study with five instructors and no experimental comparison or effect sizes. It provides useful descriptive evidence about analytics use, but not causal evidence of tool effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports some positive instructional uses of the dashboard, but impact on student outcomes is not measured and checking impact was rare. Overall influence is suggestive rather than demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: A systematic literature review of empirical research on ChatGPT in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the emerging use of ChatGPT in education and asks how students and teachers have initially used it, and what empirical studies report about its effects and concerns. The authors conduct a systematic literature review of 14 empirical studies published through April 10, 2023, using PRISMA 2020 and Okoli’s review procedures.

The review focuses on ChatGPT as a non-generative baseline AI-like educational tool in practice, examining how it has been used for learning and teaching across higher education and one elementary-school context. The included studies span multiple countries and disciplines, with participants including university students, university teachers, mixed teacher-student samples, and elementary school teachers. Data sources across the primary studies included interviews, questionnaires, and pre/post tests; most studies were qualitative or mixed-methods, and many were quasi-experimental or experimental in design.

The review concludes that ChatGPT was commonly used by students as a virtual intelligent assistant, writing/language support tool, and self-directed learning aid, while educators used it to create lesson plans, quizzes, and teaching resources and to improve productivity. Reported benefits included immediate feedback, idea generation, language support, and efficiency gains. However, the review also highlights concerns about inaccuracy, overreliance, reduced collaborative learning, weaker creativity, and academic integrity risks. The authors emphasize the need for structured training, clear guidelines, and further research on responsible integration.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on large language models, designed to generate human-like text responses, provide information, and support conversational interaction.
identified_tools.use_case: This systematic review examined empirical studies on how students and teachers used ChatGPT in educational settings, including answering questions, giving feedback, generating lesson plans, writing support, and personalized learning assistance.

findings.finding_summary: Across 14 empirical studies, ChatGPT was used as a virtual intelligent assistant for students, providing immediate feedback, on-demand answers, learning resources, and guidance. The review reports that students generally found responses relevant and detailed, though some studies noted that answers were not always accurate and that misleading information could occur.
findings.measure: Student-reported use, perceptions, and qualitative findings on learning support functions

findings.finding_summary: The review found that students used ChatGPT to improve writing and language proficiency by generating ideas, composing essays, summarizing, translating, paraphrasing texts, and checking grammar. Three studies focused on English education, and participants reported that ChatGPT supported active writing development and language use.
findings.measure: Reported writing and language support outcomes in included studies

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT was used as a resource for self-directed and personalized learning, helping students understand concepts, complete homework, follow structured learning plans, and receive tailored explanations. The review notes that this supported learning at the learner's own pace and could create a supportive home learning environment.
findings.measure: Self-directed learning and personalized learning experiences reported in included studies

findings.finding_summary: Several studies reported improvements in students' reasoning, problem-solving, and other competencies, including critical thinking, hazard recognition, and conversational social skills. At the same time, the review noted that overuse of ChatGPT may negatively affect innovative capacities, collaborative learning competencies, and higher-order thinking skills.
findings.measure: Reported competencies, reasoning/problem-solving, and negative effects of overuse
