identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI system for generating and revising text, answering questions, and supporting interactive writing and feedback tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by preservice teachers to generate lesson plans, teaching/learning content, and assessments, and to support lesson-plan development in teacher preparation activities.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative study of 2nd- and 3rd-year preservice teachers, participants reported that ChatGPT produced a general lesson plan and relevant content/assessment that provided a useful starting point for contextualising lesson plans to their own classes. Students noted that when they supplied grade level and location, ChatGPT generated more context-specific examples, which they then adapted further for teaching practice.
findings.measure: Preservice teachers' perceptions of ChatGPT-generated lesson plans and content in survey responses and class discussions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods study using questionnaires and class discussions, so it does not provide experimental causal evidence. The paper reports participant perceptions rather than controlled outcome comparisons.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests useful practical support for lesson planning, but it does not report measurable effect sizes or direct student outcome gains. Impact is therefore plausible but unclear from the evidence provided.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring High School EFL Teachers' Experiences with Magic School AI in Lesson Planning: Benefits and Insights
paper_profiles.venue: Voices of English Language Education Society
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how high school English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers in Indonesia experience the use of MagicSchool AI, a generative AI tool, for lesson planning. The study is motivated by the growing interest in AI for education and the need to understand not just whether AI can save time, but how teachers actually use and adapt AI-generated lesson materials in practice.

The intervention/approach studied was a workshop followed by teachers' use of MagicSchool AI for lesson planning, with data gathered from open-ended questionnaires, focus group interviews, and stimulated recall interviews. The participants were 38 high school EFL teachers in Central Java, Indonesia, recruited through convenience sampling from a district teacher forum. The study focused on how teachers used the tool to generate instructional materials, assessments, differentiated texts, and classroom activity ideas, and how they refined outputs to fit learner needs and classroom realities.

Findings showed four main benefits and tensions: time efficiency, differentiation, resourcefulness, and challenges/lessons. Teachers valued the tool for speeding up material and assessment preparation, supporting differentiated instruction, and prompting new teaching ideas, including practices they had previously forgotten. However, they also emphasized that AI outputs often required substantial editing, that prompting skill mattered, and that teacher judgment remained essential. The paper concludes that generative AI should be treated as a collaborative aid rather than a replacement for educators, and that targeted professional development is needed to strengthen prompt engineering and critical evaluation skills.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI tool/chatbot used to generate lesson-planning materials, assessments, differentiated texts, and instructional ideas, requiring teacher prompting and review.
identified_tools.use_case: Indonesian high school EFL teachers used MagicSchool AI in a workshop-followed lesson-planning context to create instructional materials, assessments, differentiated reading texts, and activity ideas, and to reflect on benefits and challenges in practice.

findings.finding_summary: Across 38 high school EFL teachers, MagicSchool AI was reported to reduce the time needed for material and assessment preparation. Teachers described it as faster than ChatGPT in some cases because of structured prompts and pre-designed fields, but noted that efficiency was reduced when follow-up prompting and editing were needed.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported time efficiency in material preparation and assessment design from open-ended questionnaire, focus groups, and stimulated recall interviews

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that MagicSchool AI supported differentiation by helping them level texts and vary instructional content for diverse learners. Examples included creating reading texts at different complexity levels and generating songs and jokes for icebreakers and lesson introductions.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported differentiation and personalization of lesson materials

findings.finding_summary: Teachers said the tool stimulated resourcefulness and creativity by generating new instructional ideas and reintroducing strategies they had learned earlier in their careers. The paper emphasizes that this benefit depended on teachers critically adapting outputs to fit classroom needs.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported creativity/resourcefulness in instructional planning

findings.finding_summary: Participants identified several implementation constraints: prompt quality strongly shaped output usefulness, AI-generated texts often required substantial refinement, and poor internet access limited practical use in rural areas. The paper also reframed efficiency as producing high-quality materials, not just saving time.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported challenges, prompting requirements, and contextual constraints in AI-assisted lesson planning

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative exploratory case study with 38 teachers using post-workshop questionnaires, focus groups, and stimulated recall interviews. It provides useful practice-based evidence, but it does not estimate causal effects and reports no quantitative effect sizes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful perceived benefits for lesson planning efficiency, differentiation, and creativity, but these are self-reported and not quantified. Because no effect sizes or outcome metrics are provided, the impact is clear in practice but not measurable in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how university students perceive generative AI tools such as ChatGPT in higher education. The authors ask three main questions: how familiar students are with GenAI, what benefits and challenges they associate with it, and how GenAI might be integrated effectively into teaching and learning. The study is framed by user acceptance and John Biggs’ 3P model, which emphasizes that students’ perceptions of their learning environment and tools can shape learning approaches and outcomes.

The study used an online survey with both closed-ended and open-ended questions. Participants were 399 undergraduate and postgraduate students from six universities in Hong Kong and across multiple disciplines, including STEM and non-STEM fields. The survey explored knowledge of GenAI, willingness to use it, concerns about it, and perceived educational uses. Responses were analyzed with descriptive statistics, correlation tests, and thematic analysis of open-ended answers.

Findings show that students generally understood GenAI’s strengths and limitations and had a positive attitude toward using it for learning, writing, research, multimedia creation, and administrative support. They especially valued personalized and immediate feedback, brainstorming help, and 24/7 availability. At the same time, they expressed concerns about accuracy, transparency, privacy, plagiarism, over-reliance, reduced critical thinking and creativity, job displacement, and unclear policy guidance. The paper concludes that GenAI has strong potential to support higher education, but effective integration requires improved AI literacy, ethical safeguards, and institutional policies that promote responsible use.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot based on a large language model that generates human-like text responses to user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses ChatGPT as an example of GenAI technology used in higher education and reports students' perceptions of its use for personalized learning support, writing and brainstorming assistance, research support, and potential future teaching tasks such as generating lesson plans.

findings.finding_summary: In a survey of 399 undergraduate and postgraduate students in Hong Kong, students generally expressed willingness to use ChatGPT/GenAI because it could save time and provide 24/7 support. Mean ratings were high for saving time (M=4.20, SD=0.82) and availability 24/7 (M=4.12, SD=0.83), with positive correlations between willingness and knowledge of GenAI (r=0.189, p<0.001) and frequency of use (r=0.326, p<0.001).
findings.measure: Self-reported willingness to use GenAI, including time-saving and 24/7 availability perceptions

findings.finding_summary: Students perceived ChatGPT as useful for personalized and immediate learning support, including customized recommendations and feedback. The paper reports positive ratings for providing personalized and immediate feedback and suggestions for assignments (M=3.61, SD=1.06), and qualitative responses described it as a virtual tutor that could answer questions immediately and support lesson plan generation for future teaching.
findings.measure: Self-reported perceived usefulness for personalized feedback, learning support, and lesson-plan generation

findings.finding_summary: Students viewed ChatGPT as a writing and brainstorming aid that could help generate ideas, improve grammar and paraphrasing, and provide feedback on writing. Qualitative responses highlighted its use for inspiration, citation gathering, and polishing articles, especially for non-native English speakers.
findings.measure: Self-reported perceived usefulness for writing, brainstorming, and writing feedback

findings.finding_summary: Students perceived ChatGPT/GenAI as helpful for research and analysis tasks, including literature searching, summarising readings, and generating hypotheses from data analysis. These were qualitative perceptions rather than measured performance outcomes.
findings.measure: Self-reported perceived usefulness for research and data analysis support

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General generative artificial intelligence tools and chatbots capable of producing text and other media in response to prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies university students' perceptions of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, including expected uses for learning support, writing feedback, research assistance, multimedia generation, administrative tasks, and concerns about risks and policy.

findings.finding_summary: Students were generally knowledgeable about GenAI limitations, with mean scores between 3.89 and 4.15 for items about inaccurate, biased, inappropriate, and emotionally limited outputs. They also showed positive willingness to integrate GenAI into learning and future careers (e.g., future careers M=4.05, SD=0.96; learning practices M=3.85, SD=1.02).
findings.measure: Self-reported knowledge of GenAI limitations and willingness to use GenAI

findings.finding_summary: Students saw GenAI as improving efficiency by saving time, providing 24/7 support, and offering anonymous student support services. At the same time, they expressed concerns about over-reliance, with the least positive rating on becoming over-reliant on GenAI (M=2.85, SD=1.13).
findings.measure: Self-reported efficiency benefits and over-reliance concerns

findings.finding_summary: Participants expressed concerns that GenAI could undermine the value of university education (M=3.15, SD=1.17), hinder social interaction (M=3.06, SD=1.20), and reduce development of transferable skills such as teamwork and leadership (M=3.10, SD=1.23). The paper also reports worries about privacy, plagiarism, job displacement, human values, and uncertain policies, all based on qualitative responses.
findings.measure: Self-reported concerns about educational value, social interaction, transferable skills, privacy, ethics, career prospects, human values, and policy uncertainty

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey with open-ended responses, so it is descriptive and correlational rather than experimental. The evidence is useful for understanding perceptions and intended use, but it does not test causal effects of the tool on learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceptions and intended uses of GenAI/ChatGPT, but no direct learning gains or effect sizes on achievement are measured. Reported correlations are small to modest, so the practical impact on outcomes remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in Learning Design Practice: Building an Online Course for Biomedical Sciences Research Programs
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Designs for Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This design case examines how a multidisciplinary instructional design team integrated generative AI tools into the creation of a self-paced online course on program evaluation for biomedical sciences research training programs. The paper asks how GenAI can support different stages of instructional design — from needs analysis and objective refinement to script drafting, image creation, assessment development, and multimedia production — while still preserving human judgment, pedagogical quality, accessibility, and ethical responsibility.

The intervention was not a learner-facing AI tutoring system; rather, it was an AI-supported design workflow. The team used tools such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, Canva, Audiate, Camtasia, and H5P within Moodle to develop seven online modules covering evaluation concepts, design, data collection, ethics, and reporting. They also used AI to simulate a learner needs interview, generate draft objectives and scenarios, and draft quiz items and narration, then revised all outputs through SME review, user testing, and external evaluation.

The intended audience included program directors, training grant managers, administrative staff, faculty, and graduate students in biomedical sciences at Iowa State University and similar contexts. The course was designed for asynchronous online delivery because target learners had busy and variable schedules. The case concludes that GenAI can improve efficiency and help structure design thinking, but its outputs were often inaccurate, repetitive, contextually weak, or ethically problematic, requiring substantial human oversight. The authors argue that GenAI should be treated as a scaffold rather than a replacement for instructional expertise.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General generative AI tools used for drafting, revising, and producing instructional content, assessments, visuals, and audio narration.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as co-thinkers in the instructional design process for a self-paced online course, including brainstorming, learner persona simulation, objective refinement, script drafting, image/layout generation, audio narration, assessment drafting, and accessibility support.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that GenAI tools accelerated ideation, drafting, and multimedia production, helping the team produce module content, scripts, visuals, and audio narration more quickly. However, the authors repeatedly note that substantial human revision was still required, and in some cases revising AI output took as long as writing from scratch.
findings.measure: Design workflow efficiency and production support (qualitative design reflections)

findings.finding_summary: GenAI supported early-stage learner analysis, objective drafting, and accessibility brainstorming, but the paper emphasizes risks including inaccuracies, distorted or misspelled outputs, limited contextual understanding, copyright/privacy concerns, and unclear transparency around AI-generated content. The team concluded that human oversight, SME review, and ethical guardrails were necessary throughout.
findings.measure: Reported risks and ethical/design issues during course development (qualitative reflection)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a design case and reflective report rather than an empirical evaluation of AI effectiveness, so it does not meet criteria for higher evidence tiers. The paper provides practice-based observations but no controlled comparison, quantitative effect estimates, or outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical workflow benefits from GenAI for instructional design efficiency, but the gains are qualitative and not quantified. It also documents meaningful risks and limitations, so the overall impact is positive but modest and mixed.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether AI-generated feedback can improve lesson planning quality in vocational teacher education, and whether using such a system influences students’ motivation, AI literacy, attitudes toward AI, digital self-efficacy, and digital competences. The authors position the study as a response to a practical problem in higher education: university instructors often cannot provide frequent, detailed, individualized feedback on complex lesson plans.

The intervention uses EDDA, an analytical AI platform rather than a generative chatbot. EDDA analyzes uploaded lesson plans and materials with a BERT-based classifier trained on coded lesson plans and textbook tasks, then returns expert-level textual and visual feedback across 10 main categories and 57 subcategories. In the intervention condition, 55 master’s students in business education received AI feedback throughout a semester and could then discuss it with a university teacher; 48 comparison students received human feedback only. The study was conducted across two winter-semester cycles in Germany, with lesson planning organized in small groups under the same general planning conditions for both groups.

Findings suggest that AI feedback can match or outperform human feedback on some planning dimensions, especially parts of sustainability-related planning, social competences, reflexivity, action orientation, relatedness, lesson structure, learner engagement, and some technology-use aspects. However, the study also found that using the AI platform did not automatically increase AI literacy, improve attitudes, or raise motivation. Overall, the authors conclude that analytical AI can effectively supplement traditional feedback in teacher education, but it should be embedded in a broader instructional framework and not treated as a standalone solution.

identified_tools.name: EDDA
identified_tools.description: An analytical AI platform for lesson planning that uses machine learning/NLP to analyze uploaded lesson plans and materials and return individualized expert-level text and visual feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the experimental feedback medium in a longitudinal intervention with vocational teacher education students planning lesson plans over a semester, compared against human feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In a longitudinal intervention with N=103 student teachers (experimental n=55; control n=48), the AI feedback condition improved some lesson-planning dimensions relative to human feedback. The abstract reports gains in content-related sustainability aspects, action orientation, relatedness, technology use, lesson structure, and learner engagement, while the paper also reports a significant positive effect for SDG 15 (life on land) and for social competences and reflexivity within sustainability-related planning.
findings.measure: Lesson plan content analysis of didactic/planning dimensions (including sustainability, action orientation, lesson structure, learner engagement)

findings.finding_summary: The intervention had a significant positive effect on social competences for sustainable development. The paper reports this as a higher rating for the experimental group versus the control group (N=103), with p<0.05, indicating improved communicative strategies to handle conflict in a sustainability-focused company setting.
findings.measure: Sustainable change-agent competence: social competences

findings.finding_summary: The intervention also showed a significant positive effect on reflexivity in lesson plans. The paper reports that the experimental group received higher ratings than the control group (N=103), with p<0.10.
findings.measure: Sustainable change-agent competence: reflexivity

findings.finding_summary: For the sustainability dimension, prior sustainability knowledge and prior attitudes were associated with some sub-dimensions, while the intervention effect was specific rather than uniform. The paper reports a significant positive intervention effect for SDG 15 (life on land), but not for the other SDGs, and notes that higher starting points predicted less growth across the semester.
findings.measure: Sustainability-related lesson-plan categories, including SDGs and change-agent competences

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports a limitation/risk in the AI system: EDDA tends to underestimate planning performance, rating lesson plans worse than they are because of unbalanced training data. The authors note this could potentially have demotivating effects on users by masking competence development.
findings.measure: System calibration/feedback accuracy risk noted by authors

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal comparative intervention with a control group, but it is not a randomized trial and the paper relies on several modeled outcomes and some secondary measures. The design is stronger than correlational work, yet there are implementation and sampling limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant improvements on several lesson-planning dimensions, but the effect sizes are not reported in the excerpt and the findings are uneven across outcomes. The practical impact appears meaningful but modest and domain-specific.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities, challenges, and ethical implications of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT and GPT-3, for education. Rather than testing an intervention empirically, the authors synthesize early research and outline how LLMs may support both learning and teaching, while also identifying major risks that need governance and mitigation.

On the learner side, the paper discusses uses such as generating quizzes, explanations, summaries, writing support, feedback, conversational practice, and domain-specific assistance across primary, secondary, tertiary, disability support, and professional learning contexts. On the teacher side, it highlights potential uses for lesson planning, personalized content creation, assessment, feedback generation, professional development, and supporting research and writing tasks. The paper also considers broader educational technology implications such as AR/VR integration and multilingual access.

The paper concludes that LLMs could meaningfully enhance education if used responsibly, but that they also pose risks related to bias, plagiarism, privacy, overreliance, misinformation, cost, sustainability, and difficulty distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated work. The authors argue for human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, professional development, and policy safeguards as prerequisites for trustworthy educational use.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's large language model chatbot for generating and transforming text, answering questions, and supporting dialogue-based interaction.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as a large language model for educational uses, including teacher support for lesson planning, personalized feedback, assessment, and content generation; the paper is a position paper rather than an empirical evaluation.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper and literature-discussion piece, not an empirical study or meta-analysis. It proposes opportunities and risks for ChatGPT/LLMs in education but does not report a study design, sample, or measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes or outcome data are reported, so empirical impact cannot be estimated. The paper suggests potentially substantial educational relevance, but this is only conceptual and not evidence of measured impact.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in foreign language lesson plan creation: Trends, variability, and historical biases
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how well ChatGPT can generate foreign-language lesson plans for teachers and how prompt specificity affects the quality and consistency of those outputs. The authors focus on a practical problem in teacher preparation and instructional design: whether generative AI can reliably support lesson planning, and whether more detailed prompts improve results or introduce new issues.

Using ChatGPT-4.0, the authors created five zero-shot prompts that increased in specificity from a general lesson request to a highly structured prompt with a checklist of required lesson-plan components. Each prompt was run 10 times, producing 50 lesson plans total, which were scored against a rubric based on best-practice language teaching and edTPA-related criteria used in a foreign-language teacher licensure program at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. The outputs were analyzed quantitatively for score trends, output variability, and structural differences across prompts.

The study found that ChatGPT could generate generally high-quality lesson plans, but greater prompt specificity did not produce a simple linear improvement in quality. The prompt that included a checklist of criteria performed best on average, while adding a lesson-plan template alone sometimes reduced quality in key areas such as warm-up and student interaction. Outputs from the same prompt also varied substantially, sometimes missing multiple rubric criteria and sometimes scoring near-perfectly. The authors conclude that generative AI can streamline lesson planning, but teachers must critically review and revise outputs because the model can reproduce outdated pedagogical practices, such as audio-lingual, teacher-centered patterns and weak attention to cultural connections.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model system used for conversational text generation and prompt-based content creation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as ChatGPT Version 4.0 to generate 50 foreign language lesson plans via five increasingly specific zero-shot prompts, then evaluated for lesson-plan quality, variability, and historical/pedagogical bias.

findings.finding_summary: Across 50 generated lesson plans (10 per prompt), ChatGPT was generally able to create aligned lesson plans, but quality did not increase linearly with greater prompt specificity. Mean rubric scores ranged from 19.6 to 21.6 out of 25 depending on prompt, and outputs from identical prompts varied widely (e.g., P.1 scores ranged from 16/25 to 23/25; P.5 from 20/25 to 25/25).
findings.measure: Lesson plan quality score based on 25 rubric criteria; prompt-output variability

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study with a clear comparative prompt-design method, but it is not an RCT or QED and reports descriptive/statistical analyses without causal identification. The evidence is informative but limited to one tool, one task, and one subject area.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical but mixed effects on lesson-plan quality, with no reported effect sizes and substantial output variability. The magnitude of benefit is unclear, so impact is best treated as modest or uncertain.

paper_profiles.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Personal, Academic, and Lesson Planning Purposes: Applications and Perceptions of Irish Pre-Service Primary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Irish pre-service primary teachers use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and how that use relates to their perceptions of GenAI for lesson planning. The central question is whether personal and academic experience with GenAI influences views about its value, risks, and professional development needs in lesson planning.

The study is a questionnaire-based survey conducted as the first phase of an international design-based research collaboration between teacher education institutions in Ireland and Arizona. The sample included pre-service primary teachers in two programs at one Irish institution: Bachelor of Education students and Professional Master of Education students. Participants reported their GenAI use for personal, academic, and lesson-planning purposes, and their perceptions of opportunities, challenges, ethical concerns, and the need for professional development.

Findings show that GenAI use was still in an early stage, with ChatGPT the most commonly used tool and lesson-planning use less common than personal or academic use. Participants saw GenAI as time-saving and potentially helpful for better lesson plans, but they were less confident about the creativity, originality, and reliability of AI-generated plans. They also expressed concerns about over-reliance, possible negative effects on children’s learning, educational inequity, data privacy, and the need for transparency. Importantly, personal GenAI use was not significantly related to lesson-planning perceptions, while academic use was positively associated with perceived opportunities and professional development needs, and negatively associated with perceived challenges and ethical concerns. The paper concludes that teacher education should provide foundational training for beginners and more advanced, critically oriented training for those with academic GenAI experience.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI chatbot used for generating and refining text and providing assistance across tasks such as writing and planning.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reports that most respondents who had used GenAI tools used ChatGPT the most, and ChatGPT was the predominant tool used for personal, academic, and lesson-planning-related purposes in the survey.

findings.finding_summary: In this correlational survey of n=100 Irish pre-service primary teachers, 60 participants reported using ChatGPT the most among GenAI tools. The study did not evaluate ChatGPT-specific effects on lesson planning quality or instructional practice; rather, ChatGPT was the most commonly named tool in respondents' GenAI use patterns.
findings.measure: Self-reported GenAI tool use frequency

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quantitative cross-sectional survey with descriptive statistics and Pearson correlations, not an experimental or quasi-experimental efficacy study. The evidence is useful for understanding perceptions and use patterns, but it does not establish causal effects of ChatGPT on teacher planning quality or instructional practice.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no tool-specific effect sizes for lesson planning outcomes and no evidence of measurable positive or negative impact on teacher practice. Reported correlations concern prior academic use of GenAI broadly, with no direct performance outcome, so impact on the target outcomes is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: LessonPlanner: Assisting Novice Teachers to Prepare Pedagogy-Driven Lesson Plans with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: UIST '24 (ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping novice teachers prepare high-quality lesson plans efficiently. The authors note that lesson planning is time-consuming and difficult, especially for teachers with limited experience in pedagogical strategy selection and in finding suitable teaching materials. They explore whether large language models (LLMs) can support lesson-plan creation in a way that is more structured and pedagogy-driven than a general chat interface like ChatGPT.

To do this, they first ran a formative study with six novice teachers and teaching assistants to understand their needs and concerns when using LLMs for lesson planning. Based on these findings, they built LessonPlanner, a web-based interactive system that uses GPT-4 and organizes generation around educational frameworks, especially Gagne’s Nine Events of Instruction and Bloom’s Taxonomy. The system supports goal setting, outline generation, event-based content generation, prompt presets, editable markdown, and a sidebar LLM assistant for refinement.

They then evaluated LessonPlanner in a within-subjects study with 12 university students acting as teachers, comparing it against a baseline ChatGPT workflow, and followed up with expert interviews involving six teachers across educational levels. Results showed that LessonPlanner improved the quality of produced lesson plans and reduced workload relative to the baseline. Participants also felt it better supported teaching strategy selection and content organization, though they expressed concerns about the accuracy and usefulness of generated content, especially in specialized subjects.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI system used to generate, refine, and explain text content.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the baseline web app in the within-subjects study, and also mentioned as an LLM users had previously used for lesson preparation. LessonPlanner was compared against the ChatGPT interface for lesson plan creation.

findings.finding_summary: Compared with the baseline ChatGPT interface, LessonPlanner significantly improved the quality of outcome lesson plans in a within-subjects study with n=12. The paper reports that LessonPlanner also eased users' workload in the preparation process, and expert interviews (n=6) further supported its usefulness for suggesting effective teaching strategies and meaningful educational resources.
findings.measure: Quality of outcome lesson plans; workload during lesson preparation; expert perceptions of usefulness

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods user study with a within-subjects comparison and expert interviews, but the paper does not report a randomized trial design or effect sizes in the provided text. The evidence is informative but not high-certainty experimental evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports a statistically significant improvement in lesson plan quality and reduced workload, suggesting practical relevance. However, the magnitude is not reported, so the impact level cannot be confidently graded as medium or large.

paper_profiles.title: The Effects of an Artificial Intelligence Voice Chatbot on Improving Vietnamese Undergraduate Students’ English Speaking Skills
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether an AI voice chatbot can improve Vietnamese undergraduate students’ English speaking ability, and how students perceive using it for practice. The authors focus on a persistent problem in Vietnamese EFL classrooms: students often have limited speaking opportunities, insufficient exposure to authentic English, and low confidence, which hinder fluency and accuracy. The paper asks whether a chatbot can provide a more flexible, learner-centered speaking environment than traditional classroom practice.

The intervention used Andy English Bot, an AI voice chatbot, over an 8-week quasi-experimental period. Thirty non-English-major undergraduates at Can Tho University in Vietnam practiced speaking with the chatbot in two class sessions per week, alongside five lesson plans delivered through a supporting learning website. Outcomes were measured with pre- and post-speaking tests targeting fluency and accuracy, a questionnaire, and semi-structured interviews. The design therefore combines quantitative outcome measurement with qualitative perception data.

Results showed statistically significant gains in overall speaking performance, as well as in both fluency and accuracy. Students reported that the chatbot helped them improve grammar, pronunciation, vocabulary, and confidence because it provided repeated practice, native-like input, visual text support, and unlimited speaking time. Some limitations emerged, including constrained topic coverage and voice recognition issues for Vietnamese names. The authors conclude that AI voice chatbots can be a useful classroom supplement for speaking practice and suggest teachers integrate them into lesson plans with clear objectives and guidance.

identified_tools.name: Andy English Bot
identified_tools.description: An AI voice chatbot for English conversation practice, with speech recognition, voice/text interaction, and grammar/vocabulary support.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the intervention tool for Vietnamese undergraduate students to practice English speaking during an 8-week quasi-experiment with two class sessions per week.

findings.finding_summary: In a quasi-experiment with 30 Vietnamese undergraduate students, speaking performance improved significantly after using Andy English Bot. The paired t-test showed a significant gain in overall speaking test scores (p<0.05), with significant improvements in both fluency and accuracy from pre-test to post-test.
findings.measure: Pre-speaking vs post-speaking test scores; fluency and accuracy sub-scores

findings.finding_summary: Students reported improved fluency in questionnaire and interview responses, saying they could speak with fewer pauses and hesitations after repeated practice with the chatbot. The paper attributes this to unlimited speaking time, a relaxing atmosphere, and repeated practice opportunities.
findings.measure: Questionnaire items on fluency; semi-structured interview responses

findings.finding_summary: Students reported improved speaking accuracy after the intervention, including better grammar, pronunciation, and vocabulary use. The chatbot's correct grammar, native-like voice, vocabulary suggestions, and on-screen text helped learners notice and correct errors.
findings.measure: Questionnaire items on grammar/pronunciation/vocabulary; interview responses

findings.finding_summary: The study reports that students became more autonomous and confident in speaking because they could self-check grammar and pronunciation on the chat screen and learn vocabulary through conversations. The paper also notes increased motivation and comfort from speaking anytime and anywhere.
findings.measure: Interview themes on feelings, autonomy, and confidence; questionnaire responses

findings.finding_summary: Students valued the tool's convenience and unlimited access, but the study also identified risks and limitations: limited speaking topics, occasional voice-recognition failures, inability to recognize some Vietnamese names, and installation problems on older Android devices.
findings.measure: Interview responses on usability and limitations; implementation observations

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small mixed-method quasi-experiment rather than a randomized controlled trial. The design provides useful evidence but has limited causal strength and relies partly on self-report.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant pre-post improvements, but no effect sizes are given and the sample is small. The practical impact appears promising yet is not quantifiably large from the reported data.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the implications of ChatGPT for higher education, especially assessment, learning, and teaching. The authors frame ChatGPT as a rapid development in generative AI that can produce fluent text, code, and other outputs, and they ask whether such systems threaten traditional assessment methods such as essays while also offering opportunities for teaching and learning innovation.

The paper does not report an intervention study with participants. Instead, it uses a desktop analysis / literature review approach combined with hands-on experimentation with ChatGPT. The authors review early peer-reviewed and preprint literature on ChatGPT and earlier GPT models in higher education, then test the system with example prompts such as statistical explanations, an essay-writing task, and a Chinese composition task. They also situate ChatGPT within broader AIEd frameworks, distinguishing student-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing applications.

The discussion focuses on higher education contexts and includes students, teachers, and institutions as the relevant user groups. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can be useful for conceptual explanations, drafting, and idea generation, but it is weak on higher-order reasoning, accurate referencing, and some non-English language tasks. They argue that rather than banning such tools outright, higher education should adapt assessment and pedagogy, emphasizing more innovative assessments, feedback, and AI-aware teaching practices. The paper also flags risks including hallucinated or biased content, misleading confidence, plagiarism concerns, and potential disruption to conventional assessment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational AI chatbot built on GPT-family large language models, designed to generate human-like text responses to user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reviewed ChatGPT's functionality and experimented with it for drafting essays, answering questions, translating, and generating text in educational contexts to assess strengths, limitations, and implications for higher education.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT could provide clear conceptual explanations and real-world applications, but it was less competent on tasks requiring higher-order critical and analytical thinking. It also generated a poorly structured Chinese composition and was reported to produce generic prose, occasional bogus references, and uneven factual accuracy.
findings.measure: Author's qualitative review and experimental observations of ChatGPT outputs across explanatory, essay-writing, citation, and Chinese-writing prompts

findings.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can save time by generating responses quickly, including answers and draft text within roughly 60120 seconds, and may help teachers by allowing more time for feedback and revision. However, this is presented as a potential opportunity rather than a measured effect.
findings.measure: Author's qualitative assessment of response speed and workflow implications

findings.finding_summary: The paper warns that ChatGPT may threaten traditional essay assessments, enable plagiarism-like misuse, and produce unreliable or biased outputs, while also noting potential opportunities for assessment redesign and instructional innovation. These are discussed as risks and implications rather than quantified outcomes.
findings.measure: Narrative synthesis of risks and opportunities for assessment and instructional practice

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative/review-style paper with small illustrative experiments and no controlled empirical evaluation of ChatGPT. The evidence is qualitative and descriptive, so it does not meet criteria for higher methodological rigor.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful effects on assessment, feedback, and teacher workload, but it reports no quantified effect sizes. Because the reported impacts are important yet unmeasured, the overall impact tier is modest/unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Are They Ready to Teach? Generative AI as a Means to Uncover Pre-Service Science Teachers’ PCK and Enhance Their Preparation Program
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual paper addresses how generative AI (GenAI) might be used in teacher preparation to reveal and support pre-service science teachers’ pedagogical content knowledge (PCK). The authors argue that conversations between pre-service teachers and a GenAI tool during lesson planning can expose how they think about content, pedagogy, assessment, and classroom decision-making, thereby giving teacher educators a new way to evaluate developing PCK.

The paper proposes a two-stage approach: first, record pre-service teachers’ chats with GenAI while they plan science lessons; second, have trained GenAI analyze those chats to infer PCK components. The authors illustrate the idea with example ChatGPT dialogues in chemistry, comparing an experienced chemistry educator and a pre-service teacher planning instruction on ionic versus molecular materials. They also discuss prompt engineering, the need for human verification of AI outputs, and the risk that LLMs may overestimate novice teachers’ knowledge.

The context is pre-service science teacher education, especially chemistry, although the authors argue the approach could extend to other disciplines. The main conclusion is that GenAI has promise both as a lesson-planning aid and as a formative assessment tool for teacher educators, but it should be used critically, with training in prompt engineering, content checking, and bias awareness. The paper is forward-looking and recommends empirical validation against established PCK assessment methods before broad adoption.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on large language models, used for conversational assistance, text generation, and interactive question-answering.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the conversational GenAI tool for lesson-planning dialogues and for evaluating pre-service teachers' pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) from their prompts in chemistry lesson planning.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual paper that proposes and illustrates an approach using ChatGPT rather than reporting a direct empirical evaluation of the tool. It provides examples and rationale, but no study design with measured outcomes for the tool itself.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potential benefits in teacher preparation, lesson planning, and PCK assessment, but it does not report quantified effects. Impact is therefore suggested but unmeasured in this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing mathematics education for students with special educational needs through generative AI: A case study in Greece
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can be used to create individualized mathematics lesson plans and worksheets that better support students with special educational needs. The authors frame the study around a new concept they call "mathematical familiarity," meaning the degree to which an AI-generated worksheet feels comfortable, relevant, and personally meaningful to a student.

The study reports a nine-hour teaching intervention in a Greek general education classroom. Two 8th-grade students, one diagnosed with dyslexia and one with autism spectrum disorder, received ChatGPT 3.5-generated worksheets tailored to their curriculum needs, interests, and hobbies. The worksheets were used alongside ordinary classroom teaching on square roots and irrational numbers, while the rest of the class used standard materials. Data came from classroom observation, student interviews, and a short e-questionnaire.

The authors conclude that the personalized ChatGPT worksheets increased engagement, helped the two students feel safe and confident, and supported their understanding of the target mathematics topics. They also report that the students performed well on class tests and expressed positive attitudes toward mathematics. The paper argues that generative AI can help teachers create differentiated materials more efficiently, but it also emphasizes the importance of teacher judgment, careful prompting, and training in the use of ChatGPT.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI generative AI chatbot/assistant based on GPT models that can generate text and support interactive prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate individualized mathematics lesson plans and differentiated worksheets for two 8th grade students with special educational needs (dyslexia and ASD) in a general classroom.

findings.finding_summary: In a 9-hour qualitative teaching intervention with two 8th grade students with special educational needs, ChatGPT-generated worksheets were reported to help the students understand the square root of a positive number and irrational numbers. The authors report that both students completed classroom test exercises almost correctly and that the teacher observed improved engagement and interest; no effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Student understanding/performance on class worksheets and teacher-administered tests; interview and questionnaire responses about engagement and comfort

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative case study with two participants and no experimental control group, so causal evidence is limited. The paper does provide direct classroom observations, interviews, and student responses, but the methodology is descriptive rather than rigorous comparative evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported benefits are positive, but they are based on n=2 and no effect sizes are given, so the magnitude of impact cannot be quantified. The evidence suggests possible practical value for personalized math materials, but the strength of impact remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring High School EFL Teachers' Experiences with Magic School AI in Lesson Planning: Benefits and Insights
paper_profiles.venue: Voices of English Language Education Society
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how high school English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers experienced the use of MagicSchool AI, a generative AI tool, for lesson planning. The study addresses a practical question in AI-in-education research: whether generative AI can support teacher planning quality and practice while also introducing risks or limitations that require human oversight. It is positioned against a background of growing interest in generative AI for education and concerns that AI outputs may not be pedagogically ready for direct classroom use.

The intervention/approach studied was a workshop on AI-assisted lesson planning followed by teachers' use of MagicSchool AI. Data came from 38 Indonesian high school EFL teachers in Central Java through an open-ended online questionnaire and focus group interviews, including stimulated recall. The study used an exploratory case study design and thematic analysis to identify recurring experiences and concerns.

Findings showed four major themes: time efficiency, differentiation, resourcefulness, and challenges/lessons. Teachers reported that MagicSchool AI sped up material and assessment preparation, supported differentiated instruction, and generated fresh activity ideas that could revive or extend their instructional repertoire. However, they also emphasized important risks and limitations: AI outputs often required substantial editing, effective use depended on prompt quality, and weak internet connectivity reduced usefulness in some contexts. The authors conclude that generative AI can be a helpful collaborative tool for lesson planning, but only when paired with teacher expertise, critical evaluation, and targeted professional development in prompt engineering and pedagogical review.

identified_tools.name: MagicSchool AI
identified_tools.description: A generative AI lesson-planning tool that helps teachers create instructional materials, assessments, and differentiated content through structured prompts and guided fields.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by 38 Indonesian high school EFL teachers after a workshop to support lesson planning, material preparation, assessment design, differentiation, and idea generation.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that MagicSchool AI reduced the time needed to prepare instructional materials and assessments, especially for users who could work effectively with its structured prompts and pre-designed fields. However, several teachers noted that follow-up prompting and editing were often needed, and poor internet access reduced the practical time-saving benefit. Sample size for the qualitative study was n=38.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported time efficiency in material preparation and assessment design from open-ended questionnaires, focus group interviews, and stimulated recall interviews

findings.finding_summary: Teachers said MagicSchool AI supported differentiation by helping them level reading texts, vary complexity, and generate activities aligned with diverse student needs and learning styles. The paper reports that the tool made it easier to create tailored materials, but outputs still required human review to ensure pedagogical fit. Sample size for the qualitative study was n=38.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported ability to differentiate instruction and adapt lesson materials

findings.finding_summary: Participants described MagicSchool AI as a resource that stimulated creativity and expanded their repertoire of instructional strategies, including reintroducing ideas they had not used for years. The paper emphasizes that the tool generated ideas for activities and supported teacher resourcefulness, but teachers still needed to adapt the outputs to classroom context. Sample size for the qualitative study was n=38.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported creativity/resourcefulness in instructional planning

findings.finding_summary: The study identified several risks and limitations: effective prompting was necessary, AI-generated outputs often needed substantial refinement, and human oversight was required because the tool could not adequately handle class dynamics or context. Teachers also reframed efficiency as producing quality materials, not merely saving time. Sample size for the qualitative study was n=38.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported challenges, limitations, and risks in AI-supported lesson planning

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative exploratory case study with open-ended questionnaires, focus groups, and stimulated recall interviews. It provides useful descriptive evidence, but there is no experimental design, comparison group, or quantitative causal estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are qualitatively positive for planning efficiency, differentiation, and idea generation, but no effect sizes are provided and the evidence is based on teacher perceptions rather than measured learning or instructional outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Intersections of Mind and Machine: Navigating the Nexus of Artificial Intelligence, Science Education, and the Preparation of Pre-service Teachers
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial examines the growing role of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in science education, with a particular focus on how it may affect the preparation of pre-service teachers (PSTs). The paper asks whether GenAI is genuinely transformative for education or whether it is another example of the recurring cycle of technological hype that has historically surrounded new tools such as radio, television, and computers.

Rather than testing a specific intervention, the article synthesises and positions the contributions in a special issue on GenAI and science teacher education. It discusses how GenAI can support lesson planning, personalised learning, inquiry-based learning, writing, and pedagogical content knowledge development, while also raising concerns about bias, hallucinations, privacy, data security, and over-reliance on AI-generated outputs. The context is initial teacher education and science education, especially among PSTs who are already experimenting with GenAI for university coursework and preparation for teaching.

The paper concludes that teacher education programs should provide structured support for GenAI literacy, critical evaluation of AI outputs, and ethical reflection. The authors argue that PSTs need both technical proficiency and critical judgment to use GenAI responsibly and pedagogically soundly. Overall, the editorial frames GenAI as a tool with real potential, but one whose educational value depends on careful integration, human mentorship, and sustained institutional support.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI GPT-based conversational large language model used for generating and rewriting text.
identified_tools.use_case: Used during the writing process of the editorial between July and December 2024 to rewrite sentences for improved phrasing, flow, and word choice.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an editorial/theoretical special-issue overview rather than an empirical evaluation of an AI tool. It does not report a study design, comparison group, or measured outcomes for the tool itself.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes or outcome data are reported for ChatGPT in this paper. The only described use is author-side writing assistance for the manuscript, not a measured educational impact.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can serve as a useful automated coach for teachers. The authors frame teacher coaching as a widespread but resource-intensive practice and investigate whether large language models can provide scalable feedback on classroom instruction that resembles expert coaching.

They study three coaching tasks: (A) scoring classroom transcript segments using established observation rubrics, (B) identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and (C) generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning. The model is evaluated zero-shot using the GPT-3.5-turbo version of ChatGPT on transcripts from the National Center for Teacher Effectiveness (NCTE) dataset, which contains elementary math classroom observations annotated with CLASS and MQI rubric scores. For qualitative tasks, experienced math teachers rate the model’s outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

The population is U.S. elementary mathematics classrooms, specifically 4th- and 5th-grade transcripts from 317 teachers across four school districts serving largely historically marginalized students. The study finds that ChatGPT performs poorly at rubric-based scoring, often overpredicting scores and showing low correlation with human ratings. For qualitative feedback, its responses are sometimes relevant and faithful, but often not insightful or novel; in the suggestions task, most outputs simply restate what the teacher already did. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has promise as a complement to human coaching but is not yet reliable enough to provide high-quality instructional feedback on its own.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot based on GPT-family large language models.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated zero-shot performance as an automated teacher coach for classroom transcript scoring, identifying highlights and missed opportunities, and generating actionable suggestions for eliciting student reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: On transcript scoring (Task A), ChatGPT showed low Spearman correlations with human ratings across CLASS and MQI items. Reported correlations were near zero to small at best (e.g., CLBM DA=0.35; most others ranged from -0.11 to 0.23), indicating poor alignment with expert scores on elementary math classroom transcript segments.
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between model-predicted observation scores and human raters' CLASS/MQI scores
findings.effect_size: CLPC DA=0.00; CLBM DA=0.35; CLINSTD DA=-0.01; EXPL DA=0.02; REMED DA=0.05; LANGIMP DA=0.00; SMQR DA=0.17

findings.finding_summary: For Task B (identifying highlights and missed opportunities), expert teachers generally judged the model outputs as not insightful or not relevant, with faithfulness problems present in about 20-30% of responses. MQI outputs were worse than CLASS outputs across relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness, suggesting the model struggled more with technical math-instruction judgments.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for model-generated highlights/missed opportunities
findings.sample_size: n=216 CLASS items and n=288 MQI items

findings.finding_summary: For Task C (actionable suggestions), teachers rated most suggestions as faithful, relevant, and actionable, but novelty was weak: 82% of suggestions repeated what the teacher was already doing in the transcript. The paper characterizes this as useful in some respects but with substantial redundancy and limited originality.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, actionability, and novelty of suggestions for eliciting student reasoning

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-scale empirical study with qualitative human evaluation and correlational analysis rather than an RCT or meta-analysis. The methodology is careful, but the evidence base is limited by sample size and no experimental impact on student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported associations are small or near zero for scoring accuracy, and the main qualitative finding is that outputs are often redundant or not insightful. There is some practical promise for teacher-facing use, but the demonstrated impact is modest and uncertain.

paper_profiles.title: LessonPlanner: Assisting Novice Teachers to Prepare Pedagogy-Driven Lesson Plans with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: UIST '24 (The 37th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge novice teachers face when preparing lesson plans: selecting effective teaching strategies, finding suitable materials, and organizing content into a coherent instructional flow. The authors explore whether large language models (LLMs) can support lesson-plan preparation in a way that is pedagogically grounded rather than just generating generic text.

The intervention studied is LessonPlanner, a web-based LLM-powered system built around Gagne’s Nine Events of Instruction and Bloom’s Taxonomy. LessonPlanner supports teachers in generating lesson goals, creating structured outlines, obtaining suggested teaching materials and activities for each instructional event, and refining content through preset prompts, context-aware assistance, and editable markdown outputs. The system was developed from a formative study with six novice teachers and teaching assistants, then evaluated in a within-subjects user study.

The evaluation involved 12 university students with little or no teaching experience, who prepared lesson plans for familiar data structures topics using LessonPlanner versus a baseline ChatGPT web interface. The paper also includes expert interviews with six teachers across educational levels. Results suggest LessonPlanner improved the quality of produced lesson plans and reduced workload compared with the baseline, while experts found it useful for organizing plans and suggesting teaching strategies and materials. The authors also identify concerns about prompt burden, trust in generated content, and the need for flexible user control when using LLMs for teaching support.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational LLM interface used for text generation and interactive prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the baseline web app for lesson plan preparation, and also as the underlying model family for LessonPlanner's generated content in the system implementation.

findings.finding_summary: In the within-subjects study (n=12), LessonPlanner was compared against the baseline ChatGPT web app using the same GPT-4 model. The paper reports that LessonPlanner significantly improved the quality of outcome lesson plans and eased users' workload relative to ChatGPT, but it does not provide the numerical effect size in the excerpted text.
findings.measure: Quality of outcome lesson plans; lesson-planning workload

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods, within-subjects user study with expert interviews rather than a randomized controlled trial or meta-analysis. The evidence is useful but not high-credibility experimental evidence in the K-12 framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper states statistically significant improvements in lesson plan quality and reduced workload, but no effect size is reported in the provided text. Without quantitative magnitude, the practical impact is promising but unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service elementary science teachers integrated ChatGPT into lesson planning and what they believed ChatGPT could contribute to science learning. The paper addresses a gap in empirical evidence on generative AI in education by moving beyond speculative discussions to analyze actual lesson plans and teachers’ perceptions.

The intervention/context was a short professional-learning experience on ChatGPT followed by a lesson-planning task. Twenty-nine pre-service elementary teachers at a Korean teachers’ university, enrolled in a science education course, attended four 2-hour sessions introducing ChatGPT, discussing its possible uses in science instruction, reviewing science teaching methods, and learning how to write lesson plans. They then created lesson plans for a 45-minute elementary science class using ChatGPT and submitted a simulated chat conversation plus open-ended survey responses.

The study used a modified TPACK-based rubric to rate lesson-plan quality across curriculum goals, instructional strategies, ChatGPT function selection, and overall fit, alongside qualitative analysis of survey responses and chat artifacts. Overall, the teachers designed a wide range of lessons across science domains and methods, and their plans scored above the midpoint on the rubric, suggesting moderate competence in integrating ChatGPT. Participants saw ChatGPT as useful for questioning, individualized support, role-play, and formative feedback, but they also worried about inaccurate outputs and student overdependence. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has broad perceived potential for science education, but that teacher education should more deliberately build AI literacy, critical evaluation skills, and guidance for selecting appropriate ChatGPT functions.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on GPT models, able to generate and summarize text, answer questions, and provide interactive conversational support.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by 29 pre-service elementary science teachers to design lesson plans for 45-minute science classes, integrate instructional strategies, select ChatGPT functions, and attach simulated teacher/student-chatbot conversations.

findings.finding_summary: Across 29 lesson plans, the average modified TPACK/TIAR score was M=3.29 (SD=.91) on a 4-point scale, suggesting generally strong lesson-plan quality for ChatGPT integration. Scores were higher for 'instructional strategies & ChatGPT' (M=3.48, SD=.99) than for 'ChatGPT function selection(s)' (M=3.00, SD=.93), with a significant paired difference, t(28)=2.3173, p=.0280.
findings.measure: Modified TPACK-based lesson plan rubric (TIAR-derived scores)

findings.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers anticipated ChatGPT would support high-quality questioning, self-directed and individualized learning, and formative assessment. They also identified risks: concerns about inaccurate or misleading responses (11/29) and student over-dependence on ChatGPT (13/29), including cases where ChatGPT produced non-existent or unsuitable information.
findings.measure: Open-ended survey responses on perceived usefulness and concerns

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-sample empirical study using lesson-plan analysis and open-ended survey responses, not an experiment or meta-analysis. It provides useful descriptive evidence but has limited causal strength.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally positive lesson-plan quality scores, but no standardized learning gains or effect sizes are given. The evidence suggests moderate practical promise with notable risks and implementation caveats.

paper_profiles.title: To what extent is ChatGPT useful for language teacher lesson plan creation?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can support foreign language teachers in creating lesson plans, and how the specificity of prompts affects the quality and consistency of the generated plans. The authors focus on a broader concern relevant to generative AI in education: even when outputs appear strong, they may vary substantially across repeated uses of the same prompt and may contain pedagogically outdated content.

The study used ChatGPT 4.0 in a zero-shot prompting setup. The researchers created five prompts of increasing specificity for a 45-minute high school Level I Spanish lesson in which students were novice-level learners. Across these prompts, they generated 50 lesson plans in total, with each prompt entered into 10 separate chats. The outputs were scored against a 25-item rubric derived from best practices and edTPA-aligned lesson plan expectations, including components such as warm-up, teacher input, cultural connections, standards alignment, and student engagement.

The findings suggest that ChatGPT can produce generally high-quality lesson plans, but more detailed prompting did not reliably produce better outputs. The most helpful addition was a rubric-like checklist of required components, which improved average scores. At the same time, outputs varied considerably even for identical prompts, and some responses reflected anachronistic methods such as behaviorist or audio-lingual practices rather than contemporary communicative approaches. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has practical value for lesson planning, but teachers need AI literacy to evaluate, revise, and guard against biased or outdated generated content.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on GPT models, used for conversational text generation and task completion.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate foreign-language teacher lesson plans from five zero-shot prompts of increasing specificity; outputs were scored for alignment with lesson-plan criteria and examined for variability and potential pedagogical weaknesses.

findings.finding_summary: Across 50 ChatGPT-generated lesson plans (5 prompts  10 repetitions), increasing prompt specificity did not produce a linear improvement in lesson-plan quality. Mean scores ranged from 19.6/25 to 21.6/25, with the highest mean score occurring when a checklist of criteria was added (P.5), but variability remained high within and across prompt groups.
findings.measure: Lesson-plan rubric score out of 25

findings.finding_summary: The authors conclude that ChatGPT can streamline lesson planning for foreign language teachers by generating generally high-quality lesson plans, although outputs still required human review and revision. The paper emphasizes practical usefulness for lesson-plan creation rather than a directly measured efficiency outcome.
findings.measure: Qualitative assessment of usefulness for lesson-plan creation

findings.finding_summary: The paper identified potential risks in ChatGPT outputs, including non-deterministic variation and occasional alignment with anachronistic 20th-century pedagogical practices. Specific weaknesses included limited cultural connections and occasional use of audio-lingual or teacher-centered patterns that the authors describe as research-rebuked or outdated.
findings.measure: Presence/absence of rubric elements and qualitative analysis of lesson-plan content

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study with a clear but non-randomized, simulation-style design using generated outputs rather than human learners. It is informative, but the evidence is limited by the absence of experimental comparison groups and by reliance on rubric scoring of AI outputs.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally positive but modest practical usefulness, alongside substantial variability and clear risks. No effect sizes are reported, and the strongest claims are qualitative rather than measured impacts on student outcomes or teacher performance.

paper_profiles.title: Towards Adaptive Feedback with AI: Comparing the Feedback Quality of LLMs and Teachers on Experimentation Protocols
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether large language models (LLMs) can generate educational feedback for science experimentation protocols that is comparable in quality to feedback written by human teachers and science education experts. The motivation is the growing interest in generative AI for adaptive feedback, paired with concerns that AI feedback may lack contextual understanding and pedagogical validity.

The authors developed an LLM feedback agent using GPT-3.5 and a zero-shot prompting approach. The system was given student experiment tasks, the relevant protocol section, and a defined error type, then instructed to generate structured feedback. Its outputs were compared with feedback written by 11 biology pre- and in-service teachers and 5 science education experts on 40 student protocols containing 109 identified errors. Four blinded raters with science education expertise evaluated each feedback text on six dimensions: Feed Up, Feed Back, Feed Forward, Constructive Tone, Linguistic Clarity, and Technical Terminology, along with feedback length.

The study found no significant difference in overall feedback quality between the LLM, teachers, and experts. The LLM performed similarly well on most language-related and some content-related dimensions, but it scored significantly worse on Feed Back, indicating weaker ability to explain errors in context. The authors conclude that LLMs can support classroom feedback generation, especially for forward-looking guidance and concise language, but that human oversight remains important because current models still struggle with contextual diagnosis of student mistakes.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model chatbot used to generate educational feedback from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the LLM feedback agent (GPT-3.5-turbo-0125) to generate feedback on students’ experimentation protocols and compared against teacher and expert feedback.

findings.finding_summary: The LLM agent’s feedback quality did not differ significantly from teacher or expert feedback on the overall six-dimension rating average. Mean overall scores were 3.784 (SD=1.238) for the LLM agent, 3.805 (SD=1.266) for teachers, and 3.831 (SD=1.287) for experts, with no significant difference reported.
findings.measure: Overall feedback quality score averaged across Feed Up, Feed Back, Feed Forward, Constructive Tone, Linguistic Clarity, and Technical Terminology
findings.sample_size: n=40 protocols; 109 student errors; 3 feedback sources

findings.finding_summary: The LLM agent performed significantly worse than teachers and experts on the Feed Back dimension, which assessed whether feedback described the error in the context of the current situation. The paper reports mean scores of 3.05 (SD=1.37) for the LLM agent versus 3.52 (SD=1.32) for teachers and 3.62 (SD=1.31) for experts, indicating a specific weakness in contextual error explanation.
findings.measure: Feed Back rating on 5-point Likert scale
findings.sample_size: n=40 protocols; 109 student errors; 3 feedback sources

findings.finding_summary: The LLM agent produced feedback at a length that was similar to teachers and shorter than experts, which the authors interpreted as more suitable for grade 6-8 students. The agent’s feedback was often around 50 words despite a 100-word prompt, aligning more closely with teacher-length feedback than with the much longer expert texts.
findings.measure: Word count / feedback length

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary comparative study using blinded human ratings, but it is observational/mixed-methods rather than a randomized causal design. The evidence is therefore useful but not at the highest causal confidence tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no overall difference in quality and no effect sizes, with one specific dimension showing a small disadvantage for the LLM. Without a reported effect size or clear causal intervention, the practical impact is promising but still modest/unclear.

paper_profiles.title: LLMs to Support K–12 Teachers in Culturally Relevant Pedagogy: An AI Literacy Example
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a large-language-model-based tool can help K–12 teachers adapt AI literacy lessons so they better reflect culturally relevant pedagogy (CRP). The motivation is that teachers often want to incorporate students’ cultural backgrounds into instruction but face barriers such as limited time, limited training, and lack of resources.
