The authors focus specifically on the challenge of making AI literacy activities culturally responsive, an area they argue is underdeveloped compared with CRP applications in traditional subjects.

The intervention studied is CulturAIEd, an LLM-powered system that generates culturally relevant content, offers basic and advanced lesson modifications based on a culturally responsive teaching checklist, provides rubric-based feedback, and includes just-in-time chatbot support. The pilot study used semi-structured Zoom sessions with four secondary teachers who worked through a sequence of AI literacy adaptation tasks, first without guidance, then with a checklist, and finally with CulturAIEd. Participants were teachers from North America and East Asia, including science, music education, and information technology teachers serving grades 9–12 or grade 9 in public and virtual public schools.

Findings suggest that CulturAIEd increased teachers’ confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness and making culturally responsive modifications to activities. Teachers valued the tool’s integrated demographic information, actionable feedback, and efficiency gains, especially because it reduced planning time and helped them generate ideas they had not previously considered. The authors conclude that LLMs may support CRP implementation in AI literacy lesson planning, but they also caution that the tool is only a support resource, not a replacement for teachers’ contextual judgment. They emphasize the need for larger controlled studies and note risks such as bias, stereotyping, and the possibility that AI tools could oversimplify or routinize culturally relevant pedagogy.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model chatbot or generative AI assistant used for teacher support, lesson adaptation, content generation, and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studied CulturAIEd, an LLM-powered tool for helping K-12 teachers adapt AI literacy activities to culturally relevant pedagogy. The demo used a GPT-4o-mini model, but the paper does not frame the study as an evaluation of a specific commercial product; rather, it evaluates a generative AI-supported workflow/tool.

findings.finding_summary: In an exploratory pilot with four K-12 teachers (N=4), CulturAIEd increased teachers' confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness in learning activities. The paper reports pre-survey confidence of 3-5 rising to 5/5 for all participants in the post-survey, but no inferential statistics or effect sizes are reported.
findings.measure: Self-reported confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness in learning activities (pre/post survey)

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported increased confidence in making culturally responsive modifications to existing activities after using CulturAIEd. Participants valued the tool's integrated demographic information, rubric-based feedback, and just-in-time coaching, describing it as time-saving and actionable; the study is qualitative/mixed-methods and does not report effect sizes.
findings.measure: Self-reported confidence and perceived usefulness of culturally responsive lesson modifications (survey/interviews)

findings.finding_summary: Participants perceived CulturAIEd as reducing planning burden and improving implementation efficiency by streamlining demographic integration, providing immediate feedback, and reducing the time and research needed for CRP planning. These are qualitative findings from a four-teacher pilot with no quantitative efficiency metric reported.
findings.measure: Perceived planning efficiency / time saved (interviews, post-survey)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small exploratory mixed-methods pilot with n=4 and no control group, so it provides preliminary evidence rather than rigorous causal evidence. The findings are useful but rely mainly on self-report and qualitative interviews.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceived changes in confidence and efficiency, but no effect sizes or outcome tests are provided. The impact therefore appears promising yet unquantified and limited to a very small sample.

paper_profiles.title: Fine-Tuning Large Language Models for Educational Support: Leveraging Gagné’s Nine Events of Instruction for Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.venue: Conference Proceedings of the 28th Global Chinese Conference on Computers in Education (GCCCE 2024)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how large language models (LLMs) can be adapted to better support teachers in lesson planning and instructional dialogue design. The authors argue that general-purpose LLMs are not sufficiently aligned with educational needs, requiring teachers to spend substantial time crafting prompts and manually correcting outputs. To bridge this gap, the paper proposes a pipeline for using LLMs in educational support based on Gagné’s Nine Events of Instruction.

The paper studies two approaches: prompt tuning using chain-of-thought (CoT) prompts with ChatGPT, and model tuning using fine-tuning methods such as LoRA on open-source LLMs including ChatGLM and Llama-Chinese. The resource built for this work combines Gagné-based instructional definitions, math curriculum standards, and teacher/classroom dialogue examples collected from real classrooms and manually annotated. The educational context is mathematics in compulsory education in China, with the goal of generating and analyzing teacher dialogue and lesson-planning content aligned to instructional design principles.

The paper reports a dataset construction process, model adaptation workflow, and evaluation plan using BLEU, ROUGE, and human judgments from frontline educators. Its main conclusion is that LLMs, when guided by structured prompts or fine-tuned on education-specific data, can better generate pedagogically aligned instructional dialogue and potentially support curriculum development, classroom analysis, and lesson planning. The paper is primarily a methodological contribution and does not report a completed controlled intervention study with learner outcomes.

identified_tools.use_case: Fine-tuned on the constructed dataset with LoRA to generate teacher dialogue aligned with Gagné’s instructional framework.

identified_tools.name: Qwen
identified_tools.description: Alibaba's Qwen family of open large language models used as a fine-tuning baseline for text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Included among the open-access models fine-tuned on the educational dialogue dataset.

identified_tools.description: An open large language model family used as a fine-tuning baseline for educational dialogue generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Included among the open-access models fine-tuned on the educational dialogue dataset.

Without empirical outcome data, impact remains speculative and unclear.

paper_profiles.title: AI, Expert or Peer? Examining the Impact of Perceived Feedback Source on Pre-Service Teachers Feedback Perception and Uptake
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether the perceived source of feedback affects how pre-service teachers evaluate and use feedback, with particular attention to feedback attributed to a large language model (LLM), an expert, or a peer. The central question is whether source-related biases influence perceptions such as fairness, usefulness, acceptance, willingness to improve, and affect, and whether these perceptions translate into actual feedback uptake. The work is motivated by growing use of generative AI for educational feedback and concern that negative assumptions about AI may reduce its usefulness in teacher education.

The intervention was a randomized experiment with 273 bachelor’s students enrolled in a German teacher education program. Participants received one written feedback message on a mathematics learning goal; messages had been generated by an LLM (ChatGPT-4), an expert, or a peer. After reading the feedback, participants identified the source, completed the Feedback Perception Questionnaire, and revised the learning goal to reflect the feedback. Feedback quality was independently coded and included in the analyses.

The study found that perceived source strongly shaped feedback perceptions, especially when LLM feedback was misattributed to a human expert. In those cases, LLM feedback was rated more positively on fairness and usefulness. However, perceived source and recognition accuracy did not predict actual feedback uptake once objective feedback quality was controlled for. Instead, feedback quality was the only significant predictor of implementation. Overall, the paper concludes that source-based heuristics bias judgments of AI feedback, but actual use depends mainly on feedback quality, highlighting the need for AI literacy and careful design of LLM-supported feedback in teacher education.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based large language model chatbot used to generate educational feedback text.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate one set of feedback messages on a mathematics learning goal; the paper compared feedback written by ChatGPT-4 with expert- and peer-generated feedback, while participants guessed the source and then revised the learning goal.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized experiment with 273 pre-service teachers, ChatGPT-generated feedback was recognized correctly only 36% of the time, slightly above chance. LLM feedback was evaluated more favorably on cognitive perceptions when it was falsely ascribed to a human expert, and it produced the highest relative feedback uptake (52%) compared with expert (45%) and peer (42%) feedback, but uptake was ultimately predicted only by objective feedback quality.
findings.measure: Recognition accuracy; feedback perception (fairness, usefulness, acceptance, willingness to improve, affect); feedback uptake/correction rate
findings.effect_size: Recognition accuracy: 36% correct; perceived-source effect on fairness b=1.21 and usefulness b=1.76; uptake model R²=.078; feedback quality b=1.27

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized experiment with a clear comparison of feedback sources and multiple measured outcomes, which supports relatively strong causal inference. Some concerns remain because uptake analyses were limited by missing/invalid cases and several effects were null or only trend-level.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports a meaningful source-perception effect and a moderate descriptive difference in uptake (52% vs 45%/42%), but the key behavioral predictor was feedback quality rather than source. Overall impact is modest and partly conditional, not consistently large.

paper_profiles.title: FACET: Teacher-Centred LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems—Towards Personalized Educational Worksheets
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of how generative AI can support teachers in differentiating instruction for increasingly heterogeneous classrooms. The authors argue that many current AI personalization tools are student-facing and overly focused on performance, while neglecting motivational, emotional, and pedagogical dimensions that matter for classroom teaching.

To respond to this gap, the paper introduces FACET, a teacher-facing multi-agent LLM framework for generating individualized worksheets. The system uses three specialized agents: learner agents that simulate different student profiles, a teacher agent that adapts tasks according to didactical principles and Bloom’s taxonomy, and an evaluator agent that scores the output on didactical structure, clarity, creativity, and suitability for learner needs. The implementation is demonstrated with authentic grade 8 mathematics curriculum content from German secondary education.

The study evaluates the framework through automated agent-based scoring across ten iterations per learner profile and exploratory feedback from five K-12 in-service mathematics teachers. Results suggest that the generated worksheets were stable, well aligned to the learner profiles, and perceived by teachers as suitably differentiated, especially in structure and task appropriateness. The paper concludes that multi-agent LLM systems may offer a scalable pathway for teacher support in personalized material generation, but notes that stronger classroom-based validation and richer learner profiles are still needed.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based large language model family used here for learner-agent, teacher-agent, and evaluator-agent functions within a multi-agent system.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the underlying LLM for the FACET framework: GPT-4.1 for learner and teacher agents, and GPT-4o for evaluator and formatting, to generate personalized mathematics worksheets and automated quality feedback.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports exploratory feasibility evidence that the ChatGPT-based multi-agent system could generate worksheets tailored to four learner profiles, with consistently high automated ratings across 10 iterations per profile. Agent-based evaluation found strong scores for suitability (M=4.78, SD=0.06) and clarity (M=4.76, SD=0.12), while teacher feedback from five K-12 in-service teachers also rated didactical structure and suitability positively.
findings.measure: Worksheet quality ratings from automated evaluator agent and exploratory teacher expert ratings (didactical structure, clarity, creativity, suitability)
findings.sample_size: n=10 iterations per profile; n=5 teachers

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory mixed-methods feasibility study with automated agent ratings and small-scale teacher feedback, not a controlled efficacy trial. The evidence is useful but methodologically preliminary and limited in external validity.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported outcomes are positive but are descriptive ratings rather than a measured causal effect on teacher planning quality or student outcomes. No effect size is reported, so impact cannot be quantified beyond preliminary feasibility.

paper_profiles.title: How to Align Large Language Models for Teaching English? Designing and Developing LLM based-Chatbot for Teaching English Conversation in EFL, Findings and Limitations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models (LLMs) can be aligned for English conversation practice in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education, with particular attention to pedagogical quality, conversational usefulness, and safety risks such as inappropriate or harmful content. The authors frame the problem as one of designing an LLM-based chatbot that can generate contextually appropriate, curriculum-aligned dialogue for learners, while also supporting teacher needs for feedback, customization, and classroom usability.

Using a Design and Development Research (DDR) approach, the study iteratively developed and evaluated a chatbot across six phases. The team conducted needs analysis interviews with product owners, experimented with multiple base and fine-tuned LLMs, compared prompting and instruction-tuning approaches, and used both quantitative rubric-based evaluation and qualitative expert interviews. The context was South Korea’s AI Digital Textbook initiative, and the target use case was English conversation practice aligned to elementary school textbook units, with teacher feedback also gathered from one high school English teacher.

The study found that smaller open-source models, when paired with careful prompt engineering, could perform competitively for this educational task. Teacher interviews emphasized the importance of natural feedback mechanisms, customizable AI personas, clear turn-taking, topic guardrails, and strong content filtering. The authors conclude that LLM-based chatbots are promising for EFL conversation practice, but successful educational deployment requires balancing instructional quality, user experience, and safety constraints rather than relying only on model scale.

identified_tools.name: Mistral
identified_tools.description: A family of large language models from Mistral AI used for text generation and conversation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated Mistral-family models (including Mistral-7B and Mixtral variants) as base and fine-tuned models, and selected a Mistral-based model (NeuralHermes-2.5-Mistral-7B-AWQ) with a prompt template for the third prototype of an EFL English conversation chatbot.

findings.finding_summary: Across quantitative qualitative evaluation of 10 LLMs, Mistral-7B had the highest average score among the base models (4.37) and remained among the top-performing fine-tuned models (4.01 average for fine-tuned Mistral-7B). In the prompt-engineering phase, the Mistral-based NeuralHermes-2.5-Mistral-7B-AWQ paired with prompt-v1 was selected because it balanced performance, low error, and efficiency (score=4.35, error=0.000, estimated time=5.34).
findings.measure: Quantified qualitative performance on criteria including first questions, unlearned topic question, user termination, system termination, irrelevant answer, preventing question, name recognition, and response to toxicity; plus overall score, error rate, and estimated operation time

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: A family of large open-weight language models from Meta used for text generation and dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper compared LLaMA-2 variants (7B, 13B, 70B) and fine-tuned versions as candidate backbones for an English conversation chatbot, then evaluated their performance under different prompts and training strategies.

findings.finding_summary: LLaMA-2 models showed variable performance across conversational criteria. In the base-model evaluation, Llama-13b had the highest average score among the LLaMA variants (3.63), but Llama-70b often produced long, complex responses; after fine-tuning, Llama-13b remained the strongest LLaMA variant overall (average=3.85), while some criteria improved substantially (for example, Irrelevant Answer increased from 5.0 to 4.827 and Response to Toxicity stayed high at 5.0).
findings.measure: Quantified qualitative performance across conversational criteria and average score

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI system used for text generation, dialogue, and task assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper used GPT-4 to generate synthetic dialogue data, to evaluate other LLMs in the quantitative phase, and compared GPT-4's conversational quality and adaptability against other LLMs for EFL conversation practice.

findings.finding_summary: GPT-4 was used as a strong reference model for evaluation and data generation, and it adapted its language more appropriately than Llama-2 70b in a child-directed conversation test. The paper reports that GPT-4 helped generate approximately 21,000 synthetic dialogue samples and that, in qualitative comparisons, it produced contextually appropriate responses aligned with the design principles.
findings.measure: Qualitative comparison of conversational appropriateness and use in synthetic dataset generation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a design/development study with qualitative expert interviews and model benchmarking rather than a controlled impact study on learners or teachers. The evidence is useful for tool selection and design, but it does not provide causal estimates of educational effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising model-selection outcomes and qualitative benefits for chatbot design, but it does not report learner outcome effect sizes or classroom impact. Evidence of impact is therefore suggestive but not measurable from the study as reported.

paper_profiles.title: Generating Feedback-Ladders for Logical Errors in Programming using Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of generating useful automated feedback for logical errors in student programming assignments using large language models. The authors argue that existing feedback methods often either reveal too much of the solution, fail to account for student context, or provide only a single level of help. To address this, they propose a multi-level "feedback-ladder" that offers progressively more detailed feedback for the same buggy program.

The intervention studied is a GPT-4-based prompting method that generates five feedback levels: a correctness verdict, a failing test case, a high-level explanation of the bug, a location hint, and an edit suggestion. The approach is evaluated on introductory programming problems drawn from the CSEDM dataset, focusing on submissions without syntax errors but with logical mistakes. The feedback is intended to support teachers in choosing an appropriate level of hint for different students, or to gradually increase specificity if a student remains stuck.

The study uses a user study with 10 annotators drawn from students, CS instructors, and AI researchers. They rate generated feedback on relevance and effectiveness for low-, mid-, and high-scoring student submissions across five programming problems. The paper concludes that GPT-4 can generate reasonably relevant lower-level feedback, but quality declines at higher levels, especially for high-scoring submissions where the bugs are subtle. The authors suggest the method could still reduce teacher workload, but note that more personalization and better handling of subtle errors are needed.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT family of large language models used to generate natural-language feedback from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used via the OpenAI API with model='gpt-4' to generate multilevel 'feedback-ladders' for buggy programming submissions.

findings.finding_summary: In a user study with 10 annotators evaluating 15 programming submissions, GPT-4-generated feedback ladders were judged to be highly relevant and effective at lower levels, but quality declined at higher levels. The paper reports that feedback quality was consistently better for low-level feedback than high-level feedback, and that generating good feedback was harder for higher-scoring submissions; no effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported.
findings.measure: Annotator ratings of relevance and effectiveness on a 5-point Likert scale
findings.sample_size: n=10 annotators; 15 programs (5 problems x 3 submissions)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary user study with qualitative/mixed-methods evaluation of generated feedback, not a controlled instructional outcome study or meta-analysis. The paper reports inter-rater agreement and Likert ratings, but no causal effect sizes for learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported impact is mixed: lower-level feedback was rated relatively well, while higher-level feedback and higher-scoring submissions were harder to handle and often ineffective. No quantitative effect size is reported, so the practical impact on learning quality remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Human Experts’ Evaluation of Generative AI for Contextualizing STEAM Education in the Global South
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can improve the cultural responsiveness and pedagogical quality of STEAM lesson planning in Ghana. The central problem is that STEAM curricula in the Global South are often abstract, Western-centric, and poorly connected to learners’ local realities, languages, and cultural practices. The authors focus on lesson planning as a practical point where generative AI might help teachers localize instruction while still meeting curriculum standards.

The intervention evaluated is a customized Generative AI lesson-planning tool, the Culturally Responsive Lesson Planner (CRLP), powered by interactive semi-automated prompting. Four STEAM education experts independently reviewed paired lesson plans: standardized Ghana NaCCA lesson plans and CRLP-generated culturally responsive versions. They rated the plans with a 25-item rubric covering bias awareness, cultural representation, contextual relevance, linguistic responsiveness, and teacher agency, and also wrote qualitative reflections comparing the two lesson types. The content covered Mathematics, Science, Creative Arts and Design, and Computing at the basic and junior high levels in Ghana.

Findings suggest that CRLP-generated lessons were generally stronger than the NaCCA lessons in contextual relevance, teacher agency, and linguistic responsiveness. Experts valued the inclusion of indigenous knowledge, local artifacts, bilingual elements, and community-based examples that made the lessons more engaging and relevant. However, they also identified persistent weaknesses in cultural representation, translation accuracy, and the ability of GenAI to capture Ghana’s cultural pluralism without teacher mediation. The study concludes that GenAI can support culturally responsive STEAM planning, but only as a co-designer guided by human expertise, local knowledge, and careful checking for bias and cultural fit.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI lesson-planning assistant used to produce culturally responsive STEAM lesson plans through interactive prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated a customized Culturally Responsive Lesson Planner (CRLP) powered by interactive semi-automated prompts to generate STEAM lesson plans, which were compared against NaCCA standards-based lesson plans.

findings.finding_summary: Four STEAM education experts (n=4) rated CRLP-generated lesson plans as stronger than NaCCA lesson plans on several culturally responsive dimensions, especially teacher agency (M=3.6) and contextual relevance (M=3.4). The GenAI-generated lessons were described as clearer, more student-centered, more engaging, and better connected to local community knowledge, although cultural representation remained the weakest domain (M=2.25) and translation accuracy was sometimes limited.
findings.measure: Validated 25-item Culturally Responsive Pedagogy Rubric and expert reflective comparisons across lesson plans

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a convergent mixed-methods expert review with a very small purposive sample rather than an experimental impact study. The evidence is useful for comparative judgment but remains qualitative/mixed-methods and limited in generalizability.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports favorable expert ratings for GenAI-generated lesson plans, but no causal effect size on student outcomes or teacher performance is reported. The practical signal is positive, yet the magnitude of impact is unclear because the study measures rubric scores and reflections rather than direct instructional outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Online Preference-based Reinforcement Learning with Self-augmented Feedback from Large Language Model
paper_profiles.venue: Proc. of the 24th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems (AAMAS 2025)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a reinforcement learning problem: how to obtain preference feedback for online preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) when real-time human judgments are unavailable and the usual “scripted teacher” relies on privileged task rewards. The authors identify a specific failure mode of LLM-based feedback called query ambiguity, where large language models struggle to distinguish between poor or similarly suboptimal trajectories early in training.

To address this, the paper proposes RL-SaLLM-F, a framework that uses a large language model in two ways: first, to judge which of two replay-buffer trajectories is better; and second, to generate self-augmented imagined trajectories that better achieve the task goal. A double-check mechanism reverses the order of trajectory pairs to reduce label randomness, and only consistent labels are kept. The method trains a reward model from these LLM-produced labels and imagined trajectory pairs, then uses soft actor-critic for downstream policy learning.

The context is robotic manipulation in the MetaWorld benchmark, with state information converted into text descriptions for the LLM. The paper reports experiments on eight tasks such as button press, drawer open/close, door open/unlock, window open, handle pull, and reach. Across these tasks, RL-SaLLM-F performs comparably to or better than PEBBLE with scripted teacher feedback, while using no privileged rewards or human-in-the-loop feedback. The authors conclude that self-augmented LLM feedback is a practical direction for online PbRL, though label accuracy remains limited and improves with larger models like GPT-4o at substantially higher cost.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used to judge preference between trajectory pairs and to generate self-augmented imagined trajectories for reinforcement learning feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper uses GPT-4o-mini as the main LLM feedback source and compares it with GPT-4o for trajectory preference labeling, double-checking labels, and generating imagined trajectories in online preference-based reinforcement learning.

findings.finding_summary: Using GPT-4o-mini as the LLM feedback source in RL-SaLLM-F enabled online preference labeling and self-augmented trajectory generation without privileged rewards or real-time human feedback. The paper reports that this setup achieved comparable or better task success than the scripted-teacher baseline on MetaWorld tasks, while being lightweight and cost-effective.
findings.measure: Task success rate on MetaWorld robotic manipulation tasks; feedback cost and query time

findings.finding_summary: On the Drawer Open task, scaling from GPT-4o-mini to GPT-4o improved policy performance, trajectory quality, and label accuracy. The paper reports label accuracy of 80.1% for GPT-4o versus 73.9% for GPT-4o-mini, with GPT-4o also showing a higher equal-rate behavior (28.5% vs 0.8%) and better trajectory evaluation, but at much higher cost per query ($0.081 vs $0.004) and longer query time (10.0s vs 3.9s).
findings.measure: Label accuracy, equal rate, average cost per query, average time per query, and policy/trajectory performance on Drawer Open

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary empirical paper with a clear experimental setup, but it is not an education study and does not use an RCT/QED design in the K-12 sense. Evidence is still direct and quantitative, though not aligned to the education evidence hierarchy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported improvements are meaningful within robotic RL, but the paper does not report standardized effect sizes and the outcomes are not directly educational. The practical gains are moderate and context-specific, so impact is unclear for the requested education-facing topic.

paper_profiles.title: PythonPal: Enhancing Online Programming Education through Chatbot-Driven Personalized Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of limited personalized feedback in online programming education, especially in contexts with high student-to-teacher ratios. The authors argue that novice programmers often need immediate, individualized guidance on both conceptual questions and code errors, but existing educational chatbots tend to specialize in only one part of that experience. To respond to this gap, the paper presents PythonPal, a chatbot-driven learning system designed to support Python instruction through conversational support, tutorial delivery, and automated feedback on submitted exercises.

PythonPal combines three modules: a Conversation module that classifies student intents and provides chat-based responses or routes learners to tutorial/exercise resources, a Tutorial module that retrieves video lessons, and an Exercise module that checks syntax, evaluates code against test cases, and generates natural-language feedback. The system was implemented for online Python learning and uses LINE as the user interface. The paper evaluates intent classification models, conversational response models, error-feedback accuracy, and student satisfaction, using metrics such as F1-score, BLEU, METEOR, inference time, accuracy, and survey responses.

The study population appears to be undergraduate students or undergraduate research assistants with backgrounds similar to the intended learners, and the context is online introductory Python programming. Results suggest that PythonPal can classify intents accurately, provide usable conversational support, and generate more informative feedback than raw compiler messages for common coding errors. Student feedback was generally positive, though participants wanted faster responses and improved interaction quality. Overall, the paper concludes that PythonPal is a promising step toward more personalized programming support, but also notes opportunities to improve speed, robustness, and broader educational functionality.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic chatbot/LLM-based educational AI system that can answer queries and generate feedback on student work, without a specific commercial product name.
identified_tools.use_case: PythonPal is presented as a chatbot-driven personalized feedback system for online programming education. The paper evaluates its conversation, tutorial retrieval, and exercise-feedback modules, including intent classification, response generation, and code-error feedback.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that PythonPal's intent classification performed well on 800 student-like queries. Among flat models, DistilBERT achieved the best F1-score of 0.9352, while flat SVM models were around 0.895; hierarchical models were lower, with the best at 0.8555.
findings.measure: Intent classification performance (F1-score) on student queries

findings.finding_summary: For conversational coherence, the paper fine-tuned GODEL, GPT-2, T5, and BlenderBot on 4,084 dialogue pairs from the DailyDialog 'School life' subset. BlenderBot had the highest METEOR score (0.1504), compared with GPT-2 (0.1136), GODEL (0.1056), and T5 (0.1035), indicating the best response quality among the tested models.
findings.measure: Response quality in generated chatbot dialogue (METEOR, BLEU)

findings.finding_summary: For code-error feedback, the Exercise module was evaluated on programming exercises with embedded common errors, using an accuracy-rate metric. The paper states that the system could identify syntax and testcase-related errors and generate clearer explanatory feedback than the original traceback, but it does not report a numeric accuracy value in the provided text.
findings.measure: Accuracy of coding-error detection and feedback generation

findings.finding_summary: The paper also reports inference-time comparisons. Flat intent classifiers were generally faster than hierarchical ones, and GPT-2 had the fastest response generation time among the dialogue models (0.0276 s), while BlenderBot had the best METEOR but slower inference (0.0978 s).
findings.measure: Inference time for intent classification and response generation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical system paper with quantitative experiments, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental study of educational outcomes; it mainly evaluates model performance, response quality, and user satisfaction. The evidence is therefore methodologically useful but not high-certainty causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported performance gains are promising, but the paper does not provide educational effect sizes on learner achievement or teacher practice, and several outcomes are model-metric based rather than learner-outcome based. Impact on learning is therefore plausible but unclear from the reported results.

paper_profiles.title: Automated Feedback in Math Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLMs for Open-Ended Responses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can improve automated scoring and feedback for open-ended mathematics responses. The authors compare three approaches: a fine-tuned open-source LLM called GOAT (based on Mistral), a prior similarity-based method called SBERT-Canberra, and GPT-4 used in a zero-shot prompting setup. The study asks how well these systems predict teacher-assigned scores and how well they generate feedback judged by human teachers.

The data come from an online learning platform using Illustrative Mathematics-style open-response problems. The dataset includes responses from approximately 50 teachers’ classrooms, restricted to language-based questions, and focuses on middle-school math problems. The models were trained and tested on 50 problems with 5,000 total student responses, with 100 additional responses sampled for teacher review of feedback quality. Two teachers with prior teaching experience evaluated generated feedback for accuracy, relevancy, motivation, and preference.

Results show that GOAT outperformed SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 on scoring metrics, but GPT-4 produced feedback that teachers judged to be more accurate, more relevant, less demotivating, and more preferred overall. The authors conclude that task-specific fine-tuning can improve auto-scoring, while a strong general-purpose LLM may still be better for high-quality feedback generation. They also note that teacher-provided feedback in the training data was often vague or inconsistent, which likely limited performance.

identified_tools.name: Mistral
identified_tools.description: An open-source large language model family used for text generation and downstream fine-tuning.
identified_tools.use_case: Fine-tuned (as GOAT) on student open-ended math responses and teacher-provided scores/feedback to generate automated scores and feedback; also compared against SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 Turbo.

findings.finding_summary: On the scoring task, the fine-tuned Mistral-based GOAT model outperformed SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 on all three reported metrics. Reported results were AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, and Kappa=0.422 on the test set (n=1,000 student responses).
findings.measure: Teacher score prediction on open-ended math responses

findings.finding_summary: For feedback generation, GOAT was rated by two teachers as 68% accurate, 88% relevant, 48% motivating, and 5% demotivating, and was selected as the preferred feedback 12% of the time on average. The same qualitative evaluation used 100 sampled test responses (n=100). GPT-4 was preferred more often, but GOAT was judged substantially better than SBERT-Canberra on accuracy and relevance.
findings.measure: Human ratings of feedback accuracy, relevance, motivation, demotivation, and preference

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used for text generation and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied via the GPT-4 Turbo model in zero-shot mode to score student open-ended math responses and generate feedback; compared with GOAT and SBERT-Canberra.

findings.finding_summary: On scoring open-ended math responses, GPT-4 Turbo underperformed the fine-tuned GOAT model and SBERT-Canberra on AUC and Kappa, though its RMSE was intermediate. Reported results were AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.16, and Kappa=0.266 on n=1,000 test responses.
findings.measure: Teacher score prediction on open-ended math responses

findings.finding_summary: For feedback generation, GPT-4 was rated highest by two human evaluators: 86% consensus accuracy, 91% consensus relevance, 52% consensus motivation, 1% consensus demotivation, and 77.5% average preference. The qualitative review used 100 sampled test responses (n=100), and GPT-4 was preferred over GOAT and SBERT-Canberra.
findings.measure: Human ratings of feedback accuracy, relevance, motivation, demotivation, and preference

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single comparative study with a test-train split and small human-rater component, not a randomized trial or meta-analysis. It provides useful empirical evidence, but the methodology and reporting leave some concerns, so yellow is most appropriate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear performance differences, but no standardized educational effect sizes are provided, and the outcomes are technical model metrics rather than classroom learning gains. The practical impact is promising but currently modest and uncertain for teacher practice.

paper_profiles.title: MathEDU: Feedback Generation on Problem-Solving Processes for Mathematical Learning Support
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether generative AI systems can reliably assess students’ mathematical problem-solving processes and generate useful feedback, rather than only producing a correct final answer. The authors focus on three linked tasks: classifying whether a student’s answer is correct, identifying the specific step where an error occurs, and generating teacher-like feedback that explains the mistake and suggests how to improve.

To study these questions, the authors construct MathEDU, a dataset extending MathQA with 4,048 real student solutions and teacher-written annotations. Six university students solved a balanced sample of GRE-level math word problems drawn from six MathQA categories, and three mathematics education experts annotated errors, error categories, and feedback. The study then evaluates several LLMs, including Llama3 8B, Llama3 70B, GPT-3.5, o1-mini, and fine-tuned Llama3 8B variants using LoRA under single-task, multi-task, and end-to-end setups, with and without the original rationales.

Results show that larger models and fine-tuned models can do reasonably well on answer correctness classification, especially when rationales are available, but identifying exact error steps is substantially harder. Feedback generation is the most difficult task: model outputs are often verbose, imprecise, or misaligned with teacher feedback, and sometimes they misdiagnose correct work or provide judgmental wording. The authors conclude that current generative AI systems still lack the pedagogy-aware reliability needed for trustworthy educational feedback, and that future systems need better understanding of student reasoning, more precise diagnosis, and more supportive language.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta's LLaMA family of large language models used for grading, error identification, and feedback generation in mathematical problem-solving tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as few-shot prompting baselines and as the base model for LoRA fine-tuning (Llama3 8B and Llama3 70B) to classify answer correctness, identify erroneous steps, and generate teacher-like feedback for student math solutions.

findings.finding_summary: Llama3 models varied by size and input rationale. For answer correctness classification, Llama3 70B achieved 88.23% F-score without rationale and 86.65% with rationale, while Llama3 8B improved from 66.96% to 77.04% when rationale was added. Fine-tuned end-to-end models reached 92.09%-94.38% F-score depending on rationale, with the best single-task model reaching 95.07% F-score.
findings.measure: F-score for answer correctness classification
findings.sample_size: n=603 test examples (answer correctness classification test set)

findings.finding_summary: For error identification, Llama3 8B achieved 28.40% exact match (EM) without rationale and 11.73% with rationale; Llama3 70B achieved 32.10% EM without rationale and 29.63% with rationale. Human-reviewed discussion in the paper indicates rationale sometimes reduced performance because of format mismatch, and fine-tuned end-to-end models with rationale performed better than baseline Llama3 8B.
findings.measure: Exact match and Hausdorff distance for error-span identification
findings.sample_size: n=603 test examples (overall), with error-identification evaluated on incorrect solutions

findings.finding_summary: In feedback generation, Llama3 8B obtained ROUGE-L 0.2391 without rationale and 0.1632 with rationale, BERTScore 0.7654 without rationale and 0.5515 with rationale, and an LLM rating of 2.68 without rationale and 2.14 with rationale. Human evaluation found all models remained below the ideal score of 3, with Llama3 70B sometimes producing judgmental phrasing that could discourage students.
findings.measure: ROUGE-L, BERTScore, GPT-4-based LLM rating, and human ratings of feedback quality
findings.sample_size: n=603 test examples; human evaluation on representative outputs

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language models used here for correctness classification, feedback generation, and as an automated evaluator of generated feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as GPT-3.5 on grading and feedback tasks; additionally GPT-4 was used as the LLM judge for automatic feedback evaluation, and GPT-4o was used in the automated characterization of feedback errors.

findings.finding_summary: GPT-3.5 underperformed the LLaMA models on correctness classification, with F-score 33.83% without rationale and 49.92% with rationale. The paper notes GPT-3.5 often judged answers as incorrect if intermediate steps were omitted, even when final answers were right.
findings.measure: F-score for answer correctness classification

findings.finding_summary: For error identification, GPT-3.5 achieved 30.25% EM without rationale and 27.78% with rationale, with Hausdorff distance 63.72 and 60.80, respectively. For feedback generation, GPT-3.5 obtained ROUGE-L 0.2695 without rationale and 0.2597 with rationale, BERTScore 0.8395 and 0.8366, and LLM ratings of 3.70 and 3.63.
findings.measure: Exact match/Hausdorff distance for error identification; ROUGE-L, BERTScore, and GPT-4-based LLM rating for feedback generation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmark study with annotated data and comparative model evaluation, but it is not a randomized trial or meta-analysis. The evidence is useful yet limited by single-dataset, single-domain design and model-comparison methodology.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial performance differences across models and tasks, but it does not provide causal effect sizes or intervention impacts on learners or teachers. Results are informative about model capability and risk, but the educational impact remains indirect and task-specific.

paper_profiles.title: Dual Active Learning for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a problem in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF): how to efficiently learn a reward model and resulting policy when human feedback is costly, teachers differ in expertise, and the action space for language model completions is very large. The authors argue that existing RLHF approaches often assume homogeneous teachers or select either conversations or teachers, but not both, which can lead to suboptimal reward estimation and policy learning.

The proposed approach is a dual active learning algorithm that simultaneously selects the most informative conversations (prompt-completion pairs) and the most informative teachers. It formalizes the selection problem as a D-optimal design problem and extends standard preference models to allow teacher rationality to depend on context category. The learned reward model is then used to derive a pessimistic offline RL policy that is robust to distribution shift between collected data and the target policy.

The paper is primarily theoretical and simulation-based, but it also includes experiments on public LLM preference datasets (Anthropic and UltraFeedback) using synthetic teachers derived from other LLMs. The authors report that their method improves reward estimation accuracy and policy performance relative to conversation-only selection, teacher-only selection, active preference optimization, and random sampling. They conclude that jointly selecting conversations and teachers can substantially improve RLHF data efficiency and that pessimistic policy learning further reduces suboptimality risk.

identified_tools.name: Gemma
identified_tools.description: A Google open-weight large language model used as the pretrained model / feature extractor in the paper's LLM experiments.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the pretrained model (Gemma-7b-it) to derive the feature map ϕ by removing the last layer, and as the base model for reward estimation and policy evaluation on the Anthropic and UltraFeedback datasets.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports reward accuracy results for policies built on Gemma-based features, with the proposed method outperforming benchmark policies. On Anthropic and UltraFeedback, the proposed approach achieved higher reward accuracy across evaluated sample budgets and batch sizes, but the paper does not isolate Gemma itself as a treatment effect.
findings.measure: reward accuracy
findings.sample_size: n=40000 selected samples (32000 training / 8000 test split after a 4:1 ratio)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is not an experimental study of an educational AI tool; it is a machine learning methods paper about RLHF with simulations and LLM benchmarks. The paper reports engineering performance metrics rather than education outcomes, so it does not meet evidence standards for the requested comparative teaching/planning topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No teacher planning quality, instructional practice, or educational risk outcome is evaluated. The reported gains are on reward accuracy in LLM alignment, which is not directly interpretable as educational impact.

paper_profiles.title: FEAT: A Preference Feedback Dataset through a Cost-Effective Auto-Generation and Labeling Framework for English AI Tutoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of constructing high-quality teacher feedback data for English tutoring systems, where manual generation and ranking of feedback is expensive and time-consuming. The authors argue that scalable feedback datasets are needed to support reward-based or ranking-based learning for AI tutoring models that can provide more human-friendly guidance.

To address this, the paper proposes FEAT, a framework that uses large language models to generate teacher feedback and create preference datasets under different supervision regimes. The study constructs three datasets: DIRECT-Manual (human plus LLM generation with human rankings), DIRECT-Generated (LLM-generated and LLM-annotated preferences), and DIRECT-Augmented (a hybrid combining mostly generated data with a small amount of manual data). The framework also applies five feedback criteria—Correct, Revealing, Guidance, Diagnostic, and Encouragement—intended to make the feedback educationally appropriate.

The empirical context is English tutoring, with tutoring scenarios derived from the MCTest reading comprehension dataset, which is described as serving students in grades 1–4. The paper evaluates several ranking approaches, including binary classification, reward modeling, DPO, RankNet, and an ensemble, using open-source LLMs of 1B and 3B scale. The work is not a classroom intervention; it is a dataset and model-ranking study focused on feedback generation and preference learning.

The main conclusion is that LLM-generated preference data can perform competitively with human-annotated data, and that mixing a small amount of human-annotated data into generated data (about 5–10%) can outperform training on the fully human-annotated dataset alone. The authors conclude that FEAT can reduce human annotation cost while maintaining or improving ranking performance, and they suggest extending the framework to broader educational contexts.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language models used for generating and ranking teacher feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as feedback-generation sources in the DIRECT-Manual and DIRECT-Generated datasets (e.g., GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o) and compared against human and other model-generated feedback for English tutoring.

findings.finding_summary: In the DIRECT-Manual dataset, GPT-4 feedback was ranked highest by humans among five candidate feedback sources (GPT-4 > Human > GPT-3.5 > PrepTutor > DIRECT) for an English tutoring example. In the ranking-model evaluation, LLM-generated feedback from GPT-family models contributed to preference data where models trained on DG or DA performed competitively with human-annotated DM, but the paper does not report separate quantitative effect sizes for ChatGPT-specific outputs beyond ranking examples and dataset construction.
findings.measure: Human-annotated feedback ranking; pairwise preference ranking model performance

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic large language models used for generating and annotating educational feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to automatically generate teacher feedback for the DIRECT-Generated dataset and as one of the LLMs contributing to the feedback pool compared in examples and dataset construction.

findings.finding_summary: Claude-generated feedback was included among LLM-generated teacher feedback candidates and was used in constructing the DIRECT-Generated dataset. The paper reports that adding a small amount of human-annotated DM data to LLM-generated DG improved ranking performance overall, but it does not isolate Claude-specific effects.
findings.measure: Preference data construction; ranking-model performance on DG/DA datasets

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta LLaMA-family large language models used for generating teacher feedback and training ranking models.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of the feedback generation models for DIRECT-Generated (Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct) and as the ranking-model backbone family (Llama-1B, Llama-3B, and instruct variants) for evaluating preference datasets.

findings.finding_summary: In the DG�DM comparison, LLaMA-based ranking models trained on automatically generated DG achieved competitive performance relative to human-annotated DM baselines. The paper reports that for Llama-3B-IT, binary classifier, DPO, and ensemble approaches reached or exceeded the DM�DM baseline with only 5% human-annotated DM added to DG, and several approaches surpassed the baseline in the 5�10% range.
findings.measure: Rank-biased overlap (RBO) for pairwise ranking agreement

findings.finding_summary: When varying the proportion of human-annotated DM in DA, performance generally improved as more DM was added, and Llama-3B surpassed the DM�DM baseline in all methods with at most 10�25% DM data. This supports the paper�s conclusion that high performance can be achieved with minimal human annotation cost.
findings.measure: RBO across DA�DM training ratios

identified_tools.name: Qwen
identified_tools.description: Alibaba Qwen-family large language models used for ranking teacher feedback and preference learning.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a ranking-model backbone (Qwen-3B-IT) to evaluate the quality of preference datasets and the effect of human-annotation ratios in DA.

findings.finding_summary: Qwen-3B-IT showed competitive ranking performance in the DM�DM and DG�DM settings, with DG�DM sometimes approaching DM�DM performance across ranking methods. The paper reports that Qwen-3B-IT surpassed DM�DM primarily when the DA mix contained about 50�75% or 75�100% human-annotated DM, indicating stronger gains with more human data than LLaMA-based counterparts.
findings.measure: Rank-biased overlap (RBO) for pairwise ranking agreement

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / LLM-based systems used to generate, annotate, and rank teacher feedback for tutoring.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper broadly studies an LLM-based framework (FEAT) for automatically generating teacher feedback preference datasets for English AI tutoring and comparing LLM-generated versus human-annotated feedback quality.

findings.finding_summary: Across ranking-model experiments, feedback generated by LLMs produced rankings that were highly comparable to human annotator rankings. The authors report that models trained on DG performed competitively with DM-based models, and adding only 5�10% human-annotated DM to DG yielded superior performance to using the full DM dataset alone.
findings.measure: Rank-biased overlap (RBO) of pairwise feedback rankings

findings.finding_summary: Increasing feedback criteria from two (Correct, Revealing) to five consistently improved ranking-model performance in several settings. The paper interprets this as evidence that richer feedback information improves generalization in AI-generated tutoring feedback datasets.
findings.measure: RBO comparing 2-criteria vs 5-criteria feedback generation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical NLP/education systems paper, but it is not a student learning intervention study and does not provide randomized evidence on learner outcomes. The strongest evidence concerns ranking-model performance and dataset construction quality rather than causal educational impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are about data efficiency and ranking agreement, not direct educational achievement or instructional practice outcomes. Any impact is promising but indirect and not quantified with standard educational effect sizes.

paper_profiles.title: Effects of generative artificial intelligence on instructional design outcomes and the mediating role of pre-service teachers' prior knowledge of different types of instructional design tasks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the emerging question of how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support teachers in instructional design, particularly lesson planning, and whether teachers’ prior knowledge about instructional design tasks changes the way they benefit from GenAI. The authors frame the study around concerns that default chatbots such as ChatGPT may be useful for generating ideas and structures, but may also be insufficiently systematic and require critical user judgment. They also note that little research had examined the quality of GenAI-produced instructional design outcomes or the role of prior instructional design expertise.

The paper describes an experimental research proposal rather than completed results. It plans to compare four conditions: using GenAI directly, using a GPT bot pre-trained as a co-instructional designer, using an automated GPT-based generator, and a no-GenAI control group. Participants are pre-service teachers from Flemish university colleges and universities, and they will design a lesson blueprint and lesson plan for a two-hour history lesson. The study also plans to replicate the task across two instructional design contexts: lesson personalization and 4C/ID-based lesson design.

The proposed evaluation combines expert comparative judgment of the produced lesson designs with qualitative analysis of chatbot interactions. The study is grounded in prior knowledge theory, instructional design models, and chatbot design principles. Because the paper is a proposal/pilot-oriented description of a future study, it does not report empirical findings; instead, it argues that the research is needed to determine whether GenAI can serve as a useful co-design partner for teachers and under what conditions it improves instructional design quality.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based generative AI chatbot used for conversational text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by pre-service teachers to design a lesson blueprint and lesson plan under one experimental condition; also compared against a GPT bot pre-trained as a co-instructional designer and an automated GenAI condition.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a research proposal / experimental design paper and does not report results from a completed empirical study. It outlines planned conditions, measures, and analysis, but provides no outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No empirical effects are reported yet, so there is no demonstrated impact on instructional design quality or teacher practice in this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI as a partner for teachers in building personalised learning paths for students with ease in Tanzania
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can help secondary school teachers in Tanzania design personalised learning paths more efficiently and effectively. The motivating problem is that large class sizes, limited teaching resources, and uneven access to training make it difficult for teachers to differentiate instruction, provide timely feedback, and manage workload while still meeting diverse learner needs.

The study evaluated generative AI tools, especially ChatGPT and Grok, in support of lesson planning, assessment creation, adaptive content delivery, and student feedback. The sample included 120 secondary school teachers from public schools in Dar es Salaam and Dodoma, representing both urban and rural contexts. The paper combined surveys, classroom/perception data, and student outcome measures; it reported pre/post comparisons of engagement, completion, test scores, and attendance, along with teacher perceptions of usability and workload reduction.

Findings suggest that generative AI was perceived as easy to use, helpful for reducing workload, and effective for tailoring instruction to student needs. The study also reports improved student engagement and academic performance after AI integration. However, it highlights that insufficient training and weak infrastructure, especially in rural areas, limit adoption. The paper concludes that generative AI can function as a supportive partner for teachers, but only if paired with professional development and better digital infrastructure.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM system used to generate text and support instructional tasks such as lesson planning, quizzes, and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used alongside Grok and other generative AI tools to help secondary school teachers in Tanzania create personalised learning paths, including lesson plans, quizzes, student feedback, and adaptive content.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-supported approaches improved adaptability to individual learning needs (mean 4.5 vs 2.5 under traditional methods) and timely feedback and assessment (mean 4.6 vs 2.6). The paper also reports improved student engagement (2.8 to 4.3) and mean test scores (61% to 75%) after generative AI integration, but these results are presented across the AI tools rather than isolated for ChatGPT alone.
findings.measure: Teacher-rated adaptability and feedback; student engagement; mean test scores

identified_tools.name: Grok
identified_tools.description: xAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM system designed for conversational assistance and reasoning-based text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used with ChatGPT by secondary school teachers in Tanzania for lesson planning, assessments, and adaptive content delivery to create personalised learning paths.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers using generative AI reported higher ease of use (M=4.3 vs 3.1 for non-experienced teachers) and greater helpfulness in reducing workload (M=4.1 vs 2.9). The paper attributes these advantages to generative AI use overall, not to Grok separately, so no tool-specific effect size is reported.
findings.measure: Ease of use; workload reduction; content adaptation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods, single-study evaluation with surveys, pre/post comparisons, and t-tests rather than a randomized controlled design. It provides empirical evidence, but the report does not isolate tool-specific causal effects and relies heavily on teacher perceptions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are substantial at the combined generative-AI level, including student engagement increasing from 2.8 to 4.3 and test scores from 61% to 75%. However, because the paper does not provide tool-specific effect sizes and blends multiple AI tools, the impact is best treated as modest-to-strong but not precisely attributable to one product.

paper_profiles.title: Are They Ready to Teach? Generative AI as a Means to Uncover Pre-Service Science Teachers’ PCK and Enhance Their Preparation Program
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of assessing and developing pre-service science teachers’ pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) during teacher preparation. The authors argue that generative AI (GenAI) can be used not only as a planning aid but also as a diagnostic tool that reveals what prospective teachers know about content, pedagogy, and the integration of both while they work through lesson planning tasks.

The proposed approach centers on recording pre-service teachers’ conversations with a GenAI system during lesson design, then having trained GenAI evaluate the dialogue for evidence of content knowledge, pedagogical knowledge, and PCK. The paper is conceptual rather than empirical: it illustrates the idea through example ChatGPT dialogues in chemistry, including one with an experienced educator and one with a pre-service teacher. These examples show how prompts and follow-up questions can expose the teacher’s level of understanding, including gaps related to classroom management, subject-specific teaching strategies, and lesson design.

The intended population is pre-service science teachers in initial teacher education, with examples grounded in chemistry education. The broader context is teacher preparation programs that aim to personalize instruction, support self-regulated learning, and strengthen future teachers’ ability to use GenAI responsibly and effectively. The authors conclude that GenAI dialogue analysis could help personalize teacher education and support formative assessment of PCK, but they caution that AI evaluations can be overly optimistic and should be checked by human educators and validated against established PCK assessment methods.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI conversational assistant / large language model chatbot used for interactive dialogue, content generation, and feedback/evaluation tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a conceptual paper to analyze pre-service science teachers’ lesson-planning dialogues as a way to reveal and evaluate PCK, and illustrated with example chats about molecular vs. ionic materials.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper with illustrative examples, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool. No study design, sample, or outcome data are reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that ChatGPT could support lesson planning, PCK diagnosis, and personalization, but it does not provide empirical effect estimates. Impact is therefore speculative rather than measured.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in foreign language lesson plan creation: Trends, variability, and historical biases
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, performs when asked to generate foreign language lesson plans. The authors focus on a practical question for teacher preparation and instructional design: whether increasing prompt specificity improves the quality, consistency, and pedagogical alignment of AI-generated lesson plans, and whether the model exhibits weaknesses or biases in its outputs.

The intervention/approach studied was zero-shot prompting of ChatGPT 4.0 with five prompts of increasing specificity. The prompts were designed around a 45-minute high school novice-level Spanish lesson and progressively added ACTFL proficiency guidance, a lesson-plan template, world-readiness standards, and finally a checklist of required components. Each prompt was entered 10 times in separate chats, producing 50 lesson plans that were scored against a 25-item rubric based on best practices and edTPA-aligned criteria. The study was conducted in the context of pre-service foreign language teacher training at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte, with outputs evaluated as lesson-planning artifacts rather than by human participants.

The main findings were that ChatGPT could often generate reasonably aligned lesson plans, but greater prompt specificity did not reliably produce better outputs. Adding a detailed rubric checklist produced the strongest average results, while adding a lesson-plan template sometimes reduced quality. The authors also found substantial variability across repeated outputs from the same prompt, indicating that ChatGPT is not deterministic in this task. In addition, some outputs reflected outdated pedagogical patterns, such as audio-lingual-style repetition and limited attention to culture, suggesting that generative AI may reproduce historically biased or research-rebuked teaching practices. The paper concludes that teachers can use such tools to streamline planning, but only with careful human review and AI literacy focused on critical evaluation and revision.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model used to generate and evaluate text outputs from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used via ChatGPT Version 4.0 to generate foreign language lesson plans from five zero-shot prompts of increasing specificity; outputs were scored against an edTPA-aligned rubric to examine prompt specificity, output variability, and pedagogical weaknesses.

findings.finding_summary: Across 50 ChatGPT-generated lesson plans (10 per prompt), increasing prompt specificity produced only a marginal overall difference in scores (p = 0.0442, F = 2.668, DF = 4), and pairwise tests were not significant after correction (p > 0.12). Mean scores did not increase linearly with specificity; P.3 and P.4 were lower than P.2, while P.5 had the highest mean score (21.6/25).
findings.measure: Lesson plan rubric score / presence of 25 criteria; word count

findings.finding_summary: Outputs from identical prompts showed substantial non-determinism. For example, P.1 scores ranged from 23/25 to 16/25, and P.5 scores ranged from 25/25 to 20/25; the authors state that outputs generated from identical prompts varied by at least five elements.
findings.measure: Within-prompt variability in rubric scores and Jaccard distance between outputs

findings.finding_summary: The paper identified several strengths and weaknesses in lesson-plan components. Meaningful context, teacher input aligned with objectives, and level-appropriate activities appeared in all outputs, but cultural connections and ACTFL standards in teacher input were largely restricted to P.5, while some rubric elements were present in only about 50% of outputs. The authors also report that many generated plans reflected outdated pedagogical practices such as audio-lingual, script-based instruction.
findings.measure: Presence/absence of 25 rubric categories across generated lesson plans

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical single-study analysis of ChatGPT outputs, but it is not an intervention trial and does not provide causal evidence about student outcomes. The methodology is systematic and transparent, yet the evidence is limited to one tool, one content area, and rubric-based output scoring.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports meaningful differences in output quality and substantial variability, but no standardized effect sizes are provided and the results are not directly tied to measured educational outcomes for learners or teachers. Overall impact is therefore suggestive but unclear in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT-Assisted Lesson Planning for Children’s STEAM Arts Education: An Experimental Study on Benefits, Challenges, Methods, and a Prompt Framework
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can improve lesson planning quality for children’s STEAM arts education. The authors focus on a practical problem faced by art teachers: lesson planning is time-consuming, resource-intensive, and often constrained by difficulty finding high-quality, age-appropriate, and interdisciplinary materials. The study asks what benefits and challenges arise when teachers use ChatGPT for lesson planning, how teachers can use it effectively, and what prompting approach produces better lesson plan content.

The intervention studied is ChatGPT-assisted lesson planning, compared against traditional teacher-generated planning. Teachers first created lesson plans in their usual way and then produced AI-assisted plans using GPT-4o and a structured prompt framework. The lesson theme centered on color art for primary-age children (approximately 6–12 years old), with a focus on STEAM arts instruction. A pre-study gathered teacher perceptions, then 13 art teachers created plans in Experiment 1, and 6 university professors in Experiment 2 evaluated the resulting lesson plans using a rubric adapted from the 5E model.

The study found that ChatGPT improved lesson planning efficiency and the quality of lesson plans, especially in content development, interdisciplinary integration, and resource generation. Professors scored ChatGPT-assisted plans higher than traditional plans overall, and teachers reported positive experiences and willingness to continue using the tool. At the same time, the paper identifies important limitations of ChatGPT, including weak personalization, occasional impracticality for everyday classroom use, and safety/appropriateness issues in generated content. The authors conclude that ChatGPT is best understood as a support tool for teacher-AI collaboration rather than a replacement for teachers, and they propose a prompt framework to improve future use in arts lesson planning.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot based on GPT-family large language models, used for text generation, iteration, and assistance with content creation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by teachers to collaboratively generate and refine lesson plans for children's STEAM arts education, with GPT-4o used as the specific model/account in the experiment and a prompt framework provided to guide prompting.

findings.finding_summary: In the experimental comparison of 25 lesson plans (12 traditional, 13 ChatGPT-assisted), professors rated ChatGPT-assisted lesson plans higher than traditional plans. The paper reports average total scores of 21.0 for ChatGPT-assisted plans versus 17.0 for traditional plans.
findings.measure: Professor-rated lesson plan quality score

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that ChatGPT improved lesson planning efficiency, including faster topic selection, faster generation of instructional content, and reduced planning time. Reported average scores were 3.7 for topic selection speed, 3.8 for rapid generation of high-quality instructional content, and 4.2 for reduced lesson planning time.
findings.measure: Teacher survey on lesson planning efficiency

findings.finding_summary: Teachers generally agreed that ChatGPT improved lesson planning quality. The sub-items 'The content generated by ChatGPT is accurate' and 'The lesson plan generated by ChatGPT meets my requirements' received average scores of 4.0 and 3.9, respectively.
findings.measure: Teacher survey on lesson planning content quality and fit to requirements

findings.finding_summary: For interdisciplinary integration, 61% of respondents rated ChatGPT at 4 or above, indicating that it supported cross-disciplinary lesson planning. The paper describes this as evidence of robust support for multidisciplinary integration in STEAM lesson design.
findings.measure: Teacher survey on interdisciplinary integration

findings.finding_summary: Teachers were neutral about ChatGPT's role in fostering innovation. The paper states that ChatGPT was more useful as a source of inspiration than as a generator of entirely novel content, and that true innovation still depended on human observation and creativity.
findings.measure: Teacher survey on innovation

findings.finding_summary: Overall satisfaction with ChatGPT for lesson planning was positive, with an average satisfaction score of 3.9 and a future-use score of 4.1 among 13 teachers. The authors interpret this as indicating strong willingness to continue using the tool for lesson planning.
findings.measure: Teacher satisfaction and intention for future use

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods experimental study with a small convenience sample (13 teachers, 6 professors). It includes a comparative evaluation of lesson plans, but the evidence is not a randomized controlled trial and effect sizes/confidence intervals are not reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports a meaningful improvement in professor-rated lesson plan quality (21.0 vs 17.0) and positive efficiency ratings, suggesting practical benefit. However, the magnitude is not quantified with an effect size and the study is small and context-specific, so overall impact remains somewhat unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Pedagogical Tool in Lesson Planning: Implications for Self-Confidence and Professional Development of Physical Education Student Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether artificial intelligence can support lesson planning for physical education student teachers and whether that support is associated with stronger self-confidence and professional development. The paper is motivated by the idea that lesson planning is a demanding part of teacher preparation, especially during internship periods when student teachers must translate theory into practice while managing organization, decision-making, and instructional uncertainty.

The intervention/approach studied is AI-assisted lesson planning, framed as a pedagogical scaffold rather than a replacement for professional judgment. The authors used a mixed-methods design combining a questionnaire with open-ended responses, focusing on perceptions of AI use for planning efficiency, organization of content, pedagogical differentiation, time management, and teaching-method diversification, as well as confidence, stress, competence, and professional growth.
