The sample consisted of 100 physical education student teachers at the Higher Institute of Sport and Physical Education in Tunis, Tunisia, all participating in supervised internship teaching.

Findings were generally positive: participants reported that AI helped them plan more efficiently, organize content, and feel more confident, with significant correlations between AI-supported planning and several confidence/professional-development measures. The strongest associations were observed for organization of educational content, pedagogical decision-making, and perceived professional development. At the same time, the study notes that AI did not eliminate stress entirely and that digital competence, ethical use, and pedagogical guidance remain important constraints. Overall, the paper concludes that AI can enhance planning quality and confidence in teacher preparation when implemented ethically and with adequate support.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI/LLM tool used to support lesson planning by generating ideas, structured guidance, and feedback, without a specific commercial product named in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by physical education student teachers during internship lesson planning to improve lesson organization, time management, instructional differentiation, and perceived professional confidence.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods sample of physical education student teachers (n=100), AI-supported lesson planning was associated with better perceived planning quality, efficiency, and organization. Participants reported that AI reduced lesson-preparation time, improved diversification of teaching methods, and was positively related to confidence in pedagogical decision-making and professional development.
findings.measure: Questionnaire ratings on AI use in lesson planning and perceived planning quality/efficiency

findings.finding_summary: AI use was positively associated with self-confidence outcomes. Significant correlations were reported between AI-supported lesson planning and confidence in pedagogical decisions (r=.301, p=.002), confidence using AI tools (r=.380, p<.001), and professional development (e.g., r=.457 for educational content organization with professional development), although stress reduction was weaker and not always significant.
findings.measure: Questionnaire ratings on teacher self-confidence, stress, and professional development

findings.finding_summary: Participants generally agreed that AI improved planning efficiency and reduced the time needed to prepare lessons. For example, 73% agreed or strongly agreed that AI reduces planning time, and 63% agreed that it helps them plan more efficiently. Correlations also showed that efficient planning using AI was significantly related to higher confidence and professional development (e.g., r=.415, p<.001 for professional development).
findings.measure: Likert-scale items on time management and planning efficiency

findings.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-supported lesson planning can strengthen professional identity formation during teacher training, but implementation requires ethical safeguards and guided use. It also notes variability in experiences due to digital competence and cautions that AI should support, not replace, human judgment.
findings.measure: Qualitative thematic analysis of open-ended responses and discussion of ethical use

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods correlational study with qualitative themes, not an experimental design. It provides useful empirical evidence but cannot establish causal effects of AI on planning quality or instructional practice.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported associations are mostly modest-to-moderate, with several correlations at or above r=.30 and some as high as r=.554. The strongest effects suggest meaningful practical relevance for planning quality and self-confidence, though stress reduction is weaker and the tool is not specifically named.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an analytical AI feedback platform can improve lesson planning quality in vocational teacher education, and whether using AI feedback influences related meta-dimensions such as AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competence, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and motivation. The authors argue that university instructors often cannot provide frequent, detailed, individualized feedback on complex lesson plans, creating a need for scalable alternatives.

The intervention used EDDA, an analytical AI platform that classifies uploaded lesson plans and materials and returns individualized expert feedback on didactic criteria and planning dimensions. Rather than generating free-form text like generative AI, EDDA uses an unsupervised machine-learning approach with a BERT-based model trained on coded lesson plans and textbook tasks. The experimental group received AI feedback throughout a semester and could additionally consult human instructors when needed; the control group received human feedback only.

The study involved 103 master’s students in business education in Germany, working on lesson plans in small groups across a semester. The planning tasks focused on vocational business education and included sustainability, process orientation, problem orientation, action orientation, individualization, and digitalization. Data were collected from 2023 to 2025 across two university course cycles, with lesson plans rated through content analysis and questionnaires administered for the meta-dimensions.

The main findings are that AI feedback can match or outperform human feedback on some lesson-plan dimensions, especially certain sustainability-related categories, social competences for sustainable development, reflexivity, action-related aspects, and some planning/technology dimensions. However, simply using the AI platform did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, or motivation. The authors conclude that analytical AI can effectively supplement traditional feedback, but it should be embedded in a broader, human-centered pedagogical framework. They also note that EDDA tended to underestimate planning performance in some areas because of imbalanced training data, which may have demotivating effects.

identified_tools.name: EDDA
identified_tools.description: An analytical AI platform for lesson planning that classifies uploaded lesson plans/materials into predefined didactic categories and returns individualized expert-level text and visual feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the experimental feedback medium in a longitudinal intervention with vocational teacher education students; it analyzed lesson plans throughout a semester and provided feedback that was compared with human feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In a longitudinal intervention with N=103 student teachers (experimental n=55; control n=48), the EDDA group received higher ratings on several lesson-planning dimensions than the human-feedback control group. The paper reports significant positive effects for SDG 15 (life on land), social competences for sustainable development, and reflexivity, and indicates that AI feedback could match or surpass human feedback on some planning aspects such as lesson structure, learner engagement, action orientation, relatedness, and certain content-related sustainability dimensions.
findings.measure: Content analysis ratings of lesson plans across planning dimensions and sustainability-related categories

findings.finding_summary: The study reports that the analytical AI platform did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, motivation, or related meta-dimensions simply through use. The authors note that EDDA tended to underestimate planning performance because of unbalanced training data, which could potentially have demotivating effects and mask competence development for users.
findings.measure: Self-reported AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competences, self-efficacy, and motivation; plus observed platform calibration/underestimation note

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal intervention with a comparison group, but it is not a randomized trial and several measures rely on self-report or model-based ratings. The design is stronger than a simple observational study, yet there are notable concerns about assignment, sample size, and some measurement limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports some positive effects on lesson-plan quality and selected sustainability-related dimensions, but the strongest effects are described qualitatively or with small/significance-only effects rather than robust effect sizes. Overall impact appears modest to moderate rather than large.

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT as a Lesson Planning Assistant with Preservice Secondary Mathematics Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study examines how preservice secondary mathematics teachers used ChatGPT as a lesson-planning assistant during a methods course microteaching assignment. The authors focus on two related questions: how PSTs reacted to ChatGPT’s mathematical solutions and what they found useful or not useful when using ChatGPT to plan a mini-lesson.

Participants first solved their assigned mathematics task independently, then prompted ChatGPT to solve the same task and to generate aims/objectives for a lesson based on that task. They reflected on the chatbot’s output, revised their plans, and continued using ChatGPT informally while developing their mini-lessons. The study took place in two sections of a secondary mathematics methods course at a public urban university in the northeastern United States, with 22 PSTs total (mostly undergraduates, plus graduate career changers).

Findings show that ChatGPT was often inaccurate on mathematical tasks, especially when the problems required careful interpretation or domain-specific reasoning. PSTs were usually able to judge pedagogical output as repetitive or teacher-centered, but they frequently failed to recognize mathematical errors and sometimes treated incorrect answers as merely alternative approaches. For planning, ChatGPT was most useful as a starting point for ideas, objectives, misconceptions, and assessment suggestions, but PSTs generally did not adopt its output unchanged. The authors conclude that teacher preparation should emphasize critical reflection and AI literacy, especially a framework for evaluating mathematical correctness and pedagogical quality when using generative AI in lesson planning.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model assistant used for text generation, question answering, and planning support.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by preservice secondary mathematics teachers as a lesson-planning assistant and to solve the same mathematics tasks the PSTs were assigned during microteaching planning.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative study with n=22 PSTs (19 included in the math-output analysis), ChatGPT's mathematical responses were correct in 6 of 19 coded instances. PSTs were generally accurate in judging pedagogical output as teacher-centered and repetitive, but were often inaccurate when judging incorrect mathematical output, frequently treating wrong solutions as merely a 'different approach.'
findings.measure: Correctness of ChatGPT mathematical solutions; PST accuracy in evaluating ChatGPT output; reflective judgments about pedagogical usefulness

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative study using deductive coding of PST reflections and ChatGPT outputs rather than an experimental design. It provides useful descriptive evidence, but causal claims about effects on planning quality or instruction are not supported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests mixed practical value: ChatGPT sometimes supported idea generation and planning, but also produced incorrect mathematics and teacher-centered lesson ideas. No effect size is reported, so impact appears modest and uncertain.

paper_profiles.title: Speculative Futures on ChatGPT and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Collective Reflection from the Educational Landscape
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper explores the promises and pitfalls of ChatGPT and related generative AI tools in education through a speculative methodology rather than empirical testing. The authors use collective writing and fictional storytelling to imagine positive and negative future scenarios, aiming to provoke critical reflection on how AI might reshape educational practices, roles, and values.

The paper does not evaluate a specific intervention or measure learning outcomes. Instead, it assembles narratives from a globally diverse group of education scholars, including stories about students, teachers, and researchers in future AI-rich contexts. These scenarios span school, university, and professional learning settings and consider uses such as personalized tutoring, automated feedback, language support, translation, collaborative learning, and AI-mediated academic communication.

The main conclusions are that generative AI may offer meaningful educational affordances, but its adoption raises serious concerns about bias, privacy, ethics, inequity, dependence, loss of creativity, academic integrity, and possible dehumanization of education. The authors argue that education should remain human-centered, that AI literacy and new assessment approaches are needed, and that decisions about AI use should be guided by care, intention, and critical awareness rather than blind adoption.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot and text generation system based on GPT models, used for dialogue, content creation, and assistance across tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses ChatGPT as the focal generative AI tool in speculative educational futures and includes several fictional narratives showing how it might be used by teachers and students for lesson planning, feedback, tutoring, translation, and communication.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI/chatbot systems more broadly, including conversational AI agents and large language models used for educational assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper theorizes about generative AI tools in education generally, including their potential benefits and risks, without empirical evaluation.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a speculative, conceptual paper using fictional storytelling rather than an empirical study. It does not report a study design, sample, or measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No quantitative effects or observed impacts are reported, so there is no empirical basis to judge magnitude of impact. The paper only offers imagined opportunities and risks.

paper_profiles.title: The VR-AI–Assisted Simulation for Content Knowledge Application in Pre-Service EFL Teacher Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how pre-service English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers interpret and use a VR-AI–assisted simulation designed to support content knowledge application, with a specific focus on teaching the present perfect tense. The study is motivated by the challenge of preparing future teachers for real classroom demands, especially when they must explain grammar clearly, respond to spontaneous student questions, and adapt instruction under pressure.

The intervention combines high-immersion virtual reality with AI-generated learner questions in a simulated classroom. Participants taught a virtual class of intermediate students using the Virtual Speech platform and Oculus Quest 2, then completed a qualitative e-questionnaire about their experience. The study is framed by cognitive flexibility theory, emphasizing flexible knowledge application in unpredictable situations.

The participants were 17 female graduate students in a Master of Arts program in Teaching English as a Foreign Language at a university in Poland. They were preparing for school practicum in secondary education. The findings suggest that the simulation supported reflection, confidence building, and revision of grammar knowledge, while AI-generated questions were especially helpful in prompting deeper thinking and self-assessment. At the same time, participants reported limitations such as weak interaction, lack of teaching materials, technical issues, and anxiety. Overall, the paper concludes that VR combined with AI can be a valuable tool for teacher preparation, though greater interactivity and realism are still needed.

identified_tools.name: Virtual Speech
identified_tools.description: A commercial virtual reality application for role-play and professional development simulations, including AI-generated interactions in a simulated classroom.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the VR platform for a high-immersion simulated EFL classroom in which pre-service teachers taught the present perfect tense and answered AI-generated questions from virtual students.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative case study with pre-service EFL teachers (N=17), participants generally reported that the simulation supported reflection, confidence, and the application of grammar knowledge, but some also reported technological difficulties, lack of interaction, and limits to transferability to real classrooms. The paper does not report quantitative effect sizes.
findings.measure: Participant reflections on teaching performance, content knowledge application, and transferability to real-world teaching

findings.finding_summary: Participants reported operational challenges including lack of student feedback, absence of teaching materials, VR equipment issues, and difficulties using the virtual board. The paper qualitatively notes these as barriers to the teaching experience rather than quantifying their prevalence or magnitude.
findings.measure: Participant-reported technological and instructional constraints during the VR simulation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative case study with a small sample and no quantitative causal estimate. It provides useful descriptive evidence about teacher perceptions and feasibility, but not experimental evidence of effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceived benefits such as improved confidence and reflection, but these are subjective and not quantified. Reported risks and limitations are also substantial, so overall impact is unclear rather than demonstrably large.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Frontiers of LLMs in Psychological Applications: A Comprehensive Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a comprehensive review of large language models (LLMs) in psychological applications. It examines how LLMs are reshaping psychological research across cognitive and behavioral psychology, clinical and counseling psychology, educational and developmental psychology, and social and cultural psychology. The review is motivated by the rapid growth of generative AI systems such as ChatGPT, GPT-4, Bard, Claude, and LLaMA, and by the need to understand both their benefits and their risks in psychological contexts.

Rather than reporting a single empirical intervention, the paper synthesizes 47 studies published between 2020 and 2024. These studies include experiments on LLM cognitive abilities, use of LLMs for psychological assessment and counseling support, educational applications such as tutoring and lesson-planning assistance, and social-scientific uses such as simulating human behavior or serving as proxies for human participants. The review also discusses methodological uses of LLMs for literature review, hypothesis generation, experimental design, and data analysis.

The main conclusion is that LLMs show substantial promise as research tools and support systems, but their outputs are not equivalent to human cognition and can contain important biases and safety risks. The authors emphasize ethical concerns including privacy, misuse in sensitive settings, overestimation of model competence, and the need for careful interpretation. Overall, the paper argues for responsible integration of LLMs into psychological research while maintaining caution about their limitations and potential harms.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General large language models / generative AI systems that can generate and evaluate text, support dialogue, and assist with analysis across tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a comprehensive review of large language models in psychological applications, including educational and developmental contexts, rather than an empirical evaluation of a single named product.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a review article that synthesizes prior studies rather than reporting a new empirical evaluation of a single AI tool. It does not provide original study design, sample, or effect estimates for a specific intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests broad potential and risks of LLMs in psychology and education, but it does not present a direct effect estimate from an intervention. The impact is therefore informational and field-level rather than measurable in this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Adapting Large Language Models for Education: Foundational Capabilities, Potentials, and Challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a survey of large language model (LLM) capabilities relevant to education, rather than an empirical study of a classroom intervention. It asks how LLMs can support educational tasks and what technical limitations remain before they can serve as effective intelligent education systems.

The paper reviews five foundational capability areas: mathematics, writing, programming, reasoning, and knowledge-based question answering. For each area, it summarizes representative methods, benchmarks, and current performance, and it discusses whether the methods generalize toward broader educational use. The paper also contrasts two system-level architectures for educational LLMs: a unified model and a mixture-of-experts approach.

The context is online education and intelligent tutoring, with emphasis on student-facing question answering and problem solving rather than teacher coaching or lesson-plan feedback. No participant population is studied, and no intervention is implemented. The main conclusion is that LLMs show strong promise for education, but important challenges remain, especially hallucination, weak mathematical reasoning, over-correction in writing support, limited interpretability in programming, and the need for better integration of external tools and educational knowledge.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general large language model / generative AI system used for educational tasks such as answering questions, generating text, summarizing, correcting grammar, coding assistance, and reasoning.
identified_tools.use_case: This is a survey paper that reviews the capabilities, potentials, and challenges of LLMs for education rather than evaluating one specific product in a single intervention.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/survey paper that synthesizes literature on LLM capabilities in education. It does not report a primary empirical study, RCT, or meta-analytic estimate for a specific tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No intervention effects, effect sizes, or outcome estimates are reported. The paper discusses potential applications and challenges rather than measured impact.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the frontiers of LLMs in psychological applications: a comprehensive review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a comprehensive review of large language models (LLMs) in psychological applications. It asks how LLMs are being used across major areas of psychology, what capabilities they exhibit in tasks related to cognition, assessment, intervention, and social interaction, and what technical and ethical risks accompany their use. The review is organized around four psychological domains: cognitive and behavioral, clinical and counseling, educational and developmental, and social and cultural psychology.

Rather than studying a single intervention with participants, the paper synthesizes 47 studies published from 2020 to 2024. These studies include experiments using GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, LLaMA, Claude, Bard, and related systems for tasks such as reasoning, decision-making, emotional intelligence, mental health evaluation, counseling support, lesson planning, learning support, stimulus generation, and social simulation. The review also highlights LLM use as a research tool for literature review, hypothesis generation, experimental design, and data analysis.

The paper concludes that LLMs show promising utility in psychology, including strong performance on some cognitive tasks, useful support for mental health and education, and potential as research assistants. However, it stresses important limitations and risks, including bias, safety concerns, privacy issues, overclaiming human-like capabilities, and the need for careful ethical use and interpretability. Overall, the paper argues for responsible integration of LLMs into psychological research and practice.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based conversational LLM system used for dialogue, text generation, and analysis tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: This systematic review examined multiple GPT/ChatGPT-family studies in psychological applications, including educational uses such as lesson planning and learning support, but did not report a single dedicated intervention study on teacher planning quality or instructional practice.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s conversational large language model family, formerly Bard, used for text generation, reasoning, and evaluative tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The review included Gemini/Bard in comparisons for psychological assessment and educational applications, but did not isolate a teacher-planning or instructional-practice intervention outcome for Gemini specifically.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic’s conversational large language model family used for text generation, reasoning, and safety-aligned assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: The review mentioned Claude in comparative psychological and assessment studies, but it was not studied here as a standalone teacher planning or coaching tool.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta’s open-weight large language model family used for text generation and downstream fine-tuning.
identified_tools.use_case: The review discussed LLaMA and fine-tuned LLaMA in psychological research and educational contexts, but not in a teacher lesson-plan feedback study.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI/LLM chatbot systems used for text generation, feedback, summarization, and conversational assistance when no specific product is named.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a broad systematic review of LLMs in psychology and education, including generic use of LLMs for learning support, lesson planning, and coaching-related functions.

findings.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, LLMs were presented as potentially useful for education and learning applications, including lesson planning support, personalized learning, and motivating feedback. However, the review also emphasized risks such as superficial, inconsistent, contradictory responses and the potential for users to overestimate their knowledge.
findings.measure: reviewed evidence on educational and learning applications; reported risks/benefits in included studies

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that LLMs can improve workflow efficiency in research and education-related tasks, including generating materials, summarizing text, and supporting teachers and researchers. It cites a national survey noting that 40% of US teachers used GPT weekly for lesson planning within 3 months of release, indicating rapid uptake rather than experimental effect estimates.
findings.measure: reported adoption and productivity/efficiency claims in included studies

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review synthesizing heterogeneous studies rather than a single well-controlled intervention study. The paper provides narrative evidence and some descriptive statistics, but it does not report a focused causal estimate for teacher planning quality or instructional practice.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests potentially meaningful educational and workflow benefits, including lesson-planning support and efficiency gains, but the paper does not provide a direct effect size for the target outcomes. The risk discussion also indicates that impacts may be mixed and context-dependent.

paper_profiles.title: Using AI to support education for Collective Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence can be used to support education for collective intelligence (CI), understood as thinking together, solving problems together, and making decisions together. The authors argue that prior AI in education work has focused mostly on individual learning, whereas CI requires support for group formation, collaborative dialogue, and orchestration of multi-stage group work.

To address this question, the paper conducts a scoping literature review and thematic analysis of 46 empirical studies published up to April 2023, supplemented by conceptual analysis. The review covers AI-enabled education research across classrooms, MOOCs, citizen science, crowdsourcing, and other collaborative settings. The studies include AI used as embedded analytics in environments and as explicit agents or chatbots.

The authors synthesize the literature into a three-part framework: AI for grouping, AI for process support, and AI for staging. Grouping refers to algorithms that form productive teams or recommend peers; process refers to coaching dialogue and collaborative interaction; staging refers to helping groups progress through phases of a collaborative task. The paper concludes that AI has promise for supporting CI across small groups and large or unbounded communities, but that much of the evidence remains exploratory, context-specific, and focused on feasibility or usability rather than strong causal effects.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / chatbot tool based on large language models, used conversationally for education and assistance tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generative AI and LLM-based chatbots as a potential way to support dialogue, coaching, and orchestration in education for collective intelligence, but does not evaluate a specific generative AI product in an empirical study.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a literature review and conceptual framework paper, not a primary evaluation of a specific AI tool. It synthesizes prior studies but does not report original experimental outcomes for a named system.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct effect sizes or outcome data are reported for a specific tool in this paper. The paper is about proposed uses and categories of AI support rather than measured impact.

paper_profiles.title: The PearlAI Framework: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence to Transform Education in Africa
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Scientific Research in Computer Science, Engineering and Information Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the persistent challenges facing education systems in Africa, including limited access, inequity, low learning outcomes, weak teacher support, and curriculum relevance. Rather than reporting a single empirical intervention, it proposes the PearlAI Framework as an Africa-centered, open-source approach for using artificial intelligence to improve education at scale.

The framework is built around six domains: access and equity, teacher workforce support, literacy and numeracy, curriculum relevance, assessment and evaluation, and student engagement and motivation. It draws on a systematic review of literature following PRISMA guidelines, synthesizing evidence from African and global research on mother-tongue instruction, formative assessment, retrieval practice, culturally responsive pedagogy, AI feedback systems, and teacher co-pilots. The review searched major databases, screened studies, and included 34 papers in the final synthesis.

The paper argues that effective AI in education must augment teachers rather than replace them, and that context-sensitive design is essential for African settings. It highlights the importance of offline-first deployment, small language models, privacy protections, modular architecture, and sustained teacher professional development. The main conclusion is that AI can improve learning and system efficiency only when integrated with pedagogy, local language and culture, and strong implementation and governance structures.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model chatbot or AI assistant used for educational support such as feedback, tutoring, lesson planning, and content adaptation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes PearlAI as an AI framework that includes generative AI-enabled teacher coaching, automated lesson planning, adaptive tutoring, and AI-driven formative feedback, but it does not evaluate a specific named commercial product.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual and synthesis paper proposing the PearlAI framework and summarizing prior literature; it does not report original empirical evaluation of a specific AI tool in this paper. The methodology is a PRISMA-guided review, but the paper itself provides no primary outcome data for the proposed system.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Because the paper is a framework proposal rather than an intervention study, there is no direct measured impact attributable to PearlAI in this article. The proposed design targets potentially meaningful effects on teacher workload and instructional quality, but these remain untested here.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can function as an automated coach for teachers by scoring classroom instruction and generating useful pedagogical feedback. The motivation is that many teachers lack access to consistent, high-quality coaching, and the authors explore whether an AI system could provide a scalable complement to human expert feedback.

The study evaluates ChatGPT in three zero-shot coaching tasks on elementary mathematics classroom transcripts: (1) predicting scores on classroom observation rubrics derived from the CLASS and MQI instruments, (2) identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and (3) offering actionable suggestions to elicit more student reasoning. The transcripts come from the NCTE dataset of U.S. 4th- and 5th-grade math observations, and expert teachers rate the model outputs for helpfulness, relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

The results show that ChatGPT has some promise as a feedback tool, but its performance is substantially below that of an expert coach. Score predictions correlate weakly with human ratings, and the qualitative feedback is often not insightful or novel; for suggestions, the model frequently repeats what the teacher already did in the transcript. The paper concludes that current generative AI can support teacher coaching only in limited ways and highlights the need for future work to reduce hallucination, improve novelty and insight, and better align feedback with educational practice.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model / chatbot used to generate scores, highlights, missed opportunities, and actionable suggestions from classroom transcripts.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated zero-shot on elementary math classroom transcript segments as an automated teacher coach for three tasks: scoring observation rubric items, identifying highlights and missed opportunities, and generating suggestions to elicit more student reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: On Task A, ChatGPT performed poorly at scoring classroom transcripts against CLASS and MQI observation items. The paper reports low Spearman correlations with human ratings across items (e.g., CLBM 0.35 with DA prompting, CLPC 0.00; MQI items mostly near 0), and adding rubric descriptions or reasoning did not improve performance.
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between model-predicted observation scores and human ratings

findings.finding_summary: On Task B, teachers generally did not judge the model's highlights/missed-opportunities responses to be insightful or relevant. The paper reports that 20-30% of responses were unfaithful, with MQI responses worse than CLASS responses across relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness; low scores on relevance increased from 35% to 55% and insightfulness from 51% to 71% from CLASS to MQI.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for highlights and missed opportunities

findings.finding_summary: On Task C, most suggestions were judged faithful, relevant, and actionable, but the model was highly redundant: 82% of suggestions repeated something the teacher already did in the transcript. The paper frames this as a substantial novelty problem even though the suggestions were often usable.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, actionability, and novelty for suggested coaching moves

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study using qualitative human evaluation plus correlation analysis, not an RCT or meta-analysis. The evidence is useful but limited by small samples and no causal design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clearly poor scoring performance and substantial redundancy/limited insightfulness, which indicates limited practical impact in the current form. Some outputs were judged actionable and relevant, but the overall coaching quality is not yet strong enough for higher impact.

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers and curators collaborated with a generative-AI lesson planning system, Shiksha Copilot, to create and adapt curriculum-aligned lesson plans in low-resource schools. The central question is not only whether the tool could generate useful lesson plans, but also how educators evaluated, modified, and integrated AI-generated content into their teaching work, and what new risks or constraints emerged in multilingual, resource-constrained settings.

Shiksha Copilot combined retrieval-augmented generation, human curation, and teacher customization. Curators first reviewed AI-generated learning objectives and lesson plans, then translated and refined them into English and Kannada versions. Teachers in government schools could then copy, edit, and use these plans, with optional AI features such as lesson chat, educational chat, and question generation available to some users. The system was deployed across Karnataka, India, with 1,043 teachers and 23 curators, and the study drew on logs, surveys, and semi-structured interviews.

The paper finds that AI-supported lesson planning reduced planning time, administrative burden, and stress, while helping teachers access curriculum-aligned resources and supporting a shift toward activity-based pedagogy. English lesson plans were generally high quality with few edits, but Kannada translations required substantial linguistic correction, showing the limits of literal translation for low-resource languages. Teachers typically adapted plans further using their own expertise and local networks, often off-platform. Overall, the paper argues that generative AI can support teacher planning when embedded in human-in-the-loop workflows, but its effectiveness depends on contextual alignment, language quality, and sustained human oversight.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI/LLM-based lesson planning and teacher-support system that drafts, curates, translates, and customizes curriculum-aligned lesson plans, with additional chatbot and question-generation features.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as Shiksha Copilot, a human-in-the-loop lesson planning tool used by curators and teachers in Karnataka, India to generate, review, translate, and customize lesson plans for English- and Kannada-medium classrooms.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that Shiksha Copilot reduced lesson planning time and bureaucratic workload for teachers, while also lowering teaching-related stress. Teachers used the tool for both classroom instruction and record-keeping, and survey/interview evidence indicated measurable reductions in time and effort spent on planning and documentation.
findings.measure: Lesson planning time, administrative workload, and teaching-related stress (Teacher Stress Scale and survey/interview reports)
findings.sample_size: n=406 survey; n=22 teacher interviews; n=1,043 teachers deployed

findings.finding_summary: The tool supported a shift toward activity-based pedagogy, but broader pedagogical change was constrained by staffing shortages and administrative demands. The paper describes organizational and workflow changes in how teachers prepared and used lesson plans, including the use of AI-generated plans for record-keeping and classroom delivery.
findings.measure: Reported shifts in teaching practices and workflow change from mixed-methods interviews, logs, and surveys
findings.sample_size: n=1,043 teachers deployed; n=43 interviews; log analysis of 991 curated LPs and 5,544 teacher-created LPs

findings.finding_summary: Curator review logs indicated high reliability for English lesson plans: 96.13% of 7,744 content blocks were rated suitable for classroom use, 3.53% required minor adjustments, and 0.34% were unusable. However, English learning objectives often needed substantial strengthening before downstream lesson plans were satisfactory.
findings.measure: Curator ratings of content-block quality for English lesson plans

findings.finding_summary: Kannada translations required extensive substantive revision. In a sample of 26 Kannada-medium lesson plans, 94.4% of content blocks were edited, with nearly all edits related to language rather than pedagogy, indicating that literal translation was often linguistically inadequate for classroom use.
findings.measure: Percentage of edited content blocks in Kannada-medium lesson plans

findings.finding_summary: Teachers’ final lesson plans were frequently adapted off-platform rather than through recorded edits: only 1.53% of 5,542 teacher-created lesson plans were modified in the system, and interviews suggested teachers often used the plans as a starting point and then incorporated their own expertise and informal resources mentally or offline.
findings.measure: Platform-recorded teacher edits to curated lesson plans and qualitative reports of adaptation practices
findings.sample_size: n=5,544 teacher-created LPs; n=22 teacher interviews

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods field deployment with surveys, interviews, and log analysis rather than an experimental efficacy study. The evidence is informative but largely descriptive and observational.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports practical workload and workflow benefits, but no effect sizes are provided and the magnitude of academic or instructional impact is unclear. The strongest claims concern efficiency and qualitative workflow change rather than measured learning outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service elementary science teachers integrated ChatGPT into lesson planning, with a focus on the quality of their plans, instructional uses of the tool, and their perceived benefits and risks. The paper is motivated by the lack of empirical evidence on how generative AI can be used in science teaching and learning, despite widespread optimism about ChatGPT's educational potential.

The study involved 29 pre-service elementary teachers enrolled in a science education course at a Korean teachers' university. After four 2-hour instructional sessions introducing ChatGPT, discussing its potential in science education, reviewing science teaching methods, and explaining lesson-plan design, participants wrote lesson plans for a 45-minute elementary science lesson. They were required to incorporate ChatGPT into the lesson and attach simulated chat interactions. The researchers evaluated the plans using a modified TPACK-based Technology Integration Assessment Rubric and also analyzed open-ended survey responses about why teachers chose particular content and methods, why they thought ChatGPT was useful, and what outcomes or concerns they anticipated.

Findings show that participants imagined a wide range of ChatGPT uses across science topics and instructional methods, especially cooperative learning, POE, learning cycle, analogy generation, experimentation, and concept mapping. Overall lesson-plan quality was moderately high, with strongest scores for aligning ChatGPT with curriculum goals and instructional strategies, and weaker performance on selecting appropriate ChatGPT functions. Qualitatively, participants saw ChatGPT as useful for questioning, individualized support, and formative feedback, but they also worried about inaccurate information, hallucinated resources, and student over-dependence. The paper concludes that pre-service teachers need stronger AI-focused professional development and that future research should test ChatGPT-integrated instruction in real classrooms.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM system for conversational text generation, question answering, and related language-based assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studied how 29 pre-service elementary science teachers incorporated ChatGPT into lesson plans for science learning, including lesson design, instructional strategies, role-play support, individualized learning support, and formative feedback.

findings.finding_summary: Across 29 lesson plans, pre-service teachers rated their ChatGPT-integrated plans highly on a modified TPACK-based rubric, with an overall mean of M=3.29 (SD=.91) on a 4-point scale. Scores were highest for instructional strategies & ChatGPT (M=3.48, SD=.99) and curriculum goals & ChatGPT (M=3.44, SD=.87), suggesting generally strong perceived planning quality for integration.
findings.measure: Modified TPACK-based lesson plan rubric (TIAR-derived), including curriculum goals & ChatGPT, instructional strategies & ChatGPT, ChatGPT function selection(s), and fit

findings.finding_summary: The paper identified both appropriate and inappropriate uses of ChatGPT in lesson planning. Appropriate uses included supporting role-play planning, consecutive questioning, individualized support, and feedback/reflection; inappropriate uses included requesting visual information, relying on nonexistent YouTube links, and using ChatGPT to design experiments in ways that could weaken practical inquiry skills.
findings.measure: Qualitative analysis of lesson plans and attached simulated chat data

findings.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers anticipated ChatGPT could improve efficiency by providing instant answers, summaries, additional information, and support for classroom management and lesson preparation. However, they also reported concerns about accuracy, reliability, hallucinated or incorrect information, and students becoming overly dependent on ChatGPT.
findings.measure: Open-ended survey responses on perceived usefulness, concerns, and anticipated outcomes

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods study of lesson plans and survey responses, but it is not a causal evaluation of student outcomes or teacher performance in real classrooms. Evidence is useful for understanding planning quality and perceived risks, but remains qualitative/descriptive.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally positive planning quality and perceived utility for ChatGPT, but the effects are descriptive and not tied to measured learning gains or instructional impact. Risks and limitations are substantial, so overall impact is promising but unclear.

paper_profiles.title: To what extent is ChatGPT useful for language teacher lesson plan creation?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can be useful for foreign language teacher lesson plan creation, and whether increasing prompt specificity improves the quality and consistency of generated plans. The authors note that teachers, especially in foreign language education, often lack ready-made instructional materials and may turn to generative AI for support. They also raise concerns that AI-generated lesson plans may reflect outdated pedagogical practices and be variable across repeated runs of the same prompt.

The study used ChatGPT 4.0 to generate lesson plans for a high school Level I Spanish class. Five zero-shot prompts were created, each progressively more specific: the prompts added proficiency guidance, a lesson plan template, a requirement to address ACTFL world-readiness standards, and finally a detailed checklist of required components. Each prompt was run 10 times in separate chats, producing 50 lesson plans. The outputs were scored against a 25-item rubric based on best practices and edTPA-aligned lesson plan criteria, and the authors analyzed both average quality and variability across outputs.

Results showed that greater prompt specificity did not reliably produce better lesson plans in a linear way. Adding a detailed checklist in the final prompt produced the highest average scores, but intermediate additions such as the lesson template and standards requirement sometimes reduced quality or made outputs more formulaic. The authors also found substantial variability between repeated outputs from the same prompt, including instances of strong alignment and clear misses on the rubric. They conclude that ChatGPT can be useful for lesson planning, but teachers need to critically review and revise outputs because generated plans may still include inconsistent, incomplete, or historically outdated instructional practices.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot for generating and revising text-based outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Used ChatGPT 4.0 in zero-shot prompting to generate foreign language teacher lesson plans across five increasingly specific prompts, each repeated 10 times, to examine lesson-plan quality, variability, and weaknesses.

findings.finding_summary: Across 50 generated lesson plans, outputs were generally high quality for lesson-plan creation, but quality did not increase linearly with added prompt specificity. Mean rubric scores ranged from 19.6 to 21.6 out of 25 across prompt versions; adding a checklist of criteria in P.5 produced the highest mean score (21.6/25), while intermediate specificity sometimes reduced scores.
findings.measure: Lesson plan rubric score (25-point presence/absence checklist)

findings.finding_summary: The study found that ChatGPT can streamline lesson planning and produce usable lesson plans, but outputs were highly variable even for identical prompts. Scores from the same prompt ranged by at least five criteria; e.g., P.1 ranged from 16/25 to 23/25, and P.5 ranged from 20/25 to 25/25, indicating non-determinism that limits reliability.
findings.measure: Within-prompt variability in rubric scores and Jaccard distance/dissimilarity among outputs

findings.finding_summary: The paper identified weaknesses and possible bias in generated lesson plans, including recurrence of anachronistic pedagogical practices and incomplete integration of culture and communicative interaction. Some rubric elements (e.g., cultural connection, ACTFL standards in teacher input) appeared only in about half or fewer of the outputs, suggesting historical bias in the model's training data.
findings.measure: Presence/absence of required lesson-plan components (e.g., cultural connection, communicative interaction, ACTFL standards alignment)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study using a scoring rubric and repeated prompt trials, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental evaluation of learner outcomes. The evidence is best characterized as qualitative/mixed-methods with descriptive statistics and no reported causal effect sizes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical usefulness for lesson-plan drafting and meaningful risks related to variability and historical bias, but it does not report standardized effect sizes or a direct instructional outcome effect of medium/large magnitude. The overall impact is therefore important but quantitatively unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Unbiased Teacher for Semi-Supervised Object Detection
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses semi-supervised object detection, focusing on how to train object detectors when only a small labeled set and a large unlabeled set are available. The authors argue that existing pseudo-labeling approaches used in semi-supervised image classification do not transfer well to object detection because of foreground-background imbalance, foreground class imbalance, duplicated predictions, and overfitting when labeled data are scarce.

To address these issues, the paper proposes Unbiased Teacher, a teacher-student framework. A detector is first trained in a burn-in stage on labeled data. It is then duplicated into a teacher and student model: the teacher produces pseudo-labels for unlabeled images, the student learns from them, and the teacher is updated through exponential moving average (EMA) of the student. The method also uses weak augmentation for the teacher, strong augmentation for the student, class-wise NMS, confidence thresholding, and focal loss to reduce pseudo-label bias and improve stability.

The paper evaluates the method on MS-COCO and PASCAL VOC in several semi-supervised detection settings, including COCO-standard, COCO-additional, and VOC. It reports substantial gains over prior methods such as CSD and STAC, especially in low-label regimes. The main conclusion is that continuously refined teacher-student learning, together with EMA and focal loss, produces more reliable pseudo-labels and meaningfully improves semi-supervised object detection performance.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: A semi-supervised teacher-student object detection framework that uses pseudo-labeling, exponential moving average (EMA) teacher refinement, confidence thresholding, and focal loss to improve learning from labeled and unlabeled data.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a semi-supervised object detection method for training an object detector with a small labeled set and a large unlabeled set; evaluated on MS-COCO and PASCAL VOC.

findings.finding_summary: Unbiased Teacher improved object detection performance over supervised baselines and prior semi-supervised methods. On COCO-standard, it achieved 16.94 mAP at 0.5% labeled data, 20.75 mAP at 1%, 24.30 mAP at 2%, 28.27 mAP at 5%, and 31.50 mAP at 10%, compared with the supervised baselines of 6.83, 9.05, 12.70, 18.47, and 23.86 respectively.
findings.measure: COCO-standard object detection mAP (AP50:95)

findings.finding_summary: On COCO-additional, the method outperformed supervised-only training and prior semi-supervised baselines. The reported AP50:95 was 41.30 for Ours versus 40.20 for supervised (3x), 38.82 for CSD (3x), and 39.21 for STAC (6x).
findings.measure: COCO-additional object detection AP50:95

findings.finding_summary: On VOC, Unbiased Teacher achieved 77.37 AP50 and 48.69 AP50:95 versus the supervised baseline of 72.63 AP50 and 42.13 AP50:95. This exceeded STAC on AP50:95 (44.64) and matched or slightly trailed it on AP50 (77.45 vs 77.37), while still showing a stronger overall detection-quality gain.
findings.measure: VOC object detection AP50 and AP50:95
findings.effect_size: +4.74 AP50 and +6.56 AP50:95 vs supervised baseline

findings.finding_summary: Ablation results showed that EMA training and focal loss improved pseudo-label balance and model performance. With COCO-standard 1% labeled data, the model using focal loss plus EMA had the best mAP (21.19) and the lowest KL-divergence between pseudo-label and ground-truth class distributions (0.0851), compared with cross-entropy without EMA (13.42 mAP; KL=1.7915).
findings.measure: Validation mAP and KL-divergence between pseudo-label and ground-truth class distributions
findings.effect_size: +7.77 mAP vs cross-entropy without EMA; KL-divergence reduced by 1.7064

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical conference paper with clear experimental comparisons across multiple benchmark datasets and ablation analyses. It is not a randomized educational study, but it provides a reasonably well-specified causal-style evaluation within machine learning experimentation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are large in magnitude across several settings, including double-digit mAP improvements in low-label regimes. These are substantial performance differences, though they concern computer vision detection rather than educational outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Undistillable: Making a Nasty Teacher That Cannot Teach Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a machine learning security problem: how to prevent knowledge distillation from being used to clone or steal the functionality of a released model. The authors argue that standard and data-free knowledge distillation can enable intellectual property leakage because a black-box teacher model can still be imitated from its input-output behavior, and they propose a defensive alternative called a “Nasty Teacher.”

The proposed intervention is self-undermining knowledge distillation, an adversarial training method that trains a teacher network to preserve its own accuracy while maximizing divergence from an auxiliary network’s outputs. In effect, the teacher remains a strong predictor on its own data but becomes difficult or harmful to distill from. The paper evaluates this idea on image classification benchmarks including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet using various ResNet-family teachers and lighter student architectures, as well as on data-free distillation methods such as DAFL and DeepInversion.

The main conclusion is that nasty teachers can match the accuracy of normally trained teachers with only small drops, while substantially degrading student performance under both standard KD and data-free KD. The authors also show that the approach can distort reverse-engineered images, suggesting potential protection against unauthorized model cloning and data reconstruction. Because this is a model-security paper rather than an education study, it contains no educational population, user-type, or classroom implementation information.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic knowledge distillation / teacher-student neural network setup used to transfer model behavior; not a generative AI coaching or lesson-planning product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and evaluates a 'Nasty Teacher' or 'undistillable' teacher network that preserves its own task performance while degrading student models trained by knowledge distillation, including standard KD and data-free KD settings.

findings.finding_summary: Across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, the nasty teacher largely prevented successful model stealing via KD. The paper reports that teacher accuracy stayed within about 0% to 2% of the normal teacher, while student accuracy dropped by 1.72% to 67.57% depending on dataset and student architecture.
findings.measure: Student accuracy after knowledge distillation; teacher accuracy preservation

findings.finding_summary: In data-free KD experiments using DAFL and DeepInversion, the nasty teacher reduced student performance relative to a normal teacher. The paper reports student accuracy declines of 6.34% on CIFAR-10 and 5.39% on CIFAR-100 under DAFL, and qualitatively shows distorted or noisy reconstructions under DeepInversion.
findings.measure: Student accuracy under data-free knowledge distillation; quality of inverted/reconstructed images

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical machine learning security paper about knowledge distillation, not an education intervention study. It does not evaluate a teacher-facing coaching or lesson-planning AI tool in an educational setting.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no reported educational outcome measures such as planning quality or instructional practice, and its findings are about model protection and model-stealing resistance rather than classroom impact.

paper_profiles.title: Responsive Professional Development: A Facilitation Approach for Teachers’ Development in a Physics Teaching Community of Practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a university-school partnership program, IPaSS, supports high school physics teachers’ professional learning through a responsive facilitation approach. The authors ask to what extent teachers’ perceptions align with the program’s design principles and how the program helps teachers move from peripheral participation to core membership in a community of practice.

The intervention is not an AI system; it is a professional development model built around responsiveness, co-design, and ongoing adaptation to teachers’ needs. IPaSS provides teachers with university-level physics curricular materials, peer support, and sustained PD across a school year, including summer workshops and online meetings. The facilitation approach uses daily/pre-session surveys, observations, and discussion to modify upcoming PD activities, reorganize teacher pairings, and create opportunities for teachers to share expertise, mentor one another, and lead sessions.

The study involved 13 of 14 high school physics teachers in the first two cohorts of the Illinois Physics and Secondary Schools partnership, using semi-structured interviews, survey responses, and researcher field notes. Teachers reported strong appreciation for access to materials, practical classroom resources, sustained support, collaboration, and the flexibility to adapt materials at their own pace. The authors conclude that responsive PD can strengthen pedagogical support, confidence, belonging, and leadership development, while also expanding the traditional mentor-novice model by enabling mutual learning across experience levels.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI chatbot or assistant based on large language models, without a specific named commercial or research product identified.
identified_tools.use_case: Not studied in this paper. The paper focuses on a responsive professional development program for high school physics teachers, using interviews, surveys, and observations.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods case study of teacher professional development, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool. It provides descriptive evidence about PD design and teacher perceptions, but no AI intervention, comparison group, or causal estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No AI tool effects are reported, so there is no measurable impact on teacher planning quality, instructional practice, or risks attributable to a generative AI system. The paper is relevant contextually to coaching/feedback in PD, but not to AI efficacy.

paper_profiles.title: Interdisciplinary Teams for Teacher Professional Development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the design and iterative refinement of SATTAA, the San Antonio Teacher Training Astronomy Academy, a teacher professional development program intended to strengthen secondary teachers’ astronomy content knowledge, pedagogical approaches, and comfort teaching STEM. The authors frame the problem as a persistent lack of astronomy background among secondary teachers, alongside a need to connect disciplinary content with hands-on pedagogy and technology in ways that support more confident instruction and greater student interest in STEM.

The intervention is an interdisciplinary, team-designed summer professional development program that evolved across three annual iterations (2018–2020). The program was developed and delivered by astronomers, STEM educators, and informal education partners, with formats shifting from mostly face-to-face to blended and then fully online during COVID-19. Participants were preservice and inservice teachers from the San Antonio area; the 2018 pilot involved preservice teachers only, 2019 added inservice teachers, and 2020 expanded participation further and included more online components and virtual field experiences.

Evidence reported in the paper comes from participant surveys, pre/post content quizzes, reflections, focus groups, and team observations used to guide redesign. Across iterations, participants consistently reported improved astronomy understanding, greater interest, and appreciation for the interdisciplinary and collaborative structure. The authors conclude that combining disciplinary expertise with pedagogy and informal education partnerships improved the quality and adaptability of teacher professional development, though they note that the paper mainly reports processes and lessons learned rather than a controlled evaluation of outcomes.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system is an adaptive educational software system that provides instructional support, practice, and feedback tailored to learners.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper does not evaluate an AI tool. It describes a teacher professional development program (SATTAA) and its interdisciplinary design, with astronomy content, pedagogy, and technology integration; any technology mentioned is general online meeting and field-trip tooling rather than an AI system.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive program paper about teacher professional development design and iteration, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool. No AI system is studied, and no causal evidence about an AI product is presented.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no AI intervention and no tool-level outcome to assess. The reported gains relate to teacher content knowledge within a PD program, not to AI-mediated coaching or lesson-plan feedback.

paper_profiles.title: Transforming Teacher Education in Developing Countries: The Role of Generative AI in Bridging Theory and Practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper addresses a persistent problem in teacher education in developing countries: the gap between theoretical preparation and practical teaching competence, especially the weak implementation of pedagogical modeling and performance-based assessment. Using Ghana as the main case, the paper argues that teacher education reforms have been hampered by content-heavy instruction, standardized testing, limited resources, resistance to change, and insufficient practitioner expertise among teacher educators.

The paper does not evaluate a live intervention. Instead, it proposes generative AI (GenAI) as a catalyst that could reduce the time and effort spent on content delivery, thereby allowing teacher educators to focus more on modeling effective pedagogy, supporting performance-based assessment, and improving professional development. GenAI is presented as a tool for lesson planning support, resource acquisition, digital literacy, critical thinking, and alignment of teacher education with workforce needs. The argument is that GenAI could also indirectly reduce dependence on lecture-based teaching and prompt shifts toward more authentic assessment practices.

The context is initial teacher education in Ghana, with pre-service teachers and teacher educators as the main stakeholders. The paper concludes that GenAI has promise for transforming teacher education systems in developing countries, but it also warns that misuse could undermine critical thinking and creativity. It calls for scaffolded GenAI literacy and further empirical research on responsible implementation.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI or large language model chatbots used for content support, lesson planning, feedback generation, and other educational assistance tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as a prospective tool in teacher education in Ghana and other developing-country contexts to support content knowledge acquisition, pedagogical modeling, performance-based assessment, resource acquisition, digital literacy, critical thinking, and teacher professional development.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/theoretical paper using logical deduction, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool. It proposes potential roles and risks of GenAI but reports no primary data, effect sizes, or measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that GenAI could have broad system-level influence on teacher education, but the impact is speculative rather than demonstrated empirically. Because no outcomes are measured, the impact cannot be quantified and remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Object Relation in Mean Teacher for Cross-Domain Detection
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of unsupervised domain adaptation for object detection under domain shift, where a detector trained on labeled source images performs poorly on unlabeled target images. The authors focus on cross-domain detection scenarios such as synthetic-to-real transfer and weather variation, and ask how the Mean Teacher consistency-based paradigm can be adapted to improve detection performance.

The proposed method, Mean Teacher with Object Relations (MTOR), extends Faster R-CNN with a teacher-student framework. For unlabeled target images, the model uses two augmented views and enforces three forms of consistency: region-level consistency between teacher and student predictions, inter-graph consistency between relational graphs built from region similarities, and intra-graph consistency to encourage same-class regions within the student graph to be more similar. The method is trained end-to-end with supervised detection loss on labeled source images and consistency losses on target images.

Experiments are conducted on Cityscapes to Foggy Cityscapes, SIM10k to Cityscapes, and the Syn2Real benchmark (synthetic CAD-rendered images to real COCO/YTBB images). MTOR outperforms prior domain adaptation baselines and improves mean average precision across transfers, with the authors attributing gains to the combination of region-level and graph-structured consistency. However, the paper is about computer vision domain adaptation rather than education, so it does not involve educational populations, teachers, or instructional interventions.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Computer vision / object detection research paradigm using a teacher-student consistency framework for unsupervised domain adaptation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes Mean Teacher with Object Relations (MTOR), a teacher-student domain adaptation method for cross-domain object detection, building on Faster R-CNN and consistency regularization.

findings.finding_summary: On Foggy Cityscapes for C  F transfer, MTOR achieved 35.1% mAP, which was 3.1 percentage points higher than DA [4] and better than the region-level-only variant MTORR (34.2%). The paper reports that adding inter-graph and intra-graph consistency improved performance over region-level consistency alone.
findings.measure: mean Average Precision (mAP) on Foggy Cityscapes validation set

findings.finding_summary: On SIM10k  Cityscapes (M  C), MTOR achieved 46.6% AP for car, compared with 41.9% for DA [4]. The authors attribute the gain to region-level consistency plus graph-structured consistencies.
findings.measure: Average Precision (AP) for car on Cityscapes validation set

findings.finding_summary: On the Syn2Real detection dataset for S  Y transfer, MTOR achieved 22.8% mAP on the official YTBB test set, exceeding DA [4] at 19.6% and Source-only at 18.1%. The paper describes this as state-of-the-art single-model performance for the setting.
findings.measure: mean Average Precision (mAP) on official testing set (YTBB)
findings.effect_size: +3.2 mAP points vs. DA; +4.7 vs. Source-only

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical computer vision paper with a clear experimental design and comparative evaluation, but it is not an education study and does not evaluate an educational AI tool. The evidence is strong for the reported object detection task, though not directly applicable to the requested teacher-planning domain.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful improvements in mAP/AP for object detection, but it has no relevance to teacher planning quality, instructional practice, or education-specific AI coaching/feedback. For the stated research topic, the practical impact is effectively absent.

paper_profiles.title: LessonPlanner: Assisting Novice Teachers to Prepare Pedagogy-Driven Lesson Plans with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: UIST ’24 (The 37th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge novice teachers face when preparing effective, pedagogically structured lesson plans: they must decide on instructional strategies, gather suitable teaching materials, and organize the lesson flow, often with limited experience and high time cost. The authors investigate whether large language models can support this process in a way that goes beyond generic chat-based prompting.

The proposed intervention is LessonPlanner, a web-based interactive system powered by GPT-4 that helps users generate lesson goals, create lesson-plan outlines aligned with Bloom’s Taxonomy and Gagne’s Nine Events of Instruction, and iteratively refine sections with preset prompts, contextual actions, and editable markdown-based outputs. The system was developed from a formative study with six novice teachers/teaching assistants, then evaluated in a within-subjects comparison against the ChatGPT web interface.

The main evaluation involved 12 university students acting as novice teachers and preparing lesson plans for Data Structures topics, followed by expert interviews with six teachers from university, primary, and high-school contexts. Results suggest LessonPlanner improved lesson-plan quality and reduced workload relative to the baseline, while experts found it helpful for organizing content and suggesting teaching strategies/resources. At the same time, the study highlights concerns about the accuracy, subject specificity, and trustworthiness of LLM-generated teaching content, motivating design recommendations for more controllable and theory-guided educational LLM tools.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational large language model interface used for interactive text generation and refinement.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the baseline interface in the within-subjects study, and also mentioned in formative interviews as a tool some novice teachers had used to generate lesson-planning content and student-question answers.

findings.finding_summary: In the within-subjects comparison (n=12), LessonPlanner was compared against the ChatGPT web app using the same GPT-4 model. The paper reports that LessonPlanner significantly improved the quality of outcome lesson plans and reduced workload relative to the ChatGPT baseline, but it does not provide the numerical effect size in the text provided.
findings.measure: Quality of outcome lesson plans; workload during lesson planning (NASA-TLX-based measures)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods paper with a within-subjects user study and expert interviews, but the excerpt does not report full statistical details for the main comparison. The evidence is empirical and comparative, but not presented as a fully reported RCT with effect sizes in the provided text.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports significant improvements in lesson-plan quality and reduced workload, suggesting meaningful practical benefit. However, no effect sizes or confidence intervals are given in the excerpt, so the magnitude cannot be confidently classified as medium or large.

paper_profiles.title: Attempts of Transforming Teacher Practice Through Professional Development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of improving physics and mathematics teaching through professional development, with the goal of producing lasting changes in classroom practice. The authors argue that teacher development is essential for increasing the quality of science education and, indirectly, student interest and enrolment in scientific fields.

The paper describes a series of professional development activities carried out in southern Tuscany within the Italian National Plan for Scientific Degrees. These activities included long advanced courses for qualified teachers, a summer school in physics where young teachers worked alongside expert teachers, a national master’s program in physics educational innovation, a workshop on modelling for physics and mathematics teachers, and several in-service updating courses held in specific schools.
