The interventions emphasized laboratory work, joint design of learning paths, interdisciplinary discussion, and opportunities to test materials in class when possible.

The participants were mainly secondary school teachers, many of whom were young and without permanent positions; some activities also involved expert teachers, university staff, and school administrators. The main conclusion is that professional development is most effective when it is context-specific, laboratory-based, and supported by school leadership, but that it is difficult to engage in-service teachers deeply, especially when activities are too intensive or disconnected from school constraints. The authors found that some informal, school-based updating courses worked better than broader or more demanding programs, particularly when teachers had strong management support and immediate relevance to their teaching context.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system is an AI-driven educational system that provides guided instruction, practice, and feedback/adaptation to learners.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper does not study an AI tutoring system; it discusses teacher professional development activities in physics and mathematics, including laboratory-based workshops and updating courses.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/descriptive professional development paper about teacher training activities, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool. No AI system is studied or compared, so evidence quality for AI tool effects is not applicable.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There are no measured AI-tool outcomes, effect sizes, or intervention impacts in the paper. The paper reports reflections on professional development formats and implementation challenges only.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This longitudinal intervention study examines whether an analytical AI feedback platform can support lesson-planning development in vocational teacher education. The paper addresses a practical problem: university instructors often cannot provide frequent, detailed, individualized feedback on complex lesson plans, especially when many planning dimensions and didactic principles must be considered. The authors ask whether AI-generated expert feedback can supplement or match human feedback, and whether using the platform influences related meta-dimensions such as AI literacy, attitudes toward AI, digital competences, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and motivation.

The intervention used EDDA, an analytical AI platform built on unsupervised machine learning and a BERT-based classifier. EDDA analyzed lesson plans and materials and returned individualized expert-level feedback on 10 main categories and 57 subcategories related to vocational business lesson planning, including sustainability, process orientation, problem orientation, action orientation, individualization, digitalization, and basic planning dimensions. Students in the experimental group received AI feedback throughout a semester and could also seek human clarification if needed; the control group received human feedback only. The sample consisted of 103 master's students in business education in Germany, working in small groups over a semester in 2023/2024 and 2024/2025.

Results showed that AI feedback could match or outperform human feedback in some planning dimensions. The experimental group received higher ratings in several sustainability-related categories, including social competences for sustainable development and reflexivity, and the authors report positive effects for some other planning aspects. At the same time, the mere use of AI did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, or motivation; several meta-dimensions showed little or no differential gain. Overall, the paper concludes that analytical AI can effectively supplement traditional feedback in lesson planning, but it should be embedded in a broader pedagogical framework rather than treated as a stand-alone solution.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic AI feedback platform / analytical AI system that classifies lesson-planning text and returns individualized expert feedback; here implemented as EDDA, an analytical AI platform based on BERT rather than a named commercial chatbot.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the experimental feedback medium for lesson planning in vocational teacher education. Students in the experimental group received AI feedback on their lesson plans throughout a semester, with human feedback available if needed; the control group received human feedback only.

findings.finding_summary: In a longitudinal two-group intervention with N=103 master’s students in business education, the AI-feedback group received higher ratings on some lesson-planning dimensions than the human-feedback-only control group. The paper reports significant positive effects for implementation of SDG 15 (life on land; p<0.10), social competences for sustainable development (p<0.05), and reflexivity (p<0.10), while higher prior knowledge predicted less growth on several dimensions.
findings.measure: Content analysis ratings of lesson plans on sustainability-related planning dimensions, including SDGs and competences for sustainable change agents

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic AI-supported feedback system for lesson planning that provides individualized expert-level feedback on submitted plans and materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as a substitute/supplement to human feedback in lesson planning, with outcomes assessed on both lesson-plan quality and learner meta-dimensions.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that AI feedback can match or surpass human feedback in some planning dimensions, especially certain content-related sustainability aspects, action orientation, relatedness, technology use, lesson structure, and learner engagement. However, the exact statistical coefficients and confidence intervals for these specific planning outcomes are not reported in the excerpted results tables.
findings.measure: Lesson-plan coding for didactic/planning principles and dimensions

findings.finding_summary: For the meta-dimensions measuring AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competences, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and motivation, the authors report that mere use of AI did not automatically improve AI literacy, change attitudes, or improve motivation. The intervention was intended to examine whether feedback medium changed teacher-related meta-dimensions, but the reported summary does not indicate broad positive shifts.
findings.measure: Questionnaire-based meta-dimensions: MAILS AI literacy, AI attitude, DigKomp2.2.de digital competences, SWIT digital-teaching self-efficacy, and basic need satisfaction/motivation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal two-group intervention with a control group and direct comparison between AI feedback and human feedback, which gives it stronger internal validity than a purely correlational study. However, assignment was not randomized in a traditional sense and the paper emphasizes measurement-model complexity and small sample constraints.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports some positive effects on lesson-plan quality and sustainability-related dimensions, but the magnitude of effects is mostly not reported in the excerpt and several meta-dimensions show no clear improvement. Overall impact appears modest rather than large.

paper_profiles.title: Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence: Early experiments with GPT-4
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is not an education intervention study. It reports a broad, exploratory investigation of an early text-only version of GPT-4, aiming to assess whether the model exhibits capabilities suggestive of artificial general intelligence. The authors probe the model with novel prompts across many domains, including language, coding, mathematics, vision, common-sense reasoning, tool use, and interaction with humans. They present examples where GPT-4 produces high-quality outputs on tasks such as proof writing, code generation, dialogue composition, and visual reasoning, and they contrast these outputs with ChatGPT to argue that GPT-4 is substantially more capable.

The paper does not study teachers, students, classrooms, lesson planning, professional learning, instructional coaching, or other educational interventions. Instead, it uses informal, human-designed demonstrations and comparisons to illustrate general capabilities and limitations. Some examples include GPT-4 generating pedagogical-style evaluations of model outputs, but these are not evaluations of teacher practice or instructional feedback interventions.

The main conclusion is that GPT-4 represents a major step toward more generally intelligent systems, while still having important limitations such as hallucinations, arithmetic errors, and weak planning. The authors emphasize that their evidence is exploratory rather than a rigorous benchmark evaluation and that the model is still far from fully human-like intelligence or continuous learning.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model/chatbot used to generate, revise, and evaluate text and code outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the comparison baseline in a paper demonstrating GPT-4 capabilities; no teacher planning, instructional coaching, or professional-learning intervention was studied.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is not an education intervention study and does not evaluate an AI tool for teacher planning, coaching, or professional learning. It is a demonstration paper about GPT-4 capabilities with illustrative prompts and outputs.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No teacher behavior, lesson revision, self-efficacy, or student learning outcomes are reported, so there is no educational impact evidence to rate.

paper_profiles.title: What if the devil is my guardian angel: ChatGPT as a case study of using chatbots in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines concerns about using ChatGPT in education rather than testing an instructional intervention or comparing outcomes against a control condition. The authors ask what risks and limitations early adopters perceive when using an advanced generative AI chatbot in educational contexts.

The study uses a three-stage qualitative instrumental case study of ChatGPT. First, it analyzes 2,330 tweets about ChatGPT in education using social network analysis and sentiment analysis. Second, it conducts content analysis of 19 publicly posted interviews from people with varied backgrounds who had used ChatGPT in education. Third, it reports hands-on testing by three experienced educators across ten educational scenarios, focusing on the quality, fairness, privacy, honesty, and potential misuse of ChatGPT-generated outputs.

The participants included students, educators, developers, and AI freelancers, with the educationally relevant groups being students and educators. The setting is not a single classroom or institution; rather, it is a mixed online/public discourse and user-experience exploration of ChatGPT use in education. The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is viewed as potentially useful for learning support, instructional design, and content creation, but its outputs can be inaccurate, inconsistent, manipulative, and privacy-threatening, so safe adoption requires caution, guidance, responsible design, and new teaching philosophies. The paper does not evaluate changes in teacher practice or student learning outcomes from an intervention; instead, it primarily evaluates ChatGPT-generated artifacts and user perceptions/experiences.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot based on GPT models, designed to generate and discuss text in a natural language interface.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as an early-adopter case of a chatbot in education. The paper examined ChatGPT through social media discourse, interviews, and educator user scenarios, including generating lesson content, quizzes, citations, and feedback-like responses for teaching and learning tasks.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative instrumental case study with social network analysis, interviews, and educator user-testing; it does not include a controlled comparison or experimental outcome evaluation. The evidence is therefore useful for understanding concerns and use patterns, but not for causal impact estimation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct effect sizes or controlled teacher/student outcome data are reported. The paper suggests possible instructional utility and risks, but the impact on teacher practice or student learning is not empirically measured.

paper_profiles.title: A comprehensive AI policy education framework for university teaching and learning
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the emerging need for an artificial intelligence education policy for higher education in response to the rapid spread of text-generative AI tools such as ChatGPT. Rather than testing an intervention, the study examines how university stakeholders perceive the opportunities, risks, and governance needs associated with generative AI in teaching and learning.

The authors used a mixed-methods survey design in Hong Kong universities, collecting data from 457 undergraduate and postgraduate students and 180 teachers and staff across multiple disciplines. Quantitative items assessed prior use of generative AI, attitudes toward its instructional value, concerns about misuse, and views on its impact on learning, assessment, and teacher roles. Open-ended responses were thematically analyzed to identify policy priorities.

The study proposes an AI Ecological Education Policy Framework with three dimensions: pedagogical, governance, and operational. Key recommendations include training for students and teachers, clearer rules about academic integrity and attribution, equitable access, transparency, data privacy, monitoring and evaluation, and maintaining AI as a complementary tool rather than a replacement for human teaching. The paper concludes that higher education institutions need comprehensive policy and support structures to integrate generative AI responsibly and ethically.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic text-generative AI / large language model chatbot systems used for producing and interacting with human-like text, such as ChatGPT-style tools.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper does not evaluate a specific intervention tool. It surveys students, teachers, and staff about perceptions, potential uses, risks, and policy needs related to generative AI in higher education teaching and learning.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods survey and policy framework paper, not a controlled evaluation of an AI intervention. It provides descriptive quantitative and qualitative evidence about perceptions and anticipated uses, but no causal outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests broad perceived importance and potential use of generative AI in teaching and learning, but it reports no measured effect on teacher behavior, lesson revisions, self-efficacy, or student learning. Any impact claims are speculative rather than demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review and position piece on the educational potential of artificial intelligence, with a particular focus on chatbots and ChatGPT. It asks what AI can contribute to teaching, learning, feedback, assessment, and educational administration, while also highlighting ethical, practical, and pedagogical concerns such as bias, privacy, academic integrity, and over-reliance on technology.

The article does not test an intervention or compare generative AI against human coaching, peer feedback, or business-as-usual. Instead, it synthesizes prior literature on AI applications in education, including personalized learning systems, automated feedback, intelligent tutoring, and chatbot-based supports. The discussion emphasizes how AI may support teachers by reducing repetitive work, providing instructional suggestions, and enabling more individualized student support.

Because it is a theoretical review rather than an empirical study, there is no participant population, setting, or outcome dataset reported in the paper itself. The paper concludes that AI and ChatGPT have promising uses in education, especially for feedback and personalization, but that effective and ethical implementation requires teacher preparation, oversight, and continued research.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative pre-trained transformer-based conversational AI chatbot that produces human-like text responses to natural language prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a review article discussing ChatGPT as a prominent generative AI tool in education, including its potential applications, benefits, and ethical/practical challenges. It does not report an empirical evaluation of ChatGPT in teacher planning or professional learning.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/opinion-style article with no original empirical study, no controlled comparison, and no outcome data on teacher behavior or student learning. It synthesizes prior literature and discusses implications rather than evaluating an intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes, samples, or measured impacts are reported for a direct comparison involving teacher planning or coaching. The article provides conceptual discussion only, so there is no observable impact to rate.

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how artificial intelligence is reshaping education and argues that effective use of AI in academic settings depends on three core competencies: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. Rather than evaluating a specific AI intervention with outcome measures, it presents a conceptual discussion grounded in the author’s experience at a Swiss university and supplemented by a narrative literature review.

The paper uses Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich as a case context to describe institutional responses to ChatGPT and similar large language models. It discusses internal AI guidelines for student writing, including transparency requirements for documenting model use, explaining how AI was used, and critically evaluating outputs. It also sketches classroom use cases such as AI experiments, case-study construction, AI-assisted curriculum design, gamification, and immersive technologies.

The main conclusion is that simply allowing or banning AI is insufficient; instead, institutions should build an AI culture through workshops, guidelines, budgeted support, and ongoing faculty and student development. The paper argues that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical reflection can help learners and educators use AI more responsibly, avoid overreliance and hallucinations, and better prepare for an AI-saturated future. It does not report controlled comparisons, quantitative outcome data, or direct evidence of changes in teacher practice or student learning.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI chatbot used for generating and interacting with text, supporting question answering, drafting, and other language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as an example of an AI chatbot/LLM used in education and academic writing; also referenced alongside GPT-3.5/GPT-4 as a model students might use.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's AI chatbot / large language model system for conversational text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned as an example of an AI model students might use in academic work; also referred to via Bard.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic's conversational AI assistant / large language model for text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Listed as an example of an AI model that students might declare using in academic writing.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbot category used for producing text, ideas, images, and other outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: This is a conceptual discussion paper about AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking; it does not empirically compare a named AI coaching or lesson-feedback tool against human coaching or other controls.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual discussion and narrative review with a case-study illustration, not an empirical comparison of an AI coaching or lesson-feedback intervention against human or business-as-usual controls. No causal design, sample, or outcome data are reported for teacher behavior change, revisions, self-efficacy, or student learning.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No intervention effects are reported, and there are no measurable outcomes to classify as positive, negative, or mixed. The paper offers recommendations and examples only, so impact cannot be estimated.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can function as an automated teacher coach by generating classroom-observation scores and instructional feedback from classroom transcripts. The authors frame the work as an exploration of three coaching tasks for generative AI: scoring transcript segments using established observation rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the National Center for Teacher Effectiveness (NCTE) transcript dataset, which includes elementary mathematics observations from 317 teachers across four U.S. school districts serving largely historically marginalized students. The paper evaluates ChatGPT in a zero-shot setting using two established observation systems, CLASS and MQI, and compares model-produced scores against human ratings for transcript segments. For qualitative tasks, two experienced math teachers rate ChatGPT’s responses for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

The findings show that ChatGPT’s score predictions correlate poorly with human scores, often defaulting to generic or middle/high ratings rather than transcript-specific judgments. For feedback generation, the model often produces responses that are relevant on the surface but are frequently unhelpful, non-insightful, or redundant; notably, 82% of suggestions repeat something the teacher already does in the transcript. The authors conclude that current generative AI is not yet ready to replace expert coaching, but may become a useful complement with further development and human oversight.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI assistant based on GPT models, capable of zero-shot text generation and scoring. In this paper it is evaluated as an automated teacher coach for classroom-transcript scoring and feedback generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used zero-shot to (A) predict CLASS and MQI observation scores from elementary math classroom transcript segments, (B) identify highlights and missed opportunities for instructional practice, and (C) generate actionable suggestions for eliciting more student mathematical reasoning; expert math teachers rated the outputs.

findings.finding_summary: On Task A, ChatGPT showed low correspondence with human ratings when predicting classroom observation scores. Reported Spearman correlations between model predictions and human scores were near zero or small across CLASS and MQI items (e.g., CLPC 0.00, CLBM 0.35, CLINSTD -0.01 under DA; EXPL 0.02, REMED 0.05, LANGIMP 0.00, SMQR 0.17 under DA).
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between ChatGPT-predicted observation scores and human annotator scores on CLASS and MQI transcript segments
findings.effect_size: rho range approximately -0.11 to 0.35 across items/prompts
findings.sample_size: n=100 transcript segments for Task A

findings.finding_summary: For Task B, human teachers generally rated ChatGPT's highlights and missed-opportunities feedback as not insightful or not relevant, especially for MQI items. The paper reports that 20-30% of responses were unfaithful, and the proportion of 'No' ratings increased from CLASS to MQI for faithful (22% to 29%), relevant (35% to 55%), and insightful (51% to 71%) judgments.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for model-generated highlights/missed opportunities
findings.sample_size: 216 CLASS examples and 288 MQI examples (teacher-rated subset split between 2 teachers)

findings.finding_summary: For Task C, teachers judged most suggestions to be faithful, relevant, and actionable, but novelty was weak: the model repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript 82% of the time. The paper characterizes the output as useful in some respects but often redundant rather than novel coaching advice.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, actionability, and novelty of suggestions for eliciting student mathematical reasoning

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study using qualitative human ratings plus a small quantitative correlation analysis, not an RCT. The methodology is focused and transparent, but the evidence base is limited and the sample for human evaluation is small.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not show positive downstream impact on teacher practice or student learning. It mainly evaluates the quality of AI-generated feedback artifacts, with mixed usefulness and notable shortcomings, so overall impact is unclear to modest.

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service elementary science teachers incorporated ChatGPT into lesson planning and how they perceived its usefulness and risks. The study is framed around the rapid emergence of generative AI in education and the lack of empirical evidence about how ChatGPT is actually being used for science teaching and learning, especially in teacher preparation contexts.

The intervention/context consisted of a short professional learning experience in a university science education course: participants received four 2-hour sessions introducing ChatGPT, discussing its potential uses in science instruction, and reviewing science teaching strategies. Afterward, 29 pre-service elementary teachers in South Korea created lesson plans that required at least one ChatGPT interaction and attached simulated chats. Researchers analyzed the lesson plans using a modified TPACK-based technology integration rubric and also coded open-ended survey responses about rationale, anticipated benefits, and concerns.

The main findings show that participants envisioned broad uses for ChatGPT across science topics and instructional strategies, with average lesson-plan rubric scores above the midpoint, indicating moderate-to-high competence in integrating ChatGPT. They were strongest in aligning ChatGPT with curriculum goals and instructional strategies, but weaker in selecting specific ChatGPT functions appropriately. Participants expected ChatGPT to support questioning, individualized learning, and formative feedback, but worried about inaccuracies and over-dependence. Importantly, the study evaluates planned AI-integrated artifacts and teacher perceptions, not changes in actual teaching practice or student outcomes, and the authors explicitly call for future controlled studies in real classrooms.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model system for conversational text generation, question answering, and instructional support.
identified_tools.use_case: Pre-service elementary science teachers were asked to integrate ChatGPT into lesson plans for 45-minute science classes, using it for content support, role-play scripting, individualized questioning, formative feedback, and lesson-planning support. The paper evaluated the lesson plans and teachers' perceptions of ChatGPT use; it did not compare ChatGPT against human coaching or other controls in an intervention.

findings.finding_summary: Across 29 lesson plans, the average modified TPACK-based TIAR score was M=3.29 (SD=.91) on a 4-point scale, indicating generally strong perceived quality of ChatGPT integration in lesson planning. Scores were M=3.44 for 'curriculum goals & ChatGPT,' M=3.48 for 'instructional strategies & ChatGPT,' M=3.00 for 'ChatGPT function selection(s),' and M=3.24 for 'fit'; these are evaluations of the planned lesson artifacts, not measured changes in teacher practice or student learning.
findings.measure: Modified TPACK-based TIAR rubric scores for lesson plans

findings.finding_summary: Qualitative responses suggested ChatGPT could help pre-service teachers generate questions, provide individualized support, and offer formative feedback, but also revealed inappropriate or ineffective uses such as relying on nonexistent YouTube links or using ChatGPT for visually demanding tasks. The paper explicitly notes that these are judgments about the suitability of AI-generated planning artifacts and proposed uses, not evidence of actual classroom behavior change.
findings.measure: Qualitative analysis of lesson plans and survey responses about usefulness/concerns

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small qualitative/mixed-methods study of pre-service teachers' lesson plans and perceptions, not a controlled trial or meta-analysis. It provides descriptive evidence about planning quality and anticipated use but no causal evidence of effects on teacher behavior or student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported scores suggest moderately strong lesson-plan integration quality, but there are no measured gains in teacher practice, self-efficacy, or student learning. Because no effect sizes are reported and the study is artifact-focused, the real-world impact remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: To what extent is ChatGPT useful for language teacher lesson plan creation?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can be useful for creating foreign language lesson plans and, more specifically, how prompt specificity affects the quality and consistency of the generated plans. The authors are concerned with a practical problem in language education: teachers often need to design lesson plans with limited curriculum support, and generative AI may help, but its reliability and pedagogical alignment are uncertain.

The study does not evaluate a human intervention with teachers or students. Instead, it tests ChatGPT 4.0 as a lesson-plan generator using five zero-shot prompts that progressively add more detail, including proficiency-level context, a lesson-plan template, world-readiness standards, and a checklist of required criteria. Each prompt was run 10 times, producing 50 AI-generated lesson plans that were scored against a rubric based on best practices and edTPA-related criteria. The paper distinguishes between the quality of the AI-generated artifacts themselves and any changes in teacher practice; it only evaluates the artifacts, not teacher behavior change or student learning.

Results show that ChatGPT often produced generally high-quality lesson plans, but more detailed prompts did not guarantee better outputs. Adding a rubric/checklist improved average output quality more than adding a template alone. The authors also found substantial non-determinism: the same prompt could yield highly variable outputs, sometimes including outdated or less research-aligned pedagogical practices. They conclude that ChatGPT can help streamline lesson planning, but teachers need to critically review and revise outputs, especially to avoid historic biases and weak treatment of culture and communicative practice.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on GPT models, used for conversational text generation and other prompt-based tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate 50 foreign language teacher lesson plans via five zero-shot prompts of increasing specificity; outputs were scored against a lesson-plan rubric aligned to ACTFL and edTPA criteria.

findings.finding_summary: The paper found that ChatGPT could generate generally high-quality lesson plans for language teachers, but output quality did not increase linearly with added prompt specificity. Across 50 generated lesson plans (10 per prompt), mean rubric scores ranged from 19.6/25 to 21.6/25, with the highest mean score occurring when a checklist of required criteria was added (P.5).
findings.measure: Lesson-plan rubric score (presence/absence of 25 criteria aligned to ACTFL/world-readiness standards and edTPA-based template)

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT showed substantial non-determinism: identical prompts produced lesson plans differing by at least five criteria, and scores within prompt groups ranged widely (e.g., P.1 from 16/25 to 23/25; P.5 from 20/25 to 25/25). The authors report that outputs sometimes reflected outdated pedagogical practices and that additional prompt specificity reduced variance but did not guarantee better or more consistent results.
findings.measure: Within-prompt variability in rubric scores / Jaccard dissimilarity across generated lesson plans

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-study, descriptive evaluation of AI-generated lesson plans rather than a controlled comparison against human coaching or student outcomes. It provides clear methods and quantitative rubric scoring, but it is not an experimental study of teacher behavior change.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows moderate-to-high utility for generating lesson-plan artifacts, with mean rubric scores in the 19.621.6/25 range, but no effect size was reported and there was no direct evidence of changes in teacher practice or student learning.

paper_profiles.title: LessonPlanner: Assisting Novice Teachers to Prepare Pedagogy-Driven Lesson Plans with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: UIST '24 (The 37th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge novice teachers face when preparing lesson plans: selecting effective teaching strategies, finding suitable instructional materials, and integrating them into a coherent plan. The authors argue that large language models (LLMs) can help, but that generic chat interfaces like ChatGPT leave teachers with fragmented outputs, high prompting burden, and uncertainty about content quality and pedagogical fit.

To address this, they design LessonPlanner, a web-based LLM tool that structures lesson planning around pedagogical frameworks, especially Gagne’s Nine Events of Instruction and Bloom’s Taxonomy. The system generates lesson goals and outlines, offers preset prompts for common instructional activities, supports block-based editing, and lets teachers refine or regenerate content with context-aware LLM assistance. The paper does not test student learning outcomes; it evaluates the quality of produced lesson plans and the ease of the planning process.

The study includes a formative interview/co-design phase with six novice teachers or teaching assistants, followed by a within-subjects comparison study with 12 university students acting as teachers and an expert interview study with six teachers across university, primary, and high school settings. Compared with a ChatGPT baseline, LessonPlanner improved the rated quality of outcome lesson plans and reduced perceived workload. Experts also judged the tool useful for organizing lesson plans and generating pedagogically relevant ideas, while expressing caution about accuracy and the need for human review. The main conclusion is that pedagogically structured LLM interfaces can better support lesson planning than a general-purpose chat interface, but they should preserve user control and not replace teacher judgment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based conversational large language model used for interactive text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the baseline interface (ChatGPT web app using GPT-4) for lesson-plan preparation, and also referenced by participants in the formative study as a tool for lesson planning.

findings.finding_summary: In the within-subjects study (n=12), LessonPlanner was compared against a baseline ChatGPT web app using the same GPT-4 model for lesson-plan preparation. The paper reports that LessonPlanner significantly improved the quality of outcome lesson plans and reduced workload relative to the ChatGPT baseline, but the excerpt provided does not include the numeric test statistics or effect sizes for the between-condition comparison.
findings.measure: Quality ratings of outcome lesson plans; NASA-TLX workload during lesson planning

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods within-subjects user study with expert interviews, which provides direct comparative evidence but not a randomized classroom impact trial. The excerpt does not report the full statistical detail or effect sizes for the main comparisons.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests a practical improvement in lesson-plan quality and reduced workload versus ChatGPT, but the excerpt does not provide effect sizes. Because the measured outcome is teacher planning rather than student learning, the broader instructional impact remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers and curators collaborated with an AI-assisted lesson planning system, Shiksha Copilot, in low-resource government schools in Karnataka, India. The central problem is whether LLM-based lesson planning tools can produce curriculum-aligned, context-sensitive lesson plans that teachers can actually use and adapt in multilingual, resource-constrained classrooms, while also reducing workload and administrative burden. The study is especially concerned with how teachers evaluate AI-generated lesson plans, how they modify them for classroom use, and how the tool affects their teaching work practices.

Shiksha Copilot used a human-in-the-loop workflow. LLMs generated draft learning objectives and lesson plans from ingested curriculum materials; expert curators reviewed and revised the outputs; the resulting English plans were translated into Kannada and curated again; then teachers accessed the plans and customized them for their own classrooms. The deployment included optional AI features such as lesson-specific chat, general educational chat, and question generation for power users. The study combined platform logs, interviews, and pre/post surveys, and was deployed with 1,043 teachers and 23 curators across public schools in Karnataka.

The paper reports that English lesson plans were generally high quality with relatively few edits, while Kannada translations required extensive linguistic revision. Teachers used the system mainly for both classroom instruction and bureaucratic record-keeping, and they often adapted plans beyond what was captured in the platform logs. Survey and interview findings suggest the tool reduced lesson-planning time and teacher stress, improved access to curriculum-aligned resources, and supported a shift toward more activity-based pedagogy. However, the paper also shows that broader pedagogical change was constrained by structural factors such as staffing shortages and administrative demands. The study concludes that teacher-AI collaboration can be useful in low-resource settings, but only when AI outputs are embedded in human review, local language support, and existing teacher communities of practice.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A human-in-the-loop generative AI lesson-planning system that uses LLMs with retrieval-augmented generation, translation, validation, and teacher/curator review to draft, curate, translate, and customize lesson plans and related instructional materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as Shiksha Copilot, deployed for government-school teachers in Karnataka to generate, curate, translate, and customize bilingual lesson plans, plus optional lesson-specific and general educational chat and question generation support.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods deployment with 1,043 teachers, the paper reports that Shiksha Copilot reduced bureaucratic workload and lesson planning time. Survey and interview data indicate teachers used the system to prepare lesson plans more efficiently and to satisfy record-keeping requirements, but the paper does not report a controlled comparison or a single overall effect size.
findings.measure: Lesson planning time; administrative/record-keeping workload; teacher-reported workload reduction

findings.finding_summary: The study reports lower teaching-related stress after adoption of the tool. Stress was measured with the Teacher Stress Scale in matched pre/post surveys; however, the paper excerpt provided does not report the numerical pre/post change or an effect size, and the design is not a controlled comparison against human coaching or business-as-usual.
findings.measure: Teacher Stress Scale (teaching demands and school-based support subscales)

findings.finding_summary: The paper finds a shift toward activity-based pedagogy and broader changes in teaching practices, but these are described qualitatively and through log analysis rather than as an experimentally estimated effect. Teachers adapted lesson plans, used AI-generated plans for classroom instruction, and relied on their own expertise and peer networks to refine content; however, the paper does not distinguish these practice changes from evaluation of the AI-generated lesson-plan artifacts with a causal design.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported instructional practice change; content-block edits to lesson plans; teacher ratings of lesson plans
findings.sample_size: n=22 interviews; logs for 5,544 teacher-created lesson plans; 991 curated lesson plans

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods field deployment with surveys, interviews, and log analysis, which provides useful real-world evidence but not a randomized or directly controlled comparison against human coaching, peer feedback, rubric-only self-review, or business-as-usual. The paper reports descriptive and pre/post changes, but the excerpt does not include controlled causal estimates or complete statistical results.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful practical benefits such as reduced lesson-planning burden and stress, plus qualitative shifts toward activity-based pedagogy, but no effect sizes are provided in the excerpt. Because the design is not a controlled comparison and the magnitude of change is unclear, the impact tier is best treated as modest/uncertain.

paper_profiles.title: Understanding Teacher Revisions of Large Language Model-Generated Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers revise large language model (LLM)-generated formative feedback before it is delivered to students. The central problem is that most prior evaluations of AI feedback focus on output quality in isolation, while ignoring the human mediation step that determines what students actually receive. The authors ask which textual characteristics are associated with revision, whether revision can be predicted from the AI text alone, and how revisions change the pedagogical type of feedback.

The study analyzes 1,349 AI-generated feedback drafts and corresponding teacher-delivered versions from 117 teachers using the Tutoria feedback platform. The platform was integrated with Moodle and Google Classroom and used in short open-ended response tasks across multiple educational contexts, including Brazilian high school chemistry and higher-education computer science activities. Teachers could accept feedback as-is, edit it, or fully rewrite it; the analysis compares unrevised versus revised feedback and codes feedback types such as corrective and high-information feedback.

The main findings are that teachers accepted AI feedback unchanged in about 78% of cases, and when they edited, they usually shortened the feedback while preserving most of its meaning. Revision decisions could be predicted only modestly from the AI text alone (best AUC about 0.75), suggesting that contextual factors beyond the text matter. Qualitative coding showed that revisions often moved feedback away from overly explanatory, high-information responses toward more concise corrective forms. The paper concludes that teacher revision should be treated as a key part of evaluating AI feedback systems, since default model behavior is often delivered directly to students with little modification.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model–based system that generates formative feedback drafts for students, which teachers can accept, edit, or rewrite before delivery.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as the source of AI-generated formative feedback drafts within the Tutoria platform; the paper analyzes how 117 teachers revise those drafts rather than evaluating student outcomes from the AI system itself.

findings.finding_summary: Across 1,349 feedback instances from 117 teachers, teachers accepted AI feedback without modification in 77.8% of cases (1050/1349). Edited feedback was slightly longer than unedited feedback (48.3 vs. 41.9 words; mean within-teacher difference 6.4 words), suggesting that most revisions were limited and that AI feedback often reduced teacher editing effort.
findings.measure: Teacher revision/acceptance rate; feedback length and within-teacher length difference

findings.finding_summary: Text-only models could predict whether AI feedback would be revised with above-chance performance, but only modestly. On the holdout set, ROC AUC ranged from 0.698 to 0.746 across models, with balanced accuracy ranging from 0.535 to 0.672 and Cohen’s κ from 0.095 to 0.387, indicating limited but nontrivial predictability of teacher editing behavior from the AI text alone.
findings.measure: Binary prediction of whether teacher revised AI feedback

findings.finding_summary: When AI-generated feedback was revised, its pedagogical type shifted: initial AI feedback was more often high-information (59.9%) than corrective (40.1%), but final teacher feedback became more balanced (48.0% high-information, 43.5% corrective). The shift from high-information to other forms was statistically significant (Cramér’s V = 0.12), showing that teachers often simplified or reframed AI-generated feedback rather than wholesale rewriting it.
findings.measure: Feedback type classification before vs. after teacher revision

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods observational analysis of teacher revisions to AI-generated feedback, not a controlled intervention study. The evidence is useful for describing real-world use, but causal claims about impact on teachers or students are not supported here.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows substantial teacher uptake of AI feedback and modestly predictable revision behavior, but it does not report direct effects on teacher practice change beyond editing patterns, nor any student learning outcomes. Impact is therefore informative but limited.

paper_profiles.title: Crowd Coach: Peer Coaching for Crowd Workers’ Skill Growth
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to support skill development for crowd workers without relying on expert mentors or requesters. The authors argue that crowd work platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk do not naturally support workers’ learning and advancement, even though workers want to improve their speed and quality over time. To address this, they designed Crowd Coach, a Chrome extension that lets workers both give and receive very short peer coaching snippets while completing tasks.

The system has two main parts: Micro-Coaching, which lets workers submit brief advice for specific task types, and Selective Coaching, which ranks coaching snippets using peer assessments so workers see advice others found useful. The study focuses on crowd workers doing AMT tasks, especially novice workers doing audio transcription. The controlled field experiment compared three conditions: no coaching, random coaching snippets, and selected peer coaching via Crowd Coach. Participants were 90 novice AMT workers randomly assigned to conditions.

Results showed that workers receiving selected peer coaching completed audio transcription tasks significantly faster than those in the control or random-coaching conditions, while accuracy did not significantly differ. A deployment study with 179 installed users further showed that workers actively used the system across many task types and generally found it useful. The paper concludes that lightweight peer coaching can improve worker speed without hurting quality and may support informal on-the-job skill growth in crowd work.

identified_tools.name: Crowd Coach
identified_tools.description: A browser plugin / crowd-work system that provides peer micro-coaching snippets to workers while they are completing tasks, with voting-based selection of higher-quality advice.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as an on-the-job peer coaching tool for AMT workers, compared against no coaching and random coaching snippets in a controlled field experiment, and also examined in a real-world deployment.

findings.finding_summary: In a controlled field experiment with 90 novice AMT workers, Crowd Coach was compared with a no-coaching control and a random-coaching condition on audio transcription tasks. The paper reports significant differences across conditions for task accuracy and completion time (MANOVA F(2,74)=17.53, p<0.0001); completion time was significantly lower in the Crowd Coach condition (M=184.1, SD=12.36) than control (M=262.79, SD=37.38) and random coaching (M=284.21, SD=46.44), while accuracy was not significantly different (F(2,74)=2.47, p=.09).
findings.measure: Audio transcription completion time and word error rate / accuracy
findings.sample_size: n=90 (26 control, 26 random coaching, 25 Crowd Coach completed all tasks)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled field experiment with random assignment and a real-world deployment, which provides stronger evidence than purely qualitative work. However, it is not a K-12 education study and the outcome is task performance in crowd work rather than teacher learning, so the overall evidence is moderately strong but context-limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced a clear reduction in completion time in the experimental condition, with no measurable loss in accuracy. That suggests a modest-to-medium practical effect on worker efficiency, though it does not speak to teacher practice or student learning.

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether K-12 educators prefer generative AI-produced lesson plans over human-created lesson plans, and which lesson-plan components drive those preferences. The authors address a gap in the literature by directly comparing lesson plans authored by human curriculum designers with plans generated by a customized GPT-4 model and a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model.

The study used a controlled pairwise preference design with 20 experienced K-12 mathematics educators. Participants evaluated 529 lesson-plan pairs across warm-up, main task, cool-down, and overall quality dimensions, while blinded to the source of each plan. In addition to binary preference judgments, educators provided written comments that were analyzed thematically and with topic modeling. The context was K-12 mathematics lesson planning across elementary, middle, and high school grade bands.

Results show that human-authored plans were generally preferred overall and especially for warm-up activities, main tasks, student discourse, and inclusive supports. GenAI lesson plans were comparatively stronger in cool-down activities and were more competitive at higher grade levels, particularly for structured and summarizing components. The paper concludes that GenAI is best viewed as a planning assistant that can complement, rather than replace, educator expertise; however, these findings evaluate artifacts (lesson plans) rather than downstream changes in teacher practice or student learning.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used to generate structured lesson plans and instructional text.
identified_tools.use_case: Compared customized prompt-based GPT-4 lesson plans against human curriculum designer-created plans and fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b lesson plans in K-12 mathematics lesson planning.

findings.finding_summary: This was a controlled preference study of lesson-plan artifacts, not a study of changes in teacher practice. Customized GPT-4 lesson plans were preferred 57.7% of the time in GPT-4 vs. LLaMA-2-13b comparisons, but human curriculum designer plans were preferred 58.7% over GPT-4 overall. For specific components, GPT-4 was preferred for cool-down activities (59.7% vs. human-created plans) but less often for warm-up, main tasks, and overall quality.
findings.measure: Educator binary preference for lesson-plan artifacts across warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta family large language model used here as a fine-tuned lesson-plan generator.
identified_tools.use_case: Compared fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b lesson plans against customized GPT-4 lesson plans and human curriculum designer plans in K-12 mathematics lesson planning.

findings.finding_summary: This was a controlled preference study of lesson-plan artifacts, not a study of changes in teacher practice. Fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b plans were preferred 46.4% in direct comparison with human-created plans (human 53.6%). LLaMA-2-13b performed relatively better on cool-down activities (57.9% preferred over human plans) and in high school comparisons, where it was preferred over human plans 59.2% to 40.8%.
findings.measure: Educator binary preference for lesson-plan artifacts across warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The paper uses a mixed-method comparative preference design with experienced educators, but it does not evaluate learning outcomes or causal effects on teacher practice. Evidence is observational and artifact-focused rather than an intervention study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes are reported, and the outcomes are preference shares rather than demonstrated changes in teaching behavior or student learning. The study suggests moderate practical relevance for lesson-plan generation, but impact on instruction is indirect and unquantified.

paper_profiles.title: Tailoring Education with GenAI: A New Horizon in Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a generative AI tool can support educators in creating customized lesson plans and learning scenarios more efficiently and with better personalization than traditional approaches. The authors frame the problem as one of lesson planning that often fails to account for diverse student needs, and they argue that GenAI may help educators generate more adaptive, context-sensitive instructional materials.

The intervention is a "Learning Scenario Assistant" built with interactive prompt engineering. The tool uses a staged dialogue process: positioning prompts, structured questions about audience/topic/goals/format/duration/examples, follow-up prompts, iterative revision, and a final human-editing phase. The paper presents an example lesson-planning workflow for a university Digital Humanities course and also describes use of the tool across preschool, secondary school, and university levels in English and Greek.

The evaluation is primarily about the quality of AI-generated artifacts, not direct measurement of changes in teacher practice or student learning. The authors compare outputs from ChatGPT, Llama, and Google Bard using quantitative ratings, teacher/expert qualitative feedback, and linguistic analysis (token counts and LDA topics). They report that newer models such as ChatGPT 4 and Llama 2 70B generally performed best on relevance, coherence, personalization, and related criteria, while also noting that some outputs contained inaccuracies. The paper concludes that GenAI can reduce lesson-planning time and produce useful personalized drafts, but it emphasizes the need for human oversight, ethical caution, and further validation, including future randomized trials.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based conversational AI system used for generating and revising text outputs from user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as one of several large language models for generating personalized lesson plans/learning scenarios via interactive prompting and iterative revision.

findings.finding_summary: In the English learning-scenario evaluation, ChatGPT 4 received the highest quantitative scores among the models on relevance, accuracy, creativity, engagement, personalization, and coherence, with response time also scored. The paper reports mean ratings (1–5 Likert scale) but no inferential statistics; the tool was evaluated as a lesson-plan generator, not as a change in teacher practice.
findings.measure: Expert-scored quantitative ratings of AI-generated learning scenarios (relevance, accuracy, creativity, engagement, personalization, coherence, response time)

findings.finding_summary: In the Greek learning-scenario evaluation, ChatGPT 4 again scored highest or near-highest across most quantitative categories, and the authors state it consistently produced relevant, understandable, measurable, and operationally practical outputs. No inferential statistics or sample size are reported; this is an evaluation of generated artifacts rather than evidence of teacher behavior change.
findings.measure: Expert-scored quantitative and qualitative ratings of AI-generated Greek learning scenarios

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta’s open-weight LLaMA family of large language models used for text generation and interactive prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as one of several LLMs for generating personalized lesson plans in English and Greek and for comparing output quality across model sizes.

findings.finding_summary: In the English evaluation, Llama 2 70B generally scored among the highest on several quantitative criteria, while Llama 2 13B excelled in creativity and response time; however, the paper notes that Llama 2 70B sometimes produced inaccurate content such as non-existent resource links. The study evaluates output quality only and does not measure teacher practice change, self-efficacy, or student learning.
findings.measure: Expert-scored quantitative ratings and linguistic analysis of AI-generated English learning scenarios

findings.finding_summary: In the Greek evaluation, Llama 2 70B and the other Llama models generally performed well, with Llama 2 70B described as strong in balancing simplicity and complexity. The results are descriptive, based on model outputs, and no human-comparison intervention effects on teachers are reported.
findings.measure: Expert-scored quantitative and qualitative ratings plus token/topic analysis of AI-generated Greek learning scenarios

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s conversational generative AI system, including Bard/Gemini-family models, used for text generation and interactive prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as Google Bard in the paper’s comparisons of multiple LLMs for lesson-plan generation in English and Greek.

findings.finding_summary: Google Bard was included in the model comparison and generally scored lower than ChatGPT 4 and Llama 2 70B on several dimensions such as coherence, engagement, creativity, and personalization, though it was relatively strong on response time. These are descriptive ratings of generated lesson plans, not measures of changes in teacher behavior or student outcomes.
findings.measure: Expert-scored quantitative ratings of AI-generated learning scenarios

findings.finding_summary: For Greek learning scenarios, Google Bard again tended to score lower in coherence, creativity, and personalization, while showing strength in response time. The paper discusses variability in output quality across languages but provides no causal estimate on teaching practice or learning.
findings.measure: Expert-scored quantitative and qualitative ratings of AI-generated Greek learning scenarios

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods descriptive evaluation of generated lesson-plan artifacts across several LLMs, with qualitative and Likert-scale ratings but no randomized comparison of teacher outcomes. It provides useful early evidence on output quality, but not on causal effects in teacher practice.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally favorable ratings for some models and practical time-savings claims, but no effect sizes, no controlled teacher-behavior outcomes, and no student learning data. The impact is therefore suggestive but unclear for the requested teacher-planning and professional-learning question.

paper_profiles.title: New Curriculum, New Chance – Retrieval Augmented Generation for Lesson Planning in Ugandan Secondary Schools. Prototype Quality Evaluation.
paper_profiles.venue: Ndejje University Second Annual Research Dissemination Symposium 2024
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This working paper addresses the challenge of weak or outdated lesson planning in Ugandan secondary schools, especially in the context of a new competency-based curriculum. The authors argue that teachers need support to create curriculum-aligned lesson plans efficiently and with sufficient technical quality, particularly in rural settings where access to materials and time may be limited.

To address this, they developed the NDU Lesson Plan Generator, a prototype that uses Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) with a Cohere LLM, sentence embeddings, and LangChain. The system retrieves content from government-accredited textbooks and generates lesson plans in the Ugandan lesson plan format. The prototype was trained on three Secondary 1 textbooks (ICT, Mathematics, and History/Political Education), and the generated plans were produced using a pseudo-random topic selection protocol.

The evaluation was limited to artifact quality rather than classroom impact: 24 generated lesson plans were rated by three independent raters using an adapted Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP). The plans averaged roughly 75–80% and were judged comparable to or better than human-created plans reported in related East African studies. The paper concludes that the generated lesson plans meet technical quality standards for classroom use, but it does not measure teacher behavior change, lesson revisions in practice, teacher self-efficacy, or student learning outcomes.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI / large language model-based system that uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to produce customized lesson plans from curriculum-aligned source materials.
identified_tools.use_case: A prototype lesson plan generator (NLPG) was built with Cohere LLM, Sentence Embeddings, and LangChain, then used to generate 24 lesson plans for secondary school subjects in Uganda for technical quality evaluation.

findings.finding_summary: The generated lesson plans were rated as technically strong on the LPAP by three independent raters. Across 24 plans, the average quality was reported as 75–80%, corresponding to a 'very good lesson plan'; none scored below 65%, and one plan had a topic mismatch (History07.pdf).
findings.measure: Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP) technical quality ratings of generated lesson plans

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a prototype evaluation of generated artifacts, not a controlled study of teacher behavior change or student outcomes. The methodology is transparent and uses multiple raters, but it remains a technical quality assessment in a working paper/grey literature context.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported quality scores (75–80%) suggest promising artifact quality, but no teacher practice change, self-efficacy, or student learning impact was measured. The study shows potential utility for lesson planning, yet the practical impact on education outcomes is unestablished.

paper_profiles.title: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Abductive Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of improving learning efficiency in complex reinforcement learning tasks by combining hierarchical reinforcement learning with symbolic planning. The authors argue that conventional symbolic planners used in hierarchical RL are limited when the state space is unknown, when multiple goals exist, and when reward priorities must be considered during planning.

The proposed approach uses an abductive symbolic planner at the high level and a reinforcement learning component at the low level. The abductive planner generates a plan from observations and prior knowledge, and the RL component executes subgoals derived from that plan while receiving intrinsic rewards for subgoal completion. The paper modifies weighted abduction to include task-specific expected reward so that the planner can select more promising plans, not just the most plausible explanations.

The study is implemented and evaluated in a Minecraft-like grid-world domain with partial observability, delayed reward, multiple goals, and randomized layouts. No human participants, teachers, or students are involved; the paper is a computational methods paper. Empirically, the abductive version outperforms a no-planner baseline and a fixed-goal hierarchical baseline in cumulative reward and learning efficiency, showing that abduction can help high-level planning in unpredictable domains.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: A general hierarchical reinforcement learning system that uses abductive symbolic planning as a high-level planner and reinforcement learning as a low-level planner.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a proposed architecture for hierarchical RL; the paper evaluates an abduction-based planner versus no planner and a fixed-goal planner in a Minecraft-like virtual world.

findings.finding_summary: In the evaluation domain, the proposed ABDUCTIVE model achieved much more cumulative reward than NO-PLANNER and FIXED-GOAL and learned more efficiently across training episodes. The authors report results averaged over 5 independent trials, with performance plotted over a sliding window of 500 episodes, but no numeric effect size is reported.
findings.measure: Cumulative reward over training episodes

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical / algorithmic AI paper, not an education study, and it does not evaluate teacher planning, coaching, or student learning. The reported experiment concerns reinforcement learning performance in a virtual world, so the evidence is not applicable to the requested education research topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention or teacher outcome is measured, and no interpretable effect size is reported. The paper's findings are about computational learning efficiency rather than educational impact.

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Large Language Models Creation of Interactive Learning Lessons
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can automatically generate high-quality scenario-based tutor training lessons for novice human tutors in middle school mathematics. The authors focus on the lesson creation problem itself rather than on learner outcomes, asking how much task decomposition in prompting affects lesson quality and whether LLM-generated lessons compare favorably with expert human-crafted lessons.

The intervention studied is a Retrieval-Augmented Generation workflow using GPT-4o to generate English tutor-training lessons across five sections: title page, two tutoring scenarios, instructional content, and a conclusion. The authors compare one-, two-, three-, four-, and five-segment prompting strategies, with the generated lessons evaluated by two experienced human coders using a 17-code rubric. For the human comparison, two expert lesson designers reviewed the best-performing three-segment outputs and provided structured written feedback.

The population and context are novice human tutors preparing to teach middle school mathematics online through scenario-based professional learning materials. The paper reports that three-segment decomposition produced the best overall lesson ratings, while one-segment generation was weakest and five-segment generation was not consistently better. Human reviewers praised the AI-generated lessons for saving time, producing varied scenarios, and supporting human-AI collaboration, but noted weaknesses in feedback specificity, clarity, and citation authenticity. The study concludes that LLMs can support lesson drafting, but human review remains necessary, and the paper does not test whether these AI-generated lessons change tutor behavior, teacher self-efficacy, or student learning.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI GPT-family large language model used here via GPT-4o for retrieval-augmented, prompt-engineered generation of structured tutor training lessons.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to automatically generate interactive, scenario-based tutor training lessons on three topics, with outputs created under one-, two-, three-, four-, and five-segment prompting strategies and compared against human-crafted lessons using human rubric ratings and designer feedback.

findings.finding_summary: Human raters evaluated GPT-4o-generated tutor training lessons using a 17-code rubric. The three-segment prompting strategy received the highest average lesson rating (14.67), compared with 10.67 for one-segment generation, indicating better apparent lesson quality with moderate decomposition. The paper also notes that five-segment generation was slightly worse than three-segment generation (13.33 vs. 14.67), suggesting diminishing returns from excessive decomposition.
findings.measure: Human rubric ratings of generated lesson quality
findings.sample_size: n=3 lessons generated per prompting condition

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-study, qualitative/mixed-methods evaluation of AI-generated lesson artifacts, not a controlled outcome study of teacher behavior change or learning. Evidence is useful but limited to human judgments of content quality and designer reflections.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful differences in rubric ratings across prompting strategies, but it does not provide standardized effect sizes or demonstrate impacts on teacher practice or student outcomes. The observed gains concern artifact quality rather than downstream educational impact.

paper_profiles.title: Exercise with Social Robots: Companion or Coach?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what role a social robot should play in exercise contexts: a fitness companion that works out alongside the user, or a fitness coach that demonstrates exercises and corrects mistakes. The motivation is to understand how people perceive different robot roles in physical exercise and whether a coach-like role is more acceptable or usable than a companion role.

The study used an online questionnaire built around a pictured and video-described NICO humanoid robot. Participants were shown exercise scenarios and then asked to imagine the robot either as a fitness companion or as a fitness coach. The comparison was not about actual exercise outcomes or behavior change, but about perceptions of the robot artifact, using the Coach-Athlete Relationship Questionnaire, a mind perception scale, and the System Usability Scale.

The sample was very small: 16 respondents completed the questionnaire, and the paper treats the results as preliminary. Across all three measures, the coach condition was rated slightly higher than the companion condition, suggesting that participants found the coach framing more mind-like, more relationship-supportive, and more usable. The authors conclude that the coach persona may be a promising direction for future work, but emphasize that the study is limited by its imagined, non-interactive setup and small sample size.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic social robot / AI-enabled coach concept used to deliver instruction, reminders, demonstrations, and corrective feedback in a physical exercise context.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper compares imagined roles for the NICO social robot as either a fitness companion or a fitness coach; the coach role includes showing exercises to copy and correcting movement mistakes.

findings.finding_summary: This paper does not report academic outcomes or teacher outcomes. It is a pilot questionnaire study in which participants imagined exercising with NICO; the coach condition was rated slightly higher than the companion condition on mind perception, coach-athlete relationship, and usability, but no behavioral change or learning outcome was measured.
findings.measure: Mind perception (agency, experience), CART-Q, System Usability Scale (SUS)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small questionnaire-based HRI study, not an educational intervention study, and it does not evaluate instructional coaching or teacher planning. The evidence is preliminary and descriptive with no inferential statistics reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported differences are modest and pertain only to participant perceptions of a robot coach versus companion, not to educational or teacher practice outcomes. No effect size is reported, so impact on the requested domains is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Fine-Tuning Large Language Models for Educational Support: Leveraging Gagné’s Nine Events of Instruction for Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.venue: Conference Proceedings of the 28th Global Chinese Conference on Computers in Education (GCCCE 2024)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models (LLMs) can be adapted to support educational lesson planning and classroom dialogue generation using Gagné’s Nine Events of Instruction. The authors argue that current general-purpose LLMs are not sufficiently tailored to educational contexts, requiring more structured prompting or model adaptation to produce pedagogically useful outputs.

The paper proposes two approaches: prompt tuning with chain-of-thought (CoT) prompts for models such as ChatGPT, and model fine-tuning using LoRA for open-source models such as ChatGLM and Llama-based systems. The work is built around a dataset assembled from math curriculum standards, examples of Gagné-aligned instructional dialogue, and teacher utterances from real classrooms, all manually reviewed and curated by educators and subject matter experts.

The intended context is compulsory education mathematics in East China Normal University-affiliated settings, with the system designed to support teachers in classroom dialogue assessment and in generating lesson dialogue plans. The paper mainly reports a pipeline, dataset construction process, and evaluation plan using automatic metrics and human judgment; it does not present controlled outcome evidence on teacher behavior change, lesson revisions, or student learning. Its conclusion is that structured prompting and fine-tuning can make LLMs more educationally aligned and potentially useful for instructional design and evaluation.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s generative large language model chatbot used for prompting, dialogue generation, and educational text analysis.
identified_tools.use_case: Used via the ChatGPT API and direct prompts/CoT prompting to generate teacher dialogue templates and to support analysis/alignment with Gagné’s Nine Events of Instruction; also compared as a baseline against fine-tuned/open-source models in generating educational dialogue.

findings.finding_summary: The paper does not report teacher behavior change, lesson revision outcomes, teacher self-efficacy, or student learning for ChatGPT. It describes ChatGPT-generated outputs being reviewed for alignment with Gagné’s Nine Events of Instruction and curriculum standards, but no quantitative results for educational impact are provided in the text.
findings.measure: Alignment/quality of generated teacher dialogue judged by educators; BLEU-4 and ROUGE are listed as evaluation metrics for model outputs

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta’s open-weight large language model family used for generation and fine-tuning tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as an open-source baseline/fine-tuning target (Llama2-7B) for generating teacher dialogue aligned with Gagn�e9’s Nine Events of Instruction.
