findings.finding_summary: The paper does not report downstream teacher or student outcomes for LLaMA. It only states that Llama2-7B was fine-tuned and evaluated on generated dialogue quality using BLEU-4, ROUGE, and human review, without reporting numerical performance in the provided text.
findings.measure: Generated dialogue quality/alignment with instructional events; BLEU-4 and ROUGE

identified_tools.name: ChatGLM
identified_tools.description: An open-source generative large language model used here as a fine-tuning base for educational dialogue generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Fine-tuned with LoRA to generate teacher classroom dialogue and analyze instructional alignment with Gagn�e9’s Nine Events of Instruction.

findings.finding_summary: No teacher practice, self-efficacy, or student learning outcomes are reported for ChatGLM. The paper only states that ChatGLM3-7B was fine-tuned and assessed with BLEU-4, ROUGE, and educator review of generated dialogue quality and alignment.
findings.measure: Generated dialogue quality/alignment with instructional principles; BLEU-4 and ROUGE

identified_tools.name: Qwen
identified_tools.description: Alibaba’s Qwen large language model family used for open-source generation/fine-tuning tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a baseline model (Qwen-7B) for generating educational dialogue templates aligned to Gagn�e9’s instructional events.

findings.finding_summary: The paper does not provide outcome data for teacher behavior change or learner impact from Qwen. It only indicates Qwen-7B was among the models fine-tuned and evaluated on text generation quality and human judgments.
findings.measure: Generated dialogue quality/alignment with Gagn�e9’s Nine Events; BLEU-4 and ROUGE

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a methodological/model-development paper rather than an empirical study of educator outcomes. It reports planned or in-process evaluation of generated text, but no clear quantitative outcome data on teacher behavior, self-efficacy, or student learning.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No impact estimates are reported for educational outcomes, and no direct comparison against human coaching, peer feedback, or business-as-usual is provided. The evidence in the text is limited to artifact quality and intended evaluation procedures.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This longitudinal intervention study examines whether an analytical AI feedback platform can support lesson planning in vocational teacher education, and whether it can compare favorably with human feedback. The paper addresses a practical problem in teacher education: providing detailed, individualized feedback on complex lesson plans is time-consuming for instructors, yet such feedback is important for developing planning competence.

The intervention used an analytical AI platform called EDDA, which classifies lesson plans and returns individualized expert feedback based on a trained coding framework. The experimental group received AI feedback during a semester and could then discuss results with a university teacher if needed, while the control group received human feedback only. The study involved 103 master’s students in business education in Germany, working in small groups on 90-minute lesson plans under shared course conditions.

The main outcomes were ratings of lesson-plan quality across multiple didactic dimensions, plus questionnaire-based meta-dimensions such as AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competence, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and motivation. The findings suggest that AI feedback can match or surpass human feedback on some lesson-planning dimensions, especially certain sustainability-related and didactic planning aspects. However, the authors also conclude that simply using AI did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, motivation, or digital self-efficacy, indicating that AI feedback is best understood as a supplement to, not a replacement for, human guidance within a broader pedagogical framework.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative or AI-based feedback system used to provide individualized lesson-plan feedback; in this paper the specific platform is actually an analytical AI platform rather than a named commercial chatbot.
identified_tools.use_case: Compared AI-generated lesson-plan feedback from the EDDA platform against human feedback in a longitudinal teacher-education intervention; students in the experimental group received AI feedback first and could then request human clarification.

findings.finding_summary: In a longitudinal intervention with N=103 vocational business education master's students, the AI-feedback group (n=55) received higher ratings than the human-feedback control group (n=48) on some lesson-planning dimensions, including social competences for sustainable development and reflexivity (both reported as significant positive intervention effects). The paper also reports a significant positive intervention effect for SDG 15 (life on land), while several other planning dimensions showed no significant group effect.
findings.measure: Content-analysis ratings of lesson plans on planning dimensions and sustainability-related categories

findings.finding_summary: The intervention had a significant positive effect on social competences for sustainable development, meaning students in the experimental group received higher ratings than the control group on communicative strategies for overcoming conflict in a sustainability-focused company setting. A significant positive effect was also reported for reflexivity.
findings.measure: Ratings of social competences for sustainable development and reflexivity in lesson plans

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal controlled intervention with an experimental and control group, but assignment was not randomized in a traditional sense and the sample is modest. The paper relies on coded lesson plans and self-report measures, so it is reasonably strong but not top-tier experimental evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant improvements on some planning dimensions, but effect sizes are not reported and the described effects are specific rather than large. Evidence of broader teacher-practice or student-learning impact is not clearly demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing university level English proficiency with generative AI: Empirical insights into automated feedback and learning outcomes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can improve university students’ writing outcomes when used as automated feedback during essay revision. The authors focus on large language model (LLM)-based feedback and ask whether such feedback improves the quality of revised work and how students experience the process emotionally and motivationally.

The intervention used GPT-3.5-turbo to generate feedback on an argumentative essay written by first-year English-language students at a university in Hong Kong. In a two-hour lab session, 918 students wrote an essay, then were randomly assigned to either receive AI-generated feedback or receive no feedback before revising their work. Both the original and revised essays were instructor-marked. The study also collected questionnaire data on students’ emotions, motivation, and engagement during revision, and interviewed 16 students in the feedback group about their experiences.

Results showed that students who received AI feedback improved more on their revised essays than those in the control group, with statistically significant gains, although the effect size was weak. Motivation and engagement were also slightly higher in the feedback group and were strongly associated with revision improvement, while positive emotion showed a weaker and statistically non-significant difference. Interview data suggested that students generally found the feedback useful and task-relevant, but emotional responses were mixed and some students compared AI feedback unfavorably with human feedback. The paper concludes that LLM-based feedback can modestly improve revised writing, likely by increasing motivation and engagement rather than by uniformly improving emotional experience.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-based large language model chatbot / generative AI system used to generate written feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate automated essay feedback for university students’ revision of an argumentative essay; the feedback was produced by submitting student papers plus task instructions and learning objectives to GPT 3.5.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized controlled trial with first-year university language students, the group receiving GPT-generated feedback improved more from original to revised essays than the no-feedback control group. The feedback group’s mean improvement was 7.588 versus 4.474 for controls, with a between-group mean difference of 3.113 and p=0.00360; the point-biserial correlation between receiving AI feedback and score improvement was r=0.208.
findings.measure: Difference between original and revised essay scores / essay revision score improvement

findings.finding_summary: Students who received GPT-generated feedback reported higher motivation and engagement during revision than the control group, while positive emotion differences were not statistically significant. Motivation differed by 1.701 points (p=0.00004) and engagement by 0.979 points (p=0.0346); positive emotion differed by 0.794 points but was not significant (p=0.0611).
findings.measure: Self-reported motivation, engagement, and positive emotion during revision
findings.effect_size: motivation: r=0.29; engagement: r=0.152; emotion: r=0.135

findings.finding_summary: Correlational analyses suggested that motivation and engagement were strongly associated with revision score gains across both groups, but the study could not isolate whether the AI feedback itself or the associated motivational/engagement changes drove the improvements. The authors explicitly note that the design does not allow evaluation of the accuracy, relevance, or helpfulness of the AI guidance itself, separate from changes in student practice.
findings.measure: Association between revision score gains and motivation/engagement; interpretation of AI feedback mechanism

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled trial, but it includes mixed methods and the reported outcomes are primarily post-intervention revision scores and self-reports rather than a full blinded efficacy design. The study also notes limitations in attributing effects specifically to the feedback content versus motivation/engagement changes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main academic outcome shows a statistically significant but small effect (r=0.208) on essay revision improvement, which falls in the modest-impact range. The behavioral/self-report outcomes are statistically significant for motivation and engagement but weaker in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether analytical AI feedback can support lesson planning in vocational teacher education and whether it can perform as well as or better than human feedback. The authors focus on a practical problem in teacher education: providing detailed, individualized feedback on lesson plans is time-consuming for instructors, yet essential for developing planning competence.

The intervention was EDDA, an analytical AI platform that classifies lesson-plan text and returns individualized expert feedback on didactic and planning dimensions. In the longitudinal study, an experimental group received AI-generated feedback across a semester and could then discuss the results with a university teacher if needed, while a control group received human feedback only. The participants were master’s students in business education in Germany who planned 90-minute vocational lessons in small groups under the same course conditions.

The main outcome was the quality of lesson plans, evaluated through content analysis of submitted plans at the beginning and end of the semester. The study also measured meta-dimensions such as AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competences, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and motivation through questionnaires. Results suggest that AI feedback can match or exceed human feedback on some planning dimensions, especially sustainability-related aspects, social competences, and reflexivity, but that simply using the AI tool did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, motivation, or related self-efficacy. The authors conclude that analytical AI can be a useful supplement to traditional feedback, but only within a broader pedagogical framework.

identified_tools.name: EDDA
identified_tools.description: An analytical AI platform for lesson planning that analyzes uploaded lesson plans/materials using a BERT-based classifier and returns individualized expert-level textual and visual feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used across a longitudinal intervention in vocational teacher education to provide feedback on lesson plans throughout a semester, compared against human feedback only.

findings.finding_summary: In a longitudinal intervention with N=103 teacher education students (experimental n=55; control n=48), AI feedback matched or surpassed human feedback on some lesson-planning dimensions. The experimental group received significantly higher ratings for social competences for sustainable development (p<0.05) and reflexivity (p<0.10), and a positive intervention effect was also reported for SDG 15 (life on land) (p<0.10).
findings.measure: Content analysis ratings of lesson plans for sustainability-related planning dimensions

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that higher prior starting points were associated with less growth across the semester for all sustainable change agent competence dimensions. This reflects teacher lesson-plan development rather than evaluation of AI-generated artifacts alone.
findings.measure: Growth in lesson-plan ratings across the semester

findings.finding_summary: For the meta-dimensions collected via questionnaire, the authors report that mere use of the AI platform did not automatically enhance AI literacy, change attitudes, or improve motivation. The experimental group was not described as outperforming the control group on these broader self-report outcomes.
findings.measure: AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competences, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and motivation questionnaires

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal two-group intervention with comparison to human feedback, but assignment was not randomized in a traditional sense and groups came from different course contexts, so it is stronger than qualitative work but not a fully rigorous RCT.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant improvements on some lesson-plan dimensions, but the summary does not provide effect sizes and the reported effects are generally modest and domain-specific rather than broad or large.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can function as an automated teacher coach for classroom instruction. The authors frame teacher coaching as a widespread but resource-constrained part of teacher professional learning, and investigate whether a generative AI system can provide useful feedback on instructional practice.

The study proposes three zero-shot coaching tasks for ChatGPT: scoring transcript segments using classroom observation rubrics (CLASS and MQI), identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generating actionable suggestions for eliciting more student mathematical reasoning. The model is evaluated on elementary math classroom transcripts from the NCTE dataset, which contains video-derived transcripts from 4th- and 5th-grade mathematics lessons in U.S. schools. For qualitative tasks, experienced math teachers rate the model outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty; for score prediction, model outputs are compared against human rubric ratings.

The paper finds that ChatGPT can sometimes produce relevant and actionable feedback, but its performance is generally weak. On rubric scoring, correlations with human ratings are low. On highlight/missed-opportunity generation, teachers judge many outputs as not insightful or not relevant, with some hallucination or misinterpretation. On suggestion generation, the model often repeats what the teacher already did in the transcript. The authors conclude that generative AI is not yet a substitute for expert coaching, but may become a complement if future work improves novelty, faithfulness, and pedagogical specificity.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based conversational language model used to generate text responses, including scoring, feedback, and suggestions from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluates ChatGPT zero-shot on three teacher-coaching tasks: scoring classroom transcript segments on CLASS and MQI rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit student mathematical reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: On Task A, ChatGPT’s score predictions had low Spearman correlation with human ratings across CLASS and MQI items. Reported correlations were near zero or negative for most dimensions; for example, CLBM reached 0.35 under direct-answer prompting, while several other items were at or below 0.17. The paper concludes that the model performs poorly at scoring transcripts and that added rubric descriptions or reasoning did not improve performance.
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between ChatGPT-predicted observation scores and human annotator scores on CLASS and MQI transcript segments
findings.effect_size: spearman rho mostly near 0; highest reported rho=0.35
findings.sample_size: n=100 transcript segments for Task A

findings.finding_summary: For Task B, teachers rated model-generated highlights and missed opportunities as often not insightful or relevant, and hallucination/misfaithfulness appeared in a nontrivial share of outputs. For CLASS examples, low ratings were 22% for faithfulness, 35% for relevance, and 51% for insightfulness; for MQI examples, low ratings increased to 29%, 55%, and 71%, respectively. The paper reports that the model performed worse on MQI than CLASS across all evaluation dimensions.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness of generated highlights/missed opportunities

findings.finding_summary: For Task C, most suggestions were rated faithful, relevant, and actionable, but 82% were judged redundant because they repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript. The paper interprets this as evidence that ChatGPT can generate usable suggestions, but they are often not novel or insightful enough to function as strong coaching feedback.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of faithfulness, relevance, actionability, and novelty/redundancy of generated suggestions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small empirical evaluation with human ratings and correlation analysis, but it is not an intervention study and does not test effects on teacher behavior or student outcomes. The evidence is useful for model-quality assessment, but methodological scope is limited to annotation of outputs.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear limitations in generated coaching feedback, with most quantitative associations near zero and no demonstrated downstream impact on practice or learning. Reported findings are more diagnostic than impactful in terms of educational outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Understanding Teacher Revisions of Large Language Model-Generated Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers revise large language model (LLM)-generated formative feedback before it is delivered to students. The central question is not whether the AI feedback is good in isolation, but how educators mediate, shorten, or otherwise reshape it in practice. The authors argue that evaluation of AI feedback should account for teacher editing because the final student-facing message is often the product of human-AI co-creation.

The study analyzes 1,349 instances of AI-generated feedback and the corresponding teacher-edited versions from 117 teachers using the Tutoria platform integrated with Moodle and Google Classroom. The dataset combines logs from prior controlled studies and classroom deployments in Brazilian educational contexts. The analysis focuses on three questions: which textual properties predict revision, whether revision can be predicted from the AI text alone, and how the pedagogical type of feedback changes after teacher editing.

Results show that teachers accepted AI feedback without modification in about 78% of cases, and when edits occurred, they tended to shorten feedback while preserving most of its semantic content. Revision behavior varied greatly by teacher, with many teachers rarely editing at all. Text-only models could predict revision above chance, but only modestly well. Qualitative coding showed that revisions often shifted feedback away from high-information explanations toward shorter corrective forms, suggesting teachers were simplifying AI output and reasserting pedagogical judgment rather than extensively rewriting it.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model-based feedback generation system used to draft formative feedback for student responses, which teachers could accept, edit, or rewrite before delivery.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied teacher revision behavior on AI-generated formative feedback drafts produced by an LLM-supported feedback platform (Tutoria); the paper analyzes how teachers edited the drafts and how the feedback type changed after revision.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers accepted AI-generated feedback without modification in 77.8% of cases (1050/1349). Edited feedback was only modestly longer than unedited feedback at the AI-draft stage versus the final teacher version (48.3 vs. 41.9 words within edited cases), suggesting most revisions were minor and often limited to compression rather than wholesale rewriting.
findings.measure: Teacher acceptance/editing rate; feedback length before vs. after teacher revision

findings.finding_summary: Text-only models could predict whether a draft would be revised with above-chance performance, reaching ROC AUC values from 0.698 to 0.746 on the holdout set (logistic regression, MLP, gradient-boosted trees). The best reported model achieved AUC=0.746 [0.539, 0.768], indicating that revision decisions were partially predictable from the AI-generated text alone.
findings.measure: Binary classification performance for revision decision

findings.finding_summary: When revisions occurred, teachers shifted feedback type away from the AI draft’s relatively higher share of High-information feedback and toward a more balanced distribution of Corrective and High-information feedback. Among revised cases, the initial AI feedback was High-information in 59.9% of instances (106/177) and Corrective in 40.1% (71/177), while the final teacher-delivered feedback was 48.0% High-information and 43.5% Corrective, with some Reinforcement/Punishment (7.3%) and Other (1.1%).
findings.measure: Distribution of feedback types before vs. after teacher revision
findings.sample_size: n=834 coded messages; revised subset n=177

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a retrospective observational/mixed-methods study of teacher interaction with AI-generated feedback, not a controlled comparison of competing conditions. The evidence is informative but correlational and focused on revision behavior rather than causal impacts on learning or teacher outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects relate mainly to teacher editing patterns and predictive model performance, with small-to-moderate shifts in feedback type. There is no direct evidence here of student learning gains, teacher self-efficacy change, or controlled comparisons against human coaching or business-as-usual.

paper_profiles.title: The TalkMoves Dataset: K-12 Mathematics Lesson Transcripts Annotated for Teacher and Student Discursive Moves
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces the TalkMoves dataset, a large corpus of 567 K-12 mathematics lesson transcripts annotated for teacher and student discursive moves. The authors frame the dataset around accountable talk theory, arguing that structured classroom discourse is central to equitable and rigorous mathematics learning and that curated transcript resources can support both educational research and AI development.

The paper does not evaluate a generative AI intervention against human coaching, peer feedback, rubric-only self-review, or business-as-usual. Instead, it describes the creation, annotation protocol, reliability, and composition of the dataset, along with a related TalkMoves application that uses machine learning to detect talk moves and provide automated feedback to teachers. The application is presented as a downstream use case rather than an evaluated intervention in this paper.

The transcripts come from K-12 mathematics classrooms, primarily in-person lessons with whole-class discussion and/or small-group work, plus some online lessons. Sources include public transcript collections and transcripts gathered through the TalkMoves project. The dataset is heavily oriented toward U.S. middle school classrooms, though the paper notes that some transcripts are international via TIMSS and that many descriptive fields are missing for individual lessons.

The main conclusion is that TalkMoves is a carefully curated, theory-grounded dataset that can support NLP and educational AI work, including automated feedback systems for teachers. The paper reports strong human annotation reliability and benchmark model performance for talk-move classification, but it does not report teacher behavior-change outcomes, lesson revisions, teacher self-efficacy, or student learning effects from an intervention trial.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic AI-based classroom discourse feedback and coaching system that analyzes lesson transcripts/audio and generates automated, personalized feedback for teachers; not a single named commercial product in this paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the broader category for the TalkMoves application, which provides teachers with automated, immediate feedback on mathematics instruction and discourse moves.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is primarily a dataset and system description, not an empirical evaluation of a teaching intervention. It reports model benchmarking on talk-move classification, but does not test teacher outcomes in a controlled study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The described application has potential instructional impact, but this paper provides no direct evidence of teacher behavior change, lesson revisions, self-efficacy, or student learning. Reported model performance is moderately strong, but it is an artifact-level benchmark rather than an educational impact result.

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service elementary teachers incorporated ChatGPT into science lesson planning and how they perceived its usefulness and risks. The paper responds to the lack of empirical studies on generative AI in actual educational planning, especially in science education, and asks how ChatGPT can be integrated into lesson plans, how well pre-service teachers can align it with instructional goals, and what benefits and concerns they anticipate.

The intervention/context was a short professional-learning sequence: 29 pre-service elementary science teachers at a Korean teachers' university attended four 2-hour class sessions introducing ChatGPT, discussing potential uses in science teaching, reviewing instructional methods such as cooperative learning and Predict-Observe-Explain, and learning how to write lesson plans. Participants then produced a lesson plan for a 45-minute elementary science lesson, including a simulated ChatGPT interaction and a survey about their rationale, anticipated usefulness, and concerns. The study used a modified TPACK-based rubric to evaluate the lesson plans plus qualitative analysis of survey responses and chat transcripts.

Findings show that participants envisioned ChatGPT being used across multiple science domains and instructional strategies, especially for questioning, individualized support, formative feedback, and role-play/script development. Lesson plans scored relatively high on the rubric overall, but teachers were less strong at selecting appropriate ChatGPT functions than at aligning ChatGPT with content and instructional strategies. Participants also expressed substantial concern about inaccuracies, hallucinations, and student over-dependence on ChatGPT, and they proposed safeguards such as teacher mediation, multiple information sources, structured discussion, and reflection. The paper concludes that pre-service teachers saw promise in ChatGPT for science teaching, but also that more empirical classroom research is needed to determine whether AI-supported lesson designs improve actual teacher practice and student learning.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM for conversational text generation, question answering, and interactive assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Pre-service elementary science teachers were trained on ChatGPT and asked to integrate it into 29 lesson plans for science teaching/learning activities, then explain its perceived usefulness and concerns.

findings.finding_summary: This paper does not evaluate student or teacher outcomes from using ChatGPT in instruction against a comparison group. It evaluates 29 pre-service teachers' lesson plans that incorporated ChatGPT, using a modified TPACK-based rubric; the average score was M=3.29 on a 4-point scale (SD=.91), with item means of 3.44 for curriculum goals, 3.48 for instructional strategies, 3.00 for ChatGPT function selection, and 3.24 for fit. No effect sizes or controlled outcome data on teacher behavior change, lesson revision, self-efficacy, or student learning were reported.
findings.measure: Modified TPACK-based lesson plan rubric scores; qualitative survey responses on perceived usefulness and concerns

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The study is a qualitative/mixed-methods descriptive analysis of lesson plans and survey responses, not a controlled trial. It provides useful implementation evidence but no causal estimates of impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No controlled comparison or outcome effect sizes are reported, and the paper focuses on planned integration quality rather than measured gains in practice or student learning.

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Peer, Self, and Teacher Assessments for Generative AI-Enhanced Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teacher, peer, and self-assessments align within a generative AI-enhanced collaborative feedback system (AICoFe) used in higher education. The central problem is how to provide timely, pedagogically valid feedback at scale while accounting for differences in scoring behavior across evaluators and improving the design of AI-generated feedback.

The study does not evaluate a randomized AI intervention against a human-only control. Instead, it analyzes 46 completed evaluation sets from undergraduate engineering students who delivered individual oral presentations in a compulsory communication course at Universidad Autonoma de Madrid. Each presentation was scored using the same validated rubric by the course teacher, two randomly assigned peers, and the presenter in self-assessment; the teacher also provided an independent overall grade. The analysis focused on agreement, correlations, and systematic scoring differences among evaluator types.

Results showed moderate to substantial agreement overall, with the strongest alignment between teacher rubric scores and the teacher’s global grade. Peer assessments correlated moderately with the teacher’s grade, while self-assessments were somewhat less aligned and slightly more lenient than teacher ratings. The paper concludes that peer and self-assessment can be useful inputs for GenAI feedback, but that the AI system should not treat all evaluator sources as equally reliable; instead, it should weight inputs differently, detect bias, and incorporate context-aware reasoning. The proposed contribution is primarily a design improvement for GenAI feedback generation rather than a test of effects on teacher practice, lesson revision, self-efficacy, or student learning.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI system used to aggregate human assessment inputs and generate personalized feedback with human oversight.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies the AICoFe system and proposes an enhanced GePeTo generative model within it; the GenAI component is discussed as a feedback generator informed by teacher, peer, and self-assessments rather than as a directly compared intervention.

findings.finding_summary: This paper did not evaluate student learning or teacher behavior change attributable to GenAI. Instead, it analyzed 46 evaluation sets from teacher, peer, and self-assessments to inform the design of a proposed enhanced GenAI feedback model; reported outcomes were agreement and scoring bias among human evaluators.
findings.measure: Inter-rater agreement, correlations with teacher's overall grade, and paired-sample differences among teacher, peer, and self-assessment rubric scores

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a correlational/methods study focused on agreement and bias among evaluator sources, not a controlled intervention study of AI use versus human coaching or business-as-usual. The paper proposes a GenAI-enhanced feedback design but does not report causal effects on learning or teacher practice.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported associations are moderate to strong for evaluator agreement and correlation, but they describe measurement alignment rather than impact of the AI system on outcomes. Because there is no evaluated intervention effect, practical impact on teaching or learning remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: AI, Expert or Peer? Examining the Impact of Perceived Feedback Source on Pre-Service Teachers Feedback Perception and Uptake
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether pre-service teachers’ perceptions of feedback and their actual uptake of feedback depend on the perceived source of the feedback: an LLM, an expert, or a peer. The central question is whether source labels and source misidentification shape cognitive and affective responses to feedback, and whether those perceptions translate into changes in what teachers actually revise.

In a randomized experiment, 273 bachelor’s students in a German teacher education program each received one written feedback message on a mathematics learning goal. The feedback came from a set of expert-generated, peer-generated, or LLM-generated messages (produced with ChatGPT-4), and participants first identified the source, then rated the feedback on fairness, usefulness, acceptance, willingness to improve, and affect. Finally, they revised the learning goal according to the feedback, allowing the authors to measure feedback uptake as an observed behavior rather than only perceptions.

The study found that perceived source strongly affected feedback evaluations: LLM feedback was rated more positively when it was believed to come from a human expert, indicating an expertise heuristic and a bias against AI labels. However, these perception effects did not translate into behavioral uptake. Actual implementation of feedback suggestions was driven mainly by objective feedback quality, not by perceived source, recognition accuracy, or self-reported perceptions. The authors conclude that source labels mainly shape how feedback is judged, while the quality of the message itself determines whether it is used.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based large language model / chatbot used to generate written educational feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate one set of feedback messages on a mathematics learning goal; the study compared ChatGPT-generated feedback against expert-generated and peer-generated feedback, while varying whether participants perceived the source as LLM, expert, or peer.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized experiment with pre-service teachers (N=273; analytic samples varied by outcome), feedback source strongly affected perceptions but not actual uptake once objective feedback quality was controlled. LLM-generated feedback was rated more favorably on fairness and usefulness when falsely attributed to an expert (fairness b=1.21, p=.042; usefulness b=1.76, p=.009), yet source, recognition accuracy, and their interaction did not significantly predict implementation behavior; feedback quality was the only significant predictor of uptake (b=1.27, p=.012).
findings.measure: Feedback perception (fairness, usefulness, acceptance, willingness to improve, affect) and feedback uptake/correction rate
findings.effect_size: Fairness interaction b=1.21; usefulness interaction b=1.76; uptake predictor b=1.27; R²=.078

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized experiment with direct comparison conditions and clearly defined outcomes, but it is a single study and the main analyses are correlational/regression-based rather than a full intervention trial on teacher practice over time. The paper also reports an important distinction between perception of artifacts and actual uptake behavior.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects on perceptions are small to moderate in practical terms, and the study finds no direct effect of source on uptake once quality is controlled. The strongest behavioral result is that objective feedback quality predicts revision behavior, while the AI label mainly shifts cognitive appraisals.

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a generative AI-based lesson planning system, Shiksha Copilot, supports teachers in low-resource public schools and how it changes their planning and instructional work. The core problem addressed is that teachers in multilingual, under-resourced settings face heavy administrative loads, limited teaching materials, and time scarcity, making high-quality lesson planning difficult. The authors ask how teachers collaborate with an LLM-based system, what challenges arise when using AI-generated lesson plans in non-English classrooms, and how such a tool reshapes teachers’ everyday work practices.

Shiksha Copilot combines retrieval-augmented generation, human curation, and bilingual English-Kannada support. In the system’s curation phase, 23 expert curators reviewed and revised AI-generated learning objectives and lesson plans; in the distribution phase, 1,043 teachers in Karnataka, India accessed curated lesson plans and could manually customize them, with a subset of 146 power users also receiving AI-assisted editing and chatbot features. The study used mixed methods: system logs, 43 interviews, and pre/post surveys from 406 matched respondents. The analysis focused on both the quality of AI-generated artifacts and how teachers adapted those artifacts for classroom use.

Findings suggest that AI-generated English lesson plans were generally high quality and needed only minor edits, while Kannada translations required extensive linguistic revision. Teachers used the tool to reduce lesson planning time, lower stress, and meet bureaucratic documentation requirements, but most classroom adaptation happened off-platform and was not fully captured in logs. The tool was associated with a reported shift toward more activity-based pedagogy, yet broader pedagogical change was constrained by staffing shortages and administrative demands. Overall, the paper argues that effective teacher-AI collaboration depends on human review, contextual adaptation, and alignment with local curricular and linguistic needs.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: An LLM-based, human-in-the-loop lesson planning and teacher support system that generates, translates, and helps customize curriculum-aligned lesson plans and related instructional materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Shiksha Copilot was studied as an AI-assisted lesson planning tool for curators and teachers in low-resource government schools in Karnataka, where teachers used curated AI-generated lesson plans and optional chatbot features to customize lessons for classroom use.

findings.finding_summary: In mixed-methods survey and log analyses, the paper reports that Shiksha Copilot reduced lesson planning time, reduced record-keeping burden, and lowered teacher stress. The study does not report a controlled comparison against human coaching, peer feedback, rubric-only self-review, or business-as-usual; outcomes reflect pre/post and usage-based evidence within the deployed system.
findings.measure: Weekly time spent on lesson planning and administrative tasks; Teacher Stress Scale (TSS)

findings.finding_summary: The post-intervention survey found lower teaching-related stress after adoption of the tool, with stress measured using the Teacher Stress Scale. The paper frames this as a reduction in workload-related strain rather than a comparison of AI versus human feedback conditions.
findings.measure: Teacher Stress Scale (teaching demands and school-based support subscales)

findings.finding_summary: For teacher practice, the paper reports a shift toward activity-based pedagogy and broader instructional adaptation, but also notes that systemic constraints limited more extensive pedagogical change. This is based on qualitative interview evidence and platform logs, not a controlled comparison of instructional coaching conditions.
findings.measure: Interview themes; distribution-platform edit logs; reported shifts in teaching practices
findings.sample_size: n=22 teacher interviews; log data from 5,544 lesson plans

findings.finding_summary: The study found high reliability and low editing burden for English lesson plans, with 96.13% of 7,744 content blocks rated suitable for classroom use and only 4.1% of blocks requiring modification overall. By contrast, Kannada translations required extensive substantive editing, with 94.4% of content blocks edited across 26 Kannada-medium lesson plans.
findings.measure: Curator ratings and edit rates of AI-generated lesson plan content blocks
findings.sample_size: n=991 curated lesson plans; n=26 Kannada lesson plans for detailed linguistic analysis

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods deployment study with surveys, logs, and interviews, which provides useful evidence but not a randomized or directly controlled comparison against human coaching or business-as-usual. The evidence is therefore observational and descriptive rather than causal.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful practical benefits for workload and stress, but it does not provide effect sizes for these outcomes or a direct comparison condition. Reported practice changes are promising but not quantified as medium/large impacts in a controlled design.

paper_profiles.title: Novobo: Supporting Teachers’ Peer Learning of Instructional Gestures by Teaching a Mentee AI-Agent Together
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI can support teachers’ professional learning around instructional gestures, a tacit and embodied teaching skill that is often difficult to develop through conventional teacher professional development. Rather than using AI as a coach or evaluator, the authors frame the system as a teachable mentee, so teachers can explain, critique, and demonstrate gestures to the AI agent together.

The intervention, Novobo, is a generative AI-based teachable agent that uses retrieval-augmented generation and a multi-agent workflow to generate gesture suggestions for classroom scenarios. Teachers interact with the system in four stages: posing a teaching scenario, commenting on AI-generated gestures, demonstrating gestures with a skeletal mirror interface, and explaining the reasoning behind their choices. The system also cites supporting literature and uses a posture-only mirror view to reduce self-consciousness during embodied practice.

The study involved 30 in-service teachers from seven primary schools in China, organized into 10 existing peer study groups, plus a formative design phase with six additional teachers and seven annotators who helped build the gesture knowledge base. The user study used video-based vignette analysis and focus groups to examine how teachers exchanged knowledge, reflected on AI suggestions, and co-constructed understanding through discussion and bodily demonstration. The paper concludes that positioning AI as a mentee can stimulate peer learning, surface tacit knowledge, and reduce the social pressure associated with direct peer criticism. The paper evaluates teacher collaboration and interaction with AI-generated artifacts, not changes in downstream teaching practice, teacher self-efficacy, or student learning outcomes.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model system used to generate instructional gesture descriptions and support conversational interaction in a teachable-agent workflow.
identified_tools.use_case: Novobo used OpenAI's GPT-4-turbo for intention analysis and gesture generation, and GPT-3.5-turbo for the conversation agent in a teachable AI mentee designed to stimulate teachers' peer learning of instructional gestures.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical qualitative/mixed-methods HCI study with 30 teachers, not a controlled comparison or outcomes trial. It provides process evidence about peer learning and design features, but no causal estimate of teacher or student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising collaborative-learning effects, but they are observational and not quantified with effect sizes. Impact on teacher practice is suggested through interaction analysis rather than measured behavior change.

paper_profiles.title: AI-Based Feedback in Counselling Competence Training of Prospective Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-based feedback can support the development of counseling competence in prospective teachers, especially in teacher-parent conversations. The core question is how communicative behaviors in simulated counseling sessions relate to expert ratings of conversation quality, and how students perceive AI-generated feedback after receiving it.

The intervention is an iterative four-day block seminar in which prospective elementary school teachers learn communication theory, practice peer role-play, and then complete recorded simulated teacher-parent conversations. Their recorded sessions are analyzed with AI tools: transcripts are annotated for conversational phases and communication techniques, while multimodal features such as speaking rate, pitch, loudness, gaze, smiles, and facial emotions are extracted and visualized in NOVA. Students receive collective and individual AI-based feedback, plus instructor feedback, and then participate in qualitative interviews about the experience.

The study includes 29 undergraduate prospective teachers in elementary school pedagogy at the University of Augsburg in Germany. The results reported are primarily about associations and perceptions rather than teacher behavior change: some paraverbal and nonverbal features correlated with expert ratings, model prediction performance was modest but above chance, and students generally perceived the AI feedback positively, especially when video playback and tabular summaries were combined. The paper concludes that AI-based multimodal feedback has potential to enrich teacher training, but verbal annotation guidelines need refinement and larger datasets are needed for stronger validation.

identified_tools.name: NOVA
identified_tools.description: NOVA is a tool for exploratory multimodal behavior analysis, annotation, extraction, and visualization of machine-learning and AI-based features from audio/video recordings.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to analyze simulated teacher-parent counseling conversations and to generate collective and individual AI-based feedback for prospective teachers; also used for playback during interviews and to support self-reflection.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative user study with 29 prospective teachers, the AI-based feedback system was positively perceived overall. Students especially valued the combination of NOVA playback and tabular data, and some said radar charts helped identify areas to improve; however, this paper did not report teacher behavior change, lesson revisions, self-efficacy gains, or student learning outcomes from a controlled comparison.
findings.measure: Student perceptions of AI-based feedback; interview responses about NOVA playback, tabular data, and radar charts

identified_tools.name: WhisperX
identified_tools.description: WhisperX is a time-accurate speech transcription system for long-form audio, used to transcribe speech with timestamps and align segments to audio.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to transcribe and align recorded simulated counseling sessions, enabling downstream annotation, feature extraction, and feedback preparation.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that integrating WhisperX into the transcription workflow reduced transcription time requirements by two-thirds. This is an operational efficiency outcome from the interview transcription process, not a measure of teacher learning or practice change.
findings.measure: Time required for transcription of guideline-based interviews

identified_tools.name: OpenFace
identified_tools.description: OpenFace is an open-source facial behavior analysis toolkit used for face detection, gaze estimation, facial landmarks, and action unit extraction.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to extract gaze angles and facial action units for nonverbal feedback and analysis of simulated counseling conversations.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that gaze in the main direction correlated significantly with standardized patients' satisfaction questionnaire scores on a private counseling dataset, but this was cited as prior setup for feature design rather than a result of the current teacher study. No controlled comparison of teacher coaching conditions or teacher practice outcomes was reported.
findings.measure: Correlation between gaze in main direction and standardized patients' satisfaction questionnaire (prior dataset cited in methods)

identified_tools.name: LibreFace
identified_tools.description: LibreFace is an open-source deep facial expression analysis toolkit used to infer facial action units and categorical emotions.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to detect facial expressions and categorical emotions (e.g., happiness, sadness, anger) from recorded counseling sessions for feedback generation.

identified_tools.name: WhisperX
identified_tools.description: WhisperX is a time-accurate speech transcription system for long-form audio, used to transcribe speech with timestamps and align segments to audio.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to transcribe and align recorded simulated counseling sessions, enabling downstream annotation, feature extraction, and feedback preparation.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that integrating WhisperX into the transcription workflow reduced transcription time requirements by two-thirds. This is an operational efficiency outcome from the interview transcription process, not a measure of teacher learning or practice change.
findings.measure: Time required for transcription of guideline-based interviews

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods study with a small sample and no controlled comparison of AI feedback against human coaching, peer feedback, rubric-only review, or business-as-usual. The reported outcomes are mainly perceptions and workflow efficiency, not causal evidence of teacher practice change.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests useful, actionable AI feedback and improved transcription efficiency, but it does not report measurable effects on teacher behavior, lesson revisions, self-efficacy, or student learning. Any impact on instructional practice remains untested in this study.

paper_profiles.title: Active Teacher Selection for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a core limitation in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF): most systems implicitly assume feedback comes from a single teacher, even though real settings often involve multiple teachers with different levels of expertise, rationality, and cost. The authors propose the Hidden Utility Bandit (HUB) framework to formalize reward learning when an agent can query multiple teachers and must decide not only when to ask for feedback, but also whom to ask.

The main methodological contribution is the Active Teacher Selection (ATS) algorithm, which maintains beliefs about hidden utilities and arm distributions and uses approximate POMDP planning to choose actions. ATS is designed to actively decide when teacher feedback is worth the cost and, under a specific-selection variant, which teacher to query. The paper also derives query complexity bounds and shows how teacher rationality parameters can be estimated from preference data.

The empirical section applies HUB/ATS to two simulated domains: a conference paper recommendation task and a COVID-19 vaccine-testing proof-of-concept. In the recommendation setting, the population is not human learners but simulated teachers/professors and recommendation items; in the vaccine setting, the task uses simulated patient symptoms, tests, and vaccine candidates with parameters drawn from real-world test sensitivities and costs. Across these simulations, ATS outperforms naive fixed-schedule baselines and random policies in cumulative reward and in recovering the hidden utility function, while also querying teachers more efficiently. The paper concludes that explicitly modeling heterogeneous teachers and actively selecting feedback can improve reward learning, but it is a theoretical/computational contribution rather than a study of teacher professional learning or instructional coaching.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: A general intelligent tutoring / human-feedback-driven decision support framework that learns from teacher preferences and selects which teacher to query.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a theoretical/algorithmic study of the Hidden Utility Bandit (HUB) and Active Teacher Selection (ATS) framework for selecting among multiple human teachers in reinforcement learning from human feedback; it is not an education intervention study.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical and algorithmic machine learning paper, not an empirical study of an instructional AI tool in education. It does not report a design with teacher participants, lesson planning outcomes, or student learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention effects are reported. The paper evaluates algorithm performance in simulation and two non-education domains, so there is no evidence of impact on teaching practice or student outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how K-12 teachers can be engaged in designing AI curriculum that is integrated into core non-computing subjects. The authors address a gap in AI education research: while many AI tools and lessons exist, few have been co-designed with teachers or adapted for classrooms beyond computer science. The main question is how to better support teachers’ needs and values when creating AI-integrated lessons, and how AI concepts can be meaningfully embedded in existing subject areas.

The study used a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from varied subject backgrounds, including English language arts, science, social studies, ESL, history, library science, and computer science. Teachers completed pre-work, participated in presentations on AI concepts and ethics, and worked in small groups with researchers to draft integrated lesson plans. The resulting curricula focused on social studies, ESL, and literacy for students with learning disabilities. Data sources included workshop audio, participant questionnaires, and design artifacts.

The paper concludes that teachers value curricula that support evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration. Teachers connected AI to core content through data, reflection, and ethics, and produced implementable lesson drafts. The authors argue that co-designing with teachers can make AI education more accessible across subjects and help build teacher confidence in teaching AI, though the work is exploratory and limited to a small remote workshop context.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Computer-assisted instruction / educational AI curriculum or tools used to support teaching and learning tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: A two-day co-design workshop with 15 K-12 teachers to design integrated AI curriculum lessons for social studies, ESL, literacy, and physics. The paper discusses AI tools such as Teachable Machine, Machine Learning for Kids, MIT App Inventor, Google Quick Draw, and related AI concepts as resources within the co-design process, not as a controlled intervention.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported a slight increase in familiarity with AI after the workshop and high confidence for integrating AI into their classrooms, but the study did not establish a baseline for the confidence change. The authors report participants’ familiarity with AI increased from an average of 4.8/7 before the workshop to 5.8/7 after the workshop, and confidence about integrating AI into their curriculum averaged 5.6/7 post-workshop.
findings.measure: Self-rated familiarity with AI; self-rated confidence about integrating AI into own curriculum

findings.finding_summary: The workshop produced three draft integrated AI curriculum units and surfaced teacher priorities around evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration. The paper reports that all groups successfully produced a first draft of an implementable AI curriculum, but this is an artifact/output outcome rather than evidence of changes in classroom practice or student learning.
findings.measure: Production of curriculum drafts; qualitative workshop outputs

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative co-design study with pre/post self-reports and no control group or causal comparison. It provides useful descriptive evidence about teacher perceptions and curriculum design, but not rigorous evidence of intervention effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported change in AI familiarity is modest and self-reported, and the paper does not report effect sizes or student outcome data. The main outputs are curriculum drafts and design insights rather than measured classroom impact.

paper_profiles.title: Changing Roles and Identities in a Teacher-Driven Professional Development Community
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a teacher-driven professional development community, Streamline to Mastery, supported changes in teachers’ participation, leadership, and professional identity. The central question is not about evaluating a generative AI system or comparing feedback sources, but about understanding how a collaborative, teacher-led development structure shapes growth over time.

Streamline to Mastery was a five-year professional development program for secondary physical science teachers in high-needs urban schools. Teachers were expected to help design the program, conduct classroom action research, present at conferences, and take graduate coursework. The study analyzed 42 hours of meeting video, email threads, and a focus group interview to trace shifts in agenda setting, email participation, and willingness to challenge one another’s ideas.

Findings suggest that participation became more distributed over time: teachers sent more emails, initiated more discussion threads, took over agenda setting, and increasingly engaged in skeptical but constructive challenge. The authors interpret these patterns as evidence that the group was becoming a community of practice, shifting from a hierarchy in which researchers held expertise to a more egalitarian community of expert learners. The paper concludes that professional development should focus less on making teachers change and more on creating communities where change can emerge from shared expertise and participation.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model chatbot or system used to generate or provide feedback on text, lesson plans, or instructional materials.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper does not study an AI tool. It examines a teacher-driven professional development community (Streamline to Mastery) and changes in teacher participation and leadership over time; any feedback comes from human researchers and peers, not AI.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods professional development study about teacher roles and community formation, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool. No AI system is tested, compared, or measured.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no AI intervention and no tool-related outcome data to assess. The paper reports descriptive changes in teacher participation within a PD community, not effects of AI use.

paper_profiles.title: Foundations of GenIR
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter presents a conceptual and technical overview of generative AI for information access (IA), focusing on how modern generative models change both information generation and information synthesis. The authors argue that large language models and related generative systems create new opportunities for IA because they can produce human-like responses, create tailored content, and synthesize information from external sources. The paper is not an empirical study; instead, it surveys foundational model architecture, scaling, training, prompt optimization, and multimodal applications.

A major portion of the chapter discusses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as a form of information synthesis, explaining how external documents can be retrieved and then used by LLMs to generate grounded responses. It distinguishes between naive RAG, modular RAG, and joint optimization of retrieval and generation, and also discusses retrieval planning for composite information needs. The chapter further examines generative retrieval and domain-specific modeling as alternative ways of using generative models for information access.

The context is broad and technical rather than tied to a specific participant population, educational setting, or intervention trial. The chapter summarizes prior work and research directions across IR, NLP, and multimodal generation. Its main conclusion is that generative AI can substantially enhance information access, but practical challenges remain, including hallucination, retrieval quality, prompt sensitivity, and the difficulty of maintaining and updating knowledge within model parameters.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative artificial intelligence models, especially large language models (LLMs), that produce human-like text or other content from prompts and can also synthesize information from external sources.
identified_tools.use_case: This chapter is a conceptual overview of generative AI in information access, discussing LLMs such as ChatGPT as examples rather than evaluating a specific educational intervention.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/book chapter on generative AI foundations and information access, not an empirical study of teacher planning, coaching, or professional learning. No controlled comparison, sample, or outcome data are reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No intervention outcomes are evaluated, so there is no evidence of impact on teacher practice, student learning, or related educational outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: AI-Generated Rubric Interfaces: K–12 Teachers’ Perceptions and Practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers perceive and use AI-supported rubric generation for assessment design and feedback in block-based programming contexts. The authors focus on a practical problem in teacher workflow: rubric creation is time-consuming, difficult to calibrate across performance levels, and often requires iterative refinement to match instructional goals and grade-level language. The study asks how teachers evaluate AI-generated rubrics and how hands-on exposure to such tools shapes their willingness to use them in future classroom practice.

The intervention was a summer professional development workshop in which 25 middle- and high-school teachers used MagicSchool.ai to generate rubrics for a sample block-based programming task. Teachers first created a manual rubric, then generated an AI rubric using standards and assignment information, and finally used the rubric to assess sample work both with and without a chatbot-based feedback feature (Reina). Data came from pre- and post-workshop surveys, exit tickets, and open-ended discussion responses, with quantitative Likert ratings and thematic analysis of qualitative data.

The teachers generally viewed AI-generated rubrics as useful starting drafts that improved structure, clarified vague criteria, and saved time, but they also emphasized the need for substantial teacher oversight. Survey responses were positive for clarity, alignment, and perceived transparency, while usability was weaker, especially around editing criteria. Open-ended responses highlighted a strictness-versus-detail tradeoff in AI feedback: teachers often found the feedback more detailed and scalable than their own, but sometimes harsher or misaligned with priorities. The main conclusion is that AI rubric tools are most acceptable when they preserve teacher control, support easy customization, and fit into teacher-directed assessment workflows rather than replacing human judgment.

identified_tools.name: MagicSchool.ai
identified_tools.description: An AI-powered educational platform that can generate rubrics and deliver rubric-based feedback from teacher prompts and assignment context.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers used MagicSchool.ai during a summer professional development workshop to generate rubrics for a sample block-based programming task, compare AI-generated rubrics with manually created rubrics, and then use the AI-generated rubric to assess sample student work. The paper also references the tool’s chatbot 'Reina' for generating rubric-based feedback.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the AI-generated rubrics were strong starting points that reduced the burden of drafting rubrics from scratch and improved structure/clarity. Survey responses were generally positive for clarity and alignment, but lower for editability, especially adding/removing/revising criteria (Q9 M=2.75, SD=1.23).
findings.measure: Post-survey perceptions of rubric clarity, alignment, usability, and editability

findings.finding_summary: Hands-on exposure increased teachers’ willingness to adopt AI rubric tools in future practice, but adoption was conditional on teacher control, easy customization, and alignment with classroom needs. Teachers framed the tool as a teacher-directed draft generator rather than a fixed product.
findings.measure: Post-workshop intentions to adopt AI rubric tools in future classroom practice

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large-language-model-based chatbot or generative AI system used to produce rubric-based feedback without a specific model name.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper contrasts teachers’ own feedback with AI-generated rubric-based feedback delivered by a chatbot during the workshop, focusing on perceived strictness, detail, scalability, and need for teacher oversight.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers perceived the AI-generated feedback as more detailed and scalable than their own feedback, though often harsher/stricter. The paper reports qualitative, not experimental, evidence of this perceived tradeoff rather than a measured effect on teacher behavior or student outcomes.
findings.measure: Teacher perceptions of AI-generated feedback compared with teacher feedback

findings.finding_summary: Teachers thought the AI output could help communicate evaluation expectations to students, but they also emphasized misalignment risks, rubric interpretation issues, and the need for substantial teacher oversight. This concerns evaluation of the AI-generated artifact, not a direct measure of changes in teacher practice or student learning.
findings.measure: Perceived quality and usefulness of AI-generated rubric/feedback artifacts

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods professional development study with survey and thematic analysis, not a controlled impact study. It provides useful descriptive evidence about teacher perceptions and intended use, but no causal evidence of teacher behavior change or student learning.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceptions and increased adoption intentions, which suggests practical promise, but it does not report a measurable effect size or direct learning impact. The observed influence is modest and primarily at the level of perceived usability and future intent.

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Systems that Augment Human Performed vs. Demonstrated Critical Thinking
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses a conceptual problem in research on generative AI and critical thinking: many studies appear to claim that AI improves critical thinking, but they often evaluate only the quality of AI-assisted outputs rather than whether people’s independent thinking ability has improved. The authors argue that this conflation leads to misleading conclusions about the cognitive effects of generative AI.

The paper proposes a distinction between "performed" critical thinking, meaning independent cognition without AI assistance, and "demonstrated" critical thinking, meaning thinking as expressed through AI-supported work products or interactions. The paper does not study a specific intervention, population, or educational setting empirically; instead, it synthesizes prior literature and provides a conceptual framework for designing and evaluating AI systems.

The main conclusion is that AI systems may improve demonstrated critical thinking without improving performed critical thinking, and these two goals require different evaluation methods and design choices. The authors recommend research designs that separately assess independent pre/post ability and AI-assisted performance, and they suggest that future AI tools should scaffold thinking processes rather than simply provide answers or polished outputs.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI / large language model chatbot used to assist with language, writing, or analytical tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: This is a position paper about generative AI and critical thinking, not an empirical study of a specific product. It cites prior work using various GenAI tools, but does not itself evaluate a named system.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual position paper with no original intervention, controlled comparison, or outcome data. It proposes a distinction between performed and demonstrated critical thinking rather than testing an AI tool in an empirical study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effects on teacher behavior, lesson revisions, self-efficacy, or student learning are reported. The paper does not present measurable impact estimates for any educational outcome.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring K-12 Physical Education Teachers’ Perspectives on Opportunities and Challenges of AI Integration Through Ideation Workshops
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 physical education (PE) teachers perceive opportunities and challenges for integrating AI into their classes. The authors note that AI in education has largely been explored in classroom-based STEM contexts, while PE remains underexplored despite its distinct demands, such as large open spaces, safety monitoring, heterogeneous student abilities, and the need for individualized feedback and multidimensional assessment.

To explore this issue, the researchers conducted in-person focus group ideation workshops with 17 in-service secondary school PE teachers in South Korea. The workshop included a short AI literacy lecture, individual sketching of AI-enabled ideas, group storyboard creation, and role-playing. Participants discussed current instructional challenges and envisioned four roles for AI in PE: operational assistant, personal trainer, group coach, and evaluator. These ideas centered on class management, personalized skill feedback, balanced team formation, and automated or augmented student evaluation.

The study is qualitative and does not test an intervention against a comparison condition or measure student learning outcomes. Its main contribution is a teacher-centered account of potential AI applications and the practical, ethical, and infrastructural barriers to adoption, including institutional support, teacher technology proficiency, overreliance on AI, and student data privacy. The authors conclude that AI should support rather than replace teachers and that successful integration in PE will require alignment with pedagogical goals and classroom realities.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic AI/LLM-based assistant concept used to generate feedback, support individualized instruction, and assist with evaluation or planning tasks; no specific commercial or research product is named.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper did not evaluate a deployed AI tool. It used focus-group ideation workshops with 17 in-service K-12 physical education teachers to elicit how they envisioned AI supporting class management, personalized feedback, team formation, and multidimensional assessment in PE.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative ideation/workshop paper, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool or intervention. It reports teacher perceptions and proposed use cases rather than controlled outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful applications for PE teaching practice, but it provides no measured implementation effects or student/teacher outcomes to estimate impact.

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Models: A Tool for Solving Mathematical Problems in High School
paper_profiles.venue: Annual of Sofia University “St. Kliment Ohridski”, Faculty of Mathematics and Informatics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language models (LLMs) can support mathematics education, with a focus on Bulgarian high school problem solving and practicing teachers’ perceptions of AI. The central question is whether contemporary generative AI systems can produce mathematically correct, curriculum-aligned, and linguistically appropriate solutions for Bulgarian National External Assessment (NEA) problems, and how teachers view the pedagogical value and risks of such tools.

The study has two parts. First, eleven LLMs were evaluated on eight 10th-grade NEA mathematics problems that were converted from multiple-choice to short-answer format. Models were scored not only for exact accuracy but also for structured reasoning, pedagogical alignment with the Bulgarian curriculum, error penalties, and language clarity. Second, qualitative observations were made of practicing mathematics teachers enrolled in a master’s program, who reflected on AI use in task design and instructional practice. The teacher component included coursework in online graduate classes and assignments in which participants compared AI-generated solutions with their own preferred methods.

The paper reports that some models achieved very high or perfect accuracy, but accuracy did not guarantee educational suitability. Several globally trained models produced mathematically correct answers while deviating from Bulgarian curricular methods or using awkward language, whereas locally fine-tuned models such as BgGPT showed stronger alignment with national terminology and solution conventions. In the teacher observations, participants recognized AI’s potential for personalized support and task generation, but they were cautious about adoption and preferred to retain creative and methodological control. The author concludes that effective AI use in mathematics education requires not just correctness, but also curriculum alignment and linguistically precise explanations; LLMs can complement teacher work, but should not replace it.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
