identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model/chatbot for generating and revising text, answering questions, and providing step-by-step explanations.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as one of several LLM chatbots used interactively for solving Bulgarian high school mathematics problems and for teacher-oriented task development; also referenced by teachers as a tool used in coursework and pedagogy.

findings.finding_summary: In the manual assessment, ChatGPT produced mathematically correct solutions but often used methods and presentation formats that did not align with Bulgarian curriculum expectations. The paper reports that it is the most prevalent model among students and educators in Bulgaria, but its outputs may be inapplicable in some classroom or examination contexts because of methodological mismatch.
findings.measure: Curriculum alignment / suitability of generated problem solutions for Bulgarian high school mathematics

identified_tools.name: DeepSeek
identified_tools.description: A large language model chatbot for multilingual reasoning and general-purpose text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated in automated batch testing and manual interactive problem-solving on Bulgarian 10th-grade mathematics items.

findings.finding_summary: DeepSeek R1 (7B) achieved 100.0% success on the eight NEA items in automated evaluation, but its mean rubric quality was only 54.17. The paper attributes the lower score to frequent minor deviations from Bulgarian curriculum style and to language issues, despite mathematically correct answers. In manual testing, it could be constrained to use curriculum-specific methods, but this iterative refinement was judged unrealistic for typical tenth-grade students.
findings.measure: Problem-solving success rate; rubric-based quality (structured solution, pedagogical quality, critical error, language clarity)

identified_tools.name: Mistral
identified_tools.description: Mistral AI's family of large language models/chatbots for text generation and reasoning.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated across multiple model sizes in automated testing and as Le Chat in manual interactive use for Bulgarian high school mathematics problem solving.

findings.finding_summary: Mistral (22B) achieved a 100.0% success rate and the highest mean rubric quality among the top-performing models (81.25) in the automated evaluation. The paper reports that it also showed strong pedagogical alignment with the Bulgarian curriculum and no critical errors, while Le Chat with image recognition correctly solved all interactive chat-session issues; however, its solution strategies sometimes differed from the methods students are expected to use.
findings.measure: Problem-solving success rate; rubric-based quality; curriculum alignment; interactive correctness in manual assessment

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods study with automated benchmarking and qualitative teacher observations, not a controlled intervention or randomized design. The evidence is informative but largely descriptive and model-evaluation based rather than causal.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong performance for some models on a small set of eight mathematics problems, but it does not provide effect sizes from an intervention on learners or teachers. The practical impact is promising yet unclear because findings are about solution quality and alignment rather than measured educational gains.

paper_profiles.title: The Manifesto for Teaching and Learning in a Time of Generative AI: A Critical Collective Stance to Better Navigate the Future
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a manifesto-style critical collective article examining the implications of generative AI (GenAI), chatbots, and algorithms for higher education. Rather than testing an intervention, it addresses the broader question of how GenAI should be understood and governed in teaching and learning, emphasizing ethical, pedagogical, and social concerns alongside possible affordances. The paper is framed as a call for collective responsibility and evidence-based decision-making in response to the rapid rise of GenAI after the release of ChatGPT.

The approach is a qualitative collective-writing study using a modified Delphi process. The authors are worldwide educators and researchers in higher education with expertise in GenAI. Through anonymous open-ended prompts, coding, consensus-building, and member checking, they synthesized expert reflections into a set of positive and negative thematic statements about GenAI in education. These themes include time savings, personalized learning, lifelong learning, assessment redesign, innovation, accessibility, professional development, bias, academic integrity, misinformation, and over-reliance on technology.

The population described is higher education educators/researchers, not K-12 participants. The paper does not report a controlled implementation or student outcome study; instead, it offers a theoretical and normative framework for interpreting GenAI’s role in education. Its main conclusion is that GenAI is not neutral and should be integrated cautiously, with attention to equity, human oversight, transparency, and preservation of human values, critical thinking, and authentic learning.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbot systems used for text and multimedia generation, question answering, feedback, tutoring, and content support.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a critical manifesto about generative AI in education and discusses GenAI/chatbots/LLMs at a conceptual level rather than evaluating a specific product.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an editorial/manifesto using collective writing and Delphi-style qualitative synthesis, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool. It does not report controlled outcomes or subgroup analyses.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No intervention effects, effect sizes, or measured impacts are reported. The paper offers conceptual claims and critical reflections only.

paper_profiles.title: Epistemic authority and generative AI in learning spaces: rethinking knowledge in the algorithmic age
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the epistemological and pedagogical consequences of generative AI in learning spaces, focusing on how tools such as ChatGPT reshape what counts as knowledge, who is seen as authoritative, and how students and teachers relate to one another. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention, the article argues that generative AI can function as a “surrogate knower,” encouraging automation bias, weakening traditional norms of justification, and shifting epistemic authority away from human educators toward algorithmic outputs.

The authors discuss generative AI as embedded in classroom learning, feedback, and assessment contexts, but the paper itself is a conceptual/opinion piece rather than an empirical study. It draws on prior literature and philosophical framing to describe how AI-generated outputs may reinforce dominant discourses, reproduce bias, and operate as a hidden curriculum that privileges fluency, certainty, and speed over critical reflection and pluralistic inquiry. The article also highlights the potential for AI use by both students and instructors to blur teacher-student boundaries and alter perceptions of expertise and objectivity.

The paper concludes by arguing for “epistemic agency” and a model of the teacher as an “epistemic mentor.” It recommends reflective pedagogies such as comparing AI responses with peer or instructor feedback, trust audits, journaling, source checking, and critical AI literacy. The central conclusion is that education should not simply adopt AI for efficiency, but should actively frame its use in ways that preserve human judgment, critical discernment, and democratic learning values.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI / large language model chatbots used for producing and transforming text, answering questions, giving feedback, and supporting instruction.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is an opinion/theoretical discussion about generative AI in learning spaces, with examples including ChatGPT and other large language models; it does not evaluate a specific tool in an empirical study.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an opinion/theoretical paper rather than an empirical controlled, quasi-controlled, or review study. It does not report a systematic methodology or original outcome data on any AI tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No causal or descriptive effect estimates are reported, so there is no measurable instructional or learning impact to rate.

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular emphasis on chatbots and ChatGPT. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it reviews the broader literature on AI technologies, their educational uses, and the ethical and practical issues involved in adopting them. The paper is framed as an overview of the state of the field and a discussion of how AI may reshape teaching, learning, feedback, assessment, and administrative work.

The article discusses AI tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, automated grading, personalized learning platforms, and chatbots, explaining how they can provide individualized instruction, instant feedback, and workload reduction for teachers. It also outlines the main technical and ethical challenges, including bias, privacy, reliability, transparency, academic integrity, and the need for teacher preparation and support. The discussion is conceptual and literature-based, drawing examples from prior studies rather than reporting a new controlled evaluation.

The paper concludes that AI has substantial promise for improving student engagement, learning outcomes, and personalized support, while also assisting teachers with feedback, assessment, and administrative tasks. At the same time, the authors stress that these benefits depend on responsible implementation, adequate teacher training, and attention to fairness and privacy. The piece calls for further research on how tools like ChatGPT can be integrated effectively and ethically into education.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative pre-trained transformer chatbot that produces human-like text responses to natural language prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a narrative review focused on ChatGPT and related educational uses, discussing its potential for personalized learning, instant feedback, tutoring, and teacher support.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a review/opinion-style overview article, not a controlled, quasi-controlled, or meta-analytic evaluation of an AI tool. It does not report a study design with empirical effect estimates for subgroup or moderation analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No empirical impact estimates are reported. The paper discusses potential benefits and challenges of ChatGPT in education, but provides no measured outcomes or effect sizes.

paper_profiles.title: A classification tool to foster self-regulated learning with generative artificial intelligence by applying self-determination theory: a case of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how ChatGPT, as a form of generative AI, can be used to support students’ self-regulated learning (SRL) and satisfy self-determination theory (SDT) needs from the perspective of school teachers. The study is positioned as a response to a gap in the literature: while generative AI is increasingly used in education, there is still limited clarity about which AI-supported learning activities help students’ autonomy, competence, relatedness, and SRL phases.

The authors used a Delphi design with 36 Hong Kong school teachers who had experience with technology-enhanced learning, SDT-based teaching, and ChatGPT-supported learning design. Across three rounds, participants reviewed, refined, combined, removed, and added candidate activities until consensus was reached. The panel represented several subjects, including English, Chinese, mathematics, science, humanities and art, and technology, and the schools covered different student levels in Hong Kong. The process produced a classification tool of 20 ChatGPT-based learning activities.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT-based activities were seen as especially useful for supporting competence, followed by autonomy, while relatedness was least supported. The activities were also mapped to SRL phases, with performance and self-reflection supported more often than forethought. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can support SRL, but not fully on its own; teacher guidance remains important, especially in school settings. The resulting tool is intended to guide future research, classroom practice, and AI-in-education policy, but it is exploratory rather than an outcome study of student learning.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot for generating, revising, and discussing text and other content in a human-like, interactive manner.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the focal GenAI tool in a Delphi study to classify learning activities that school teachers believed could use ChatGPT to support self-regulated learning and satisfy SDT needs.

findings.finding_summary: Using a three-round Delphi with 36 Hong Kong school teachers, the study developed a classification tool of 20 ChatGPT-based learning activities that teachers agreed could support self-regulated learning. The paper does not report causal effects on student outcomes; it reports consensus patterns indicating ChatGPT was seen as especially useful for competence support, and less so for relatedness.
findings.measure: Teacher consensus on ChatGPT learning activities, mapped to SDT needs and SRL phases

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative Delphi consensus study, not a controlled trial or meta-analysis. It provides expert-derived classifications rather than outcome effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect size is reported and no student outcome was measured. The paper suggests potential utility for SRL support, but the impact is descriptive and unquantified.

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT in teaching and learning: a systematic review through SWOT analysis approach
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats of using ChatGPT in teaching and learning are, and organizes the evidence using Biggs’s Presage-Process-Product (3P) model. The review is not an evaluation of a single intervention; rather, it synthesizes findings from published studies on educational uses of ChatGPT and related chatbots to understand where the technology appears helpful, where it is risky, and how it may fit into teaching and learning workflows.

The authors conducted a systematic review following PRISMA guidance, searching Scopus, ERIC, and Google Scholar for empirical studies from 2022–2023. After screening, 51 studies were included. Most were higher-education studies, with a smaller set in general education; the review covered a wide range of countries and subject domains, especially English language education, health education, and computer science/programming. The paper does not focus on a single controlled intervention or subgroup comparison, but it does summarize descriptive patterns across studies, including that ChatGPT is often viewed positively, can support personalized learning and rapid feedback, and may help with course material development and writing tasks.

The main conclusions are that ChatGPT has clear perceived strengths in the presage, process, and product stages of education, including support for personalized learning, immediate responses, idea generation, assessment support, and some learning gains. At the same time, the review highlights important weaknesses and threats such as generic outputs, response-length limits, bias, inaccuracy, fabricated citations, plagiarism concerns, and potential academic dishonesty. The authors conclude that ChatGPT should complement, not replace, teachers, and that effective use depends on learner skills, teacher judgment, and careful verification of outputs.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI chatbot used for generating responses, explanations, writing support, feedback, and other instructional assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: This systematic review examined empirical studies on the use of ChatGPT in teaching and learning across presage, process, and product stages of the 3P model.

findings.finding_summary: Across 51 included studies, the review synthesized perceived strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats of using ChatGPT in teaching and learning. Descriptive patterns suggested positive perceptions, personalization, immediate response, and improved learning outcomes, alongside concerns about inaccuracy, bias, forged citations, plagiarism, and reduced critical thinking. The paper did not report subgroup analyses by teacher experience, subject area, grade band, school context, or deployment format beyond descriptive differences across contexts.
findings.measure: Systematic review thematic synthesis of included empirical studies

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review synthesizing mostly qualitative and descriptive empirical studies rather than a controlled intervention study or meta-analysis. The evidence is useful for mapping themes, but it does not provide causal subgroup estimates or effect sizes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review reports potentially meaningful benefits and risks, but impact is not quantified and no medium/large effect size is available. Descriptive patterns suggest broad relevance, yet the absence of controlled subgroup evidence makes the practical impact uncertain.

paper_profiles.title: The Perception by University Students of the Use of ChatGPT in Education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines university students’ perceptions of ChatGPT in education, focusing on perceived benefits, barriers, and possible ways to use the tool more effectively. The study was motivated by the rapid rise of generative AI in education and a lack of empirical evidence about how students actually experience ChatGPT in academic work.

The authors used a mixed-methods design with an online questionnaire and semi-structured interviews. The sample consisted of 200 Vietnamese university students who had previously used ChatGPT for academic purposes; 30 of these students were interviewed. The survey used 5-point Likert items and the data were analyzed with descriptive statistics and one-sample t-tests, while interview responses were coded into themes.

Results indicated generally positive perceptions of ChatGPT. Students strongly agreed that it is easy to use, can function as a search engine, can work across languages, and is useful for study. Reported benefits included saving time, accessing information across diverse fields, improving writing through idea generation and feedback, and providing personalized tutoring/adaptive learning. Reported barriers centered on reliability and academic accuracy, such as inability to verify source quality, cite correctly, handle idioms well, and deal with difficult mathematical formulas. Students suggested verifying responses against reliable sources, using ChatGPT as a consultant rather than copying answers, providing clear guidelines, and promoting academic integrity. The study did not test learning outcomes or compare ChatGPT with a control group; it mainly documents perceptions and concerns among students.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s generative language model / conversational chatbot for natural-language interaction, text generation, and instructional assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed university students’ perceptions of using ChatGPT for learning, including perceived benefits, barriers, and suggested solutions; also interviewed a subset of students about their experiences.

findings.finding_summary: Students reported generally favorable perceptions of ChatGPT for learning (general mean=3.61/5; use of ChatGPT mean=3.62). The one-sample t-test showed the mean was significantly above the neutral point of 3 (t=31.868, df=199, p=0.000).
findings.measure: Overall perception/use of ChatGPT on a 5-point Likert scale

findings.finding_summary: Students perceived several benefits of ChatGPT in learning, with an overall benefits mean of 3.58/5. Highest-rated benefits were saving time (mean=3.74) and providing information in diverse fields (mean=3.66). The one-sample t-test indicated the benefits score was significantly above neutral (t=18.051, df=199, p=0.000).
findings.measure: Perceived benefits of ChatGPT on a 5-point Likert scale

findings.finding_summary: Students also reported barriers, with an overall barriers mean of 3.64/5. Top concerns were inability to examine source quality/reliability (mean=3.73), inability to replace words and use idioms wisely (mean=3.72), and inability to handle difficult mathematical formulas (mean=3.72). The barriers score was significantly above neutral (t=27.331, df=199, p=0.000), indicating substantial concern as well as perceived usefulness.
findings.measure: Perceived barriers/limitations of ChatGPT on a 5-point Likert scale

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods perception study with survey and interviews, not a controlled intervention study. It provides useful descriptive evidence about perceived benefits and barriers, but it does not test causal effects of ChatGPT coaching or feedback.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceptions of ChatGPT and specific perceived affordances such as time-saving and personalized tutoring/feedback, but there are no outcome effect sizes on learning. The practical impact is therefore suggestive but unquantified.

paper_profiles.title: Impact of ChatGPT on ESL students’ academic writing skills: a mixed methods intervention study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether using ChatGPT as a formative feedback tool improves undergraduate ESL students’ academic writing skills. The study responds to the lack of empirical evidence on generative AI for writing feedback and asks both whether ChatGPT changes writing performance and how students perceive its usefulness. The work is positioned within feedback theory, especially feedback as a dialogic process, and treats ChatGPT as a writing support tool that can provide immediate, tailored responses.

The intervention was conducted in a first-year undergraduate science and engineering context in an elite private university in India. Students in the experimental group received a short training session on using ChatGPT for self-assessment and peer assessment, then used it during six hours of instruction on process, comparison, and cause-effect writing. A comparison group followed the same general course without the ChatGPT feedback intervention. Quantitative data came from pre-test, post-test, and delayed post-test writing assessments; qualitative data came from focus group discussions with experimental-group students.

Results showed a strong positive effect of ChatGPT on writing performance. The experimental group significantly outperformed the comparison group on both the post-test and delayed post-test, and gains persisted over time. Students described ChatGPT as helpful for generating ideas, staying on topic, organizing content, and improving grammar, while also noting minor risks such as dependence and reduced creativity. The paper concludes that, with training, ChatGPT can function as a useful formative feedback tool in large writing classes.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI generative AI chatbot based on a large language model that can provide conversational assistance, explanations, and feedback on text and writing tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a formative feedback tool for self-assessment and peer-assessment in an undergraduate ESL academic writing intervention, where students used it for idea generation, organization, grammar checking, and revision support.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed-methods quasi-experimental intervention, the experimental group using ChatGPT for self- and peer-feedback improved from pre-test to post-test and delayed post-test on academic writing scores. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed a significant effect across time, F(2,72)=330.704, p=5.146e-37, b72=0.902; Bonferroni comparisons were significant for pre-test vs post-test (d=-3.300), pre-test vs delayed post-test (d=-3.898), and post-test vs delayed post-test (d=-0.598).
findings.measure: Academic writing test scores across pre-test, post-test, and delayed post-test
findings.sample_size: n=37 (EG); n=35 EG included in reported data per methods section, but tables/reporting use n=37

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods quasi-experimental intervention study with quantitative and qualitative components rather than a randomized controlled trial. The design is informative but still subject to selection and classroom-context confounds.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects on writing performance are very large, with b72=0.902 and multiple statistically significant pairwise comparisons. The positive gains persisted at delayed post-test, indicating a strong educational impact on the measured writing outcome.

paper_profiles.title: Towards Synergistic Teacher-AI Interactions with Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter addresses the growing role of generative AI in education and the concern that it may automate teaching work in ways that reduce teacher agency, cognitive engagement, and professional judgment. Rather than evaluating a single intervention with measured outcomes, the paper proposes a conceptual framework for understanding how teachers and AI interact across different degrees of shared control and mutual adaptation.

The authors introduce five levels of teacher-AI teaming: transactional, situational, operational, praxical, and synergistic. These levels are defined by how information, decisions, actions, and feedback flow between teachers and AI systems, ranging from one-shot request-response use to iterative co-adaptation and potential mutual challenge. The framework is positioned as a way to analyse GenAI-supported teacher-facing tools in educational contexts and to distinguish productivity-oriented automation from deeper cognitive teaming.

To illustrate the framework, the chapter draws on a systematic review of empirical AI-in-education studies from 2010 to 2025, with a secondary focus on GenAI-powered teacher-facing tools. The review suggests that current applications are mostly transactional, situational, or operational, with some praxical examples, but no clear empirical cases of true synergistic teaming. The authors argue that synergy may require stronger teacher AI literacy, better pedagogical design, and more human-centred co-design, while also noting that current GenAI systems may have limited capacity to genuinely push back or negotiate with teachers.

Because this is a conceptual and review-based chapter, it does not report controlled subgroup analyses by teacher experience, subject area, grade band, school context, or deployment format. Its main contribution is a taxonomy and interpretive lens for future empirical work on teacher-AI interactions.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI / large language model-based conversational and multimodal systems used to generate, adapt, evaluate, or provide feedback and instructional content.
identified_tools.use_case: The chapter does not evaluate a single product; it synthesizes empirical examples of teacher-facing GenAI use in education and proposes a five-level teacher-AI teaming framework, including use for feedback generation, lesson planning, tutoring, grading, and situational feedback.

findings.finding_summary: Across the reviewed empirical examples, GenAI was associated with improved efficiency in teacher-facing tasks. The chapter reports that AI-assisted grading decreased grading time by 44% and increased grading accuracy by 6% compared with manual grading, and that co-produced feedback reduced production time while maintaining comparable quality to manual feedback.
findings.measure: Grading time, grading accuracy, feedback production time, and feedback quality in reviewed teacher-facing GenAI studies

findings.finding_summary: The chapter reports that co-produced feedback using GenAI yielded comparable quality to manual feedback and statistically significant learning gains. The text does not provide study-level effect sizes, sample sizes, or confidence intervals for these findings.
findings.measure: Quality of student feedback and learning gains in reviewed studies

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual chapter with a narrative review of prior studies rather than a primary controlled evaluation of a specific tool. The reported evidence is synthesized from other papers and no subgroup or moderation analyses are presented here.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The chapter describes potentially meaningful practical effects such as reduced grading and feedback time and improved accuracy, but these are secondary summaries without full study details or pooled estimates. The impact direction is generally positive, but the underlying evidence is not directly evaluated in this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Do Teachers Dream of GenAI Widening Educational (In)equality? Envisioning the Future of K-12 GenAI Education from Global Teachers’ Perspectives
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers think about and enact generative AI (GenAI) education in relation to educational equality. The authors ask how teachers use GenAI instruction to reduce existing inequities, what barriers prevent equitable implementation, and what broader support teachers believe is needed to make GenAI education more inclusive.

The study is based on 30 semi-structured interviews with K–12 teachers in the United States, South Africa, and Taiwan. The teachers taught across multiple grade bands and subjects, including elementary, middle, and high school settings, with some teaching dedicated IT or computer science courses and others integrating GenAI into English, science, social studies, math, and special education classrooms. The work is therefore not an intervention study but a qualitative cross-national investigation of current practice and teacher perspectives.

Across the interviews, teachers described GenAI education as serving two linked purposes: helping students overcome pre-existing inequities and preventing new inequities from emerging. They used GenAI to address gaps in awareness, learning resources, digital literacy, and personalized support, especially for marginalized students. At the same time, they warned about shortcut use, bullying, cultural bias in outputs, and overreliance on AI for emotional support. The paper concludes that equitable GenAI education depends not only on teacher initiative, but also on infrastructure, training, culturally responsive tools, and support from schools, policymakers, communities, and technology companies.
paper_profiles.study_region: North America / Sub-Saharan Africa / East Asia & Pacific

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI chatbot or model used for education-related interaction, content generation, explanation, and feedback; no specific commercial product or model family is named in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers across the United States, South Africa, and Taiwan discussed teaching students about GenAI and using GenAI tools in classroom instruction, mainly for explaining concepts, generating examples/materials, supporting practice, and providing feedback-like responses within GenAI education.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, interview-based study of teachers’ perspectives and practices rather than an experimental evaluation of a specific AI tool. It provides rich contextual evidence but no causal estimates or controlled comparisons.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests important equity-related patterns in how GenAI is used in K-12 teaching, but it does not report quantified impacts or effect sizes. The influence is conceptually significant yet empirically unmeasured in this study.

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can help teachers personalize mathematics tasks for students, and what happens when the teacher remains in the loop while using the model. The core question is how teachers use ChatGPT to modify existing curriculum problems into personalized versions, how students react to those personalized problems, and whether the process becomes more efficient or improves over time with reflection and iteration.

The intervention involved 7 middle school mathematics teachers working with GPT-4o/ChatGPT to revise Illustrative Mathematics problems for their 7th-grade classes. Teachers first received a 2-hour training on personalization, bias, readability, and cultural relevance, then completed two personalization rounds: Unit 4 and Unit 6. In Zoom sessions with researchers, they wrote personalized problem versions, and students in ASSISTments received the resulting assignments. The study combined prompt-log analysis, video/transcript coding, student ratings, and open-ended student feedback. It also used mixed-effects models to test whether the number of prompts and unit (first versus second round) were associated with student ratings and teacher time.

The sample included 7 teachers across 6 U.S. schools and 521 7th-grade students. Teachers were experienced on average and came from geographically diverse schools serving varied levels of economic disadvantage and racial/ethnic marginalization. The main findings were that teachers most often used ChatGPT to add or swap popular-culture references and to improve realism, age appropriateness, and numerical plausibility. Students generally preferred specific, fine-grained references over broad categories, but also often disliked references that did not match their own interests. Efficiency was limited: creating one problem took about 4 minutes on average, and teachers did not clearly become faster over time. However, the second round involved more prompts and more time, and student ratings of interestingness and closeness improved significantly. The study concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization is useful but time-consuming, and that iterative reflection may improve quality even if it does not improve efficiency.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s generative AI chatbot/LLM system used to generate and revise text, including personalized instructional tasks and problem variants.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by 7 middle school mathematics teachers to rewrite existing Illustrative Mathematics problems into personalized versions aligned with students’ interests, with iterative prompting and teacher oversight.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers used an average of 3.2 prompts per problem (SD=2.6) and took about 4 minutes per problem (M=246 seconds, SD=165.7) to create 143 personalized mathematics problems for 512-521 7th grade students. Efficiency did not clearly improve over time; from Unit 4 to Unit 6, prompts increased by 1.26 per problem and time increased by 70.4 seconds per problem, suggesting iterative coaching made the work more time-consuming rather than more efficient.
findings.measure: Teacher prompts per problem; time spent creating each problem; change from Unit 4 to Unit 6
findings.effect_size: B=1.26 for prompts from Unit 4 to Unit 6; B=70.4 seconds for time from Unit 4 to Unit 6; B=0.240 for the 3-5 prompt zone vs other prompt counts on student ratings

findings.finding_summary: Using 3-5 prompts was associated with higher student ratings of both interestingness and closeness to interests by approximately 0.24 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073). The authors describe this as a 'Goldilocks Zone' suggesting that some iterative prompting improved outcomes, but too many prompts may reduce effectiveness.
findings.measure: Student ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests
findings.sample_size: 52 problems with rating data; student-level ratings

findings.finding_summary: Student ratings improved from Unit 4 to Unit 6. Mean interestingness increased from 2.27 to 2.56 and mean closeness increased from 2.28 to 2.66; a mixed-effects model found the increase significant (B=0.33, SE=0.095, t=3.49, p=0.0012). This suggests teachers’ second-round prompting, after reviewing student feedback, produced somewhat better personalized problems.
findings.measure: Student 1-5 ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single mixed-methods, quasi-experimental/observational study with no control group for performance outcomes. The paper includes quantitative models and rich qualitative analysis, but it is not a randomized efficacy trial.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main statistically significant effects are modest in size and mostly concern student interest ratings and teacher workflow rather than achievement. The reported 0.24 and 0.33 point gains on a 5-point scale are meaningful but not large, and efficiency gains were not demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can function as an automated teacher coach by generating classroom-observation scores and pedagogical feedback from transcript segments. The authors focus on three tasks: scoring transcript segments using classroom observation rubrics, identifying instructional highlights and missed opportunities, and providing actionable suggestions for eliciting more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the NCTE transcript dataset, which contains U.S. elementary mathematics classroom transcripts from 317 teachers across four districts serving largely historically marginalized students. The evaluation is zero-shot: ChatGPT is prompted without fine-tuning to score transcript segments with CLASS and MQI instruments, and expert math teachers judge the quality of its qualitative feedback for highlights/missed opportunities and suggestions.

Results show that ChatGPT performs poorly on all three tasks overall. Its score predictions have low correlation with human ratings, and added rubric detail or chain-of-thought style prompting does not meaningfully improve performance. For qualitative feedback, teachers generally find the outputs only partly relevant and often not insightful, with the MQI-based feedback performing worse than CLASS-based feedback. For suggestions, most outputs are actionable and faithful, but the model is highly repetitive and frequently restates what teachers already do. The paper concludes that current generative AI is not yet a reliable teacher coach, though it may eventually complement human coaching if improved.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot powered here by gpt-3.5-turbo, used zero-shot to score classroom transcript segments, identify highlights and missed opportunities, and generate actionable feedback suggestions.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as an automated teacher coach on elementary math classroom transcripts from the NCTE dataset across three tasks: predicting CLASS/MQI observation scores, identifying highlights and missed opportunities, and suggesting ways to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: Across 100 randomly sampled transcript segments, ChatGPT showed low Spearman correlations with human scores on CLASS and MQI observation items. For CLASS, correlations ranged from -0.06 to 0.35 across prompting methods; for MQI, correlations ranged from -0.11 to 0.17. Adding rubric descriptions or reasoning generally did not improve performance.
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between model-predicted observation scores and human ratings

findings.finding_summary: In qualitative evaluation of highlights and missed opportunities, teachers generally judged the model's responses as not very relevant or insightful. For CLASS items, 22% of responses were rated not relevant, 51% not insightful, and 22% unfaithful; for MQI items, 29% were not faithful, 71% not relevant, and 71% not insightful. The paper notes MQI results were worse than CLASS across all evaluation dimensions.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for generated highlights/missed opportunities

findings.finding_summary: For actionable suggestions, teachers rated most outputs as faithful, relevant, and actionable, but novelty was weak. The model produced redundant suggestions repeating what the teacher already did in 82% of cases, indicating limited originality even when the advice was usable.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of faithfulness, relevance, actionability, and novelty of generated suggestions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-study evaluation with expert teacher judgments and correlation analyses, but it is small-sample and exploratory rather than a controlled efficacy trial. The paper provides useful diagnostic evidence, though not causal evidence of instructional impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Effects are generally modest to unclear and often negative for scoring accuracy and insightfulness, with no reported medium/large positive effect sizes. The main positive pattern is usability/actionability of some suggestions, but novelty and scoring performance remain weak.

paper_profiles.title: GenAI at the Edge: Comprehensive Survey on Empowering Edge Devices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a comprehensive survey of research on deploying generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) models on edge devices. It addresses the problem that modern GenAI systems, including large language models and diffusion models, are typically too computationally and memory intensive for resource-constrained edge hardware, while cloud-only deployment raises latency, privacy, and connectivity concerns.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or any teacher- or student-facing program. Instead, it organizes the technical literature into three broad categories: software optimization, hardware optimization, and deployment frameworks. Within software optimization, it reviews model compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation, along with neural architecture search and open-source model adaptation. Within hardware optimization, it surveys accelerator designs and attention-optimization methods for LLMs and diffusion models. It also reviews systems and frameworks such as TensorRT, TVM, EdgeMoE, CoreInfer, and super-resolution acceleration pipelines.

Because this is a survey rather than an empirical study, it does not report a participant population, controlled comparison, subgroup analyses, or outcome effects. Its main conclusion is that progress in co-design across algorithms, hardware, and frameworks is making GenAI increasingly feasible on edge devices, but important challenges remain around personalization, security, latency, and energy efficiency.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI systems based on large language models and foundation models that generate new data or content such as text and images.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a survey of GenAI techniques for deployment on edge devices; it does not evaluate an instructional coaching or lesson feedback product.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a survey paper on edge deployment of generative AI, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It does not report controlled, quasi-controlled, or subgroup analyses relevant to teacher coaching or feedback.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational outcomes or impact estimates are reported. The paper provides background and synthesis on system optimization only, so there is no measured instructional impact to rate.

paper_profiles.title: Bridging Cultural Distance Between Models Default and Local Classroom Demands: How Global Teachers Adopt GenAI to Support Everyday Teaching Practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers experience and adapt to generative AI (GenAI) when using it for everyday teaching tasks. The authors ask why GenAI outputs sometimes align well with classroom needs, sometimes require substantial teacher labor to make usable, and sometimes fail entirely because of cultural, linguistic, curricular, or policy mismatches. To explain these differences, the paper introduces the concept of "cultural distance," defined as the gap between a model’s default cultural repertoire and the situated demands of teaching practice.

The study is based on 30 in-depth, semi-structured interviews with K–12 teachers who were actively using GenAI in South Africa, Taiwan, and the United States. Participants discussed using general-purpose and education-specific tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Meta AI, MagicSchool, Mindjoy, Doubao, ERNIE Bot, and others for tasks including stakeholder communication, brainstorming instructional activities, generating assessment questions, and designing culturally relevant materials. The paper does not evaluate a coaching intervention or feedback tool; instead, it develops a qualitative framework from teachers’ descriptions of how they prompt, revise, localize, or abandon GenAI outputs.

Findings organize teachers’ experiences into three levels of cultural distance: low-distance tasks like communication and activity brainstorming, mid-distance tasks like assessment generation and culturally relevant lesson design, and high-distance tasks involving unsupported local languages or policy restrictions. Teachers generally needed little effort for low-distance tasks, significant iterative prompting and editing for mid-distance tasks, and often could not overcome high-distance barriers even with repeated effort. The paper concludes that cultural alignment in educational GenAI is not binary but a spectrum, and that reducing mismatches will require both better model/data coverage and more context-aware design, policy, and infrastructure.
paper_profiles.study_region: Sub-Saharan Africa, East Asia & Pacific, North America

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Chat-based generative AI systems used by teachers to draft, rewrite, simplify, brainstorm, and localize teaching materials and communications.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as the everyday GenAI tools K–12 teachers used for lesson design, communication, assessment generation, and culturally relevant adaptation across South Africa, Taiwan, and the United States.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, interview-based conceptual paper rather than a controlled or quasi-controlled study. It provides rich empirical description, but no causal estimates or subgroup analyses.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful variation in usability and adaptation effort by task and context, but it does not report effect sizes or measured student/teacher outcome impacts. Evidence is descriptive and exploratory, so impact is unclear rather than demonstrably large.

paper_profiles.title: Transforming Teacher Education in Developing Countries: The Role of Generative AI in Bridging Theory and Practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a perspective/theoretical study about how generative AI (GenAI) could address longstanding problems in teacher education in developing countries, using Ghana as the main case. The central problem is the persistent gap between theory-heavy teacher preparation and the limited implementation of pedagogical modeling and performance-based assessment in initial teacher education programs.

Rather than reporting an empirical intervention, the paper argues that GenAI can reduce the burden of content delivery and content knowledge acquisition, allowing teacher educators to spend more time on modeling teaching practices, supporting authentic assessment, and strengthening professional development. The author also suggests that GenAI may help reduce resistance to curricular change, improve access to resources, and encourage digital literacy and critical thinking among pre-service teachers.

The context is Ghanaian initial teacher education, especially the four-year colleges of education reform and its constructivist/experiential orientation. The paper concludes that GenAI could catalyze broader systemic change in teacher education and, downstream, improve K-12 teaching and workforce readiness, but it warns about misuse and the possible erosion of critical thinking and creativity. It calls for scaffolded GenAI literacy and future empirical research on responsible integration.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative artificial intelligence / large language model tools used for content synthesis, drafting, feedback, and instructional support.
identified_tools.use_case: This is a perspective/theoretical paper arguing that generative AI could support teacher education in developing countries by reducing content-delivery burden, enabling pedagogical modeling, supporting performance-based assessment, and aiding professional development; it does not evaluate a specific deployed product in an intervention.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/theoretical paper using logical deduction and literature citation rather than an empirical controlled or quasi-controlled evaluation. It does not report original outcome data, subgroup analyses, or moderation findings.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Because no empirical effects are reported, there is no measurable impact estimate to classify as positive or negative. The paper argues for potentially substantial system-level influence, but this remains speculative rather than demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: Guardrails for avoiding harmful medical product recommendations and off-label promotion in generative AI models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the risk that generative AI models may recommend medical products for unapproved uses, creating both safety and regulatory concerns. The authors focus on “off-label promotion,” defined as recommending a medical product for an indication not included in its FDA-approved labeling, and argue that this can be harmful when produced at scale by general-purpose generative models.

The paper proposes a post-hoc detection method for identifying potentially harmful product-indication associations in multimodal large language model outputs. The method standardizes user queries, uses biomedical named entity recognition to extract products and diseases, matches entities to FDA labeling data, and then determines whether a response is making an off-label recommendation. The study demonstrates the approach with Anthropic Claude 3 Sonnet in a shopping-style medical product question-answering setting, where the user supplies an image of a product label and asks a question about it.

For experimentation, the authors generated 14,300 synthetic queries across 35 pharmaceuticals with 143 known off-label uses. They report that 15.4% of model responses contained off-label indications, and that their detector achieved reasonably strong precision and recall on a human-annotated sample. The paper concludes that generalist GenAI can surface unvetted medical product uses and that guardrails are needed to filter or prevent harmful recommendations. No teacher, student, school, or education-related populations were studied.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic’s multimodal large language model / generative AI assistant for text and image understanding and generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the evaluated MLLM in a shopping-style medical product question-answering setting; given product-label images and user queries, its responses were analyzed for off-label product promotion.

findings.finding_summary: Across 14,300 synthetic customer queries for 35 pharmaceuticals, 15.4% of Claude 3 responses were identified as containing off-label indications. Using 2,000 random human-annotated samples, the proposed detection method achieved precision of 85.75%, recall of 80.47%, and F1 of 83.02% for identifying off-label promotion in model outputs.
findings.measure: Off-label indications in model responses; detection performance of the proposed off-label identification method (precision, recall, F1)
findings.sample_size: n=14300 synthetic queries; n=2000 human-annotated sample

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a proof-of-concept empirical paper with one model and no controlled comparison of instructional outcomes; it does not provide educational intervention evidence. The study design is technical and descriptive rather than an education experiment or review.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports a notable rate of off-label outputs (15.4%), but this is not an educational effect size and no instructional impact is measured. The findings mainly indicate a moderate safety/guardrail issue in model behavior.

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Models are In-context Teachers for Knowledge Reasoning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can function as better in-context teachers than humans for knowledge reasoning tasks. The core problem is that standard few-shot chain-of-thought prompting depends on human-written rationales, which are expensive to create and may not match what a student model can best learn from. The authors propose an "encoding specificity" view of in-context learning: rationales used as demonstrations should resemble the student model’s training distribution as closely as possible.

To operationalize this idea, the paper introduces two methods. First, Self-Explain prompts an LLM to generate explanations for question-answer pairs from the task domain, then uses those self-generated rationales as in-context exemplars. Second, Teach-Back first fine-tunes a teacher model on a student’s self-explanations so the teacher can produce more student-aligned rationales. The experiments use knowledge-intensive multiple-choice QA datasets in both general and expert domains, specifically StrategyQA, MedMCQA, and MedQA, with several LLMs including Llama2, Mistral, Phi-3-mini, and GPT-3.5.

The main findings are that self-explanations usually outperform human-crafted CoT examples, and generating multiple self-explanations can improve performance further. The paper also shows that a model’s own self-explanations are often the best demonstrations for that model, while stronger or larger teacher models are not necessarily better if their rationales differ from the student’s. Teach-Back can improve cross-model teaching effectiveness, especially when the teacher is aligned to the student through fine-tuning. Overall, the paper argues that rationale similarity to the student’s internal knowledge, rather than human plausibility alone or teacher scale, is a key factor in effective in-context teaching.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model used for generating in-context explanations/rationales and few-shot prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the student/teacher model in in-context teaching experiments; GPT-3.5-turbo generated self-explanations and also served as a student and teacher model in comparisons with human-crafted CoTs and other LLM teachers.

findings.finding_summary: Across knowledge-reasoning tasks, GPT-3.5-turbo prompted with its own self-explanations outperformed human-crafted CoTs by around 2 percentage points on MedQA and the general-domain task, and reached similar performance to human CoT on MedCQA. With five generated self-explanations per exemplar, performance improved further to 56.6% on MedCQA, 59.6% on MedQA, and 59.7% on StrategyQA.
findings.measure: Test accuracy on MedCQA, MedQA, and StrategyQA under few-shot prompting

findings.finding_summary: When GPT-3.5-turbo was taught using another model's explanations, its performance depended on similarity between teacher and student explanations. Teach-Back further improved GPT-3.5-turbo's few-shot performance; the paper reports that a fine-tuned Mistral-7B could teach GPT-3.5 to surpass human teachers by around 5% in test accuracy and Self-Explain by around 4%.
findings.measure: Test accuracy after in-context teaching with LLM/human teachers and Teach-Back

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical study with controlled comparisons, but it is not a randomized classroom or teacher-intervention study; it evaluates prompting and model-teacher configurations on benchmark QA tasks. The evidence is methodologically solid for ML experimentation but only indirectly relevant to education practice.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are mostly modest-to-moderate in benchmark accuracy (about 2% to 5% depending on setting). The results are promising for LLM prompting and instructional-teaching analogies, but they do not directly demonstrate educational impact in real classrooms.

paper_profiles.title: Understanding Parents’ Desires in Moderating Children’s Interactions with GenAI Chatbots through LLM-Generated Probes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how parents want to moderate their children’s interactions with generative AI chatbots, and what kinds of chatbot behaviors make interactions feel concerning. The authors focus on moderation and transparency preferences at the level of individual conversations, rather than broad device-level parental controls. They are motivated by the rapid rise of GenAI use among children and the gap between existing coarse-grained parental controls and the more nuanced risks parents anticipate in child–AI conversations.

To study this, the authors generated synthetic child–chatbot scenarios using an LLM, iteratively refined them with a small parent validation group, and then used 12 selected scenarios as probes in semi-structured interviews with 24 parents of children aged 6–18 in the United States. Parents reviewed the scenarios, rated concern, explained why they found them troubling, and described how they would prefer a chatbot to respond and how they would want to be informed. The analysis was thematic and qualitative, using grounded-theory-informed coding across interviews.

The main findings are that parents are concerned not only about obviously unsafe or inappropriate chatbot outputs, but also about subtler issues such as misunderstanding a child’s intent, emotionally impactful responses, developmental mismatch, exposure to unsafe ideas, signs of harmful child intent, overdependence, and children trying to bypass safeguards. Parents wanted fine-grained, conversation-level moderation that explains refusals, corrects misunderstandings, adapts to age, and sometimes defers to human support. They also preferred personalized transparency controls, especially alerts about flagged activity and different levels of access to content and conversation history. Overall, the paper concludes that parental controls for GenAI should be more personalized, conversational, and sensitive to context than current coarse-grained tools.

identified_tools.use_case: The paper used synthetic child–GenAI chatbot scenarios, generated with GPT-4.1-nano, to probe parents’ concerns and preferences about moderating children’s interactions. The evaluated system was a generic GenAI chatbot rather than a single named child-facing product.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, interview-based study using scenario probes and thematic analysis, not a controlled effectiveness study. It provides rich descriptive evidence but no causal estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports important descriptive patterns about parental moderation preferences and concerns, but it does not measure learning or behavioral impact with effect sizes. Impact is therefore informative but not quantifiable.

paper_profiles.title: Teacher agency in the age of generative AI: towards a framework of hybrid intelligence for learning design
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how generative AI (genAI) affects teachers’ professional agency in educational settings. Rather than evaluating a specific tool with experimental data, the authors discuss the risks that genAI may reduce teachers’ capacity to act, affect decisions, and take stances when it is used for learning design, lesson creation, grading, and related educational tasks.

The paper situates this discussion within broader debates about educational technology adoption, teacher trust in AI, and the tendency for edtech to prioritize learner agency while limiting teacher influence over the technology. It draws on concepts from teacher agency, contextual knowledge in TPACK, and hybrid intelligence to argue that AI systems should be designed as human-AI collaborative partners rather than autonomous substitutes for teachers.

The proposed approach is a theoretical framework in which hybrid intelligence supports co-creation between teachers and genAI so that teachers retain agency while benefiting from AI assistance. The paper uses prior literature and conceptual arguments, with illustrative examples such as genAI supporting learning design and tailoring explanations for learners. Its main conclusion is that genAI should be designed to extend, not diminish, teacher agency, and that human-centred hybrid intelligence may help align AI use with educational and ethical goals.

identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses genAI as a broad class of tools that can support teachers’ learning design, provide feedback, generate teaching materials and lesson plans, and act as a human-AI collaborator; it is not an empirical evaluation of a specific product.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper about teachers’ agency and hybrid intelligence, not an empirical study of an AI tool. It does not report controlled, quasi-controlled, or subgroup analyses.

paper_profiles.title: Relief or displacement? How teachers are negotiating generative AI’s role in their professional practice
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Conference proceedings (venue not otherwise specified in text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers are responding to the introduction of generative AI (genAI) in their professional practice, with attention to the tensions between perceived relief and perceived displacement. Rather than studying student outcomes or testing a specific instructional intervention, the authors ask how teachers perceive genAI, what opportunities and challenges arise when districts introduce it, and how teachers negotiate its use within professional, pedagogical, and ethical boundaries.

The study is based on semi-structured interviews with 22 teachers from a large U.S. school district that was an early adopter of genAI and had encouraged use of MagicSchool AI and other tools. Participants taught across elementary, middle, and high school levels and across subject areas including STEM, social studies, special education, CLDE, literacy, and media/CTE. Interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis informed by the Teacher Response Model, focusing on teachers’ value-driven decisions, contextual constraints, and perceptions of what was possible with genAI.

The paper finds that teachers were neither simply adopting nor rejecting genAI. Instead, they described adoption as motivated by district encouragement, peer validation, burnout prevention, and creative instructional possibilities, while reluctance stemmed from lack of time, stigma around “cheating,” preference for established routines, and environmental concerns. Teachers also described carefully setting boundaries around AI use to preserve professional judgment, ensure factual accuracy, protect student data, and regulate student exposure. The authors conclude that sustainable genAI integration depends less on the tool itself than on district policy clarity, teacher-led professional development, ethical guidance, and support for students’ critical AI literacy.

paper_profiles.title: The Design and Implementation of an Educational Chatbot with Personalized Adaptive Learning Features for Project Management Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to design and evaluate a generative AI-enabled educational chatbot that supports personalized adaptive learning (PAL) in higher education project management training. The authors argue that although educational chatbots and PAL systems have been studied in STEM and language learning, there is little work on multidisciplinary domains such as project management, and even less on chatbot designs grounded in explicit PAL principles.

The intervention is PMTutor, a chatbot built using design science research and implemented with rule-based dialog logic, natural language understanding, and an OpenAI GPT-3 fallback for out-of-scope questions. PMTutor included five PAL features: self-assessment, topic recommendation, tailored feedback for correct/incorrect answers, the ability to view/resume exercises, and question answering. Content was organized by topic and designed by teaching staff/domain experts. The system was piloted in an online project management course, where postgraduate students in a Finnish university of applied sciences completed activity network exercises and then filled out a retrospective pre/post survey plus open-ended feedback questions.

The pilot found that students generally had positive experiences, with the tailored exercise feedback receiving the strongest praise. Self-reported competence increased significantly from pre- to posttest, and qualitative feedback suggested that the chatbot was useful for recapping concepts and supporting learning at an individual pace. Participants also reported usability issues, especially navigation between modules and exercises, the use of English in a Finnish course, and some limitations in question-answering quality. The paper concludes that PAL chatbots can engage learners and complement project management instruction, but that better usability, localization, and more sophisticated personalization remain important future directions.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used as a conversational AI component to answer learner questions beyond the chatbot's rule-based dialog logic.
identified_tools.use_case: PMTutor incorporated OpenAI GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) to generate answers for learner questions outside the scope of the system's NLU and dialog rules, while warning learners about possible inaccuracies.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is primarily a design science and pilot implementation paper with qualitative feedback and a small pre/post self-assessment, not a controlled comparison of AI tool effectiveness across subgroups. The study includes some quantitative change in self-assessment, but the evidence base is limited and non-randomized.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports a statistically significant within-group increase in retrospective self-assessment (median 3 to 4, n=29) and positive user feedback, but no effect size for the AI tool and no subgroup analyses of teacher experience, subject area, grade band, school context, or deployment format. Overall impact is suggestive but unclear and modest.

paper_profiles.title: The effect of AI-powered chatbots in social studies education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether an AI-powered chatbot can improve learning outcomes in middle school Social Studies and how students and the teacher experience its use. The paper addresses a gap identified by the authors: while chatbots have been studied in language and computer science education, their use in Social Studies had not previously been investigated.

The intervention was a closed-domain, hybrid chatbot called SosyalciBot, built with Dialogflow and MindBehind. It provided short instructional explanations, question-answer activities, hints, instant feedback, motivational messages, visual support, and some audio-based delivery. The chatbot was integrated into 6th-grade Culture and Heritage lessons, sometimes used before teacher instruction to build readiness and sometimes after teacher instruction to reinforce learning. A pilot was conducted, and then the main study used a pretest-posttest control group quasi-experimental design with three intact classes: one experimental group and two control groups taught with a constructivist approach. Quantitative outcomes were measured with a researcher-developed achievement test and a delayed permanence test five weeks later; qualitative data came from interviews with 17 students and the practitioner teacher.

Results showed that the experimental group outperformed both control groups on post-test and retention measures, with large effect sizes. Interview data suggested the chatbot improved readiness, engagement, enjoyment, and reinforcement of learning, and both students and the teacher viewed it as a useful teaching support. Participants especially valued the chatbot’s instant feedback, constructive language, visual and audio support, and opportunities for repeated practice. Limitations were also noted, including lack of voice input, limited dynamism, and the need for stronger AI communication capacity. Overall, the paper concludes that chatbots have strong potential for Social Studies education, but further refinement is needed for broader and more flexible classroom use.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general AI-powered chatbot used for instructional dialogue, lesson explanation, question-answering, hints, instant feedback, and reinforcement in a closed-domain educational setting.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as 'SosyalciBot' to teach and reinforce 6th-grade Social Studies content, provide Q&A practice, clues, instant feedback, and motivational support; deployed in both written and audio forms in a web-based platform.

findings.finding_summary: In a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design with 78 6th-grade students, the experimental group taught with the chatbot scored significantly higher on the post-test than both control groups after adjusting for pretest scores. The corrected post-test means were 20.897 for the experimental group, 17.027 for Control 1, and 16.478 for Control 2; the group effect was significant with F(2,74)=7.646, p=.001, η²=.171.
findings.measure: 6th Grade Culture and Heritage Success Test post-test scores (ANCOVA-adjusted)

findings.finding_summary: On the delayed permanence test, the experimental group again outperformed both control groups after adjustment for pretest scores. The corrected permanency-test means were 21.944 for the experimental group, 18.394 for Control 1, and 17.233 for Control 2; the group effect was significant with F(2,74)=9.019, p<.001, η²=.196.
findings.measure: 6th Grade Culture and Heritage Success Test permanency test scores (ANCOVA-adjusted)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods quasi-experimental study with one nonrandomly assigned teacher/classroom implementation and qualitative interviews, not a randomized trial. The design is credible for classroom intervention evidence, but there are no subgroup analyses or randomized controls to raise the tier higher.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The adjusted group effects were statistically significant and in the modest-to-large range (η²=.171 and .196). This indicates meaningful positive impact on academic outcomes for the chatbot-assisted instruction.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether an analytical AI feedback platform can support lesson planning in vocational teacher education, and whether its effects differ from standard human feedback. The study is motivated by the challenge university instructors face in providing frequent, detailed, individualized feedback on lesson plans, especially in complex vocational business education settings.

The intervention used EDDA, an analytical AI platform that classifies lesson plans and returns expert-level text and visual feedback on 10 main planning dimensions and 57 subcategories, including action orientation, process orientation, problem orientation, motivation, digitalization, sustainability, and basic lesson-structure dimensions. In the experimental condition, student teachers used EDDA throughout a semester and could also seek human clarification when needed; the control group received human feedback only. The study also measured broader meta-dimensions such as AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competences, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and motivation.

Participants were 103 master’s students in business education in Germany, working in small groups on 90-minute lesson plans under the same course structure and planning constraints. The intervention ran across a semester and was implemented in two cycles at two universities, with the comparison group recruited from an elective module at a different university. The design was not randomized, so it is best described as quasi-experimental.

The main findings suggest that AI feedback can match or exceed human feedback on several lesson-planning dimensions. The experimental group showed stronger results on some sustainability-related and didactic categories, including social competences for sustainable development and reflexivity, and a positive effect on SDG 15. However, the study also found that prior competence mattered: higher initial performance often predicted less growth, and some sustainability knowledge/attitude variables were associated with specific planning outcomes. For the meta-dimensions, simply using AI did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, or motivation, indicating that AI feedback works best as part of a broader instructional framework rather than as a stand-alone tool.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI / chatbot tool category used for producing or evaluating text-based outputs, without a specific commercial or model name.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper situates its study in the broader literature on generative AI feedback and compares its analytical AI platform to human feedback and to generic generative AI tools discussed in prior work; it does not evaluate a named generative product itself.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled longitudinal intervention study, but the paper evaluates an analytical AI platform rather than a named generative AI product. The design is stronger than descriptive work, yet the sample is relatively small and the setting is specialized.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are mostly modest to moderate and concentrated in specific planning dimensions, with several outcomes showing no effect. The most notable positive findings are limited to selected sustainability-related and competence-related subdimensions, not broad across all measures.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI-assisted feedback and EFL writing: a study on proficiency, revision frequency and writing quality
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-assisted writing feedback improves EFL academic writing more effectively than traditional teacher feedback. The central question is how a commonly available AI writing assistant, Grammarly Premium, affects overall writing proficiency, revision behavior, and specific dimensions of writing quality in postgraduate EFL learners.

The intervention compared two feedback conditions in a pre-test/post-test control-group study. Sixty postgraduate students enrolled in an English for Academic Purposes writing course at a public university in Egypt were randomly assigned to an experimental group using Grammarly Premium and a control group receiving traditional written teacher feedback. The study ran for 6 weeks within an 8-week timeframe. All students completed the same writing tasks and were taught by the same instructor; the experimental group also received a training session on using Grammarly critically for revision.

Results showed that the AI-assisted feedback group outperformed the control group on the overall post-test writing score, with especially strong gains in Language Use and Organization. Content did not differ significantly between groups, suggesting that the tool was more effective for surface-level and structural aspects of writing than for higher-order idea development. Within the experimental group, more frequent use of Grammarly’s generative and corrective features and more revisions were positively associated with better outcomes, and generative feature use during assignments predicted post-test performance beyond prior assignment scores. Qualitative interviews reinforced these findings by showing that students perceived the tool as increasing confidence, speeding revision, and improving accuracy, while also emphasizing the need for critical judgment and noting limitations in fluency and broader language support.

identified_tools.name: Grammarly
identified_tools.description: An AI-powered writing assistant and grammar/style feedback tool that provides automated corrective suggestions, clarity, style, vocabulary, and limited rewrite support.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as Grammarly Premium to provide immediate AI-assisted feedback on EFL students’ drafts during practice and assignment writing tasks, compared against traditional written teacher feedback.
