findings.finding_summary: In a randomized pre-test/post-test control group study with 60 postgraduate EFL students (n=30 Grammarly, n=30 control), the Grammarly group achieved significantly higher total post-test writing scores than the control group. The reported means were 54.37 (SD=5.54) versus 45.50 (SD=5.32), with Welch’s t(47.35)=10.89, p<0.001; Mann–Whitney U=16.50, z=6.42, p<0.001.
findings.measure: Total post-test academic writing score

findings.finding_summary: Effects varied by writing component. The Grammarly group did not differ significantly from control on Content scores (17.05 vs 16.10; t(58)=1.68, p=0.098), but it scored significantly higher on Organization (18.12 vs 15.65; Welch’s t(51.88)=4.31, p<0.001) and Language Use (19.20 vs 13.75; Welch’s t(40.15)=9.55, p<0.001).
findings.measure: Post-test writing component scores: Content, Organization, Language Use

findings.finding_summary: Within the Grammarly group (n=30), higher feature use and more revisions were positively correlated with better post-test performance. Correlations with total post-test score were significant for generative AI use in practice (r=0.346, p=0.049) and assignments (r=0.373, p=0.032), grammar/vocabulary feature use in practice (r=0.374, p=0.032) and assignments (r=0.348, p=0.047), and total revisions in practice (r=0.359, p=0.040) and assignments (r=0.375, p=0.032).
findings.measure: Correlations between Grammarly usage behaviors/revisions and total post-test writing score

findings.finding_summary: In the Grammarly group (n=30), feature use was differentially associated with specific writing components. Generative AI feature use correlated significantly with Content (r=0.360 practice; r=0.369 assignment) and Organization (r=0.346 practice; r=0.389 assignment), and with Cohesion/Consistency for assignments (r=0.369). Grammar/vocabulary feature use correlated significantly only with Grammar and Vocabulary scores (r=0.415 practice; r=0.395 assignment).
findings.measure: Correlations between Grammarly usage behaviors and specific writing component scores

findings.finding_summary: More frequent use of Grammarly’s generative AI features was associated with more total revisions in the experimental group. The correlations were significant for practice activities (r=0.421, p=0.012) and assignment activities (r=0.398, p=0.018), suggesting that tool engagement was linked to a more active revision process.
findings.measure: Correlations between generative AI feature use and total revisions

findings.finding_summary: Hierarchical regression showed that assignment score explained initial variance in post-test performance (R2=0.162), and adding generative AI use during assignments improved the model by ΔR2=0.113 to a final R2=0.275. In the final model, assignment score (β=0.38) and generative AI use (β=0.34) were significant predictors; adding revision frequency did not significantly improve prediction (ΔR2=0.010).
findings.measure: Hierarchical regression predicting post-test writing score

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control-group study with random assignment after pretest, plus correlational and qualitative components. It is useful evidence, but it is not a full-blown RCT and includes subgroup-like descriptive analyses rather than true moderation tests.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects on total writing score, organization, and language use are large and statistically robust, with substantial mean differences and strong t values. The study also reports meaningful positive associations between tool engagement and outcomes, indicating strong practical impact in this setting.

paper_profiles.title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can be used effectively as automated writing evaluation (AWE) feedback in English as a new language (ENL) writing instruction, and whether students prefer AI-generated feedback to feedback from a human tutor. The authors frame the study around broader concerns about how tools such as ChatGPT and GPT-4 should be ethically and pedagogically integrated into education, especially for writing support and feedback.

The paper reports two longitudinal studies conducted at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region. In Study 1, 48 university ENL learners participated in a six-week repeated-measures quasi-experimental comparison between an experimental group that received GPT-4-generated feedback and a control group that received human tutor feedback. Writing quality was measured using pre- and post-tests and weekly writing revisions. In Study 2, a separate group of 43 ENL students received both AI and human feedback and completed weekly preference surveys plus open-ended responses about their experiences.

Study 1 found no significant difference in writing gains between students who received GPT-4 feedback and those who received human tutor feedback, suggesting AI-generated feedback was not superior but could be used without harming learning outcomes. Study 2 found a near-even split in preference between AI and human feedback: human feedback was valued for interpersonal interaction and speaking practice, while AI feedback was valued for clarity, specificity, and availability. The authors conclude that a blended model combining AI feedback with human discussion may be the most beneficial approach, and they note that further research is needed on proficiency level, prompt design, and broader populations.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based chatbot interface used to generate text responses from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used via GPT-4 to generate individualized corrective writing feedback for ENL students in a six-week quasi-experimental study, and to provide AI feedback alongside human tutor feedback in a separate preference study.

findings.finding_summary: In Study 1 (n=48; EG n=23, CG n=25), repeated-measures ANOVA found no significant interaction between feedback source and time on writing scores (F=3.094, p=0.085, partial eta squared=0.063). The between-subjects effect of group was also not significant (F=0.241, p=0.626, partial eta squared=0.005), indicating AI-generated feedback did not outperform human tutor feedback on the writing rubric.
findings.measure: Pretest-posttest analytic rubric scores for content, coherence, language use, and sources/evidence (max 40)
findings.effect_size: partial eta squared=0.063 (interaction); partial eta squared=0.005 (group)

findings.finding_summary: In Study 2 (n=43, with weekly survey responses varying from 32 to 41), students showed a near-even split in preference between AI-generated and human tutor feedback. The grand means slightly favored human tutor feedback on satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and overall preference, but all mean differences were nonsignificant; qualitative comments indicated some students valued AI clarity/specificity while others preferred human interaction and the ability to ask follow-up questions.
findings.measure: Weekly feedback preference survey items and qualitative responses

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental comparative study plus a separate preference survey with mixed methods, but not a randomized controlled trial. The paper provides clear procedures, sample sizes, and inferential statistics, though subgroup/moderation analyses were not reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main quantitative effects were null or near-null (partial eta squared=0.063 for the non-significant interaction and 0.005 for group). Preferences were split, suggesting useful but not clearly impactful evidence rather than a demonstrable positive effect.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can serve as a useful automated teacher coach. The authors frame the problem around three coaching tasks: scoring classroom transcript segments using observation rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the National Center for Teacher Effectiveness (NCTE) transcript dataset, which contains classroom observation transcripts from U.S. elementary mathematics lessons. The population is 4th- and 5th-grade classrooms taught by 317 teachers across four school districts. The model is evaluated in a zero-shot setting using gpt-3.5-turbo on CLASS and MQI rubric items, and human math teachers rate the quality of the generated qualitative feedback.

Results show that ChatGPT performs poorly at score prediction, with low correlations against human ratings and a tendency to predict generic, similar scores across items. For qualitative feedback, teachers judged many outputs as not insightful or not relevant, though many responses were still faithful and actionable. For suggestion generation, the model often repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript, indicating low novelty. The paper concludes that current ChatGPT-style models may complement coaching but are not yet reliable substitutes for expert instructional feedback.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational large language model used for zero-shot scoring, identifying highlights and missed opportunities, and generating actionable instructional feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as an automated teacher coach on elementary math classroom transcripts using three zero-shot tasks: scoring observation items (CLASS and MQI), identifying highlights and missed opportunities, and generating suggestions to elicit more student reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: On Task A (scoring transcripts), ChatGPT showed low correlation with human ratings across CLASS and MQI items. Spearman correlations were near zero or negative for most items (e.g., CLPC 0.00, CLBM 0.35, CLINSTD -0.01; EXPL 0.02, REMED 0.05, LANGIMP 0.00, SMQR 0.17 under direct-answer prompting), indicating poor alignment with expert scores.
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between model-predicted observation scores and human annotator scores
findings.effect_size: rho mostly near 0; best reported rho=0.35 (CLBM)

findings.finding_summary: Performance did not improve with added rubric descriptions or reasoning prompts; in some cases it worsened. For example, CLBM dropped from rho=0.35 (DA) to 0.23 (DA+) and 0.07 (RA), while several MQI dimensions remained near zero or negative across prompting methods.
findings.measure: Spearman correlation under different prompting methods (DA, DA+, RA)
findings.effect_size: best reported rho change CLBM 0.35  0.23  0.07; other items largely near 0

findings.finding_summary: For Task B, teachers generally did not find the model's highlights/missed-opportunity feedback insightful or relevant. The paper reports that 35-50% of CLASS responses and 55-71% of MQI responses were rated not relevant, and 51-71% of CLASS/MQI responses were rated not insightful, with MQI worse than CLASS across all criteria.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for generated highlights and missed opportunities

findings.finding_summary: Faithfulness was a nontrivial issue but not the dominant failure mode: around 20-30% of Task B responses were rated unfaithful. The paper also reports worse MQI performance than CLASS, with low-score proportions increasing from CLASS to MQI for faithful (22% to 29%), relevant (35% to 55%), and insightful (51% to 71%).
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of faithfulness plus comparison of low-score proportions across CLASS vs MQI

findings.finding_summary: For Task C, the majority of model suggestions were actionable, relevant, and faithful, but novelty was weak. The most notable result is redundancy: 82% of suggestions described what the teacher already did in the transcript, although most responses were still rated actionable and faithful to context.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, actionability, and novelty for generated suggestions

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports descriptive patterns that the model tended to predict the same score for a given rubric dimension regardless of transcript evidence, often overpredicting CLASS scores and defaulting to the middle MQI score (or highest score for REMED). This suggests prompt/dimension-driven behavior rather than transcript-sensitive scoring.
findings.measure: Distributional comparison of human vs. model ratings and score histograms

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small empirical study with human evaluation and quantitative comparisons, but it is not experimental in the causal sense and uses limited samples (e.g., 100 scored segments, 2 human raters for qualitative tasks). The evidence is informative but methodologically constrained.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The findings suggest limited practical performance for ChatGPT as a teacher coach, with mostly near-zero correlations and substantial qualitative shortcomings, so the impact on outcomes is unclear to modest at best. Some Task C suggestions were actionable, but the dominant pattern is weak or mixed performance.

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how teachers should remain in the loop when using generative AI to personalize mathematics tasks. The central question is not whether AI can generate personalized problems, but how teachers interact with the system, how much time the process requires, and whether the resulting tasks match student preferences and perceptions of relevance.

Seven middle school mathematics teachers used ChatGPT/GPT-4o to modify existing Illustrative Mathematics problems for their seventh-grade students. The teachers participated in a two-hour training, then worked in short Zoom-based problem-writing sessions for Unit 4 and again for Unit 6, with their prompts, speech, and ChatGPT logs recorded. The personalized problems were delivered through ASSISTments to 521 seventh-grade students in six U.S. schools. Students completed closed-ended ratings of interestingness and closeness to their interests, and a subset provided open-ended feedback.

The study found that teachers typically used broad topic prompts first and then refined outputs through multiple additional prompts, focusing heavily on realism, numerical accuracy, age appropriateness, and specific popular-culture references. Students preferred smaller-grain, more specific references, while broader categories were less satisfying for many students. A mixed-effects analysis showed that using about 3–5 prompts per problem was associated with the best student ratings, but personalization was still time-consuming: about four minutes per problem on average, with no clear evidence of becoming faster over time. After reflecting on student feedback, teachers used more prompts and more time in Unit 6, and students rated Unit 6 problems more positively than Unit 4 problems. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization supports professional learning and quality control, but it limits grain size and does not appear to be highly time efficient.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM system used for text generation and task adaptation.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers used ChatGPT (with underlying model GPT-4o) to modify existing middle school mathematics problems into personalized versions aligned with students' popular culture interests, while researchers observed prompting, revision, and reflection.

findings.finding_summary: Across 143 personalized problems, teachers used an average of 3.2 prompts per problem (SD=2.6) and 246 seconds per problem (SD=165.7). Efficiency did not improve over time; from Unit 4 to Unit 6, teachers used 1.26 more prompts per problem and spent 70.4 more seconds per problem, both statistically significant.
findings.measure: Prompts per problem and time to create each problem
findings.effect_size: B=1.26 (unit effect on prompts); B=70.4 seconds (unit effect on time)

findings.finding_summary: Teachers' personalization work with ChatGPT appeared to provide professional learning opportunities, but it was time-consuming and did not become clearly more efficient with experience. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization is feasible only at a relatively broad grain size, which limits alignment with students' desire for finer-grained personalization.
findings.measure: Descriptive teacher growth, reflection, and feasibility judgments

findings.finding_summary: Student ratings of personalized problems were higher when teachers used 3-5 prompts than when they used other numbers of prompts; the paper reports this as approximately a 0.24-point increase on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073). The authors describe this as a 'Goldilocks Zone' for prompting.
findings.measure: Student-rated interestingness and closeness of the personalized problem

findings.finding_summary: Student ratings improved from Unit 4 to Unit 6. Mean interestingness increased from 2.27 to 2.56 and mean closeness from 2.28 to 2.66; the combined regression model found the unit effect significant (B=0.33, SE=0.095, t=3.49, p=0.0012).
findings.measure: 1-5 student ratings of interestingness and closeness

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI/large language model chatbot systems used to generate and adapt instructional content.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generic teacher-facing and student-facing GenAI approaches as conceptual comparisons, including broader claims about context personalization and possible future multi-agent systems, but the empirical study itself specifically used ChatGPT.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods, quasi-experimental/descriptive study with no control group and no random assignment, so it does not meet blue/green causal-evidence standards. It does provide direct empirical observations of teacher prompting, student feedback, and within-teacher changes across two units.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The prompting-performance association is modest but nontrivial (B=0.240 on a 5-point scale) and unit-to-unit gains in student ratings are statistically significant. However, the practical implications are limited by the small sample, exploratory design, and lack of a comparison group.

paper_profiles.title: SenseBERT: Driving Some Sense into BERT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to make BERT-style language models more sensitive to lexical semantics, especially word sense and WordNet supersenses. The authors argue that standard word-level self-supervision forces the model to infer meaning only indirectly from form, which can leave it weak at disambiguating word senses.

They propose SenseBERT, a modified BERT pretraining approach that adds an auxiliary masked-word supersense prediction objective. The model is trained jointly to predict both the masked word and its WordNet supersense, using weak supervision from WordNet rather than human-annotated sense labels. The architecture also injects supersense information into the input embeddings and changes masking to prioritize words with a single supersense; for out-of-vocabulary words, they test alternative handling strategies.

The empirical evaluation is on NLP benchmark tasks, not education. They test supersense disambiguation on a SemEval-based dataset and the WiC word-in-context task, with additional GLUE results to check general language understanding. SenseBERT improves over vanilla BERT, including strong gains in a frozen-probe setting and state-of-the-art WiC performance for SenseBERTLARGE, while maintaining comparable GLUE performance. The paper provides no teacher, student, or school-related intervention context.

identified_tools.name: SenseBERT
identified_tools.description: A BERT-based language model augmented with weak supervision for predicting WordNet supersenses alongside masked-word prediction, producing a semantic-level language model.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and evaluates SenseBERT as a pre-trained model, comparing it against vanilla BERT on lexical semantic tasks (SemEval-SS and WiC) and GLUE.

findings.finding_summary: SenseBERT improved supersense disambiguation in the SemEval-SS task relative to BERT. In the frozen-embedding setting, SenseBERTBASE scored 75.6 versus 65.1 for BERTBASE, and SenseBERTLARGE scored 79.5 versus 67.3 for BERTLARGE; in the fine-tuned setting, SenseBERTBASE scored 83.0 versus 79.2 and SenseBERTLARGE scored 83.7 versus 81.1.
findings.measure: SemEval-SS supersense disambiguation accuracy

findings.finding_summary: SenseBERT improved performance on the Word in Context (WiC) task. SenseBERTBASE scored 70.3 compared with 69.6 for BERTLARGE, and SenseBERTLARGE scored 72.1, which the paper describes as state of the art for this benchmark.
findings.measure: WiC accuracy

findings.finding_summary: On GLUE, SenseBERTBASE performed on par with BERTBASE overall rather than showing a clear gain or loss. The paper reports an overall score of 77.9 for SenseBERTBASE versus 77.5 for BERTBASE, with mixed task-level differences across the GLUE subtasks.
findings.measure: GLUE benchmark scores across 9 tasks

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a model development paper proposing and evaluating a pretraining architecture, not an education study. It does not examine instructional coaching, lesson feedback, teachers, or school context, and it provides no K-12 intervention evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention outcomes are reported, so there is no demonstrated instructional impact to rate. The reported gains are limited to NLP benchmark performance.

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers in low-resource public schools collaborate with a generative AI system, Shiksha Copilot, to create and customize lesson plans. The central question is how an LLM-based, human-in-the-loop lesson planning workflow can support teachers’ instructional work while fitting the realities of multilingual, resource-constrained classrooms.

Shiksha Copilot was deployed in government schools across Karnataka, India. The system used retrieval-augmented generation to draft curriculum-aligned lesson plans in English, which were then reviewed by human curators and translated into Kannada before being distributed to teachers. Teachers could manually customize the curated plans, and a subset of “power users” also accessed AI-based regeneration, lesson chat, edu chat, and question-generation features. The study included 1,043 teachers in the deployment, 23 curators in the curation phase, 43 interviews, pre/post surveys, and log analysis of thousands of lesson plans.

The findings suggest that the tool reduced lesson-planning time, administrative burden, and stress, while helping teachers produce curriculum-aligned materials and, in some cases, shift toward more activity-based pedagogy. English lesson plans were generally high quality with relatively few edits, whereas Kannada translations required substantial human correction, mainly for linguistic and contextual reasons. Teachers used the plans flexibly and often supplemented them with their own expertise and off-platform resources. Overall, the paper concludes that generative AI can support teacher work in low-resource settings, but only when embedded in a human-in-the-loop workflow with strong local curation, curriculum alignment, and attention to language and context.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI/LLM-based lesson planning and teacher support system that drafts, translates, revises, and customizes lesson plans, with additional chatbot and question-generation features.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied through Shiksha Copilot, a human-in-the-loop lesson planning platform for government-school teachers in Karnataka, India. Teachers and curators used the system to generate, curate, translate, customize, and discuss lesson plans and related instructional materials.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods deployment with 1,043 teachers and 23 curators, the system reduced lesson planning time and bureaucratic workload. The paper reports measurable reductions in lesson planning time and teacher stress, but does not provide a single effect size for the overall intervention in the text provided.
findings.measure: Lesson planning time; self-reported teacher stress; workload/record-keeping burden
findings.sample_size: n=406 matched survey responses for quantitative analyses; n=1,043 teachers in deployment

findings.finding_summary: The intervention lowered teaching-related stress in post-survey analyses, based on the Teacher Stress Scale. The paper states that the tool produced measurable reductions in teacher stress, but no subgroup effect sizes or moderation analyses are reported in the provided text.
findings.measure: Teacher Stress Scale (teaching demands and school-based support subscales)

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported and logs showed increased access to curriculum-aligned, context-sensitive lesson plans and a shift toward activity-based pedagogy. The paper describes this as a qualitative/descriptive finding rather than a causal estimate, and no subgroup moderation by experience, subject, grade band, or context is reported beyond descriptive patterns.
findings.measure: Teacher perceptions, interviews, and platform logs about lesson plan quality and pedagogy
findings.sample_size: n=22 teacher interviews; log analysis of 5,544 teacher-created lesson plans

findings.finding_summary: Platform logs indicate low rates of on-platform editing of teacher-created lesson plans: only 85 of 5,542 plans (1.53%) were modified, and 19 of 1,480 Kannada-medium plans (1.28%) were edited. This suggests teachers often used the curated plans with minimal recorded changes, though interviews indicate additional off-platform adaptation was common.
findings.measure: Rate of teacher edits to generated lesson plans in platform logs
findings.sample_size: n=5,542 lesson plans; Kannada subset n=1,480

findings.finding_summary: Descriptive analyses show strong language- and subject-dependent variation in curation burden. English-medium content was largely usable with 96.13% of 7,744 content blocks rated suitable, whereas 94.4% of Kannada content blocks required edits; among Kannada LPs, edit rates differed by subject (Mathematics 99.0%, Science 97.2%, Social Science 88.9%).
findings.measure: Curator ratings and edit rates of generated lesson-plan content blocks by language medium and subject
findings.sample_size: English n=7,744 content blocks; Kannada n=26 lesson plans across three subjects

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods field deployment with surveys, interviews, and log analysis, but not a controlled or quasi-controlled causal study in the text provided. The evidence is informative yet largely descriptive and qualitative for most outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear practical benefits such as reduced planning time, lower stress, and improved access to lesson plans, but the provided text does not report causal effect sizes. Subgroup or moderation effects by teacher experience, subject, grade band, school context, or deployment format are mostly descriptive rather than quantified.

paper_profiles.title: Consensus Sampling for Safer Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a theoretical AI safety problem: how to aggregate outputs from multiple generative models so that the combined system inherits safety properties from the safest subset, even when some models may be unreliable or adversarial. The authors focus on risks that are hard or impossible to detect by inspecting outputs alone, such as steganography and hidden code vulnerabilities.

The proposed approach, called consensus sampling, takes k generative models and a parameter s indicating how many are assumed safe, then samples from a mixture of the models and accepts outputs only when enough probability mass agrees across the models. If agreement is insufficient, the algorithm abstains. The method is designed to be model-agnostic and to use access to model probabilities rather than just sampled outputs.

The paper analyzes the algorithm formally, proving that its risk is bounded by a factor R times the average risk of the safest s models, and that it has bounded information leakage on the order of log(R+1) bits. It also derives abstention guarantees under overlap assumptions among the safe models and proves Pareto optimality of the tradeoff between robustness and abstention. The work is entirely theoretical and does not study learners, teachers, or classrooms.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / language model ensemble used to sample from and evaluate probabilities across multiple models for safety-robust output aggregation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and analyzes consensus sampling over k generative models, using model output probabilities to accept or abstain from generations based on agreement among constituent models.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/framework paper about consensus sampling and AI safety, not an empirical education study. It reports formal lemmas and theorems rather than controlled or quasi-controlled outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational outcome is measured, and no intervention effect size or student/teacher impact is reported. The paper is about safety properties of generative model aggregation, so educational impact is not applicable.

paper_profiles.title: Analysis and experiments of the dissipative Twistcar: direction reversal and asymptotic approximations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies the dynamics of a dissipative Twistcar, a two-link underactuated wheeled vehicle inspired by the Roller Racer toy. The central question is how adding viscous rolling resistance changes the system’s behavior relative to earlier non-dissipative and frictional models, especially with respect to bounded motion and direction reversal. The authors revisit the vehicle using a planar nonholonomic model with dissipation and derive asymptotic approximations for small-amplitude periodic steering inputs.

The intervention/approach is theoretical and computational rather than educational: the authors formulate the constrained equations of motion, perform perturbation analysis, and compare analytic results with numerical simulations. They also build a modular robotic prototype to experimentally validate the model, including open-loop actuation of the steering joint and the ability to change geometry and mass distribution. The work further estimates dissipation parameters by fitting simulation to experimental tracking data and explores additional effects such as wheel skidding and slight floor slope.

The paper does not involve human educational populations, teachers, students, or classrooms. Its main findings are that the dissipative model yields bounded steady-state oscillatory motion, that direction reversal can occur when geometry or mass distribution is changed, and that the asymptotic predictions match simulations well for small actuation amplitudes. Experiments with the robot corroborate the predicted direction reversal, while also showing that skidding and ground slope can substantially affect observed motion and parameter fitting.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Not applicable here: the paper is a robotics/mechanical systems study of the dissipative Twistcar and does not study an AI tool.
identified_tools.use_case: No AI tool is evaluated in this paper.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/experimental robotics paper, not an education or AI-in-education study. It does not present empirical evidence about any AI instructional tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational AI intervention is studied, so there is no measurable instructional impact to rate.

paper_profiles.title: The Harvard Science Research Mentoring Program
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the founding, design, and first two years of operation of the Harvard Science Research Mentoring Program (SRMP), a year-long mentoring program intended to give high-school students authentic research experiences in astrophysics while also providing graduate students and postdoctoral scholars with mentoring experience. The author frames SRMP as a response to gaps in STEM mentoring and the need for role models, research exposure, and advisor-training opportunities that are often not provided in graduate education.

The intervention is not a controlled instructional study but a program model: students are recruited from Cambridge Rindge and Latin School, selected through essays and interviews, then paired with mentors for September-to-May independent research projects. The program includes an orientation, introductory astrophysics sessions, twice-weekly student-mentor meetings, monthly cohort meetings, and an end-of-year symposium. Mentors are primarily advanced graduate students and postdocs, and the author emphasizes flexible, hands-on or hands-off supervision depending on the project and student needs.

The paper reports descriptive implementation details and testimonials from students and mentors, along with limited survey-based evaluation. The main conclusions are that the program appears to support student engagement, coding and research skill development, and professional identity exploration, while also benefiting mentors’ professional development as novice advisors. The author argues that the long timescale and authentic research context are important features of SRMP and that the model could be replicated at other institutions.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI instructional coaching or lesson-feedback system. In this paper, no AI tool is actually studied; the paper is about a science research mentoring program in astronomy.
identified_tools.use_case: Not applicable; the paper does not evaluate any generative AI coaching/feedback tool.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive/programmatic paper about a science research mentoring program, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tutoring, coaching, or feedback system. No controlled or quasi-controlled analysis of an AI tool is reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no reported AI intervention effect to assess, so impact on instructional coaching or lesson feedback cannot be estimated from this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Tensorial Mixture Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a theoretical generative modeling framework called Tensorial Mixture Models (TMMs). The main problem addressed is how to combine tractable inference and tractable marginalization with neural-network-style architectures, especially for classification under missing data. The authors argue that many contemporary generative neural models are expressive but do not support exact marginalization, while classical tractable generative models are often too limited or require handcrafted structure.

The proposed approach builds a generative model by viewing the prior over mixture components as a tensor and then factorizing it using tensor decompositions such as CP and Hierarchical Tucker. This yields convolutional arithmetic circuit architectures with a generative interpretation. The paper emphasizes that this algebraic formulation makes tractability, expressivity, and inductive bias easier to analyze and control. It also shows that TMMs can be trained with standard SGD in a log-space implementation and can perform exact marginalization over missing inputs.

Empirically, the paper evaluates TMMs on image classification with missing data using MNIST and small NORB, and on speech recognition using TIMIT. The experiments compare TMMs against discriminative classifiers, imputation-based baselines, sum-product networks, and other generative methods. The reported results show that TMMs are more robust under missing-data corruption and often outperform the baselines, especially when the missingness pattern at test time differs from training. However, these are illustrative benchmark experiments rather than a controlled educational intervention study, so there are no teacher-, school-, or grade-related subgroup analyses relevant to education.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: A general intelligent tutoring system / generative model category that provides structured inference and prediction; in this paper, the relevant AI system is a generative convolutional architecture for classification under missing data, not an educational tutoring product.
identified_tools.use_case: Not an education study. The paper proposes Tensorial Mixture Models / generative ConvACs and evaluates them on image and speech classification with missing data.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical machine learning paper with model derivations and experiments outside education, not a controlled or quasi-controlled study of instructional coaching or lesson feedback. No educational intervention or teacher subgroup analysis is present.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No K-12 instructional outcome or educator impact is studied, so there is no relevant educational effect size or impact to assess.

paper_profiles.title: Late-Time Observations of Type Ia Supernova SN 2014J with the Hubble Space Telescope Wide Field Camera 3
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an astrophysics observational study of late-time photometry of Type Ia supernova SN 2014J, not an education or AI-in-education intervention study. The author presents complementary Hubble Space Telescope Wide Field Camera 3 observations of SN 2014J taken roughly 365 to 1296 days after B-band maximum light, focusing on the late-time light curves in the F438W, F555W, and F814W filters.

The main analytical goals are to determine whether the measured photometry is contaminated by unresolved light echoes and to test whether the late-time decline rates of SN 2014J are consistent with previously reported correlations between supernova luminosity and late-time light-curve flattening. The author compares SN 2014J colors to those of SN 2011fe to rule out unresolved echo contamination, and directly compares F438W and F555W decline rates for several supernovae (SN 2011fe, 2012cg, 2014J, 2015F, and ASASSN-14lp) to avoid pseudo-bolometric reconstruction assumptions.

The study concludes that SN 2014J’s photometry is not contaminated by an unresolved light echo and that the late-time decline-rate pattern remains consistent with the earlier claim that more intrinsically luminous SNe Ia have flatter, slower-declining late-time light curves. The paper emphasizes that the main remaining limitation is the small supernova sample size, which prevents a definitive test of the correlation.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: No AI instructional tool is studied in this paper; the article is an astronomy observation/analysis paper about late-time photometry of Supernova SN 2014J.
identified_tools.use_case: Not applicable. The paper does not evaluate any generative AI, tutoring, feedback, or educational technology tool.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is not an education or AI-in-education study and contains no empirical evaluation of an instructional AI tool. It is an astrophysics observational paper, so there is no relevant educational evidence to assess.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational or instructional AI intervention is studied, so there is no measurable instructional impact on teachers, students, or schools.

paper_profiles.title: Optically induced flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether flat electronic bands, normally accessible only near the magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene, can be created and controlled using light. The authors ask if coherent optical driving can flatten bands, open spectral gaps, and potentially induce topological properties in small-angle twisted bilayer graphene where undriven bands are not sufficiently flat or isolated.

The intervention studied is not an educational intervention but a theoretical Floquet-engineering scheme: a circularly polarized optical field is applied to a continuum model of twisted bilayer graphene. The authors analyze the resulting Floquet band structure under different twist angles, driving frequencies, field strengths, and lattice-relaxation parameters, using numerical calculations of quasi-energy spectra, time-averaged density of states, and Chern numbers.

The paper considers low-angle twisted bilayer graphene and shows that sufficiently strong but still sub-bandwidth light in the visible to near-infrared range can open gaps between the upper and lower bands near charge neutrality, isolate them from remote bands, and reduce their bandwidth. These effects are reported to be robust to realistic lattice relaxation and to persist over a wide range of twist angles below the magic angle. The authors also find that, in an off-resonant regime, the driven system can acquire nonzero Chern numbers for the flat bands, suggesting the possibility of topological flat-band states.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Computer-assisted instruction systems that provide automated instructional support, feedback, or adaptive learning activities.
identified_tools.use_case: Not studied empirically in this paper. The paper is a condensed-matter physics article about optically induced flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene, not an education or AI-in-education study.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The paper is not an education research study and does not evaluate any AI instructional tool, so there is no empirical evidence to assess. Its content is a theoretical physics paper about Floquet engineering in graphene.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational or AI-coaching intervention is studied, and no learning, teaching, or school outcome is reported. Therefore there is no impact evidence relevant to the requested taxonomy.

paper_profiles.title: The Design and Implementation of an Educational Chatbot with Personalized Adaptive Learning Features for Project Management Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how educational chatbots can be designed using personalized adaptive learning (PAL) principles for project management training in higher education. The authors note that prior educational chatbot research has largely focused on STEM and language learning, with little work in multidisciplinary fields such as project management, and even less on chatbots that combine personalization, adaptivity, and generative AI. They therefore ask how an educational chatbot can be designed utilizing PAL for project management training.

To answer this, the paper presents PMTutor, a chatbot built using design science research. PMTutor combines rule-based dialog logic, natural language understanding, and an OpenAI GPT-3 service, and it includes five PAL features: self-assessment, topic recommendation, tailored exercise feedback for correct/incorrect answers, the ability to resume or review exercises, and answering learner questions. Content was designed by teaching staff and domain experts using a topic configuration template, and the system was piloted in project management courses.

The main empirical context was a one-and-a-half-hour online pilot in a Finnish postgraduate project management course, with 30 students participating and 29 completing retrospective pre/post self-assessments. The study also incorporated student feedback from open-ended survey responses and earlier testing workshops used during development. Results suggest that PMTutor can complement learning, provide engaging interactive exercises, and support learners through immediate customized feedback. Participants particularly valued the exercise feedback, though they also reported usability issues such as language mismatch and navigation difficulties. The authors conclude that PAL chatbots can support project management learning, but they emphasize the need for stronger usability testing, incremental design, and further development of generative-AI-supported personalized interaction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM system for natural-language question answering and response generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used via OpenAI GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) to answer learner questions beyond the scope of PMTutor's NLU and dialog logic.

findings.finding_summary: In the pilot, PMTutor's GPT-3-backed question-answering feature was perceived as useful by some learners, with 1 respondent in the UX analysis explicitly noting the ability to answer open questions as positive. However, 2 respondents also reported that PMTutor did not adequately answer their open questions, indicating mixed user experience rather than a clear learning gain attributable to the LLM feature.
findings.measure: Qualitative survey feedback on user experience and ability to answer open questions

identified_tools.name: PMTutor
identified_tools.description: An educational chatbot system for project management training that combines rule-based dialogue, NLU, and an LLM service to provide interactive exercises, adaptive topic recommendations, self-assessment, resumable exercises, and question answering.
identified_tools.use_case: Designed and piloted as a minimum viable personalized adaptive learning chatbot integrated into a project management course for postgraduate students.

findings.finding_summary: Among 30 postgraduate students, 25 provided positive UX feedback and 16 said PMTutor was moderately to very helpful in achieving the learning objective 'I can calculate a project's schedule and critical path using an activity network.' Retrospective self-assessment on activity network competence increased from median 3 to 4 among n=29, with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test showing the increase was statistically significant (Z = -4.354, p = 0.0000134).
findings.measure: Retrospective pre/post self-assessment of activity network competence; qualitative feedback on user experience and learning outcome

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single mixed-methods pilot with survey and thematic analysis rather than a controlled experimental design. The evidence is useful but limited by the small sample and reliance on self-report.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports a statistically significant improvement in retrospective self-assessment, but no standardized effect size is provided and the outcome is self-reported competence. The practical impact appears promising yet modest and preliminary.

paper_profiles.title: A cross-sectional look at teacher reactions, worries, and professional development needs related to generative AI in an urban school district
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers in a large urban school district perceived generative AI, especially chatbot tools such as ChatGPT, shortly after their emergence in education. The study asks whether teacher reactions and AI allowability differ by grade level taught, subject area, and years of teaching experience, and it also explores the concerns, perceived benefits, and professional development needs teachers associate with AI use in schools.

The authors used a mixed-methods survey design embedded in the district’s annual employee survey. The sample included 1,454 completed teacher responses from a single large urban district in the United States. Teachers reported prior chatbot use, whether they had explicit classroom policies for AI use, their views on whether AI should be allowed for specific tasks (idea generation, paper editing, full paper writing, concept explanation, and code generation), and open-ended concerns/benefits for both teacher and student use. The open responses were thematically coded, and the closed-ended items were analyzed with regression and chi-square tests.

Findings show that willingness to allow AI decreased as grade level increased: elementary teachers were generally more permissive than middle and high school teachers, and more experienced teachers were more restrictive than less experienced ones in several contexts. Teachers were especially skeptical of AI for editing or completing papers, and experienced humanities teachers tended to be the most conservative about writing-related uses. Across the sample, teachers viewed AI differently for teachers versus students, with plagiarism and student overreliance dominating concerns about students, while teachers more often cited lack of knowledge and their own overreliance for teacher use. Professional development needs varied by grade level: elementary and middle school teachers wanted basic AI literacy, while high school teachers wanted help guiding student use and detecting AI-generated work. The paper concludes that AI professional learning should be tailored to grade level and teacher role, with a focus on pedagogy, policy, and responsible use rather than only technical familiarity.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI chatbot systems used for conversational text generation and assistance, such as ChatGPT-like tools.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed K-12 teachers’ reactions, concerns, allowability judgments, and professional development needs regarding generative AI chatbots in schools; the paper references ChatGPT as an example but does not evaluate a specific product intervention.

findings.finding_summary: This is not an intervention study of teacher uptake or reflective practice with a specific AI coaching system. Instead, 1,454 teachers reported allowability judgments about generic AI chatbot uses; willingness to allow use decreased as grade level increased (e.g., marginal effects of -0.121 for idea generation, -0.117 for editing, -0.135 for writing all paper, -0.125 for concept explanation, and -0.150 for code generation, all p<0.001).
findings.measure: Teachers’ reported allowability of students’ use of AI chatbots for idea generation, paper editing, writing an entire paper, concept explanation, and code generation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The study is a cross-sectional mixed-methods survey with descriptive and regression analyses, not an experimental evaluation of an AI coaching system. It provides useful evidence about teacher attitudes and needs, but not direct evidence of iterative dialogic AI coaching or actual uptake.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are mostly modest-to-large negative associations in allowability judgments, but they concern policy preferences rather than measured learning or coaching impact. Because the paper does not test a coaching intervention, practical impact for the requested topic is indirect and unclear.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and risks of large language models, especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention, it synthesizes early applications and argues for ways these models may support learning and teaching while also introducing challenges such as bias, privacy concerns, overreliance, copyright issues, and difficulty distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated text.

The paper discusses potential uses across educational levels and contexts, including content generation, personalized feedback, tutoring, lesson planning, assessment support, and professional development for teachers. It highlights examples from the emerging literature on quizzes, pedagogical agents, adaptive feedback, and conversational systems, but these are reviewed as prior work rather than evaluated in the paper itself. The population context is broad, spanning learners and educators in primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional settings, with examples also relevant to group, remote, and language-learning scenarios.

The main conclusion is that large language models could become valuable educational tools if they are integrated responsibly, with human oversight, critical thinking, transparency, and appropriate governance. The authors emphasize that further research is needed on effective pedagogical designs, trustworthy use, bias mitigation, and equitable access before these systems can be broadly and safely adopted in education.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's large language model chatbot for natural-language dialogue, content generation, question answering, and related assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as an example of a large language model in education, including potential uses for teaching, feedback, lesson planning, assessment, and tutoring. The paper does not empirically evaluate ChatGPT in a teacher-coaching setting.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper and literature-oriented discussion, not an empirical study of a tool in classrooms or teacher coaching. It offers no primary outcome data, sample sizes, or effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that LLMs such as ChatGPT may have broad educational value, but it reports no measured impact. Because there is no empirical effect, impact is unclear rather than demonstrably positive or negative.

paper_profiles.title: Rankings and Reactivity: How Public Measures Recreate Social Worlds
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines how public rankings become consequential social measures rather than neutral descriptors. The authors ask how quantitative rankings shape behavior, expectations, and institutional change, using U.S. News and World Report law school rankings as their case study. The central problem is reactivity: the process by which being measured changes what is measured.

The paper is not an intervention study or a coaching system evaluation; instead, it develops a conceptual framework for understanding how rankings produce effects. The authors analyze two mechanisms—self-fulfilling prophecy and commensuration—to explain how rankings alter decisions, redistribute resources, and change how actors interpret quality. They argue that rankings do not merely reflect social worlds but actively help recreate them by changing incentives, attention, and organizational identities.

The empirical context is U.S. legal education in the United States. The study draws on 136 open-ended interviews with law school administrators, faculty, and staff, plus additional interviews and document analysis, to trace how schools respond to rankings in admissions, budgeting, recruitment, marketing, and internal goal-setting. The main conclusion is that rankings have strong reactive effects: they can intensify stratification, encourage gaming and conformity to ranking criteria, and make quantitative measures more authoritative by embedding them in everyday institutional decisions.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Computer-assisted or other quantified evaluation systems used to measure and rank institutions rather than an interactive AI tutoring product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper analyzes U.S. News and World Report law school rankings as a public performance measure shaping institutional behavior; it does not study an AI coaching or generative AI tool.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a sociological article about rankings and reactivity, not an empirical evaluation of an AI educational tool. It contains qualitative case-study methods but no AI system intervention or learner/teacher outcome evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No AI tool is studied, and no instructional or coaching impact is reported. The paper’s relevance is conceptual for measurement and accountability, not evidence of AI coaching effectiveness.

paper_profiles.title: War of the chatbots: Bard, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, Ernie and beyond. The new AI gold rush and its impact on higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the rapid rise of generative AI chatbots and their implications for higher education, with a particular emphasis on the comparative capabilities of major systems such as ChatGPT, Bing Chat, Bard, and Baidu’s Ernie. The central problem is not an educational intervention study, but rather how universities should respond to the spread of chatbot technology amid concerns about assessment integrity, plagiarism, hallucinations, and the reliability of AI-generated output.

The paper provides a broad conceptual and critical review of the chatbot landscape, including brief histories of conversational agents, the role of major technology firms, and an English-language literature review on ChatGPT and higher education. It describes a systematic comparison of selected chatbots on tasks relevant to academic work, such as answering questions and handling higher-education-related prompts, but the article is primarily a position/review piece rather than an empirical study of learners or teachers.

No participant population is studied directly. The context is higher education in general, with discussion of students, faculty, and institutions, and the authors note that the findings are preliminary because the field is changing quickly. The paper concludes that GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 performed best among the compared bots, while Bing Chat and Bard lagged behind, and it recommends that higher education stakeholders adapt assessment and teaching practices to the new AI environment.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's large language model chatbot, formerly Bard/LaMDA-based conversational assistant for search and general dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses Bard as one of the major chatbot systems in the higher-education landscape and includes it in a comparative overview of leading LLM-based chatbots; it also notes a literature search finding no academic articles on Bard and higher education at the time.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on GPT models for conversational text generation and question answering.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reviews ChatGPT extensively as the central example of a generative chatbot affecting higher education, and summarizes prior academic work comparing ChatGPT's performance to human students or exam standards.

findings.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes prior studies showing ChatGPT can perform strongly on some academic tasks but has clear weaknesses. Reported examples include passing or exceeding thresholds on some professional and standardized exams (e.g., bar, medical, SAT/AP), while also producing hallucinations, weak reasoning, and unreliable outputs; the review notes that these issues affect assessment integrity and teaching practice.
findings.measure: Performance on academic exams and tasks; reliability/limitations in higher-education contexts

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an opinionated, narrative review article rather than a primary empirical study of an AI coaching system for teachers. It does not evaluate an interactive coaching intervention, teacher uptake, or reflective practice outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has discussion-level relevance to generative AI in higher education, but it provides no measurable intervention effect. Its practical impact for teacher coaching is indirect and not evidenced with outcome data.

paper_profiles.title: Interacting with educational chatbots: A systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the growing use of chatbots in education and the lack of a focused synthesis of how educational chatbots are designed, interacted with, and evaluated. The authors specifically aim to analyze evidence-based chatbot-learner interaction design techniques, as well as the field of application, platform, educational role, interaction style, design principles, empirical evidence, and limitations across prior studies.

The study is a systematic review of 36 articles published between 2011 and 2021, identified through searches in ACM Digital Library, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and SpringerLink. The reviewed chatbots span multiple educational contexts, including computer science, general education, language learning, mathematics, and other smaller application areas. Most systems were web-based and commonly served as teaching agents or peer agents; interaction styles were usually chatbot-driven and often flow-based or intent-based, with fewer user-driven systems.

The review finds that educational chatbots are frequently designed around personalized learning, experiential learning, social dialogue, collaborative learning, affective learning, learning by teaching, and scaffolding. Empirical evidence in the reviewed studies generally suggests improved learning, engagement, satisfaction, or interest, though the authors note uneven methodological quality and a lack of attention to usability heuristics. Overall, the paper concludes that educational chatbots show promise, but future work should better address design quality, localization, personality, and more robust evaluation.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Conversational/educational chatbot or conversational agent used in educational settings to tutor, answer questions, provide feedback, scaffold interaction, or support learning tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a systematic review of 36 educational chatbot studies, examining their fields of application, platforms, roles, interaction styles, design principles, evaluation methods, and limitations.

findings.finding_summary: Across 36 reviewed papers, the authors report that educational chatbots were mainly used as teaching agents or peer agents, most often on web platforms. The review synthesis indicates that more than a third of the chatbots were evaluated with experiments and that results primarily point to improved learning and subjective satisfaction.
findings.measure: Review synthesis of reported evaluation outcomes across included chatbot studies

findings.finding_summary: The review found that most chatbot studies used chatbot-driven, flow-based interaction styles, while a smaller set used user-driven conversations. The paper reports that some systems included personalized learning, experiential learning, collaborative learning, affective learning, learning by teaching, and scaffolding, with the overall evidence base suggesting improved learning, engagement, and satisfaction in several studies.
findings.measure: Review synthesis of interaction styles, design principles, and reported outcomes

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of prior chatbot studies rather than a new controlled trial. The evidence is synthesized from heterogeneous studies, with the paper itself not reporting a single pooled effect size.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests generally positive educational effects, but the paper does not provide a quantitative aggregate effect size for teacher coaching or reflective-practice uptake. Reported impacts are qualitative and broad rather than precise.

paper_profiles.title: Conversational Agents in Health Care: Scoping Review and Conceptual Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly growing use of conversational agents (chatbots and similar dialogue systems) in health care, asking what kinds of systems have been studied, how they are used, and what evidence exists regarding their accuracy, acceptability, and effectiveness. The authors note that the field was fragmented, descriptive, and lacked a clear overview of applications and evaluation approaches.

The paper is a scoping review and conceptual analysis of literature published up to April 2019. The authors searched major biomedical databases and gray literature sources, ultimately including 47 study reports (45 studies and 2 ongoing trials). Because the review is about health care rather than education, there is no teacher, student, or school-based intervention context. The included studies covered a range of health applications, such as treatment and monitoring, service support, education, lifestyle behavior change, and diagnosis, with most systems delivered through smartphone apps and often using text-based interaction.

Across the included studies, the review found that conversational agents were usually evaluated through case studies, surveys, or randomized controlled trials, with generally positive findings for accuracy, acceptability, and effectiveness. However, the evidence base was dominated by small, descriptive studies, with limited reporting on adverse effects, cost, and implementation in real-world health systems. The authors conclude that more robust evaluations are needed, especially for safety, effectiveness, and integration into existing services.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Conversational agents or chatbots that simulate human text or voice conversations using rules-based or machine-learning/NLP methods.
identified_tools.use_case: This scoping review examined health care conversational agents in general, including their applications, characteristics, and evaluation across the literature, rather than one specific product.

findings.finding_summary: The review identified 47 study reports (45 studies and 2 ongoing clinical trials) on health care conversational agents. The literature was largely descriptive, with most agents delivered via smartphone apps, using free-text input/output, and only 11 randomized controlled trials; the authors concluded there is an urgent need for more robust evaluation focused on acceptability, safety, and effectiveness.
findings.measure: Study characteristics and evaluation outcomes across included literature
findings.sample_size: n=47 study reports (45 studies, 2 ongoing clinical trials)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a scoping review, not an empirical evaluation of a single AI tool. It synthesizes heterogeneous conversational-agent studies and does not provide a rigorous causal estimate for one product.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests broad use and generally positive evaluations across health care conversational agents, but it does not report a pooled effect size or a clear measured impact for one tool. The evidence is therefore informative but not directly quantifiable for impact.

paper_profiles.title: Speculative Futures on ChatGPT and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Collective Reflection from the Educational Landscape
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapid emergence of ChatGPT and other generative AI tools and asks what their possible futures might mean for education. Rather than evaluating a deployed intervention or collecting outcome data, the authors use a speculative methodology to explore both optimistic and pessimistic scenarios for AI in educational contexts. The paper is framed as a collective reflection from a diverse group of scholars, intended to provoke critical thought about the promises, pitfalls, ethical risks, and changing human-AI relationships in education.

The approach studied is not an interactive coaching system or empirical implementation, but a set of fictional narratives written by the coauthors and one narrative generated by ChatGPT. These narratives imagine AI supporting personalized learning, collaboration, assessment, accessibility, language learning, and teacher productivity, while also raising concerns about bias, privacy, surveillance, academic integrity, dependency, and dehumanization. The paper emphasizes that technology should not replace the human role in education, and that educators need new literacies, policies, and assessment practices to respond responsibly to generative AI.

The population is not a participant sample in the empirical sense. Instead, the paper draws on the perspectives of an international group of higher education scholars and presents imagined educational scenarios involving students, teachers, and researchers across multiple contexts. The conclusions argue for cautious, ethical, and human-centered integration of generative AI in education, while recognizing that the value and impact of these tools depend heavily on how they are positioned and used.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI language model for text generation, dialogue, and assistance across tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses ChatGPT as the exemplar of conversational generative AI in education and includes speculative narratives imagining its use for student support, grading, translation, personalized learning, and teacher assistance; one narrative was explicitly generated by ChatGPT.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a speculative, conceptual paper using fictional narratives and collective reflection rather than an empirical evaluation of an AI tool. No study design, sample, or measured outcomes are reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No impact can be estimated because the paper does not report outcome data or effect sizes for actual tool use. The discussion is about possible future affordances and risks, not demonstrated effects.

paper_profiles.title: The Personalization of Conversational Agents in Health Care: Systematic Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews how personalization has been implemented in health care conversational agents. The authors were interested in understanding what kinds of personalization have been used, for whom they were targeted, how the personalization was automated, and how these features were evaluated. The review is framed around conversational agents with unconstrained natural language input, including chatbots and embodied conversational agents.

Across 13 included studies, personalization most commonly affected the content of dialogue, such as tailored feedback, reminders, warnings, alerts, and recommendations. A smaller number of studies adapted conversational style or the user interface, and a few used either explicit user input, implicit sensing from interaction history or audiovisual cues, or a combination of both to drive adaptation. The reviewed systems were used for mental health support, mindfulness coaching, asthma self-management, diabetes monitoring, pain reporting, exercise and sun protection promotion, and reflection on physical activity.

The review concludes that personalization in health care conversational agents was limited and generally not evidence-based. Most studies did not use explicit theoretical frameworks for personalization and rarely evaluated personalization itself as a distinct factor. Only a few studies directly assessed personalized features, and the authors argue that future research should more carefully examine how personalization affects user engagement, health outcomes, privacy, safety, and decision-making.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Conversational artificial intelligence system: an interactive natural-language dialogue agent that can deliver personalized content, feedback, reminders, and adaptive conversational responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Systematic review of 13 health-care conversational agents with unconstrained natural-language input, focusing on how personalization was implemented and evaluated across studies rather than on a single named product.

findings.finding_summary: Across 13 included studies, personalization was commonly implemented for tailored content, but the review reports that it was usually not supported by a theoretical framework and was only directly evaluated in 2 studies. The authors conclude that personalization features were associated in the reviewed literature with higher user satisfaction, engagement, and dialogue quality, but the role of personalization in improving health outcomes was not directly assessed.
findings.measure: User satisfaction, user engagement, dialogue quality, and reported health outcomes across included studies

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review, so the evidence is synthesized rather than a single controlled evaluation. However, the paper explicitly notes limited direct assessment of personalization and little ability to attribute outcomes to the personalization features themselves.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests potential benefits for satisfaction, engagement, and dialogue quality, but it does not provide pooled effect sizes or direct evidence of impact on outcomes. The overall impact is therefore promising but unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Reflecting in the Reflection: Integrating a Socratic Questioning Framework into Automated AI-Based Question Generation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint addresses the challenge of designing high-quality reflection questions for education. The authors argue that reflection prompts are important for metacognition and deeper learning, but they are time-consuming to create and often uneven in quality. Prior automated question generation work has focused mostly on factual recall or closed-ended item types, leaving a gap for reflective, open-ended prompts that are pedagogically grounded.

To address this gap, the paper proposes a reflection-in-reflection framework that uses two role-specialized LLM agents: a Student–Teacher agent that drafts a reflection question and a Teacher–Educator agent that responds with Socratic coaching questions to iteratively refine it. The system takes as input a topic, key concepts, optional student level information, and optional instructional materials. It is designed to support iterative revision, explicit rationales, and adaptive stopping when the question is judged satisfactory.

The paper evaluates the framework in an authentic lower-secondary ICT context using instructional materials for 8th–9th grade students in Czechia, focusing on internet fundamentals such as servers, routers, packets, and decentralization. However, the evaluation is performed on generated questions using a stronger LLM as evaluator rather than on teachers or students using the system in practice. The main findings are that dynamic stopping and contextual information improve question quality, and that the two-agent Socratic protocol produces questions judged more relevant and deeper than a one-shot baseline. The authors conclude that structured Socratic prompting can improve AI-generated reflective questions and may help educators author better prompts more efficiently.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used here as the backbone model for two LLM-based agents (Student–Teacher and Teacher–Educator) and as the external GPT-4-class evaluator.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate reflection questions through a two-agent Socratic dialogue (GPT-4o-mini backbone) and to evaluate outputs with a stronger GPT-4-class model in pairwise comparisons.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that the two-agent reflection-in-reflection protocol using a GPT-4o-mini backbone outperformed a one-shot GPT-4o-mini baseline on generated question quality. Across context settings, the protocol was judged better for relevance (gamma ranging from 0.60 to 0.92) and generally better for depth (average above 0.6, with values such as gamma(depth)=0.77 and 0.91 in underspecified conditions), while clarity and overall quality were also usually slightly above 0.5 but with smaller gains.
findings.measure: Pairwise LLM-evaluated clarity, relevance, depth, and overall quality of generated reflection questions
findings.effect_size: gamma ranges: relevance 0.60-0.92; depth average >0.6; clarity around 0.50-0.64 in most conditions; overall quality around 0.50-0.58 in most conditions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preprint describing an empirical comparison, but the evaluation relies on LLM-based pairwise judgments rather than human-rated or experimental classroom outcomes, and sample sizes/effect estimates are not fully reported. The design is informative but not strong enough for blue/green evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported preference indices show modest-to-substantial advantages over the one-shot baseline, especially for relevance and depth, with gamma values often well above 0.20 above chance. However, the evidence is about generated-question quality rather than direct teacher uptake or learning impact.

paper_profiles.title: PACEE: Parent-Centered AI Scaffolding for Emotion Education in Early Childhood Conversations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of supporting emotion education for children aged 3 to 6, a period when children have limited verbalization and self-regulation skills and parents often lack practical guidance. The authors argue that most prior AI tools for emotional development target children directly, which is a poor fit for preschoolers and ignores the central role of parents in everyday emotion coaching at home.

To address this, the paper introduces PACEE, an LLM-based parent-centered scaffold for family emotion education. PACEE has three main modules: a real-time Parent-Child Conversational Scenario module that guides parents through Gottman’s five steps of emotion coaching, a Parental Feedback Report that summarizes and critiques parental guidance, and a Child Emotional Modeling module that builds a profile of the child’s emotional understanding, expression, and regulation from parent input and conversation analysis. The system is designed to support parents rather than replace them, and it includes trackable feedback so parents can reflect on what guidance was useful.

The study began with formative interviews with five kindergarten teachers and five parents, plus observations of five parent-child pairs, all in China. The evaluation then used a within-subject study with 16 parent-child pairs, comparing PACEE to a baseline voice-based LLM chatbot.
