Results suggest PACEE increased parent-child engagement, produced richer emotional dialogue, improved parents’ immediate experience and confidence, and helped parents reflect more deeply on their children’s emotional states. The authors conclude that AI can be effective as a reflective partner for parents in early childhood emotion coaching, but they also caution that the system is supportive rather than a validated measure of coaching skill.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: An LLM-based assistant that provides real-time conversational support, stage-aware guidance, scenario generation, actionable feedback, and child emotional profiling for parent-led early childhood emotion coaching.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as PACEE, a parent-centered AI scaffolding system to support parents in guiding children aged 3–6 through emotion-related conversations, compared against a generic voice-based LLM chatbot baseline (Doubao) with no PACEE features.

findings.finding_summary: In a within-subject study with 16 parent-child pairs, PACEE increased interaction duration (M=892.37s, SD=310.96) compared with the baseline LLM chatbot (M=560.17s, SD=194.61), with p<0.01. It also increased dialogue turns (M=60 vs. 38, p<0.05), parent word count (M=1597 vs. 994, p<0.05), child word count (M=370 vs. 165, p<0.001), and emotion-related word usage by both parents (M=111 vs. 70, p<0.05) and children (M=19 vs. 10, p<0.01).
findings.measure: Interaction duration, dialogue turns, word count, and emotion-related word usage during parent-child emotional conversations

findings.finding_summary: Parents reported better immediate interaction experience with PACEE than with the baseline, including higher satisfaction (M=5.06, SD=1.12 vs. 3.94, SD=1.57, p<0.05), lower effort (M=2.56, SD=1.79 vs. 3.62, SD=2.03, p<0.01), and reduced frustration (M=2.06, SD=1.24 vs. 3.06, SD=1.57, p<0.05). The paper notes that self-efficacy did not change significantly in this short study.
findings.measure: NASA-TLX and PSOC post-questionnaire ratings of interaction experience

findings.finding_summary: PACEE was rated as significantly better than the baseline in addressing the three family emotion-education challenges (limited parental expertise, insufficient feedback, and lack of understanding of children’s emotional states), each at p<0.01. Qualitatively, 14 of 16 parents found PACEE’s emotional-profile analysis useful as an external perspective, and parents reported adopting real-time suggestions such as collaborative problem-solving and open-ended questioning.
findings.measure: Post-questionnaire ratings and semi-structured parent interviews about system support for emotion coaching challenges

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single within-subject mixed-methods evaluation with qualitative interviews and non-randomized comparison to a baseline chatbot. It provides useful empirical evidence, but not the level of control or validation needed for a higher tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are practically meaningful in engagement and parent experience, but the paper does not report standardized effect sizes, and the study is short-term with no evidence of long-term coaching impact.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an analytical AI feedback platform can support lesson-planning development in vocational teacher education, and whether such feedback can improve the quality of student teachers’ lesson plans compared with human feedback. The authors focus on lesson planning as a complex professional skill that requires integrating multiple didactic principles and domain-specific considerations, and they argue that instructors often cannot provide frequent, detailed, individualized feedback at scale.

The intervention used EDDA, an analytical AI platform that classifies uploaded lesson plans and teaching materials into a structured coding scheme and returns individualized expert feedback. Unlike generative AI, EDDA is designed to provide reproducible, domain-specific feedback based on pre-coded categories covering planning dimensions such as action orientation, process orientation, problem orientation, motivation, digitalization, sustainability, and basic planning dimensions. In the experimental condition, student groups received AI feedback first and could then seek human clarification; the control group received human feedback only. The study was conducted longitudinally across a semester in two master’s-level business education courses in Germany.

The sample included 103 master’s students preparing to become vocational business educators, working in small groups on a 90-minute lesson plan. Outcomes were assessed through content analysis of lesson plans and questionnaire measures of AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competences, self-efficacy, and motivation. The study found that AI feedback could match or outperform human feedback on some lesson-planning dimensions, especially certain sustainability-related and structural aspects, and that the experimental group showed advantages on some competence-related dimensions. However, the authors also found that simply using the AI platform did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, or motivation, suggesting that AI feedback works best as part of a broader pedagogical framework rather than as a standalone tool.

identified_tools.name: EDDA
identified_tools.description: An analytical AI platform for lesson planning feedback. It uses a BERT-based transformer model to classify uploaded lesson plans/materials against a coded framework and returns individualized expert-level text and visual feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a longitudinal intervention with vocational teacher education students to provide feedback on lesson plans throughout a semester; students in the experimental group received EDDA feedback first and then could request human feedback to discuss the AI results.

findings.finding_summary: In a longitudinal intervention with N=103 master’s students in business education, the experimental group using EDDA received higher ratings on some lesson-plan dimensions than the human-feedback control group. The paper reports significant positive effects for implementation of social competences for sustainable development (p<0.05) and reflexivity (p<0.10), and a significant positive effect for SDG 15 (life on land) (p<0.10).
findings.measure: Content analysis ratings of lesson plans and teaching materials across didactic/planning dimensions, including SDGs, sustainable change agent competences, and planning principles

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal two-group intervention with an experimental and control condition, but assignment was not randomized in the traditional sense and the control group came from a different university. The study is empirical and fairly well specified, but some quasi-experimental concerns remain.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported positive effects are statistically significant but generally small in magnitude (e.g., p<0.10 for some outcomes) and the paper does not report standard effect sizes for these findings. The impact appears modest rather than large.

paper_profiles.title: The effects of over-reliance on AI dialogue systems on students’ cognitive abilities: a systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the growing concern that students may over-rely on AI dialogue systems, especially generative tools used in academic research and writing, and that such dependence may weaken key cognitive abilities. The review focuses on three cognitive domains: decision-making, critical thinking, and analytical thinking. It also identifies the ethical issues that the authors argue contribute to over-reliance, including hallucination, algorithmic bias, plagiarism, privacy concerns, and lack of transparency.

The study is a systematic review following PRISMA procedures. The authors searched four databases (ProQuest, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science) for English-language journal articles and conference proceedings published from 2017 to 2023. After screening, 14 studies were included in the synthesis. The included evidence largely concerns higher education contexts, with student users and some educator/faculty perspectives, especially around academic writing, paraphrasing, and research assistance.

Across the reviewed studies, AI dialogue systems were found to offer practical benefits such as faster research, writing support, immediate feedback, and personalized assistance. However, the paper concludes that these benefits come with important risks: users may become overly dependent on AI-generated outputs, which can reduce independent judgment, creativity, and critical/analytical reasoning. The review argues that ethical weaknesses in AI systems, rather than the tools alone, are central drivers of over-reliance and that more responsible use is needed to protect cognitive development and academic integrity.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI/chatbot system used for generating and interacting with natural-language outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reviewed studies that used ChatGPT/GPT-4 and related GPT-based dialogue systems in research and education, especially for academic writing, paraphrasing, scientific questions, and feedback support.

findings.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT was reported to improve efficiency in academic writing and research tasks, streamline workflows, and provide immediate feedback or 24/7 availability. However, the review also synthesized concerns that over-reliance on ChatGPT may reduce critical thinking, analytical thinking, creativity, and decision-making, and may increase plagiarism, hallucination, bias, and transparency problems.
findings.measure: Synthesized outcomes from included studies on writing efficiency, feedback, and cognitive/ethical risks
findings.sample_size: 14 studies reviewed; tool-specific sample sizes varied and were not pooled

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that ChatGPT can support academic writing, help overcome language barriers, and improve writing productivity. At the same time, it may contribute to reduced originality and writing dependence, with some included studies warning about academic dishonesty and plagiarism risks.
findings.measure: Synthesized outcomes on academic writing support and writing quality
findings.sample_size: 14 studies reviewed; tool-specific sample sizes varied and were not pooled

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review synthesizing 14 articles, but it does not provide pooled effect sizes or a single controlled evaluation of ChatGPT. The evidence is mainly descriptive and mixed-method in nature, so it does not meet blue/green experimental standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests meaningful potential benefits for writing efficiency and feedback, but also substantial risks to critical thinking and academic integrity. Because no quantified effect size is reported, impact is best characterized as promising but unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Pedagogical AI conversational agents in higher education: a conceptual framework and survey of the state of the art
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly expanding use of pedagogical AI conversational agents in higher education and the need for a structured account of their current state of the art. The authors ask how these agents are being used, what pedagogical and technological functions they serve, and which areas remain underexplored. Rather than testing a single intervention, the paper surveys and synthesizes prior work to build a conceptual framework for categorising conversational agents in higher education.

The study reviews 92 papers published between 2014 and 2022, identified through searches of ACM Digital Library, ScienceDirect, ProQuest, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and Web of Science. Using thematic template analysis, the authors organise agents along two main dimensions: pedagogical applications and technological functions. Pedagogical uses are grouped into instructional, pastoral, and cognitive purposes, with finer-grained intents such as mentoring and coaching, motivation, communication, assessment, reflective/metacognitive support, FAQ/knowledge-base support, and simulation/experience. Technological functions are organised by embodiment, functional type, and implementation features such as NLP, machine learning, external data sources, and social/IM platform integration.

The review covers higher education contexts that include both face-to-face and distance/online delivery, and the examples span students in undergraduate and graduate-level settings. The paper concludes that conversational agents are most commonly used for instructional and pastoral purposes, while cognitive and assessment-oriented uses are less explored. The authors argue that future research should place greater emphasis on reflective practice, personalisation, richer interaction, and more advanced pedagogical applications, including better support for assessment and administration.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Conversational AI / pedagogical conversational agents used for instructional, pastoral, and cognitive educational interactions, including chatbots, virtual agents, voice bots, and virtual humans.
identified_tools.use_case: Systematic review and conceptual framework of pedagogical AI conversational agents used in higher education from 2014-2022.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a review/conceptual framework paper rather than a primary evaluation study. It synthesizes prior literature and does not report an empirical trial of a single tool with effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has conceptual and field-mapping value, but it does not report measured learning or teacher outcomes for a specific intervention. Any impact is therefore indirect and not quantifiable from this paper.

paper_profiles.title: A Study on Reflective Reciprocal Peer Coaching for Pre-service Teachers: Change in Reflectivity
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Education and Training Studies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether a reflective reciprocal peer coaching (RRPC) program can improve the reflectivity of pre-service teachers. The central question is whether training on RRPC and participation in the RRPC process lead to measurable changes in how pre-service teachers think about and reflect on their teaching, moving them from technical reflection toward contextual and dialectical reflection.

The intervention involved 12 pre-service English language teaching teachers at a Turkish university during their field experience course. Participants first received 12 weeks of training on reflection, RRPC, observation forms, and reflective diary keeping, followed by 8 weeks of peer coaching practice in triads at state schools. Each cycle used pre-conference, observation, and post-conference discussion, with structured observation tools and video-based intervention sessions to support analysis. Quantitative data came from the Profile of Reflective Thinking Attributes administered three times, and qualitative data came from reflective diaries, video recordings of post-conference sessions, and focus-group interviews.

Findings showed statistically significant gains in reflectivity after training and again after RRPC practice. Descriptively, participants shifted from mostly technical and contextual reflection to more contextual and dialectical reflection by the end of the study. Qualitative evidence suggested that participants increasingly focused on student needs, rationale for teaching decisions, and ethical dimensions of classroom practice. The author concludes that reflective reciprocal peer coaching, when paired with training and structured support, can foster deeper reflective practice in pre-service teacher education.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Collaborative peer coaching / reflective coaching model where teachers observe each other, give structured feedback, and reflect on teaching practice.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studied reflective reciprocal peer coaching (RRPC) for pre-service teachers, including training, observation forms, pre-conferences, post-conferences, reflective diaries, and focus-group interviews to examine changes in reflectivity.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-method study with 12 Turkish ELT pre-service teachers, reflectivity scores on The Profile of Reflective Thinking Attributes increased significantly after RRPC training and again after RRPC practice. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests showed significant pre-post differences after training (z=-3.061, p=.002) and after practice (z=-3.065, p=.002), and the distribution shifted from 6 technical/6 contextual/0 dialectical at baseline to 0 technical/5 contextual/7 dialectical after practice.
findings.measure: The Profile of Reflective Thinking Attributes; reflective diaries; post-conference recordings; focus-group interviews

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods peer coaching study, not an evaluation of an AI tool or generative coaching system. The evidence is qualitative/mixed-method and focused on reflective practice, so it is not a high-causal-inference AI study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No AI system was studied, and no effect size was reported. While the reflective coaching intervention showed positive changes in reflectivity, the paper does not support an AI tool impact estimate.

paper_profiles.title: Mindset matters: Fostering teachers’ responsible AI use through professional development
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of New Approaches in Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether professional development for future teachers about generative AI is more effective when it includes not only tool training, but also a mindset component focused on ethics, human-centered pedagogy, and critical reflection. The authors frame the problem as a gap in teacher AI preparation: most PD is tool-centric and may increase confidence without sufficiently developing responsible, reflective AI use.

The intervention was a one-day PD workshop with two conditions. One group received tools-only training on using generative AI for teaching tasks. The other group received the same tools training plus a mindset module covering AI ethics, human-centered education, growth mindset, and pedagogical reflection. The study used a mixed-method randomized design with 57 preservice teachers in a teacher education program in Vietnam. Data came from pre/post surveys measuring AI anxiety and AI competence self-efficacy, plus written reflections analyzed qualitatively.

Results showed that both groups had reduced AI anxiety after training, but the tools-only group showed broader gains in self-efficacy across multiple AI competence dimensions. The mindset-inclusive group showed a more limited quantitative gain, mainly in human-centered AI competence, but their written reflections showed deeper ethical awareness, more caution about AI limitations, and stronger attention to pedagogical responsibility. The authors conclude that mindset-oriented PD may not produce immediate boosts in confidence, but it better supports reflective, ethically grounded AI use, and should be integrated alongside technical training in teacher preparation.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI/chatbot system used for creating teaching materials and supporting teacher work; no specific commercial product is named in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a one-day professional development workshop for preservice teachers; one condition received tools-only training on efficient use of GenAI in teaching and learning, and the comparison condition also received mindset-oriented content on ethics and human-centered pedagogy.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-method pre-post comparison with 57 preservice teachers, both groups showed reduced AI anxiety over time, but only the tools-only group had a statistically significant pre-post decrease. The overall Time effect was significant (b=-0.49, p=.003, η2p=.05), while the Time×Group interaction was not significant (p=.128).
findings.measure: AI anxiety scale

findings.finding_summary: Overall competence self-efficacy did not differ significantly by time or group, but the tools-only group showed a significant pre-post increase in self-efficacy, whereas the mindset-inclusive group did not. At the subscale level, the mindset-inclusive group showed a significant gain only in Human-Centered Education, while the tools-only group improved in AI Knowledge, AI Pedagogy, AI Assessment, Human-Centered Education, and Professional Engagement.
findings.measure: TAICS competence self-efficacy scale and six subscales (AI Knowledge, AI Pedagogy, AI Assessment, AI Ethics, Human-Centered Education, Professional Engagement)
findings.effect_size: motivation predictor η2p=.11; subscale effects not pooled

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small mixed-method experimental study with pre-post measures and random assignment, but outcomes are self-reported and immediate post-test only. The paper provides useful comparative evidence on teacher PD, yet it is not a fully powered RCT with long-term or behavioral validation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The quantitative effects are modest and uneven: anxiety reduction is small (η2p=.05) and broader self-efficacy gains are limited to specific subdomains rather than a strong overall effect. The qualitative findings suggest meaningful reflective benefits from mindset-inclusive training, but the evidence does not show clear large impact on actual teacher uptake or classroom implementation.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can serve as an automated teacher coach by producing feedback that resembles classroom observation and coaching practices. The authors frame three teacher-coaching tasks for generative AI: scoring transcript segments using classroom observation rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student reasoning. A central concern is not just whether the model can generate plausible text, but whether its feedback is relevant, faithful to the transcript, insightful, and actually different from what teachers are already doing.

The study uses the NCTE transcript dataset of elementary mathematics lessons from the United States, with transcripts linked to expert ratings on CLASS and MQI observation instruments. The researchers evaluate zero-shot prompting of gpt-3.5-turbo/ChatGPT on selected transcript segments from 4th- and 5th-grade math classrooms. For the qualitative tasks, two experienced math teachers rate model outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty; for score prediction, model outputs are compared with human ratings using Spearman correlation.

Results show that ChatGPT has substantial limitations as a teacher coach in this setting. It performs poorly at predicting rubric scores, often outputs generic or non-novel feedback, and frequently repeats suggestions already present in the transcript. The strongest negative finding is that 82% of its suggestions describe what the teacher already does. The authors conclude that current LLMs may complement human coaching only with substantial improvement, and they propose future directions such as involving educators in tuning and integrating automated feedback into human coaching workflows.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI system used for zero-shot scoring and generating instructional feedback/suggestions.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as a teacher coach on elementary math classroom transcripts by scoring CLASS/MQI items, identifying highlights and missed opportunities, and generating actionable suggestions for eliciting more student reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT showed low agreement with human ratings when asked to score classroom transcript segments on CLASS and MQI observation items. Reported Spearman correlations were low across items and prompting methods; for example, CLBM reached 0.35 under direct-answer prompting, while many other item correlations were near zero or negative.
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between model-predicted observation scores and human annotator scores

findings.finding_summary: For identifying highlights and missed opportunities, teachers generally rated ChatGPT's outputs as not insightful or not relevant. On MQI items, the share of 'No' ratings was high, including 55% for relevance and 71% for insightfulness, and faithfulness problems were present in 29% of examples.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for generated feedback examples

findings.finding_summary: For actionable suggestions to elicit more student reasoning, most outputs were judged faithful, relevant, and actionable, but they were usually redundant. The paper reports that 82% of suggestions described what the teacher was already doing in the transcript, indicating low novelty despite practical usefulness.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, actionability, and novelty for generated suggestions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study using qualitative human ratings and correlational validation, not a controlled intervention. The methodology is clear and the sample is concrete, but evidence is limited to a small set of transcript segments and raters.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports one moderately positive finding on suggestion actionability, but the main results are mostly null or negative, with low correlations and high redundancy. Overall impact on teacher coaching quality appears modest and unclear rather than strong.

paper_profiles.title: LearnLens: An AI-Enhanced Dashboard to Support Teachers in Open-Ended Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping teachers interpret open-ended student responses in exploratory learning environments, where much of students’ thinking is difficult to see in real time. The authors argue that existing classroom tools often organize data but do not provide actionable summaries or feedback, making it hard for teachers to quickly identify misconceptions and adjust instruction.

To address this problem, the paper presents LearnLens, a generative AI-enhanced teacher-facing dashboard. LearnLens ingests digital assessment responses such as check-ins, exit tickets, and formative assessments, then provides tables of student responses, filtering, sample response viewing, word clouds, bar charts, and AI-generated summaries of class understanding and common misconceptions. The GenAI component was developed with iterative prompt engineering and human validation, using GPT-4o, and refined using real classroom data from a middle school Earth science curriculum.

The study was conducted with two 6th-grade science teachers from one urban public school in the United States. Teachers were co-design participants in prior professional development sessions and were shown the dashboard through guided, semi-structured interviews rather than using it independently in class. The teachers valued the visualizations and the AI-generated insights for sense-making and planning future instruction, but they were cautious about AI suggestions that went beyond the evidence in the student data. Overall, the paper concludes that AI-supported dashboards can improve teachers’ ability to interpret open-ended responses and support instructional adaptation, while noting that more longitudinal and broader evaluation is needed.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used to generate summaries and identify misconceptions from student open-ended responses in a teacher-facing dashboard.
identified_tools.use_case: Powered the LearnLens AI-generated insights feature via GPT-4o to summarize collective student understanding and detect common misconceptions or gaps for teacher review.

findings.finding_summary: In semi-structured interviews, two middle-school science teachers reported that the GPT-4o-based insights were useful for quickly identifying gaps and misconceptions in students’ open-ended responses. Teachers valued the summaries as data-grounded support for instructional decision-making, but remained cautious about prescriptive recommendations that went beyond the data.
findings.measure: Teacher interview perceptions of usefulness/trust in AI-generated summaries and misconception identification

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, interview-based study with two teachers and no experimental comparison, so it does not meet high-causality evidence standards. The methodology is structured and directly examines teacher perceptions of the AI feature, supporting a moderate qualitative evidence tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceived usefulness for teacher sense-making, but no quantitative effect size or demonstrated change in student outcomes. Because impact is suggestive rather than measured, the impact tier is yellow.

paper_profiles.title: Transforming Teachers’ Roles and Agencies in the Era of Generative AI: Perceptions, Acceptance, Knowledge, and Practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a conceptual gap in the generative AI in education literature: existing studies often examine teachers’ perceptions, acceptance, knowledge, and classroom practices separately, rather than as interconnected dimensions shaping how teachers engage with GenAI. The author argues that GenAI is transforming teachers’ roles and agencies in ways that traditional technology frameworks such as TPACK do not fully capture, because GenAI can actively co-create content, provide feedback, and participate in instructional processes.

The paper proposes a four-stage framework for teacher engagement with GenAI: Awareness (GenAI Observer), Exploration (GenAI Adopter), Integration (GenAI Collaborator), and Innovation (GenAI Innovator). Rather than reporting a new empirical intervention, the article synthesizes prior literature to describe how teachers may progressively move from passive awareness to active experimentation, routine classroom integration, and finally innovation and leadership in GenAI-supported teaching.

The context is education broadly, with examples drawn primarily from pre-service teachers, in-service teachers, and teacher education settings, including lesson-planning activities and collaborative learning with AI speakers. The paper concludes that meaningful GenAI adoption requires continuous professional development, institutional support, and stronger teacher knowledge so that educators can use GenAI critically, ethically, and creatively, rather than only at a superficial or exploratory level.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI systems used in education to generate content, support personalized learning, and provide feedback or instructional assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a conceptual framework paper about teachers’ roles and agencies in the era of generative AI. It discusses GenAI broadly, including tools such as ChatGPT, but does not evaluate a single named product empirically.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/framework article rather than an empirical evaluation. It proposes a teacher-role framework and summarizes prior literature, but does not report a study design, sample, or measured outcomes for an AI tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes, outcome measures, or tool-specific impacts are reported in this paper. The paper is about theoretical implications and adoption stages, so there is no direct evidence of impact on teachers or students.

paper_profiles.title: Distance Teaching Experience of Campus-based Teachers at Times of Pandemic Confinement
paper_profiles.venue: ACM 5th International Conference on Education Technology Management (ICETM 2022)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how campus-based university teachers experienced the sudden shift to distance teaching during COVID-19 pandemic confinement. The authors were interested in the practical challenges teachers faced, how they adapted their teaching, what they learned from the experience, and whether those lessons might improve future campus-based teaching after the pandemic.

The study is based on online, semi-structured interviews with six teachers from the Computer Science department at Blekinge Institute of Technology in Sweden. The interview prompts focused on adaptation, session recording, Zoom fatigue, virtual reality, and lessons learned. The authors then applied inductive qualitative thematic analysis to the transcripts. The paper is therefore about teacher perceptions and reflections rather than a tested coaching or generative AI intervention.

The main findings were that interaction with students was much harder online, especially when webcams were off and nonverbal cues were missing. Teachers valued asynchronous communication tools such as chat, polls, Kahoot, Mentimeter, and Padlet because these reduced shyness barriers and sometimes increased participation. Recorded lectures were widely seen as useful for flexibility and review, but they also reduced opportunities for live questioning and could promote procrastination. Teachers reported increased workload, technical strain, and Zoom fatigue, but many expected to keep some online elements, especially hybrid or flipped approaches, in future campus teaching.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic AI system or chatbot based on generative AI/LLM capabilities; no specific commercial or research product is named in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Not actually studied as an AI tool. The paper discusses distance teaching during COVID-19 and mentions digital tools such as Zoom, polls, Mentimeter, Kahoot, Padlet, and Discord, but no generative AI coaching system for teachers.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative interview study, but it does not evaluate an AI tool or teacher-coaching system. The paper provides contextual findings about remote teaching practices rather than evidence for generative AI coaching.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No AI intervention effect is reported, so there is no measurable impact on teacher uptake or reflective practice attributable to a tool. The paper only suggests general digital tools for engagement.

paper_profiles.title: Understanding Teacher Revisions of Large Language Model-Generated Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how teachers actually revise large language model (LLM)-generated formative feedback before it reaches students, and what those revisions reveal about the alignment between AI feedback and teacher priorities. The authors argue that most existing evaluations focus on output quality in isolation, while ignoring the human-in-the-loop process that determines what students ultimately receive. They therefore study teacher edits as a concrete trace of pedagogical judgment and uptake.

The study analyzes 1,349 AI-generated feedback drafts paired with final teacher-delivered feedback messages from 117 teachers using the Tutoria platform. Tutoria is integrated with Moodle and Google Classroom and supports a workflow in which the LLM drafts feedback for short open-ended student responses, and teachers can accept, edit, or rewrite it before delivery. The dataset combines logs from controlled studies and in-the-wild classroom deployments across Brazilian high school chemistry and higher-education computer science contexts, with additional extracurricular computer science tasks.

Results show that teachers accepted AI feedback without modification in about 78% of cases, and that revision was highly heterogeneous across teachers: about half never edited feedback at all, while a small minority edited most messages. When teachers did revise, they typically shortened the feedback and preserved much of its meaning, suggesting compression rather than wholesale rewriting. The authors also found that feedback texts alone could predict revisions only modestly well, indicating that contextual factors beyond the message itself matter. Qualitative coding further showed that revisions often reduced overly explanatory or high-information feedback and moved it toward more concise corrective forms. The paper concludes that teacher revision is a useful indicator of pedagogical alignment and that AI feedback systems should better account for teacher preferences while minimizing unnecessary editing effort.

identified_tools.name: DeepSeek
identified_tools.description: A DeepSeek large language model used to generate formative feedback drafts for short open-ended student responses within the Tutoria platform.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of the LLMs that generated initial feedback drafts which teachers could accept, edit, or rewrite before delivery to students. The paper analyzed teacher revisions of these AI-generated drafts rather than comparing model variants.

findings.finding_summary: Across 1,349 AI-generated feedback drafts from 117 teachers, teachers accepted DeepSeek-based/LLM-generated feedback without modification in 77.8% of cases (1050/1349). Teacher revision was modestly predictable from the AI text alone, with holdout ROC AUC values of 0.698 to 0.746 across models, but the paper does not isolate DeepSeek-specific effects from other LLMs used in the platform.
findings.measure: Teacher acceptance vs. revision of AI-generated feedback; binary prediction of revision from text features

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI GPT-family large language model used to generate formative feedback drafts for student responses in Tutoria.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as an early-version LLM in the platform to generate feedback drafts that teachers then accepted, edited, or rewrote. The study analyzed how teachers revised these drafts in practice.

findings.finding_summary: Across the combined dataset of 1,349 feedback instances from 117 teachers, teachers accepted AI feedback without modification in 77.8% of cases (1050/1349), and edited feedback was slightly longer than unedited feedback before being shortened by teachers. The paper reports overall predictive performance for revision decisions from AI text alone (best ROC AUC=0.746), but does not report ChatGPT-only outcomes.
findings.measure: Teacher acceptance/revision behavior; text-only prediction of revision

identified_tools.name: Tutoria
identified_tools.description: An AI-supported feedback platform integrated with Moodle and Google Classroom that generates an initial feedback draft for teacher co-creation and delivery.
identified_tools.use_case: Served as the platform within which teachers reviewed, accepted, edited, or fully rewrote LLM-generated formative feedback. The paper studies teacher revision traces logged by Tutoria.

findings.finding_summary: In Tutoria, teachers accepted AI-generated feedback without modification in 77.8% of 1,349 instances (1050/1349), suggesting the platform frequently reduced the need for manual rewriting. However, when revisions occurred, teachers typically compressed and simplified the feedback rather than substantially changing its semantic content (mean cosine similarity between AI and final feedback = 0.97 overall).
findings.measure: Acceptance rate; similarity between AI draft and final teacher feedback; revision patterns

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a correlational, log-based analysis of teacher revisions rather than an experimental study. It provides descriptive and predictive evidence about real-world teacher uptake, but does not establish causal effects on learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed teacher acceptance rate is large in magnitude (77.8% unchanged), and the paper also reports meaningful behavioral heterogeneity and above-chance prediction of revision. However, the impact on student outcomes is not measured, so the practical effect is clearer for workflow than for learning.

paper_profiles.title: Teacher training in the age of AI: Impact on AI Literacy and Teachers' Attitudes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether an online professional development program can improve in-service teachers’ AI literacy, their attitudes toward AI, and their self-reported willingness to use AI in teaching. The authors position the study as a response to the rapid spread of generative AI in education and the need for teachers to develop both conceptual understanding and practical confidence, rather than simply being aware of AI in the abstract.

The intervention was a four-week certificate course offered by the digital professional development platform fobizz, titled “Artificial Intelligence in Everyday School and Classroom Practice.” The course combined a kickoff webinar, self-paced learning modules, optional supplementary webinars and workshops, and a project phase in which participants created an AI-supported lesson plan using tools such as the fobizz AI Assistant. The sample consisted of German in-service teachers from a range of school types, with some participants also coming from adult education, higher education, and school administration. Outcomes were measured with pre-post questionnaires assessing AI literacy and attitudes toward AI, including self-reported current use, intended classroom integration, perceived preparedness, and beliefs about opportunities and risks.

The findings show statistically significant gains in overall AI literacy and in most competency domains, along with large positive shifts in self-reported use of AI in daily life and teaching practice, and in feeling prepared to integrate AI into lessons. The authors conclude that structured training can improve teachers’ AI-related knowledge, confidence, and willingness to use AI educationally. However, they also note that post-training knowledge remained incomplete, that the sample was self-selected, and that the study did not assess long-term sustainability or whether teachers actually implemented AI practices beyond the immediate post-test.

identified_tools.name: fobizz AI Assistant
identified_tools.description: A digital AI assistant offered within the fobizz professional development platform for generating and supporting classroom materials and lesson planning.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by participating teachers during the training course to develop an AI-supported lesson plan and to practice pedagogically reflective AI use in classroom contexts.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers in the training program showed increased self-reported use of AI tools for lesson planning and teaching materials after the intervention. The paper reports that agreement increased significantly for "I use AI to help create my lessons and teaching materials" (pre M=1.27, post M=2.35, p<0.001, d=1.32; n=436) and for "I feel well-prepared to integrate AI technologies into my teaching" (pre M=1.03, post M=2.28, p<0.001, d=1.65; n=436).
findings.measure: Self-reported use of AI for lesson creation and perceived preparedness to integrate AI into teaching

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI generative AI chatbot based on large language models used for conversational text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Included in the core training module "ChatGPT & fobizz AI in Your Classroom" and discussed as a generative AI tool teachers should learn to use in educational practice.

findings.finding_summary: After the training, teachers reported significantly higher current and intended use of AI in daily and educational practice. Items increased for regular AI use in daily life (pre M=1.37, post M=2.28, p<0.001, d=1.07; n=436), use for lesson/material creation (pre M=1.27, post M=2.35, p<0.001, d=1.32; n=436), use for assessments/grading (pre M=0.41, post M=1.04, p<0.001, d=0.67; n=436), and imagining AI integration into teaching (pre M=2.45, post M=2.72, p<0.001, d=0.49; n=436).
findings.measure: Self-reported AI use, intended integration, and preparedness for teaching

findings.finding_summary: The training also increased critical beliefs about AI risks while increasing belief in AI's instructional value. Agreement that "AI in schools is more of a threat than an opportunity" rose slightly (pre M=0.98, post M=1.37, p<0.001, d=0.42; n=436), and concern that "AI will replace teachers in the future" also increased slightly (pre M=0.45, post M=0.67, p<0.001, d=0.25; n=436), but belief that AI offers an opportunity to support students increased as well (pre M=2.39, post M=2.67, p<0.001, d=0.50; n=436).
findings.measure: Self-reported beliefs about AI opportunities and risks in education

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a pre-post intervention study with self-reported outcomes, not a randomized controlled trial. It provides useful evidence on teacher attitudes and reported use, but the design limits causal inference and the paper does not isolate effects of a single tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effect sizes for several self-reported outcomes are medium to very large (e.g., d=1.32 and d=1.65). Even though the evidence is self-reported, the magnitude of change suggests substantial perceived impact.

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines how secondary teachers used and evaluated Colleague AI Classroom, a generative AI platform designed as a teaching partner rather than a teacher replacement. The central question is how teachers design, implement, and reflect on AI-assisted classroom tools, and how teacher judgment and AI competency shape the quality of student-AI interactions and instructional outcomes.

The intervention consisted of four AI-powered features: Teaching Aide for structured student-AI dialogue, Assessment and AI Grading for rubric generation and formative feedback, AI Tutor for student-initiated support, and Student Growth Insights for surfacing patterns in student activity. The pilot ran for seven weeks in spring 2025 with 21 in-service teachers from five Washington State districts and one independent school. More than 600 students in grades 6-12 used the system in live classroom settings. Teachers co-designed activities, implemented them with students, and provided weekly reflections; the researchers also collected surveys, planning documents, group meetings, interviews, and platform usage logs.

Findings suggest that AI was most useful when teachers provided clear framing, monitored use closely, and aligned activities to instructional goals. Teachers valued narrative feedback more than numeric scores, often using AI-generated comments as a first draft for revision and retaining final grading authority. Student engagement and learning were strongest when teachers iterated on prompts, used the tools repeatedly, and matched scaffolds to grade level and subject area. The report concludes that generative AI can support formative feedback and student inquiry in classrooms, but only when integrated with strong teacher mediation, pedagogical purpose, and ongoing refinement.

At the same time, the study highlights that teachers' prior AI experience, beliefs about AI, and subject/grade context strongly influenced uptake. The authors emphasize that AI currently functions best as a third agent in a teacher-student-AI collaborative model, extending instructional reach while leaving human judgment central to teaching and assessment.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI classroom platform with multiple teacher-configurable features for student conversation, AI-assisted grading/feedback, tutoring, and teacher-facing student growth insights.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied through the Colleague AI Classroom pilot, where secondary teachers co-designed and implemented four features: Teaching Aide, Assessment & AI Grading, AI Tutor, and Student Growth Insights.

findings.finding_summary: Across the Teaching Aide feature, 28% of teachers reported classrooms where most students engaged thoughtfully, 66% reported mixed engagement, and 6% reported limited engagement. Teachers attributed stronger engagement to clear framing, active monitoring, and repeated implementation; by the final session, 44% of teachers reported being very confident reusing the tool and 56% somewhat confident.
findings.measure: Teacher-rated student engagement with Teaching Aide conversations; teacher confidence in reusing the tool

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the Teaching Aide helped most students learn in 35% of classrooms and helped some students learn in 62%; only 3% reported no student benefit. The report notes that learning gains were strongest when teachers aligned conversations to instructional goals and provided scaffolds such as conversation starters and participation norms.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported student learning from Teaching Aide

findings.finding_summary: For AI-assisted assessment and grading, 57% of teachers said the AI feedback was useful (41% for both teachers and students, 14% for students only, 3% for teachers only), while 42% said it was not useful (24% vague/unhelpful; 18% incorrect/misleading). Teachers valued narrative feedback more than numeric scores and often used the AI output as a first draft to revise.
findings.measure: Teacher survey of AI-generated assessment feedback quality

findings.finding_summary: In assessment logs, median AI grading coverage on submitted work was 92.2% across 58 assessments, with mean submission rate 54.8% and average student resubmission rate 8.7%. This indicates high automation coverage, but actual iterative uptake of feedback through resubmission was comparatively limited and varied by classroom.
findings.measure: Platform log metrics for submission rate, AI grading coverage, and resubmissions

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that Student Growth Insights and related conversation summaries reduced oversight burden and supported real-time instructional adjustment by surfacing common questions, misconceptions, and patterns of progress. The report presents this as a teacher-facing efficiency and decision-support benefit, not as a student achievement effect.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported usefulness of student growth summaries and instructional adjustments

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods pilot with teacher surveys, interviews, reflections, and platform logs rather than a controlled causal design. The evidence is useful for implementation and uptake, but it is not strong experimental evidence of learning impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The report suggests meaningful implementation effects such as improved teacher confidence, high AI grading coverage, and some reported student learning support, but it does not report effect sizes and most outcomes are qualitative or descriptive. The impact on actual uptake is notable, but the magnitude for student outcomes remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Grounding AI-in-Education Development in Teachers’ Voices: Findings from a National Survey in Indonesia
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how K–12 teachers in Indonesia are currently using AI in their instructional work, what kinds of support they need, and what barriers they face. The motivation is that AI is increasingly present in Indonesian classrooms, but there is limited large-scale, teacher-centred evidence to guide the design of context-appropriate tools and policies.

The study is a nationwide online survey of 349 Indonesian teachers across elementary, junior high, and senior high schools. Respondents reported on AI use across six teaching domains: content knowledge development, pedagogy, assessment and evaluation, curriculum development, teaching media, and professional practice. The survey also examined usage of several AI tool categories, including LLM-based text assistants, translation systems, image/video generators, grammar checkers, and speech technologies. Participants were recruited through education offices, teacher networks, and digital channels, and data were collected over four weeks in 2025.

The results show that teachers most often use AI to reduce preparation workload, especially for content development and teaching media creation. Teachers’ highest priorities for future support were generating assessment items, syllabus and lesson plan design, and creating interactive teaching media. At the same time, they reported problems such as overly generic feedback, infrastructure constraints, overreliance concerns, and unclear or contextually misaligned outputs. The authors conclude that Indonesian AI-in-education tools should be more context-aware, pedagogically grounded, and lightweight enough to work in uneven connectivity environments.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / LLM-based text assistants used for instructional support, content creation, and related teaching tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper surveyed Indonesian K–12 teachers about their use of generic LLM-based text assistants and other AI tools across teaching components, as well as their needs and challenges when using them.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional national survey of teachers’ reported AI use and needs, so it provides descriptive correlational evidence rather than an experimental evaluation of an AI tool. It is nevertheless systematic and based on a reasonably large sample (n=349).
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports broad teacher adoption and perceived needs, but no causal impact estimates or learning outcome effects. Any impact is indirect and the study does not evaluate actual tool effectiveness beyond self-reported use and satisfaction.

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper examines how a human-in-the-loop generative AI system, Shiksha Copilot, supported lesson planning for teachers in low-resource government schools in Karnataka, India. The authors investigate a central question for teacher-facing AI: not just whether the system can generate plausible lesson plans, but how teachers and curators actually review, edit, adapt, and use AI-produced materials in everyday practice. The paper is especially concerned with teacher-AI collaboration in multilingual settings and with the practical constraints of public schooling, including heavy administrative workload, limited instructional resources, and the need to align with a state-mandated curriculum and the 5E instructional model.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general LLM-based AI lesson-planning and chat assistance system with human-in-the-loop curation, curriculum-grounded retrieval, translation, and teacher-customizable lesson plans.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as Shiksha Copilot, a bilingual teacher-AI collaboration system used by curators and teachers in Karnataka, India to generate, review, translate, customize, and query lesson plans.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods deployment with 1,043 teachers, the paper reports that Shiksha Copilot reduced lesson planning time and bureaucratic workload, and lowered teacher stress. Teachers used the curated lesson plans for both classroom instruction and record-keeping, with the system supporting faster preparation and less administrative effort.
findings.measure: Teacher survey and interview reports on lesson planning time, administrative workload, and teaching-related stress

findings.finding_summary: The post-survey and interviews indicate reduced teaching-related stress after adoption of the tool. The authors attribute this to easier access to ready-made, curriculum-aligned lesson plans and reduced burden from record-keeping and planning.
findings.measure: Teacher Stress Scale (TSS), pre/post survey

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported a shift toward activity-based pedagogy and broader changes in teaching practices. The system also improved access to contextualized, curriculum-aligned instructional resources, although systemic constraints limited larger pedagogical change.
findings.measure: Custom access-to-resources scale; interviews on teaching practice changes
findings.sample_size: n=406 matched responses for survey; n=22 teacher interviews

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods field deployment with surveys, interviews, and log analysis rather than a randomized or quasi-experimental impact study. The evidence is informative but largely descriptive and qualitative, with no causal identification or reported effect sizes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful practical benefits such as reduced planning time, lower stress, and improved workflow fit, but it does not provide quantified effect sizes. The impact appears substantial in use, yet the magnitude cannot be precisely estimated from the reported results.

paper_profiles.title: The AI Teacher Test: Measuring the Pedagogical Ability of Blender and GPT-3 in Educational Dialogues
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how to evaluate whether generative conversational models are capable of functioning as AI teachers in educational dialogues. The authors argue that existing automatic text-generation metrics are not sufficient because they do not assess pedagogical qualities such as sounding like a teacher, understanding the student, and helping the student improve. They therefore propose an AI Teacher Test based on comparative judgments between human teachers and AI-generated responses.

To build the test, the authors ran Blender and GPT-3 in parallel with human teachers on real student-teacher dialogue data from language-learning and mathematics settings. They generated candidate responses to student utterances, then had human raters compare pairs of replies in context across three pedagogical dimensions: likely said by a teacher, understanding the student, and helping the student. A Bayesian Bradley-Terry model was used to estimate latent ability scores and rank responses.

The evaluation used two dialogue corpora, but the direct human rating study focused on the Teacher-Student Chatroom Corpus in second-language learning, with crowdworkers from the UK and US serving as evaluators rather than the actual students or teachers in the dataset. The main finding is that Blender and GPT-3 can show reasonable conversational uptake, but both remain substantially behind human teachers on pedagogical ability, especially helpfulness. Blender performs better than GPT-3 overall, yet neither model matches human performance. The authors conclude that their method is a first step toward more meaningful evaluation of AI teachers and could eventually support autonomous model development.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI generative language model / chatbot family used for open-domain dialogue and text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as GPT-3 (Ada and Davinci completions) to generate AI teacher responses to student utterances in educational dialogues for comparison against human teacher replies.

findings.finding_summary: In comparative judgments of teacher responses in educational dialogues, GPT-3 was rated significantly worse than human teachers on all measured pedagogical abilities. Relative to the actual teacher, mean ability differences were = -0.67 for speaking like a teacher, = -0.67 for understanding the student, and = -0.93 for helping the student (all p < .001).
findings.measure: Pairwise comparative judgments on three pedagogical dimensions: likely said by a teacher, understanding the student, helping the student

findings.finding_summary: GPT-3's responses were positively evaluated in only 33-35% of dialogue contexts across the three abilities, and 2-12% of estimates had credible intervals excluding zero. The paper reports that some GPT-3 responses were still preferred over human teacher responses in specific cases, but overall performance was substantially lower than human teachers.
findings.measure: Per-item posterior ability estimates and proportion of responses with positive alpha

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary comparative study using human judgments and Bayesian modeling, but it is not an RCT/QED of teacher outcomes. The evidence is observational and evaluative, so it fits a lower-confidence tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported negative differences for GPT-3 vs. human teachers are large in magnitude, especially for helping the student ( = -0.93). That indicates substantial underperformance on pedagogical ability, even though the direction is adverse.

paper_profiles.title: Understanding Teacher Perspectives and Experiences After Deployment of AI Literacy Curriculum in Middle-School Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle-school teachers experienced implementing modules from the MIT RAICA (Responsible AI for Computational Action) curriculum and how their beliefs about AI and teaching evolved through the process. The study is motivated by a gap in AI education research: much prior work has centered researchers as instructors, leaving limited evidence from classroom teachers about what supports are needed for successful implementation of AI literacy curricula.

The intervention consisted of three project-based AI literacy modules deployed in middle-school classrooms. Teachers received ongoing professional development, interacted with RAICA researchers during weekly debrief sessions, and then participated in semi-structured interviews after implementation. Seven teachers from interdisciplinary backgrounds (art, business, and computer science) were interviewed about how they adapted the modules, their attitudes toward AI before/during/after implementation, and their perceptions of the curriculum and support resources. The classroom modules included activities such as building an interactive art installation, creating a chatbot, or designing an app for the school community.

Findings show that the curriculum expanded teachers’ AI knowledge, increased attention to ethical and societal implications of AI, and encouraged teachers to draw on their own interdisciplinary strengths to engage students. Teachers valued the flexibility of the curriculum but also reported needing more technical support, clearer guidance, more time for preparation, and better accommodations for diverse learners. Overall, the paper concludes that AI literacy curricula for middle school are more effective when paired with sustained teacher support, concrete scaffolding, and opportunities for continuous feedback during development and early deployment.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Computer-assisted instruction / AI-enabled curriculum or educational software used to support teaching and learning.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies teacher experiences implementing the MIT RAICA AI literacy curriculum in middle-school classrooms, including teacher professional development and classroom deployment of curriculum modules.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the RAICA curriculum expanded their knowledge of AI concepts, helped them recognize AI's daily applications and ethical implications, and supported more confident adaptation of lessons to their classrooms. They also described increased appreciation for peer support and the curriculum's flexibility, but requested more scaffolding, technical support, and one-on-one code review during PD.
findings.measure: Teacher interview themes on AI knowledge growth, confidence, adaptation of curriculum materials, and implementation challenges

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods study based on semi-structured interviews with seven teachers, not an experimental evaluation. It provides useful implementation insight but no causal evidence or quantitative effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceived impact on teacher knowledge and confidence, but impact is not quantified and is based on self-reported experiences. Any effect on uptake or practice is suggestive rather than measured with robust outcome data.

paper_profiles.title: The ADAIO System at the BEA-2023 Shared Task on Generating AI Teacher Responses in Educational Dialogues
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents the ADAIO team’s submission to the BEA 2023 shared task on generating AI teacher responses in educational dialogues. The overarching question is whether large language models, especially GPT-3, can generate teacher-like responses that are contextually appropriate, pedagogically useful, and suitable for use in dialogue-based intelligent tutoring systems. The paper is framed as a system description and benchmark result rather than a study of a deployed educational intervention.

The intervention/approach is a set of prompt-engineering and model-configuration experiments using OpenAI GPT-3, including zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuning settings. The authors test several prompts that vary the tutor’s stance, including polite/helpful responses, probing student understanding, and encouraging conversational skills. They use examples from the Teacher-Student Chatroom Corpus (TSCC), a dataset of ESL teacher-student chatroom dialogues, and evaluate candidate systems with automatic metrics such as BERTScore and DialogRPT.

The population/context is real teacher-student dialogue data from ESL chatrooms in the TSCC corpus, where teachers interact with students on language-learning tasks. The paper does not report a classroom deployment with human participants, teacher training, or learner outcomes. Its main conclusion is that few-shot GPT-3 with Prompt A performed best for their submission and achieved second place in the shared task, suggesting that LLMs can generate plausible teacher responses in this benchmark setting. However, the authors also note the limits of automatic evaluation and call for further work on pedagogical validity and longer discourse contexts.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT family of large language models used for text generation and dialogue response generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the generative model for the ADAIO system to produce AI-teacher responses in educational dialogues; evaluated in zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuning settings, with the final submitted system using few-shot text-davinci-003 (normalized to ChatGPT).

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports automatic benchmark performance for the GPT-3-based ADAIO system on teacher-response generation in the BEA 2023 shared task. For the final few-shot system, official scores were BERTScore P=0.67, R=0.71, F1=0.69 on the DEV phase and P=0.72, R=0.69, F1=0.71 on the EVAL phase; DialogRPT final scores were 0.35 (avg) / 0.71 (best) on DEV and 0.37 (avg) / 0.65 (best) on EVAL. The authors state the system placed 2nd overall, but they did not conduct human evaluation of teacher uptake or reflective practice.
findings.measure: BERTScore and DialogRPT on shared-task teacher-response generation
findings.sample_size: n=273 test dialogues (shared task test set); internal model-selection on n=50 training samples

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a system paper for a shared-task benchmark, not a randomized or quasi-experimental study of teacher users. Evaluation is primarily automatic text-generation scoring, with no human uptake or reflective-practice outcomes measured.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported performance is moderate at the task level, but no educational effect size is provided and there is no evidence of actual teacher behavior change. The impact on teachers is therefore unclear rather than demonstrably positive.

paper_profiles.title: Focus on conceptual ideas in quantum mechanics for teacher training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that teacher training for quantum mechanics should prioritize conceptual understanding before formal mathematics, especially as quantum ideas move earlier into the curriculum and become more relevant to the emerging quantum workforce. The author identifies five core conceptual ideas that teachers should master: superposition, entanglement, complementarity, tagging, and measurement. The paper is framed as a call to action rather than a conventional empirical education study, and it draws on physics education research, existing instructional materials, and the author’s instructional experience.

The proposed approach is to use a sequence of concrete thought experiments and visual/computer-based tools, including Stern-Gerlach analyzer loops, two-slit experiments, beam splitters, Mach-Zehnder interferometers, and delayed-choice/interaction-free measurement examples. The paper emphasizes algebra- and trigonometry-level reasoning, computer animations, tutorials, lectures, readings, problem solving, and reflective writing as teaching methods. It also references an online edX course that reportedly spans 4–6 weeks and has been used with tens of thousands of learners, but the paper does not present a formal evaluation of that course in this article.

The target population is teachers or prospective teachers who need to become quantum literate, especially adults without prior quantum expertise. The context is teacher preparation for quantum mechanics and quantum information science, with a focus on the United States and the broader second quantum revolution. The paper concludes that teachers need substantial conceptual grounding in order to answer student questions, teach quantum ideas confidently, and support the introduction of quantum topics earlier in schooling. It also states that the ideas are field-tested and evidence-informed, but not evidence-based, and calls for more curriculum development and research.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system or structured instructional platform that provides guided learning support, feedback, and practice in a domain.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper cites and discusses online course materials and computer-based tutorials/animations used to teach quantum mechanics concepts to teachers, including the edX course Quantum Mechanics for Everyone, but it does not evaluate an adaptive tutoring system as such.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual, opinion-driven paper about how quantum mechanics should be taught to teachers. It explicitly states that education research has not yet been performed on these ideas, so there is no empirical evaluation of an AI tool or tutoring system.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No quantitative outcomes, effect sizes, or uptake measures are reported for any AI-enabled coaching or tutoring tool. The paper discusses instructional materials and course design, not measured impact on teacher practice.

paper_profiles.title: Are they just delegating? Cross-Sample Predictions on University Students' & Teachers' Use of AI.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether university teachers and students differ in how often they use generative AI for academic work, how much they delegate tasks to it, and how accurately they predict the other group’s AI use. The authors frame the study as a trust problem in higher education: if teachers and students misjudge each other’s AI practices, this may undermine confidence, assessment, and communication.

The study used online surveys with German university teachers and students. Participants reported their own AI use across six overlapping academic tasks: information research, literature research, writing, coding, translating, and visualizing. They also made incentivized predictions about the other group’s use and delegation levels on the same tasks. No intervention was delivered; the work is a comparative survey study with cross-sample prediction measures.

Results showed that students reported higher AI use and greater delegation than teachers on most tasks, although teachers reported more use for translation. Both groups substantially overestimated the other group’s AI use, and neither group was clearly more accurate overall. The authors conclude that there is a meaningful perception gap between teachers and students, and they argue that open discussion and transparency about AI practices are needed to support trust and equitable use of AI in higher education.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / AI chatbot tools used for academic tasks such as information research, writing, programming, translating, and visualizing; the paper does not identify a specific product in the main study measures.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers and students self-reported frequency of use and degree of delegation to AI across overlapping academic tasks, and predicted the other group’s use and delegation.

findings.finding_summary: This was a survey study of university teachers (n=113) and students (n=123) in which participants reported their own AI use and delegation across academic tasks and made cross-sample predictions. Students reported higher frequency of AI use than teachers for five of six tasks (overall b=-0.35, d=0.36), and higher delegation (overall b=-15.72, d=0.66); teachers reported higher use for translation only.
findings.measure: Self-reported frequency of AI use and self-reported degree of AI delegation across six overlapping academic tasks

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a correlational survey study with self-reports and cross-sample predictions, not an experiment or intervention. It provides useful descriptive evidence about AI use patterns but does not test a coaching system or causal effect on teacher practice.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported group differences are modest to medium in size, with d=0.36 for frequency and d=0.66 for delegation. However, the paper is about general AI use perceptions rather than interactive coaching, so direct instructional impact is limited.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether ChatGPT can serve as a useful automated coach for teachers by generating feedback on classroom instruction. The authors frame the problem around a real need in teacher professional development: high-quality coaching is valuable but often scarce, and prior automated tools have tended to provide low-level analytics rather than actionable feedback. They ask whether a generative language model can score classroom observation segments and provide high-level instructional feedback that resembles human coaching.

The study uses the NCTE Transcript dataset, which contains anonymized video-derived transcripts from 317 U.S. elementary mathematics teachers in grades 4 and 5 across four school districts. The authors evaluate ChatGPT in three zero-shot tasks: (A) predicting scores on selected CLASS and MQI observation items from transcript segments, (B) identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and (C) offering actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning. Two experienced math teachers, including one instructional coach, rated model outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

Results show that ChatGPT performs poorly on score prediction and only modestly on feedback generation. Its score predictions correlate weakly with human ratings, and its qualitative feedback is often not especially insightful or novel; for suggestions, the model frequently repeats what the teacher already did in the transcript. The paper concludes that generative AI has promise as a complement to human coaching, but current off-the-shelf models are not yet reliable enough to replace expert feedback. The authors emphasize the importance of future work on reducing hallucination, involving educators in tuning, and integrating automated feedback within human coaching systems.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational large language model / chatbot used for zero-shot text generation and scoring.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluates ChatGPT (accessed via gpt-3.5-turbo through the OpenAI API) as an automated teacher coach for three tasks: scoring classroom transcript segments against CLASS and MQI rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities, and generating actionable suggestions for eliciting more student mathematical reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: On Task A, ChatGPT showed low correspondence with human ratings when predicting CLASS and MQI observation scores from transcript segments. Reported Spearman correlations were near zero to weak across items, with values ranging from -0.11 to 0.35 depending on rubric item and prompting method, indicating poor calibration to expert scores (sample for quantitative scoring: n=100 transcript segments).
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between model-predicted observation scores and human ratings on CLASS and MQI items

findings.finding_summary: For Task B, teachers generally did not find ChatGPT’s highlighted examples of good instruction or missed opportunities to be insightful or relevant, especially for MQI items. The paper reports that hallucination/non-faithfulness was present in a nontrivial share of responses, with around 20-30% marked unfaithful, and that MQI responses were rated worse than CLASS responses across relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness (Task B evaluation: 216 CLASS examples and 288 MQI examples rated by 2 teachers).
