findings.measure: Human ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for highlighted examples and missed opportunities

findings.finding_summary: For Task C, ChatGPT’s suggestions were often judged actionable, relevant, and faithful to the transcript context, but they were usually redundant rather than novel. The paper reports that 82% of suggestions repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript; despite this, most suggestions were still rated actionable and faithful by the two teachers who evaluated 36 suggestions.
findings.measure: Human ratings of relevance, faithfulness, actionability, and novelty for teacher suggestions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical study with a clear evaluation setup, but it is not a randomized intervention and relies on a small number of human raters plus qualitative judgments. The evidence is useful but correlational/benchmark-style rather than causal.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported quantitative associations are weak overall (e.g., Spearman correlations near zero to 0.35), and the paper’s key qualitative finding is that outputs are often redundant or not insightful. That suggests limited demonstrated impact in the study as conducted.

paper_profiles.title: The Promises and Pitfalls of LLMs as Feedback Providers: A Study of Prompt Engineering and the Quality of AI-Driven Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can generate high-quality instructional feedback and what prompt characteristics are needed to elicit that quality. The authors are motivated by the broader challenge in higher education that expert feedback is time-consuming, while novice feedback is often lower in quality. They therefore develop a theory-driven prompt engineering manual and compare feedback produced by ChatGPT-4 under three prompts of varying quality.

The intervention studied is not a school-based coaching program, but an LLM feedback workflow in which ChatGPT-4 is prompted to comment on a learning goal containing three intentional errors. The researchers first code and compare LLM outputs across low-, medium-, and high-quality prompts, then use the best-performing prompt to elicit feedback from novice pre-service teachers and expert educators for comparison. The population is higher-education actors in teacher education: pre-service teachers, teacher trainers, educational science professors, and a headmaster, all working with a teacher-education feedback task.

The study finds that prompt quality strongly shapes feedback quality: only the best prompt reliably produced strong LLM feedback, while a superficially good prompt could still generate hallucinated errors. Overall, ChatGPT-4 outperformed novice feedback and in some dimensions even exceeded expert feedback, especially in specificity, questions, and explanations. The authors conclude that LLMs can be efficient and high-quality feedback providers in higher education, but only when guided by careful prompting and human oversight; they also emphasize ethical concerns such as privacy, data security, and the need for experts to monitor and revise AI-generated feedback.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based chatbot/LLM system used to generate feedback from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as ChatGPT-4 to generate feedback on a learning goal given prompts of varying quality, and then compared against novice and expert feedback.

findings.finding_summary: Using three prompt variants, ChatGPT-4 produced feedback that differed significantly by prompt quality. The highest-quality prompt (prompt 3) yielded better feedback than prompts 1 and 2 on assessment criteria, explanation, first person, questions, explanation of suggestions, and specificity; prompt quality was also associated with fewer errors than prompt 2. Sample sizes for this part were 20 feedback instances per prompt (n=60 total).
findings.measure: Feedback quality subdimensions coded with a prompt manual and content analysis (assessment criteria, explanation, first person, questions, explanation of suggestions, specificity, errors)
findings.effect_size: MDiff values reported: assessment criteria 1.50 vs prompt 1 and 0.90 vs prompt 2; explanation 0.75 vs prompt 1 and 0.40 vs prompt 2; first person 1.05 vs prompt 1 and 0.95 vs prompt 2; questions 0.70 vs prompt 1 and 1.00 vs prompt 2; explanation of suggestion 0.60 vs prompt 1; specificity 1.25 vs prompt 1; errors prompt 2 vs prompt 1 MDiff = -0.85 and vs prompt 3 MDiff = -0.95
findings.confidence_interval: Multiple 95% CIs reported in text for pairwise prompt comparisons, e.g. assessment criteria 95% CI [1.10, 1.90] vs prompt 1 and [0.50, 1.30] vs prompt 2; other CIs not fully repeated here

findings.finding_summary: Compared with novice and expert feedback, ChatGPT-4 feedback generated using the highest-quality prompt was superior to novice feedback across all subdimensions except valence and first person. Relative to expert feedback, ChatGPT-4 was significantly better in explanation, questions, and specificity. The comparison included 30 novice feedback instances, 11 expert feedback instances, and 30 LLM feedback instances.
findings.measure: Feedback quality subdimensions coded with the same feedback quality scheme
findings.effect_size: MDiff values reported vs experts: explanation 0.46, questions 0.50, specificity 0.96; versus novices, no effect sizes were reported in the summary text
findings.confidence_interval: For expert comparisons: explanation 95% CI [0.17, 0.74], questions 95% CI [0.07, 0.93], specificity 95% CI [0.52, 1.41]
findings.sample_size: n=30 LLM feedback, n=30 novice feedback, n=11 expert feedback

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical comparative study using coded feedback outputs rather than a randomized field trial. The methodology is quantitative and reasonably clear, but it is situated in a higher-education prompt/feedback task rather than a school implementation study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported differences are substantively meaningful, with several moderate-to-large mean differences in feedback quality subdimensions and clear advantages for higher-quality prompts. However, the paper does not report a single standardized effect size like d, so impact is best treated as modest-to-moderate rather than definitive.

paper_profiles.title: Perceptions and preparedness of K-12 educators in adopting generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 educators perceive generative AI and how prepared they feel to adopt it in school settings. The study addresses a practical problem in education: AI tools such as ChatGPT and DALL-E are becoming more visible, but schools vary widely in readiness, policy support, and teacher confidence. The author focuses on educators’ familiarity with AI, their perceptions of its benefits and risks, and the institutional conditions that shape adoption.

The study uses a mixed-methods survey design with 250 K-12 educators from rural, suburban, and urban schools across public, charter, and private institutions in the United States. Participants included teachers, principals, vice principals, superintendents, and instructional coaches. Quantitative survey items measured AI familiarity, perceived impact, and institutional planning stage, while open-ended responses were thematically analyzed to identify common concerns and opportunities. Data collection occurred online over 2024, and the survey was anonymous and IRB-approved.

Findings suggest that educators generally view generative AI positively, especially for operational efficiency, lesson planning, personalized learning, and student engagement. However, readiness is uneven: leaders reported higher preparedness than teachers, and many respondents cited insufficient professional development, funding constraints, infrastructure gaps, and ethical concerns such as data privacy and algorithmic bias. The paper concludes that effective AI integration in K-12 education requires targeted training, strong leadership support, equitable access to resources, and clear institutional policies governing responsible use.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools and chatbots used for producing text, images, lesson materials, and other educational outputs in K-12 settings; includes systems such as ChatGPT and DALL-E when discussed generally rather than as evaluated products.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed K-12 educators’ perceptions, familiarity, preparedness, and institutional readiness for adopting generative AI in teaching, lesson planning, administrative work, and broader school integration. The paper also discussed potential classroom uses and policy/implementation considerations, but did not evaluate a specific deployed tool in a school coaching system.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed-methods survey of 250 K-12 educators, institutional readiness for AI integration varied substantially: 25% reported pilot programmes in progress or completed, 15% reported being fully invested and successfully deployed, and 20% were in short-term planning. The study also found a significant positive association between AI familiarity and perceived readiness (r = 0.45, p < 0.05), and regression results indicated that AI familiarity and institutional planning stage significantly predicted AI adoption (R² = 0.35).
findings.measure: Institutional planning stage, AI familiarity, perceived readiness, and AI adoption
findings.effect_size: r = 0.45; R² = 0.35; B = 0.40 (AI familiarity), B = 0.30 (institutional planning stage)

findings.finding_summary: Educators reported that generative AI was viewed positively for streamlining administrative and instructional preparation tasks, especially grading, lesson planning, and data analysis. The mean perception of AI’s impact was 4.1/5, with 40% rating it as extremely positive and 35% somewhat positive.
findings.measure: Perceptions of AI’s impact on efficiency and teaching work

findings.finding_summary: Participants described generative AI as useful for personalised learning and differentiated instruction, noting its ability to tailor lessons to student needs and support more advanced learners. However, the study also reported substantial concerns about lack of funding, infrastructure gaps, teacher preparedness, data privacy, algorithmic bias, and plagiarism, indicating that benefits were viewed alongside significant implementation barriers.
findings.measure: Qualitative thematic responses on personalised learning, differentiation, and implementation challenges

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods survey study with descriptive statistics, correlations, and regression, not an experimental evaluation. The evidence is useful for implementation context but remains observational and self-reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Reported effects are modest to moderate in readiness/adoption associations (e.g., r = 0.45), but the paper does not test learning outcomes or a deployed intervention. The main contribution is implementation insight rather than demonstrated student impact.

paper_profiles.title: Leak, Cheat, Repeat: Data Contamination and Evaluation Malpractices in Closed-Source LLMs
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Volume 1: Long Papers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates a methodological problem in large language model (LLM) evaluation: indirect data contamination and evaluation malpractice when researchers assess closed-source models such as OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. The authors argue that because these models may learn from user interactions, benchmark data sent through the ChatGPT web interface can leak back into future model updates, creating unfair advantages and undermining the credibility of evaluation results. In addition to contamination, the paper examines reproducibility and fairness issues in the way proprietary LLMs are commonly tested.

The study is a systematic literature review of 255 papers that evaluated ChatGPT-related models between late November 2022 and early October 2023. The authors screened the literature, identified which studies used the web interface versus the API, and estimated how much benchmark data was exposed in ways that could be used for further training. They also checked whether papers reported prompts, code repositories, model versions, sampling procedures, and comparable baselines.

The review found that 90 papers accessed ChatGPT through the web interface, exposing over 4.7 million benchmark samples from 263 datasets. Many leaks were substantial, with more than half of leaked datasets classified as highly leaked. The paper also reports widespread reproducibility gaps and unfair comparisons, such as evaluating ChatGPT on small samples while comparing open models on full benchmarks. The authors conclude with recommended best practices for evaluating closed-source LLMs, including using API access when possible, reporting model versions and prompts, sampling all systems equally, and explicitly disclosing contamination.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's closed-source chat-based large language model service, accessed via web interface or API; in this paper it refers to GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 as used through ChatGPT.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper systematically reviewed prior research using ChatGPT (GPT-3.5/GPT-4) and classified papers by whether they accessed it via the web interface or API, focusing on indirect data contamination and evaluation practices.

findings.finding_summary: Across 255 reviewed papers, 90 papers (about 42% of the relevant set) accessed ChatGPT through the web interface in ways that could leak data to OpenAI for training. The review reports a total of 4,714,753 leaked samples from 263 unique datasets, with 142 datasets categorized as high leakage (>95%).
findings.measure: Number of leaked papers, leaked datasets, and leaked benchmark samples via web-interface use
findings.sample_size: n=255 papers reviewed; n=90 leaked papers

findings.finding_summary: The review documents widespread reproducibility and fairness problems in ChatGPT evaluations, including incomplete reporting of prompts, missing repositories, unclear model versions, and comparisons on different sample sizes. It specifically notes that 71 pre-prints and 30 published papers lacked comparison to open-source or non-LLM baselines, and that 54 pre-prints and 34 peer-reviewed papers compared results on different samples.
findings.measure: Presence/absence of prompts, code repositories, model version reporting, and fairness of comparative evaluation protocols

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of prior papers, not an empirical study of ChatGPT in a school setting. The evidence is descriptive and audit-oriented rather than experimental, so it does not meet criteria for higher-tier causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports large-scale contamination and evaluation-practice issues, which are important at the field level, but it does not estimate educational effect sizes or school-based outcomes. Impact is therefore substantial for research integrity, but not directly for learning outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: The Data Coach Chronicles: A systematic review of human support for making data-based decision-making a success
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what data coaches do in school-based data-based decision-making (DBDM) initiatives and how those coaches are prepared for their role. The authors frame DBDM as a process in which schools use assessment and other data to inform instructional and school-improvement decisions, and they argue that human support is often essential because teachers and school teams struggle to interpret and act on data effectively.

The study is a systematic review of 20 studies published between 2005 and 2021, drawn from primary and secondary education settings. The included cases involved data coaches or similar support roles in school improvement, professional development, and data-use interventions, mostly in the United States and the Netherlands, with one Canadian case and one New Zealand case. The review synthesizes how data coaches were appointed, what expertise they brought, what tasks they performed, and what professionalization activities supported them.

The main conclusion is that data coaching is highly variable but generally centered on helping school teams analyze, interpret, and act on data. Coaches were often temporary and external, frequently with teaching experience, and their work included data support, analysis, presentation, artifact development, and facilitation of team discussions. Only a minority of studies described explicit professionalization, and the authors conclude that more tailored training, clearer role definitions, and flexible, context-sensitive coaching models are needed to strengthen DBDM in schools.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI / LLM chatbot used for writing assistance and outlining, rather than a specific named AI product with an educational coaching function.
identified_tools.use_case: The authors disclosed using ChatGPT to assist with outlining the structure of the article, and QuillBot to generate alternative phrasings and help refine language during manuscript preparation. The paper did not study AI for instructional coaching or lesson-plan feedback in schools.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of human data coaching, not an empirical evaluation of an AI instructional coaching tool. The only AI mention is a writing-assistance disclosure (ChatGPT/QuillBot), which is not part of the study’s research focus or evidence base.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational or school-based AI intervention outcomes were measured. The paper reports no impact of AI on coaching, feedback, learning, or school implementation.

paper_profiles.title: A Review of AI Tools: Definitions, Functions, and Applications for K-12 Education
paper_profiles.venue: AI, Computer Science and Robotics Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews artificial intelligence tools and platforms relevant to K-12 education, with the goal of giving teachers a practical reference for understanding what AI tools exist, how they are used, and what risks accompany their use. Rather than testing a single intervention, the article synthesizes definitions, functions, and categories of AI in education and then surveys a set of currently popular tools. The review is especially concerned with classroom uses such as instructional support, lesson planning, assessment, tutoring, and predictive analytics.

The paper discusses AI applications including machine learning, intelligent tutoring systems, automated essay scoring, natural language processing, chatbots, adaptive learning systems, and early warning systems. It also classifies tools into instructional, administrative, and analytical categories, and provides examples such as ChatGPT, Chat for Schools, Class Companion, Copilot, Diffit, DreamBox, Eduaide.AI, Khanmigo, MagicSchool, PowerBuddy, and SchoolAI. These tools are framed as supports for teachers, students, parents, and school systems in K-12 settings, including uses for lesson planning, feedback, differentiated instruction, and monitoring student progress.

The main conclusions are that AI can enhance teaching and learning, support personalization, reduce administrative burden, and help identify student needs, but it also raises important concerns about privacy, bias, misinformation, surveillance, and overreliance on automation. The authors emphasize that teachers and administrators should choose tools carefully, align them with curriculum and student needs, and consider ethical safeguards such as data protection, transparency, and human oversight. The article is positioned as a reference and guidance document for educators and future researchers rather than an empirical study of implementation in schools.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / chatbot systems used for drafting, tutoring, summarizing, feedback, and other language-based educational tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a review of AI tools for K-12 education; it discusses generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and other generative AI applications as examples of tools students and teachers can use, but does not evaluate a single generic system empirically.

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Instructional Quality: Leveraging Computer-Assisted Textual Analysis to Generate In-Depth Insights from Educational Artifacts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the emerging use of AI, machine learning, and natural language processing to analyze educational text artifacts for instructional improvement. Using Elmore’s Instructional Core Framework, it organizes the discussion around three instructional components: teachers, students, and content. The paper argues that text-rich educational data such as classroom transcripts, student responses, lesson plans, textbooks, and online resources can provide more detailed and scalable insight than traditional structured data.

A major focus is generative AI for teacher coaching. The paper discusses prior work on automated detection of instructional features such as authentic questions and accountable talk moves, and reviews a case study where ChatGPT was asked to score classroom transcript segments using CLASS and MQI rubrics, identify instructional strengths and misses, and generate actionable suggestions. The paper reports that ChatGPT could produce relevant responses but did not consistently provide novel or deeply insightful feedback, highlighting the need for more task-specific training data and stronger alignment with human coaching practices.

The paper also surveys AI applications for student support and assessment, including automated essay scoring, constructed-response scoring, and intelligent tutoring. In the content domain, it highlights work on evaluating and generating lesson plans and open educational resources, including a large-scale project to assess the quality and curricular alignment of middle-grades mathematics lesson plans using human coding and machine learning. Overall, the paper concludes that AI can help scale feedback, assessment, and curriculum analysis, but it must be combined with human expertise, domain knowledge, and ethical safeguards such as privacy protection, bias mitigation, and responsible deployment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational generative AI system for text generation, analysis, and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Reviewed as a generative AI tool for teacher coaching, including scoring classroom transcript segments against CLASS and MQI rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities, and generating actionable pedagogical suggestions.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT could provide relevant responses for teacher-coaching tasks, but its feedback was not novel or especially insightful. In the three-task evaluation using classroom transcripts, the model performed zero-shot scoring and feedback generation, but the authors conclude that it falls short of a complete coaching solution without further training and fine-tuning.
findings.measure: Validity of ChatGPT outputs against human ratings on CLASS and MQI rubric-based tasks; quality of generated pedagogical suggestions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/small empirical evaluation of a named generative AI tool, not a randomized or large-scale quasi-experimental study. The paper itself describes a zero-shot assessment against human judgments but does not provide a rigorous causal design or full quantitative reporting.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effect is directionally positive for relevance, but the paper explicitly notes that ChatGPT failed to provide novel or insightful coaching feedback. Because no effect sizes are reported and the overall impact appears limited, the evidence is modest and unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can function as an automated teacher coach by generating classroom-observation scores and feedback on instructional practice. The authors focus on a practical question in teacher professional development: whether a general-purpose generative model can complement expert coaching by producing useful, actionable feedback from classroom transcripts.

The study evaluates three zero-shot coaching tasks using ChatGPT via the OpenAI API: (1) predicting rubric scores for classroom observation items from the CLASS and MQI instruments, (2) identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and (3) suggesting ways to elicit more student mathematical reasoning. The data come from the NCTE transcript dataset of anonymized elementary mathematics classroom observations in U.S. schools, and expert math teachers rate the model’s outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

Results show that ChatGPT has clear limitations as a stand-alone teacher coach. Its score predictions correlate poorly with human ratings, and its qualitative feedback is often relevant but frequently uninsightful, unfaithful, or redundant—especially for MQI-based tasks. The authors conclude that generative AI may eventually support instructional coaching, but current models require substantial improvement and should be used with human oversight, privacy safeguards, and coaching expertise in the loop rather than as replacements for expert coaches.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative conversational AI / LLM chatbot used for zero-shot scoring and generating feedback or suggestions from text prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used zero-shot via the OpenAI API (gpt-3.5-turbo powering ChatGPT) to score classroom transcript segments against CLASS and MQI rubrics, identify highlights and missed opportunities, and generate actionable suggestions for eliciting more student mathematical reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: On Task A, ChatGPT showed low correspondence with human ratings when predicting classroom observation scores from transcript segments. The paper reports Spearman correlations that were near zero or small across all CLASS and MQI items (e.g., CLPC DA=0.00, CLBM DA=0.35, EXPL DA=0.02, SMQR DA=0.17; many others were close to 0 or negative), indicating poor scoring performance on the sampled segments (n=100 segments for Task A).
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between model-predicted observation scores and human annotator scores

findings.finding_summary: On Task B, teachers generally did not find ChatGPT’s highlighted examples and missed opportunities to be insightful or relevant, though faithfulness/hallucination was somewhat less problematic than relevance and insightfulness. The paper reports that for CLASS examples, 22% were rated not faithful, 35% not relevant, and 51% not insightful; for MQI examples, the corresponding 'No' rates were 29%, 55%, and 71% (human ratings of model outputs, n=216 CLASS items and n=288 MQI items).
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for generated highlights/missed opportunities
findings.sample_size: n=216 CLASS items; n=288 MQI items

findings.finding_summary: On Task C, ChatGPT produced suggestions that were usually faithful, relevant, and actionable, but they were often redundant rather than novel. The paper reports that 82% of suggestions repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript, while most responses were still judged actionable and aligned with the classroom context (n=36 suggestions).
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, actionability, and novelty for generated suggestions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study with expert human ratings and correlational analysis, not a randomized trial. The methodology is clear and informative, but the evidence is limited to a small sampled set of transcript segments and teacher raters.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are mostly low, near zero, or negative for scoring accuracy, and the qualitative benefits are mixed. The paper does not report a clear medium-or-large positive effect on instructional coaching outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Bridging the Novice-Expert Gap via Models of Decision-Making: A Case Study on Remediating Math Mistakes
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to scale high-quality tutoring responses when many tutoring systems rely on novice tutors who struggle to respond effectively to student math mistakes in real time. The authors ask whether large language models can be guided to better remediate mistakes by explicitly modeling the decision process used by expert teachers.

The intervention introduced is Bridge, a cognitive task analysis-based method that decomposes expert remediation into three steps: inferring the student’s error, selecting a remediation strategy, and identifying the intention behind that strategy. The paper uses this framework to annotate 700 real tutoring conversations and to prompt/evaluate LLMs such as GPT-4 and Llama-2-70B on the task of generating better remediation responses. The work also includes human evaluation by teachers comparing generated responses under different decision-making conditions.

The population/context is 1st–5th grade students in Title I schools, drawn from real tutoring sessions delivered through an online tutoring provider serving a Southern U.S. school district. Experienced math teachers collaborated in developing the framework and annotations. The main conclusion is that embedding expert decision-making substantially improves LLM tutoring responses, especially when decisions are context-sensitive and aligned with expert reasoning, while random or absent decision guidance leads to weaker, more superficial feedback. The paper positions this as a promising step toward human-LLM tutoring systems that better support novice tutors and scalable instructional coaching.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model chat system used for text generation and feedback-style responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated GPT-4 and GPT-3.5-turbo on math mistake remediation, with and without expert-guided decision-making (Bridge).

findings.finding_summary: In human pairwise evaluations of remediation responses, GPT-4 with expert decisions was 76% more preferred than GPT-4 without decisions and 80% more useful. The paper also reports that expert decision-making significantly improved overall response quality for all models under a two-tailed t-test (p < 0.05).
findings.measure: Teacher pairwise ratings of prefer/useful/care/human-soundingness/overall response quality
findings.sample_size: 40 pairs per model, 3 annotators each (exact n of evaluated responses not otherwise reported)

findings.finding_summary: In the self decision-making condition, GPT-4 significantly outperformed its no-decision baseline on prefer and useful, with improvements up to +95%. However, random decision-making performed worse than expert decision-making and could even underperform no decision-making on some outcomes.
findings.measure: Teacher pairwise ratings of response quality under no, expert, self, and random decision-making conditions

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta's open-weight large language model family used here in a chat/instruction-tuned form for response generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated Llama-2-70b-chat / Llama-2-70b-instruct on remediation of student math mistakes, both directly and with Bridge decision inputs.

findings.finding_summary: In human evaluations, expert decision-making improved Llama-2 response quality over the no-decision baseline on prefer and useful, though the paper notes it did not improve care. The authors also report that self decision-making significantly outperformed the no-decision condition on prefer and useful.
findings.measure: Teacher pairwise ratings of response quality
findings.sample_size: 40 pairs per model, 3 annotators each (exact n of evaluated responses not otherwise reported)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study with a human evaluation design, but it is not a randomized classroom intervention and the paper evaluates generated tutoring responses rather than student learning outcomes. The evidence is therefore useful but methodologically limited for causal claims about educational impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported response-quality improvements are substantial in relative terms (e.g., +76% preference for GPT-4 with expert decisions), but the outcomes are proxy measures from teacher ratings rather than direct student achievement. That makes the practical impact promising but still modest/indirect.

paper_profiles.title: Ethical AI for Young Digital Citizens: A Call to Action on Privacy Governance
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how artificial intelligence systems, including generative AI and other AI-driven digital platforms, create privacy, transparency, consent, and accountability risks for young digital citizens. The authors argue that current privacy regulations and AI governance approaches are largely reactive and adult-centric, leaving youth insufficiently protected in contexts where AI systems collect, infer, share, and monetize personal data.

Rather than testing a specific intervention, the paper proposes a stakeholder-centered governance and education framework for ethical AI privacy management. It synthesizes concerns from young people, parents, educators, AI professionals, and policymakers, and recommends privacy-by-design principles, age-appropriate consent practices, transparency statements, internal audits, independent oversight, and stronger regulatory standards. The paper also argues for integrating AI privacy education into school curricula and for training educators so they can guide students in responsible AI use.

The context is youth-facing AI across digital platforms and educational settings, with specific attention to schools in Canada and broader international regulatory examples such as GDPR, PIPEDA, and OPC guidance. The authors emphasize that educational institutions should adopt privacy education, student privacy audits, and multi-stakeholder collaboration, but the paper does not report an empirical school-based implementation study. Its main conclusion is that protecting young users requires coordinated governance, education, and technical safeguards that prioritize transparency, youth agency, and accountability.

Because there are no outcome data, impact on student learning or school implementation cannot be determined from the paper.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI can serve as an automated teacher coach by scoring classroom observation segments and producing actionable instructional feedback. The authors focus on three tasks: predicting rubric-based observation scores, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and suggesting ways to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the National Center for Teacher Effectiveness (NCTE) transcript dataset of elementary mathematics classroom observations. These transcripts come from U.S. fourth- and fifth-grade classrooms across four school districts and are annotated with expert scores using two observation instruments: CLASS and MQI. The authors test zero-shot ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) on these transcripts and ask experienced math teachers, including one instructional coach, to judge the quality of the model’s qualitative feedback.

Results show that ChatGPT performs poorly on score prediction and often produces feedback that is relevant but not novel or insightful. For qualitative feedback, teachers rated a substantial portion of responses as unhelpful or unfaithful, and for suggestion generation the model frequently repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript. The paper concludes that ChatGPT has promise as a scalable complement to human coaching, but current systems need major improvements in truthfulness, novelty, and pedagogical usefulness before they can support real coaching practice.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model system used for zero-shot scoring, identifying highlights/missed opportunities, and generating actionable coaching suggestions from classroom transcripts.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as an automated teacher coach for elementary math classroom transcripts using CLASS and MQI observation rubrics, and for generating feedback on instructional practice.

findings.finding_summary: On Task A (score prediction), ChatGPT showed low correlation with human ratings across CLASS and MQI items. Reported Spearman correlations were small or near zero across prompting methods; for example, CLPC was 0.00/0.04/-0.06 and EXPL was 0.02/0.12/-0.11 for DA/DA+/RA respectively.

The paper reports that 35-50% of CLASS responses and 55-71% of MQI responses were rated not relevant, and 50-71% were rated not insightful depending on instrument; faithfulness problems were present in about 20-30% of responses.

findings.sample_size: CLASS: n=216 examples; MQI: n=288 examples

Teachers rated 82% of suggestions as redundant, meaning they repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript; nonetheless, most suggestions were still considered relevant and actionable.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical, mixed qualitative/quantitative evaluation of ChatGPT rather than a controlled intervention study. It provides useful evidence about model performance in teacher-coaching tasks, but the sample is small and the human evaluation is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear shortcomings and only limited promise, with correlations mostly near zero and high redundancy/non-relevance in feedback. Any positive effect is unclear or modest rather than demonstrated at a meaningful operational level.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Needs Adaptive Governance
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that generative AI develops too quickly and across too many domains for traditional, static governance approaches to remain effective. The authors frame the central problem as a pacing mismatch: laws and regulatory processes are slow, while generative AI capabilities, deployment contexts, and associated risks evolve rapidly. They contend that one-and-done disclosure, registration, and risk-management regimes are prone to regulatory misalignment and may fail to address new harms as they emerge.

To address this, the paper proposes an adaptive AI governance framework inspired by adaptive governance in environmental policy and agile methods in software development. The framework expands the relevant actors beyond government, industry, and academia to include civil society and citizens, and organizes responsibilities into shared activities (share best practices, collaborate, use, monitor, inform, adapt) and actor-specific activities (financing, anticipating, challenging, training, innovating). The paper also gives examples of how adaptive governance could be operationalized, such as permanent government AI committees, structured review cycles, centralized incident repositories, and dedicated AI governance R&D funding.

The paper is conceptual rather than empirical and does not study a school, classroom, or educational intervention. Its conclusions are broad policy recommendations: AI governance should be iterative, monitored, transparent, and revisable over time, while still maintaining oversight and safeguards against regulatory capture, insufficient depth, and uncertainty. The authors also note that adaptive governance should account for both current harms and longer-term risks, and they suggest that AI literacy and education initiatives can support responsible public participation in governance.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)

identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a governance/theoretical discussion of generative AI broadly, using examples such as ChatGPT and Claude to motivate adaptive governance; it does not evaluate a specific instructional coaching or lesson-feedback tool.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/governance paper with no empirical evaluation of an AI tool, no study design, and no outcome data. It proposes an adaptive governance framework rather than testing a tool in schools or coaching systems.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No instructional, educational, or school-implementation impact is measured. The paper discusses potential governance relevance only, so there is no reported effect on learner, teacher, or system outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: How Close is ChatGPT to Human Experts? Comparison Corpus, Evaluation, and Detection
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how close ChatGPT is to human experts in question-answering quality, what linguistic differences distinguish its outputs from human-written answers, and how well automated systems can detect ChatGPT-generated text. The authors frame these questions around the rapid spread of generative AI and the risks of AI-generated content on online platforms, including concerns about accuracy, reliability, and misuse.

The core contribution is the Human ChatGPT Comparison Corpus (HC3), a large bilingual dataset of question-answer pairs collected from existing QA sources and Wikipedia-style materials, with both human answers and ChatGPT answers for the same prompts. The paper then reports human evaluations (Turing-style detection and helpfulness judgments) and linguistic analyses comparing the two sources across domains such as open-domain QA, computer science, medicine, finance, psychology, and law.

The study is not an educational intervention study; it does not involve schools, teachers, or students. Instead, it evaluates content quality and detectability in a general QA setting. The main findings are that ChatGPT is often more organized, longer, and more neutral than humans, but can still fabricate facts in domain-specific contexts. The authors also show that RoBERTa-based detectors generally outperform simpler GLTR-style methods, that sentence-level detection is harder than full-text detection, and that adding question context improves detection robustness.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational LLM chatbot based on the GPT-3.5 series, fine-tuned with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) to generate responses to user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the focal generative model for comparison against human expert answers in the HC3 corpus, and as the source of text to evaluate detectability and linguistic characteristics.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports human evaluation results comparing ChatGPT answers with human answers across multiple QA domains. Expert Turing-test detection rates for ChatGPT-generated answers were 0.90 overall for paired text and 0.81 overall for single-text English, while amateurs reached 0.48 overall on single-text English; helpfulness tests found ChatGPT was judged more helpful than human answers in 0.57 overall of English cases and 0.54 overall of Chinese cases. The paper also reports that ChatGPT can be easier to detect when a human answer pair is shown, and that it is generally more helpful than humans in finance and psychology but less helpful in medicine.
findings.measure: Human evaluation: Turing test detection accuracy and helpfulness preference in domain-specific QA

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-study empirical comparison with human evaluation and linguistic analysis, not a controlled educational intervention study. The methods are systematic but the outcome is not an education outcome and no causal effect on learning is tested.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported results show detectable differences and modest helpfulness preferences, but there is no educational effect size tied to instruction or learning. The paper is mainly about text characteristics and detection performance rather than instructional impact.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Impact of Community Oversight for Managing Mobile Privacy and Security
paper_profiles.venue: USENIX Symposium on Usable Privacy and Security (SOUPS) 2023
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether community-based oversight can help people manage mobile privacy and security together. The authors focus on the problem that users often struggle to understand app permissions and privacy risks on their own, and instead rely on advice from trusted peers. To address this, they propose and evaluate a community oversight model that emphasizes transparency, awareness, trust, individual participation, and community participation.

The intervention is CO-oPS (Community Oversight of Privacy and Security), an Android app that lets members of a self-selected community view one another’s installed apps and granted permissions, send direct feedback, discuss privacy concerns, and receive weekly educational tips. The app also includes controls for hiding selected apps and links to Android settings so users can change permissions. The study used a four-week mixed-method longitudinal field design with 101 participants in 22 self-formed groups in the United States.

Participants ranged from teens to older adults, though most were young adults. Communities were mainly composed of family members, friends, coworkers, and acquaintances. Data sources included pre- and post-surveys, weekly surveys, app usage logs, and follow-up interviews. The authors found increases in transparency, awareness, trust, individual participation, community participation, self-efficacy, and collective efficacy; community belonging did not change significantly. They conclude that community oversight can support real-world privacy and security co-management, but effectiveness depends on trust, relationship closeness, and differences in technical expertise.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)

identified_tools.use_case: Not an AI tool study for instructional coaching or lesson plan feedback; the paper evaluates the CO-oPS mobile app for peer/community oversight of mobile privacy and security decisions.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods field study with surveys, logs, and interviews, but it does not evaluate an AI instructional tool. The empirical design is clear, yet it is outside the requested AI-in-education use case.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful changes in privacy/security behaviors and perceptions, but not educational AI outcomes. Since no instructional coaching or lesson-feedback system is studied, impact for the target domain is not established.

paper_profiles.title: A Blueprint for Auditing Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: Research Handbook of the Law of Artificial Intelligence (book chapter preprint; based on AI and Ethics article)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter addresses the question of how generative AI systems should be audited in order to identify and manage ethical, legal, and technical risks. The authors argue that existing auditing procedures are too narrow for generative AI because these systems are adaptable across many downstream tasks and can display emergent capabilities, making it difficult to rely on a single audit point or a single standard set of checks.

The paper proposes a three-layer auditing blueprint. At the governance level, providers of generative AI systems should undergo audits of organizational procedures, accountability structures, and quality management systems. At the model level, pre-trained systems should be audited for technical characteristics such as performance, information security, and robustness. At the application level, downstream products and services built on generative AI should undergo continuous audits of functionality and impact, with attention to legality, ethical alignment, and real-world effects over time.

The chapter is conceptual rather than empirical and does not study a school or education setting. Its target audience is technology providers, policymakers, and independent auditors. The main conclusion is that effective oversight of generative AI requires coordinated governance, model, and application audits, ideally conducted by independent third parties with appropriate levels of access. The authors also emphasize that auditing can improve transparency and accountability, but it cannot by itself eliminate all harms or resolve all normative disagreements about fairness, privacy, and acceptable use.

identified_tools.use_case: The paper does not evaluate a specific classroom product; it proposes a governance and auditing blueprint for generative AI systems and their downstream applications in general.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/legal policy chapter proposing an auditing blueprint, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool in educational settings. There is no study design, sample, or measured outcome to assess.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention or outcome was tested, so there is no empirical impact to judge. The paper discusses governance mechanisms rather than student or teacher effects.

paper_profiles.title: Foundations of GenIR
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter/paper provides a conceptual and technical foundation for generative AI in information retrieval and information access. It asks how modern generative models, especially large language models, change the design of information access systems and what new paradigms they enable. The paper does not evaluate an educational intervention; instead, it surveys model architecture, scaling, training, prompting, and multimodal capabilities as background for understanding generative information retrieval (GenIR).

The main approach discussed is twofold: information generation, where generative models directly create tailored outputs for user needs, and information synthesis, where models integrate external evidence to produce grounded responses. Within information synthesis, the paper reviews retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), modular retrieval strategies, retrieval planning for composite information needs, and related questions of reliability, hallucination mitigation, and multi-source information use. It also covers generative retrieval and domain-specific modeling as alternatives or complements to traditional retrieval pipelines.

Because the chapter is theoretical, there is no participant population, school setting, or intervention implementation context. Its conclusions are that generative AI can substantially enhance information access, but reliability, hallucination, grounding, controllability, and system design remain central challenges. The paper argues that future progress will depend on better integration of retrieval and generation, stronger methods for external knowledge use, and more transparent and controllable model-based information systems.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI / large language model paradigm that produces human-like text and can also synthesize or integrate external information (e.g., via retrieval-augmented generation).
identified_tools.use_case: This chapter reviews foundational generative AI concepts, including information generation and information synthesis, with examples such as ChatGPT, Bing with retrieval-augmented generation, and multimodal generative systems; it is not an empirical study of a single tool.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical chapter about generative AI foundations and information access, not an empirical evaluation of an instructional-coaching or lesson-feedback tool. No study design, sample, or outcome evidence is reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The chapter is influential as background synthesis on generative AI and retrieval-augmented generation, but it reports no measured educational impact. Because no direct outcomes are evaluated, practical impact for the requested school coaching use case is not established.

paper_profiles.title: Demystifying Instruction Mixing for Fine-tuning Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how to mix different instruction-tuning datasets when fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). The authors ask whether combining general chat instructions, NLP downstream-task instructions, and coding instructions improves overall model behavior, or whether certain mixtures help some capabilities while harming others.

The study fine-tunes LLaMA-2 7B and 13B models on Alpaca (general instructions), CodeAlpaca (coding instructions), and P3 (NLP downstream-task instructions), both separately and in all combinations. The evaluation covers NLP benchmarks, HumanEval code generation, and an alignment-focused chat evaluation using the FLASK framework with GPT-4 scoring. No human participants, students, teachers, or school settings are involved; this is a model-training and benchmark-evaluation paper.

The main findings are that specialized instruction datasets improve performance in their own domains, but mixing all instruction types does not uniformly improve every task. Alpaca contributes the strongest alignment and broad NLP performance, CodeAlpaca improves coding and can also help chat alignment when combined with general instructions, while P3 improves NLP benchmark performance but tends to hurt alignment/chat ability. The paper concludes that instruction mixture should be chosen based on model size and target use case, and that larger models can better exploit diverse instruction sources.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta's open-weight large language model family used for instruction tuning and chat-style generation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper fine-tunes LLaMA-2 7B and 13B models on different mixes of instruction datasets (Alpaca, CodeAlpaca, and P3) and evaluates the resulting models on NLP benchmarks, code generation, and alignment/chat ability.

findings.finding_summary: Across zero-shot NLP and code benchmarks, instruction mixing produced task-dependent gains and tradeoffs. For LLaMA-2-7B, the best NLP average was 58.2 with P3 alone, while the best code pass@1 was 25.0 with AC; for LLaMA-2-13B, the best code pass@1 was 32.9 with ACP and the best NLP average was 61.9 with CP.
findings.measure: Zero-shot benchmark averages on ARC, Winogrande, PIQA, MMLU, RACE, HellaSwag; HumanEval pass@1 and pass@10
findings.sample_size: n=2 model sizes; benchmark sizes not reported in aggregate

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language models used here as the evaluator in the FLASK alignment framework.
identified_tools.use_case: GPT-4-0613 was used to score alignment skills of fine-tuned LLaMA models on 1,180 instruction samples.

findings.finding_summary: Using GPT-4-0613 as the evaluator, the paper reports alignment-skill scores for models fine-tuned with different instruction mixes. Alpaca performed best overall, while adding P3 lowered alignment scores by 2.8 points for 7B and 3.6 points for 13B; combining CodeAlpaca with general instructions improved alignment by +0.6 (7B) and +1.6 (13B).
findings.measure: FLASK alignment skill assessment (logical correctness, factuality, commonsense understanding, comprehension, completeness, insightfulness, readability, conciseness)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmark study, but it is not a school-based education intervention and does not test instructional coaching use in authentic classrooms. The evidence is experimental but limited to model fine-tuning/evaluation rather than educational deployment.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no direct educational impact, only model benchmark changes and alignment-skill scores. It does not evaluate classroom learning, coaching outcomes, or school implementation effects.

paper_profiles.title: Transforming Software Development with Generative AI: Empirical Insights on Collaboration and Workflow
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot are changing everyday work practices and collaboration in software development. The authors focus on how GenAI affects productivity, learning, communication, and team dynamics, arguing that while these tools can accelerate routine work and support individual problem-solving, they may also reduce human-to-human knowledge sharing.

The study is an exploratory multi-case qualitative interview study conducted across companies that had introduced GenAI into product development. The authors interviewed 13 adult professionals, including data scientists, managers, developers, designers, and frontend developers, about how they use GenAI and how it affects their workday. Reported uses included getting unstuck, learning new topics, creating virtual environments, copywriting, boilerplate generation, and working with existing code.

The paper concludes that GenAI increases perceived efficiency, motivation, and enjoyment, but can also disrupt established teamwork and learning loops by shifting interactions away from colleagues toward the AI tool. It also identifies practical concerns around confidentiality, anonymization, tool integration, prompt engineering skill, and the need to carefully contextualize outputs for local team practices. Overall, the paper frames GenAI as a useful but double-edged addition to software teams rather than a fully reliable replacement for peer collaboration.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on GPT-family large language models, used for conversational assistance, text and code generation, and interactive prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by software professionals for assistance when stuck, learning, copywriting, boilerplating code/text, working with existing code, and prompt-engineered interactions; also used in simulated/virtual environment creation.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative interview study with 13 software professionals, participants reported that ChatGPT helped them get unstuck, work more efficiently, and reduce time spent on repetitive or menial tasks. It was described as faster than asking colleagues or searching Google, but the paper reports perceptions rather than quantified effects.
findings.measure: Interview-reported productivity, speed, and ease of use

findings.finding_summary: Participants reported that ChatGPT supported interactive learning, acted like a 'personal tutor,' and helped them learn new topics faster. The paper also notes that prompt engineering and role-based prompting improved precision and quality of responses.
findings.measure: Interview-reported learning and skill development

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that using ChatGPT reduced some human-to-human interaction and pair programming, disrupting the team's learning loop and knowledge sharing. It also notes concerns about data confidentiality, anonymization of input, cultural bias in outputs, and the need to align prompts with agile context, but these are reported as perceived challenges rather than measured outcomes.
findings.measure: Interview-reported collaboration, knowledge sharing, and workflow disruption

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative multi-case interview study with 13 participants, so it provides useful practice-based evidence but not experimental causal estimates. The paper reports perceptions and themes rather than measured intervention effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported benefits are meaningful but unquantified, and the paper does not provide effect sizes. Because the evidence is qualitative and centered on workflow perceptions rather than measured impact, the overall impact tier is unclear/modest.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Privacy Questions From Stack Overflow: Can ChatGPT Compete?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether ChatGPT can serve as a viable alternative to Stack Overflow for answering privacy-related technical questions. The authors focus on privacy concerns raised by software developers, especially those involving choice/consent, aggregation, identification, disclosure, and onward transfer, and ask whether generative AI can produce answers comparable to community-vetted responses.

To study this, the authors extracted 932 Stack Overflow questions posted between 2016 and 2023, randomly sampled 270 question-answer pairs, and manually annotated them using two privacy taxonomies and a natural-language-inference-inspired labeling process. After several annotation and discussion rounds, they created a dataset of 92 privacy-related QAs. They then generated ChatGPT answers to the same questions using the original question text as prompts and compared ChatGPT responses with accepted or highest-voted Stack Overflow answers using expert annotators.

The paper finds that ChatGPT responses matched Stack Overflow answers in 56.1% of cases, and that Stack Overflow was slightly more accurate when the answers did not match. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can sometimes provide acceptable privacy guidance, but both ChatGPT and Stack Overflow should be used cautiously for privacy-sensitive questions because accuracy is not consistently high enough for full reliance.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on GPT-family large language models, capable of producing conversational responses and assisting with text/code generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate answers to Stack Overflow privacy-related questions using the original question text as the prompt, then compared against accepted or highest-upvoted Stack Overflow answers.

findings.finding_summary: Across 82 Stack Overflow privacy-related QAs with available answers, ChatGPT responses were judged to agree with Stack Overflow answers in 46/82 cases (56.1%) when at least two of three annotators agreed. For the non-agreed cases, ChatGPT was considered more accurate for 12/36 (33.3%) and less accurate than Stack Overflow for 15/36 (41.7%), with 9/36 inconclusive.
findings.measure: Annotator judgment of agreement and relative accuracy between ChatGPT-generated answers and Stack Overflow answers

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-method comparative study with manual annotation and expert judgment, not an experiment with controlled outcome testing. The evidence is useful but has moderate methodological limitations, including small sample size and subjective agreement coding.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effect is modest and mixed: ChatGPT matched or was judged acceptable in just over half of cases, but Stack Overflow remained slightly more accurate overall. No standardized effect size is reported, so impact is best treated as unclear-to-modest.

paper_profiles.title: Making AI-Enhanced Videos: Analyzing Generative AI Use Cases in YouTube Content Creation
paper_profiles.venue: Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI EA '25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI tools are being used in real-world YouTube content creation workflows. The authors ask what specific tasks GenAI supports across the video production pipeline and how creators incorporate these tools in practice. Rather than evaluating learning outcomes, the paper maps practical use cases and discusses implications for future GenAI tool design.

The study analyzes 274 YouTube how-to videos posted between September 2023 and February 2024. Using YouTube Data API retrieval, manual screening, and thematic analysis of 2,829 segmented clips, the authors identified GenAI use cases across four phases of video creation: planning, production, editing, and uploading. Examples include identifying topics, generating scripts, creating prompts, producing visuals and voiceovers, lip-syncing avatars, upscaling visuals, translating speech, and generating subtitles and titles.

The context is an online creator community rather than a school setting. The paper shows that creators use GenAI to streamline labor-intensive creative tasks and that prompting skill is emerging as an important form of expertise. The authors also note concerns about originality, authenticity, and transparency of AI-generated content, including questions about labeling and platform visibility rules. Overall, the paper provides a conceptual framework for GenAI in video creation and suggests future research directions for supporting creators with more integrated and responsible tools.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods content analysis of YouTube how-to videos, not an intervention study or controlled evaluation. The paper provides descriptive evidence about tool use but no causal impact estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper documents broad creator use cases across many tools, but it does not measure learning, coaching outcomes, or other educational impact. Reported effects are descriptive only, so the impact on schooling or instruction is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: AI to the rescue: Exploring the potential of ChatGPT as a teacher ally for workload relief and burnout prevention
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can help reduce teacher workload and mitigate burnout by assisting with time-consuming non-teaching tasks. The authors frame the problem around lesson planning and content development, which they identify as major contributors to teacher stress and overload, especially in secondary schooling.

The intervention studied is not a live classroom deployment but an explanatory, prompt-based evaluation of ChatGPT’s ability to generate and refine lesson plans and teaching materials. The researchers tested ChatGPT with tailored prompts for English, science, and math across secondary grade bands (ages 12–15 and 16–18), then judged the outputs using the 5Es instructional model. They also asked follow-up prompts to improve plans, add differentiation, and generate formative assessment or real-life problem examples.

The study context is secondary education in the United Arab Emirates, where the authors connect the work to broader national efforts to integrate AI into education. The main conclusion is that ChatGPT can produce useful planning support when prompts are specific and iterative, but its first outputs are often insufficient and require substantial human refinement. The authors emphasize human oversight, careful prompt design, and ethical use, and they recommend training teachers to use AI as a supportive assistant rather than a replacement for professional judgment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s generative AI chatbot based on GPT models that produces human-like text responses and can assist with a range of language-based tasks, including lesson planning and feedback generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a teacher assistant to generate and revise lesson plans and teaching materials for English, science, and math at secondary-school level (ages 12-18), with prompts aligned to the 5Es instructional model and curriculum needs.

findings.finding_summary: In this exploratory study, ChatGPT produced lesson plans for Grade 8 math, Grade 10 science (chemistry), and Grade 7 English that were judged to have useful strengths but also notable shortcomings on the first attempt. The authors report that quality improved after iterative prompting and human review, but no quantitative effect sizes or sample sizes for learners were reported because the study assessed generated lesson plans rather than student outcomes.
findings.measure: Author evaluation of ChatGPT-generated lesson plans using the 5Es instructional model

findings.finding_summary: The paper concludes that ChatGPT can help reduce teacher workload by streamlining lesson planning and content development, thereby freeing time for other teaching responsibilities. This is presented as a potential operational benefit rather than a measured classroom effect, and no numerical effect estimate is reported.
findings.measure: Perceived workload relief / time saved in lesson planning and material development

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory, non-randomized study that evaluates AI-generated lesson plans with qualitative author judgment rather than direct student outcomes. It provides useful applied evidence but lacks controlled methodology and quantitative estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical workload-reduction potential, but the impact is not quantified and is based on lesson-plan quality rather than demonstrated learner gains or measured time savings. The evidence therefore indicates possible benefit, but the magnitude is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT-like systems, for education. Rather than reporting a single empirical intervention, it surveys the emerging literature and argues that LLMs may support both learning and teaching by generating educational content, providing explanations, offering personalized feedback, assisting with lesson planning, and supporting assessment and professional development.

The paper is framed around both learner and teacher perspectives across primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional development contexts. It discusses possible uses such as quiz generation, curiosity prompting, code explanations, language-learning support, adaptive feedback, and semi-automated grading. It also emphasizes that these applications should be embedded in educational systems with human oversight, curriculum alignment, critical thinking, and fact-checking practices.

The main contribution is a set of challenges and mitigation strategies rather than experimental findings. The authors highlight risks including bias, plagiarism, privacy and security issues, overreliance by students and teachers, difficulty distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated text, lack of expertise, and inequitable access. They conclude that LLMs can be beneficial in education only if used responsibly, with governance, transparency, privacy protections, and ongoing human monitoring.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Large language model–based generative AI systems that can produce and transform text, answer questions, generate feedback, and support personalized or instructional outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Position paper discussing opportunities, risks, and mitigation strategies for using large language models in education, including lesson planning, personalized feedback, assessment, and professional development; not an empirical evaluation of a specific deployed system.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper with no empirical study, no evaluated intervention, and no outcome data. It offers conceptual discussion and recommendations rather than a testable research design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes, sample sizes, or measured impacts are reported. The paper does not present evidence of educational impact from a deployed tool.

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service elementary teachers think about and plan to use ChatGPT in science education, addressing a gap in empirical work on the practical classroom use of generative AI. The authors ask how broadly ChatGPT can be integrated into science lesson plans, how well pre-service teachers can design such integration, and what benefits and concerns they associate with it.

The study involved 29 pre-service elementary science teachers at a Korean teachers' university. Participants completed a four-session instructional sequence about ChatGPT and science pedagogy, then designed a 45-minute elementary science lesson plan that had to incorporate ChatGPT and include a simulated chat. The researchers evaluated the lesson plans with a modified TPACK-based rubric and analyzed open-ended survey responses, triangulating these with the attached chat examples.

Findings suggest that participants saw ChatGPT as useful across multiple science domains and teaching methods, especially cooperative learning, POE, learning cycles, analogy generation, and concept mapping. Their plans scored relatively high overall, but they were stronger at aligning ChatGPT with curriculum goals and instructional strategies than at choosing the most appropriate ChatGPT functions. Participants expected ChatGPT to support questioning, individualized learning, and formative feedback, but they also worried about inaccuracy, hallucinations, and student over-dependence. Proposed safeguards included using multiple information sources, teacher checking, and structured classroom interactions. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has promise for science learning, but better professional development and more real classroom research are needed before broad implementation.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM for conversational text generation, question answering, and other language-based assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Pre-service elementary science teachers were asked to integrate ChatGPT into 45-minute science lesson plans and simulate teacher/student interactions, using it for instructional support, role-play structuring, adaptive questioning, formative feedback, and lesson planning.

findings.finding_summary: Across 29 pre-service teachers' lesson plans, the average TIAR-derived integration score for ChatGPT was M=3.29 (SD=.91) on a 4-point scale, suggesting moderately strong planned integration. Scores were highest for instructional strategies & ChatGPT (M=3.48, SD=.99) and curriculum goals & ChatGPT (M=3.44, SD=.87), but lower for ChatGPT function selection(s) (M=3.00, SD=.93).
findings.measure: Modified TPACK-based lesson plan rubric (TIAR-derived scores)

findings.finding_summary: The study identified both appropriate and inappropriate proposed uses of ChatGPT in lesson plans. Appropriate uses included supplementary information, role-play support, adaptive instruction, and feedback/reflection; inappropriate uses included asking ChatGPT for visual information, relying on nonexistent YouTube links or summaries, and using it to design experiments in ways that could undermine practical inquiry skills.
findings.measure: Qualitative analysis of lesson plan use cases and simulated chat data

findings.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers reported that ChatGPT could provide instant answers, support continuous questioning, summarize lengthy student-generated scenarios for a 45-minute lesson, and offer individualized learning support that one teacher could not provide alone. These anticipated affordances were discussed as helping manage classroom instruction and feedback more efficiently.
findings.measure: Open-ended survey responses on perceived usefulness

findings.finding_summary: Participants expressed concerns about accuracy, reliability, and security, including that ChatGPT may produce incorrect information, outdated science content, or misconceptions. They also worried that students could become overly dependent on ChatGPT, and proposed mitigation strategies such as using teachers, peers, textbooks, diverse sources, critical thinking, and structured classroom interactions.
findings.measure: Open-ended survey responses on concerns and remedies

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods pre-service teacher study using lesson-plan analysis and open-ended responses, not an experimental evaluation of student outcomes. The evidence is useful for understanding perceived integration quality and concerns, but it does not establish causal impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no effect sizes on learning outcomes, only descriptive integration scores and perceptions. Impact on achievement or implementation quality is therefore suggestive but unclear rather than demonstrated.}

paper_profiles.title: Exploring High School EFL Teachers' Experiences with Magic School AI in Lesson Planning: Benefits and Insights
paper_profiles.venue: Voices of English Language Education Society
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how high school English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers perceive and use MagicSchool AI, a generative AI tool, for lesson planning. The central question is whether and how such a tool can support lesson preparation while still preserving pedagogical quality, contextual fit, and teacher judgment.

The study was conducted as an exploratory case study with 38 Indonesian high school EFL teachers in Central Java. Data came from a post-workshop online open-ended questionnaire, focus group interviews, and stimulated recall interviews after teachers had been introduced to AI-assisted lesson planning. The intervention was not a schoolwide coaching system but a workshop-based introduction and subsequent reflection on use of the tool for planning materials, assessments, differentiated texts, and classroom activities.

Findings show that teachers valued MagicSchool AI mainly for speeding up material and assessment preparation, generating diverse instructional ideas, and supporting differentiation for varied learner needs. At the same time, teachers reported that AI outputs often needed substantial refinement, careful prompting, and ongoing human oversight to align with classroom dynamics, vocabulary level, and curriculum goals.
