The authors conclude that generative AI can be a useful collaborator in lesson planning, but only when paired with teacher expertise, critical evaluation, and professional development in prompt engineering and adaptation.

identified_tools.name: MagicSchool AI
identified_tools.description: A generative AI education tool designed to help teachers create lesson plans, instructional materials, assessments, and other classroom resources through structured prompts and pre-built fields.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a lesson-planning assistant for 38 Indonesian high school EFL teachers after a workshop; teachers used it to generate instructional materials, assessments, differentiated texts, and activity ideas.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that MagicSchool AI reduced the time needed for lesson-material and assessment preparation, especially when using its structured prompts and pre-designed fields. However, some gains were offset by the need for follow-up prompting and refinement, and rural internet connectivity problems reduced practicality for some users.
findings.measure: Teachers’ open-ended questionnaire responses and focus group interviews about time efficiency in material preparation and assessment design

findings.finding_summary: Teachers said the tool supported differentiation by helping them level reading texts, vary complexity, and generate activities aligned with different student needs and learning styles. Respondents emphasized that the outputs were useful starting points but still required human review and adaptation to align with classroom context and curriculum goals.
findings.measure: Teachers’ qualitative reports of differentiation support and adaptability of AI-generated lesson materials

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative exploratory case study based on open-ended questionnaires and focus group interviews, not an experimental or quasi-experimental impact evaluation. The evidence is useful for implementation insights but does not provide causal estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceived benefits such as faster planning and easier differentiation, but no effect sizes, standardized outcomes, or student achievement data are reported. The magnitude of impact is therefore unclear and based on teacher self-report.

paper_profiles.title: Editorial: Generative AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial introduces a Frontiers Research Topic on generative AI in education and synthesizes the themes addressed across 11 papers in the volume. The piece focuses on how generative AI may reshape educational practice through personalized content generation, AI tutors, automated feedback, assessment support, and learner modeling, while also highlighting risks and governance concerns such as privacy, ethics, transparency, bias, and accuracy.

Rather than reporting a single empirical study, the editorial summarizes the contributions of multiple articles spanning perspectives, original research, opinion pieces, and a mini-review. The included papers cover uses such as LLM-based feedback generation, adolescent schoolwork use of AI chatbots, support for critical thinking, pre-service teacher mathematical proof generation, whole-learner support, personalized assessment, AI mentors for STEM career exploration, responsible integration, interactive listening task generation, and deception detection with educational robots.

Because this is an editorial, it does not focus on one participant population or school implementation setting. The paper’s main conclusion is that generative AI has significant promise for education, but its effective and ethical adoption will require continued research and careful attention to human oversight, interpretability, responsible use, and alignment with educational goals and standards.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbot systems used for educational content generation, tutoring, feedback, and personalization.
identified_tools.use_case: This editorial surveys a research topic on generative AI in education and summarizes multiple included papers rather than evaluating one named product. It discusses generative AI chatbots and LLMs for feedback, tutoring, assessment, mentoring, and related educational uses.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an editorial/opinion piece summarizing a research topic, not a primary empirical evaluation or systematic review with an explicit search and synthesis method. It does not report original tool-level outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes, controlled comparisons, or outcome data are reported for a specific AI tool in this paper. The article is descriptive and conceptual rather than evidentiary.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of ChatGPT and asks what it means for learning, teaching, and assessment in higher education. The authors are especially concerned with the rapid public attention around generative AI and the possibility that tools like ChatGPT could disrupt traditional written assessments, enable plagiarism, or otherwise change how educators evaluate student work.

The paper does not report a formal empirical study of a school intervention. Instead, it combines a literature review, background discussion of OpenAI and GPT-3/ChatGPT, and the authors’ own exploratory testing of the chatbot with sample prompts. It situates ChatGPT within the broader Artificial Intelligence in Education literature, using Baker and Smith’s student-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing framework to discuss possible educational uses.

The context is higher education, with references to university-level learning, teaching, assessment, and writing support. The paper discusses implications for students, teachers, and institutions, including opportunities for AI-assisted feedback and assessment redesign, as well as threats related to academic integrity and the difficulty of reliably detecting AI-generated text. Its main conclusion is that ChatGPT is likely to become part of educational practice, but institutions must adapt assessment and policy rather than assume the technology can simply be banned.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot built on GPT-family large language models, designed to generate and revise text through natural-language prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reviews ChatGPT's functionality and uses it sparingly for brainstorming and experimentation, while discussing its implications for higher education assessment, teaching, and learning.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a review/opinion-style paper with desktop analysis and informal experimentation, not a controlled empirical evaluation of ChatGPT in a school implementation setting. It provides no causal evidence on instructional coaching or lesson plan feedback outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues ChatGPT may affect assessment, writing, and teaching practices, but it reports no measured effect sizes or outcome data. Any impact is speculative and based on discussion rather than demonstrated school-based implementation results.

paper_profiles.title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines university students’ perceptions of generative AI (GenAI), especially tools such as ChatGPT, in higher education. The authors focus on how familiar students are with GenAI, what benefits they expect from it, what concerns they have, and how it might be integrated responsibly into teaching and learning. The study is framed around the idea that student perceptions shape uptake and learning outcomes, and it responds to the rapid rise of GenAI in higher education.

The study used an online survey with both closed-ended and open-ended questions, administered to 399 undergraduate and postgraduate students from six universities in Hong Kong. Quantitative analysis assessed students’ knowledge of GenAI, willingness to use it, and concerns about it, while thematic analysis of open responses explored perceived benefits and risks in more depth. The context was general higher education use, not a specific classroom intervention or coaching system.

Findings suggest that students generally view GenAI positively and see value in personalized learning support, writing and brainstorming help, research assistance, multimedia creation, and administrative efficiency. At the same time, they express substantial concerns about accuracy, transparency, privacy, plagiarism, over-reliance, effects on creativity and critical thinking, career displacement, and unclear institutional policies. The paper concludes that GenAI can support higher education, but effective implementation requires AI literacy, ethical guidance, privacy protections, transparency, and institutional safeguards.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI conversational large language model chatbot that generates human-like text responses to prompts and can assist with writing, feedback, brainstorming, and question answering.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses ChatGPT as an example of generative AI in higher education and reports students’ perceptions of using it for personalized learning support, writing and brainstorming, research support, and administrative tasks. It is not evaluated as a formal intervention in a school coaching system.

findings.finding_summary: Students reported a generally positive attitude toward using ChatGPT-like generative AI in higher education. In the survey of 399 undergraduate and postgraduate students in Hong Kong, perceived benefits included personalized and immediate learning support, writing feedback, research assistance, and 24/7 anonymous support; concerns remained about accuracy, privacy, ethics, over-reliance, and uncertain policies.
findings.measure: Survey responses on willingness to use generative AI, perceived benefits, and concerns

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey with open-ended responses, so it provides useful descriptive evidence but not causal impact evidence. The paper studies perceptions and policy implications rather than testing an intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceived usefulness but no measured learning effect sizes or outcome gains. Its impact is therefore suggestive and indirect rather than demonstrated through effect estimates.

paper_profiles.title: What if the devil is my guardian angel: ChatGPT as a case study of using chatbots in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines concerns about using ChatGPT in education, with a focus on early adopters, and asks what issues should be considered to ensure safe and responsible adoption of advanced chatbots in educational settings. The authors frame ChatGPT as a representative generative AI chatbot and investigate it through a qualitative instrumental case study.

The study uses three complementary stages: social network analysis and sentiment analysis of Twitter posts about ChatGPT in education, content analysis of 19 publicly recruited interviewees (including educators, students, developers, and AI freelancers), and hands-on user experience testing by three experienced educators over one week across 10 educational scenarios. The educational scenarios explored cheating, content accuracy, fairness, assessment design, learning assistance, emotional response, honesty/truthfulness, privacy, and manipulation.

Findings suggest that although public sentiment and stakeholder perceptions are generally optimistic, major concerns remain around cheating, misleading or inaccurate outputs, inconsistent responses across users, lack of emotion or reflection, privacy risks, and manipulative or untruthful behavior. The paper argues that ChatGPT can potentially support teaching and learning, but only if used cautiously with stronger guidelines, responsible design, human oversight, and new teaching philosophies that emphasize critical thinking and other non-text-based assessment approaches.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational generative AI chatbot based on GPT-3, designed to interact in natural language and generate human-like text.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a representative advanced chatbot in education across early adopters; educators tested it for instructional design, lesson/content generation, quiz creation, feedback-like assistance, and general teaching/learning scenarios.

findings.finding_summary: In qualitative interviews and user experience testing, participants generally found ChatGPT useful for instructional design, lesson/material creation, and immediate feedback-like support, and said it could reduce teacher workload. However, its utility was limited by occasional errors, generic answers, inconsistent outputs across users, and missing context-specific information.
findings.measure: Perceived usefulness, instructional workload, and quality of generated educational outputs from interviews and scenario-based user testing
findings.sample_size: n=19 interviewees; 3 educators in user-experience testing

findings.finding_summary: The study identified several concerns in educational use: cheating/plagiarism, reduced critical thinking, dishonesty, privacy misleading, manipulation, and inaccurate or vague information. In the user-experience scenarios, ChatGPT sometimes produced wrong or overly generic content, different answers to the same prompt, and misleading claims about privacy and citation handling.
findings.measure: Observed concerns in tweets, interviews, and 10 educator-led usage scenarios

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, instrumental case study with sentiment analysis, interviews, and scenario testing rather than a controlled experiment. It provides useful evidence about risks and perceived usefulness, but no causal estimates or experimental effect sizes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful practical implications for school adoption, but it does not quantify learning gains or implementation effects. The overall impact is important yet unclear because findings are descriptive and mixed rather than effect-size based.

paper_profiles.title: Large language models encode clinical knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models (LLMs) can encode and apply clinical knowledge well enough to support medical question answering, and how such systems should be evaluated for safety, factuality, bias, and usefulness. The authors argue that existing benchmark-style evaluations are too narrow for safety-critical medical use, especially for open-ended consumer health questions and real-world clinical workflows.

To address this, they introduce MultiMedQA, a benchmark combining six existing medical question-answering datasets with a new consumer-health dataset, HealthSearchQA. They also propose a human evaluation framework in which clinicians and lay users rate long-form answers along multiple axes, including scientific consensus, correctness, omission of important content, possible harm, and bias. They evaluate PaLM, Flan-PaLM, and an instruction prompt-tuned version called Med-PaLM on these tasks.

The evaluated populations are adult users only: consumer medical questions from real-world adult search behavior, plus clinician and lay rater assessments. The study is not a school-based educational intervention; rather, it is a domain benchmark and model-evaluation paper in a medical context. The main conclusion is that scaling and instruction tuning improve performance substantially, and Med-PaLM narrows the gap with clinicians on several safety and quality dimensions, but the models remain below clinician level and require stronger grounding, uncertainty handling, bias mitigation, and safeguards before real-world deployment.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google PaLM/Flan-PaLM/Med-PaLM family of large language models for medical question answering and instruction tuning.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated PaLM and Flan-PaLM on MultiMedQA and developed Med-PaLM via instruction prompt tuning to improve long-form medical question answering and alignment.

findings.finding_summary: On MedQA (USMLE-style questions), Flan-PaLM 540B achieved 67.6% accuracy, exceeding the previous state of the art by more than 17%. The paper also reports 57.6% on MedMCQA and 79.0% on PubMedQA.
findings.measure: multiple-choice accuracy on medical QA benchmarks
findings.effect_size: more than 17% above prior SOTA on MedQA

findings.finding_summary: In human evaluation of long-form consumer medical questions, clinicians judged 92.6% of Med-PaLM answers to be aligned with scientific consensus versus 61.9% for Flan-PaLM and 92.9% for clinician answers. Med-PaLM also reduced the share of answers rated as potentially leading to harm from 29.7% to 5.9%.
findings.measure: clinician ratings of scientific consensus alignment and potential harm on long-form answers
findings.effect_size: 29.7% to 5.9% for potential harm; 61.9% to 92.6% for scientific consensus alignment
findings.sample_size: n=140 questions total in human evaluation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study with substantial human evaluation, but it is not a school-based education study and does not use a randomized or educational implementation design. The evidence is therefore indirect for the requested school coaching context.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are large within the medical QA setting, but the paper does not evaluate instructional coaching, lesson-plan feedback, or school implementation. Because the target educational use case is absent, impact for this topic is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can function as an automated teacher coach by scoring classroom instruction and generating feedback that is useful for instructional improvement. The authors focus on three coaching tasks: predicting rubric scores from classroom transcripts, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and offering actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the NCTE Transcript dataset of U.S. elementary mathematics classroom observations. The dataset includes anonymized transcripts from 4th- and 5th-grade classrooms collected across four school districts and already scored by expert raters using two established classroom observation instruments: CLASS and MQI. The authors evaluate ChatGPT in a zero-shot setting, using transcript segments and prompts derived from the observation rubrics. They compare model-generated numerical scores with human scores and also recruit experienced math teachers, including one with instructional coaching experience, to rate the model’s qualitative feedback for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

Overall, ChatGPT performs poorly at matching human rubric scores and often produces feedback that is repetitive, not especially insightful, or only weakly aligned with the instructional evidence in the transcript. For suggestion generation, the model is frequently redundant, often restating what the teacher already does. The paper concludes that current generative AI can complement, but not replace, expert coaching, and it highlights the need for better guardrails, human oversight, and future model tuning with educator input before such systems can be reliable for school coaching use.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / GPT-based large language model system used for zero-shot natural-language generation and evaluation tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used zero-shot to (A) predict classroom observation scores from transcript segments, (B) identify highlights and missed opportunities in teacher instruction, and (C) generate actionable suggestions for eliciting more student mathematical reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: On score prediction (Task A), ChatGPT showed low Spearman correlation with human ratings across CLASS and MQI items, even when prompts included rubric descriptions or reasoning. Reported correlations were near zero or negative for most dimensions; for example, CLPC DA=0.00, CLBM DA=0.35, CLINSTD DA=-0.01, and MQI correlations ranged from -0.11 to 0.17.
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between model-predicted observation scores and human ratings on CLASS and MQI transcript segments
findings.effect_size: correlations reported: CLPC 0.00; CLBM 0.35; CLINSTD -0.01; EXPL 0.02; REMED 0.05; LANGIMP 0.00; SMQR 0.17 (DA); other prompt variants also near zero

findings.finding_summary: For highlights/missed-opportunities generation (Task B), teachers generally rated the model outputs as not insightful or not relevant, with hallucination present in a nontrivial share of responses. The paper reports around 20-30% of responses as unfaithful, and CLASS/MQI 'No' proportions were high for relevance and insightfulness (e.g., CLASS no-relevant 35%, no-insightful 51%; MQI no-relevant 55%, no-insightful 71%).
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for model-generated highlights and missed opportunities

findings.finding_summary: For actionable suggestions to elicit more student reasoning (Task C), most model outputs were rated faithful, relevant, and actionable, but novelty was poor: the model repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript 82% of the time. The paper characterizes the suggestions as often redundant despite being mostly implementable.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of faithfulness, relevance, actionability, and novelty for generated teaching suggestions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical study with human ratings of model outputs, but it is not an RCT or causal field study. The evidence is qualitative/mixed-methods with correlational analysis, so it fits a yellow tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports mostly small or unclear quantitative effects, with correlations near zero for many outcomes and qualitative judgments of limited insightfulness. While some suggestions were actionable, the overall measured impact is modest and inconsistent.

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-service elementary teachers imagine and design the use of ChatGPT in science lesson planning, with a focus on the pedagogical range, appropriateness, and perceived value of the tool. The authors respond to a gap in empirical research on how generative AI is being integrated into actual educational planning, especially in science education, and ask how ChatGPT can be incorporated into lesson plans, how well teachers can align it with curriculum and pedagogy, and what concerns they have about its use.

The study involved 29 pre-service elementary science teachers in Korea who were enrolled in a science education course. After a four-session instructional sequence introducing ChatGPT, its potential uses, science teaching methods, and lesson-planning procedures, participants drafted lesson plans for a 45-minute elementary science class. They also attached simulated ChatGPT conversations and completed open-ended survey questions about their choices and concerns. The lesson plans were evaluated with a modified TPACK-based rubric, and the survey responses were analyzed qualitatively.

Findings suggest that participants envisioned ChatGPT across multiple science topics and teaching approaches, especially cooperative learning, POE, learning cycles, analogy generation, concept mapping, and experimentation. Overall, they scored moderately high on the rubric, showing stronger alignment with curriculum goals and instructional strategies than with selecting appropriate ChatGPT functions. Participants saw ChatGPT as useful for questioning, individualized support, and formative feedback, but expressed concern about inaccurate information, bias, and student overdependence. They proposed safeguards such as using multiple information sources, teacher mediation, structured peer interaction, and reflection to reduce misuse. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has promise for science lesson planning, but more research is needed in real classroom settings and on how to support teachers in selecting and supervising AI use effectively.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot based on GPT models, capable of generating text, answering questions, and supporting multi-turn dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: Pre-service elementary science teachers were asked to integrate ChatGPT into lesson plans, attach simulated conversations, and describe how it would support science learning, instructional strategies, feedback, and individualized support.

findings.finding_summary: In 29 pre-service teachers' lesson plans, ChatGPT-integrated plans received an average TIAR score of M=3.29 (SD=.91) on a 4-point scale, indicating reasonably strong integration quality. Scores were highest for instructional strategies & ChatGPT (M=3.48, SD=.99) and curriculum goals & ChatGPT (M=3.44, SD=.87), with lower performance on ChatGPT function selection(s) (M=3.00, SD=.93).
findings.measure: Modified TPACK-based Technology Integration Assessment Rubric (TIAR) scores for lesson plans

findings.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers anticipated ChatGPT would support high-quality questioning, self-directed and individualized learning, and formative assessment. They also identified concerns about inaccurate or misleading outputs, hallucinated or non-existent resources, and students becoming overly dependent on ChatGPT; proposed safeguards included using multiple sources, teacher oversight, structured group discussion, and post-ChatGPT reflection.
findings.measure: Open-ended survey responses about perceived usefulness and concerns

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods study of lesson plans and survey responses rather than an experimental evaluation of student outcomes. The design is useful for understanding implementation thinking, but it does not establish causal effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports relatively strong lesson-plan integration scores, but no learning gains or behavioral effect sizes are provided. Reported benefits are largely anticipated rather than measured outcomes, so impact is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the challenge of helping teachers in low-resource schools create curriculum-aligned lesson plans while managing heavy workloads, administrative documentation, multilingual instruction, and limited pedagogical support. The authors focus on whether generative AI can support lesson planning in a way that is practical for real school settings, especially where English and local-language instruction coexist and where teachers need materials that align with state-mandated curricula and classroom realities.

The intervention studied is Shiksha Copilot, a human-in-the-loop lesson-planning system that combines LLM-generated drafts with human curation and teacher customization. The system was built around Retrieval-Augmented Generation, curriculum ingestion from textbooks, bilingual English-Kannada translation, and structured workflows for drafting, reviewing, and refining learning objectives and lesson plans. Teachers could use curated lesson plans, manually customize them, and for some users access additional AI features such as lesson-specific chat, general educational chat, and question generation. Human curators reviewed AI output for pedagogical quality, accuracy, formatting, and contextual relevance before teachers received the plans.

The study was deployed in government schools across Karnataka, India, with 1,043 field teachers and 23 curators. Teachers taught grades 5–10 in Kannada- and English-medium public schools, mostly in low-resource settings with limited digital infrastructure. The authors used a mixed-methods design, combining interviews, surveys, and log analysis to examine how educators collaborated with the system and how it affected their work. They found that the tool reduced lesson-planning time, lowered stress, and supported both instructional and bureaucratic tasks, while also encouraging more activity-based pedagogy.

The main conclusion is that generative AI can be useful in school-based lesson planning when it is tightly constrained by curriculum grounding, human review, and local adaptation. English lesson plans were generally high quality with few edits, while Kannada translations required much heavier human correction, showing the importance of language-specific oversight. Teachers often adapted plans beyond what was recorded in the system, using their own expertise and peer networks to fit local classroom needs. The paper argues that effective school AI systems in low-resource contexts must be human-in-the-loop, curriculum-aligned, and embedded in existing teacher workflows rather than treated as standalone automation.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI lesson-planning and teacher-support system built with LLMs, retrieval-augmented generation, human-in-the-loop curation, and bilingual English-Kannada support for curriculum-aligned instructional materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as Shiksha Copilot, an AI-assisted lesson planning tool deployed in government schools in Karnataka, India. Teachers and curators used it to co-create, review, translate, customize, and deploy curriculum-aligned lesson plans, with optional chat and question-generation features.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that Shiksha Copilot reduced the time and effort spent on lesson planning and record-keeping, and lowered teacher stress. The study is mixed-methods with 1,043 teachers and 23 curators in field deployment; however, the text provided does not report a numeric effect size for these outcomes.
findings.measure: Lesson planning time, administrative workload/record-keeping burden, and teacher stress (survey and interview data)

findings.finding_summary: Teachers used the system to satisfy administrative documentation needs as well as classroom instruction, indicating that the tool fit into existing school accountability practices. The paper describes this as easing bureaucratic workload and supporting curricular compliance, but no quantitative effect size is reported in the provided text.
findings.measure: Use of AI-generated lesson plans for bureaucratic documentation and curricular compliance

findings.finding_summary: The system supported a shift toward activity-based pedagogy and helped teachers access curriculum-aligned lesson plans. The paper presents this as a qualitative/mixed-methods finding from real school deployment rather than as a controlled causal estimate.
findings.measure: Perceived pedagogical usefulness and reported shift toward activity-based teaching

findings.finding_summary: For English-medium lesson plans, curators found the AI-generated content highly reliable: 96.13% of 7,744 content blocks were rated suitable for classroom use, 3.53% required minor adjustments, and 0.34% were unusable. Only 4.1% of blocks required edits overall, showing low curation burden for English outputs.
findings.measure: Curator ratings and edits to English-medium lesson-plan content blocks

findings.finding_summary: Kannada translations required extensive human editing because literal translation often produced unnatural or semantically confusing text. In an analysis of 26 Kannada-medium lesson plans, 94.4% of content blocks were edited, with almost all edits being substantive language changes.
findings.measure: Curator edits to Kannada-medium translated lesson plans

findings.finding_summary: Teachers rarely edited the curated plans on-platform after receiving them: only 85 of 5,542 lesson plans (1.53%) were modified, and only 19 of 1,480 Kannada-medium plans (1.28%) showed edits. The authors interpret this as low recorded edit burden, though they note teachers often adapted plans mentally or off-platform.
findings.measure: Teacher on-platform edits to curated lesson plans
findings.sample_size: n=5,542 lesson plans; n=1,480 Kannada-medium plans

findings.finding_summary: The tool supported both single-day and multi-day planning workflows, with 60.8% of users (n=622) generating all term lesson plans in one sitting. This suggests the system was used to compress planning work into fewer sessions, though no causal effect size is reported.
findings.measure: Usage pattern for lesson-plan generation sessions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods field deployment study with surveys, interviews, and platform logs in genuine schools, which gives it strong ecological validity. It is not an RCT or meta-analysis, so evidence quality is best classified as yellow.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear practical benefits such as reduced planning burden and high usefulness, but it does not provide causal effect sizes for the main outcomes in the text provided. That makes the impact meaningful but quantitatively unclear, fitting yellow.

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 mathematics educators evaluate lesson plans created by generative AI models versus human curriculum designers. The study is motivated by the growing use of GenAI for lesson planning and the need for evidence on whether AI-generated lesson plans can meet teachers’ pedagogical expectations and standards-aligned instructional needs.

The authors compare three lesson-plan sources: human-created plans from open educational repositories, a customized prompt-based GPT-4 system, and a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model trained on expert-designed lesson plans. Lesson plans were structured around Common Core-aligned mathematics queries spanning elementary, middle school, and high school grades. Twenty experienced educators participated in a web-based pairwise preference study, evaluating anonymized lesson-plan pairs on warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality, and providing optional comments. The design combines quantitative preference analysis with qualitative thematic analysis of educator feedback.

Results show that human-authored lesson plans are generally preferred overall, especially for elementary grades and for sections requiring student engagement, scaffolding, discourse, and inclusive supports. GenAI performs more competitively in structured components, particularly cool-down activities and, in some cases, higher-grade instruction. The customized GPT-4 model often outperforms the fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model, while LLaMA-2-13b can be competitive in high school contexts. The authors conclude that GenAI is best used as an assistive tool in a human-AI collaborative lesson-planning workflow rather than as a replacement for curriculum expertise.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used for generating customized lesson plans and structured instructional content.
identified_tools.use_case: Compared customized GPT-4 lesson plans against human curriculum designer-created plans and fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b plans for K-12 mathematics lesson planning.

findings.finding_summary: In pairwise educator preference comparisons across all measures, customized GPT-4 lesson plans were preferred 57.7% of the time over fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b plans, but human curriculum designer plans were preferred 58.7% of the time over customized GPT-4. This indicates GPT-4-generated lesson plans were competitive with other AI-generated plans but were still less preferred than human-authored plans overall.
findings.measure: Binary educator preference across warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality
findings.effect_size: preference margin 15.4% vs LLaMA-2-13b; 17.4% vs human-created
findings.sample_size: n=529 lesson plan pairs; n=16 educators

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta LLaMA-family large language model used here as a fine-tuned open-weight model for lesson plan generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b was compared with customized GPT-4 and human curriculum designer lesson plans for K-12 mathematics lesson planning.

findings.finding_summary: Fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b lesson plans were preferred 46.4% of the time in comparisons with customized GPT-4, and human curriculum designer plans were preferred 53.6% of the time over LLaMA-2-13b. The model was especially competitive in high school, where educators preferred LLaMA-2-13b over human-authored plans 59.2% to 40.8%.
findings.measure: Binary educator preference across warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality
findings.effect_size: preference margin 7.2% vs human-created; 15.4% vs GPT-4 in the opposite direction
findings.sample_size: n=529 lesson plan pairs; n=16 educators

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI/LLM-based lesson planning systems used to generate instructional materials and lesson plan sections.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generative AI lesson plan generation more broadly and compares AI-generated plans with human-created plans, with qualitative emphasis on responsible AI integration and human-AI collaboration.

findings.finding_summary: Across specific lesson plan sections, educators preferred human-authored plans for warm-up activities, main tasks, and overall quality, while GenAI-generated plans were preferred for cool-down sections. Qualitatively, educators praised GenAI for structure and adaptability but noted weaker scaffolding, discourse prompts, and differentiated support than human-authored plans.
findings.measure: Section-level educator preferences and qualitative comments
findings.sample_size: n=529 lesson plan pairs; n=2,979 comments

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods comparative user study, not an RCT or meta-analysis. It provides useful empirical evidence on educator preferences, but the design is preference-based and observational rather than causal.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports preference percentages rather than educational outcome gains, so impact on learning is unclear. The findings suggest moderate practical relevance for lesson-planning workflows, but no direct effect on student achievement is measured.

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines how a generative AI platform can be integrated into real secondary school classrooms as a teaching partner, rather than as a standalone tutoring or laboratory tool. The central question is how teachers design, frame, and supervise AI-supported activities so that AI adds instructional value while preserving human judgment, curricular alignment, and teacher authority.

The intervention was the Colleague AI Classroom pilot, a seven-week co-design study in which 21 in-service teachers from Washington State public school districts and one independent school used four AI features: Teaching Aide, AI-assisted Assessment and Grading, AI Tutor, and Student Growth Insights. More than 600 students in grades 6-12 participated in classroom activities designed and facilitated by their teachers. Teachers planned lessons, implemented AI-supported activities in live classrooms, and provided weekly reflections, interviews, surveys, planning forms, and usage logs that informed iterative tool refinement.

The study found that AI was most effective when teachers actively scaffolded its use, aligned it to instructional goals, and retained oversight over prompts, grading, and interpretation of feedback. Teachers valued the platform most for formative feedback, conversational support, and class-level insight generation, especially when AI outputs were short, clear, standards-aligned, and editable. The report concludes that generative AI can meaningfully extend classroom instruction as a "third agent" only when teachers remain central mediators, and it emphasizes the importance of teacher AI competency, developmentally appropriate design, and human oversight for trustworthy school-based implementation.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI / LLM-based classroom platform used for teacher-guided student conversations, rubric generation, automated formative feedback, AI tutoring, and student-growth analytics.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied through the Colleague AI Classroom pilot in real K-12 classrooms, where in-service teachers co-designed and implemented four features: Teaching Aide, Assessment & AI Grading, AI Tutor, and Student Growth Insights.

findings.finding_summary: In a seven-week pilot with 21 in-service teachers across four Washington State public school districts and one independent school, teachers reported that the platform could support classroom instruction when teacher-framed and scaffolded. The report emphasizes that pedagogical judgment and AI competency jointly shaped implementation quality, with teachers using the system as a 'third agent' while retaining final authority.
findings.measure: Teacher surveys, planning/reflection forms, group meetings, one-on-one interviews, and platform usage logs; teacher-reported implementation quality and confidence

findings.finding_summary: For the Teaching Aide feature, 35% of teacher-reported implementations indicated the AI helped most students learn, 62% indicated some students learned from the tool, and 3% indicated no student benefit. Teachers said thoughtful engagement and learning were strongest when they provided clear framing, modeled prompts, and tied the AI activity to instructional goals.
findings.measure: Teacher-rated student learning from AI-assisted conversations

findings.finding_summary: For AI-assisted conversations, 28% of teacher-reported implementations had most students engage thoughtfully, 66% were mixed, and 6% showed limited engagement. Engagement improved with repeated use, strong teacher presence, explicit norms, and clear finish lines, but outcomes varied by grade band and subject.
findings.measure: Teacher-rated student engagement in Teaching Aide conversations

findings.finding_summary: In the assessment workflow, the system produced high automated-grading coverage: median AI grading coverage on submitted work was 92.2% across 58 classroom-level assessment records, with a mean submission rate of 54.8% and an average resubmission rate of 8.7%. Teachers used the tool mainly for in-class formative assessments and revision cycles.
findings.measure: Platform usage logs for assessment grading and resubmissions

findings.finding_summary: Teachers found the AI-generated rubrics moderately useful: 60% indicated the rubrics could be used in classroom assignments with minor revisions, while 12% did not use AI-generated rubrics, 4% said they needed major revisions, 3% said the rubrics covered all key criteria, and 7% said the rubrics could not be applied. Teachers valued the generated feedback more than the numeric scores, but many reported score inconsistency and misalignment with their rubrics.
findings.measure: Teacher survey responses on rubric usefulness and assessment feedback quality
findings.sample_size: n=13 teacher survey responses on assessment feedback; n=19 teachers used assessments

findings.finding_summary: On assessment feedback quality, 57% of teachers said the AI provided clear, actionable feedback for teachers or students; 41% said it was useful for both teachers and students, 14% for students only, and 3% for teachers only. At the same time, 42% said the feedback was not useful, including 24% who found it vague or unhelpful and 18% who found it incorrect or misleading.
findings.measure: Teacher survey responses on AI-generated feedback usefulness

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods pilot and implementation report rather than a controlled efficacy study. It provides rich real-world evidence, but outcomes are mostly teacher-reported and descriptive, with no causal design or formal effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The report suggests practical instructional value, especially for formative feedback and teacher workflow support, but it does not report effect sizes or directly measured student outcome gains. Impact is promising yet unclear in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: New Curriculum, New Chance – Retrieval Augmented Generation for Lesson Planning in Ugandan Secondary Schools. Prototype Quality Evaluation.
paper_profiles.venue: Ndejje University Second Annual Research Dissemination Symposium 2024
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This working paper addresses the problem of weak or outdated lesson planning in Ugandan secondary schools, especially as the country rolls out a new competency-based curriculum. The authors argue that teachers need tools that can quickly generate lesson plans aligned to government-approved textbooks and the new curriculum, while still fitting the local lesson plan format and instructional approach.

The paper presents the NDU Lesson Plan Generator (NLPG), a retrieval-augmented generation prototype built with Cohere LLM, sentence embeddings, LangChain, and a web interface. The system retrieves content from government-accredited textbooks for Secondary 1 ICT, Mathematics, and History, then prompts the model to generate lesson plans in the Ugandan format. The interface was designed to be lightweight for rural teachers and made publicly available on a website.

The evaluation is based on 24 generated lesson plans rated by three independent raters using an adapted Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP). The authors report average scores of about 75–80%, which they interpret as very good quality and better than comparable human-created lesson plans in cited East African studies. They conclude that the prototype can produce lesson plans that meet technical standards for classroom use, though they also note a serious hallucination risk when the retrieved textbook lacks enough information and recommend future safeguards such as confidence indicators and plausibility checks.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model system that produces text outputs from prompts, here augmented with retrieval from external documents to constrain generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Built as the NDU Lesson Plan Generator (NLPG), a retrieval-augmented generation prototype that generated lesson plans for Ugandan secondary school subjects using government-accredited textbooks and the Ugandan lesson plan format.

findings.finding_summary: Across 24 generated lesson plans, three independent raters using the adapted Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP) found an average quality of 75–80%, described as a 'very good lesson plan.' None of the lesson plans scored below 65%, and the authors conclude the plans met the technical quality criteria for classroom implementation, though human adaptation was still recommended.
findings.measure: Lesson plan technical quality rated with the adapted Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a working paper/prototype evaluation with a small sample of generated lesson plans and qualitative/technical rubric-based assessment rather than a controlled impact study. The paper reports inter-rater ratings and protocol-based evaluation, but no experimental design or learner outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported lesson-plan quality is moderately high (75–80% LPAP average) and the authors judge it classroom-ready on technical grounds. However, the evidence is limited to prototype outputs and rubric scores, so the practical impact is promising but not directly measured in classroom learning effects.

paper_profiles.title: An Evaluation of the Pedagogical Soundness and Usability of AI-Generated Lesson Plans Across Different Models and Prompt Frameworks in High-School Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a practical problem in the use of generative AI for education: how well large language models can produce lesson plans that are pedagogically sound, usable, accurate, and aligned with curriculum expectations. The study is motivated by concerns that AI-generated lesson plans may be convenient but still suffer from weak instructional design, factual errors, and limited alignment with standards or higher-order learning goals.

The paper compares lesson plans generated by five models—ChatGPT (GPT-5), Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek V3.2, and Grok 4—using three structured prompt frameworks: TAG, RACE, and COSTAR. Fifteen lesson plans were generated for a single high-school physics topic, The Electromagnetic Spectrum, intended for mixed-ability Grades 9–12 classrooms. The plans were evaluated with automated metrics for readability, hallucination/factual reliability, standards alignment to NGSS, and Bloom’s taxonomy cognitive demand.

The findings suggest that model choice mainly determines readability, while prompt framework choice more strongly affects factual completeness and curricular alignment. RACE generally produced the best balance of completeness and alignment, while DeepSeek produced the most readable plans and Grok the lowest hallucination scores. Across all models and prompt types, however, the lesson objectives mostly remained at lower Bloom levels such as Remember and Understand, with very limited higher-order thinking. The study concludes that educators should not use AI-generated lesson plans uncritically; instead, they should pair a readable model with a structured prompt framework and add explicit curriculum and cognitive-demand requirements.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI chatbot/LLM used to generate and evaluate text outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of five LLMs to generate high-school physics lesson plans on the electromagnetic spectrum under TAG, RACE, and COSTAR prompt frameworks; also mentioned in the declaration as being used to refine Python code snippets.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic's conversational AI chatbot/LLM used for text generation and analysis.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of five LLMs to generate high-school physics lesson plans on the electromagnetic spectrum under TAG, RACE, and COSTAR prompt frameworks.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's conversational AI chatbot/LLM used for text generation and analysis.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of five LLMs to generate high-school physics lesson plans on the electromagnetic spectrum under TAG, RACE, and COSTAR prompt frameworks.

identified_tools.name: DeepSeek
identified_tools.description: DeepSeek's conversational AI model/chatbot used for text generation and analysis.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of five LLMs to generate high-school physics lesson plans on the electromagnetic spectrum under TAG, RACE, and COSTAR prompt frameworks.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbot systems used to produce instructional text.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper compares multiple generative AI chatbots and prompt frameworks for producing lesson plans, but the studied outputs are specific named models rather than an unnamed single tool.

findings.finding_summary: Across five models and three prompt frameworks, the generated lesson plans showed moderate incidental alignment with NGSS and low cognitive demand overall, but performance varied substantially by model and prompt. The paper reports that readability depended mostly on model choice (e.g., DeepSeek mean FKGL=8.64; Claude mean FKGL=19.89), while the RACE framework produced the lowest hallucination index (mean HI=2.00) and the highest framework-level NGSS mean (0.082).
findings.measure: Readability and linguistic complexity (FKGL, FRE, FOG, TTR), factual accuracy/hallucination index, NGSS alignment similarity, Bloom-based cognitive demand index

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single study with an automated, non-experimental comparison of generated lesson plans rather than a controlled classroom intervention. The methodology is systematic, but evidence is limited to one topic, one topic domain, and fifteen generated plans.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports practically relevant differences in readability, hallucination, and standards alignment, but no causal classroom outcome effect sizes are provided. The findings suggest moderate utility for prompt/model selection, yet the direct instructional impact remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: ClassMind: Scaling Classroom Observation and Instructional Feedback with Multimodal AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of scaling classroom observation and instructional coaching, which are widely viewed as effective for teacher development but are constrained by cost, limited coach availability, and inconsistency across observers. The authors ask how multimodal generative AI can support teachers by analyzing classroom videos and producing feedback that is aligned with instructional rubrics and professional standards.

They present ClassMind, an open-source system that ingests classroom recordings and optional supporting materials such as lesson plans, slides, and notes, then uses a multimodal agent framework (AVA-Align) to generate timestamped, rubric-grounded feedback. The system is designed around established frameworks including Danielson, Bloom’s taxonomy, and COPUS, and outputs strengths, growth opportunities, and actionable advice. The design was informed by a narrative review, a survey of 75 PK–12 teachers in the United States, and interviews with four teachers and two instructional coaches.

The evaluation also included a controlled simulated-user role-play study with six secondary-school teachers who used feedback generated from ATLAS classroom videos. Findings suggest that teachers found the system useful, easy to use, fair, and helpful for reflection, especially because it linked feedback to evidence and professional standards. At the same time, participants raised concerns about privacy, accountability, explainability, and the appropriate boundary between AI and human coaching. The paper concludes that multimodal AI can scale instructional feedback, but it should complement rather than replace human judgment and coaching relationships.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s multimodal large language model family used for video, text, and other multimodal reasoning and generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the core video foundation model in the AVA-Align pipeline for classifying classroom video segments, generating rubric-aligned feedback, and supporting long-context multimodal analysis in ClassMind.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports technical evaluation results for ClassMind’s Gemini-based video agent on 10 ATLAS videos. The system achieved 100% factuality, mean significance 4.40/5 (SD 0.66), mean feasibility 4.50/5 (SD 0.50), and temporal coverage entropy 0.85 (SD 0.07), outperforming the Gemini-2.5-Pro baseline on all reported metrics.
findings.measure: Video feedback quality: factuality, significance, feasibility, temporal coverage entropy

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods systems paper with formative studies, a technical evaluation, and a small user study, but not a randomized educational impact study. The evidence is informative for system performance and teacher perceptions, yet limited in scale and causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are technical and descriptive rather than instructional outcome effect sizes. With n=10 videos in benchmarking and n=6 teachers in the user study, the impact on real educational outcomes remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Tailoring Education with GenAI: A New Horizon in Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI can be used to support educators in creating customized lesson plans and learning scenarios. The authors argue that traditional, one-size-fits-all lesson planning often fails to address differences in students’ abilities, interests, and learning needs, and they propose an interactive GenAI-based assistant intended to make lesson design more adaptive and efficient.

The intervention is a “Learning Scenario Assistant” built around iterative prompt engineering. The system first positions the model in the lesson-planning domain, then uses an interactive prompt to gather structured information from the educator (target audience, topic, goal, format, duration, examples, and optional additional questions), followed by user feedback and human-led refinement. The paper reports an example use case in a university Digital Humanities course and describes testing the assistant across preschool, secondary school, and university levels in both English and Greek, using ChatGPT, Llama 2, and Google Bard.

Evaluation combined quantitative ratings from experts, qualitative feedback from teachers and educational experts, and linguistic analysis of generated outputs. The authors conclude that GenAI can substantially reduce lesson-planning time while producing tailored outputs that educators judge as useful and adaptable. They also emphasize that human oversight remains essential, and they call for continued evaluation, ethical governance, and broader testing, including stronger evidence through randomized trials in future work.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-based conversational AI system for generating and refining text through interactive prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of the evaluated large language models for generating tailored lesson plans and learning scenarios; also explicitly tested in the prompt workflow for lesson planning.

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT 4 (09/2023) and ChatGPT 3.5 (09/2023) were evaluated on lesson-plan generation quality across English and Greek scenarios. The paper reports that ChatGPT 4 generally scored highest across most quantitative and qualitative categories, including relevance, accuracy, creativity, engagement, personalization, and coherence, and was also described as effective in producing detailed and operationally practical outputs.
findings.measure: Expert ratings of generated lesson plans on Likert-scale criteria; linguistic analysis (tokens, LDA topics)

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta family of large language models used for conversational text generation and prompt-based completion.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated alongside ChatGPT and Google Bard for generating lesson plans and learning scenarios in English and Greek.

findings.finding_summary: Llama 2 70B generally scored highly across several English and Greek evaluation categories and was noted for strong creativity, personalization, and detailed outputs, but the paper also reports accuracy problems, including material that was not existent (for example, non-existent links for additional resources). Llama 2 13B was noted to excel in creativity and response time.
findings.measure: Expert ratings of generated lesson plans on Likert-scale criteria; linguistic analysis (tokens, LDA topics)

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s conversational large language model family, formerly Bard, used for text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as Google Bard in the paper for generating lesson plans and learning scenarios in English and Greek.

findings.finding_summary: Google Bard was competitive in the lesson-plan generation task but generally scored lower than ChatGPT 4 and Llama 2 70B in several categories, particularly coherence, engagement, creativity, and personalization. The paper notes it tended to perform better in response time than in content quality.
findings.measure: Expert ratings of generated lesson plans on Likert-scale criteria; linguistic analysis (tokens, LDA topics)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods comparative evaluation of LLM outputs rather than a controlled educational intervention. The paper provides structured human ratings and linguistic analysis, but no experimental student outcome data or effect sizes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical utility for lesson planning efficiency and personalization, but the impact is based on qualitative and rating-based assessments without quantified educational effect sizes. Overall impact appears promising but remains unclear for actual learner outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: LLMs to Support K–12 Teachers in Culturally Relevant Pedagogy: An AI Literacy Example
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can help K–12 teachers adapt AI literacy lessons to be more culturally relevant. The authors focus on a longstanding instructional challenge: teachers often want to implement culturally relevant pedagogy (CRP), but they face barriers such as limited time, insufficient training, and difficulty finding appropriate resources. The paper positions AI literacy as an especially important and still-emerging content area, making it a useful test case for culturally responsive lesson adaptation.

The intervention studied is CulturAIEd, an LLM-powered teacher support tool that combines student demographic information, a culturally responsive teaching checklist, rubric-based feedback, and an interactive chatbot for just-in-time pedagogical support. The tool was prototyped with GPT-4o-mini and used in a structured pilot study. The study procedure included baseline lesson design, checklist-guided adaptation, and then refinement using CulturAIEd.

Participants were four secondary teachers: three from North America and one from East Asia. All taught grades 9–12 or grade 9, and the study was conducted through semi-structured Zoom sessions with pre/post surveys and interviews. The findings suggest that teachers valued the tool’s ability to save time, surface cultural responsiveness opportunities, and provide actionable feedback. They reported higher confidence after using the system, though the authors emphasize that the evidence is preliminary and that larger studies are needed to assess generalizability and sustained impact.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model / generative AI chatbot used for generating, adapting, and giving feedback on instructional materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in the paper as the underlying generative AI capability for CulturAIEd and as an available comparison/resource (e.g., ChatGPT) for teachers adapting AI literacy lessons to culturally responsive pedagogy.

findings.finding_summary: In an exploratory pilot with 4 K-12 teachers, CulturAIEd improved teachers' confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness in learning activities. The paper reports that post-survey confidence rose from 3-5 pre-survey to all 5 post-survey on this item, and participants described the tool as helpful for concrete examples and culturally responsive modifications.
findings.measure: Teacher self-reported confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness in learning activities

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that CulturAIEd increased confidence in making culturally responsive modifications to existing activities and helped them produce more meaningful CRP/CRT-aligned lesson adaptations. Participants emphasized that the tool saved time, streamlined integration of student demographics, and provided rubric-based feedback and just-in-time coaching.
findings.measure: Teacher self-reported confidence and perceived usefulness for culturally responsive lesson modification

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small exploratory mixed-methods pilot with 4 teachers, based on interviews and pre/post surveys. It provides useful early evidence, but it is not a controlled efficacy study and relies heavily on self-report.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported change is positive and appears practically meaningful, but no effect size is reported and the sample is very small. The evidence supports promising utility rather than a clearly quantified medium or large impact.

paper_profiles.title: How K-12 Educators Use AI: LLM-Assisted Qualitative Analysis at Scale
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 educators use generative AI in authentic professional practice, and separately demonstrates how large language models can support scalable qualitative analysis of those interactions. The authors address a gap in understanding real-world educator-AI use beyond small surveys, lab studies, or preservice settings, focusing instead on unscripted conversations from a live, open-registration AI platform.

The intervention or approach studied is not a classroom intervention in the traditional sense, but an LLM-assisted qualitative analysis pipeline. The researchers used grounded-theory-inspired methods with human oversight and successive LLM support for inductive theme discovery, codebook development, and deductive annotation. They analyzed more than 13,000 educator-AI conversations, using triadic units and later single-message coding, with enterprise API use and privacy protections. The platform supported tasks such as lesson planning, differentiation, assessment, and communication.

The population comprised practicing K-12 educators and school administrators using the platform in the United States, with prompts spanning elementary, middle school, and high school contexts as well as some educator-preparation content that was not the primary focus. The study finds that educators most often used AI for instructional planning, content design, differentiation, assessment, and professional responsibilities, while also actively revising and evaluating AI outputs rather than using them as full automation. The paper concludes that LLMs can meaningfully augment qualitative research at scale when kept under human control, and that educator use of generative AI is deeply embedded in instructional reasoning and real professional workflows.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic's family of LLM chat assistants used for natural-language generation, summarization, and analysis.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the LLM in the study's human-led qualitative analysis pipeline to perform open coding, axial coding, selective coding, and deductive annotation of educator-AI conversations. The paper specifically names Claude 3 Sonnet and Claude 3.5 Haiku as the models employed.

findings.finding_summary: This paper is primarily a qualitative/methods study of educator-AI conversations rather than an intervention study of learner outcomes. It reports that Claude 3.5 Haiku achieved moderate agreement with human coders on educator requests (Cohen's kappa = 0.38; F1 = 0.40) and responses (kappa = 0.34; F1 = 0.38), but much higher agreement in a verification condition (requests kappa = 0.83, F1 = 0.84; responses kappa = 0.87, F1 = 0.88) when human coders checked Claude's labels rather than coding independently.
findings.measure: Interrater agreement / annotation quality in qualitative coding of educator-AI messages
findings.sample_size: n=1,000 sampled messages for validation; dataset of 13,071 conversations overall

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods study with methodological validation, not a causal outcome evaluation. The reported evidence concerns coding agreement and analytic workflow performance rather than student achievement or experimental effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report an educational effect size on learner outcomes; its quantitative results are agreement metrics for annotation reliability. These are useful for method assessment but do not establish instructional impact.

paper_profiles.title: Designing for human–AI complementarity in K-12 education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how to design effective human–AI partnerships in K-12 education, focusing on the challenge of helping teachers work productively with AI tutoring systems during live instruction. The authors argue that many human–AI systems fail because they are not designed around real classroom practices, local context, or the complementary strengths of teachers and AI. To address this, they frame the problem as one of augmenting teachers’ situational awareness and decision-making, rather than replacing teacher judgment.

The intervention studied is Lumilo, a pair of mixed-reality smart glasses that give teachers real-time classroom analytics drawn from an AI tutor, including indicators of students’ learning, metacognition, and behavior. The design process was participatory and iterative: teachers with prior experience using AI tutors contributed through field observations, storytelling, card sorting, speed-dating exercises, co-design sessions, replay enactments, and pilot studies. The system was refined using Causal Alignment Analysis, which linked intended student outcomes to teacher behaviors and tool features, and it was piloted in authentic classrooms before a larger field evaluation.

The main field study involved 343 middle school students across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools and school districts in AI-supported math classes using the Lynnette tutor. Classrooms were randomly assigned to business-as-usual, a glasses-only monitoring condition, or glasses plus analytics. Results showed that Lumilo improved student learning and shifted teacher attention toward students who needed help most, especially lower-performing students. The paper concludes that real-time teacher-facing AI support can improve outcomes when it is designed through deep stakeholder involvement, tested in authentic settings, and explicitly oriented toward complementarity between human judgment and algorithmic analytics.

identified_tools.name: Lumilo
identified_tools.description: A mixed-reality teacher awareness tool implemented with Microsoft HoloLens that overlays real-time analytics, alerts, and student-specific detail screens above students during AI-supported classroom instruction.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by teachers in K-12 classrooms to monitor students working with the AI tutor Lynnette and to support teacher decisions about whom to help and when during live instruction.

findings.finding_summary: In a field experiment with 343 middle school students across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools/districts, the Glasses + Analytics condition using Lumilo produced higher student learning gains than both business-as-usual and the Glasses-only control. The authors report that Lumilo also reduced the usual 'rich get richer' pattern by shifting teacher attention toward students with lower initial knowledge.
findings.measure: Pre/post learning gains on linear equation solving; teacher attention allocation across students by incoming knowledge
findings.sample_size: n=286 analyzed students (343 enrolled; 57 excluded for absence)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a real-world field experiment in K-12 classrooms with random assignment of classrooms to conditions, but the paper excerpt does not report effect sizes or confidence intervals. The evidence is stronger than qualitative work, yet some methodological detail and full statistical reporting are not present here.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive learning and attention-allocation effects, but no effect size is provided in the excerpt, so the magnitude cannot be verified. Given the likely educational relevance but incomplete quantitative reporting, the impact is best treated as modest or unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers should remain “in-the-loop” when using generative AI to personalize instructional tasks, focusing on middle school mathematics. The authors investigate a central tension in GenAI-supported personalization: teachers can improve the realism, appropriateness, and instructional fit of AI-generated tasks, but doing so may reduce efficiency and still may not produce the fine-grained personalization students prefer.

The study involved 7 middle school math teachers in 6 U.S. schools who used GPT-4o/ChatGPT to modify existing Illustrative Mathematics problems for their students’ interests, mainly in popular culture areas. Teachers participated in training on personalization, bias, readability, and cultural relevance, then worked in recorded Zoom sessions to create personalized versions of Unit 4 and Unit 6 problems. Their 521 seventh-grade students completed the resulting assignments in ASSISTments and provided closed-ended ratings and open-ended feedback about interest, fit, and accuracy.

Findings showed that teachers used prompting to control grain size, depth, and ownership of personalization. They often asked the model to insert or refine specific references, fix realism issues, and improve numerical or contextual plausibility. Students tended to prefer very specific personal references, while teachers often operated at broader interest categories. Personalizing one problem took about 4 minutes on average, and this process did not become clearly more efficient over time; in fact, teachers used more prompts and more time in Unit 6, though student ratings improved. The paper concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support professional learning and quality control, but it is time-consuming and may not achieve the fine-grained personalization students want.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot used to generate and revise text, including instructional content and personalized problem variants.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by 7 middle school mathematics teachers to modify existing Illustrative Mathematics problems into personalized versions aligned to students' interests, while researchers logged teacher prompts and interactions.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers needed an average of 3.2 prompts per problem (558 prompts for 143 problems) and about 246 seconds per problem to personalize tasks with ChatGPT. The study found a 'Goldilocks Zone' in which using 3-5 prompts was associated with higher student ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests by about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073).
findings.measure: Teacher efficiency (prompts, time per problem) and student ratings of interestingness/closeness to interests

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods, observational study with teacher prompting logs and student feedback, not a controlled trial. The design is informative but does not isolate causal effects of ChatGPT use on learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported association between 3-5 prompts and student ratings is modest in magnitude (about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale). The study suggests practical usefulness for personalization workflow, but the measured impact is limited to perceptions rather than achievement.

paper_profiles.title: AI-Generated Rubric Interfaces: K–12 Teachers’ Perceptions and Practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a practical question in K–12 assessment design: how teachers perceive and use AI-generated rubrics, and whether hands-on exposure changes their willingness to adopt such tools. The authors focus on AI-supported rubric generation because rubric creation is time-consuming, cognitively demanding, and often difficult to align precisely with assignment goals, curriculum standards, and grade-level language.

The intervention studied was a summer professional development workshop in which 25 middle- and high-school teachers used MagicSchool.ai to generate rubrics for a block-based programming task. Teachers first created rubrics manually, then produced AI-generated rubrics using North Carolina standards and assignment descriptions, and finally used the rubric to assess sample student work both with and without an AI chatbot for feedback. Data came from pre- and post-workshop surveys, exit tickets, and open-ended discussion responses, combining quantitative Likert-scale analysis with thematic analysis of qualitative data.

Teachers generally viewed the AI rubrics as useful starting drafts that improved structure, clarified vague criteria, and could support more scalable feedback. However, they also reported that outputs often required substantial editing, sometimes used generic or grade-misaligned language, and could miss instructional priorities. Across the workshop, teachers emphasized the need for teacher oversight, editable workflows, alignment with standards and classroom goals, and safeguards around fairness, privacy, and transparency. Overall, the study concludes that teacher-directed AI rubric tools are promising when they preserve educator control rather than presenting fixed or fully automated assessment products.

identified_tools.name: MagicSchool.ai
identified_tools.description: An AI-enabled education platform that can generate rubrics and provide chatbot-based feedback for teachers.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by middle- and high-school teachers in a summer professional development workshop to generate AI rubrics for a block-based programming assignment, compare them with manually created rubrics, and use the platform’s chatbot ('Reina') to generate rubric-based feedback.
