findings.finding_summary: In a summer PD workshop with K–12 teachers (n=25), participants generally rated the AI-generated rubric positively on clarity, assignment alignment, and transparency. Mean ratings were high for clearly written criteria (M=3.9375), clear performance-level distinctions (M=4.125), assignment goal alignment (M=4.0), and grading transparency (M=4.0625), but lower for ease of adding/removing/revising criteria (M=2.75) and grade-level language appropriateness (M=3.5).
findings.measure: Pre/post workshop survey ratings of rubric clarity, alignment, usability, ethical factors, and transparency

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-generated rubrics were helpful starting points that reduced workload and improved structure, but they required teacher oversight because outputs could be generic, misaligned with instructional priorities, or need substantial editing. Open-ended responses also highlighted a strictness-versus-detail tradeoff in AI-generated feedback, with some teachers perceiving the feedback as harsher but more detailed than their own.
findings.measure: Thematic analysis of open-ended survey responses and discussion/exit-ticket data

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods workshop study rather than an experimental efficacy trial. It provides useful evidence about teacher perceptions and implementation concerns, but not causal impact on student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally positive teacher perceptions and moderate usability/alignment, but no student achievement effect sizes and no quantified improvement beyond survey means. The practical impact appears promising but modest and clearly conditional on teacher oversight and customization.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring K-12 Physical Education Teachers’ Perspectives on Opportunities and Challenges of AI Integration Through Ideation Workshops
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how in-service K-12 physical education (PE) teachers think about artificial intelligence (AI) in their teaching practice, with a focus on opportunities, concerns, and practical constraints for real PE classes. The authors note that while AI has been widely studied in STEM and classroom-based settings, PE presents distinct challenges because instruction often occurs in large open spaces, requires active supervision for safety, and involves balancing physical ability differences, team dynamics, and assessment burden.

To explore this, the researchers conducted in-person focus group ideation workshops with 17 secondary school PE teachers in South Korea. The workshops included short AI literacy lectures, idea sketching, storyboarding, voting, and role-playing, allowing teachers to imagine possible AI uses in authentic PE contexts. Participants were asked to identify classroom challenges, envision AI-supported solutions, and discuss barriers to adoption. The study was designed as a participatory, qualitative inquiry rather than an intervention trial.

Teachers envisioned AI in four main roles: operational assistant, personal trainer, group coach, and evaluator. These roles included automating attendance and safety monitoring, giving individualized movement feedback, supporting balanced team formation, and streamlining multidimensional assessment. At the same time, teachers emphasized that AI should remain a supporting tool rather than replace educators, and they raised concerns about institutional support, infrastructure, teacher readiness, overreliance on AI, alignment with PE educational goals, and student data privacy and autonomy. The paper concludes that successful AI integration in PE requires curricular alignment, clear guidelines, and attention to ethical and practical safeguards.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / AI system concept discussed as a supportive tool for education, capable of analysis, feedback, automation, and content-related assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: In-service secondary school PE teachers in South Korea were asked to ideate how AI could be integrated into K-12 physical education. The paper discusses envisioned roles such as operational assistant, personal trainer, group coach, and evaluator, with no specific named product evaluated.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative ideation/workshop paper with no empirical evaluation of a specific AI tool, no intervention, and no outcome measures. It is best classified as a framework/needs-analysis study rather than evidence of tool effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has conceptual relevance for school-based AI implementation because it surfaces teacher concerns about alignment, privacy, and oversight, but it does not measure student or teacher outcomes. Therefore there is no demonstrable intervention impact, only design insight.

paper_profiles.title: Understanding Teacher Revisions of Large Language Model-Generated Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers actually revise large language model (LLM)-generated formative feedback before it reaches students. The core question is not whether the model can generate useful feedback in isolation, but how human mediation changes AI output in real educational workflows. The authors analyze whether certain textual features of AI feedback predict teacher edits, how often teachers revise versus accept the feedback, and how the pedagogical type of feedback changes after revision.

The study uses log data from the Tutoria platform, an AI-supported feedback system integrated with Moodle and Google Classroom. Tutoria generates an initial feedback draft for short open-ended student responses, and teachers can accept it, edit it, or rewrite it before delivery. The dataset includes 1,349 AI-generated feedback messages and corresponding teacher-delivered versions from 117 teachers, with contributing contexts including Brazilian high school chemistry, introductory computer science instruction, and extracurricular computer science tasks. The paper combines descriptive analysis, predictive modeling, and qualitative coding of feedback types.

The main findings are that teachers accepted AI feedback unchanged in about 78% of cases, and most teachers edited very little. When edits occurred, they usually shortened the feedback and preserved most of the original meaning, suggesting compression rather than wholesale rewriting. Revised feedback often shifted away from high-information explanations toward more concise corrective feedback. The authors conclude that default LLM behavior is highly consequential because most feedback is delivered without modification, and they argue that future systems should better align with teacher preferences and reduce unnecessary editing burden.

identified_tools.name: DeepSeek
identified_tools.description: A DeepSeek large language model used to generate formative feedback drafts in an educational feedback platform.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of the LLMs in Tutoria to generate initial feedback drafts that teachers could accept, edit, or rewrite before delivery to students; later stages adopted DeepSeek-V3, including multi-agent configurations.

findings.finding_summary: The paper does not evaluate DeepSeek against an outcome for student learning; it examines teacher revision of DeepSeek-generated feedback within Tutoria. Across 1,349 feedback instances from 117 teachers, teachers accepted AI feedback without modification in 77.8% of cases (1050/1349), while edited feedback was modestly longer than unedited feedback and teacher revisions often simplified or shortened the original message.
findings.measure: Teacher revision rate; semantic similarity and length of AI feedback vs final teacher-delivered feedback
findings.effect_size: AUC=0.75 for predicting revision decisions from AI text (best model); Cram�e9r's V=0.12 for shift in feedback type after revision
findings.confidence_interval: AUC 0.75 [0.54, 0.77] for gradient-boosted trees; AUC 0.70 [0.53, 0.72] logistic regression; AUC 0.74 [0.52, 0.78] MLP

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an observational/mixed-methods analysis of platform logs and coded feedback revisions, not an experimental efficacy study. The paper reports descriptive, predictive, and qualitative analyses rather than causal impact on learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported predictive and distributional effects are modest, and the paper does not report student learning gains from DeepSeek itself. The main contribution is about teacher mediation and workflow, not demonstrated outcome impact.

paper_profiles.title: Listening with Language Models: Using LLMs to Collect and Interpret Classroom Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language model (LLM)-powered chatbots can improve the classroom feedback process compared with traditional end-of-quarter surveys. The authors argue that standard surveys are often too delayed, generic, and poorly aligned with instructors’ needs, making them weak tools for obtaining actionable teaching feedback.

To address this, the paper presents a three-part system: PromptDesigner for instructors to co-design course-specific feedback prompts, FeedbackCollector for students to provide conversational feedback through a GPT-4-powered chatbot, and FeedbackAnalyzer for instructors to review anonymized responses and AI-generated summaries. Instructors could upload syllabi, choose topics such as assignment clarity or lecture engagement, and revise prompts over the quarter. Students interacted asynchronously through a secure platform, and faculty later reviewed dashboards summarizing themes from the conversations.

The system was piloted in two graduate courses at the University of California, Santa Cruz—Game Data Science and Ethics in HCI—with one instructor and 40 students. The study used co-design sessions, a mid-quarter deployment of the chatbot, and post-course semi-structured interviews with six students and the instructor. The results suggest that the LLM-based system produced richer, more contextual, and more timely feedback than standard surveys, helped instructors make mid-course adjustments, and was generally appreciated by students for its conversational style. However, students also raised concerns about anonymity and wanted stronger privacy reassurance in the interface.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI GPT-based large language model chatbot used for conversational interaction, text generation, and summarization/analysis tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the GPT-4-powered student-facing FeedbackCollector chatbot to gather classroom feedback conversationally, and within FeedbackAnalyzer to generate summaries of anonymized student responses.

findings.finding_summary: In two graduate courses (n=40 total students), the LLM-based feedback system was reported to be quicker and more efficient than the university’s standard end-of-quarter survey. The instructor said it took about five minutes and yielded 23 feedback responses, substantially more than they typically received through SETS; students also found the conversational format engaging.
findings.measure: Instructor-reported efficiency and response volume; student interview feedback about engagement compared with standard surveys
findings.sample_size: n=40 (pilot classes); n=6 student interviews + 1 instructor interview

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative pilot study with semi-structured interviews and a small case-study deployment, not a controlled trial. It provides useful implementation insight but limited causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear practical benefits in timeliness, response volume, and perceived usefulness, but no quantitative effect size is reported. Impact is promising yet currently unclear in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: Democratizing Foundations of Problem-Solving with AI: A Breadth-First Search Curriculum for Middle School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to broaden access to AI education by embedding foundational AI problem-solving ideas into regular K–12 subject instruction rather than offering stand-alone AI activities. Specifically, it asks whether middle school students can learn Breadth-First Search (BFS) as a concrete example of AI reasoning when the content is integrated into a science unit on virus transmission and contact tracing.

The intervention was a seven-day, co-designed curriculum delivered in a rural public middle school health science course in the United States. The curriculum combined an interactive Snap!-based environment (I-SAIL) with unplugged tracing tasks, map-based pathfinding, and science applications involving disease spread and contact networks. Students practiced BFS through scaffolded simulation activities, then applied the idea in paper-based and hands-on science contexts. The study collected pre/post assessments, student work artifacts, and a teacher interview.

Results showed significant gains in students’ BFS understanding from pre- to post-assessment, and most students could correctly identify a shortest path on the unplugged worksheet, though many had difficulty documenting every procedural step. The teacher reported that the module fit well within the existing science curriculum and helped students connect AI reasoning to science concepts. The paper concludes that AI problem-solving can be productively taught in ordinary subject classrooms when curricula are carefully designed, scaffolded, and co-developed with teachers.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Computer-assisted instruction or AI-supported instructional system used in K–12 learning contexts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper describes a classroom curriculum and interactive learning environment for teaching Breadth-First Search (BFS) as an AI problem-solving procedure within middle school science instruction. The system is i-SAIL, a Snap!-based environment, but the paper does not study a named commercial AI product or an LLM chatbot.

findings.finding_summary: Students showed improved performance on a matched five-item BFS knowledge assessment after the four core I-SAIL activities. Mean score increased from 0.683 (SD=0.219) pre-test to 0.790 (SD=0.232) post-test, with the improvement statistically significant in a paired t-test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The within-subject effect was moderate (Cohen’s dz=0.453).
findings.measure: Matched pre/post BFS knowledge assessment (5 multiple-choice items)

findings.finding_summary: On a paper-based BFS tracing worksheet completed after the I-SAIL activities, 64.5% of students accurately identified the shortest path to the goal state. However, many students omitted intermediate steps and had incomplete exploration-order records, indicating partial procedural understanding.
findings.measure: Paper-based BFS tracing worksheet accuracy and step-by-step procedural completeness

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a classroom implementation study with pre/post assessment and interview data, but it is not an experimental evaluation of a named AI product. The evidence is mixed-methods and observational, so it fits a lower-than-experimental tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported learning gain on the BFS assessment is moderate (dz=0.453), which meets the threshold for medium impact. The worksheet results suggest useful but incomplete procedural learning, so overall impact is positive but bounded.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a generative AI writing assistant, CyberScholar, can support K-12 students’ writing through formative feedback. The central question is how well the tool can help students improve writing in authentic school subjects while aligning feedback with teacher rubrics, instructional materials, and classroom expectations. The study is framed by formative assessment and metacognition, and it is positioned as an exploration of GenAI in real school settings rather than a laboratory demo.

CyberScholar was piloted in four public schools in the United States across grades 7, 8, 10, and 11, in English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History classes. The tool was customized using teachers’ materials, prompts, and rubrics through retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering. The implementation involved 121 students and 4 teachers, with data gathered through observations, surveys, and interviews. Teachers and students received training, and the researchers used iterative development cycles during the pilot.

Findings from thematic qualitative analysis suggest that students viewed the AI feedback as detailed, specific, interactive, and helpful for improving writing quality. Participants especially valued the alignment between AI feedback and teacher rubric criteria, and they appreciated the chance to ask follow-up questions. The paper concludes that CyberScholar has promise as a pedagogically grounded formative feedback tool that can support teacher guidance, but it should complement rather than replace teacher feedback. The authors also note that the system is still under development and that broader testing is needed.

identified_tools.name: CyberScholar
identified_tools.description: A generative AI writing assistant for K-12 education that provides formative feedback on student writing, aligned with teacher rubrics, instructional materials, and classroom expectations, using retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering.
identified_tools.use_case: Piloted in four U.S. public schools to provide formative feedback on writing assignments for students in grades 7, 8, 10, and 11, with teachers supplying rubrics, prompts, and classroom materials; students revised drafts based on AI feedback and follow-up questioning.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative multi-site pilot, students generally perceived CyberScholar as helpful for improving writing through detailed, specific, and rubric-aligned feedback. Of 54 post-survey respondents, 36 said they would like to use it again, while 11 were hesitant; students also reported improvements in grammar, transitions, sentence clarity, and revision quality.
findings.measure: Student post-survey responses, interviews, and implementation observations about writing support and feedback usefulness
findings.sample_size: n=121 students, n=4 teachers; post-survey n=54; interviews n=8 students, n=1 teacher

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, exploratory multi-case study with surveys, interviews, and observations rather than an experimental design. It provides useful implementation evidence but does not support causal claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceived effects on writing support and revision, but no quantitative effect size is reported. Impact is therefore suggestive but unclear in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an analytical AI feedback platform can support lesson-planning development in teacher education, and how it compares with traditional human feedback. The authors focus on a gap in the literature: while generative AI for feedback has received attention, there is less direct evidence on analytical AI systems that provide individualized, expert-level feedback in educational settings.

The intervention used EDDA, an analytical AI platform built on a BERT-based classifier trained on coded lesson plans and materials. EDDA analyzed student lesson plans and returned individualized text and visual feedback on didactic principles and planning dimensions. The study compared an experimental group that received AI feedback plus follow-up human discussion with a control group that received human feedback only. The comparison was conducted over a semester in a vocational business education master’s course in Germany, with lesson plans collected at the beginning and end of the term.

Participants were 103 master’s students in vocational business education, working in small groups. The main outcome was the quality of the lesson-plan artifacts, coded for planning dimensions such as sustainability, action orientation, process orientation, problem orientation, individualization, digitalization, learner activation, and lesson structure. The study also tracked self-reported meta-dimensions including AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competence, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and motivation. The authors report that AI feedback matched or exceeded human feedback on several lesson-plan dimensions, but mere exposure to the AI system did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, or motivation.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI/LLM chatbot or AI feedback system without a named commercial or research product specified.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generative AI tools in the background literature, but the empirical intervention evaluated is an analytical AI platform rather than a generative chatbot.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal intervention study with a comparison group and repeated measures, which is stronger than purely descriptive work. However, assignment was not randomized in the traditional sense and the control came from a different university, so internal validity is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports some positive differences in lesson-plan ratings for the AI-feedback group, but effects are mixed and often reported only as significance values rather than clear standardized effect sizes. Several broader outcomes such as AI literacy and motivation did not clearly improve from the intervention alone.

paper_profiles.title: Identifying the characteristics of effective teacher professional development: a critical review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper critically examines the evidence base behind the widely cited consensus that effective teacher professional development (PD) is sustained, collaborative, subject-specific, includes outside expertise, has teacher buy-in, and is practice-based. The authors argue that this consensus has influenced policy and practice in multiple countries, but that the reviews supporting it often rely on weak inclusion criteria and flawed inferential logic.

Rather than evaluating a single PD intervention, the paper is a methodological review of prior reviews and meta-reviews. It traces the literature from policy guidance back through umbrella reviews and then to the primary studies they relied on, focusing on studies that used pupil achievement as the outcome. The paper uses instructional coaching as an illustrative example of how to identify effective PD characteristics by combining causal evidence of impact with separate evidence on mechanisms such as habit formation and repeated practice.

The population of interest is K-12 teachers and their students, especially in elementary, middle, and high school settings, with much of the cited evidence centered on mathematics, literacy, and science PD. The authors conclude that many commonly asserted PD features lack strong evidential warrant, especially collaboration and buy-in, and that apparent regularities in effective interventions do not by themselves prove those features are causally important. They recommend a more theory-informed approach that links rigorous intervention evaluations with independent evidence about learning and behavior-change mechanisms.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring / adaptive instructional support system that provides guided practice, feedback, and/or individualized instructional assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Not the focus of this paper. The paper is a critical review of teacher professional development and does not evaluate a specific AI tool; it mentions instructional coaching and several non-AI PD studies as illustrative examples.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a critical review of teacher professional development, not an empirical study of an AI tool. It contains no direct evaluation of any generative AI system or other AI educational product.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No tool was evaluated, so there are no measurable effects on teacher practice or student outcomes to classify. The paper is theoretical/methodological rather than impact-evaluative.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what the current state of artificial intelligence (AI) research in higher education is, using a systematic review of peer-reviewed journal articles published from 2016 to 2022. The authors aim to map where the research was conducted, who the intended users were, which academic levels and subject domains were studied, and how AI was being used across higher education settings.

The review identified 138 articles through PRISMA-based searching and screening. Rather than evaluating a single AI intervention, the paper categorizes the literature into major usage types such as assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. The review found that undergraduate students were the most frequently studied population, with a smaller share of graduate-level work; the main user groups were students, instructors, and managers/administrators. The most common subject areas were language learning, computer science, and engineering.

The main conclusions are descriptive and field-mapping rather than causal. The literature grew sharply in 2021–2022, China had become the leading country by publication count, and education departments were now the most common first-author affiliation. The authors argue that most current AI use in higher education supports existing practices such as feedback, prediction, tutoring, and learning analytics, and they call for more research on underrepresented countries, graduate learners, instructor support, and more innovative uses of AI, including new tools such as ChatGPT.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic artificial intelligence and AI-enabled systems used in higher education, including assessment/evaluation, predictive analytics, AI assistants/chatbots, intelligent tutoring systems, and learning management/analytics functions.
identified_tools.use_case: Systematic review of 138 peer-reviewed higher-education studies (2016-2022) examining how AI was used, rather than evaluating one specific AI product.

findings.finding_summary: Across 138 studies, AI in higher education was most commonly used for assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistant functions, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. The review also reports that 72% of studies focused on students, 17% on instructors, and 11% on managers, but it does not report causal effects on teacher practice or student outcomes.
findings.measure: Distribution of study uses, intended users, and subject/domain coding across included studies

findings.finding_summary: The review describes AI as supporting instructors by reducing grading time, generating questions/tests, and providing automated personalized feedback. These are described as affordances observed in the literature, not experimentally estimated effects.
findings.measure: Reported uses/affordances of AI for grading, question generation, and feedback provision

findings.finding_summary: The review identifies predictive uses of AI for forecasting academic performance, at-risk students, dropouts, and future grades, with 21 studies focused on predicting. No pooled effect sizes or comparative outcome estimates are reported.
findings.measure: Reported predictive applications and associated study counts
findings.sample_size: n=21 studies on predicting within n=138 total

findings.finding_summary: The review notes 18 studies that explicitly used intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) to provide adaptive instruction, customized strategies, and personalized learning paths. The paper does not provide experimental comparisons versus human coaching, peer review, or no-feedback baselines.
findings.measure: Reported ITS use and counts

findings.finding_summary: The review reports 19 studies focused on managing student learning, including learning analytics, curriculum sequencing, instructional design, and clustering of students. These were described as efficiency and decision-support uses rather than direct outcome evaluations.
findings.measure: Reported management/learning analytics applications and study counts

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review, but it synthesizes heterogeneous higher-education AI studies and does not report a meta-analysis or direct experimental comparison of a single tool. The evidence is descriptive and review-based rather than causal.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports broad use patterns and potential affordances, but no pooled effect sizes or direct outcome impacts are provided. Because impact is not quantified, the practical impact remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a tertiary review (review of reviews) that maps the scope, quality, and characteristics of artificial intelligence in higher education (AIHEd) evidence syntheses published between 2018 and mid-2023. The authors ask what kinds of evidence syntheses are being conducted, where they are published, who is producing them, what AI applications they focus on, and how rigorously they are reported. The motivation is to reduce research waste and provide a clearer foundation for future AI research and policy in higher education.

The study does not evaluate a single AI intervention. Instead, it synthesizes 66 secondary studies that themselves reviewed primary AI research in formal higher-education and continuing-education settings. The corpus includes systematic reviews, scoping reviews, meta-analyses, mapping reviews, bibliometric reviews, and related evidence syntheses. The reviewed primary literature covers applications such as adaptive systems and personalization, profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, and intelligent tutoring systems. The most common settings and populations discussed are higher-education learners, especially undergraduate and graduate/doctoral students, along with some studies involving institutional and administrative functions.

The main conclusions are that AIHEd evidence synthesis has grown rapidly, is mostly collaborative, and is concentrated in systematic reviews, but methodological reporting quality is uneven. Many reviews fail to report inter-rater reliability, exact coding schemes, full quality appraisal, or reflections on limitations. The field is heavily oriented toward learner-facing applications, while administrative uses are less common. The authors call for greater methodological rigor, better ethics and transparency, and stronger interdisciplinary collaboration in future AI in education research.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system is an AI-driven educational system that supports instruction through guided learning, diagnosis, and automated feedback, often adapting to learner needs.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a tertiary review of AI in higher education and includes intelligent tutoring systems as one of the main application categories, but it does not evaluate a specific ITS product or primary study directly.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a tertiary review of secondary studies, not a primary evaluation of an AI tool. It does not provide direct experimental evidence on a specific tool in the target K–12 teacher coaching or lesson-feedback domain.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct outcome effect is reported for a specific tool, and the paper is not an intervention study. Its findings are descriptive about the state of the literature rather than impacts on teacher practice or student outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a perspective article that examines the role of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in human learning. Rather than reporting a primary empirical study, it synthesizes current research and discusses the promises, risks, and research needs associated with GenAI across learning, resource creation, feedback, and assessment. The authors frame GenAI as a potentially transformative tool for supporting personalized learning, generating instructional materials, producing feedback, and enabling more adaptive assessment practices.

The paper does not study a specific intervention, participant sample, or educational setting. Instead, it reviews illustrative examples from existing studies and products such as tutoring chatbots, AI-generated learning materials, AI feedback systems, and generative assessment agents. It also highlights concerns including hallucinations, privacy, transparency, bias, inequality, and the possibility that GenAI may create an illusion of performance gains without durable learning.

The main conclusion is that GenAI should be developed and used in ways that are human-centred, evidence-based, and methodologically rigorous. The authors argue that researchers, educators, policymakers, and technologists need stronger empirical evidence—especially longitudinal and randomized studies—to determine when GenAI genuinely improves cognition, metacognition, creativity, and learning outcomes, and to distinguish artifact quality from actual behavior change or learning gains.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI systems, especially large language models and other generative models, used to create text, images, video, feedback, assessments, and adaptive support.
identified_tools.use_case: This perspective paper discusses GenAI broadly as a tool for human learning, including tutoring/support, resource generation, feedback provision, and assessment design. It does not evaluate one specific product in an empirical study.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/theoretical article rather than an empirical study. It synthesizes prior literature and proposes research directions, but does not present original experimental, quasi-experimental, or longitudinal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct outcome data, effect sizes, or measured impact on K-12 teacher coaching, lesson-plan feedback, or student outcomes are reported in this paper. The paper discusses potential impacts only at a conceptual level.

paper_profiles.title: The effect of ChatGPT on students’ learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking: insights from a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT improves student learning and under what conditions its effects are strongest. The authors note that prior studies on ChatGPT in education have reported mixed results, ranging from positive effects on achievement and motivation to null or negative effects, which motivated a quantitative synthesis.

The study uses a meta-analysis of 51 quasi-experimental and experimental studies published between November 2022 and February 2025. The included studies cover primary, secondary, and college contexts, although nearly all moderator analyses were driven by secondary and college samples. Outcomes were grouped into three categories: learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking. The paper also codes moderating variables including grade level, type of course, learning model, intervention duration, ChatGPT role, and application area.

The main finding is that ChatGPT has a large positive effect on learning performance and moderate positive effects on learning perception and higher-order thinking. Effects were strongest in skills/competencies courses, problem-based learning, and interventions lasting 4–8 weeks for performance; learning perception improved across durations, with larger effects after longer use; and higher-order thinking benefits were most pronounced when ChatGPT functioned as an intelligent tutor. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can support learning when embedded in structured pedagogical designs, but they also caution that future studies should better examine how it is used and for what learning purpose.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model system used for conversational text generation, tutoring, feedback, and related instructional tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: This meta-analysis examined ChatGPT as the intervention across experimental and quasi-experimental studies on student learning outcomes; the paper also discusses ChatGPT's role in education broadly, including tutoring, assessment, personalized recommendation, and learning support.

findings.finding_summary: Across 44 independent effects from 51 studies, ChatGPT had a large positive effect on learning performance (Hedges's g=0.867, 95% CI 0.683 to 1.052, p<0.001). The paper notes substantial heterogeneity (I2=89.243%) and reports stronger effects in problem-based learning and 4-8 week interventions.
findings.measure: Learning performance (tests/exams; standardized mean difference across experimental vs control groups)

findings.finding_summary: Across 19 independent effects, ChatGPT had a moderate positive effect on learning perception (Hedges's g=0.456, 95% CI 0.287 to 0.625, p<0.001). The paper reports that intervention duration moderated the effect, with longer interventions (>8 weeks) showing larger gains.
findings.measure: Learning perception (scales/questionnaires)

findings.finding_summary: Across 9 independent effects, ChatGPT had a moderate positive effect on higher-order thinking (Hedges's g=0.457, 95% CI 0.255 to 0.650, p<0.001). The paper reports that ChatGPT was most effective when used as an intelligent tutor, and that effects varied by course type.
findings.measure: Higher-order thinking (scales/questionnaires)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis of 51 experimental/quasi-experimental studies with quantified pooled effects and heterogeneity analyses. The review explicitly reports inclusion criteria, effect-size computation, and moderator analyses, which supports high evidence quality despite heterogeneity.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effects are medium to large by the paper's own conventions, including a large effect on learning performance (g=0.867) and moderate effects on learning perception and higher-order thinking (both g=0.456-0.457). These exceed the threshold for blue impact.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can function as an automated teacher coach for classroom instruction. The authors frame coaching as a key component of teacher development and investigate whether a generative AI system can provide useful classroom-observation scoring and feedback in ways that resemble human coaching.

The study evaluates ChatGPT zero-shot on three teacher-coaching tasks using elementary mathematics classroom transcripts from the NCTE dataset: (A) predicting rubric scores for selected CLASS and MQI observation items, (B) identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instructional practice, and (C) generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning. For the qualitative feedback tasks, experienced math teachers rate model outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty. The population is elementary school math teachers/classrooms in four U.S. school districts; the work does not involve an intervention in live classrooms, but rather an offline evaluation of model outputs against human ratings and expert judgment.

The main findings are that ChatGPT shows some promise but falls well short of expert coaching quality. Its score predictions correlate weakly with human ratings, and prompt additions such as rubric descriptions or reasoning do not materially improve performance. For qualitative feedback, teachers generally find the model’s comments relevant but often not insightful or novel, and many suggestions simply restate what teachers already did in the transcript. The paper concludes that generative AI may eventually complement human coaching, but substantial improvements are needed to reduce unhelpful, redundant, and sometimes unfaithful feedback.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational generative AI chatbot/model used for zero-shot text generation, scoring, and feedback generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated zero-shot as an automated teacher coach on elementary math classroom transcripts for three tasks: predicting rubric scores (CLASS and MQI), identifying highlights and missed opportunities, and generating actionable suggestions for eliciting more student reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: On Task A, ChatGPT showed low Spearman correlations with human ratings across CLASS and MQI observation items. The paper reports correlations near zero or negative for most dimensions, and adding rubric descriptions or reasoning did not improve performance.
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between model-predicted observation scores and human annotator scores

findings.finding_summary: For Task B, expert math teachers generally judged ChatGPT's highlights and missed-opportunities feedback as not insightful or not relevant. The paper reports that around 20-30% of responses were unfaithful, and MQI results were worse than CLASS across relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for generated highlights/missed opportunities
findings.effect_size: CLASS no-ratings: faithful 22%, relevant 35%, insightful 51%; MQI no-ratings: faithful 29%, relevant 55%, insightful 71%
findings.sample_size: n=216 CLASS examples; n=288 MQI examples

findings.finding_summary: For Task C, teachers found many suggestions actionable, relevant, and faithful, but 82% were redundant, repeating what the teacher already did in the transcript. The paper characterizes the outputs as generally actionable but lacking novelty.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, actionability, and novelty for generated suggestions
findings.effect_size: Redundant/novelty-negative suggestions in 82% of cases; actionability/relevance/faithfulness mostly rated yes or somewhat (exact proportions not fully reported in text)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative and correlational evaluation of model outputs against human ratings, not an RCT or quasi-experiment. The methodology is clear, but it does not test downstream teacher or student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows some potential for actionable feedback generation, but the strongest findings are about limitations: low score-correlation, low relevance/insightfulness, and high redundancy. Any positive impact is modest and not demonstrated on behavior or student outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using generative AI to personalize mathematics problems for students. The core question is not whether AI can generate personalized tasks, but how teachers actually interact with ChatGPT while adapting existing curriculum problems and whether that process is efficient, realistic, and responsive to students’ interests.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers from six U.S. schools were trained to use GPT-4o/ChatGPT to personalize Illustrative Mathematics problems for students’ interests in popular culture. Across two units, teachers modified 143 problems and students (about 521 total) completed the resulting assignments in ASSISTments. The study analyzed teacher prompts, recorded teacher-AI interactions, time spent creating tasks, and student survey ratings and open-ended feedback about interestingness and fit to their interests.

The study found that teachers often used ChatGPT to work at a relatively broad grain size, such as broad topics like sports or music, but also repeatedly edited outputs to improve realism, numerical plausibility, age appropriateness, and specific cultural references. Students tended to prefer smaller-grain, more specific references, and often judged problems based on whether the reference matched their personal interests. Teachers took about four minutes per problem on average, and there was no clear evidence that the process became faster over time; in fact, after reflection on student feedback, teachers used more prompts and spent more time in the second unit, though student ratings improved. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support professional learning and quality control, but it is time-consuming and may not satisfy students’ desire for more individualized personalization.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational generative AI chatbot based on GPT-family large language models, used for generating and revising text responses through prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers used ChatGPT (with underlying model GPT-4o) to modify Illustrative Mathematics problems into personalized mathematics tasks aligned with students’ interests, then iterated based on student feedback.

findings.finding_summary: Across 143 personalized problems created by 7 middle school teachers for 521 7th grade students, using 3-5 prompts per problem was associated with higher student ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests than other prompt counts. The regression coefficient for this prompt range was B=0.240 (SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073), on a 5-point scale.
findings.measure: Student ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests (1-5 scales)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods exploratory field study with teacher and student reports, not a randomized or quasi-experimental comparison of tools. It provides useful descriptive and correlational evidence, but causal claims are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported association between 3-5 prompts and higher student ratings is modest (B=0.240 on a 5-point scale). However, the outcome is student-perceived task quality/fit rather than direct achievement or durable behavior change.

paper_profiles.title: To what extent is ChatGPT useful for language teacher lesson plan creation?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can be useful for creating lesson plans for foreign language teachers, with a focus on how prompt specificity affects the quality and consistency of AI-generated instructional materials. The authors do not study teacher behavior change or student outcomes; instead, they evaluate the quality of generated lesson-plan artifacts. Their central question is whether adding more detailed prompting leads to better, more standards-aligned lesson plans and whether repeated prompting yields stable outputs.

The intervention-like approach consists of using ChatGPT 4.0 with five increasingly specific zero-shot prompts to generate 50 Spanish lesson plans. The prompts were designed around a high school Level I Spanish lesson and progressively added more context: proficiency level clarification, a lesson-plan template, alignment to ACTFL world-readiness standards, and finally a checklist of required components. Each prompt was entered 10 times in separate chats to assess output variability. The resulting lesson plans were scored against a 25-item rubric based on best practices and edTPA-related criteria, and the authors analyzed scores, word counts, dissimilarity, clustering, and patterns of omitted elements.

The study was conducted in the context of pre-service foreign language teacher training at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte, using lesson-plan expectations tied to North Carolina teacher licensure requirements and ACTFL guidance. The population is not a participant sample in the usual sense; the study concerns AI-generated outputs intended for educators, so the only user type represented is educator. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can generate generally high-quality lesson plans, but increased prompt specificity does not always improve output quality in a linear way. A rubric/checklist prompt produced the best average scores, while adding a template sometimes reduced quality. The authors also found substantial non-determinism across repeated runs of the same prompt and noted recurring weaknesses related to cultural integration and occasional reliance on outdated pedagogical practices. They argue that teachers should critically evaluate and revise AI outputs rather than adopt them directly.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative chatbot / large language model system used to generate text-based outputs from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate 50 foreign-language lesson plans via five increasingly specific zero-shot prompts; outputs were scored against an edTPA-aligned rubric and analyzed for quality and variability.

findings.finding_summary: Across 50 generated lesson plans (5 prompts � 10 chats each), increasing prompt specificity produced a non-linear change in rubric alignment. Mean scores were 21.2/25 for P.2, dropped to 19.8/25 for P.3, 19.6/25 for P.4, and rose to 21.6/25 for P.5; the overall difference across prompt groups was marginally significant (p=0.0442; F=2.668; DF=4), but pairwise comparisons were not significant after correction (p > 0.12).
findings.measure: edTPA-aligned lesson plan rubric score (presence/absence of 25 criteria)

findings.finding_summary: Adding prompt specificity significantly affected output length; word count differed across prompt groups (p=0.0047; F=4.338; DF=4). P.3 was significantly shorter than P.1 and P.2, and P.4 was significantly shorter than P.1, indicating that prompt design changed the amount of generated material, though not always in a quality-improving direction.
findings.measure: word count of generated lesson plans

findings.finding_summary: Output variability was high even for identical prompts. For example, P.1 scores ranged from 16/25 to 23/25 and P.5 scores ranged from 20/25 to 25/25, with outputs from the same prompt often differing by at least five rubric elements. Jaccard-distance, NMDS, PERMANOVA (F=3.1556; p=0.001), and ANOSIM (R=0.141, p=0.001) analyses showed some separation between prompt groups but also substantial overlap and convergence across groups.
findings.measure: variability/dissimilarity in rubric scores across repeated prompt runs

findings.finding_summary: Several rubric components were inconsistently or infrequently generated, including cultural connections and ACTFL standards integration in some sections. The authors concluded that ChatGPT sometimes reflected outdated 20th-century pedagogical practices (e.g., audio-lingual/teacher-centered routines) and that such weaknesses require human review when using generated lesson plans.
findings.measure: presence/absence of specific lesson-plan components and alignment with contemporary pedagogy

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-study, descriptive/mixed-methods evaluation of generated artifacts rather than a causal trial with teacher or student outcomes. It provides useful systematic evidence about prompt sensitivity and output quality, but the methodology does not reach RCT/QED standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests moderate practical value for lesson-plan drafting, but the measured effects are primarily on artifact quality and variability, not demonstrated changes in teacher practice or student learning. The reported gains are inconsistent and non-linear, with substantial output variability and several pedagogical weaknesses.

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-service elementary science teachers envisioned using ChatGPT in their lesson planning, in a context where empirical evidence on generative AI in science education was still scarce. The authors were interested in what kinds of science topics and instructional strategies teachers would pair with ChatGPT, how well they could align the tool with lesson goals, and what benefits and concerns they associated with its use.

The study involved 29 pre-service elementary teachers enrolled in a science education course at a Korean teachers' university. After four instructor-led sessions introducing ChatGPT, discussing its potential uses, and reviewing science teaching methods, participants wrote lesson plans for a 45-minute elementary science class. They also attached simulated ChatGPT conversations and completed open-ended survey questions about why they chose specific content, how ChatGPT would help, and what outcomes they expected. Lesson plans were scored with a modified TPACK-based rubric, and survey responses were analyzed qualitatively.

Results showed that participants imagined ChatGPT being used across several science domains, especially biology, chemistry, and earth science, and with multiple pedagogical strategies such as cooperative learning, Predict-Observe-Explain, learning cycles, analogy generation, and concept mapping. On average, lesson plans were rated relatively high on the rubric, suggesting moderate competence in integrating ChatGPT into science instruction, although participants were weaker at selecting the most appropriate ChatGPT functions for particular tasks. The authors also found that participants valued ChatGPT for supporting questioning, individualized learning, and formative feedback, but worried about inaccuracy, bias, and over-dependence. They concluded that ChatGPT has perceived instructional promise, but real classroom effects still need to be tested through stronger empirical studies, including quasi-experimental research on student outcomes.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational large language model chatbot for generating text, answering questions, and supporting interactive dialogue-based tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Pre-service elementary science teachers were asked to integrate ChatGPT into 29 lesson plans for a 45-minute class, using it to support lesson content, instructional strategies, simulated teacher/student queries, and feedback/reflection.

findings.finding_summary: This paper did not evaluate student learning or teacher performance outcomes from using ChatGPT in class. Instead, it assessed 29 pre-service teachers’ ChatGPT-integrated lesson plans with a modified TPACK-based rubric; the average score was M=3.29 (SD=.91) on a 4-point scale, indicating reasonably strong planned integration quality.
findings.measure: Modified TIAR/TPACK-based lesson-plan rubric score

findings.finding_summary: Scores differed by rubric dimension: curriculum goals & ChatGPT (M=3.44, SD=.87), instructional strategies & ChatGPT (M=3.48, SD=.99), ChatGPT function selection(s) (M=3.00, SD=.93), and fit (M=3.24, SD=.83). The paper reports a significant difference between instructional strategies & ChatGPT and ChatGPT function selection(s), t(28)=2.3173, p=.028, suggesting stronger planning for strategy integration than for choosing appropriate ChatGPT functions.
findings.measure: TIAR subscale scores and paired-samples t-test

findings.finding_summary: Qualitative analysis found both appropriate and inappropriate intended uses of ChatGPT in lesson planning. Pre-service teachers saw it as useful for questioning, individualized support, formative assessment, and summarizing role-play scenarios, but also noted risks such as inaccuracies, hallucinated/nonexistent resources, and potential overdependence.
findings.measure: Open-ended survey responses and lesson-plan content analysis

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory qualitative/mixed-methods study of lesson-plan artifacts, not a causal evaluation of classroom implementation or student outcomes. It provides useful descriptive evidence about planned use and perceived benefits/risks, but no randomized or quasi-experimental evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive planning quality and perceived instructional promise, but no measured effect on teacher behavior or student achievement. Any impact is therefore indirect and uncertain rather than demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: LessonPlanner: Assisting Novice Teachers to Prepare Pedagogy-Driven Lesson Plans with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: UIST '24 (The 37th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge novice teachers face when preparing lesson plans: deciding on effective instructional strategies, finding appropriate teaching materials, and organizing those materials into a coherent plan. The authors ask whether large language models can support lesson-plan preparation in a way that is more structured and pedagogy-informed than a generic chat interface.

To study this, the authors built LessonPlanner, a web-based system powered by GPT-4 that guides users through lesson-goal setting, outline generation, and section-by-section refinement using Gagne’s Nine Events of Instruction and Bloom’s Taxonomy. The system includes preset prompts, instructional-event templates, a sidebar assistant, editable markdown output, and options to regenerate or contextualize LLM responses. The study focused on novice teachers and teaching assistants, plus a few more experienced teachers in follow-up interviews.

The evaluation combined a formative interview/co-design study, a within-subjects comparison between LessonPlanner and a baseline ChatGPT web interface, and expert interviews. In the within-subjects study, 12 university students with teaching experience prepared lesson plans for familiar computer-science topics; an expert teacher rated the resulting plans for quality, and participants reported workload and usability perceptions. The paper concludes that LessonPlanner improves the quality of produced lesson plans and reduces workload relative to a generic ChatGPT interface, while also surfacing important concerns about accuracy, trust, and the need for teacher control over generated content.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational large language model interface for generating and refining text.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the baseline web interface in a within-subjects study; participants could use the ChatGPT web app to prepare lesson plans, with GPT-4 as the underlying model.

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT served as the baseline comparator rather than the intervention. The paper reports that LessonPlanner significantly improved the quality of outcome lesson plans and reduced workload compared with the baseline ChatGPT interface, but it does not provide a separate quantitative result for ChatGPT itself.
findings.measure: Lesson plan quality and planning workload compared against the baseline ChatGPT web app

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a within-subjects user study with qualitative interviews and Likert-scale ratings, not a randomized controlled trial of instructional outcomes in classrooms. The evidence is useful for usability and artifact quality but does not establish causal effects on teacher behavior or student learning.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports improved lesson-plan artifact quality and reduced planning workload when using LessonPlanner versus the ChatGPT baseline, but no effect sizes are reported. The practical impact appears modest and is limited to planning artifacts rather than demonstrated classroom or student outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: How Can Video Generative AI Transform K-12 Education? Examining Teachers’ Perspectives through TPACK and TAM
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers perceive the educational potential and limitations of video generative AI (Video GenAI), an emerging form of AI that can create video from natural-language prompts. The study is framed by TPACK and TAM, and asks what teachers’ first impressions are, what educational uses they envision, and what barriers they anticipate for classroom adoption.

The researchers conducted online semi-structured interviews with 10 purposively selected participants: eight elementary school teachers, one high school English teacher, and one former elementary teacher who worked as a data analyst. Participants were given access to Luma Dream Machine and an instructional guide so they could experiment with the tool before discussing it. The context was K-12 education in South Korea, and the study focused on teachers with comparatively strong interest in and experience with educational technology and AI.

Findings suggest that teachers saw Video GenAI as promising for visualizing abstract content, supporting creative expression, enriching project-based learning, and enabling new forms of formative and summative assessment. At the same time, they raised substantial concerns about technical quality, language support, hallucinations, safety, copyright, age restrictions, infrastructure, and the lack of institutional guidance. The paper concludes that Video GenAI could be pedagogically valuable, but only if technical, ethical, and policy barriers are addressed and teachers receive appropriate professional development and support.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI video creation tool for producing dynamic, customized visual content from natural language prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers were given access to Luma Dream Machine, a video generation AI platform, and an educational guide so they could experiment with video generation and discuss its K-12 instructional applications in interviews.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative interview study of ten selected teachers’ perceptions and hands-on impressions, not an experimental or quasi-experimental evaluation of outcomes. It does not measure teacher-practice change or student outcomes, so causal evidence strength is low.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes or outcome impacts are reported, and the paper focuses on perceived potential, barriers, and intended use rather than demonstrated impact. The evidence does not establish measurable benefit on instruction or learning.

paper_profiles.title: AI Coach Assist: An Automated Approach for Call Recommendation in Contact Centers for Agent Coaching
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of helping contact center supervisors identify which customer-agent calls are most useful for coaching. The authors argue that manual review and random sampling of calls are time-consuming and inefficient, and propose an AI-based call recommendation system that prioritizes calls likely to contain coachable moments.

The intervention studied is AI Coach Assist, a text classification system that combines a supervisor’s quality-assurance question with an ASR transcript of a call and predicts whether the call is coachable for that question. The system is implemented with fine-tuned transformer models, especially DialogLED for higher accuracy and DistilBERT for a more efficient deployment option. The paper also compares these models against TF-IDF plus classical machine-learning baselines and reports ablation results showing that including the question text and allowing longer input sequences improve performance.

The data come from real-world contact centers and include 58 coaching questions paired with call transcripts annotated by contact center managers and supervisors. The paper does not study K-12 teachers or students; instead, it focuses on adult contact-center personnel in a business setting. The authors conclude that their system can improve the efficiency of coaching workflows by helping managers select calls for manual review, while explicitly not replacing human judgment or automating performance scoring.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A transformer-based text classification system that uses a query and call transcript to predict whether a call is coachable for agent coaching.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to recommend contact-center calls for coaching by predicting whether a call/transcript pair is coachable for a given manager question; specifically compared DistilBERT and DialogLED variants, but no single commercial named product was studied.

findings.finding_summary: On the QA Scorecard test set, the DialogLED-based AI Coach Assist model achieved accuracy of 70.52 and precision of 67.92, outperforming the DistilBERT variant (accuracy 66.25, precision 62.53). The paper frames this as improving call selection efficiency for human coaching, not replacing human review.
findings.measure: Classification performance for coachable vs. not coachable call-transcript pairs

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single technical model-development paper with offline classification experiments, not an RCT, QED, or field study of coaching outcomes. The paper evaluates prediction performance only, without causal evidence on teacher or agent behavior change.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported model performance is moderate and relevant for operational triage, but there is no reported effect size on downstream coaching effectiveness. Because the outcome is predictive accuracy rather than behavior or learning impact, the practical impact remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Garbage Collection Makes Rust Easier to Use: A Randomized Controlled Trial of the Bronze Garbage Collector
paper_profiles.venue: ICSE ’22 (44th International Conference on Software Engineering)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether adding an optional garbage-collection abstraction to Rust can make the language easier and more productive to use for novice programmers. The authors focus on a common pain point in Rust: ownership, borrowing, lifetimes, and aliasing, especially when implementing data structures that need multiple references or mutable aliases.

To test this, they designed Bronze, a library-based garbage collector for Rust with a GC reference type (GcRef<T>) that simplifies aliasing and mutable shared access. They ran a randomized controlled trial in a sophomore-level programming languages course, assigning students to either use Bronze or use traditional Rust across a multi-part programming assignment. The assignment moved from basic syntax to ownership/borrowing and then to a more difficult aliasing task involving parent-child links and caches.

The study involved students enrolled in a required programming course at one university in the United States. Quantitative outcomes included task completion and self-reported time; the authors also collected survey responses and free-text comments. Bronze improved completion and reduced time on the hardest aliasing task among those who finished it, but did not improve total time across the whole assignment because Bronze students later redid the aliasing task without GC. The paper concludes that GC can substantially reduce architectural and aliasing complexity for Rust newcomers, though learning Rust’s core ownership concepts remains necessary.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / chatbot-style system that produces or adapts text and could be used for feedback or instructional support, without a specific named product identified in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Not studied in this paper. The paper is about the Bronze garbage collector for Rust, a programming-language usability intervention, not an AI tool.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an RCT, but it does not evaluate any AI tutoring, feedback, or generative tool. The intervention is a Rust garbage-collection library, so there is no AI-tool evidence to extract.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No AI system is studied, so there is no instructional or learning impact attributable to an AI tool. The reported effects concern programming-language usability, not teacher coaching or lesson feedback.

paper_profiles.title: Teacher-student relationship and teaching styles in primary education. A model of analysis.
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Professional Capital and Community
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether students’ perceptions of their teachers’ teaching styles are associated with their perceptions of the teacher-student relationship in primary education. The authors focus on two teaching-style dimensions—directive and participative—and two relationship dimensions—emotional and educational—arguing that these constructs are often studied separately but should be analyzed together.

Using survey data from the 2018/2019 Diagnostic Assessment in the Canary Islands, the study applies structural equation modeling to 21,126 sixth-grade students in 623 schools. The latent variables are constructed from existing questionnaire items rather than from direct observation. The paper also compares perceptions across student subgroups defined by gender, relative age, and parents’ educational level.

The findings indicate that participative teaching style is more strongly associated with both emotional and educational teacher-student relationships than directive style. The directive style relates more to the educational relationship than the emotional one, while participative style is more strongly linked to the emotional relationship. The study also finds that perceptions differ by gender and parental education, with girls generally perceiving more participative teaching and more positive relationships, and students from less-educated families perceiving directive teaching more clearly. The paper concludes that student feedback can be used to model classroom relationships, but it is limited by the use of pre-existing questionnaire data and the absence of some dimensions such as discipline/conflict management.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system is an adaptive educational system that provides instruction, practice, and feedback based on learner responses.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper does not study an AI tool; it cites prior literature on teaching styles and teacher-student relationships, including references to student feedback questionnaires and related educational constructs.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a correlational, non-AI paper analyzing relationships between teaching styles and teacher-student perceptions using survey data and SEM. It does not evaluate an AI tool, so there is no tool-level evidence quality to rate beyond the paper being non-experimental for AI.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No AI intervention or AI-assisted coaching tool is studied, so there is no direct impact on instructional coaching or lesson-plan feedback to assess.

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper examines how elementary school students and teachers perceived a generative-AI-powered tool for creative mathematical writing. The central question is not whether the tool improves test scores or teacher practice relative to another condition, but rather what educational benefits and challenges participants experienced when using GenAI to co-create math stories.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI system based on GPT models for text and image generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in the developed classroom technology to generate draft mathematical stories from student inputs; the paper states the platform integrated OpenAI’s GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 for story and image generation.

findings.finding_summary: This was a qualitative classroom study, not a comparative trial. Across 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers, participants reported benefits such as supporting creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and interest/ownership, but also challenges including weak critical evaluation, limited room for improvement, reduced autonomy, weak social connection, and limited accessibility.
findings.measure: Students’ and teachers’ perceptions from semi-structured interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI system used to create text and images in educational settings.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies a GenAI-powered classroom tool for creative mathematical writing, but the specific product is anonymized in the paper and only its use with GPT-4/DALL�e8 3 is described.

findings.finding_summary: This was a qualitative classroom implementation with 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers. Participants perceived the GenAI-supported writing activity as beneficial for creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and engagement, while also identifying problems such as insufficient feedback, over-perfection, lack of autonomy, and lack of social/accessible communication features.
findings.measure: Perceptions from interviews, open-ended surveys, and observation notes

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The study is a qualitative/mixed-methods classroom implementation with interviews, surveys, and observations, not a randomized or quasi-experimental comparative evaluation. It provides useful descriptive evidence, but not causal evidence on teacher coaching, lesson-plan feedback, or student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes or comparative outcome data are reported, so impact on practice or achievement cannot be quantified. The paper suggests potentially meaningful pedagogical value, but the evidence is perception-based rather than outcome-based.

paper_profiles.title: One Small Step for Generative AI, One Giant Leap for AGI: A Complete Survey on ChatGPT in AIGC Era
paper_profiles.venue: ACM (survey article; manuscript submitted to ACM / arXiv preprint)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of ChatGPT and related generative AI systems in the AIGC era. It addresses the rapid emergence of ChatGPT after its 2022 release and the need for a consolidated review of its technology, capabilities, applications, challenges, and future trajectory toward AGI. Rather than focusing on a single empirical question or a specific educational intervention, the paper synthesizes existing literature and public reports on the model and its uses.

The survey organizes prior work around the technical foundations of ChatGPT, including Transformer architectures, autoregressive modeling, and the GPT model lineage from GPT-1 through GPT-4. It also reviews application areas such as scientific writing, education, medicine, software development, and management, with education discussed as one application domain among several. The education section describes potential uses for teaching, learning, assessment, and course-material generation, but does not report a primary study of teachers, students, or classrooms conducted by the survey authors.

The paper’s main conclusion is that ChatGPT is a highly capable general-purpose generative AI tool with broad promise, but it remains limited by factual errors, logical inconsistency, lack of self-awareness, and misuse risks such as plagiarism and misinformation. The authors argue that ChatGPT may substantially reshape writing, learning, and professional workflows, while emphasizing the need for careful human oversight and stronger safeguards. For the specific research topic of comparative evidence on teacher coaching or lesson-plan feedback, this paper does not provide direct experimental evidence; it is a descriptive synthesis rather than an evaluation of intervention effects.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot based on the GPT family, capable of text generation and multimodal input in newer versions.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a survey of ChatGPT, describing its technology, capabilities, applications, and challenges across domains including education.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative survey paper, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool. It does not report a controlled study, quasi-experiment, or field study with measurable outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No intervention effects or outcome measures are reported, so there is no evidence of impact to rate.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Effect of Activity-Based Method of Teaching Mathematics on Nigerian Secondary School Students’ Achievement in Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an activity-based teaching method improves secondary school students’ achievement in mathematics compared with the conventional lecture method. The study is motivated by persistent poor performance in mathematics among Nigerian secondary school students and asks whether a more interactive, student-centered approach can produce better test outcomes.

The intervention was an activity-based mathematics teaching approach applied to topics in circle geometry and construction. The comparison condition was lecture-based instruction. The study used a pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design with intact classes and ANCOVA to adjust for pretest differences, allowing comparison of posttest achievement between the two groups.

Participants were 96 Senior Secondary II students from two government-owned schools in Calabar Metropolis, Cross River State, Nigeria.
