The paper reports that students in the activity-based group outperformed those in the lecture group on the posttest after controlling for pretest scores. The author concludes that activity-based instruction can increase mathematics achievement and recommends teacher training and the provision of materials to support its use in secondary schools.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Computer-assisted instruction or teacher-led instructional intervention used to support learning, typically through structured lessons or activities rather than a specific commercial AI product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studied an activity-based teaching method versus lecture method in secondary school mathematics; no AI system, generative model, or named educational technology product was evaluated.

findings.finding_summary: This paper is not an AI-tool study; it reports a quasi-experimental comparison of activity-based teaching versus lecture teaching in mathematics. Students in the activity-based group had higher posttest mean scores (51.71) than the lecture group (29.56) after controlling for pretest scores, with ANCOVA showing a significant group effect (F=114.461, p<0.05, partial eta squared=0.261).
findings.measure: 20-item Mathematics Test (pretest/posttest essay test)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The paper uses a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design with ANCOVA, but it evaluates a conventional teaching method rather than an AI tool. This is empirical education research, but not evidence about generative AI or instructional coaching technology.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported group effect is moderate to large (partial eta squared=0.261), indicating meaningful academic impact for the instructional intervention. However, because the intervention is not an AI tool and the study does not address teacher coaching or feedback systems, the relevance to the requested topic is limited.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an analytical AI platform can improve lesson-plan quality in vocational teacher education, and whether it performs as well as or better than human feedback. The authors focus on a practical problem in teacher education: providing detailed, individualized feedback on complex lesson plans is time-consuming for university instructors, especially when many didactic principles must be addressed.

The intervention was EDDA, an analytical AI system that classifies lesson plans and returns expert-level feedback on ten main and 57 subcategories related to vocational business education. In the study, one group of student teachers received AI feedback throughout a semester, supplemented by human feedback when needed; the comparison group received human feedback only. Both groups completed the same course tasks and planning conditions, and lesson plans were evaluated at the beginning and end of the semester using content analysis. The study also measured several meta-dimensions, including AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competences, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and motivation.

The sample consisted of 103 master’s students in business education in Germany, organized into small planning groups. The results suggest that AI feedback can match or exceed human feedback on some lesson-planning dimensions, including certain sustainability-related criteria, action orientation, relatedness, technology use, lesson structure, and learner engagement. However, simply using the AI system did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes toward AI, or motivation. The authors conclude that analytical AI can effectively supplement traditional feedback, but should be embedded in a broader pedagogical framework rather than treated as a standalone solution.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI/LLM chatbots used to generate or provide feedback on text-based educational artifacts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper contrasts its analytical AI feedback platform with the broader class of generative AI tools discussed in the literature; however, the empirical study itself evaluates the named analytical platform EDDA rather than a generative chatbot.

identified_tools.name: Adaptive Feedback System (General)
identified_tools.description: An AI-based feedback system that analyzes learner-created artifacts and returns individualized, criterion-linked feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies EDDA, an analytical AI platform for lesson-plan feedback in teacher education. EDDA classifies uploaded lesson plans/materials and provides expert-level text and visual feedback, then compares that feedback with human feedback over a semester.

findings.finding_summary: In a longitudinal intervention with N=103 vocational teacher education students (n=55 AI feedback; n=48 human feedback), the AI feedback platform matched or surpassed human feedback on some lesson-plan dimensions but not all. The abstract reports improvements in certain content-related sustainability aspects, action orientation, relatedness, technology use, lesson structure, and learner engagement, while the Results section specifies significant positive effects for some sustainability-related subdimensions (e.g., SDG 15, social competences, reflexivity) but not others.
findings.measure: Content analysis ratings of lesson plans for didactic criteria and planning dimensions

findings.finding_summary: For the meta-dimensions, the study found that the mere use of AI did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, motivation, or related self-efficacy. The authors report no clear intervention effect on the broader attitudinal/motivational measures, even though some planning-dimension ratings improved.
findings.measure: Questionnaire-based measures of AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competences, SWIT self-efficacy, and basic-needs motivation across the semester

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal quasi-experimental intervention study with a comparison group and repeated measures, but assignment was not randomized and groups came from different course contexts/universities. The design is fairly strong for field evidence, yet there are notable threats to internal validity.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive effects on some lesson-plan quality dimensions and no broad gains on AI literacy or motivation, suggesting modest and domain-specific impact rather than a large generalized effect.

paper_profiles.title: Improving Instructional Practice through Peer Observation and Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what is known about peer observation and feedback as a way to improve instructional practice, especially in light of concerns that principal-led teacher evaluation is time-consuming, uneven in quality, and often insufficiently useful for instructional improvement. The authors frame peer coaching as a potentially more scalable and collaborative alternative to traditional administrator-centered supervision.

The paper is a systematic review of peer observation and feedback literature. The authors searched multiple education databases and, after screening, included 38 documents spanning 1984 to 2019. The reviewed studies covered pre-service and in-service teachers in a range of settings, with most studies qualitative or mixed-methods and only a small number using quantitative or quasi-experimental designs. The population contexts included elementary, secondary, and some higher-education teacher preparation settings across multiple countries.

The review concludes that peer observation and feedback is promising for instructional improvement, but the evidence base remains limited and uneven. Across studies, the most consistent reported benefits were increased collaboration, reflection, confidence, and some changes in instructional practice; however, the literature was small-scale, heterogeneous, and often lacked rigorous comparison groups. The authors emphasize that more piloting and stronger research are needed to identify which peer coaching models work best and under what conditions.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring or coaching system that provides instructional support, feedback, or guidance to learners or teachers.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper does not study an AI tool; it is a systematic review of peer observation and feedback among human teachers, including peer coaching and reciprocal coaching models.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of human peer observation and feedback, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool. The paper synthesizes heterogeneous teacher coaching studies rather than testing a specific intervention with randomized or quasi-experimental design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No AI tool or measurable AI-related intervention effect is reported. The review discusses potential instructional-improvement benefits of peer coaching, but these are human-to-human processes and not attributable to an AI system.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can function as an automated teacher coach for classroom instruction. The authors focus on three tasks: scoring transcript segments using established classroom observation rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the NCTE transcript dataset of elementary mathematics classrooms in the United States. The dataset includes video-derived transcripts from 317 teachers across four school districts, with human expert ratings from the CLASS and MQI observation instruments. ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) is evaluated in zero-shot mode on transcript segments, and its outputs are compared against human ratings for score prediction and assessed by experienced math teachers for helpfulness, relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

The paper finds that ChatGPT performs poorly at predicting observation scores and often produces feedback that is relevant but not insightful or novel. For task-based suggestions, 82% of the model’s suggestions simply restate something the teacher already does in the transcript. The authors conclude that current generative AI may be a useful starting point for scalable teacher feedback, but it is not yet a substitute for expert coaching and needs substantial improvement before being used as a reliable teacher-coaching tool.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational large language model / chatbot system used for text generation and evaluation tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated zero-shot as an automated teacher coach for K-12 elementary math classroom transcripts, including scoring rubric items, identifying highlights and missed opportunities, and generating actionable suggestions for eliciting student reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: Across CLASS and MQI scoring tasks, ChatGPT showed low correspondence with expert human ratings. Reported Spearman correlations were near zero to modest at best across items and prompting methods (e.g., CLBM reached 0.35 under direct-answer prompting, while most other correlations were close to 0 or negative), indicating weak alignment with human rubric scores on transcript segments (sample sizes for the correlation analysis were not fully reported; the paper states 100 transcript segments were sampled for Task A).
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between model-predicted observation scores and human annotator scores on CLASS and MQI transcript segments

findings.finding_summary: For identifying highlights and missed opportunities, teachers generally rated ChatGPT’s responses as insufficiently relevant and insightful, though faithfulness was somewhat better. The paper reports that on CLASS items, 22% of responses were rated not faithful, 35% not relevant, and 51% not insightful; on MQI items, the corresponding 'No' rates were 29%, 55%, and 71%, respectively. The authors note that MQI results were worse than CLASS across all evaluation dimensions (n=216 CLASS items; n=288 MQI items).
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for model-generated highlights and missed opportunities
findings.sample_size: n=216 CLASS items; n=288 MQI items

findings.finding_summary: For generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student reasoning, teachers found the suggestions largely faithful, relevant, and actionable, but often redundant. The most notable result was that 82% of suggestions repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript, indicating poor novelty; at the same time, most suggestions were judged actionable and contextually faithful (n=36 suggestions).
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, actionability, and novelty for generated suggestions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-scale empirical validation study using expert ratings, not a randomized or quasi-experimental field study. It provides useful evidence about model output quality, but the design is primarily qualitative/correlational and does not test real-world teacher or student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows limited and mixed utility for ChatGPT in coaching-related tasks, with weak score prediction and substantial redundancy/non-insightfulness in feedback. Because no meaningful behavior-change or student-outcome effect is demonstrated, the practical impact appears modest and unclear.

paper_profiles.title: ClassMind: Scaling Classroom Observation and Instructional Feedback with Multimodal AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of scaling classroom observation and instructional coaching, which are widely regarded as effective but are constrained by cost, limited coach availability, and inconsistent coverage of classroom practice. The authors argue that recent generative multimodal AI can help provide more timely and personalized instructional feedback by analyzing full-length classroom recordings and related artifacts.

The intervention studied is ClassMind, an open-source AI system that ingests lesson videos, transcripts, slides, and optional lesson materials, then generates rubric-aligned feedback grounded in established frameworks such as Danielson, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and COPUS. Its core technical component, AVA-Align, is designed to provide temporally precise, evidence-linked feedback with strengths, weaknesses, and actionable suggestions. The system was technically evaluated against video-agent baselines on a small set of ATLAS videos and showed stronger factuality and more pedagogically meaningful feedback.

The empirical component included formative studies with PK–12 teachers in the United States and semi-structured interviews with secondary teachers and instructional coaches. These studies were not randomized or comparative user trials; instead, they focused on design requirements, perceptions of usefulness, trust, privacy, and workflow fit. Participants generally valued the system’s objectivity, full-lesson coverage, and actionable suggestions, while also expressing concerns about accountability, explainability, and the limits of AI relative to human coaching. Overall, the paper concludes that multimodal generative AI may complement human coaching by scaling observation and feedback, but it does not provide direct evidence of teacher behavior change or student outcomes.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A multimodal generative AI classroom observation and instructional feedback system that analyzes lesson recordings, transcripts, slides, and other context to produce rubric-aligned teaching feedback, annotations, and actionable suggestions.
identified_tools.use_case: ClassMind was proposed and evaluated as an AI coaching prototype for classroom observation and instructional feedback for teachers, including feedback on full lessons, lesson-level reflection, and rubric-aligned comments.

findings.finding_summary: In a simulated-user role-play study with n=6 secondary-school teachers, participants rated the system as highly usable overall (USE M=5.9/7, 95% CI [5.5, 6.4]). Ease of Learning was strongest (M=6.7), followed by Ease of Use (M=6.1), suggesting the prototype was easy to adopt for reviewing instructional feedback.
findings.measure: Usefulness, Satisfaction, and Ease of use Questionnaire (USE)

findings.finding_summary: Self-reported workload was modest overall (NASA-TLX raw overall M=28.5/100, 95% CI [18.1, 38.9]). Participants reported relatively higher mental demand and effort than physical, temporal demand, or frustration, indicating that the main burden was interpreting feedback rather than using the tool itself.
findings.measure: NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX)

findings.finding_summary: Perceptions of responsible AI were positive overall (FATE total M=5.8, 95% CI [5.4, 6.2]). Teachers rated fairness and causability especially highly, but noted some concerns about accountability and explainability, indicating trust in the system’s impartiality with a desire for more transparency.
findings.measure: Fairness, Accountability, Transparency, and Explainability Questionnaire (FATE)

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the system helped them identify classroom patterns, connect observations to professional frameworks, and reflect on their own practice. The paper presents these as qualitative gains in reflection and sense-making, but it does not report student outcomes or a controlled comparison against human coaching or no-feedback baselines.
findings.measure: Semi-structured interview themes and reflection logs

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods formative prototype study with a very small sample and no randomized, quasi-experimental, or longitudinal impact evaluation. The evidence is useful for design and usability but does not establish causal effects on teacher practice or student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potential operational benefits such as usability and manageable workload, but reported outcomes are mostly self-report and qualitative. There is no demonstrated medium or large effect on teacher behavior or student learning, so impact remains exploratory.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring LLM-Generated Feedback for Economics Essays: How Teaching Assistants Evaluate and Envision Its Use
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-generated feedback can support instructors’ grading of student writing, focusing on the question of how teaching assistants (TAs) perceive the quality and usability of LLM-generated feedback as suggestions in their workflow. Rather than testing student learning outcomes, the study investigates instructor-facing use of generative AI for feedback provision and the conditions under which it may be useful.

The authors built an LLM-powered feedback engine for short economics essays in a foundational college ECON101 course. The system decomposes feedback generation into three steps: identifying relevant evidence in the essay, judging whether rubric criteria are met, and generating rubric-aligned feedback. It also visualizes highlights and intermediate outputs in a Word plugin, and in one variant retrieves historic instructor feedback when a rubric is missed. The study involved 5 teaching assistants who first graded essays as usual and then participated in think-aloud sessions reviewing AI feedback on the same essays across 4 writing assignments over 20 one-hour sessions.

The TAs reported that AI feedback was often more detailed, more positive, and more closely aligned to rubrics than their own comments, and that the highlighting interface could speed up reading and make AI suggestions easier to verify. They also noted important limitations: the AI could be overly rigid, miss deeper conceptual issues, and over-focus on rubric fragments rather than holistic writing quality. Overall, the paper concludes that AI feedback has promise as a suggestion tool for grading support, but only when paired with clear rubrics, transparent highlights, and human judgment; it does not evaluate downstream effects on student performance.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI GPT-based large language model used to generate and evaluate feedback text.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the underlying model (GPT-4o) in a feedback engine that identified relevant essay sentences, made rubric judgments, and generated feedback comments for economics essays shown to teaching assistants.

findings.finding_summary: In think-aloud sessions, 5 teaching assistants across 20 one-hour sessions reported that AI feedback could expedite grading, save time constructing comments, and improve consistency in their workflow. This was a qualitative mixed-methods study; no experimental effect sizes were reported.
findings.measure: TA perceptions of grading speed, time savings, and grading consistency

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative think-aloud study with 5 TAs and no experimental comparison of outcomes. It provides useful user-perspective evidence, but not causal evidence about learning or practice change.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Participants perceived the tool as potentially helpful for speeding grading and improving consistency, but the paper did not report measured effect sizes or demonstrated behavior or student outcome impacts.

paper_profiles.title: Language Alignment via Nash-learning and Adaptive feedback
paper_profiles.venue: ICML 2024 Workshop on Models of Human Feedback for AI Alignment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of aligning large language models without relying on a learned preference model or a human-annotated preference dataset. The authors position their work in the broader alignment literature, contrasting reinforcement learning from human feedback and related Nash-learning approaches with a new method that can operate using adaptive self-evaluation.

The proposed approach, Language Alignment via Nash-learning and Adaptive feedback (LANA), reformulates alignment as a two-player game solved with mirror descent / mirror ascent updates. In the proposed training loop, each policy generates candidate responses, then uses an evaluation prompt to compare responses and treat the preferred answer as coming from an improved opponent. This creates a self-rewarding alignment process intended to improve the model without external preference labels.

Experiments are conducted on instruction-tuned language models, primarily Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct, using 3K prompts from public instruction datasets and evaluated with automatic benchmarks such as AlpacaEval, MT-Bench, and LLM-Evaluation Harness tasks. The paper reports modest gains in preference-based evaluation and claims no clear degradation on reasoning benchmarks, while noting that performance depends strongly on the base model quality. Overall, the paper is a theoretical/methods contribution for LLM alignment rather than a study of educational interventions, teachers, or K–12 settings.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model / instruction-tuned generative AI system used for self-alignment and preference-style feedback without a named commercial product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and evaluates LANA, a self-rewarding alignment algorithm in which the model generates two responses to a prompt and then uses adaptive self-evaluation feedback to choose the preferred response during training. Experiments are conducted on instruction-following and benchmark tasks using Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct as the base model, with comparisons to other open models in ablations.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that training with LANA on 3K prompts improved AlpacaEval results versus the base model. Table 1 shows LANA at 22.50 LC win rate and 21.35 win rate compared with Phi-mini at 20.84 LC win rate and 19.98 win rate (standard deviations 1.26 and 1.20, respectively).
findings.measure: AlpacaEval LC win rate and win rate

findings.finding_summary: On reasoning benchmarks, the paper reports no noticeable drop relative to the base model, and a slight improvement on GSM8K in MT-Bench, although the tableed values on GSM8K-5shot are slightly lower for LANA than base (0.7703 vs 0.7756). The reported benchmark set also includes HellaSwag and ARC-Challenge, where LANA is marginally below the base model.
findings.measure: LLM-Evaluation Harness / MT-Bench reasoning benchmark scores

findings.finding_summary: Using UltraFeedback test data and OpenHermes preference categories, the authors report that LANA improved win rate across all task categories, with more noticeable gains in riddle, theory-of-mind, and plan categories. No numerical effect sizes are provided in the text excerpt.
findings.measure: Win rate across preference-data categories

findings.finding_summary: An ablation study found negligible improvements when the base model was Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1 or Gemma-2b-it, suggesting that the base model choice is important for the method to work well. The paper does not report quantitative effect sizes for this ablation in the excerpt.
findings.measure: Ablation comparison across base models

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical / algorithmic paper on LLM alignment, not an empirical K-12 education study. It does not evaluate teacher coaching, lesson-plan feedback, or student outcomes in an educational setting.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct instructional-coaching or K-12 classroom impact measured. The reported results are limited to model-alignment and benchmark performance, so educational impact is not established.

paper_profiles.title: Using Transformers to Provide Teachers with Personalized Feedback on their Classroom Discourse: The TalkMoves Application
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes TalkMoves, an AI-enabled system intended to automatically analyze K–12 mathematics classroom recordings and provide teachers with personalized feedback on their instructional discourse practices. The core instructional target is the use of “talk moves,” a set of accountable-talk strategies that support student participation, mathematical reasoning, and more productive classroom conversations. The paper’s main technical contribution is the development and evaluation of transformer-based models for classifying teacher utterances into six talk-move categories plus a none class, with the goal of turning those classifications into actionable feedback for teachers.

The system uses speech recognition and natural-language processing to process classroom audio/video recordings, generate transcripts, classify teacher-student sentence pairs, and present dashboards summarizing discourse features such as talk-move frequency, teacher versus student talk, wait time, and student one-word responses. The paper reports multiple model experiments on 501 transcripts of K–12 math lessons, with best test performance around F1 = 79.33% for RoBERTa-Large. It also describes the feedback interface and a pilot deployment to 21 teachers in two Midwestern U.S. school districts during the 2019–2020 academic year, where teachers recorded lessons, reviewed feedback, and participated in surveys and interviews.

The main conclusion is that modern transformer models can approximate expert annotation of classroom discourse reasonably well and can be integrated into an end-to-end system that provides scalable feedback to teachers. However, the paper is primarily a system-development and model-evaluation study rather than a causal impact study of teacher coaching or student outcomes. It emphasizes technical feasibility, dashboard design, and early pilot feedback rather than experimental evidence that the tool changes teacher practice or improves learning.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: An AI/NLP-based application that automatically analyzes classroom recordings and teacher-student discourse to classify talk moves and generate personalized instructional feedback for K-12 teachers.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as the TalkMoves application for providing K-12 mathematics teachers with automated feedback on classroom discourse and talk moves from lesson recordings.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports model performance for talk-move classification, not teacher or student outcomes. The best-performing model, ROBERTA-LARGE, achieved F1=79.33% and MCC=0.7779 on the test set for classifying six accountable talk moves plus 'none' across 176,757 labeled sentences.
findings.measure: Talk-move classification performance on a held-out test set

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a system-development / model-evaluation paper rather than an experimental study of teacher behavior or student outcomes. It reports classifier performance and pilot use but no controlled comparison against human coaching, peer review, rubric-only self-review, or no-feedback baselines.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported model accuracy is substantial for the classification task (F1=79.33%), but it reflects artifact quality, not demonstrated instructional or learning impact. The paper does not provide causal evidence that the feedback changes teacher practice or student outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Older Adults’ Preferences for Feedback Cadence from an Exercise Coach Robot
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how older adults perceive different cadences of feedback from a robot exercise coach. The authors focus on whether changing the frequency of verbal and nonverbal feedback changes perceived usefulness, clarity, timeliness, and helpfulness of the feedback, rather than measuring exercise performance or behavioral change.

The intervention studied is a robot coach that evaluates bicep curls and lateral raises and provides multimodal feedback through speech, facial expressions, and body movements. The study manipulates the cadence of verbal feedback and nonverbal feedback across six conditions, using prerecorded videos of the robot interacting with an exerciser. The design is intended to isolate preferences for feedback frequency in each modality and how one modality influences perceptions of the other.

The population is 100 adults aged 60+ recruited online through Prolific, so the context is an online video-based user study rather than an in-person coaching trial. Participants watched randomized videos and rated the robot’s feedback on Likert scales. The main finding is that medium or high verbal feedback is generally preferred over low verbal feedback, and medium nonverbal feedback is preferred over low nonverbal feedback. The paper also reports cross-modal effects: altering the cadence of one modality changes perceptions of the other modality as well. The authors conclude that feedback cadence should be tuned to older adults’ preferences, while noting that the results are based on viewing videos of another person and may not generalize to being coached directly.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic AI/robot coach system that evaluates user performance and provides verbal and nonverbal feedback with adjustable cadence.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies an exercise coach robot that gives verbal and nonverbal feedback at different cadences; participants viewed videos of the robot and rated the feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In an online study of older adults (n=100), changing the cadence of verbal feedback affected perceived clarity and helpfulness of the robot’s verbal feedback. Participants preferred medium and high verbal cadence over low cadence for helpfulness, and high over medium for clarity; no effects on actual exercise performance were measured.
findings.measure: 5-point Likert ratings of verbal feedback clarity and helpfulness after viewing robot exercise-coach videos

findings.finding_summary: Changing the cadence of nonverbal feedback affected perceived timeliness and helpfulness of the robot’s nonverbal feedback. Participants preferred medium nonverbal cadence over low cadence for both measures; the study reports repeated-measures ANOVA significance values but no standardized effect sizes.
findings.measure: 5-point Likert ratings of nonverbal feedback timeliness and helpfulness after viewing robot exercise-coach videos

findings.finding_summary: The cadence of verbal feedback also influenced perceptions of nonverbal feedback: medium and high verbal cadence were associated with better perceived clarity and timeliness of nonverbal feedback than low cadence. This was a perception study only, not a comparison of learning or coaching effectiveness on behavior change.
findings.measure: 5-point Likert ratings of nonverbal feedback clarity and timeliness after viewing robot exercise-coach videos

findings.finding_summary: The cadence of nonverbal feedback affected perceptions of verbal feedback timeliness. Participants preferred medium nonverbal cadence when judging verbal feedback timeliness, but the paper does not report a standardized effect size.
findings.measure: 5-point Likert ratings of verbal feedback timeliness after viewing robot exercise-coach videos

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical user study with a clear repeated-measures design, but it is not a K-12 instructional coaching or lesson-feedback study and it measures perceptions from videos rather than behavior change. The evidence is therefore methodologically recognizable but only weakly applicable to the requested educational-use case.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant preference/perception differences, but no effect sizes and no educational or student-outcome impact. Because the outcomes are subjective ratings rather than behavior change, the practical impact for K-12 coaching is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: CANDERE-COACH: Reinforcement Learning from Noisy Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of learning reinforcement learning policies from human-style binary feedback when that feedback is noisy. The authors argue that existing learning-from-feedback methods such as Deep COACH assume perfect teacher feedback, which is unrealistic in practice because human evaluative signals can be incomplete or incorrect due to cognitive load, distraction, or limited expertise.

To address this, the paper proposes CANDERE-COACH, a classifier-augmented noise-detecting and relabeling framework. The method trains a classifier to identify likely clean and noisy feedback from state-action-feedback tuples, filters low-loss samples as clean, and actively relabels suspected noisy samples by flipping binary labels. The approach is evaluated in simulated RL environments rather than in educational settings: Cart Pole, Lunar Lander, and MiniGrid DoorKey, with a scripted expert teacher that provides binary feedback at fixed intervals and injected symmetric noise levels up to 40%.

The experiments show that standard Deep COACH degrades substantially under noisy feedback, especially with limited feedback budgets, while CANDERE-COACH improves robustness and generally outperforms the baselines. The active relabeling component improves performance over the version without relabeling, and online classifier updates help adapt to state-distribution shifts. The paper concludes that the proposed denoising mechanism can enable feedback-based RL under noisy teacher signals and can also be plugged into Deep TAMER, but it remains a simulation-based algorithmic study rather than an empirical study of teachers, students, or classrooms.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning feedback system where a teacher provides binary evaluative feedback to train an agent; in this paper, the system is CANDERE-COACH, a classifier-augmented noise-detecting and relabelling version of COACH for learning from noisy feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and evaluates CANDERE-COACH for RL agents learning from noisy teacher feedback, comparing it against Deep COACH, Deep COACH (Preload), and ablations, with scripted-teacher feedback in Cart Pole, Lunar Lander, and Minigrid Door Key.

findings.finding_summary: Across three Gymnasium domains (Cart Pole, Lunar Lander, and Minigrid Door Key), CANDERE-COACH generally outperformed Deep COACH and Deep COACH (Preload) under noisy feedback, especially at 30% noise. The paper reports that CANDERE-COACH could learn successfully with up to 40% symmetric label noise, while baselines often failed or were unstable; no standardized effect sizes were reported.
findings.measure: Episodic return / accumulated reward during evaluation episodes
findings.sample_size: 10 runs of different seeds; exact trial n not otherwise reported

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/algorithmic RL paper with simulation experiments, not a K-12 instructional coaching study and not an education field trial. The paper does not evaluate a teacher-facing coaching or lesson-feedback product in classrooms.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational practice, teacher behavior, or student outcome impact is measured. Reported gains are confined to simulated RL agent reward in benchmark environments, so there is no K-12 instructional impact evidence.

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Peer, Self, and Teacher Assessments for Generative AI-Enhanced Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teacher, peer, and self-assessments align within a generative AI-enhanced collaborative feedback system (AICoFe) for oral presentations. The central question is not whether AI replaces human feedback, but how human evaluative sources differ in agreement, bias, and correlation when used as inputs for AI-supported feedback generation.

The study uses rubric-based assessments from 46 full evaluation sets collected during a compulsory course for final-year telecommunications engineering undergraduates at Universidad Autonoma de Madrid in Spain. Each presentation was scored by the teacher, two randomly assigned peers, and the presenting student via self-assessment while reviewing a video recording. The same validated 15-item rubric was used across all raters, and the teacher also assigned an independent global grade. The paper analyzes inter-rater agreement, correlations with the teacher’s overall grade, and systematic score differences.

Results show moderate to substantial agreement under Gwet’s AC2, though weighted Cohen’s kappa was lower. Teacher rubric scores aligned most strongly with the teacher’s own global grade, peer ratings were moderately aligned, and self-assessments were the least aligned but still correlated significantly. Peers and students tended to score slightly higher than the teacher. The authors conclude that teacher, peer, and self-assessment each contribute distinct perspectives, and they propose a more nuanced GenAI model that weights evaluator inputs differently and detects bias rather than averaging all sources equally.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model–based feedback system that can aggregate human assessments, detect bias, and generate personalized feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies the AICoFe collaborative feedback system and proposes an enhanced GenAI model (GePeTo) that integrates teacher, peer, and self-assessments to generate personalized feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In this correlational study with n=46 evaluation sets, the proposed GenAI-enhanced feedback approach was informed by moderate-to-substantial agreement across teacher, peer, and self-assessment sources. The paper reports that combining evaluators yielded strong alignment with the teacher’s overall grade (r=0.85, ρ=0.86 for the mean rubric score across all evaluators), but the study did not test downstream changes in teacher practice or student learning.
findings.measure: Agreement/correlation between rubric-based evaluations and the teacher’s overall grade; inter-rater agreement indices

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical correlational study with a small sample (n=46) and no randomized or quasi-experimental comparison of GenAI versus human feedback. It provides descriptive evidence about evaluator agreement and bias, but not causal evidence of impact on teacher practice or student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The strongest reported association is large (r=0.85), but it reflects correlation among ratings rather than a demonstrated intervention effect. Because no behavior-change or learning outcome was measured, practical impact remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: How Useful is Intermittent, Asynchronous Expert Feedback for Bayesian Optimization?
paper_profiles.venue: 6th Symposium on Advances in Approximate Bayesian Inference (Workshop, non-archival)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether small amounts of intermittently arriving expert feedback can improve Bayesian optimization (BO) when feedback must be incorporated asynchronously and without blocking the optimization loop. The motivation is self-driving laboratory settings, where minimizing human interruption is important, but occasional expert intuition may still be valuable for steering search.

The proposed approach separates BO into two concurrent threads: one performs standard BO over a black-box objective, while the other gathers sparse pairwise expert preferences and fits a Bayesian Bradley-Terry preference model. The learned preference model is then injected into the BO acquisition function through a Thompson-sampling-style scalarization, allowing the optimizer to balance objective improvement with expert preferences. The paper also explores variants for selecting which pairs are shown to the expert, including random selection and active-learning-style acquisition rules.

Experiments are conducted on synthetic toy functions and on real-world chemistry / drug-discovery benchmark datasets. No human participants are studied directly; instead, expert feedback is simulated from hidden scoring functions or pretrained preference models. The results suggest that even low-frequency asynchronous feedback can improve BO performance and can also bias solutions toward constrained or preferred regions of the search space, although some surrogate-feedback combinations perform worse and active-learning heuristics are not consistently better than random pair selection.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic AI feedback system using Bayesian optimization with asynchronous expert preference learning; no specific commercial LLM or named educational product is studied.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies an online, non-blocking Bayesian optimization framework that incorporates intermittent expert pairwise feedback via a Bayesian Bradley-Terry neural network and uses it to steer exploration-exploitation.

findings.finding_summary: In toy optimization tasks and chemistry datasets, intermittent asynchronous expert feedback improved Bayesian optimization relative to a no-feedback baseline. The authors report that with feedback probability pfb=0.1, 'less than 100 randomly-arriving labeled pairs on average' made the GP surrogate significantly better across all test problems; for the LA surrogate, results were mixed and in some cases (Hartmann) performance degraded when γ was fixed at 1.
findings.measure: Optimization performance on toy benchmark functions and docking score optimization on real-world chemistry datasets

findings.finding_summary: When the feedback-selection policy used BALD or minimized pairwise Thompson-sample differences, performance was worse than random selection across the board. The authors conclude these active-learning strategies were not suitable in this intermittent-feedback setting.
findings.measure: BO performance under active-learning selection strategies for expert feedback versus random selection

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a methodological/algorithmic workshop paper, not an educational RCT, QED, or field study. It provides simulation results only, with no K–12 teacher or student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not evaluate an educational intervention, instructional coaching tool, or teacher practice outcome. Any reported gains are in Bayesian optimization simulations, not in schooling contexts.

paper_profiles.title: AI, Expert or Peer? Examining the Impact of Perceived Feedback Source on Pre-Service Teachers Feedback Perception and Uptake
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether pre-service teachers’ perceptions and uptake of feedback depend on the perceived source of the feedback, specifically comparing LLM-generated feedback with expert- and peer-generated feedback. The authors focus on a key gap in feedback research: whether bias toward or against AI changes not only how feedback is judged, but also whether it is actually used.

In a randomized experiment, 273 bachelor’s students in a German teacher-education program received one piece of written feedback on a mathematics learning goal during their practicum-related coursework. The feedback came from one of three sources: an LLM (ChatGPT-4), an expert, or a peer. Participants identified the presumed source, completed a feedback perception questionnaire, and then revised the learning goal to measure feedback uptake. Objective feedback quality was independently coded and controlled for in the analyses.

Results showed that source perceptions strongly shaped cognitive feedback judgments: LLM feedback was rated more favorably when it was misattributed to a human expert, while expert-labeled feedback was often assumed to be higher quality regardless of its true source. Recognition accuracy was low, especially for LLM feedback. However, actual uptake of feedback suggestions was driven only by objective feedback quality, not by perceived source, recognition accuracy, or subjective perceptions. The study concludes that source labels bias perceptions, but behavioral implementation depends primarily on artifact quality rather than the label attached to it.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI GPT-based large language model chatbot used to generate written feedback on a learning goal.
identified_tools.use_case: Generated the LLM feedback messages on a mathematics learning goal; ChatGPT-4 was used with a structured prompt to produce feedback comparable to expert and peer feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized experiment with 273 pre-service teachers, ChatGPT-generated feedback was correctly identified only slightly above chance (36%). Participants rated LLM feedback more positively on cognitive perceptions when they believed it came from a human expert; however, feedback uptake was driven by feedback quality rather than source or recognition accuracy. The LLM condition showed the highest relative uptake at 52% (103 implemented suggestions out of 198 recognized mistakes), but source did not independently predict implementation in the regression model.
findings.measure: Source recognition accuracy; feedback perception (fairness, usefulness, acceptance, willingness to improve, affect); feedback uptake/correction rate
findings.effect_size: recognition accuracy = 36%; relative uptake = 52%; source effects on perception significant for fairness/usefulness (b not reported here)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized experiment with a teacher-education sample and clearly specified measures, but it is a single study with some modeling/measurement limitations and no student achievement outcome. The design is strong for source-perception and uptake effects, but not a full classroom efficacy trial.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports a modest behavioral effect in uptake metrics and stronger effects on perceptions, but the key behavioral predictor was feedback quality rather than the LLM itself. Because the observed impact is real but limited and context-specific, it fits a modest-impact tier.

paper_profiles.title: Distilling Feedback into Memory-as-a-Tool
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes a framework for amortizing inference-time reasoning in large language models by converting transient feedback into persistent, retrievable guidelines stored in a file-based memory system. The core idea is that instead of repeatedly performing self-critique on each new task, the model distills feedback from one interaction into structured memory files and later rereads those lessons when facing related tasks.

The approach is evaluated on the Rubric Feedback Bench, a newly introduced benchmark of 42 rubric-based scenarios spanning creative writing, analytical writing, behavioral/persona-following tasks, and ethical reasoning. The experiments compare a zero-shot baseline, an inference-time self-critique baseline, and the proposed memory-augmented method across three frontier models: Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.1, and Gemini 3 Pro. The setup is not a human-learner study; it is an LLM-agent evaluation in which another model generates rubric-based feedback and scores.

Results show that the memory-based approach rapidly improves over repeated tasks, often matching or approaching the self-critique baseline while substantially reducing inference cost. In a longer mixed-task sequence, the memory-augmented agent outperforms a no-memory baseline and demonstrates that feedback can be consolidated across tasks. The paper concludes that explicit, interpretable memory files can preserve useful critiques as reusable guidelines, yielding a favorable cost-performance tradeoff, although scalability and retrieval complexity remain open issues.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic's Claude family of large language models, used here in an agentic setup with tool calling and persistent file-based memory.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of three frontier LLM agents (alongside GPT-5.1 and Gemini 3 Pro) in a memory-augmented feedback-learning framework. The paper tested Claude Sonnet 4.5 with zero-shot, self-critique, and memory-plus-feedback configurations on the Rubric Feedback Bench and a long-horizon mixed-task sequence.

findings.finding_summary: On the Rubric Feedback Bench continual-learning setup, the memory-plus-feedback configuration for Claude Sonnet 4.5 improved over the zero-shot baseline and matched or exceeded the self-critique baseline after two rounds of feedback. The paper reports that all models benefited from memory, with Claude showing the steepest learning curve, but it does not report task-level n or formal statistical tests.
findings.measure: Mean rubric-based judge scores across sequential tasks on Rubric Feedback Bench

findings.finding_summary: In the long-horizon mixed-task experiment (H = 12), Claude Sonnet 4.5 with memory and feedback achieved a higher final aggregated score than the baseline without memory, with lower variance. The paper reports scores of 0.78 � 0.10 with memory versus 0.52 � 0.25 without memory, but these are judge scores rather than student outcomes and no inferential statistics are reported.
findings.measure: Aggregated judge scores on final tasks of each category in mixed-task sequence

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT family of large language models, used here as an agentic LLM with tool access and persistent memory.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of the frontier models in the same memory-augmented framework, using the GPT-5.1 variant with zero-shot, self-critique, and memory-plus-feedback settings.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that GPT-5.1 benefited from the memory mechanism on the Rubric Feedback Bench, with memory-plus-feedback improving over the zero-shot baseline and approaching the self-critique baseline after iterative feedback. Results are described only at the aggregate trajectory level; the paper does not provide GPT-specific numeric effect sizes, confidence intervals, or sample sizes beyond the 15-example per-model setup.
findings.measure: Mean rubric-based judge scores across sequential tasks on Rubric Feedback Bench

findings.finding_summary: Across the long-horizon mixed-task experiment, the memory-augmented GPT agent is described as showing substantially better performance than the no-memory baseline, consistent with the overall framework result. The paper does not report GPT-specific final scores or inferential statistics for this condition.
findings.measure: Aggregated judge scores on long-horizon mixed-task sequence

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's Gemini family of large language models, used here as an agentic LLM with tool access and persistent memory.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of the three frontier models in the memory-as-a-tool framework, using the Gemini 3 Pro variant under the same zero-shot, self-critique, and memory-plus-feedback conditions.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that Gemini 3 Pro benefited from the memory mechanism on the Rubric Feedback Bench, with performance increasing after feedback and eventually matching or exceeding self-critique on later rounds. No Gemini-specific numerical effect sizes, confidence intervals, or sample sizes are reported beyond the shared experimental design.
findings.measure: Mean rubric-based judge scores across sequential tasks on Rubric Feedback Bench

findings.finding_summary: In the longer mixed-task sequence, the memory-based agent is reported to generalize across heterogeneous tasks better than the baseline without memory. The paper does not provide separate Gemini-only final scores or statistical tests.
findings.measure: Aggregated judge scores on long-horizon mixed-task sequence

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conference paper on an LLM memory framework, not a K-12 teacher coaching study. It reports benchmark scores from synthetic rubric-based tasks rather than classroom, teacher-practice, or student-outcome evidence, and does not use a rigorous educational field-study design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported benchmark gains are moderate in at least one comparison (e.g., 0.78 vs 0.52 on the mixed-task score), but they reflect artifact quality on an AI evaluation benchmark rather than demonstrated instructional impact in K-12 settings.

paper_profiles.title: Attitudes towards and expectations on the role of artificial intelligence in the classroom among digitally skilled Finnish K-12 mathematics teachers
paper_profiles.venue: LUMAT: International Journal on Math, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how digitally skilled Finnish K-12 mathematics teachers view artificial intelligence in school, with a focus on their expectations, attitudes, and perceived opportunities and risks. The authors frame AI adoption through the Will, Skill, Tool framework, arguing that teachers’ existing digital competence can serve as a proxy for readiness to adopt AI tools even when few have direct classroom experience with advanced AI systems.

The study used a web-based survey with 85 in-service mathematics teachers who taught across primary, lower secondary, and upper secondary levels in Finland. Respondents were recruited through teacher and university networks and completed questions about their current digital tool use, the pedagogical functions of those tools, their awareness of AI, possible classroom uses of AI, perceived risks, and attitudes toward AI in society and education. The survey was conducted in Swedish and Finnish before ChatGPT-3 was introduced.

Findings show that the teachers were already heavy users of digital mathematics resources and generally described themselves as technologically interested and experienced. They saw AI as potentially useful for individualized learning, scaffolding, differentiation, homework support, and teacher assessment tasks, but they also worried about privacy, data security, overreliance on algorithms, reduced student collaboration, and a shift away from core mathematical reasoning. Overall, the sample was characterized by interest and openness toward AI, tempered by ambivalence about risks. The authors conclude that these mathematics teachers appear likely to be early adopters of AI tools, though successful implementation would still require suitable tools, curriculum resources, and teacher preparation.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI / AI-tool category, including adaptive and individualized teaching materials, assessment support, exercise generation, and related AI-based classroom tools; no specific commercial product is named in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper surveyed K-12 mathematics teachers about their expectations, attitudes, and early experiences with AI-based tools in mathematics education, including potential uses such as individualized learning paths, homework support, assessment assistance, and automatic exercise generation.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods web survey of digitally skilled Finnish K-12 mathematics teachers (N=85), 78% thought AI-tools could create individual learning paths, 81% thought they could offer challenges for interested students, and 66% thought they could make it easier for the teacher to follow up and assess students. The paper reports no effect sizes because this was a survey of expectations rather than an intervention study.
findings.measure: Teacher survey responses on perceived potential uses of AI-tools in mathematics learning

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods survey study with descriptive and correlational analysis, not an intervention or causal design. The evidence is useful for understanding teacher attitudes and expectations, but it does not test AI-tool effects on student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper indicates substantial perceived potential for AI tools in mathematics teaching, especially for personalization and assessment, but it provides no measured impact on learning or teaching performance. The impact is therefore plausible but unquantified.

paper_profiles.title: A cross-sectional look at teacher reactions, worries, and professional development needs related to generative AI in an urban school district
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers in a large urban school district perceived generative AI, especially chatbot tools such as ChatGPT, shortly after these tools became widely available. The authors ask whether teachers’ reactions differ by grade band taught, subject area, and years of teaching experience, and what concerns, perceived benefits, and professional development (PD) needs teachers report for themselves and for students.

The study is not an intervention trial; instead, it uses districtwide survey data supplemented by qualitative coding of open-ended responses. The survey was administered to certificated educators in a large West Coast urban district in 2023, producing 1,454 complete teacher responses. Teachers reported their AI chatbot usage, allowability policies for student use, concerns, benefits, and PD needs. Quantitative analyses used logistic regression and chi-square tests, while qualitative responses were coded thematically.

The sample included elementary, middle, and high school teachers, with comparisons also made by subject area for middle/high school teachers (STEM, humanities, and other) and by experience level (less than vs. more than 10 years). The findings show that willingness to allow AI use decreased as grade level increased, and more experienced teachers were generally more restrictive. Elementary and middle school teachers most often wanted basic AI literacy, while high school teachers more often wanted guidance on how to manage student AI use and detect AI-generated work.

Overall, the paper concludes that teacher attitudes toward generative AI are strongly shaped by instructional context and experience, suggesting that AI-related PD and policy should be differentiated by grade band and teaching role. It also highlights that teachers distinguish sharply between AI’s possible uses for teachers versus students, with different perceived benefits and risks for each.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI chatbot / large language model system used for conversational text generation, answering questions, and assisting with tasks such as writing support, concept explanation, code generation, and lesson-planning help.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed K-12 teachers’ perceptions, allowability, concerns, and professional development needs related to generative AI chatbots in schools; the paper explicitly references ChatGPT as an example but does not study a specific product beyond generic chatbot use.

findings.finding_summary: In a cross-sectional survey of 1,454 teachers in a large urban school district, teachers in secondary settings were less willing to allow generative AI chatbot use than elementary teachers. More experienced elementary teachers (>10 years) were also significantly less likely to allow AI for idea generation, paper editing, writing entire papers, concept explanation, and code generation; the paper reports marginal effects such as dy/dx = -0.489 for idea generation and -0.500 for code generation in elementary settings.
findings.measure: Teachers’ allowability / willingness to permit student use of AI chatbots for idea generation, editing/completing a paper, writing a paper, explaining a concept, and generating code
findings.effect_size: dy/dx = -0.121 to -0.150 by grade level; elementary more-experienced teacher dy/dx = -0.489 to -0.587 across writing-support outcomes
findings.confidence_interval: see paper tables; e.g., grade-level models 95% CI [ -0.126, -0.116 ] to [ -0.156, -0.144 ]; elementary more-experienced models 95% CI [ -0.633, -0.346 ] to [ -0.826, -0.348 ]

findings.finding_summary: Teachers’ reported professional development needs varied significantly by grade level (χ²_dof=21 = 63.949, p=0.000), but not by subject or experience level. Elementary and middle school teachers emphasized basic AI literacy, while high school teachers emphasized how to instruct/manage student AI use and how to detect AI-generated work.
findings.measure: Open-ended professional development needs coded by grade level, subject, and years of experience
findings.sample_size: n=1,454; coded needs analyses reported for subgroups

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods cross-sectional survey study, not an experiment. It provides subgroup analyses and coded qualitative responses, but causal inference is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported subgroup differences are meaningful for implementation and professional development, but the study does not test an intervention and the effect sizes are mostly directional/marginal rather than outcome impacts on learning.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper asks how large language models such as ChatGPT can be used in education, and what opportunities and risks they create for learners, teachers, and educational systems. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention, the paper synthesizes early examples and broader considerations around educational use of large language models, including content generation, feedback, assessment support, tutoring, and professional development.

The paper discusses potential applications for students across elementary, secondary, tertiary, and professional learning contexts, and for teachers in lesson planning, personalized feedback, assessment, and instructional support. It emphasizes that these systems may support writing, question generation, problem solving, and differentiated instruction, while also requiring human oversight, critical thinking, and fact checking. The text also notes that such tools could be integrated into broader digital learning environments, including remote and immersive settings.

The authors conclude that large language models hold substantial promise for education but should be deployed cautiously because of risks related to bias, privacy, copyright, misinformation, overreliance, and inequitable access. They argue for responsible, ethical, and transparent use, supported by teacher professional development, governance, and ongoing human monitoring. The paper is primarily a conceptual roadmap rather than a study of a specific implementation.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s generative large language model chatbot for dialogue, text generation, question answering, and related language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as an example of a large language model that could support teaching processes, including personalized feedback, lesson planning, assessment, and content creation; the paper does not report an empirical study of ChatGPT in K–12 coaching or lesson-plan feedback.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper and literature discussion rather than an empirical evaluation of an AI tool in K–12 settings. It does not present a study design, sample, or outcome data for tool effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No measurable intervention outcomes are reported, so there is no evidence of impact to rate.

paper_profiles.title: Co-designing AI Education Curriculum with Cross-Disciplinary High School Teachers
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI-24 (The Thirty-Eighth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how high school teachers from different disciplines think about teaching about and with artificial intelligence (AI), especially generative AI, in their classrooms. The authors are motivated by the rapid rise of public-facing AI tools such as ChatGPT and DALL·E and by the challenge of creating AI curriculum that works across subject areas rather than only in computer science. The central question is how teachers interpret AI in relation to disciplinary goals and what opportunities and challenges they see in using AI tools for instruction.

The study used a co-design approach: five collaborative sessions were conducted with eight high school teachers teaching humanities and STEM subjects, including social studies, English/ELA, economics, art, engineering, statistics, and computer science. The sessions were held over Zoom across four months, and the teachers reviewed and adapted AI curriculum resources on topics such as AI in everyday life, facial recognition, generative AI in art, AI and math/data, and AI and society. The sessions were designed to let teachers critique resources and develop their own lesson ideas, with generative AI becoming a stronger focus in later sessions after ChatGPT and DALL·E gained prominence.

The teachers generally framed AI through both technical and ethical lenses, but the relative emphasis varied by discipline. For example, engineering and CS-oriented teachers emphasized technical structure and model behavior, while English and social studies teachers were more interested in ethical argumentation, social impact, and disciplinary frameworks such as SOAPSTone or OPCVL. Several teachers saw value in a "dual exploration" approach, where students use their subject-specific analytic frameworks to examine AI-generated content and simultaneously learn about the limitations and assumptions of AI. Overall, the paper concludes that AI curriculum can be made more adaptable and meaningful when it is co-designed with teachers across disciplines and aligned with both technical and ethical goals.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools built on large language models and image-generation models, used to generate or transform text and images.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers co-designed AI curriculum and discussed using generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and DALL·E in high school lessons across art, math, social studies, English, engineering, and economics; the paper focused on teachers' perspectives on teaching with and about generative AI rather than evaluating student outcomes.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, formative co-design study with eight high school teachers. It provides rich descriptive evidence but no experimental comparison or causal effect estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report measurable outcome effects on students or teachers. Its contribution is conceptual and design-oriented, so impact is meaningful but not quantified.

paper_profiles.title: Teachers and AI: Understanding the factors influencing AI integration in K-12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the psychological and pedagogical factors that shape K-12 teachers’ readiness to integrate generative AI into instructional practice. The authors focus on why teachers embrace or resist AI, including perceived usefulness, student engagement, curriculum alignment, cultural fit, ethical concerns, technical barriers, and workload. The study is positioned as a response to the growing interest in AI in education and the need to understand teachers’ roles in successful implementation.

The empirical work was conducted in a 14-week professional development course at a private school in Türkiye. Sixty-six teachers from 11 disciplines participated, with representation across pre-school, primary school, and high school. Participants engaged with generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, MagicSchool, Canva, Gamma, and Character.ai through online discussion forums and an AI-supported learning activity design task. Their reflections and designed activities were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis.

Findings suggest that teachers valued AI for efficiency, adaptability, interactive learning, and support for lesson planning and differentiation. At the same time, they reported barriers related to technical problems, device access, time demands, curriculum mismatch, language and cultural issues, and ethical concerns such as privacy, fairness, plagiarism, and reduced student creativity. The paper concludes that effective AI integration in K-12 education requires targeted teacher support, infrastructure, ethical guidance, and better alignment between AI tools and local curricular and cultural contexts.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on GPT models, used for dialogue, content generation, and instructional support.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by teachers in a professional development course and in designed classroom activities for lesson planning, generating instructional content, creating questions, summaries, stories, presentations, and feedback/improvement tasks.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative study of 66 teachers from a private school in Türkiye, ChatGPT was the most commonly used AI tool in the 59 analyzed designed activities. Teachers reported it supported lesson planning, content creation, differentiated instruction, story/dictation generation, and feedback-oriented tasks, but also noted curriculum misalignment, language, and cultural limitations.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported tool use and thematic analysis of designed learning activities and forum reflections

identified_tools.name: MagicSchool
identified_tools.description: An AI-powered teacher tool platform offering multiple utilities for lesson planning, content creation, student support, and related classroom tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used and discussed by K-12 teachers as a lesson-planning and instructional support tool during AI-focused professional development and activity design.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative study of 66 teachers, MagicSchool was among the most valued tools after ChatGPT. Teachers highlighted its variety of tools, usefulness for adapting materials to lessons, and support for planning, differentiation, progress tracking, and performance evaluation, while also noting broader implementation barriers such as alignment and workload.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported preferences, reflections, and thematic analysis of designed activities

identified_tools.name: Canva
identified_tools.description: A digital design platform with AI-enabled features for creating visual content, presentations, and educational materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned by teachers as one of the AI tools used in designed activities and as a preferred tool for visual and interactive learning materials.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers included Canva among the preferred tools in their designed activities and associated it with visual design, animated characters, and interactive story/presentation creation. The paper does not report quantitative effects, but the qualitative findings indicate teachers viewed it as useful for visual and differentiated instruction.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported preferences and thematic analysis of designed activities

identified_tools.name: Gamma
identified_tools.description: An AI-assisted presentation/content creation tool used for generating slide decks and visual materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by teachers for generating presentations in designed activities and discussed as a tool that made work easier.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported Gamma as helpful for quickly preparing presentation files and supporting presentation-related classroom activities. The study provides qualitative evidence of perceived efficiency and ease of use rather than quantitative impact.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported preferences and reflections

identified_tools.name: Character.ai
identified_tools.description: A chatbot platform that allows users to create and interact with character-based conversational agents.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in teachers' designed activities for discussions, role-play, and creative learning tasks.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers used Character.ai in designed activities for character creation, discussion, and reflective tasks. In the qualitative analysis, it was associated with constructivist, critical-thinking, and creative-expression strategies, but no quantitative effect was reported.
findings.measure: Teacher-designed activities and thematic coding

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory qualitative study with 66 teachers from a single private school and no experimental comparison group. It provides rich descriptive evidence but not causal impact estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong perceived usefulness across several tools, but it does not provide effect sizes or outcome metrics. Impact is therefore suggestive rather than measurable from the reported data.

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when generative AI is used to personalize mathematics tasks for students. The authors focus on a central tension in AI-assisted lesson/task design: teacher-mediated personalization may preserve pedagogical judgment and contextual realism, but it may also take substantial time and may not produce the fine-grained personalization students prefer.

The study partnered seven middle school mathematics teachers with ChatGPT (GPT-4o) to modify existing Illustrative Mathematics problems into personalized versions aligned to students’ popular-culture interests. Teachers worked on problems from two units of 7th-grade mathematics, first Unit 4 (proportional relationships and percentages) and then Unit 6 (expressions, equations, and inequalities). In total, 521 7th-grade students in six U.S. schools received the resulting assignments through ASSISTments. Data included teacher prompt logs and video/audio, student closed-ended ratings of interestingness and closeness to their interests, and student open-ended feedback.

Findings show that teachers often used ChatGPT to add or swap specific popular-culture references, but they also spent substantial effort correcting realism, quantities, age appropriateness, and other contextual details. Students tended to prefer specific, small-grain references, while teachers often had to work at broader grain sizes due to practical constraints. On average, creating a problem took about four minutes and teachers used about three prompts, with a “Goldilocks zone” of roughly 3–5 prompts associated with the best student ratings. Teachers became more elaborate, not more efficient, from Unit 4 to Unit 6, and student ratings improved in Unit 6. The paper concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization is pedagogically valuable but time-intensive, and that future systems may need automation or agent support to reduce teacher burden while preserving teacher judgment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based generative AI chatbot and text generation assistant used for drafting, rewriting, and modifying content through iterative prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by 7 middle school mathematics teachers to personalize existing Illustrative Mathematics problems for seventh-grade students’ interests; teachers prompted ChatGPT (with underlying model GPT-4o) to rewrite problems and adjust realism, references, readability, and mathematical clarity.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed-methods study, teachers used ChatGPT to personalize 143 middle-school math problems for 521 seventh-grade students across 6 U.S. schools. Teachers used an average of 3.2 prompts per problem and about 246 seconds per problem; student ratings were significantly higher when teachers used 3–5 prompts, with ratings increasing by about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073).
findings.measure: Teacher prompting efficiency; student ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests

findings.finding_summary: From Unit 4 to Unit 6, teachers used more prompts and spent more time on problem personalization, while student ratings also improved.
