Teachers averaged 3.2 prompts/problem in Unit 4 versus 4.6 in Unit 6 (B=1.26, SE=0.41, t=3.08, p=0.0025), and time increased from 204 seconds/problem to 286 seconds/problem (B=70.4, SE=29.6, t=2.38, p=0.0189); student ratings of interestingness and closeness rose by 0.33 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.33, SE=0.095, t=3.49, p=0.0012).
findings.measure: Number of prompts, time per problem, and student ratings across Unit 4 vs Unit 6

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods observational study with teacher prompting logs, student surveys, and regression analyses, not a randomized controlled trial. The design provides useful empirical evidence but with limited causal strength and only one classroom cohort.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are statistically significant but modest in size for student ratings, and the practical time burden for teachers remains substantial. The study suggests meaningful classroom relevance, but not a large demonstrated impact on learning outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary students and teachers perceived a generative AI-supported creative mathematical writing activity. The authors focus on the pedagogical question of whether GenAI can support young learners in composing math-related stories and how both benefits and challenges are experienced in real classrooms.

The intervention used a researcher-developed GenAI-powered learning platform that guided students through three steps: Ask, Represent, and Transform. Students first unpacked a math story, then represented mathematical ideas visually, and finally co-created culturally relevant math stories with the help of GPT-4 and DALL·E 3. The system also included prompts and a checklist for evaluating AI-generated stories. The study was implemented in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools, involving 79 students and six teachers. After several class sessions, 10 students and all six teachers were interviewed; open-ended survey responses and observation notes were used to triangulate the findings.

Using thematic analysis, the authors identified perceived benefits including creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, interest/curiosity, and ownership of learning. They also identified challenges such as weak student critical evaluation of AI output, difficulty generating coherent stories, overly perfect AI responses, limited pedagogical feedback, reduced autonomy, limited social connection, and lack of multiple communication modes. Overall, the paper argues that GenAI can support elementary mathematical writing, but effective educational use depends on careful instructional and interface design that preserves opportunities for human judgment, feedback, and collaboration.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI-powered learning technology using large language and image generation models to create and revise math stories with supporting prompts and feedback scaffolds.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in elementary classrooms to support 5th-grade students’ creative mathematical writing: students supplied goals, characters, settings, and events; the system generated story drafts and corresponding images; students then evaluated and revised the AI-generated stories.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative classroom study with 79 5th-grade students and 6 teachers, participants reported that the GenAI-supported activity fostered creativity in mathematics, including divergent thinking, convergent thinking, originality, and flexible thinking. The paper reports these as thematic findings from interviews, open-ended surveys, and observations; no effect sizes were reported.
findings.measure: Student and teacher perceptions of creativity in mathematical writing

findings.finding_summary: Participants reported that the GenAI-supported story-writing process helped students understand math problems, represent mathematical knowledge, and surface misconceptions. Teachers said the Ask and Represent steps supported breakdown of problems and visualization of mathematical ideas; no effect sizes were reported.
findings.measure: Student and teacher perceptions of mathematical understanding and representation

findings.finding_summary: The study found that working with GenAI promoted AI literacy, especially prompt engineering and evaluating AI strengths and weaknesses. This was based on thematic analysis of interview and survey data; no quantitative impact estimate was reported.
findings.measure: Perceived AI literacy development

findings.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived improvements in interest, curiosity, and ownership of learning when using the GenAI-supported writing activity. The paper describes these as affective-domain benefits from qualitative data, without effect sizes or statistical tests.
findings.measure: Interest, curiosity, and ownership in learning

findings.finding_summary: The study also identified challenges, including students’ lack of critical evaluation of AI-generated content and difficulty formulating coherent story prompts aligned to learning objectives. These were qualitative barriers reported by students and teachers; no quantitative estimates were provided.
findings.measure: Perceived challenges in critiquing and generating AI-assisted stories

findings.finding_summary: Participants reported that the system lacked pedagogical supports such as adaptive/formative feedback, autonomy-preserving options, social connection features, and multiple communication modes (e.g., speech-to-text). These design limitations were identified through thematic analysis and not measured with numerical outcomes.
findings.measure: Perceived pedagogical/interaction limitations of the system

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-method classroom study with interviews, open-ended surveys, and observations rather than a controlled causal design. It provides useful evidence about perceptions and implementation context, but not high-causal-confidence impact estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no effect sizes or statistical impacts, only perceived benefits and challenges. As a result, the practical impact is promising but remains unclear and not quantifiable from the study.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether CyberScholar, a generative AI writing assistant, can support K-12 students’ writing through formative feedback aligned to classroom rubrics and materials. The central question is how a GenAI tool can be used for writing support in authentic school contexts, and whether its feedback is perceived as useful by students and teachers.

The intervention was piloted in four public schools in the United States across middle and high school grades, with writing tasks in English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History. CyberScholar was customized using teachers’ prompts, rubrics, books, and slides through retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering. The study involved 121 students and 4 teachers, with data gathered through observations, surveys, and interviews over an implementation period from August 2024 to January 2025.

Using an exploratory multiple case study and thematic qualitative analysis, the authors found that students valued the tool’s detailed feedback, interactivity, perceived improvements in writing quality, and rubric-based scoring. Teachers were positioned less as sole evaluators and more as managers of AI-supported feedback loops. The paper concludes that GenAI can complement teacher feedback in K-12 writing instruction when it is contextually aligned, interactive, and pedagogically grounded, though it should not replace teachers.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI writing assistant/chatbot used to generate formative feedback on student writing and support revision in K-12 settings.
identified_tools.use_case: Piloted as CyberScholar, a GenAI assistant customized with teachers’ rubrics, instructional materials, and expectations to provide formative feedback on student writing across grades 7, 8, 10, and 11 in four U.S. schools.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative multiple-case study, 121 K-12 students used CyberScholar for writing revisions across English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History. Students reported that the tool supported writing development through detailed and specific feedback, interactive clarification, perceived improvements in writing quality, and ratings aligned with rubric criteria; 36 students said they would use it again, while 11 were hesitant.
findings.measure: Student post-survey comments, interviews, and classroom observations of perceived usefulness for writing support
findings.sample_size: n=121 students; n=4 teachers; post-survey n=54; interviews n=8 students and 1 teacher

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports subgroup and setting variation descriptively rather than with statistical tests. Interactive follow-up questioning was available only in Schools C and D, and student comments varied by school/context; the authors also note that the tool was customized to different rubrics, subject areas, and school settings, but no comparative effect sizes were reported by grade band, subject, teacher experience, or school context.
findings.measure: Descriptive qualitative differences across schools, grades, and subjects

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative multiple-case study with surveys, interviews, and observations rather than an experimental design. It provides contextual evidence of use, but there are no causal estimates or statistical tests.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceived usefulness and practical alignment with teacher rubrics, but no effect sizes are available. Impact appears promising yet uncertain because outcomes are based on participant perceptions and descriptive evidence.

paper_profiles.title: LLMs to Support K–12 Teachers in Culturally Relevant Pedagogy: An AI Literacy Example
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a large language model (LLM)-based tool can help K–12 teachers adapt AI literacy lessons in ways that better reflect culturally relevant pedagogy (CRP). The authors frame the problem as a practical one: teachers often want to make instruction culturally responsive, but they face barriers such as limited time, limited training, uncertainty about how to adapt materials, and lack of ready-made resources tailored to students’ cultural backgrounds.

To address this, the paper presents CulturAIEd, an LLM-powered system that uses student demographic information, a culturally responsive teaching checklist, rubric-based feedback, and chatbot-style just-in-time guidance to support lesson adaptation. The tool was used in an exploratory pilot with four K–12 teachers completing AI literacy lesson-design tasks over Zoom. The tasks focused on adapting activities from AI4K12-related content, including prompt engineering, AI risks, and AI hallucinations, while integrating CRP elements.

The participants were four secondary teachers from North America and East Asia: two science teachers, one music education teacher, and one information technology teacher. All had at least four years of teaching experience, and the schools included a virtual public school and public schools. The study found that teachers felt CulturAIEd improved their confidence, efficiency, and ability to identify culturally responsive modifications, especially because it streamlined demographic integration and offered actionable feedback.

The main conclusion is that LLMs can support teacher planning for culturally responsive AI literacy instruction, but the evidence is preliminary. The authors emphasize that the study is small and exploratory, and they call for larger, controlled, and longer-term studies to test whether such tools can meaningfully improve practice across subjects and contexts.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model / chatbot used to generate, adapt, and give feedback on instructional materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the underlying LLM capability in CulturAIEd to support K-12 teachers adapting AI literacy activities for culturally relevant pedagogy, including demographic customization, rubric-based feedback, and just-in-time coaching. The paper also notes that participants had access to generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, but the study’s focal tool is the unnamed LLM-powered system CulturAIEd rather than a separately named commercial product.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative-dominant mixed-methods exploratory pilot with four K-12 teachers (N=4), CulturAIEd increased teachers' confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness in learning activities and in making culturally responsive modifications to activities. Post-survey results showed all participants rated themselves 5/5 on confidence in implementing CRP modifications, up from pre-survey ratings of 3-5.
findings.measure: Teacher self-reported confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness and implementing CRP modifications

findings.finding_summary: Participants reported that the tool saved time and reduced the burden of researching and integrating student demographics into lesson adaptation. The paper characterizes this as streamlined workflow and high implementation efficiency, but provides no quantitative effect size.
findings.measure: Perceived time savings, workflow efficiency, and usability/satisfaction from post-survey and interviews

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory qualitative-dominant mixed-methods pilot with a very small sample (n=4), so it provides useful formative evidence but not strong causal evidence. The paper reports perceptions and pre/post self-ratings rather than rigorous experimental outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported impact is positive but unquantified, with no effect sizes or controlled comparison. The study suggests meaningful usability and confidence gains, but the magnitude of educational impact remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Do Teachers Dream of GenAI Widening Educational (In)equality? Envisioning the Future of K-12 GenAI Education from Global Teachers’ Perspectives
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers think about and teach generative AI (GenAI) in relation to educational equality. The central question is how teachers are already integrating GenAI into classroom practice, what structural barriers constrain those efforts, and what kinds of support they believe are needed to make GenAI education more equitable.

The study is based on 30 semi-structured interviews with K–12 teachers in the United States, South Africa, and Taiwan. Participants taught across elementary, middle, and high school settings, with subject areas including English, social science, math, science, special education, information technology, and computer science. Some teachers taught formal AI/IT courses, while others incorporated GenAI into ordinary subject teaching. The paper is therefore not an intervention study but an exploratory qualitative study of teachers’ current practices and future visions in diverse school contexts.

The main findings are that teachers see GenAI as both an opportunity and a risk for educational inequality. They described using GenAI to help students in under-resourced settings, support learners with limited digital literacy, and provide personalized assistance for marginalized students. At the same time, they worried that GenAI could intensify inequality through shortcut learning, bullying, cultural bias, and overreliance that replaces human care. Teachers also reported systemic barriers such as unequal infrastructure, limited professional training, and restrictive norms, and they called for support from schools, policymakers, and technology companies. The paper concludes that equitable GenAI education depends on broader sociotechnical support, not only individual teacher effort.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI tools/chatbots used for generating and interacting with text, explanations, and other content; no specific commercial or research product is named in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: K–12 teachers were interviewed about how they teach students about generative AI, including using it in lessons, assignments, and classroom discussions across subjects and settings.

findings.finding_summary: This qualitative interview study with 30 K–12 teachers across the United States, South Africa, and Taiwan found that teachers viewed GenAI as both a tool for reducing pre-existing educational inequalities and a source of new risks. Teachers described using GenAI to address resource shortages, support digital literacy, and personalize learning, while also reporting structural barriers such as unequal infrastructure, insufficient training, and restrictive norms.
findings.measure: Teacher interview accounts of GenAI integration, constraints, and perceived equality implications

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, cross-national interview study rather than an experimental evaluation. It provides rich descriptive evidence about teacher experiences and contexts, but no causal effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports important systemic and practice-level implications, but it does not measure outcome gains or provide effect sizes. Impact is therefore important but empirically unquantified.

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI ’26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how middle school students perceive and want to design generative AI peers for collaborative mathematical problem solving, rather than AI tutors. The authors focus on a gap in prior K-12 GenAI work: most systems have emphasized one-on-one tutoring, feedback, or teacher-facing support, while much less is known about AI participation as a peer inside small-group work.

To study this, the researchers ran a five-day summer camp with 24 rising grades 6–8 students at a public university in the United States. The camp combined collaborative math problem solving, direct experience with a web-based AI peer technology probe, and participatory design activities in which students sketched, discussed, and refined their ideal AI peers. Students experienced both human-only and AI-involved collaboration, first individually and then in small groups, using grade-aligned mathematics tasks in ratio/proportional reasoning, expressions and equations, and early functions/geometry.

The main findings show that students wanted an AI peer that supports co-agency rather than acting like a teacher: they preferred hints, checks, and gradual scaffolds over full solutions; wanted control over when the AI speaks and how much it says; and disliked behaviors that felt repetitive, overly directive, or emotionally inattentive. They also preferred a peer-like but expert tone and minimal persona exaggeration. The paper concludes that effective AI peers for middle-school mathematics should be scaffold-first, collaborative, socially attuned, and configurable to fit classroom norms.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family conversational AI model used for dialogue, reasoning, and content generation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper used GPT-4o as the LLM backbone powering the AI peer technology probe; it was also demonstrated to students as a commercial GenAI tool (e.g., ChatGPT) during the camp.

findings.finding_summary: In a five-day summer camp with N=24 middle-school students, the GPT-4o-powered AI peer probe reduced perceived temporal demand during collaborative math problem solving (M=5.67 vs 9.62; p=0.002; d=1.15) but increased physical demand (M=8.48 vs 4.90; p=0.014; d=1.14). Students also reported lower group social attraction (M=5.21 vs 6.50; p=0.029; d=0.94) and lower task coordination (M=4.76 vs 5.54; p=0.047; d=0.81) relative to human-only CPS.
findings.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand and physical demand; GEQ attractions to group-social and group integration-task
findings.sample_size: n=22 for paired comparisons; N=24 enrolled

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods participatory design study with within-subject quantitative comparisons and qualitative analysis, not a randomized controlled trial. The evidence is informative but context-specific and exploratory.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects on workload and group climate are large (all reported d values exceed 0.80), indicating substantial impact in the measured setting.

paper_profiles.title: LitLinker: Supporting the Ideation of Interdisciplinary Contexts with Large Language Models for Teaching Literature in Elementary Schools
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge elementary school Chinese-language teachers face when designing interdisciplinary contexts for literature instruction. The authors argue that effective interdisciplinary lesson planning requires teachers to explore many candidate topics, connect them to reading materials, and then turn those connections into usable lesson plans and classroom activities, which is time-consuming and cognitively demanding.

To support this work, the paper introduces LitLinker, a human-AI collaborative web application powered by a large language model (GLM-4). LitLinker uses a multi-agent workflow to recommend interdisciplinary contexts, analyze relationships between contexts and texts at multiple levels, let users refine and question the generated content, and finally produce structured lesson plans with introductions and activities. The design was informed by three interview sessions with an experienced elementary literature teacher and her team, plus prototype feedback from additional teachers.

The evaluation includes a within-subjects experiment with 16 novices of literature teaching and qualitative expert interviews with 10 elementary Chinese-language teachers with varying experience, all in mainland China. The system was compared against a baseline LLM web app. Results suggest LitLinker produced deeper subject integration, reduced workload, and was viewed as more satisfying and efficient than the baseline. Expert teachers also valued its support for interdisciplinary ideation, while expressing concerns about the reliability of purely generated content and the need for grounded subject databases and editable outputs.

identified_tools.name: Qwen
identified_tools.description: An LLM-based interactive system for teachers to ideate interdisciplinary contexts for teaching literature in elementary schools, analyze reading materials, and generate lesson plans and related classroom activities.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper introduces and evaluates LitLinker, a human-AI collaborative system powered by the GLM-4 LLM family, used by elementary Chinese language teachers to explore interdisciplinary contexts, connect them to texts, and generate course plans and activities.

findings.finding_summary: Compared with a baseline LLM web app, LitLinker improved the quality of outcome lesson plans for interdisciplinary literature instruction in a within-subjects study (n=16). The paper reports that LitLinker led to deeper integration of different subjects, was rated more satisfying and efficient, and reduced workload, but the excerpt does not provide the exact effect sizes for these outcomes.
findings.measure: Quality ratings of outcome lesson plans; integration depth; satisfaction; efficiency; workload (NASA-TLX)

findings.finding_summary: In the within-subjects study (n=16), LitLinker significantly reduced perceived task workload during interdisciplinary lesson planning relative to the baseline system. Workload was measured with NASA-TLX, but the excerpt does not report the exact statistics or effect sizes.
findings.measure: NASA-TLX workload during lesson-planning task

findings.finding_summary: In qualitative expert interviews and iterative design sessions with elementary Chinese language teachers, participants reported high satisfaction with LitLinker and strong appreciation for its usefulness in supporting interdisciplinary course design. The study is qualitative/mixed-methods and reports no numeric effect size for these perceptions.
findings.measure: Expert interview feedback on usability, usefulness, and creative support
findings.sample_size: n=10 interviewees; 17 teachers involved in design/evaluation overall

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods HCI study with a within-subjects comparison and qualitative interviews, but it is not a randomized controlled trial and the excerpt does not report full statistics for the main outcomes. The evidence is useful but not high-certainty in the K-12 evidence hierarchy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive, practically meaningful improvements in lesson-plan integration and reduced workload, but the excerpt does not provide effect sizes for the key outcomes. Impact therefore appears promising but remains somewhat unclear from the reported statistics.

paper_profiles.title: When Scaffolding Breaks: Investigating Student Interaction with LLM-Based Writing Support in Real-Time K-12 EFL Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language models can function as real-time writing support in K–12 English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classrooms, with a focus on the tradeoffs of step-by-step AI scaffolding. The authors investigate a tension common in classroom AI: while such systems can provide immediate, individualized feedback at scale, they may also create dependency, frustration, or uneven participation when used under time pressure and with students of different proficiency levels.

To study this, the authors developed WriteAid, a chat-based LLM writing support tool, and deployed it in a South Korean public middle school English class. The deployment lasted six weeks and involved 157 eighth-grade students across six classes; 133 consented to data analysis. The system supported sentence construction, vocabulary/grammar explanations, and grammar checking. The study combined log analysis of 14,863 student-LLM messages, qualitative coding of a sampled subset of interactions, written assessment results, and naturalistic classroom observations across three sessions, plus a follow-up teacher interview.

The findings show that higher-proficiency students tended to use the LLM for lower-level support such as vocabulary translation and validation, whereas lower-proficiency students more often outsourced full sentence generation and revision. Although WriteAid improved grammatical accuracy during class, step-by-step scaffolding sometimes demotivated lower-proficiency students and increased reliance on the system, especially under time constraints. Classroom observations also showed that the LLM changed student-teacher dynamics: some students asked the teacher less often, a few extroverted students still dominated teacher attention, and the teacher had more difficulty identifying common student difficulties. The paper concludes that classroom LLMs should be proficiency-aware, syntax-aware, and designed to support teachers’ awareness and equity, rather than simply withholding answers.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: An unnamed large language model (LLM)-based writing support chatbot providing step-by-step scaffolding, sentence construction, vocabulary/grammar explanations, and grammar checking in a chat interface.
identified_tools.use_case: Deployed as 'WriteAid' in real-time K-12 EFL classrooms to support eighth-grade students' English writing during two classroom writing tasks over six weeks.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that LLM-assisted sentence construction improved students' grammatical accuracy during in-class writing. Across the fall semester, students constructed 632 sentences with LLM assistance, and 309 (48.9%) were incorporated verbatim into final essays; 82.3% of those incorporated sentences were grammatically correct. The authors state that the tool improved grammatical accuracy, but no experimental effect size or confidence interval is reported.
findings.measure: Grammatical correctness of LLM-constructed sentences incorporated into final essays

findings.finding_summary: Effects varied by proficiency level: high-performing students correctly incorporated 65.8% of LLM-constructed sentences into their final written assessments, compared with 37.8% for middle-performing students and 14.0% for low-performing students. The paper interprets this as evidence that the tool supported grammatical accuracy overall, but retention and transfer were much weaker for lower-performing students.
findings.measure: Correct incorporation of LLM-constructed sentences into final written assessment by proficiency group

findings.finding_summary: Lower-proficiency students were reported to become demotivated and more reliant on the system when step-by-step scaffolding required many exchanges. The paper also reports more frequent confusion/annoyance among middle- and low-performing students (12.2 and 11.4 affective behaviors per session, respectively) than among high-performing students (3.8 per session).
findings.measure: Observed negative affective behaviors and reported demotivation during LLM interaction
findings.sample_size: n=133 consented students; qualitative subset n=15

findings.finding_summary: Teachers could redirect repetitive low-level questions to the LLM, which freed teacher time for other classroom tasks. In the follow-up interview, the teacher said they had more time to walk around the classroom and check students' progress because they no longer needed to respond to every simple question.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported classroom workload/time freed from answering simple questions

findings.finding_summary: The LLM changed classroom dynamics in both helpful and problematic ways. It reduced some barriers for lower-proficiency students and helped more students complete tasks, but it also made it harder for teachers to identify struggling students, reduced some peer interaction, and concentrated teacher attention on a few extroverted students.
findings.measure: Classroom equity, teacher-student interaction, and peer-learning dynamics from observation and interview
findings.sample_size: 3 observed class sessions; 157 students in deployment

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods deployment study in a single middle school classroom, not a controlled trial or meta-analysis. It provides rich observational evidence but limited causal identification.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful classroom-level benefits and harms, but no numerical causal effect sizes are given for learning outcomes. Impacts appear practical and mixed rather than clearly large or medium by the framework.

paper_profiles.title: A Benchmark for Math Misconceptions: Bridging Gaps in Middle School Algebra with AI-Supported Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of identifying and diagnosing student misconceptions in middle school algebra, with the broader aim of supporting AI systems that can better assist math learning and teacher decision-making. The authors argue that existing math tutoring and educational AI systems often lack grounding in real, research-based misconceptions and may miss important topic-specific patterns in student errors.

To address this, the paper introduces a benchmark of 55 algebra misconceptions and common errors, each paired with four diagnostic examples for a total of 220 examples, compiled from 145 peer-reviewed and related academic sources. The benchmark is organized by algebra topic and evaluated using GPT-4 Turbo in two in-context learning experiments: one with random train/test splits across the full dataset and another with topic-constrained splits. The study also includes educator feedback from five middle school math teachers and follow-up expert review from two additional algebra educators, making it a mixed-methods design combining model evaluation with human judgment.

The population of interest is middle school learners in grades 6 through 8, especially in algebra-relevant topics, though the direct participants were educators rather than students. The teachers worked in U.S. public schools serving underserved populations, including one youth correctional facility context, and they had 4 to 10+ years of experience. Their feedback suggested the benchmark was clear and relevant, and most reported encountering the misconceptions in their classrooms.

Overall, the paper concludes that GPT-4 Turbo can identify algebra misconceptions with moderate accuracy, improving substantially when testing is constrained by topic and when educator feedback is incorporated. The authors emphasize the value of topic-specific testing, human expertise, and multimodal support, and they position the benchmark as a resource for diagnostic tools, teacher support, and future AI-assisted math instruction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model chatbot/system used for generating and evaluating educational text-based outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: GPT-4-turbo was used to diagnose middle school algebra misconceptions from question/answer pairs in an in-context learning benchmark, and the paper also discusses its potential use for teacher support and diagnostic feedback. Educators reviewed GPT-4 results and provided feedback on benchmark clarity and classroom relevance.

findings.finding_summary: Using GPT-4-turbo on the algebra misconception benchmark, the model achieved precision of 0.526 and recall of 0.529 per misconception in Experiment 1 (all examples mixed). When testing examples were constrained within topic in Experiment 2, performance improved to precision 0.753 and recall 0.748 per misconception. After expert educator relabeling of some cases, accuracy rose to 65.45% in Experiment 1 and 83.91% in Experiment 2.
findings.measure: Precision and recall per misconception (MaE), plus expert-adjusted classification accuracy
findings.sample_size: n=5,500 iterations in Experiment 1; n=1,100 iterations in Experiment 2

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods study using repeated subsampling validation and educator feedback, but it is not a randomized controlled trial and the paper focuses on benchmark evaluation rather than a classroom intervention. The evidence is useful but methodologically limited for causal claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported classification performance is moderate to strong after topic constraint and expert adjustment, but no standardized effect size is reported. The impact is promising for diagnostic tooling, yet the study does not demonstrate downstream student learning effects.

paper_profiles.title: Research on the Application of Large Language Models in Automatic Question Generation: A Case Study of ChatGLM in the Context of High School Information Technology Curriculum
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a large language model, ChatGLM, can automatically generate written exam questions for a high school information technology curriculum. The central problem is the heavy workload of question setting for information technology teachers and whether AI-generated questions can approach or exceed the quality of human-generated questions.

The intervention studied is prompt-engineered question generation using ChatGLM. The authors used textbook content from two high school information technology chapters, "Data and Information" and "Algorithm Basics," to generate 20 questions with ChatGLM and compare them against 20 manually written questions. The prompts framed ChatGLM as a high school information technology teacher and asked it to output questions in pseudocode-like format.

Five experienced high school information technology teachers evaluated the questions on hitting/alignment, fitting/core competency alignment, clarity, and willingness to use. The study found no significant difference between ChatGLM and human questions for hitting, fitting, or clarity, but ChatGLM scored significantly higher on willingness to use. The authors conclude that ChatGLM shows promise for reducing teachers' workload and improving the acceptability of generated assessment items, especially in high school information technology contexts.

identified_tools.name: ChatGLM
identified_tools.description: A Chinese large language model used for text generation and question generation tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used with prompt engineering to generate high school information technology exam questions, which were compared against human-generated questions and evaluated by five experienced teachers.

findings.finding_summary: In a case study of 20 human-generated and 20 ChatGLM-generated questions for high school information technology, five teachers rated ChatGLM slightly lower on Hitting (mean 4.17 vs 4.32) and essentially equal on Fitting (4.10 vs 4.11), but higher on Clarity (4.14 vs 4.03) and much higher on Willingness to use (3.98 vs 3.05). Welch's ANOVA found no significant differences for Hitting (p=0.067), Fitting (p=0.891), or Clarity (p=0.149), but Willingness differed significantly (p<.001).
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of Hitting, Fitting, Clarity, and Willingness to use for generated exam questions
findings.sample_size: n=20 questions per condition; n=5 teachers

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small case study with teacher ratings rather than a controlled educational outcome trial. The methodology is clear, but evidence is limited to expert evaluation of generated questions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The strongest reported difference is on teacher willingness to use the questions, but no effect size is reported and the study does not measure student learning outcomes. Overall impact is modest and mostly centered on perceived usefulness.

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Text: Probing K-12 Educators’ Perspectives on Designing Learning Opportunities Leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 educators envision using multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for learning, and what concerns arise when teachers try to design educational experiences with them. The authors focus on a gap in the literature: while many AI-for-education papers discuss student-facing applications or teacher productivity tools, less is known about what educators themselves think about emerging multimodal AI capabilities beyond text.

To investigate this, the researchers ran workshops with 12 K-12 educators in New York City. Participants viewed demo videos of commercial MLLMs, discussed possible classroom uses, and then prototyped their own learning activities using Claude 3.5 and its Artifacts feature. The sample included public school, charter school, magnet school, and museum educators teaching elementary, middle, and high school students, with varied years of experience and mostly novice familiarity with LLMs. The workshop format let participants experiment with image input, text prompting, and interactive code-based outputs.

The paper finds that educators were broadly enthusiastic about MLLMs, especially for creating multimedia simulations, personalized supports, research scaffolds, and interactive learning tools. However, many teachers preferred using MLLMs themselves to generate student-facing materials rather than having students interact directly with the model, especially in elementary and middle grades. High school educators were more open to student-direct use. The authors conclude that MLLMs may be useful for teacher-authored interactive content and student research support, but they also highlight concerns about output quality, literacy-level fit, access, policy, and the need for professional development.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic’s conversational large language model assistant capable of text and image input, with code-based interactive output via Artifacts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a November 2024 workshop with 12 K-12 educators to prototype student-facing learning activities, test multimodal inputs/outputs, and explore educator perspectives on designing with multimodal LLMs.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative workshop study with 12 educators using a commercial AI tool, not an experimental impact study. It provides rich descriptive evidence about educator perceptions and design choices, but no causal estimate of learning effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no measured student outcomes or effect sizes. Its contribution is mainly prospective and design-oriented, so the educational impact is suggested rather than demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI as a lab partner: a case study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how high school students used ChatGPT during a physics laboratory session and what that reveals about the potential role of generative AI in school laboratory work. The authors were interested in how students perceived useful interactions with ChatGPT, how they actually used it while working on a lab, and whether such interactions supported problem solving and conceptual understanding.

The intervention was an intentionally designed high school physics lab on acoustic levitation and the speed of sound in air. Students were given access to the free version of ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) alongside the lab manual, textbook, formula book, and calculator. The lab instructions were deliberately somewhat vague so that students would likely need to consult ChatGPT for help with formulas, analysis, and conceptual questions. Data came from video recordings of seven student groups, chat logs, written notes, and pre/post group interviews.

The study involved 19 Swedish high school students across Physics 1, 2, and 3 courses, including both second- and third-year students. The context was a school/university-linked physics lab in Sweden, and the analysis focused on qualitative patterns in how students interacted with ChatGPT and how prior knowledge shaped their ability to judge its answers.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT can function as a kind of lab partner or quick source of information, but its usefulness depends strongly on students’ prior physics knowledge and their ability to evaluate output critically. More knowledgeable groups used ChatGPT more productively, while less knowledgeable groups were more easily misled or used it in a superficial way. The paper argues that generative AI may support lab work and problem solving, but only when students have enough subject knowledge and guidance to avoid over-trusting inaccurate or confusing responses.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot based on GPT models, used for answering questions, explaining concepts, and generating text or formulas.
identified_tools.use_case: High school physics students used the freely accessible GPT-3.5 version of ChatGPT during an acoustic levitation lab to get help with understanding the phenomenon, identifying equations for analysis, converting units, and answering discussion questions.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative case study (n=19 across 7 lab groups), ChatGPT was sometimes useful for providing equations, brief explanations, and quick guidance during the physics lab, especially for students with more prior knowledge who could evaluate its answers. However, it also produced vague, confusing, or incorrect guidance in some cases, and weaker-knowledge groups often accepted outputs uncritically or were misled by them.
findings.measure: Qualitative observations from lab video, chat histories, and pre/post group interviews about usefulness, trustworthiness, and problem-solving interactions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods case study rather than an experimental design, so the evidence is best classified as yellow. The paper provides rich observational detail, but no causal estimate or controlled comparison.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported impact is mixed and context-dependent: some groups benefited from concise explanations and formula lookup, while others were confused or misled. No effect size is reported, so the overall impact is unclear rather than clearly positive or large.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Usage of Generative AI for Group Project-Based Offline Art Courses in Elementary Schools
paper_profiles.venue: CSCW '25 (Proceedings of the 2025 ACM SIGCHI Conference on Computer-Supported Cooperative Work & Social Computing)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI can support elementary school students in group-based, project-based art courses in offline classrooms. The authors focus on a gap in prior work: although GenAI is increasingly studied for education, little is known about how younger K-12 students use it in authentic classroom settings, especially for collaborative art projects and teacher-mediated activities rather than student-facing writing feedback.

The study was conducted as a four-phase field study in China with two experienced K-6 art teachers and 132 students across multiple sessions. In Phases 1 and 2, students used DALL-E and GPT through a standard chat interface to support information seeking and ideation for handcrafted dragon-themed projects. The researchers then designed AskArt, an interface that integrated GPT and DALL-E with features such as project-specific introductions, audio-to-text input, suggested follow-ups, and a select-and-generate workflow. Phases 3 and 4 evaluated AskArt in additional classroom sessions, including a between-groups comparison in Grade 6 classes with and without AskArt.

The paper finds that GenAI can help elementary students generate ideas, obtain background information, and move from text-based exploration to visual inspiration, while teachers perceived increased engagement. However, students struggled with prompt formulation and typing, and the audio input feature did not work well in practice. AskArt improved students’ understanding of appropriate tool use and increased overall satisfaction in the comparison study, but did not significantly change perceived challenge, collaboration, or creativity. The paper concludes that GenAI can be useful in offline elementary art classrooms when carefully tailored to children’s interaction needs and classroom workflows, but concerns remain about misuse, interface suitability, and the limitations of group-based deployment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-based large language model chatbot used for conversational text generation, question answering, and guidance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in the study as GPT-4 Turbo (later GPT-4o in AskArt) to support elementary students’ information seeking and project-implementation guidance in group-based offline art courses.

findings.finding_summary: In Phase 2, students reported that GPT helped provide background information and personalized guidance for their art project, and it supported idea implementation. Six respondents rated the generated content as helpful for coming up with more ideas (M=5.67, SD=0.82 on a 7-point scale).
findings.measure: Student rating of whether generated content helped the group come up with more ideas; interview and observation evidence on background information and implementation guidance
findings.sample_size: n=6 respondents (Phase 2 questionnaire); class A n=24 students overall

findings.finding_summary: Students used GPT sequentially for information seeking before switching to DALL-E for visual inspiration. However, many students struggled with typing and query formulation, and some GPT outputs were perceived as incorrect or unhelpful. In Phase 2, 9 queries were perceived as incorrect and 11 as correct but unhelpful.
findings.measure: Interaction logs, screen recordings, and coded student responses to GPT outputs

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that GenAI increased students’ engagement in the classroom, but they also expressed concerns about misuse and interface suitability. This was based on interviews across the four phases.
findings.measure: Teacher interview themes on classroom impact

identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies generative AI in general within elementary school art project-based learning, including DALL-E and GPT-based conversational assistance, and then the AskArt interface combining them.

findings.finding_summary: Across phases, GenAI helped elementary students generate project ideas, obtain background knowledge, and receive guidance for implementing their art projects. In Phase 4, students using AskArt reported significantly higher overall satisfaction than the baseline group (M=6.64 vs. 5.46; t=3.62, p=0.0005).
findings.measure: Overall satisfaction in class; qualitative reports on ideation and implementation support
findings.sample_size: n=108 valid responses in Phase 4 overall; n=43 AskArt, n=54 baseline

findings.finding_summary: GenAI use did not significantly change perceived challenge, team collaboration, or creativity expression in Phase 4. The experimental group with AskArt was not significantly different from the baseline on challenge (t=0.57, p=0.57), team engagement (t=0.70, p=0.48), or creativity expression (t=-0.37, p=0.72).
findings.measure: Perceived challenge, team collaboration, and creativity expression ratings
findings.sample_size: n=108 valid responses in Phase 4 overall; n=43 AskArt, n=54 baseline

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods field study in authentic classrooms rather than a randomized or strongly controlled trial. It provides useful contextual evidence, but the evidence base is limited by small teacher samples in earlier phases and nonrandomized classroom comparisons.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The clearest quantitative result is a statistically significant satisfaction increase in Phase 4, but no effect sizes were reported and several other outcomes were null. Overall impact appears modest and context-specific rather than broadly demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: Physics task development of prospective physics teachers using ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT 3.5 can support the development of physics assessment tasks by prospective teachers, compared with a traditional textbook-based approach. The central question is not student learning, but the quality of the tasks prospective teachers create and how they revise them after receiving either AI-generated prompts or textbook examples.

The study used a randomized controlled trial with 26 prospective physics teachers from Ludwig-Maximilians-University Munich. Participants were divided into an intervention group that used ChatGPT 3.5 and a control group that used a high-school physics textbook. All participants created four text-based conceptual tasks for 10th-grade high school physics, focused on kinematics and Newton’s laws. The intervention group also completed a usability and perceived usefulness survey about ChatGPT.

Results showed that ChatGPT-supported and textbook-supported groups produced similarly correct tasks and tasks of comparable overall quality, but the textbook group produced clearer tasks and more often embedded them in meaningful context. Both groups struggled most with task specificity, meaning they often omitted information needed to solve the tasks. ChatGPT was rated as easy to use, but its output quality was judged only neutral to slightly poor. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can support prospective physics teachers, but prompt design and teacher training are still needed to improve the pedagogical quality of the tasks produced.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational large language model chatbot for generating and revising text based on prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a support tool by prospective physics teacher students to generate four conceptual physics assessment tasks for 10th-grade German high school students, compared with a textbook condition.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized controlled trial with n=26 prospective physics teachers, task correctness did not differ significantly between ChatGPT and textbook conditions. However, ChatGPT tasks scored lower on clarity (p=0.04, d=0.38) and context (p=6�b710^-5, d=1.04), while specificity, misleading phrasing, and adequacy of difficulty showed no significant differences.
findings.measure: Task quality ratings: specificity, clarity, correctness, misleading phrasing, adequate difficulty, context, relevance to target concept, overall quality

findings.finding_summary: Participants rated ChatGPT usability highly (mean 4.1/5) but judged its output quality as slightly below neutral (mean 2.76/5) and perceived usefulness as neutral (mean 3.24/5). Response time was not viewed as a major barrier (mean 2.09/5 for the slowdown item).
findings.measure: System Usability Scale, Technology Acceptance Model 2 items on perceived usefulness and output quality

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled trial with a small sample and clear comparison condition, using direct task-quality ratings and usability measures. There are some concerns about small n and single-site sampling, but the design is experimental and credible.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports a medium-to-large positive effect for context quality in favor of the textbook and a small effect for clarity, with no difference on correctness. Overall impact is modest and mixed rather than strongly positive.

paper_profiles.title: HESEIA: A community-based dataset for evaluating social biases in large language models, co-designed in real school settings in Latin America
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of community-grounded, context-sensitive benchmarks for evaluating social bias in large language models (LLMs). The authors argue that existing bias datasets are often crowdsourced, centered on dominant cultures, and insufficiently representative of the lived experiences of educators and students in Latin America.

To address this, they developed HESEIA, a Spanish-language dataset of 46,499 stereotype-bearing sentences co-created in a professional development course for high-school teachers. The course combined in-person classes, asynchronous activities, and classroom-based lesson-plan implementation. Teachers used minimal-pair and other participatory methods to generate and validate examples drawn from their school subjects and local communities, and students in those teachers’ classes contributed under teacher supervision. The course also included educator reflection on AI bias, data governance, and lesson-plan co-design, with optional use of a web tool (EDIA) or paper-based alternatives.

The study involved 370 high-school teachers from 189 Latin American schools and 5,370 students ages 13–19, with teachers’ experience and school context varying across urban, peri-urban, and rural settings. The dataset was organized by school subject and demographic axis, with substantial intersectionality across gender, socioeconomic status, geography, age, and other categories. The authors also tested several LLMs on the resulting dataset and found that HESEIA elicited more 'don't know' responses and fewer stereotype rejections than comparison datasets, suggesting that current models are less able to recognize or reject locally grounded stereotypes.

Overall, the paper concludes that participatory, educator-centered dataset creation can reveal forms of bias that are missed by standard benchmarks and can support more contextually valid evaluation of LLM social bias in educational settings.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: A Google generative AI / large language model chatbot family used for text generation and evaluation tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reports experiments where Gemini-1.5-Flash was queried on stereotype datasets, including HESEIA, to assess whether it recognized and rejected stereotypes.

findings.finding_summary: In Experiment 1, Gemini-1.5-Flash had a 52.75% rate on HESEIA, representing the proportion of responses indicating the model failed to recognize the sentence as a stereotype. In Experiment 2, Gemini-1.5-Flash had a 44.24% rate on HESEIA for failing to reject stereotypes among those it first identified as stereotypical. The paper compares these proportions across datasets but does not report inferential statistics or effect sizes.
findings.measure: Proportion of responses indicating failure to recognize stereotypes (Exp. 1) and failure to reject stereotypes (Exp. 2)

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbot use in educational settings, without a specific named product beyond examples of language models.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies generative AI in the context of a professional development course for high-school teachers, using ChatGPT-like language models and EDIA to explore bias and stereotypes in school subjects and real school settings.

findings.finding_summary: The professional development course involved 370 high-school teachers from 189 Latin American schools and 5,370 students, and it produced the HESEIA dataset with 46,499 sentences. The paper reports that teachers’ pre/post responses shifted toward stronger disagreement with statements expressing automation and societal bias in AI; all five items showed statistically significant paired t-test differences, but no t statistics, p values, or effect sizes are reported in the excerpt.

findings.sample_size: n=245 teachers completing both tests; n=370 teachers in course; n=5,370 students

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary empirical study with a structured professional development intervention and model evaluation, but the excerpt does not provide inferential statistics or effect sizes for the reported outcomes. The design is mixed-methods and participatory rather than a tightly controlled causal study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial participation and clear descriptive changes in teacher perceptions, but effect sizes are not provided and the outcomes are not directly tied to a tested instructional outcome with quantified magnitude. The model-comparison results are descriptive proportions only, so impact is suggestive rather than clearly established.

paper_profiles.title: EZYer: A simulacrum of high school with generative agent
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the gap in educational AI tools for generating high-school-level mathematics teaching materials and supporting interactive learning. The authors argue that existing systems often have incomplete service, weak interactivity, limited quality assurance, and insufficient support for LaTeX Beamer generation. To address this, they propose EZYer, a generative educational agent designed for high school mathematics.

EZYer has three main components. The Teacher Module turns user-entered content or uploaded documents into structured teaching materials, exercises, and LaTeX Beamer courseware. The Student Module simulates classroom interaction through five roles—Teacher, Assistant, Top Student, Struggling Student, and Note Taker—to produce collaborative notes. The Controller screens inputs and outputs using keyword filtering, content scoring, role co-validation, and dynamic correction to maintain pedagogical appropriateness and academic quality.

The intended population is high school teachers and students, specifically in high school mathematics. The paper frames the system as useful for instructional preparation, in-class style interaction, and note summarization, rather than as a tested classroom intervention. Evaluation is conducted by having five large language models score 100 generated Beamer and Notes outputs on content accuracy, knowledge coverage, usability, formatting correctness, and visual appeal. The authors report generally strong scores and conclude that EZYer shows promise for high school math instruction, while noting that broader applicability, speed, and manual evaluation remain areas for future work.

identified_tools.name: DeepSeek

identified_tools.use_case: Used as the underlying LLM API when the text corpus did not match the user input, to generate high school mathematics teaching materials, exercises, classroom dialogue, and notes; also used in the controller for content scoring and correction.

The paper reports these as evaluation scores for 100 generated Beamer and Notes documents, but no effect sizes or confidence intervals are reported.

findings.sample_size: n=100 generated Beamer and Notes documents
