No effect sizes are reported, so impact remains unclear rather than demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: MusicScaffold: Bridging Machine Efficiency and Human Growth in Adolescent Creative Education through Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a central tension in generative AI for creative education: while prompt-output systems make creation fast and accessible, they may not help learners develop deeper expressive strategies, reflection, or autonomy. The authors ask whether generative AI can be redesigned to support not just efficient music production, but also cognitive, behavioral, and affective growth in adolescent learners.

To study this, they introduce MusicScaffold, a framework and prototype that repositions AI as a guide, coach, and co-creation partner. The system turns vague natural-language intentions into symbolic musical attributes with explanations, supports iterative refinement through reflective prompts, and then generates full music outputs while preserving learner agency. The framework is evaluated in mixed-methods studies in middle school music classes, including an exploratory four-week study with 60 students and a comparative four-week study with 270 students across three conditions: direct generation, attribute selection, and MusicScaffold.

The findings show that conventional prompt-output and attribute-selection tools mainly support completion efficiency, but leave students with low prompt specificity, limited strategic adjustment, low intrinsic motivation, and weak self-efficacy. In contrast, MusicScaffold improves students’ ability to translate emotions into structured musical choices, encourages more reflective and strategic revisions, and increases participation and confidence. The paper concludes that generative AI can support adolescent growth when designed as an educational scaffold rather than a one-shot generator.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model/chatbot system used for text-based generation and interpretation tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the LLM in MusicScaffold for structure-oriented intent interpretation and symbolic prompt explanation; the paper specifies GPT-4o in the prototype and describes an LLM that translates natural-language intent into musical attributes with explanations.

findings.finding_summary: In the MusicScaffold prototype, the ChatGPT/GPT-4o-based LLM helped transform vague student intents into structured musical attributes with explanations, and the comparative study found that the MusicScaffold condition significantly improved prompt specificity versus both control conditions. Group C had a mean specificity score of 3.00 compared with 1.53 and 1.80 in the two controls, with 38.9% at Level 3, 21.1% at Level 4, and 8.9% at Level 5 (N=270).
findings.measure: Prompt specificity in music expression

findings.finding_summary: The MusicScaffold condition also improved the breadth of musical elements used. Experimental Group C reached an average coverage score of 2.88, compared with 1.47 and 1.84 in the two control groups, and 68.8% of prompts in Group C invoked three or more dimensions. The paper reports significant group effects for element coverage (KruskalWallis H(2)=91.50, p<.001; chi-square (8, N=270)=96.31, p<.001).
findings.measure: Creative coverage across musical elements

findings.finding_summary: MusicScaffold increased strategic adjustment behavior relative to direct generation and attribute selection. In the comparative study, Group C showed 51.1% prompt modifications and only 28.9% regenerations, whereas Control A relied on 76.7% non-strategic regeneration and Control B on 54.4% template switching; the group difference was significant (chi-square (6, N=540)=194.27, p<.001).
findings.measure: Adjustment behavior during AI interaction

findings.finding_summary: The framework improved sustained motivation and confidence. Group C had higher after-class participation, rising more than the controls across four weeks, and higher self-efficacy in expressing emotions through music (mean=3.60 vs. 2.01 and 2.37 in controls). The paper reports significant group effects for self-efficacy (chi-square (8, N=270)=33.89, p<.001; H(2)=27.97, p<.001).
findings.measure: After-class participation and self-efficacy in musical expression

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods comparative study with quantitative analyses and interviews, but it is not a randomized controlled trial in a typical education-intervention sense and the paper does not report effect sizes or confidence intervals for the main outcomes. Evidence is still reasonably structured and multi-armed, so it is stronger than purely qualitative work.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported group differences are substantial and statistically significant, especially for prompt specificity, coverage, and strategic behavior. However, the paper does not provide standardized effect sizes, so the precise magnitude is somewhat unclear despite likely meaningful practical impact.

paper_profiles.title: A cross-sectional look at teacher reactions, worries, and professional development needs related to generative AI in an urban school district
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how K-12 teachers in a large urban school district perceive generative AI chatbots, especially ChatGPT, and what professional development (PD) they say they need. The paper asks whether reactions to AI vary by grade band, subject area, and teaching experience, and it also compares teachers’ perceived benefits and concerns for teachers versus students.

The study is not an AI intervention or coaching program; instead, it analyzes responses from the district’s annual employee survey after AI-focused items were added. The sample included 1,454 certificated educators from one large urban district on the U.S. West Coast. Teachers reported their grade level, subject area, years of experience, prior AI use, allowability judgments for several AI uses (idea generation, paper editing/completion, full paper writing, concept explanation, and code generation), open-ended concerns and benefits, and PD needs.

Findings show clear subgroup variation. Teachers in higher grade bands were less willing to allow student use of AI than elementary teachers. Elementary teachers with more experience were especially restrictive about writing support, concept explanation, and code generation. Among high school teachers, more experienced humanities teachers were particularly conservative about allowing AI for idea generation and paper editing. Teachers also differentiated between risks and benefits for teachers versus students, with plagiarism and overreliance seen as more serious for students, while misinformation and lack of AI knowledge were more salient for teachers. For PD, elementary and middle school teachers wanted basic AI literacy, whereas high school teachers more often wanted guidance on managing student use and detecting AI-generated work.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI chatbot/large language model system used for school-related tasks such as writing support, concept explanation, code generation, lesson planning, and information retrieval.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers in a large urban K-12 district reported their attitudes toward AI chatbots, including ChatGPT as the example, and responded to survey items about allowable uses, concerns, benefits, and professional development needs. The paper did not evaluate a specific deployed product; it studied teachers’ perceptions of generative AI chatbots generally.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods cross-sectional survey of 1,454 teachers in one large urban district, teachers in secondary settings were less willing than elementary teachers to allow AI chatbot use. Grade level was negatively associated with allowability for all five queried uses; for example, the marginal effects were dy/dx=-0.121 for idea generation (N=254), -0.117 for paper editing (N=254), -0.135 for writing an entire paper (N=216), -0.125 for concept explanation (N=232), and -0.150 for code generation (N=100).
findings.measure: Teacher allowability of AI chatbot use for five tasks (idea generation, paper editing, full paper writing, concept explanation, code generation)
findings.effect_size: dy/dx range: -0.117 to -0.150 for grade-level effects; elementary more permissive than secondary
findings.confidence_interval: see tables in paper; exact CI varies by outcome

findings.finding_summary: Among elementary teachers, more experienced educators (>10 years) were substantially less likely to allow student AI use for writing-related tasks. Relative to less experienced teachers, the marginal effects were -0.489 for idea generation (N=113), -0.502 for editing a paper (N=115), and -0.587 for writing an entire paper (N=113).
findings.measure: Teacher allowability of AI chatbot use for writing support tasks by experience level
findings.confidence_interval: [0.633, -0.346] for idea generation; [0.657, -0.348] for editing; [0.826, -0.348] for full paper writing as reported

findings.finding_summary: For high school teachers, more experienced educators and humanities teachers were generally more restrictive about AI chatbot use for writing support. For idea generation, more experienced humanities teachers had dy/dx=-0.329 (N=97), and for paper editing more experienced humanities teachers had dy/dx=-0.378 while more experienced STEM teachers had dy/dx=-0.404 (N=96). For writing an entire paper, more experienced educators had dy/dx=-0.435 (N=69).
findings.measure: Teacher allowability of AI chatbot use by subject and experience within high school

findings.finding_summary: For elementary teachers, more experienced educators were less likely to allow AI use for concept explanation and code generation, with marginal effects of -0.457 (N=114) and -0.500 (N=60), respectively. For high school teachers, more experienced educators were also less likely to allow concept explanation (dy/dx=-0.232, N=81).
findings.measure: Teacher allowability of AI chatbot use for concept explanation and code generation by experience
findings.confidence_interval: see tables 9 and 11 for reported intervals

findings.finding_summary: Teachers distinguished sharply between concerns/benefits for teachers versus students. Chi-square tests showed significant differences in both benefits (χ2_dof=6=77.817, p=0.000) and concerns (χ2_dof=7=273.019, p=0.000). Teachers most often worried about teachers’ own insufficient AI knowledge (18.37%) and overreliance (18.21%), while for students the leading concerns were overreliance (29.52%) and plagiarism/misuse (26.35%).
findings.measure: Ranked open-ended concern categories for teachers’ vs students’ AI use
findings.sample_size: n=668 for teachers' concerns; n=669 for students' concerns

findings.finding_summary: Teachers also differed in perceived benefits for teachers versus students. Chi-square tests found significant differences in benefits (χ2_dof=6=77.817, p=0.000). Teachers most often named lesson planning/material preparation (21.41%) and efficiency (13.62%) as benefits for teachers, whereas for students the top benefits were information retrieval (20.33%) and other benefits (22.57%).
findings.measure: Ranked open-ended benefit categories for teachers’ vs students’ AI use
findings.sample_size: n=626 for teachers' benefits; n=630 for students' benefits

findings.finding_summary: Professional development needs varied significantly by grade level (χ2_dof=21=63.949, p=0.000), but not by subject area (χ2_dof=14=17.376, p=0.237) or experience level (χ2_dof=7=4.165, p=0.761). Elementary and middle school teachers more often wanted basic AI literacy, while high school teachers more often wanted guidance on managing student AI use (12.195%) and detecting AI-generated work (11.707%).
findings.measure: Open-ended professional development needs for generative AI
findings.sample_size: n=256 elementary; n=114 middle; n=205 high for grade comparisons

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional mixed-methods survey study from a single district, so it provides correlational evidence rather than experimental causal evidence. The analyses are systematic and sample size is large, but the paper does not evaluate an intervention or product efficacy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial subgroup differences in willingness to allow AI use and in professional development needs, but these are attitudinal and policy-relevant rather than direct learning impacts. Effect sizes for the regression models are modest-to-large in direction, but they concern perceptions and allowability, not measured student outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI use in K-12 education: a systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews empirical research on generative AI (GenAI) use in K-12 education, focusing on how GenAI has been used, in what contexts, and with what reported impacts. The author conducted a systematic review using Scopus and Web of Science plus snowballing, screening papers against inclusion criteria that required empirical use of GenAI in teaching or learning within K-12 or closely related vocational settings.

Across 30 included papers, the review finds that GenAI work in K-12 has concentrated on high school and pre-service teachers, with much less attention to in-service teachers, elementary grades, or special populations. ChatGPT was by far the dominant tool, although some studies used Midjourney, Copilot, Canva, and custom GenAI-based tools. Subject coverage skewed strongly toward STEM, especially mathematics and physics, but also included programming, science, writing, English, history, and AI-related activities.

The review concludes that quasi-experimental designs are the most common, but that the evidence base relies heavily on self-reported outcomes such as attitudes, trust, self-efficacy, and engagement rather than objective learning measures. It also notes that teacher professional development is frequently recommended, yet actual studies involving in-service teachers, instructional practice, parent involvement, rural settings, and long-term or rigorous classroom evaluation remain sparse. The paper argues that future work should examine real-time classroom use, broader subject areas, and better outcome measures to support effective GenAI integration in schools.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools or chatbots used for educational content generation, assistance, and feedback tasks in K-12 settings.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a systematic review of empirical K-12 studies using GenAI tools; it synthesizes how tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot, Midjourney, and others were used across subjects, grade bands, and settings.

findings.finding_summary: Across 30 included studies, the review found that most existing work focused on high school and preservice teachers, with middle school also represented; in-service teachers were barely targeted. Subject coverage was concentrated in STEM, especially mathematics and physics, while non-STEM areas such as writing and English were less common. The review also notes a lack of evidence in early childhood, special needs, and rural contexts, and very limited work involving instructional coaches or teacher professional development beyond general calls for training.
findings.measure: Distribution of included studies by educational level, subject area, country/context, and study design

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review synthesizing heterogeneous primary studies rather than a single controlled evaluation. The evidence is informative but largely descriptive and based on the included studies' varied designs and measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review indicates clear patterns of use and gaps, but it does not report a pooled causal effect size. The practical impact is therefore suggestive rather than quantitatively established.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI for Teachers’ Self-Directed Professional Development: A Mixed-Methods Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study examines how K-12 teachers use generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, for self-directed professional development (SDPD). The authors ask how ChatGPT supports instructional practice, how teachers use it within their own professional learning processes, and how teachers perceive its usefulness for SDPD. The study is framed by Garrison’s self-directed learning model, focusing on self-management, self-monitoring, and motivation.

The quantitative phase surveyed 298 U.S.-based K-12 teachers who had experience using ChatGPT for teaching and professional development. The qualitative phase included five semi-structured interviews and analysis of teachers’ ChatGPT interaction logs or related documents. Participants reported using ChatGPT mainly for lesson planning, generating pedagogical ideas, creating activities or materials, and saving time in planning and organization. Interviewees included elementary and high school teachers as well as teachers working in adult/community and college/university contexts; the findings highlighted experience differences and varied subject areas, including English language arts, reading, social science, and social studies/history/government/economics.

Overall, the paper concludes that ChatGPT can function as a flexible, just-in-time support tool that lowers the barrier to engaging in SDPD, especially when teachers face time pressure and limited formal PD opportunities. Teachers generally used the tool critically, revising outputs based on their expertise and classroom needs. The authors argue that generative AI may expand teachers’ informal professional learning by providing structure, ideas, and motivation, while also raising concerns about shallow engagement, uneven digital literacy, and the need for stronger institutional support and AI-specific training.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI chatbot used to generate, revise, and discuss text, ideas, and feedback through natural-language prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a self-directed professional development tool for K-12 teachers in the United States; teachers used it for lesson-plan inspiration, course planning, generating materials, answering questions, and reflecting on teaching practice.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed-methods study of 298 K-12 U.S. teachers, participants reported using ChatGPT most often for inspiration for classroom pedagogies, class activities, and lesson plans (19.49%), generating practice questions/quizzes (17.97%), and creating customized educational content (15.75%). Interviewees likewise described using it to structure lesson planning and curriculum design, including an 18-week pacing guide for a high school anthropology course.
findings.measure: Self-reported educational activities/use cases with ChatGPT; interview descriptions of lesson-planning use

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that ChatGPT supported self-management in SDPD by helping them organize activities, manage time, and apply learning strategies (e.g., organizing activities M=4.81, managing time M=4.70). Interviewees repeatedly said the tool saved planning time and reduced cognitive load, allowing them to focus on other classroom responsibilities.
findings.measure: Likert-scale self-management items and interview themes about time management/organization

findings.finding_summary: Teachers were motivated to use ChatGPT for SDPD, with strong agreement on wanting to improve teaching practice (M=3.87), learn new ideas (M=3.94), and enjoy learning through ChatGPT (M=3.96), but the paper also notes passive motivation due to teaching pressure and limited room for professional advancement. Several teachers said ChatGPT lowered the entry threshold for SDPD by making it easier to start planning and learning.
findings.measure: Motivation to use ChatGPT for SDPD; interview accounts of barriers and motivators

findings.finding_summary: Teachers generally felt responsible for and capable of directing their own learning with ChatGPT, including setting goals, seeking help, and following plans (e.g., responsibility for learning M=4.19; high learning standards M=4.04). Interviewees described iterative refinement of AI-generated lesson materials and using ChatGPT to break ideas into smaller pieces.
findings.measure: Self-monitoring and self-management Likert items; interview themes on reflection and revision

findings.finding_summary: Participants generally agreed that they critically evaluated ChatGPT's instructional ideas (M=4.17) and felt confident interacting with the tool (M=4.04), but confidence in the accuracy of its information was more variable (M=3.46). The authors interpret this as teachers using a critical mindset and relying on their own expertise to edit and humanize AI outputs.
findings.measure: Perceptions of ChatGPT's functionality and accuracy; interview reflections on critical use

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods empirical study with a moderate sample size, but it relies on self-report survey data, a very small interview sample, and descriptive analysis rather than experimental or quasi-experimental estimation. That makes it useful evidence, but not high-credibility causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally positive perceived effects on planning, motivation, self-management, and critical reflection, but it does not provide causal effect sizes or student outcome gains. Impact is therefore promising but quantitatively unclear.

paper_profiles.title: A cross-sectional look at teacher reactions, worries, and professional development needs related to generative AI in an urban school district
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers in a large urban school district perceived generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT soon after their widespread release. The study asks whether teachers’ reactions, concerns, and professional development needs vary by grade level taught, subject area, and years of teaching experience. It is motivated by uncertainty about how generative AI should be used in schools and by the need to understand teacher-facing guidance needs rather than only student-facing uses.

The researchers used a district-wide annual survey augmented with AI-specific questions. The sample included 1,454 certificated educators from a single large urban school district on the U.S. West Coast. Teachers reported their prior chatbot use, the degree to which they would allow students to use AI for specific tasks, their concerns and perceived benefits for both teachers and students, and their desired professional development topics. The analysis combined quantitative logistic regression and chi-square tests with qualitative coding of open-ended responses.

Findings showed clear subgroup differences. Teachers in higher grade bands were less willing to allow AI use, especially for writing-related tasks; elementary teachers were generally more permissive than middle and high school teachers. Within elementary grades, more experienced teachers were more restrictive than less experienced teachers. Among high school teachers, more experienced humanities teachers were especially likely to disallow AI for idea generation and paper editing. Across all grades, teachers’ main professional development need was learning how to use AI pedagogically, but elementary and middle school teachers wanted basic AI literacy while high school teachers especially wanted guidance on managing student AI use and detecting AI-generated work. The paper concludes that professional learning and policy support should be tailored to grade band and, to a lesser extent, subject and experience.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI chatbot / large language model tool used for conversational text generation, explanation, editing, and related school tasks; the paper mentions ChatGPT as an example but does not evaluate a specific product beyond generic chatbot use.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed K-12 teachers’ perceptions of generative AI chatbots in schools, including allowability for idea generation, paper editing/completion, full paper writing, concept explanation, and code generation; also asked about benefits, concerns, and professional development needs.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers in a large urban district reported substantially lower allowability for generative AI as grade level increased. In logistic regression, moving from elementary to middle/high school reduced likelihood of allowing idea generation (dy/dx=-0.121), paper editing (-0.117), full paper writing (-0.135), concept explanation (-0.125), and code generation (-0.150), all p<0.001; models used survey responses from 1,454 teachers, with outcome-specific analytic samples ranging from N=100 to N=254.
findings.measure: Teacher allowability of student use of AI chatbots for five academic tasks (idea generation, paper editing, full paper writing, concept explanation, code generation)
findings.confidence_interval: [0.975] range reported as approximately -0.156 to -0.116 across models

findings.finding_summary: Among elementary teachers, more experienced educators (>10 years in district) were much less likely to allow AI writing support. Relative to less experienced elementary teachers, more experienced teachers showed lower allowability for idea generation (dy/dx=-0.489), paper editing (-0.502), and writing an entire paper (-0.587), all p<0.001; the elementary models used N=113-115.
findings.measure: Teacher allowability of AI use for writing support tasks among elementary teachers

findings.finding_summary: For high school teachers, experience and subject area also shaped allowability for AI writing support. More experienced high school teachers were more likely to disallow idea generation (dy/dx=-0.329 for humanities; -0.279 for other; p�3c0.05), and more experienced teachers were more likely to disallow paper editing/completion, with the largest negative marginal effects for humanities (dy/dx=-0.378) and STEM (dy/dx=-0.404, p=0.036); the paper writing model also showed a negative effect for more experienced educators (dy/dx=-0.435, p<0.001).
findings.measure: Teacher allowability of AI use for writing support tasks among high school teachers, by subject and experience

findings.finding_summary: For concept explanation and code generation, more experienced elementary teachers were again less likely to allow student AI use. The reported marginal effects were dy/dx=-0.457 for concept explanation and dy/dx=-0.500 for code generation, both p<0.001, indicating substantially lower allowability among more experienced educators.
findings.measure: Teacher allowability of AI use for concept explanation and code generation among elementary teachers

findings.finding_summary: Teachers identified different benefits and concerns for teachers versus students. For teachers, the top benefits were insufficient personal knowledge about AI (22.16%), preparing lesson plans/materials (21.41%), and increased efficiency (13.62%); for students, the most common benefit was information retrieval (20.33%) and other uncategorized benefits (22.57%). Concerns also differed: teachers’ top concerns were insufficient AI knowledge (18.37%) and teacher overreliance (18.21%), whereas for students the dominant concerns were overreliance (29.52%) and plagiarism/misuse (26.35%).
findings.measure: Open-ended survey responses about perceived benefits and concerns for teachers’ versus students’ use of AI chatbots

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods cross-sectional survey with regression and coded open-ended responses, not an experimental study. Evidence is useful for subgroup variation but is correlational and district-specific, so causal inference is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The subgroup effects are often statistically significant and sometimes sizable in magnitude, but they describe attitudes/allowability rather than student outcomes or implemented coaching effects. The practical impact is important for PD targeting, yet outcome evidence is indirect.

paper_profiles.title: Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence: Early experiments with GPT-4
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents an exploratory assessment of an early, text-only version of GPT-4, arguing that it displays many signs of broad, general intelligence. Rather than using conventional benchmark evaluation alone, the authors adopt a human-curiosity-driven approach: they create novel prompts and tasks intended to probe whether the model can generalize across domains, combine skills, and handle tasks that are difficult to solve by memorization.

The paper examines GPT-4’s behavior across several areas, including interdisciplinary composition, coding, mathematics, tool use, interaction with humans, and discrimination/hallucination checks. Examples include generating code for graphics, writing poetry-style mathematical proofs, solving math problems, comparing generated outputs, and handling common-sense reasoning tasks. The model is shown to perform strongly on many of these demonstrations, often outperforming ChatGPT and producing outputs the authors judge to be close to human quality.

The paper’s broader conclusion is that GPT-4 represents a significant step toward AGI, while still showing important limitations such as hallucinations, arithmetic errors, weak planning, and bias. The work is not an educational intervention study and does not examine teachers, students, or school settings; it is a position/exploratory paper about model capabilities and limitations.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family conversational language model used for text generation, question answering, and evaluation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper uses early GPT-4, normalized here to ChatGPT per the provided LLM family rules, as the focal model in informal demonstrations of broad language, coding, reasoning, and comparison tasks. It is compared against ChatGPT-style outputs across several prompts, including teaching-style evaluations of generated text.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a demonstration/opinion-style paper rather than a controlled empirical study, meta-analysis, or systematic review. It does not evaluate a K–12 coaching or lesson-feedback intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No K–12 educational outcome is measured, and there are no reported effect sizes or outcome data relevant to teacher coaching or lesson-plan feedback.

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment: Definitions and Relationships
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a conceptual problem in the assessment literature: the lack of agreement about what counts as formative assessment and how it differs from related ideas such as feedback, assessment for learning, and assessment of learning. Wiliam reviews the historical origins of feedback and formative assessment, arguing that effective assessment must be understood as part of a broader instructional system rather than as a standalone intervention. The paper synthesizes findings from earlier reviews and meta-analyses to show that feedback can improve learning, but only when it is used by teachers and/or students to change subsequent instructional or learning activity.

The paper does not report a single new empirical intervention. Instead, it analyzes a wide range of prior research spanning elementary, middle, high school, and college-aged learners, with especially strong attention to K-12 classroom assessment. It discusses classroom feedback practices, teacher use of assessment data, student self-assessment, and systems of formative assessment embedded in instruction. The paper also notes subject-specific examples, including mathematics, reading, history, figurative language, and chemistry, to illustrate how feedback must be domain-specific and tied to the learning task.

The main conclusion is that formative assessment should be defined by whether evidence is actually used to adapt teaching to student needs, not merely by the collection of information about student performance. Wiliam emphasizes that effective formative assessment depends on the learning milieu, teacher responses, and student responses, and that simple feedback or grades alone are often insufficient. The paper concludes that classroom-level reform in formative assessment is central rather than marginal and will require sustained support, but it does not identify a single best model for practice.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system or related instructional feedback system that provides adaptive guidance, feedback, or assessment support within a learning environment.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses formative assessment and feedback as general instructional concepts and reviews evidence from feedback/assessment systems, but it does not study a specific AI product or generative AI tool.

findings.finding_summary: Across prior research on formative assessment and feedback, the paper reports that effective classroom assessment can improve student achievement, with reviews finding effects typically around 0.4 to 0.7 standard deviations. The paper also notes that feedback is more effective when it is task-focused, timely, and used to adapt instruction, rather than merely providing grades or praise.
findings.measure: Student achievement / learning outcomes in classroom assessment and feedback studies
findings.effect_size: 0.4 to 0.7 SD (reviewed literature); also 0.32 SD in one classroom implementation cited

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/review paper about formative assessment and feedback, not an empirical evaluation of a specific AI tool. It synthesizes prior literature rather than reporting a new controlled study of an instructional AI system.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper summarizes moderate positive effects reported in prior research on formative assessment (often above 0.20 SD), but these are not findings about a specific AI tool in this paper. The direct evidence for the paper itself is therefore not tool-specific and remains indirect.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can serve as an automated teacher coach. The authors frame three teacher-coaching tasks for the model: scoring classroom transcript segments using established observation rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student reasoning. The motivation is that classroom coaching is important for teacher development, but many teachers lack access to consistent high-quality feedback because of limited expertise and resources.

The study evaluates ChatGPT in a zero-shot setting on elementary mathematics classroom transcripts from the National Center for Teacher Effectiveness (NCTE) dataset. The transcripts come from 4th- and 5th-grade classrooms in four U.S. school districts serving largely historically marginalized students. For the quantitative scoring task, the authors compare model predictions against expert human ratings on CLASS and MQI observation items. For the qualitative feedback tasks, they recruit experienced math teachers, including one with decades of instructional coaching experience and one with six years of teaching experience in Title 1 public schools, to rate the model’s outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT shows some promise for scalable instructional feedback, but its performance is weak overall. It has low correlation with human ratings for scoring tasks, often produces feedback that is not insightful or relevant, and frequently repeats what teachers already do instead of offering novel suggestions. The authors conclude that current generative AI is not yet a reliable replacement for human instructional coaches, but could become a useful complement with further development and coach-in-the-loop refinement.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based conversational large language model used for zero-shot text generation and scoring.
identified_tools.use_case: Used zero-shot as an automated teacher coach to (A) score classroom transcript segments with CLASS and MQI observation rubrics, (B) identify highlights and missed opportunities in instructional practice, and (C) generate actionable suggestions for eliciting more student mathematical reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: On the quantitative scoring task, ChatGPT showed low correspondence with expert human ratings across CLASS and MQI items. Reported Spearman correlations were small to near-zero across prompting methods (e.g., CLASS CLPC/CLBM/CLINSTD with DA: 0.00/0.35/-0.01; MQI EXPL/REMED/LANGIMP/SMQR with DA: 0.02/0.05/0.00/0.17), and adding rubric descriptions or reasoning did not consistently improve results.
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between ChatGPT-predicted observation scores and human rubric scores on CLASS and MQI transcript segments

findings.finding_summary: For highlight/missed-opportunity generation, teachers rated outputs as often not insightful or relevant, with MQI worse than CLASS. The paper reports that for CLASS, low scores were 22% faithful, 35% relevant, and 51% insightful; for MQI, low scores were 29% faithful, 55% relevant, and 71% insightful. Faithfulness problems (hallucination/misinterpretation) appeared in about 20-30% of responses.
findings.measure: Human teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for generated feedback on CLASS and MQI items
findings.sample_size: n=504 examples total (216 CLASS, 288 MQI) rated by 2 teachers

findings.finding_summary: For actionable suggestions on eliciting student reasoning, most responses were judged actionable, faithful, and relevant, but they were frequently redundant. The paper reports that 82% of suggestions repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript; nonetheless, 76% were rated novel? Actually the text says the majority were actionable and faithful, while novelty was poor due to redundancy.
findings.measure: Human teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, actionability, and novelty for suggested coaching moves

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small empirical study with qualitative human ratings and correlational analysis, not an RCT or meta-analysis. The evidence is useful but limited by the small evaluation sample and lack of experimental comparison groups.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear limitations in ChatGPT’s coaching usefulness: correlations are near zero to small, and many outputs are irrelevant, uninsightful, or redundant. Any positive signal is modest and inconsistent rather than clearly medium or large.

paper_profiles.title: To what extent is ChatGPT useful for language teacher lesson plan creation?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can be used to generate effective foreign-language teacher lesson plans and how prompt specificity affects the quality and consistency of the outputs. The authors frame the problem as a practical and research gap: teachers increasingly need support for lesson planning, but it is unclear how reliable generative AI is when used for this purpose, especially when prompted in simple, zero-shot ways.

The intervention/approach was not a human-subjects intervention but an experimental prompt-evaluation study using ChatGPT 4.0. The authors created five zero-shot prompts that progressively increased in specificity for a 45-minute high school Level I Spanish lesson on a Costa Rican restaurant. Each prompt was run in 10 separate chats, producing 50 lesson plans that were scored against a 25-item rubric based on best practices and edTPA-aligned lesson criteria. The rubric and context were derived from teacher-education expectations at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte.

The study context is K-12 teacher preparation, specifically foreign language teacher education in the United States, with the sample materials centered on a high school Spanish classroom. The paper does not study students directly; instead, it evaluates AI-generated materials intended for preservice and practicing teachers. Findings suggest ChatGPT can produce generally strong lesson plans, but added specificity does not reliably improve quality in a linear way. Including a lesson template sometimes reduced quality, while including explicit scoring criteria improved outputs most. Outputs also showed substantial non-determinism, with the same prompt producing lesson plans that varied widely in quality.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT can be useful for lesson-plan creation, but teachers must critically review and revise generated materials because outputs may include outdated pedagogical practices and inconsistent inclusion of key instructional components such as cultural connections and communicative interaction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model system used for conversational text generation and prompting-based assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate foreign language teacher lesson plans from five zero-shot prompts of increasing specificity; each prompt was run 10 times to assess prompt specificity, output variability, and alignment with lesson-plan criteria.

findings.finding_summary: Across 50 ChatGPT-generated lesson plans (5 prompts � 10 iterations), increasing prompt specificity had a marginal effect on overall rubric scores (p=0.0442; F=2.668; DF=4), but pairwise tests were not significant after correction. The mean score did not increase linearly: P.2 averaged 21.2/25, P.3 19.8/25, P.4 19.6/25, and P.5 21.6/25.
findings.measure: Lesson-plan rubric score out of 25

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT outputs showed substantial non-determinism within identical prompts. For example, P.1 outputs ranged from 16/25 to 23/25 and P.5 from 20/25 to 25/25, with outputs from the same prompt varying by at least five rubric elements. Distances and clustering showed only partial separation by prompt group, indicating both convergence and divergence across repeated runs.
findings.measure: Within-prompt variability in rubric scores and Jaccard-distance similarity of output components

findings.finding_summary: Several lesson-plan components were consistently present, including meaningful context, teacher input aligned to objectives, and activities appropriate to proficiency level. Other components were inconsistently or weakly represented, including cultural connections and integration of ACTFL standards; some prompt features (especially the checklist in P.5) improved inclusion of required elements, while template-only prompting sometimes reduced quality in specific sections such as the warm-up and teacher input.
findings.measure: Presence/absence of 25 rubric criteria across generated lesson plans

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-study, mixed-methods/quantitative evaluation of ChatGPT outputs rather than a controlled effectiveness trial. The design is systematic and transparent, but it does not establish causal impacts on teacher or student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports some meaningful improvements in rubric alignment with stronger prompting, but effects are modest and inconsistent, with substantial variability across repeated outputs. No effect sizes were reported, and the main results are about output quality rather than downstream educational impact.

paper_profiles.title: LessonPlanner: Assisting Novice Teachers to Prepare Pedagogy-Driven Lesson Plans with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: UIST '24 (The 37th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge novice teachers face when preparing lesson plans: choosing effective teaching strategies, finding appropriate instructional materials, and organizing those materials into a coherent lesson flow. The authors argue that while large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4 can generate useful lesson-plan content, using them through a standard chat interface can be cognitively demanding and can produce fragmented or hard-to-use outputs.

To address this, they develop LessonPlanner, a web-based interactive system that structures LLM assistance around educational theory, especially Bloom’s Taxonomy and Gagne’s Nine Events of Instruction. Users input course metadata and lesson goals, generate an outline, and then refine each lesson section with preset prompts, contextual actions, editable markdown, and a sidebar assistant for regeneration, explanation, and slide-oriented suggestions. The system is explicitly designed for lesson-plan preparation rather than student-facing writing feedback.

The study includes a formative interview/co-design phase with six novice teachers and teaching assistants, a within-subjects evaluation with 12 university students acting as teachers, and expert interviews with six teachers from university, primary, and high school settings. The quantitative and qualitative findings suggest that LessonPlanner improved the perceived quality of lesson plans and reduced workload relative to a ChatGPT baseline, while experts valued its structured outline and pedagogically informed prompts. The paper concludes that LLMs can support teacher lesson planning effectively when embedded in a guided, theory-based interface with flexible user control.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM system used for interactive text generation and refinement.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the baseline interface for lesson-plan preparation, and also referenced by participants as a tool they had used to generate answers, lesson-plan content, and instructional materials.

findings.finding_summary: In the formative study, 3 participants reported prior use of ChatGPT for lesson preparation, including generating precise answers to student questions and suggesting teaching flow/materials. The paper reports perceptions that ChatGPT can help, but also notes concerns about prompting burden, accuracy, and subject-specific usefulness; no controlled effect size was reported for ChatGPT itself.
findings.measure: Qualitative interview reports of prior use, perceived usefulness, trust, and prompting burden
findings.sample_size: n=6 (formative study participants mentioning LLM use: n=3)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods HCI study with interviews, co-design, and a within-subjects comparison, but the excerpt provides no formal effect sizes for ChatGPT specifically and largely reports qualitative perceptions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical utility of ChatGPT in lesson planning, but the excerpt does not provide a tool-specific impact estimate beyond qualitative reports, so impact is unclear/modest.

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether K-12 mathematics educators prefer lesson plans generated by generative AI systems or by human curriculum designers, and how those preferences vary by grade band and lesson-plan component. The study is motivated by the growing use of GenAI tools for lesson planning, alongside concerns that AI-generated materials may lack pedagogical nuance, contextual fit, or student-support features.

The intervention or comparison involved pairwise evaluations of three lesson-plan sources: a customized GPT-4 model, a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model, and human curriculum designer-created plans retrieved from open educational resources. The authors generated or matched lesson plans across K-12 mathematics topics and asked experienced educators to compare them on warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality. Participants were blinded to source and also provided written comments explaining their choices. The study used both quantitative preference analysis and qualitative thematic analysis.

The sample consisted of 20 experienced K-12 mathematics educators spanning elementary, middle, and high school levels; 16 completed the full study, producing 529 usable lesson-plan pair evaluations. The work was conducted online over several weeks in 2024, with participants completing practice comparisons and weekly check-ins. The context was U.S.-based K-12 mathematics lesson planning, with comparisons made across grade bands and instructional components.

The main findings were that human-created lesson plans were generally preferred overall, especially for elementary grades and for warm-up, main-task, and overall-quality measures. GenAI, especially customized GPT-4, performed comparatively better on cool-down sections, and the fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model became more competitive in high school settings. The qualitative analysis suggested that educators valued human plans for student discourse, differentiation, and scaffolding, while AI plans were appreciated for structure and adaptability. The authors conclude that GenAI is best positioned as an assistive tool for lesson planning rather than a replacement for educator expertise.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-family conversational large language model used to generate customized lesson plans from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a customized prompt-based GPT-4 model to generate K-12 mathematics lesson plans for comparison against human curriculum designer lesson plans and fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b outputs.

findings.finding_summary: In pairwise comparisons across 2,116 total evaluations from 16 educators, customized GPT-4 was preferred over fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b 57.7% vs. 42.3% overall. However, human curriculum designer plans were still preferred over GPT-4 overall 58.7% vs. 41.3%, and the pattern varied by grade band: GPT-4 was stronger in middle school and especially in cool-down activities, but weaker than human-authored plans in elementary settings.
findings.measure: Educator binary preference for lesson plans overall, by grade level, and by lesson-plan section (warm-up, main tasks, cool-down)
findings.sample_size: n=16 educators; 529 lesson-plan pairs; 2,116 measure-level evaluations

findings.finding_summary: GPT-4 was preferred over human curriculum designer lesson plans for cool-down sections: 59.7% vs. 40.3% in pairwise comparisons. Bootstrapped aggregate analysis also ranked GPT-4 first for cool-down activities at 38%, suggesting comparatively strong performance on lesson wrap-up and reflection tasks.
findings.measure: Preference for cool-down section quality and coherence
findings.confidence_interval: 95% bootstrap CIs reported but values not given in text

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta’s open-weight large language model family, here fine-tuned on expert-designed K-12 lesson plans to generate structured instructional content.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model to generate K-12 mathematics lesson plans for comparison with customized GPT-4 and human curriculum designer plans.

findings.finding_summary: Fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b was preferred less often than customized GPT-4 overall (42.3% vs. 57.7% in their direct comparison), but it remained competitive with human curriculum designer lesson plans, which were preferred 53.6% vs. 46.4%. The study reported stronger relative performance in higher grade levels, especially high school, and in cool-down activities.
findings.measure: Educator binary preference for lesson plans overall and by grade level/lesson section
findings.sample_size: n=16 educators; 529 lesson-plan pairs; 2,116 measure-level evaluations

findings.finding_summary: For high school lesson plans, fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b outperformed human curriculum designer plans, with educators preferring LLaMA-2-13b FT 59.2% vs. 40.8%. The paper interprets this as evidence that domain-specific fine-tuning helps the model better capture higher-grade complexity.
findings.measure: Preference in high school grade band
findings.sample_size: subset of the overall sample; exact n for high school comparisons not reported

findings.finding_summary: LLaMA-2-13b also performed well in cool-down activities: it was preferred over human-created lesson conclusions 57.9% vs. 42.1%. In the bootstrapped aggregate analysis, it scored 33.7% on cool-down tasks, behind GPT-4 but ahead of human-authored plans, indicating relative strength in summarization and reinforcement activities.
findings.measure: Preference for cool-down section quality and coherence
findings.confidence_interval: 95% bootstrap CIs reported but values not given in text

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-method comparative user study with experienced educators, but it is not a randomized trial and does not report formal effect sizes. The evidence is useful for preference patterns and subgroup variation, but causal strength is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports clear directional preference differences by grade band and lesson section, but no standardized effect sizes are provided. The practical impact appears meaningful for lesson-planning workflows, yet the magnitude is not quantified.

paper_profiles.title: An Evaluation of the Pedagogical Soundness and Usability of AI-Generated Lesson Plans Across Different Models and Prompt Frameworks in High-School Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-generated lesson plans for K-12 teaching are pedagogically sound and usable, and how output quality varies by large language model and prompt framework. The author focuses on a practical classroom planning problem: educators increasingly use generative AI to draft lessons, but there is limited evidence on which models and prompting structures produce the most usable and instructionally reliable plans.

The study generated fifteen lesson plans for one high-school physics topic, The Electromagnetic Spectrum, using five LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Grok) crossed with three prompt frameworks (TAG, RACE, and COSTAR). The plans were evaluated automatically on readability/linguistic complexity, factual accuracy and hallucination detection, standards alignment to NGSS, and cognitive demand of learning objectives.

The paper reports that model choice primarily affected readability, with DeepSeek producing the most accessible plans and Claude the most linguistically complex. Prompt framework structure mattered more for factual completeness and curriculum alignment, with RACE generally producing the best results. Across all models and prompts, learning objectives were concentrated at the lowest Bloom’s taxonomy levels (Remember and Understand), indicating that the generated plans often lacked higher-order cognitive demand. The author concludes that AI can help draft lesson plans, but teachers should use structured prompts, explicit curriculum references, and higher-order objective requirements to improve classroom usability.

paper_profiles.title: Understanding Teacher Revisions of Large Language Model-Generated Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how teachers actually revise large language model (LLM)-generated formative feedback before it is delivered to students, and what characteristics of the AI output are associated with revision. The authors focus on teacher mediation as a core part of evaluating generative AI in education, arguing that model output alone does not determine what learners receive.

The study analyzes 1,349 AI-generated feedback drafts and corresponding teacher-edited messages from 117 teachers using the Tutoria platform. The platform integrates with Moodle and Google Classroom and supports a co-creation workflow in which teachers can accept, edit, or rewrite feedback generated for short open-ended responses. Data came from prior controlled studies and classroom deployments, including Brazilian high school chemistry tasks, introductory computer science feedback by higher-education instructors, and extracurricular computer science contexts.

Across the dataset, teachers accepted LLM feedback unchanged in about 78% of cases, and many teachers rarely edited at all. When they did revise, edits usually shortened the feedback and preserved much of its meaning, suggesting compression rather than wholesale correction. Text-only models could predict revision decisions above chance, but only modestly. Qualitative coding showed that revisions often reduced overly explanatory, high-information feedback in favor of more concise corrective forms. The authors conclude that teacher revision is selective and heterogeneous, and that generative feedback systems should better align with teacher preferences while accounting for classroom constraints and pedagogical judgment.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative large language model system used to draft formative feedback for students, which teachers could accept, edit, or rewrite before delivery.
identified_tools.use_case: Used within the Tutoria platform to generate initial feedback drafts for short open-ended student responses; the study examined how 117 teachers revised those LLM-generated drafts before students received them.

findings.finding_summary: Across 1,349 feedback instances from 117 teachers, teachers accepted AI feedback without modification in 77.8% of cases (1050/1349). Edited feedback was modestly longer in the comparison reported, but teachers usually shortened or simplified the AI draft rather than fully rewriting it; 51.3% of teachers edited at least once, and half of teachers edited fewer than 6% of messages while the top decile revised roughly two-thirds.
findings.measure: Teacher revision rate / acceptance rate of AI-generated feedback; length and semantic similarity of revised vs. unrevised feedback

findings.finding_summary: Text-only models could predict whether feedback would be revised above chance, with the best holdout performance reaching ROC AUC=0.75 (gradient-boosted trees), compared with logistic regression AUC=0.70 and a shallow neural network AUC=0.74. This suggests revision-prone feedback can be identified from the AI text alone, though performance was modest.
findings.measure: Binary classification of whether AI-generated feedback would be revised; holdout ROC AUC, balanced accuracy, accuracy, Cohen’s κ

findings.finding_summary: When AI-generated feedback was revised, the pedagogical type shifted: unrevised feedback was more often Corrective (58.1%) than High-information (41.9%), whereas revised feedback began as more often High-information (59.9%) than Corrective (40.1%) and moved toward a more balanced distribution after teacher editing. The authors interpret this as teachers often simplifying overly explanatory feedback, sometimes due to disagreement with the AI’s assessment, language/context issues, or concerns about feedback efficiency.
findings.measure: Feedback-type distribution before and after revision (Corrective, High-information, Reinforcement/Punishment, Other)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods/observational analysis of teacher revisions of LLM-generated feedback, not a randomized efficacy trial. The evidence is useful but mainly descriptive and predictive, with subgroup/setting variation only discussed indirectly rather than tested as causal effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed effects on teacher behavior and feedback type are modest but practically meaningful: most feedback was accepted unchanged, and revision behavior varied sharply by teacher. The reported associations and classification performance are above chance but not large.

paper_profiles.title: Fine-Tuning Large Language Models for Educational Support: Leveraging Gagné’s Nine Events of Instruction for Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.venue: Conference Proceedings of the 28th Global Chinese Conference on Computers in Education (GCCCE 2024)
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper examines whether large language models can be adapted to support educational work by generating and analyzing teacher classroom dialogue and lesson-planning content aligned with Gagné’s Nine Events of Instruction. The central problem is that general-purpose LLMs are not optimized for educational use, so teachers must spend substantial effort crafting prompts and still may not receive pedagogically appropriate outputs. The authors propose a pipeline to make LLMs more useful for instructionally grounded teacher support.

paper_profiles.title: Using Transformers to Provide Teachers with Personalized Feedback on their Classroom Discourse: The TalkMoves Application
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of giving K-12 mathematics teachers timely, scalable, and personalized feedback on classroom discourse practices. The authors focus on “talk moves,” a set of instructional discourse strategies associated with accountable talk, which are used to support student participation, reasoning, and mathematical understanding. Because human observation and transcript coding are costly and difficult to scale, the paper explores whether natural language processing can automatically identify these discourse moves from classroom transcripts and use them to generate feedback for teachers.

The intervention/approach is the TalkMoves application, an end-to-end system that processes classroom audio/video recordings, uses automated speech recognition to create transcripts, and then applies deep learning models to classify teacher utterances into six talk-move categories plus a none label. The paper compares multiple model architectures, including BiLSTM, attention-based models, and transformer-based models such as BERT, RoBERTa, XLNet, and DistilRoBERTa. The best-performing model is RoBERTa-Large, and a smaller DistilRoBERTa model is deployed in the application for efficiency.

The study context is K-12 mathematics classrooms in two midwestern school districts in the United States. The paper reports on a pilot group of 21 teachers serving grades 3-12 who used the application during the 2019-2020 academic year, recorded multiple lessons, reviewed feedback, and participated in surveys and interviews. Human annotators also coded 501 math lesson transcripts to create the training and evaluation data. The authors conclude that transformer-based NLP substantially improves talk-move classification and can support automated feedback for teacher professional learning, while noting technical challenges such as noisy classroom speech and ASR errors with children’s speech.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A transformer-based NLP system for automatically analyzing K-12 classroom speech transcripts and generating personalized feedback for teachers on their use of accountable talk / talk moves.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as the TalkMoves application for K-12 mathematics teachers; it classifies teacher-student sentence pairs into accountable talk move categories and presents automated lesson feedback dashboards to teachers.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that the best-performing model for talk-move classification was RoBERTa-LARGE, achieving F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the held-out test set. This improved over the prior BiLSTM baseline (F1 = 65%) for classifying 6 talk-move labels plus 'None' in 501 transcripts (176,757 sentences) from K-12 math lessons.
findings.measure: Talk-move classification performance on the test set (F1 and Matthews correlation coefficient)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary machine-learning systems paper with model evaluation on a train/validation/test split, but it is not an educational impact trial and does not report causal effects on teacher or student outcomes. The evidence is therefore useful but methodologically limited for K-12 coaching impact questions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported performance improvement in classification is substantial for the model task, but it is not a direct measure of educational impact. There is no reported effect on teacher practice, student learning, or coach effectiveness, so the practical impact for coaching remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Multimodal Feedback Using Multiple External Representations: Strategy Profiles and Learning in High School Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether students’ use of elaborated feedback in a digital high-school physics platform is associated with learning gains, and whether different patterns of feedback-format selection relate to performance. The authors are motivated by the growing relevance of adaptive feedback and multimodal large language models, but the study itself evaluates a computer-based learning environment rather than a generative AI coaching system for teachers.

The intervention-like component is a web platform (KI4SCool) that gave students verification feedback after multiple-choice physics exercises and optional elaborated feedback in three external representations: verbal, graphical/pictorial, and mathematical. Students could choose one, two, or all three formats after each item. The study analyzed naturally occurring usage patterns, linear mixed-effects models, and clustering of feedback-selection logs rather than assigning learners to conditions experimentally.

Participants were high-school students in grades 10 and 11 in Germany. Data came from 29 schools across four federal states, with 661 students who completed pre- and post-tests and at least one exercise included in the main analyses. The main findings were that greater use of elaborated feedback was modestly and positively associated with post-test performance, but the study was observational so causal claims are not warranted. The authors also found stable strategy groups in how students selected the three feedback formats, yet no strong evidence that these strategy groups were explained by initial representational competence. Overall, the paper suggests that multimodal, adaptive feedback may support physics learning, especially when students engage with multiple representations, but it does not study K–12 teacher coaching or lesson-plan feedback.

identified_tools.name: Adaptive Feedback System (General)
identified_tools.description: A computer-based instructional system that provides immediate verification feedback and optional elaborated feedback in multiple representational formats.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in high school physics to deliver verification feedback plus optional elaborated feedback (textual, graphical/pictorial, and mathematical) after multiple-choice exercises; the study examined how students selected and used these feedback formats and how that related to post-test learning.

findings.finding_summary: In two observational cohorts of high school physics students, more frequent use of elaborated feedback was associated with higher post-test scores. The association was statistically significant in Cohort 1 (standardized b2 = 0.13, 95% CI [0.05, 0.22]) and positive but not conventionally significant in Cohort 2 (b2 = 0.08, 95% CI [0.00, 0.16], p = .054); sample sizes were n = 351 and n = 310, respectively.
findings.measure: Post-test score

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an observational cohort study with no randomized comparison of the feedback system, so causal claims are limited. The paper does provide quantitative modeling and cluster analyses, but the design remains correlational.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported association between elaborated feedback use and post-test performance is small but positive (standardized b2 around 0.080.13). That places the impact in the modest range rather than a large-effect tier.

paper_profiles.title: Coaching a Robotic Sonographer: Learning Robotic Ultrasound with Sparse Expert’s Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of improving training efficiency and performance in robotic ultrasound (RUS) systems by incorporating sparse real-time expert coaching. The authors argue that while prior work in RUS has focused on learning from demonstrations or self-supervised reinforcement learning, it has not examined active expert engagement during training.

The proposed approach combines soft actor-critic reinforcement learning with sparse corrective feedback from expert sonographers. Coaching is formalized as a partially observable Markov decision process, where expert corrections are used to update both the policy and reward structure. The expert feedback is delivered as kinesthetic corrections to the robot arm during training, and the corrected trajectories are used to refine the policy through replay-buffer updates and KL-regularized policy learning.

The empirical evaluation uses a robotic ultrasound setup with a Sawyer 7-DOF arm, a Telemed probe, and urinary bladder phantoms. Human expert sonographers provided sparse coaching while the robot learned to acquire high-quality ultrasound images. The study reports that coaching improved convergence speed and increased the number of high-quality images acquired, suggesting that real-time expert feedback can substantially improve robotic ultrasound learning.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: A general intelligent tutoring or coaching system that adapts guidance based on learner actions and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and tests a coaching framework for robotic ultrasound training using sparse expert corrective feedback during reinforcement learning, which functions as a general coaching/tutoring system rather than a named product.

findings.finding_summary: In phantom testing, adding coaching improved learning efficiency. Policies coached every 20k and 10k timesteps converged at approximately 150k and 120k steps, respectively, versus no convergence by 200k steps for the no-coaching condition; coaching every 5k steps converged at 100k steps. The authors report an approximate 25% improvement in convergence rate.
findings.measure: Training convergence rate / number of training steps to convergence

findings.finding_summary: Coaching improved task performance on urinary bladder phantoms P0 and P1. For P0, the number of high-quality images (HQI) increased from 2.1 �b1 0.5 without coaching to 8.2 �b1 4.6 with coaching every 20k steps, and further to 21.5 �b1 2.3 with coaching every 5k steps. For P1, HQI increased from 1.5 �b1 0.3 without coaching to 5.9 �b1 1.6 with coaching every 20k steps, and to 16.2 �b1 2.9 with coaching every 5k steps; the abstract reports a 74.4% increase in HQI on phantom testing.
findings.measure: Number of high-quality ultrasound images (q  4) during execution trials on phantoms P0 and P1

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a robotics/controls framework paper, not an education study, and it does not evaluate a K-12 instructional AI tool or coaching product in classrooms. The evidence is experimental but entirely outside the target domain, so it is not usable as educational AI efficacy evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are specific to robotic ultrasound training and do not translate to K-12 teaching or lesson-plan feedback. No educational impact on teachers, students, or schools is measured.

paper_profiles.title: Feedback Indicators: The Alignment between Llama and a Teacher in Language Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how well large language model (LLM)–generated feedback indicators align with human teacher ratings in a foreign-language learning context. The authors frame the problem as one of making automated formative feedback more transparent and explainable by first extracting interpretable indicators from student texts, rather than directly asking the model to score submissions end-to-end.

The intervention/approach studied is an indicator-extraction pipeline using Llama 3.1. The model is prompted with binary and list-style queries to identify textual indicators such as form of address, sociolinguistic appropriateness, vocabulary use, coherence, grammar, and related features from student submissions. These indicator values are then compared with teacher ratings from an established rubric through correlation analysis.

The study took place in an online French-as-a-foreign-language course at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin. The participants were 22 university students enrolled in a B1-level course; 11 students submitted the analyzed task and consented to the use of their submissions. Teacher feedback was given using a Moodle rubric with 10 criteria, and the paper examines whether LLM-extracted indicators can serve as useful proxies for those criteria.

The main conclusion is that many extracted indicators showed moderate to strong correlations with at least one teacher-rated criterion, suggesting that LLMs can support a transparent feedback pipeline. However, the alignment between the intended indicator and criterion was often weaker than expected, indicating that high-level feedback criteria are complex and may be captured indirectly by different textual features. The authors argue that their approach could support teacher-assistive automated feedback and also help reveal which indicators teachers implicitly use when grading.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: A family of open-weight large language models developed by Meta for text generation and other language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the LLM to extract binary and list-based feedback indicators from students’ French language submissions and compare those extracted indicators with teacher ratings on a rubric.

findings.finding_summary: In an online French-as-a-foreign-language course (level B1), Llama 3.1-generated indicators showed statistically significant moderate-to-high alignment with teacher ratings across multiple rubric criteria. The paper reports that 44 of 63 extracted indicators (70%) had acceptable correlations with at least one criterion (|PCC|  .5), and 15 indicators had high correlations (|PCC|  .70); the study involved 11 consenting students who completed the analyzed task.
findings.measure: Pearson correlation between LLM-extracted feedback indicators and teacher ratings on feedback criteria

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single correlational study rather than an experimental impact evaluation. The paper provides quantitative alignment evidence, but not causal evidence of learning gains or teacher performance improvements.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effect is promising but indirect: correlations between extracted indicators and teacher ratings, not student outcome gains. The study suggests moderate to high alignment, but impact on instruction or learning is not established.

paper_profiles.title: Stable matchings of teachers to schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies the computational properties of assigning teachers to schools in a centralized matching system. The motivation comes from teacher labor markets in which teachers specialize in two subjects and schools have subject-specific staffing capacities. The central question is whether stable assignments exist under different preference structures and, when they do not, how hard it is to find the most stable assignment.

The authors formalize the Teachers Assignment Problem (TAP), define two notions of blocking pairs/stability, and analyze several variants. In the basic variant, teachers rank schools and schools rank applicants; in the subject-specific variant, schools can rank applicants differently by subject. The paper proves NP-completeness for the existence of a stable matching in the general case, but shows polynomial-time solvability when preferences are generated by a master list of applicants or a master list of schools.

The paper is purely theoretical and uses reductions from satisfiability problems rather than empirical data. It also proves that finding a matching with the minimum number of blocking pairs is strongly inapproximable unless P=NP, for both TAP variants. The results are positioned as characterizing the boundary between tractable and intractable versions of teacher-to-school matching with subject constraints.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general classroom/education matching or assignment algorithmic system, not an AI tutoring or feedback product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies the computational problem of assigning teachers to schools under stable matching constraints, including variants with master lists and subject-specific preferences. It does not evaluate an AI coaching or lesson-feedback tool.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/computational matching paper, not an empirical study of an AI educational tool or coaching system. It contains no intervention, usage, or outcome evidence related to teacher coaching or lesson-plan feedback.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational AI tool impact is measured or reported. The paper addresses algorithmic tractability of teacher-school assignments rather than instructional outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging learning analytics to enhance immersive teacher simulations: Challenges and opportunities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how learning analytics can be used to enhance immersive teacher simulations, with a particular emphasis on making teachers’ cognitive, behavioral, and perceptual processes visible and actionable. The paper situates this work within teacher education and argues that immersive simulation environments can serve as a testbed for data-informed professional learning, especially when they are combined with analytics dashboards and multimodal feedback.

The chapter’s central contribution is conceptual and methodological rather than an evaluation of a single intervention. It reviews the broader evolution of teacher analytics and then presents TeacherGen@i, a generative AI-enhanced immersive teacher simulation that collects multimodal data including transcribed speech, interaction logs, and gaze information. The simulation is designed so that preservice teachers create and enact lesson scenarios in a web-based VR classroom with AI-driven student agents powered by a large language model.

The empirical portion describes a case study conducted at one university in South Korea with 33 preservice teachers enrolled in a Digital Education course.
