The authors analyze the recorded simulation sessions using BERT-based classification aligned to Bloom’s taxonomy, lag sequential analysis, and gaze-based visualizations, then use these outputs to inform a prototype dashboard. Across the chapter, the authors conclude that multimodal analytics can surface novice teaching patterns such as reliance on remembering/understanding-level discourse, structured interaction sequences, and selective visual attention, and that dashboards may support reflective practice and lesson redesign.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI-enhanced immersive teacher simulation platform that uses a large language model to generate adaptive student-agent responses in a virtual classroom for teacher practice and analytics.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the TeacherGen@i web-based VR simulation in a university digital education course to let 33 preservice teachers teach AI-driven student agents, generate lesson scenarios, and then review multimodal analytics dashboards.

findings.finding_summary: Across 33 dialogue sessions (n=33 preservice teachers; 1,269 interaction turns), BERT-based coding showed a predominance of Remembering and Understanding questions, indicating mainly lower-order pedagogical discourse. Sequential analysis identified 215 significant behavioral patterns, including structured TT scaffolding chains, SS reasoning sequences, and less frequent but high-impact ST feedback loops, suggesting the simulation elicited both novice-like and more complex dialogic patterns.
findings.measure: BERT-based Bloom's taxonomy coding of verbal discourse; sequential analysis / lag sequential analysis of interaction patterns

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single case study with multimodal analysis of preservice teachers in one course, so the evidence is qualitative/mixed-methods rather than experimental. The paper does not report causal estimates for the AI tool's effects on learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows potentially useful analytic and instructional design implications, but no effect sizes are reported for student/teacher outcomes. Impact is therefore suggestive but unclear rather than demonstrated at a measurable level.

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Peer, Self, and Teacher Assessments for Generative AI-Enhanced Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing timely, meaningful feedback in higher education, particularly in large courses where instructors must balance depth of feedback with scalability. The authors investigate whether teacher, peer, and self-assessments can be combined to improve generative AI-enhanced feedback in a human-centered way.

The study is conducted within AICoFe, an AI-based collaborative feedback system that supports rubric-based assessment of engineering students’ oral presentations. Forty-six undergraduate students in the final year of a telecommunications engineering program at Universidad Autónoma de Madrid participated. Each presentation was evaluated by the teacher, two randomly assigned peers, and the presenter via self-assessment, using the same validated 15-item rubric. The teacher also assigned an independent overall grade. The paper analyzes agreement, correlations, and scoring biases across these evaluators.

Results show moderate to substantial agreement overall, with peer-to-peer agreement slightly stronger than teacher-self agreement. Teacher rubric scores aligned most strongly with the teacher’s own overall grades, while peer and self-scores were somewhat less aligned but still significantly correlated. The teacher tended to score more strictly than peers and self-assessments, and students showed a mild positive bias. Based on these findings, the authors propose a more advanced GenAI feedback model that weights evaluator inputs differently, detects bias, and generates context-aware feedback while preserving human oversight.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI-based feedback system that uses large language model capabilities to generate personalized feedback from human assessments and rubric data, with human oversight.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as part of the AICoFe system and proposed GePeTo enhancement for integrating teacher, peer, and self-assessments into AI-generated feedback for engineering students’ oral presentations.

findings.finding_summary: In this study of 46 presentation evaluation sets, the GenAI-enhanced AICoFe/GePeTo approach was informed by observed evaluator differences rather than directly tested against an alternative AI condition. The paper reports substantial agreement among human evaluators by Gwet’s AC2 (0.58-0.66) and correlations between rubric-based scores and the teacher’s overall grade (teacher r=0.88, peers r=0.69, self r=0.59), which the authors use to justify weighted AI feedback integration.
findings.measure: Inter-rater agreement and correlations between rubric-based scores and teacher’s overall grade

findings.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI-supported feedback can reduce teacher workload by aggregating multiple evaluative sources and producing personalized feedback, but this is presented as a design implication rather than an evaluated outcome. No direct efficiency effect size is reported in this paper.
findings.measure: Proposed feedback system efficiency/design implications

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical correlational study of teacher, peer, and self-assessment data used to inform a GenAI feedback design, but it does not experimentally evaluate the GenAI system itself. The evidence is therefore informative but indirect for AI effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported agreement and correlation values are moderate to substantial, but they concern human assessment alignment rather than measured gains from the GenAI tool. Because the AI component is proposed/inferred rather than tested, impact is unclear for actual instructional outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Teacher transfers: equalizing deficits across schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies a theoretical teacher-reassignment problem motivated by India’s Right to Free and Compulsory Education Act (RTE) and related state policies on redeploying teachers from surplus schools to deficit schools. The central question is how to reassign teachers so that post-transfer school deficits are reduced in a way that is fair, efficient, and strategy-proof.

The authors model the situation as a network flow problem in which each surplus school has a limited surplus of teachers, each teacher has an acceptable set of deficit schools, and each deficit school has a maximum number of teachers it can receive. A transfer is feasible only if it respects individual rationality for teachers and surplus schools, and no fractional transfers are allowed. The planner evaluates outcomes only by the post-transfer deficit vector, with the goal of equalizing deficits across schools.

Using convex cooperative game theory and the Megiddo-Dutta-Ray algorithm, the paper proves that a Lorenz-dominant post-transfer deficit vector always exists. Because the algorithm initially yields a fractional solution, the authors develop a second-stage rounding procedure via an auxiliary max-flow network to recover an integral transfer that preserves Lorenz dominance. They also show that a fixed tie-breaking version of the mechanism is strategy-proof for teachers. Extensions cover transfers between surplus schools and subject-specific teacher specializations.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / LLM chatbot tool. No specific commercial or research product is identified in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Not studied in this paper. The paper is a theoretical/combinatorial optimization study of teacher transfers, not an AI coaching or lesson-feedback intervention.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is not an empirical education study of AI use. It is a theoretical operations/matching paper about teacher transfers and network flows, with no study design evaluating an AI tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no reported educational AI intervention, outcome, or effect size. The paper has no direct AI-related impact on K–12 teaching or coaching.

paper_profiles.title: Active Teacher Selection for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a core limitation in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF): standard approaches assume feedback comes from a single teacher, even though real systems often draw on multiple annotators or experts who differ in rationality, expertise, and cost. The authors argue that these differences matter for learning accurate reward models and for deciding when feedback is worth requesting.

To model this setting, the paper introduces the Hidden Utility Bandit (HUB) framework, which treats learning as a partially observable sequential decision problem with hidden item utilities, multiple arms, and multiple teachers. It then proposes Active Teacher Selection (ATS), an algorithm that maintains a belief over hidden utilities and actively decides both when to query a teacher and, in the specific-selection variant, which teacher to query. The framework is solved approximately via POMDP methods, specifically POMCPOW with custom rollout policies.

The paper evaluates the framework in two non-education domains: a paper recommendation task and a COVID-19 vaccine testing proof-of-concept. In the paper recommendation domain, the “teachers” are professors with different rationality levels, and in the vaccine domain the “teachers” are COVID-19 test types with different accuracies and costs. Across these experiments, ATS generally outperforms naive and random baselines, especially when it can choose specific teachers rather than relying on general/random teacher selection.

The main conclusion is that explicitly modeling teacher heterogeneity and actively selecting feedback sources can improve both reward learning and decision quality. The paper does not study K–12 education, teacher coaching, lesson-plan feedback, instructional coaches, or any school-based setting; it is a theoretical and algorithmic RLHF paper with simulation-based evaluations.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: A general intelligent tutoring or feedback system that learns from human teacher feedback; in this paper, the focus is on a reward-learning / teacher-selection framework rather than a specific commercial product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and evaluates the Hidden Utility Bandit (HUB) framework and Active Teacher Selection (ATS) as a general method for learning from multiple teachers with different rationality and costs, illustrated with paper recommendation and COVID-19 testing domains.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/methods paper introducing a framework and algorithm, not an empirical study of a K–12 coaching or lesson-feedback tool. There is no student-, teacher-, or school-based education intervention outcome reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has conceptual relevance for teacher-feedback systems, but it does not report education outcome effects or K–12 implementation results. Its impact for the requested topic is therefore unclear and indirect.

paper_profiles.title: Design language learning with artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots based on activity theory from a systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews research on how AI chatbots are used in language learning and, more specifically, how different sociocultural and instructional factors shape student outcomes when chatbots are used in educational settings. The authors argue that prior reviews have focused too much on whether chatbots work and not enough on the mechanisms and contextual factors that explain why outcomes vary.

Using Activity Theory as the organizing framework, the review synthesizes 37 empirical studies published from January 2014 to January 2025. The studies included K–12 and higher education contexts, with most conducted in higher education and in traditional classroom settings. The review examines the roles of rules/course design, tools/chatbots, community, and division of labor among students, teachers, peer students, researchers, and the AI systems themselves.

The review concludes that chatbot-supported language learning produces four main outcome types: cognitive, emotional, behavioral, and agentic. Cognitive outcomes were most common, followed by emotional and behavioral outcomes, while agentic outcomes were least frequent and especially underexplored. The authors find that outcomes are shaped by instructional design, teacher support, chatbot capabilities, and the degree of collaboration and feedback in the activity system. They recommend stronger teacher-AI collaboration models, more professional language-education chatbots, and more research in K–12 settings, collaborative learning, and agentic outcomes.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI chatbots/LLM-based assistants used for conversational language support, feedback, and task completion.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a systematic review of 37 studies on AI chatbots in language learning, including generic GenAI tools and named products; it also discusses teacher-AI collaboration, prompt-like instructional design, and risks.

findings.finding_summary: Across 37 reviewed studies, chatbot-supported language learning was associated mainly with cognitive outcomes (43% of studies) and emotional outcomes (38%), with some behavioral (15%) and agentic outcomes (4%). The review synthesizes that well-designed course rules, teacher support, and chatbot-mediated interaction can help students attain language-learning outcomes, though the paper does not report pooled effect sizes.
findings.measure: Reported frequency and thematic synthesis of learning outcomes across reviewed studies

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that most studies found improved linguistic performance and language knowledge, especially in writing, speaking, listening, reading, pronunciation, vocabulary, and grammatical accuracy. It also notes that some studies found no significant improvement in listening performance, and one study found higher GPA students did not write significantly better with a chatbot than with traditional instruction.
findings.measure: Language performance/achievement in writing, speaking, listening, reading, pronunciation, vocabulary, and grammar

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that chatbot-supported learning often increased motivation, confidence, willingness to communicate, enjoyment, and positive attitudes, while lowering anxiety in many studies. It also highlights a four-staged ChatGPT-based rapport-building protocol that was reported to improve teacher-student rapport and L2 grit, but no effect size was given in the review text.
findings.measure: Motivation, attitude, confidence, willingness to communicate, enjoyment/interest, anxiety, and grit

findings.finding_summary: The review identifies behavioral gains such as increased language practice frequency, greater class engagement, and more frequent or varied interactions with chatbots. It also notes a small set of agentic outcomes, including using English for realistic purposes and proactively seeking information or help from the chatbot when encountering unfamiliar content.
findings.measure: Language practice frequency, class engagement, interaction frequency/types, and agentic behaviors

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review synthesizing prior studies rather than a single empirical intervention or meta-analysis with pooled effects. The evidence is useful for mapping patterns, but it does not provide primary causal estimates for one tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests broadly positive associations between chatbot use and several language-learning outcomes, but it reports no effect sizes or pooled estimates. The impact is therefore directionally promising but quantitatively unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Teacher Effectiveness with AI based Prompt Engineering: A Proof of Concept
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a proof-of-concept on using AI prompt engineering to support K-12 teachers, especially middle school teachers, in creating instructional materials more efficiently and with better alignment to curriculum goals. The authors frame the problem as one of teacher workload, burnout, and the need for AI-supported tools that can help teachers generate high-quality, differentiated lesson materials while still preserving instructional intent and standards alignment.

The intervention described is a structured prompt engineering workflow built around four components: Task Context, Task Input/Variable, Task Instructions, and Task Criteria. The authors used Microsoft Copilot to generate materials such as informational texts, assessment questions, quizzes, rubrics, and differentiated activities. Their examples focus on middle school social studies and STEAM-related instruction in Georgia, with prompts explicitly tied to Georgia standards and learning targets. The workflow is iterative, with educators refining prompts when outputs are not satisfactory and collaborating to improve prompt quality.

The paper argues that this structured approach helps teachers produce more consistent, standards-aligned, and differentiated outputs across uses and users. The authors claim the process can reduce the mental effort and time spent on curriculum development, allowing more attention to student interaction and feedback. Because the paper is primarily descriptive and reflective, it offers practical design guidance and claims of benefit, but it does not present controlled outcome evidence about student learning or teacher effectiveness beyond the authors’ experiences.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI system for generating and refining text, instructions, and other content.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of the example large language model tools referenced in the paper; the authors state they used Microsoft Copilot for their process, while also discussing ChatGPT as an AI tool with educational potential.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's conversational generative AI system for text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned as an example LLM alongside ChatGPT; the paper does not report empirical results for Gemini specifically.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbot used to assist with drafting, revising, and generating instructional materials.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies a prompt-engineering framework for teachers using Microsoft Copilot, with prompt scaffolds for creating standards-aligned informational texts, quizzes, and differentiated materials.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a proof-of-concept and reflective framework paper rather than a controlled empirical study. It reports no quantitative outcome data, effect sizes, or comparison condition.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that the approach can improve efficiency, differentiation, and teacher effectiveness, but these claims are not backed by measurable impact estimates. Because the study is implementation-focused and qualitative, the impact remains plausible but unquantified.

paper_profiles.title: Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This reflection paper examines how artificial intelligence, especially generative AI and large language models (LLMs), may affect learning, with a focus on cognitive learning processes and outcomes. The authors argue that current enthusiasm about AI in education often outpaces the evidence, and they call for a more systematic, theory-driven approach to understanding when AI helps learning, when it simply replaces existing instructional functions, and when it may actually harm learning through over-reliance or shallow processing.

The paper does not report a new empirical intervention. Instead, it synthesizes prior research and proposes the ISAR model, which distinguishes inversion, substitution, augmentation, and redefinition effects of AI in educational settings. The discussion covers mechanisms such as AI-generated content, feedback, scaffolding, conversational tutoring, and teacher-assisted workflows like write-curate-verify, as well as safeguards including retrieval-augmented generation, teacher oversight, prompt quality, and domain-specific fine-tuning. It emphasizes that these features shape output quality, pedagogical alignment, and the risk of students or teachers uncritically relying on AI outputs.

Because the paper is conceptual rather than empirical, it does not focus on a single population or setting. Its implications span students and educators across educational contexts, including K–12 and higher education, but the paper’s core contribution is a framework for future research and practice rather than evidence from one intervention. The authors conclude that AI should complement, not replace, human instruction, and that successful integration depends on AI literacy, pedagogical skill, careful validation, and attention to cognitive engagement and instructional quality.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI / large language model systems that generate text and other outputs and can provide tutoring, feedback, scaffolding, and content generation across educational contexts.
identified_tools.use_case: This reflection paper discusses generative AI and LLMs broadly, focusing on how they may be used to support or redesign learning, including teacher planning, feedback, scaffolding, conversational tutoring, and content generation. It does not evaluate one specific product as the main focus, but cites examples such as ChatGPT, GPT-4, Jill Watson, AutoTutor, Socratic Playground for Learning, and Ruffle & Riley.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a reflection/theoretical paper rather than an empirical evaluation of a specific AI tool. It synthesizes prior studies and proposes the ISAR framework, but does not report primary data, effect sizes, or a study design for a tool intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper is conceptually influential and offers a broad framework for thinking about AI effects in education, but it does not provide direct outcome evidence from a single intervention. Its practical impact is therefore potentially meaningful but not empirically quantified here.

paper_profiles.title: Feedback sources in essay writing: peer-generated or AI-generated feedback?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can serve as a useful source of feedback for complex writing tasks and how its feedback compares with peer-generated feedback. The central question is not whether ChatGPT improves essay writing directly, but whether the feedback it produces differs in quality and characteristics from student peer feedback, and whether essay quality is associated with feedback quality from either source.

The study used ChatGPT as a feedback provider in an online argumentative essay-writing module. Students wrote essays first, then provided peer feedback and also received ChatGPT-generated feedback using essentially the same prompt. The feedback was coded with established schemes covering affective, cognitive, and constructive dimensions, while essays were coded for argumentative quality. The sample included 74 graduate students in food sciences at a Dutch university, and the work was conducted over two weeks in an online Brightspace module with the FeedbackFruits peer-feedback tool.

Results showed that peer feedback was overall higher quality than ChatGPT feedback, mainly because peers were better at identifying problems in the essays, while ChatGPT produced more descriptive summaries. There was no overall significant relationship between essay quality and feedback quality for either peers or ChatGPT, although some small correlations appeared for affective feedback features. The authors conclude that ChatGPT may complement peer feedback rather than replace it, especially for large writing-intensive courses, but they also note that prompt wording, model behavior, and validation of AI-generated feedback require further study.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on GPT-family large language models, capable of producing natural-language responses and feedback from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a feedback source on students' argumentative essays. The paper provided ChatGPT the same feedback prompt given to peers (with minor wording changes) and compared the quality of ChatGPT-generated feedback with peer feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In a sample of 74 graduate students, ChatGPT-generated feedback differed significantly from peer feedback. ChatGPT scored higher on description (M=2.00, SD=0.00) but lower on identification of problems (M=1.29, SD=0.70) than peer feedback (description M=1.91, SD=0.29; identification M=1.52, SD=0.49), while affective, justification, and constructive components did not differ significantly.
findings.measure: Feedback quality coding scheme: affective, description, identification, justification, constructive components
findings.effect_size: eta2=0.03 for description; eta2=0.02 for identification

findings.finding_summary: There was no significant overall relationship between essay quality and ChatGPT-generated feedback quality. A positive correlation appeared between essay quality and the affective feature of ChatGPT feedback for some essay elements, while a negative relationship appeared for justification on one essay element; the overall correlation was not significant.
findings.measure: Spearman correlations between essay quality and ChatGPT feedback quality/features

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-institution exploratory study with correlational and group-comparison analyses, not a randomized trial. The methodology is clear and coder reliability is reported, but the evidence is limited by the small sample and one-course context.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports statistically significant differences, but the effects are small (eta2=.02-.03) and the practical impact is mixed. Overall influence on feedback quality is suggestive rather than strong.

paper_profiles.title: Assessing student perceptions and use of instructor versus AI-generated feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examined whether AI-generated feedback could match instructor feedback in an authentic programming course setting, and how students perceived and used each type of feedback. The core question was not only whether students liked the feedback, but whether they could use it to improve their work. The authors focused on usefulness, fairness, developmental value, and encouragement as perception dimensions, and on actual score improvement as the behavioral outcome.

The intervention took place in an undergraduate Java programming course at a public university in Türkiye. Students were randomly assigned to receive either instructor feedback or ChatGPT-4-generated feedback on a lab exam submission. Both conditions used the same rubric, and both kinds of feedback were written to provide hints and explanations rather than direct solutions. Students then revised their submissions during a supervised feedback session and completed a perception questionnaire afterward. The study also controlled for prior knowledge using midterm scores.

Results showed that students viewed both feedback sources positively, but instructor feedback was rated significantly more useful. Although instructor feedback was also rated higher on fairness, developmental value, and encouragement, those differences were not statistically significant. More importantly, students receiving instructor feedback improved their lab scores significantly more than those receiving AI feedback, even after controlling for prior knowledge. The authors conclude that current LLM-based feedback may need stronger educational-context grounding and that hybrid human–AI feedback models are likely to be more effective than AI alone.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI system used to generate natural-language feedback from prompts and uploaded files.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the AI feedback provider for students' Java lab submissions. The study uploaded the same rubric, lab instructions, and student Java file to ChatGPT 4 and used one fixed prompt to produce feedback that mirrored the instructor's plain-language, hint-based feedback style.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized controlled trial with 35 analyzed students (18 instructor-feedback, 17 AI-feedback), students receiving ChatGPT-generated feedback reported significantly lower usefulness than those receiving instructor feedback. The Mann-Whitney U test found a difference for usefulness (U=191.0, p=0.04), while fairness, development, and encouragement were not significantly different.
findings.measure: Student feedback perceptions: usefulness subscale

findings.finding_summary: After controlling for midterm scores, students receiving ChatGPT-generated feedback improved less on their Java lab resubmissions than students receiving instructor feedback. The robust ANCOVA showed a significant group effect (coefficient=-4.97, SE=2.40, t=-2.07, p=0.04), indicating lower score gains for the AI-feedback group.
findings.measure: Change in lab assignment scores from initial to revised submission

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled trial with between-subjects assignment and a controlled comparison of AI versus instructor feedback. The study uses clear measures, a pre-specified rubric, and appropriate statistical analyses, though the final analytic sample is small and one ANCOVA assumption was violated and addressed with robust standard errors.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study found statistically significant differences, but effect sizes were not reported and the practical magnitude is not directly quantifiable from the paper. The direction suggests AI feedback underperformed instructor feedback, but the evidence supports a negative/uncertain impact rather than a clearly large one.

paper_profiles.title: Challenges and opportunities for classroom-based formative assessment and AI: a perspective article
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) may affect classroom-based formative assessment, with particular attention to both the opportunities and the risks created by AI-enabled tools. The paper focuses on the core formative assessment cycle: eliciting evidence of learning, interpreting it, and using it to guide next instructional steps. The authors argue that while formative assessment is pedagogically valuable, it is difficult for teachers to implement consistently and at scale because of time constraints, large class sizes, feedback demands, and contextual pressures such as accountability systems and resource limitations.

The paper does not report an empirical intervention. Instead, it synthesizes prior research and uses examples such as automated essay scoring, intelligent tutoring systems, computerized formative assessment, AI-supported peer assessment, longitudinal learner profiling, and AI-assisted rubric design to illustrate how AI could support teachers and students. It also discusses practical and ethical concerns, including bias in training data, reduced interpretability of machine-learning outputs, privacy, and the possibility that AI may be over-trusted or used inappropriately. The discussion specifically notes that generative AI can help teachers generate rubric samples and feedback support, but these outputs require careful curation and human judgment.

The context is classroom formative assessment, with examples drawn from K-12 and broader education settings, including references to classroom teaching, peer assessment, and policy shifts in Australian government schools. The authors emphasize that AI should augment, not replace, teachers, and that students will need stronger self-regulated learning and critical thinking skills to use AI responsibly. They conclude with recommendations for feedback assistance, ethical use, teacher guidance, co-design research, and attention to teacher roles in interpreting AI outputs and supporting learning.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model systems used to generate text, feedback, rubrics, and other adaptive outputs for educational tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: A perspective discussion of how generative AI and related AI systems could support classroom formative assessment, including rubric generation, feedback assistance, peer-assessment prompts, and teacher support. The paper does not evaluate a specific named product beyond mentioning ChatGPT as an example.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective article with no empirical evaluation, no study design, and no reported outcomes. It discusses opportunities and risks conceptually rather than testing an AI tool in classrooms.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potential practical relevance for K-12 formative assessment and teacher workflows, but it reports no measured effect sizes or direct impact evidence. Because impact is only argued conceptually, the tier is limited to yellow.

paper_profiles.title: Embracing LLM Feedback: the role of feedback providers and provider information for feedback effectiveness
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether learners’ perceptions of feedback change depending on whether the feedback is attributed to a large language model (LLM) or to a human educator, and whether additional information about the feedback provider improves those perceptions. The central problem is that AI-generated feedback is increasingly used in education, but it is unclear how learners judge its trustworthiness, fairness, and usefulness compared with human feedback, and whether simple provider information can mitigate bias or improve acceptance.

The study used a 2×2 between-subjects experiment in which 169 German-speaking student teachers evaluated a fictional feedback interaction. Participants were randomly assigned to receive feedback from either an educator or an LLM, with or without accompanying provider-information. The provider-information for the LLM was a brief textual explanation adapted from global xAI-style explanations, while the human-provider information described the educator’s expertise. Outcomes were measured using self-report scales for trustworthiness and feedback message perceptions, and the authors also explored feedback literacy as a learner characteristic.

Results showed that provider-information improved overall feedback message perceptions and especially affective reactions, but it did not directly increase trustworthiness overall. The LLM was generally perceived as more trustworthy than the educator, but provider-information changed this pattern for some subscales: it eliminated differences in perceived expertise and reversed fairness judgments in favor of the LLM when information was present. Higher feedback literacy was associated with better feedback message perceptions but lower trust in the provider, suggesting that more feedback-literate learners focus more on the feedback content than on the source. The authors conclude that provider-information can shape how AI- or human-generated feedback is received, but its effects depend on the provider and the content of the explanation.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model / AI chatbot that generates written feedback on student work.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the feedback provider in a 2x2 between-subjects experiment comparing feedback from an LLM versus an educator, with or without provider-information. The paper used a screenshot oriented on ChatGPT, but did not evaluate a specific named model as the intervention.

findings.finding_summary: Participants rated feedback from the LLM more positively on trustworthiness than feedback from the educator. Overall trustworthiness was higher for the LLM (beta=0.58, p<=0.001), including expertise (beta=0.74, p<=0.001), benevolence (beta=0.62, p<=0.001), and integrity (beta=0.39, p<=0.05).
findings.measure: Muenster Epistemic Trustworthiness Inventory (METI): overall trustworthiness, expertise, benevolence, integrity
findings.effect_size: beta=0.58 overall; beta=0.74 expertise; beta=0.62 benevolence; beta=0.39 integrity

findings.finding_summary: The presence of provider-information improved feedback message perceptions overall (beta=0.53, p<=0.05) and affective reactions to the feedback (beta=0.79, p<=0.01). The effect was small according to the authors.
findings.measure: Feedback Perceptions Questionnaire (FPQ): overall score and affect subscale

findings.finding_summary: Provider-information changed how the LLM was evaluated relative to the educator. Without provider-information, the LLM was rated as less fair than the educator (t=2.52, p<=0.05, d=0.53), but with provider-information this difference disappeared (t=-0.44, p=0.66, d=0.09).
findings.measure: FPQ fairness subscale
findings.effect_size: d=0.53 without provider-information; d=0.09 with provider-information

findings.finding_summary: Without provider-information, the LLM was perceived as more trustworthy on expertise than the educator (MLLM=3.34, MEducator=2.19, t=-4.46, p<=0.001, d=0.94). When provider-information was provided, this difference disappeared (MLLM=2.62, MEducator=2.31, t=-1.29, p=0.201, d=0.28).
findings.measure: METI expertise subscale
findings.effect_size: d=0.94 without provider-information; d=0.28 with provider-information

findings.finding_summary: Exploratory analyses showed that higher feedback literacy was associated with better feedback message perceptions (F(1,167)=10.61, p<=0.01, R2=0.05) but lower perceived trustworthiness of the feedback provider (F(1,167)=8.22, p<=0.01, R2=0.04).
findings.measure: Feedback message perceptions and provider trustworthiness

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single randomized between-subjects survey experiment, but the tool is a generic LLM/chatbot rather than a named product. The design is controlled, yet outcomes are perceptual and not direct learning gains.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Reported effects on trustworthiness and feedback perceptions are small-to-moderate in places (e.g., d=0.53, beta=0.79), so the practical impact is modest rather than large. The study focuses on user perceptions, not achievement or instructional outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: AI in academia: An overview of selected tools and their areas of application
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly expanding use of artificial intelligence tools in academic work, especially after the rise of ChatGPT, and asks how educators and researchers can make sense of the available tools, their functions, and their risks. Rather than evaluating one intervention empirically, the paper offers a narrative overview of selected AI applications used in higher education for literature search, paper analysis, and academic writing/editing.

The author approaches the topic from the perspective of a university educator and compiles a review of tools such as Elicit, Litmaps, Scite, ChatPDF, Scholarcy, Jenni.ai, Quillbot, Trinka, and others. The paper describes how these tools support semantic search, citation mapping, document questioning, summarization, paraphrasing, and language correction. It also notes some implementation features, such as use of GPT-4 in certain tools, custom-document-based AI, and integration with citation managers, but does not study classroom deployment or coaching workflows.

The context is higher education rather than K–12, and the paper is centered on academic users: educators, researchers, and students. Its main conclusion is that AI tools can save time, improve readability and writing quality, and support literature work, but they also raise concerns about authenticity, privacy, bias, and academic integrity. The paper emphasizes that users need critical judgment, ethical awareness, and institutional guidance when adopting these tools, because they are best used to complement human work rather than replace it.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model chatbot or writing assistant used for academic tasks such as answering questions, summarizing, drafting, editing, and providing feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a narrative review of selected AI tools in academia. It discusses generative AI and LLMs in general, including ChatGPT, GPT-4, and GPT-3, but does not evaluate a specific AI tool in K–12 teacher instructional coaching or lesson-plan feedback.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/overview article with no empirical evaluation of an AI tool in K–12 teacher coaching or lesson-plan feedback. The paper summarizes tools and their potential uses rather than testing outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that AI tools may improve efficiency and quality of academic work, but it reports no measurable effect sizes or outcome data for the target use case. Any impact claims are descriptive and not directly evidenced in this study.

paper_profiles.title: Impact of Guidance and Interaction Strategies for LLM Use on Learner Performance and Perception
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how different guidance strategies shape the way learners interact with large language models (LLMs), and how those strategies affect performance, confidence, trust, and self-perception while using an LLM tutor. The authors focus on whether students should be given direct instructions, example-based guidance, metacognitive prompts, or a workflow that requires solving first and refining with the LLM afterward.

The intervention is a set of four guidance strategies: list-based suggestions, example-based instruction, metacognitive questioning, and solve-then-refine. In addition, the authors compared a prompted versus unprompted GPT-3 chatbot in the online study. In the classroom deployment, the model was also constrained by a system prompt telling it to act as a database instructor, give brainstorming help only, and never provide SQL solutions directly. The study examined how these design choices changed the content of students’ first queries, assignment performance, and perceptions of the chatbot.

The paper reports two studies. Study 1 was a formative classroom study in a third-year undergraduate database course at a North American university (N=145 students who completed the assignment), and Study 2 was a controlled online experiment on Prolific with adults solving math problems (N=356). The results show that structured guidance reduced unrelated queries and verbatim copy-pasting, while the solve-then-refine workflow shifted students toward clarification-seeking and self-first problem solving. However, the interventions did not reliably improve task performance overall in the controlled study; confidence in using LLMs rose briefly after guidance but often fell after actual task use, and trust in LLM responses declined after experience with the system. The authors conclude that guidance can shape interaction quality and learner behavior, but it does not automatically improve outcomes and may also reveal risks such as overconfidence, shallow engagement, or reduced trust after use.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: A GPT-family large language model chatbot used as a dialogue-based support system / tutoring assistant. In this paper it is configured via system prompts to behave as a database instructor or K-12 math teacher and provide guided, open-ended help rather than direct answers.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the LLM tutor in two studies: (1) a classroom database assignment support chatbot based on GPT-3, and (2) a controlled math-problem-solving chatbot with prompted vs. unprompted variants.

findings.finding_summary: In Study 1 (n=145), the prompted database tutor was used under four guidance conditions. The paper reports that G4 (solve then refine with LLM) may not have helped homework performance as much as the other guidance strategies, while Study 2 (n=356) found no significant performance difference between prompted and unprompted LLMs (Kruskal-Wallis d 0.13, p=1; Mann-Whitney W=15025, p=0.37).
findings.measure: Homework score / task accuracy in assignment and math problems

findings.finding_summary: In Study 1, structured guidance reduced unrelated student queries and reduced copy-pasting of assignment questions into the chatbot. The paper reports that absence of G1, G3, and G4 led to more unrelated questions, while G1, G2, and G4 reduced the likelihood of verbatim assignment-question copy-pasting.
findings.measure: First-query category distribution and occurrence of verbatim question copy-pasting

findings.finding_summary: Across Study 2, confidence in using LLMs increased after guidance but dropped after completing the task (mean 4.51 initial, 5.19 after guidance, 4.57 after use; Friedman d 72.82, p<0.001). Trust in LLM responses also declined after task experience (mean 4.36 initial to 3.49 post-task; Friedman d 80.31, p<0.001).
findings.measure: Confidence in using LLMs and trust in LLM responses across stages

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports negligible or non-significant change in self-confidence / confidence in one's own answers. In Study 2, confidence in math-solving ability was stable from pre- to post-task (mean 5.04 to 5.16, p=0.079). In Study 1, changes in self-confidence were negligible across conditions.
findings.measure: Self-confidence in topic / math-solving ability

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that pre-prompting the model changed the interaction environment but did not improve overall task performance. Exploratory analysis suggested that examples (G2) and metacognitive questioning (G3) appeared to improve performance when paired with an unprompted LLM, with G2 yielding 68.13%�.68% versus 58.09%�.32% with a prompted LLM.
findings.measure: Performance across prompted vs. unprompted LLM conditions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical randomized classroom study plus a controlled online experiment, but it is not a single fully powered RCT for the main classroom outcomes and includes exploratory subgroup analyses. The methodology is still reasonably strong and directly observes actual student-LLM interactions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports several statistically significant attitude and interaction-pattern changes, but the core performance effects are null or small and no standardized effect sizes are reported. Overall impact on learning outcomes is unclear/modest rather than clearly large.

paper_profiles.title: The promise and peril of Coding & Robotics education in South Africa: A scoping review of teacher preparation and generative artificial intelligence’s potential for delivering equity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) might help address teacher preparation challenges associated with introducing Coding & Robotics (C&R) in South African schools. The central problem is that the new Grades R–9 C&R subject depends on teachers who often lack sufficient pedagogical content knowledge, programming confidence, ongoing professional development, and adequate technological infrastructure in their schools.

The authors conducted a scoping review using Arksey and O’Malley’s framework. They searched ERIC, Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus for peer-reviewed studies published from 2022 to May 2024, screened 221 abstracts, and included 10 studies. The review synthesized evidence from studies involving teachers, learners, and pre-service teachers in school and university contexts, with most evidence drawn from GenAI tools such as ChatGPT, Codex, Copilot, and related LLM-based systems.

Across the reviewed literature, GenAI was found to support teacher learning through personalized pathways, immediate feedback, code generation, lesson-plan feedback, and support for professional learning communities. The paper also reports risks: biased or inaccurate outputs, overreliance on automated assistance, weak prompt specification, and inequities tied to infrastructure and internet access. The authors conclude that GenAI can complement C&R teacher development and resource creation, but only if paired with teacher judgment, quality assurance, ethical guidance, and professional development.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative artificial intelligence tools, typically based on large language models, that can generate text/code, provide explanations, feedback, and personalized support.
identified_tools.use_case: This scoping review examined how GenAI could support K–12 Coding & Robotics teacher preparation in South Africa, including lesson-plan feedback, content generation, tutoring, and personalized learning support.

findings.finding_summary: Across 10 included studies, GenAI was reported to help teachers with personalized learning routes, content generation, code explanations, and feedback on lesson plans and teaching methods. The review also notes that tools such as ChatGPT, Codex, and Copilot could support programming practice and reduce workload, but benefits depend on prompts, learning objectives, and teacher verification.
findings.measure: Synthesized findings from included studies on teacher preparation, lesson-plan feedback, code generation, and programming support

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a scoping review synthesizing heterogeneous qualitative, mixed-methods, and quasi-experimental studies rather than a single controlled evaluation. The paper does report a systematic search and screening process, but no pooled causal effect estimates are provided.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests potentially meaningful benefits for teacher preparation and feedback support, but it provides no effect sizes and the evidence base is indirect and heterogeneous. Reported impacts are promising but remain unclear in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: Defining AI companions: a research agenda—from artificial companions for learning to general artificial companions for Global Harwell
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual and agenda-setting article that defines AI companions and argues that generative AI is pushing education beyond AI as a mere tool or assistant toward more companion-like systems. The authors distinguish AI tools, assistants, and companions, emphasizing that companions involve mixed initiative interaction and require some form of user model that accounts for intellectual, emotional, social, and value dimensions.

A major focus is the historical development and design logic of artificial learning companions (ALCs). The paper traces the idea back to Chan and Baskin’s learning companions and reviews design approaches such as simulation and machine learning. It then synthesizes prior work on ALC roles, including collaborators, competitors, tutees, negotiators, and animal companions, and links these to educational theories such as Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development, cognitive conflict, cognitive load sharing, and interest-driven creator theory. The paper also highlights AI-related mechanisms relevant to current generative AI, including large language models and retrieval-augmented generation, as well as multimodal, robotic, metaverse, and seamless-learning environments.

The paper does not report an empirical study of a specific student sample or school context. Instead, it proposes a research agenda organized around four questions: emergent technologies, learning theories, educational roles and strategies, and expected outcomes/evaluations. Its main conclusion is that AI companions and ALCs have broad potential to support cognition, metacognition, affect, behavior, social interaction, and wellbeing, but their design and evaluation should be theory-driven, adaptive, and sensitive to the distinct roles companions may play in learning environments.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI systems and large language models used as adaptive conversational or content-generating educational companions, assistants, or tutoring tools; may include retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for more contextually relevant answers.
identified_tools.use_case: This is a theoretical/review paper on AI companions for learning, discussing how generative AI, LLMs, and RAG could support AI learning companions and educational assistance, including tutoring, feedback, and personalized materials.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/review agenda paper rather than an empirical evaluation of a specific AI tool. It does not report primary data, study design, sample sizes, or measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that generative AI and related companion designs may support learning, personalization, and feedback, but it provides no empirical effect sizes or outcome evidence. Impact is therefore speculative and not measurable from this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Mobile-Optimized AI-Driven Personalized Learning: A Case Study at Mohammed VI Polytechnic University
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies (iJIM)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an AI-driven personalized learning platform, Campus+, improves undergraduate students’ academic achievement, engagement, motivation, and retention of course material. The authors frame the problem as a need to move beyond conventional uniform teaching toward personalized, adaptive support that can better fit learners’ needs, especially in a mobile-learning context.

The intervention is a mobile-optimized platform built with LangChain, Pinecone, and an LLM model. It lets instructors upload course materials and allows students to interact with an AI tutor through a chat interface embedded in their course documents. The system uses document retrieval and semantic search to provide personalized, real-time feedback and support, with the paper noting that it is based on GPT-4 and is positioned as an alternative to fine-tuning. The platform was used for four weeks by an experimental group, while a control group continued without the AI intervention.

The study was conducted at Mohammed VI Polytechnic University in Morocco with undergraduate students enrolled in thermodynamics, operational research, neuroanatomy, and embryology. Quantitative pre-test/post-test comparisons and survey feedback were used to evaluate the platform. The authors report that students using Campus+ showed greater gains than the control group, and that most users perceived it as effective for learning efficiency, engagement, motivation, and retention. The paper also notes risks and constraints, including possible bias in personalization and limited support for graphics, numbers, and mathematical formulas.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used as the conversational AI engine for question answering and personalized support in a retrieval-augmented learning platform.
identified_tools.use_case: Used within Campus+ / Tutor GPT to answer student questions from uploaded course documents and provide personalized guidance and instant feedback; the system is described as using OpenAI GPT-4, LangChain, and Pinecone for document-based Q&A.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports improved post-test performance for the experimental group using Campus+ compared with the control group across four subjects. In thermodynamics, the experimental group increased from 14.3375 to 15.0375 (mean diff. 0.7, t=5.83, p<0.001, df=7), while the control group increased only from 14.4 to 14.575.
findings.measure: Pre-test and post-test course scores

findings.finding_summary: In operational research, the experimental group increased from 14.12 to 14.74 (mean diff. 0.62, t=5.49, p<0.001, df=9), compared with a smaller increase in the control group from 14.68 to 14.81. The authors interpret this as evidence that the AI intervention improved learning outcomes.
findings.measure: Pre-test and post-test course scores

findings.finding_summary: In neuroanatomy, the experimental group rose from 14.27 to 14.93 (mean diff. 0.665, t=6.02, p<0.001, df=10), whereas the control group increased from 14.66 to 14.84. The paper states that the experimental group consistently improved more than the control group.
findings.measure: Pre-test and post-test course scores

findings.finding_summary: In embryology, the experimental group increased from 15.67 to 16.22 (mean diff. 0.55, t=5.24, p<0.001, df=8), compared with the control group’s increase from 14.74 to 14.91. The paper reports a stronger improvement for the AI-supported group.
findings.measure: Pre-test and post-test course scores

findings.finding_summary: Survey results suggest favorable learner perceptions of the system: 84% rated Campus+ as moderately or highly effective for improving learning efficiency, 80% reported feeling slightly or highly engaged, 73% said it increased their enthusiasm to learn, 80% reported moderate or excellent retention, and 88% rated the experience as slightly better or far superior to traditional methods.
findings.measure: Student self-report survey on effectiveness, engagement, motivation, retention, and comparison with traditional learning

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental primary study with a control group and pre/post measures, plus survey data. It provides direct empirical evidence, but it is not a randomized trial and the paper does not report effect sizes or confidence intervals.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are moderate in magnitude in raw score change and consistently favor the AI-supported group across subjects, but the study does not provide standardized effect sizes. The evidence suggests meaningful positive impact, though the overall strength is limited by design and reporting constraints.

paper_profiles.title: Comparing individual vs. collaborative processing of ChatGPT-generated feedback: Effects on L2 writing task improvement and learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether students’ processing of ChatGPT-generated feedback on L2 writing works better when done individually or with support from teachers and/or peers. It is motivated by the shift from viewing feedback as something merely delivered to viewing it as something learners actively process within a sociocultural context. The paper also responds to concerns that AI feedback may be used too passively or uncritically, and that teacher mediation may be important for effective and ethical use.

The intervention was a seven-week experiment conducted with 117 sophomore EFL learners at a Chinese university and six teachers. Students completed three during-intervention writing tasks and one delayed new writing task. All students used ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) to obtain automated feedback using a uniform prompt pattern: feedback requirement + rating criteria + essay, with iterative multi-turn prompting encouraged. Participants were randomly assigned to individual processing, teacher-scaffolded processing, peer-scaffolded processing, or teacher-peer-scaffolded processing. Teachers received training on using ChatGPT for feedback and on scaffolding students’ use of it; peer groups discussed feedback through collaborative writing tools and chat platforms.

Results showed that students who processed ChatGPT feedback individually had the largest immediate task improvements, while groups with collaborative processing showed smaller gains during the intervention but stronger longer-term learning on subsequent draft scores. Teacher-involved groups, especially teacher-scaffolded and teacher-peer-scaffolded conditions, showed the strongest learning progression during the intervention. The authors conclude that collaboration can make AI feedback use more careful and developmentally beneficial, and that teacher presence remains important for helping learners interpret, validate, and apply ChatGPT feedback. They also caution that individual use of ChatGPT may produce unrealistically large revisions and raise concerns about academic integrity and overreliance on AI.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s chatbot powered by the GPT family of large language models, used for interactive, iterative text generation and feedback provision.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the automated feedback source for L2 writing drafts in a seven-week experiment. Students prompted ChatGPT using a uniform pattern ('feedback requirement + rating criteria + essay') and were trained to use multi-turn, trial-and-error prompting; feedback was then processed individually or collaboratively with teacher/peer scaffolding.

findings.finding_summary: On L2 writing task improvement (gain scores from draft to final products across T1-T3; n=117), the individual-processing control group outperformed the teacher-, peer-, and teacher-peer-scaffolded groups overall. The group main effect was significant, F(3,113)=44.61, p<.001, η2p=.542, and the interaction was significant, F(6,226)=2.78, p=.013, η2p=.069; pairwise comparisons showed the control group had significantly larger improvements than experimental groups on T1-T3.
findings.measure: L2 writing task improvement (final score minus draft score)
findings.effect_size: η2p=.542; η2p=.069; pairwise d=0.71 (IP vs TS on T3)

findings.finding_summary: On L2 writing learning measured by draft scores across T1-T3 and the delayed new task NT (n=117), the collaborative groups with teacher involvement (TS and TPS) showed stronger learning progression than the individual-processing group. The group main effect was significant, F(3,113)=37.75, p<.001, η2p=.501, and the interaction was significant, F(9,339)=3.91, p<.001, η2p=.094; the study reports small pairwise effects for teacher-involved groups on draft scores (e.g., TPS vs IP on NT, d=0.66).
findings.measure: L2 writing learning (draft score progression across tasks, including delayed new task)
findings.effect_size: η2p=.501; η2p=.094; pairwise d=0.66 (TPS vs IP on NT)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary experimental study with random assignment to four conditions, clear measures, and reported inferential statistics. However, it is not blue because it is a single-site educational study with design and generalizability limitations noted by the authors.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are large for the main group outcomes (η2p=.542 and .501), indicating substantial impact on both immediate task improvement and learning progression. Although findings are mixed across outcomes, the magnitude on the primary analyses is clearly medium-to-large.

paper_profiles.title: Development of REGAI: Rubric Enabled Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes and evaluates REGAI (Rubric Enabled Generative Artificial Intelligence), a retrieval-augmented generation and large language model-based system designed to improve automated evaluation of unstructured text. The main problem addressed is that LLMs can produce plausible but inaccurate or inconsistent judgments, especially in high-stakes evaluation settings where human-like reasoning, consistency, and alignment with explicit criteria are required.

REGAI combines several components: a rubric that may be manually created or LLM-generated and then reviewed by a human expert; a scoring LLM that produces an initial numeric score and justification; a critiquing LLM that checks the score against the rubric and provides corrective feedback; and an iterative draft-critique-revision workflow. It also uses retrieval from a knowledge base of expert-created rubrics, grades, and critiques, with the goal of grounding outputs in prior human examples and strengthening performance over time. The paper explicitly discusses possible applications in academic grading, applicant screening, performance evaluation, client interaction assessment, proposal review, email prioritization, paper review, and transcript analysis.

Although the system is presented as broadly applicable, the only empirical evaluation reported uses the first 500 essays from the Hewlett Foundation Automated Essay Scoring dataset. In that experiment, REGAI is tested in two configurations: a single critique iteration versus a rubric-only approach. Results suggest that the critique cycle improves error reduction, weighted agreement, and score calibration relative to rubric-only scoring, but both approaches still fall short of human raters and show signs of overfitting due to a very small knowledge base. The paper concludes that REGAI is promising, but requires more robust knowledge bases, better prompt engineering, and additional validation across domains.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A rubric-enabled generative AI system built from large language models and retrieval-augmented generation to evaluate unstructured text using human-created or human-reviewed rubrics, iterative critique, and a growing knowledge base.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and preliminarily evaluates REGAI for automated essay scoring and discusses prospective use in academic grading; the system is also framed for rubric-based evaluation tasks more broadly.

findings.finding_summary: On the Hewlett Foundation Automated Essay Scoring Dataset (first 500 essays from essay set 8), the single-critique REGAI configuration showed better error and agreement metrics than the rubric-only approach, but not consistently better correlation. Reported overall metrics were Corr=0.49, MAE=4.37, and QWK=0.49 for single critique versus Corr=0.55, MAE=7.86, and QWK=0.26 for rubric-only; human raters were Corr=0.60, MAE=2.03, and QWK=0.59.
findings.measure: Automated essay scores compared with human-provided scores; correlation, mean absolute error, and quadratic-weighted kappa

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preliminary evaluation of a proposed system using one dataset and limited human-approved examples, not a rigorous experimental study. The paper also reports the results as indicative/proof-of-concept rather than definitive, with limited methodological detail.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported differences suggest the critique cycle may improve scoring accuracy and agreement, but the impact is mixed and the system remains below human raters. The effect is meaningful for the specific essay-scoring setting, but the paper does not report a single effect size and the evidence is early-stage.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Thematic Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how educators perceive the benefits, risks, and pedagogical implications of generative AI in education, with a particular focus on tools such as ChatGPT, Bard, and Bing AI. The central question is not an intervention study but a thematic exploration of educator viewpoints on how GenAI affects learning, assessment, academic integrity, prompt construction, programming support, and responsible use. The authors aim to surface both opportunities and concerns, especially around plagiarism, hallucinated outputs, over-reliance, bias, transparency, and the need for updated assessment practices.

The study is based on seven unstructured essays written by education-sector professionals, all of whom taught in higher education contexts across subjects such as machine learning, programming, databases, statistics, and research methods. The paper combines thematic analysis with exploratory data analysis of the essays, including word-frequency and bigram analyses. The educators discuss GenAI as a tool for boilerplate code generation, troubleshooting, iterative prompting, and personalized support, while also warning about misuse, inaccurate outputs, weak arithmetic performance, and the erosion of independent thinking.

The main conclusions are that educators see GenAI as both promising and risky, and that effective use depends heavily on prompt quality, human oversight, and curricular guidance. The most prominent concern is academic integrity, with strong emphasis on replacing traditional essay-heavy assessment with more authentic forms of evaluation such as oral questioning, project-based work, and monitored interaction. The paper also argues that students and staff need explicit instruction on responsible GenAI use, and that institutions should develop clearer policies, better assessment designs, and more transparent practices for integrating these tools into teaching and learning.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI / large language model system for text generation, question answering, coding help, and other prompt-based outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as a generative AI tool used by students and educators for coding help, simulated data generation, essay writing, troubleshooting, and as a general education example; also referenced in relation to prompts, hallucinations, arithmetic errors, and assessment misuse.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's conversational generative AI / large language model system for text generation and question answering.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned via the prior name Bard and discussed as an example of generative AI in education, including differences from ChatGPT and use in writing/response generation.

identified_tools.name: Turnitin
identified_tools.description: An originality/similarity detection system used to compare submitted text against existing sources and produce a similarity score.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the example originality detector to explain how similarity scoring works, and to argue that such tools can be misinterpreted as definitive plagiarism detectors.

identified_tools.name: GPTZero
identified_tools.description: A product claiming to detect whether text was generated by AI or written by humans.
identified_tools.use_case: Cited as an example of an LLM-generated-content detector discussed in terms of claimed accuracy and limitations.

identified_tools.name: ZeroGPT
identified_tools.description: A product claiming to detect AI-generated text versus human-written text.
identified_tools.use_case: Cited alongside GPTZero as an example of AI-content detection software and its limitations.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative thematic analysis of educator opinions rather than an empirical evaluation of a tool. It discusses mechanisms, concerns, and examples, but reports no experimental outcome data or effect sizes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical implications for how generative AI and detection tools are used in education, especially around assessment and academic integrity, but it does not measure impact on learner outcomes. The influence is therefore suggestive but unquantified.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial muses: Generative Artificial Intelligence Chatbots Have Risen to Human-Level Creativity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI chatbots can produce creative output comparable to humans. The authors test a common assumption in creativity research and AI discourse: that human creativity is uniquely superior, and that chatbots mainly recombine existing text without producing genuinely original ideas. Rather than studying a classroom intervention or educational use case, the paper focuses on a basic question about the creative capabilities of generative AI systems.

The study compares responses from 100 adult human participants with responses from five generative AI chatbots (Alpa.ai, Copy.ai, ChatGPT-3, Studio.ai, and YouChat), and includes GPT-4 in follow-up analyses. All human participants were native English-speaking adults recruited via Prolific in the United States. Participants completed the Alternative Uses Test, generating as many uses as possible for five everyday objects. The same prompts were given to the chatbots, with repeated prompting used to elicit more responses. Human raters and a trained AI independently scored originality and fluency.

The main finding is that the chatbots produced ideas that were, on average, indistinguishable from human responses in originality, although GPT-4 outperformed earlier models. The paper also emphasizes that human prompting, problem definition, and selection of outputs remain essential parts of the creative process. The authors conclude that generative AI can serve as a useful assistant for idea generation, but its value depends heavily on the quality of prompts and the human task framing. The paper also notes risks and limitations such as unreliable outputs on factual tasks, the need for careful prompting, and the broader ethical concerns of misuse.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based conversational language model/chatbot for generating human-like text from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of five generative AI chatbots in an Alternative Uses Test (AUT) to generate ideas for everyday objects; GPT-4 was added in follow-up analyses.

findings.finding_summary: For originality in the AUT, ChatGPT (GPT-3 and GPT-4 normalized to ChatGPT) was compared with human responses across five prompts (pants, ball, tire, fork, tooth). In the main analyses, human- and AI-rated originality did not differ overall between humans and the GAIs (human-rated B=-0.21, p=.218; AI-rated B=-0.18, p=.241), and GPT-4 outperformed the other five GAIs except on ball; however, 9.4 humans on average were more creative than GPT-4 across prompts.
findings.measure: AUT originality ratings by six human raters and a trained LLM rater
findings.effect_size: Human-rated B=-0.21; AI-rated B=-0.18; fork human-vs-GAI t=2.75, d=1.15; tooth AI-rated human-vs-GAI t=3.99, d=0.65; GPT-4 follow-up not pooled into a single effect size
findings.sample_size: n=100 humans; 5 GAI chatbots (ChatGPT versions 3 and 4 included in analyses)
