paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary experimental comparison with blind ratings and quantitative analyses, but it is about creativity tasks rather than education, and the paper does not study K-12 coaching or lesson feedback. The design is clear, yet the evidence is indirect for the stated research topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects on originality are mixed and often null, with no single consistent medium-or-large impact across tools. The study suggests potential for idea generation, but the practical impact on K-12 instructional coaching or lesson-plan feedback is not demonstrated here.

paper_profiles.title: What Generative Artificial Intelligence Means for Terminological Definitions
paper_profiles.venue: 3rd International Conference on Multilingual digital terminology today. Design, representation formats and management systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence, especially ChatGPT and similar large language model chatbots, is changing the creation and use of terminological definitions. The author argues that these tools can reduce the time and effort required to draft definitions, but also raise concerns about factual errors, hallucinations, bias, plagiarism, and inconsistency across repeated queries.

The paper is primarily a conceptual and position-oriented analysis rather than an empirical study. It discusses AI-assisted terminography, with particular emphasis on post-editing workflows in which the terminologist uses ChatGPT to draft a definition and then verifies, corrects, or refines it. It also outlines prompt strategies, such as specifying contextual and functional constraints, requesting non-redundant term-initial wording, using templates, and asking for multiple definitions when a term is polysemous.

The context is professional terminology work, not education. The paper suggests that ChatGPT can support definition writing by helping analyze existing definitions, extract semantic traits from concordance lines, and refine drafts, especially when combined with corpus tools such as Sketch Engine. The main conclusion is that AI will likely become integrated into terminology workflows, increasing productivity while making human and AI-generated terminological content increasingly difficult to distinguish; however, reliability concerns mean human validation remains essential.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI large language model chatbot for general-purpose conversational text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a generative AI tool for creating, refining, analyzing, and validating terminological definitions; the paper also includes example prompts and responses from ChatGPT 4 in March 2024.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper rather than an empirical evaluation. It discusses possible uses, risks, and workflows for ChatGPT in terminography, but reports no experimental design, sample, or measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes or outcome data are reported, so there is no measurable impact evidence to rate. The paper’s claims are speculative and illustrative rather than empirical.

paper_profiles.title: The Emerging Generative Artificial Intelligence Divide in the United States
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether awareness of generative AI is unevenly distributed across the United States in ways that resemble older digital divides. Rather than studying classroom use or instructional effects, it asks where interest in ChatGPT was concentrated during the first six months after its public release and what county-level demographic, socioeconomic, and industry factors were associated with that awareness.

The study uses de-identified Bing search logs from December 1, 2022 to May 31, 2023, aggregated to ZIP code and county level, and combines them with American Community Survey data. The authors map spatial clustering of ChatGPT search interest, test for hotspots and coldspots, and fit multilevel negative binomial regression models with state random effects. The population is U.S. residents at the county level, with analysis focused on adult search behavior rather than any education-specific subgroup.

The main finding is that early ChatGPT awareness was concentrated in more urban, educated, and economically advantaged counties, especially along the West Coast and in major metropolitan areas, while coldspots appeared in the Gulf South, Appalachia, and parts of the Midwest. Educational attainment was the strongest predictor and substantially attenuated other associations in adjusted models. The paper concludes that generative AI adoption is already reflecting existing socioeconomic and spatial inequalities, raising concerns that the technology could reinforce rather than reduce disparities without targeted intervention.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational generative AI chatbot built on a GPT-family large language model.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the focal technology for measuring awareness/adoption via Bing search interest in the first six months after its public release; the paper does not evaluate instructional use or educational outcomes.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a correlational, observational study using search-log and county-level census data, not an intervention or causal evaluation of AI use in education. It provides descriptive evidence about awareness patterns rather than experimental evidence of effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports sizable geographic and socioeconomic disparities in awareness of ChatGPT, but it does not test learning, coaching, or classroom outcomes. Its impact is therefore indirect and primarily about adoption patterns rather than demonstrated educational effect.

paper_profiles.title: Generative Agent-Based Modeling: Unveiling Social System Dynamics through Coupling Mechanistic Models with Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces Generative Agent-Based Modeling (GABM), a modeling approach that couples a mechanistic model of interactions with a large language model to represent agent decision-making. The main question is how generative AI can be integrated into simulation models of social systems so that human behavior emerges from LLM-informed reasoning rather than from hand-coded decision rules.

The paper is primarily methodological and pedagogical. It uses ChatGPT (GPT-3.5-Turbo) as the LLM and presents a simple office-based diffusion model in which 20 workers choose daily between green and blue shirts. Each agent receives prompt-based information about the social context, prior choices, and persona traits, then generates a response that drives the simulation. The authors systematically vary personas, prompt wording, temperature, and initial conditions to study sensitivity and reproducibility.

The paper concludes that GABMs can produce plausible path-dependent social dynamics and that persona definitions and prompt design materially affect outputs. It argues that the approach can reduce reliance on manually specified behavioral rules and may help model more realistic decision-making, but it also highlights risks such as prompt sensitivity, bias from training data, and reproducibility issues. The paper does not study a K–12 educational intervention; its educational contribution is as a tutorial example for modelers.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s large language model chatbot used for generating and reasoning over natural-language prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the LLM in a generative agent-based model (GABM) to simulate individual agents’ decisions in a norm-diffusion toy model; specifically GPT-3.5-Turbo was used via the OpenAI API.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/methodological paper that introduces and illustrates a modeling framework rather than evaluating an AI tool in an educational intervention study. It does not present K–12 empirical evidence or causal estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational outcome is measured, and no effect sizes or student/teacher impact results are reported. The paper only provides a proof-of-concept simulation and sensitivity discussion.

paper_profiles.title: Search engines post-ChatGPT: How generative artificial intelligence could make search less reliable
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This commentary examines how generative AI is being integrated into search engines and argues that this shift can reduce the reliability of search results. The paper focuses on problems such as hallucinated content, decontextualized quotations, incorrect or misleading citations, hidden provenance, and the amplification of bias when large language models are used to synthesize answers rather than simply rank documents.

The authors illustrate these concerns with examples from contemporary generative search systems, including Google’s Search Generative Experience, Perplexity AI, Arc Search, BingChat, and You.com. They show that small query changes and typos can trigger confidently written but factually incorrect answers, and that these systems may fabricate support for claims or misattribute source material. They frame this behavior as an instance of retrieval-augmented generation that is not sufficiently protected by guardrails, especially when the system prefers generating an answer over refusing to answer.

The paper does not study a K–12 population or an educational intervention; it is a position/commentary piece about information systems. Its main conclusion is that generative search trades efficiency and convenience for reduced reliability, lower transparency, and increased risk of biased or misleading outputs. The authors call for stronger mitigation techniques, better refusal behavior, more attention to provenance and verifiability, and further research on how users interpret and trust generative search results.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI / large language model systems that produce natural-language text, sometimes used in retrieval-augmented or question-answering interfaces.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a commentary on generative search systems and uses examples from ChatGPT-like, Perplexity AI, BingChat, Google SGE, YouChat, and Arc Search to illustrate risks in generated search responses; it does not evaluate a single educational tool.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a commentary/opinion piece rather than an empirical study, meta-analysis, or systematic review. It discusses risks and mechanisms of generative search systems but reports no original study design, sample, or measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes, samples, or outcome measurements are reported, so there is no empirical impact estimate to assess. The paper is useful for conceptual understanding of GenAI risks, but not for evidence of instructional or learning impact.

paper_profiles.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Internet of Things Computing: A Systematic Survey
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Proceedings (venue not fully reported in text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly growing body of work on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for Internet of Things (IoT) computing and argues that the literature is fragmented across many narrow applications. The authors aim to provide a holistic survey of the opportunities, challenges, and implications of combining GenAI with IoT, rather than focusing on a single use case or vertical domain.

The paper is a systematic literature review conducted according to PRISMA. It searches major digital libraries and screenes studies from 2020 to March 2025, ultimately analyzing 74 eligible records. The review organizes prior work using a tripartite IoT framework—Internet-oriented, object-oriented, and semantic-oriented perspectives—and further maps studies to categories of generative models such as auto-regressive models, flow-based models, variational auto-encoders, energy-based models, diffusion models, and GANs. It also compares applications, model choices, and recurring technical constraints such as resource limitations, interoperability, data quality, and privacy/security.

Because the paper is a survey rather than an intervention study, it does not involve a participant population such as students or teachers. Its context is broad cross-domain IoT computing, with examples drawn from networking, edge intelligence, healthcare, smart cities, and security. The authors conclude that GenAI can support synthetic data generation, uncertainty handling, optimization, and human-machine interaction in IoT, but practical deployment is constrained by computational cost, scalability, training instability, and the need for better domain-specific datasets and robust integration frameworks.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative artificial intelligence systems in general, including generative models and LLMs, used to create or synthesize outputs from data.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a systematic survey of generative artificial intelligence for Internet of Things (IoT) computing. It does not study a single educational AI product or a K-12 coaching tool; instead it reviews generative model families and their roles in IoT contexts.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic survey, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool in K-12 education. It synthesizes prior literature across IoT generative modeling and reports no direct study outcomes for a specific tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No student, teacher, or coaching outcome is measured, and no effect sizes or intervention impacts are reported. The paper is outside the requested K–12 instructional coaching/lesson-feedback use case.

paper_profiles.title: A perishable ability? The future of writing in the face of generative artificial intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether human writing ability could erode over time as generative artificial intelligence becomes more capable and widely used. Rather than presenting an empirical study, it makes a conceptual argument that writing may become a “nonperennial” technology: once a society can outsource routine writing to machines, the incentive for individuals to practice and maintain writing skills may decline.

The article develops this argument through historical analogy, especially the abandonment of Linear B in the Greek Dark Ages, and then connects it to current large language models such as ChatGPT. It includes examples of prompting ChatGPT to generate text, including a love letter and arguments about the possibility of skill loss, to illustrate how convincingly AI can produce human-like writing even without genuine emotion or understanding.

No population or educational intervention is studied. The paper’s main conclusion is cautionary: as AI text generation improves, humans may increasingly rely on machines for writing in many domains, which could reduce the practical need for human writing competence. The author also notes that current models still have important limitations, including reasoning failures, factual errors, and bias, but suggests that continued investment could make them substitutes for human writers in more contexts.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot and virtual assistant for generating and editing text via prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in an illustrative discussion and conversational examples about whether generative AI could erode human writing ability; the author prompted ChatGPT to generate a love letter and arguments about writing-skill loss.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/opinion preprint, not an empirical evaluation of ChatGPT or any educational intervention. It contains illustrative prompts and quoted outputs, but no systematic method, sample, or measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No impact estimate is reported and there is no measured educational effect. The paper discusses hypothetical risks and capabilities rather than demonstrating observable outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Text-to-Text: An Overview of Multimodal and Generative Artificial Intelligence for Education Using Topic Modeling
paper_profiles.venue: The 40th ACM/SIGAPP Symposium on Applied Computing (SAC ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper maps the research landscape of multimodal and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in education. The authors ask what the high-level topic structure of educational GenAI research looks like, especially beyond the dominant text-to-text large language model literature. They argue that educational AI research has become heavily concentrated around tools such as ChatGPT, while other modalities like text-to-speech, speech-to-text, text-to-image, and text-to-video remain comparatively underexplored.

To answer this, the study conducts a large-scale literature search in Dimensions.ai, supplemented by Scopus and Web of Science, yielding 4,175 abstracts after filtering. The authors then apply BERTopic-based topic modeling using sentence-transformer embeddings, UMAP dimensionality reduction, HDBSCAN clustering, and c-TF-IDF topic labeling. Hyperparameters were searched over 5,000 random combinations, and the resulting topics were interpreted and merged into 38 final topics grouped into 14 thematic areas. No participants were recruited; the analysis is based entirely on published research abstracts.

The review identifies strong concentration in areas such as LLMs in education, text-to-speech for learning support, writing feedback, educational chatbots, automated question generation, assessment, and academic integrity. The authors conclude that the field is skewed toward text-centered GenAI and largely centered on higher education, with K–12 and multimodal applications receiving much less attention. They recommend broader investigation of multimodal foundation models and educationally focused AI systems, including applications that better support personalized learning, creativity, and accessibility, while also highlighting ethical, integrity, and policy concerns.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative artificial intelligence / large language model chatbots and multimodal foundation models used to produce text and other content modalities for educational contexts.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a topic-modeling overview of the education literature on multimodal and generative AI; it does not evaluate a single tool experimentally, but maps which tools and use areas appear in the corpus. It reports that OpenAI ChatGPT is the most frequently mentioned named service, while the broader literature is dominated by text-to-text LLM use.

findings.finding_summary: Across 4,175 education articles, the corpus was heavily concentrated on text-to-text LLMs, with OpenAI ChatGPT the most frequently mentioned named service. The authors note that multimodal capabilities such as text-to-speech, speech-to-text, and text-to-image were comparatively underexplored, indicating an uneven research landscape rather than a measured effectiveness result.
findings.measure: Topic modeling of titles/abstracts; keyword occurrence counts in the corpus

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic, topic-modeling overview rather than an intervention study. It synthesizes a large corpus, but it does not estimate causal effects or evaluate tool outcomes directly.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has broad descriptive influence on the field by mapping where GenAI research is concentrated, but it does not report measurable learning gains or operational effects for a specific tool.

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Teacher Effectiveness with AI based Prompt Engineering: A Proof of Concept
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI prompt engineering can help teachers create instructional materials more efficiently and with better alignment to standards and classroom goals. The authors frame the work as a proof of concept focused on improving teacher effectiveness, reducing the burden of curriculum creation, and supporting differentiated instruction in K-12 settings, especially middle school STEAM/social studies contexts.

The intervention is a structured prompting framework built around four elements: task context, task input/variable, task instructions, and task criteria. The authors used Microsoft Copilot and demonstrated the process through example prompts for creating simplified informational texts and advanced learning questions aligned to standards, learning targets, and assessment questions. The workflow also emphasized iterative refinement of prompts when outputs were not satisfactory, as well as collaboration among educators to improve prompts.

The paper focuses on middle school teachers in Georgia, with examples drawn from 7th grade social studies and STEAM instruction aligned to Georgia standards and NGSS. The evidence is primarily reflective and descriptive, based on the experiences of two teacher-authors who piloted the process. The main conclusion is that structured prompt engineering can produce higher-quality, standards-aligned instructional materials more consistently, save time, and support differentiated instruction, but it depends on teachers having strong curriculum design knowledge and clear instructional goals.

identified_tools.use_case: The paper presents a prompt-engineering framework for teachers using generative AI to create informational texts, quizzes, rubrics, differentiated materials, and standards-aligned lesson components.

The authors state that the process enabled production of multiple standards-aligned texts at varying complexity levels and supported differentiated instruction, but no quantitative outcome data, sample size, or statistical effect is reported.

These benefits are described qualitatively in reflections from two teachers; no numerical estimate of time saved is provided.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a proof-of-concept / reflective paper with no controlled design, no quantitative outcome analysis, and no inferential statistics. The evidence is qualitative and descriptive, so it does not meet criteria for higher-tier causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful practical benefits for teacher productivity and instructional material quality, but it provides no effect sizes or measured student outcomes. Impact is therefore plausible but empirically unclear.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an analytical AI platform can improve lesson-planning feedback in teacher education, and whether such AI-mediated feedback affects both lesson-plan quality and broader student outcomes such as AI literacy, attitudes, digital competence, self-efficacy, and motivation. The motivation for the study is that university instructors often cannot provide frequent, detailed, individualized feedback on complex lesson plans, especially in vocational business education where multiple planning principles must be balanced.

The intervention used an analytical AI platform called EDDA (electronic didactic assistance for lesson planning). EDDA was built with unsupervised machine learning and a German BERT-based transformer model trained on 1,304 lesson plans/materials from universities in Germany and Austria plus 4,679 coded textbook tasks. It classified uploaded lesson plans into 10 main and 57 subcategories aligned to didactic criteria and planning dimensions such as action orientation, process orientation, problem orientation, motivation, digitalization, sustainability, and basic lesson-structure dimensions. The experimental group used EDDA first and then could consult a university teacher to discuss AI results; the control group received human feedback only. The setting was a master’s didactics course in vocational business education, with lesson plans developed in small groups over a semester.

The sample included 103 master’s students in Germany, split between an experimental group and a control group recruited from different university course contexts. The study followed participants across a semester and included repeated measurement of lesson-plan quality and questionnaire-based measures of AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competences, digital-teaching self-efficacy, and motivation. The study found that AI feedback could match or sometimes outperform human feedback on some lesson-plan dimensions, especially certain sustainability-related aspects, action orientation, relatedness, technology use, lesson structure, and learner engagement. However, simply using AI did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, or motivation, suggesting that benefits depend on a broader pedagogical framework rather than exposure alone. The authors conclude that analytical AI can effectively supplement traditional feedback, but it should be integrated as part of a human-centered, collaborative approach.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI/LLM-based chatbot or platform used to generate or provide feedback, without a named commercial product specified.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper contrasts generative AI tools for feedback with the analytical AI platform EDDA and discusses their general opportunities and risks in lesson-planning feedback, but does not evaluate a named GenAI product.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical intervention study, but the named system under evaluation is EDDA, an analytical AI platform rather than a generative AI product. Since the request focuses on generative AI implementation details and no named GenAI tool is actually studied, evidence for a GenAI product is absent.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful instructional-feedback effects for the non-generative EDDA platform, but there is no direct impact estimate for a generative AI tool. For generative AI specifically, impact is not established in this paper.

paper_profiles.title: A Large Language Model Approach to Educational Survey Feedback Analysis
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs), specifically GPT-4 and GPT-3.5, can support analysis of open-ended educational survey feedback. The authors focus on a practical problem in education: qualitative survey comments are valuable for identifying course strengths, weaknesses, and areas for improvement, but they are time-consuming to code manually and often difficult to analyze consistently at scale. The study asks whether modern LLMs can perform a broad set of common text-analysis tasks on such data with little or no labeled training data.

The approach treats survey analysis as a pipeline of natural-language-processing tasks, including multi-label classification, multi-class classification, binary classification, extraction, inductive thematic analysis, and sentiment analysis. The models were accessed through the OpenAI API using zero-shot prompting, zero-shot chain-of-thought reasoning, function calling for structured output, and prompt tuning based on inspection of model reasoning. The authors also developed a generalizable label set for course-feedback analysis and compared LLM outputs with human annotations and, in some cases, specialized baseline models.

The evaluation used 2,500 open-ended end-of-course survey comments drawn from 15 online biomedical science courses at a single educational program, with an additional development set for prompt refinement. The paper concludes that GPT-4 in particular can achieve human-level performance on several survey-analysis tasks and can produce useful reasoning traces that may help with confidence, debugging, and prompt improvement. The results suggest that LLMs can make qualitative survey analysis more accessible and scalable, though performance depends on careful prompting, task specification, and the quality of the label scheme.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT family of large language models used for zero-shot text analysis, classification, extraction, thematic analysis, sentiment analysis, and structured JSON output via function calling.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on educational survey feedback analysis tasks, including multi-label classification, binary and multi-class classification, extraction, inductive thematic analysis, and sentiment analysis; it also examined chain-of-thought reasoning and prompt engineering practices.

findings.finding_summary: On the multi-label classification task, GPT-4 achieved average Jaccard similarity of 80.60% when compared with human annotators across pairings, close to the 81.24% average Jaccard similarity among the four human raters. The paper reports that GPT-4 reached human-level performance on multiple tasks with effective prompting; exact per-task effect sizes were not reported.
findings.measure: Multi-label classification agreement using average Jaccard similarity coefficient

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary empirical study with clear methods, but it is not an experimental intervention study in K-12 and relies on qualitative/mixed evaluation of LLM outputs rather than a controlled design. The evidence is useful but narrower in scope and setting than the strongest tiers.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported performance is strong and close to human agreement, but the paper does not report a numeric effect size meeting the stated threshold. The main practical impact is enabling efficient survey feedback analysis rather than demonstrating a clearly measured medium-or-large outcome.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can function as an automated teacher coach by scoring classroom transcripts and generating actionable instructional feedback. The authors focus on three tasks: predicting observation scores from transcript segments using established classroom observation rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and offering suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the National Center for Teacher Effectiveness (NCTE) transcript dataset, consisting of elementary mathematics classroom observations from U.S. 4th and 5th grade teachers. The data are linked to expert ratings from two established observation instruments: CLASS and MQI. The authors test ChatGPT in a zero-shot setting using the gpt-3.5-turbo model, with prompt variants for direct scoring, scoring with rubric descriptions, and reasoning-then-answer prompts. For qualitative tasks, experienced math teachers evaluate model outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

Results show that ChatGPT has promise but performs substantially below expert coaching quality. Score predictions correlate weakly with human ratings, and adding rubric descriptions or chain-of-thought reasoning does not improve performance much. For feedback generation, teachers often judged outputs as not insightful or not relevant, especially for MQI-based items, and many suggestions repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript. The paper concludes that generative AI may eventually support teacher coaching, but current models need better grounding, reduced hallucination, and stronger human-in-the-loop design.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational large language model used for generating scores, identifying highlights/missed opportunities, and producing actionable feedback from text prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated zero-shot as an automated teacher coach on elementary math classroom transcripts. The model was prompted to score CLASS and MQI observation items, identify highlights and missed opportunities, and generate suggestions for eliciting more student reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: On Task A, ChatGPT showed low correlation with human ratings across CLASS and MQI observation items. Reported Spearman correlations were generally near zero (e.g., CLPC DA=0.00, CLBM DA=0.35, CLINSTD DA=-0.01; EXPL DA=0.02, REMED DA=0.05, LANGIMP DA=0.00, SMQR DA=0.17), and adding rubric descriptions or reasoning did not reliably improve performance.
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between model-predicted observation scores and human annotator scores
findings.effect_size: See reported Spearman correlations in Table 1 (e.g., 0.35 max on CLBM; many near 0)

findings.finding_summary: For Task B, teachers generally did not find model outputs insightful or relevant for identifying highlights and missed opportunities. Faithfulness was somewhat better than the other dimensions, but around 20-30% of responses were still marked unfaithful; MQI results were worse than CLASS across relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness.
findings.measure: Human ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for generated feedback examples

findings.finding_summary: For Task C, most suggestions were judged actionable, relevant, and faithful to the transcript context, but novelty was poor: 82% of suggestions repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript. The paper characterizes the suggestions as often useful in form, but highly redundant.
findings.measure: Human ratings of relevance, faithfulness, actionability, and novelty for teacher suggestions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study using qualitative and correlational evaluation rather than an RCT or meta-analysis. The methods are clear and systematic, but the evidence is limited by small human-evaluation samples and no causal design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported performance is mixed to negative for scoring and insight generation, with one notable positive on actionability but strong redundancy and low scoring accuracy. Because no positive outcome reaches a clear modest-to-large effect threshold, overall impact is unclear to modest at best.

paper_profiles.title: Changing Roles and Identities in a Teacher-Driven Professional Development Community
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a teacher-driven professional development community, Streamline to Mastery, changed teachers’ participation, leadership, and identities over time. The central question is whether a professional learning environment built around teacher agency, shared inquiry, and skeptical discourse can foster a community of practice in which teachers move from peripheral participation to more central, expert-like roles.

The program was not a generative AI intervention; rather, it was a long-term professional development model for secondary physics and physical science teachers. Teachers were responsible for setting their own goals, planning classroom action research, sharing lessons, designing workshops, and preparing conference presentations. The research team observed the program through videos of meetings, email threads, and interviews/focus groups, and coded these data to track agenda setting, email initiation, and instances of challenge/disagreement in discussion.

The sample included four teachers from two urban high schools in high-needs districts in the United States. Teachers met with researchers every other week in 2.5- to 3-hour evening sessions in teachers’ classrooms. The study found that teachers increasingly initiated emails, set meeting agendas, and challenged one another’s ideas, indicating a shift from researcher-led professional development to a more egalitarian community of expert learners.

The authors conclude that professional development may be more effective when it creates conditions for teacher agency and community formation rather than simply delivering outside expertise. They argue that teacher knowledge and resources already reside within teachers’ everyday practice, and that vulnerability, skepticism, and shared inquiry can support both individual and collective growth.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI or large language model chatbot, with no specific commercial or research product named.
identified_tools.use_case: Not studied in this paper. The paper is a teacher professional development/community-of-practice study and does not evaluate any AI tool.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods study of teacher professional development and community participation, not an empirical evaluation of an AI system. No AI tool is tested, compared, or analyzed for outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There are no AI-related outcomes or effects reported, so there is no measurable tool impact to rate. The paper is outside the scope of AI tool effectiveness evidence.

paper_profiles.title: AI-Generated Rubric Interfaces: K–12 Teachers’ Perceptions and Practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers perceive and use AI-supported rubric generation for assessment and feedback, with a focus on whether such tools can reduce the burden of creating rubrics while still preserving teacher control and instructional alignment. The authors specifically ask how teachers view large language models for generating rubrics and assessments in block-based programming contexts, and whether hands-on exposure changes their willingness to adopt these tools in practice.

The intervention studied was a summer professional development workshop in which 25 middle- and high-school teachers used MagicSchool.ai to generate rubrics, practiced prompting to tailor criteria and performance levels, and then used the AI-generated rubrics to assess a sample block-based programming task. Teachers also used the platform’s chatbot, Reina, to generate rubric-based feedback for the same work. Data came from pre- and post-workshop surveys, open-ended reflections, discussions, and exit tickets, and the qualitative component was analyzed thematically.

Across both survey and qualitative findings, teachers viewed AI-generated rubrics as useful starting drafts that improved structure, clarity, and speed, especially for vague or creative tasks. However, they repeatedly emphasized that the outputs often required substantial editing, sometimes used generic or grade-misaligned language, and could miss instructional priorities. Teachers were generally positive about clarity, transparency, and ethical acceptability, but less satisfied with usability, especially the ability to add, remove, or revise criteria. Overall, the study concludes that AI rubric tools are most promising when they are teacher-directed, editable, standards- and goal-aligned, and supported by scaffolded prompting rather than presented as fixed automated products.

identified_tools.name: MagicSchool.ai
identified_tools.description: An AI-enabled educational platform that can generate and help refine teacher-authored classroom materials such as rubrics and feedback via prompting and chat-based interaction.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers used MagicSchool.ai to generate AI rubrics for a block-based programming task, practiced prompting to tailor criteria and performance levels, and then used the generated rubrics to assess a sample assignment; they also used the platform's chatbot (Reina) to produce rubric-based feedback.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that MagicSchool.ai-generated rubrics were useful as strong starting drafts that reduced the time and effort of creating rubrics from scratch. The tool was seen as improving structure and clarifying vague criteria, but many teachers said outputs still required substantial editing and teacher oversight.
findings.measure: Teacher perceptions of rubric generation usefulness, workload reduction, and editability from surveys, open-ended responses, and thematic analysis

findings.finding_summary: Teachers rated the generated rubrics positively for criteria clarity (M=3.9375), performance-level differentiation (M=4.125), assignment alignment (M=4.0), and transparency (M=4.062), but were more mixed on grade-level language appropriateness (M=3.5) and curriculum/learning-outcome alignment (M=3.5). The lowest usability rating concerned adding/removing/revising criteria without difficulty (M=2.75), indicating friction in customization.
findings.measure: Post-survey Likert ratings of clarity, alignment, usability, and ethical factors

findings.finding_summary: Teachers perceived AI-generated feedback as more detailed and scalable but sometimes harsher than their own feedback, creating a strictness-versus-detail tradeoff. They emphasized that adoption should remain teacher-directed, with outputs calibrated and reviewed before use with students.
findings.measure: Open-ended reflections on feedback quality and willingness to use AI-generated feedback

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large-language-model chatbot or generative AI system used to draft rubrics and provide rubric-based feedback when no specific model product is identified beyond the platform context.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper also refers generically to a chatbot/LLM workflow within the rubric-generation platform and to the use of a chatbot for delivering rubric-based feedback, without naming a standalone model beyond MagicSchool.ai's integrated chatbot.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the chatbot-enabled workflow could provide scalable, detailed feedback and support quicker rubric-based assessment than manual grading alone. Adoption was conditional on the system remaining configurable so teachers could retain control over criteria, weighting, and final judgments.
findings.measure: Teacher perceptions from surveys and open-ended responses about AI-assisted grading and feedback workflow

findings.finding_summary: Teachers found that prompt clarity and detail affected output quality: more descriptive prompts yielded deeper feedback, while vague prompting could produce outputs that were generic or misaligned with instructional priorities. This supports an iterative human-in-the-loop workflow rather than fixed automation.
findings.measure: Open-ended reflections on prompt quality, output depth, and alignment

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods workshop study with surveys and thematic analysis, not an experimental impact study. It provides useful evidence about teacher perceptions and workflow features, but not causal effects on student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful practitioner uptake and workflow benefits, but these are perception-based and no quantitative student-performance effect sizes are reported. Impact is promising for teacher workflow, but the educational outcome impact remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Changing Identities and Evolving Conceptions of Inquiry through Teacher-Driven Professional Development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a teacher-driven professional development program shaped secondary science teachers’ understanding of scientific inquiry and their participation in a professional community. The central problem is that teachers often hold ambiguous or incomplete conceptions of inquiry, and the authors ask whether sustained, collaborative, minimally facilitated professional development can help teachers develop a more coherent, expert-like shared understanding.

The intervention studied is Streamline to Mastery, a five-year professional development program in which teachers partner with university researchers to co-design professional learning. Teachers and researchers met every other week to share inquiry-oriented lessons, discuss classroom experiences, reflect on lessons, and plan conference presentations and other activities. The study analyzed lesson reflections, inquiry survey responses, videotaped meetings, email threads, and interviews, using both qualitative coding and frequency counts aligned with the NRC five essential features of inquiry.

The participants were four secondary physical science teachers from two urban high schools in the Rocky Mountain West of the United States. They taught in high-needs contexts, and most were teaching outside their primary science discipline. Over time, the teachers’ talk about inquiry became more aligned with the five essential features, while also preserving themes such as real-world relevance, ownership, and social construction of knowledge. The paper concludes that the program supported growth in teacher agency and leadership as teachers increasingly initiated emails, set agendas, and challenged one another’s ideas, and that shared, experience-grounded discourse was central to this development.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system is a computer-based instructional system that provides individualized guidance, practice, and feedback based on learner responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Not studied in this paper. The paper is a teacher professional development study about inquiry talk and community participation, not an AI tool evaluation.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods STEM teacher professional development paper, not an AI or generative AI tool evaluation. No AI system was implemented, compared, or assessed.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no reported AI tool outcome, effect, or instructional impact to evaluate. The paper’s findings concern teacher discourse and participation in a professional community.

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of making AI education more accessible and relevant for K–12 teachers and learners by integrating AI concepts into core non-computing subjects. The authors argue that many existing AI curricula are standalone or computer-science-centered, which makes them difficult for teachers of English, social studies, science, and other subjects to adopt. They investigate what K–12 teachers need in order to design and potentially implement integrated AI curricula.

The study used a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K–12 educators from a range of subjects and grade levels. The workshop included presentations to establish shared AI knowledge, tool demonstrations, a card-sorting activity, a pre-work assignment in which teachers connected one AI tool to their own curriculum, and co-design sessions where teachers and researchers worked in small groups to draft integrated lesson plans. The researchers analyzed workshop audio, questionnaires, and participant artifacts using open coding.

The resulting curricula embedded AI into social studies, ESL, literacy for students with learning disabilities, and an exemplar physics curriculum. Across the workshops, teachers emphasized four design needs: evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration. The paper concludes that integrated AI curriculum should leverage data already produced in classroom activities, support student reflection, and include explicit scaffolding for ethics. It also notes that teacher-researcher co-design, even in a remote format, can surface practical pathways for making AI education more accessible beyond computing classrooms.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI / AI learning tool category; in this paper, the workshop explored several AI learning tools rather than a single named GenAI product.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers co-designed integrated K-12 lesson plans around AI learning tools and discussed how AI concepts could be embedded into core subjects. The paper references tools such as Teachable Machine, Machine Learning for Kids, Google Quick, Draw!, MIT App Inventor AI, Arbitrary Style Transfer, and related AI learning tools as examples used in the workshop.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative co-design study about teacher needs and curriculum design, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool’s learning effects. The methodology is clear, but it does not test a specific product or report causal outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has meaningful design implications for K-12 AI curriculum implementation, but it does not measure student achievement or compare tool impacts. As a result, impact is important but indirect and not quantifiable from the study.

paper_profiles.title: LLM Performance Predictors: Learning When to Escalate in Hybrid Human-AI Moderation Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of deciding when an LLM’s moderation output can be trusted and when it should be escalated to a human reviewer in hybrid human-AI content moderation systems. The authors frame this as an uncertainty quantification and cost-sensitive selective classification problem: the system should automate easy cases, but defer high-risk or ambiguous cases to humans.

The proposed approach is an LLM Performance Predictor (LPP) framework that learns a meta-model from signals extracted from the base LLM’s outputs, including token log-probabilities, entropy, verbalized confidence, and moderation-specific abstention indicators. The workflow uses structured prompts, a fixed integer-token output schema, deterministic retries for malformed outputs, and a learned ridge-regression meta-classifier that outputs a probability of correctness. A threshold policy then routes cases either to automated trust or to human review.

The paper evaluates the framework on text-only and multimodal content moderation benchmarks using several proprietary and open-source LLMs. The results show that the meta-model generally improves error prediction and reduces expected moderation costs relative to standard uncertainty heuristics such as MSP, entropy, and top-2 margin. The authors also find that their abstention indicators improve explainability by distinguishing evidence deficits from policy gaps, though Chain-of-Thought prompting was not beneficial in this setting because it inflated confidence and hurt calibration.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A large language model-based AI system used to generate structured moderation judgments, confidence signals, and uncertainty indicators from text and multimodal inputs, with human-in-the-loop escalation when uncertainty is high.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies multiple LLMs in a hybrid human-AI moderation workflow; models are prompted to produce fixed-schema outputs and their uncertainty is predicted to decide whether to trust the model or escalate to human review.

findings.finding_summary: Across the evaluated moderation datasets, the LPP meta-model improved cost-aware routing relative to standard uncertainty baselines. For example, on the OpenAI Moderation Dataset, expected cost for gpt-4o-mini decreased from $132 (best baseline) to $38, with escalations reduced from 331 to 148; on the Multimodal Moderation Dataset, expected cost for gpt-4o-mini decreased from $37 to $22, with escalations reduced from 107 to 80.
findings.measure: Expected cost ($) and escalation count/ratio in selective trust-vs-escalate routing

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical systems paper with controlled evaluations and held-out test sets, but not a randomized educational intervention and not K–12-specific. The evidence is quantitative yet domain-specific to content moderation rather than instructional coaching.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported improvements are operational and can be substantial in the moderation setting, but there is no standardized effect size and the outcome is not educational achievement. Relevance to K–12 teacher coaching is indirect, so the impact for the requested topic is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service elementary science teachers incorporated ChatGPT into science lesson planning, and how they perceived its usefulness and risks. The study addresses a gap in empirical work on actual educational uses of generative AI, especially for science instruction and lesson design rather than speculative commentary.

The intervention/context was a short professional-learning experience in which 29 pre-service teachers at a Korean teachers’ university learned about ChatGPT across four 2-hour class sessions, including its basic functions, potential educational uses, science-teaching strategies, and lesson-plan construction. Participants then produced lesson plans for a typical 45-minute elementary science class, were required to include at least one instructional strategy learned in the course, and attached simulated ChatGPT conversations. Lesson plans were evaluated with a modified TPACK-based technology integration rubric, and open-ended survey responses were analyzed qualitatively; the chat transcripts were used for triangulation.

Overall, the pre-service teachers showed broad but uneven understanding of ChatGPT’s educational affordances. They most often envisioned using it to support questioning, self-directed and individualized learning, role-play, formative feedback, and classroom discussion across multiple science topics and instructional strategies. Quantitatively, lesson plans scored above the rubric midpoint, with stronger performance in aligning ChatGPT to curriculum goals and instructional strategies than in selecting the most appropriate ChatGPT functions. The paper concludes that pre-service teachers see substantial promise in ChatGPT for science instruction, but they need more professional development on function selection, accuracy checking, and avoiding over-dependence or misuse of AI-generated information.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot for text generation, question answering, and dialogue-based assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Pre-service elementary science teachers used ChatGPT in lesson plans and simulated conversations to support science content exploration, role-play scripting, adaptive questioning, individualized support, and formative feedback in 45-minute lessons.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative/mixed-methods study of 29 pre-service elementary science teachers, ChatGPT-integrated lesson plans scored highly on a modified TPACK-based rubric (M = 3.29, SD = .91 on a 4-point scale). Scores were highest for instructional strategies & ChatGPT (M = 3.48, SD = .99) and curriculum goals & ChatGPT (M = 3.44, SD = .87), while ChatGPT function selection(s) was lower (M = 3.00, SD = .93).
findings.measure: Modified TPACK-based lesson plan rubric (TIAR-derived)

findings.finding_summary: Participants perceived ChatGPT as useful for question-driven learning, individualized support, and formative feedback, but also expressed concerns about inaccurate or misleading outputs and student over-dependence. The paper reports that 11/29 raised accuracy/reliability concerns and 13/29 raised over-dependence concerns, with many proposing mitigation through diverse sources, teacher feedback, and structured classroom interaction.
findings.measure: Open-ended survey responses and lesson-plan analysis

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical qualitative/mixed-methods study with lesson-plan analysis and survey responses, but no controlled outcome comparison or causal estimate. The evidence is informative for implementation, yet not strong enough for blue/green under the framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported lesson-plan quality scores are positive and relatively high, but they are not outcome effects on student learning and have no effect size. Reported benefits and risks are important, but the measurable impact on K-12 outcomes is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: LLMs to Support K–12 Teachers in Culturally Relevant Pedagogy: An AI Literacy Example
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge K–12 teachers face in implementing culturally relevant pedagogy (CRP), especially when adapting emerging AI literacy curricula to students’ cultural contexts. The authors argue that teachers often lack the time, training, and resources needed to meaningfully integrate CRP into lesson planning, and that this gap is particularly salient in AI education, where culturally responsive learning materials are limited.

To explore whether generative AI can help, the paper presents CulturAIEd, an LLM-powered tool that combines demographic information about students, a CRT checklist, rubric-based feedback, and just-in-time chatbot coaching. The system was prototyped with Streamlit and GPT-4o-mini-2024-07-18. Teachers could use it to generate culturally relevant examples and to receive basic versus advanced lesson modifications aligned with CRT levels (Contributions, Additive, Transformation, Social Action), along with formative feedback on lesson quality.

The study used an exploratory pilot with four secondary teachers from North America and East Asia: science, music education, and information technology teachers working in grades 9–12. Participants completed adaptation tasks across multiple phases, including baseline lesson design, unaided revision, checklist-guided revision, and revision using CulturAIEd. The main conclusion is that the tool improved teachers’ confidence in identifying culturally responsive opportunities and reduced planning burden by making demographic integration and feedback more immediate and actionable. The authors also note risks, including biased or stereotyped outputs, routinizing CRP into a checklist, and the need for teacher judgment and professional development to refine AI suggestions.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general large language model chatbot / generative AI system used to generate, adapt, and provide feedback on educational content and lesson plans.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studied CulturAIEd, an LLM-powered teacher support tool for adapting K–12 AI literacy activities to culturally responsive pedagogy (CRP), using student demographics, a CRT checklist, rubric-based feedback, and just-in-time coaching. The demo used Streamlit and a GPT-4o-based model, but no standalone named product beyond general GPT/ChatGPT-family use was evaluated as a separate commercial tool.

findings.finding_summary: In an exploratory pilot with four K–12 teachers (N=4), participants reported increased confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness in learning activities and making culturally responsive modifications after using the LLM-based CulturAIEd workflow. The paper reports pre-survey confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness rose from 3-5 to all 5 in post-surveys, but does not report inferential statistics or effect sizes.
findings.measure: Self-reported confidence in identifying opportunities for cultural responsiveness in learning activities; post-survey ratings

findings.finding_summary: Teachers said CulturAIEd streamlined CRP-related lesson adaptation by integrating student demographics, providing concrete examples, and offering rubric-based feedback and just-in-time coaching. The paper characterizes the tool as highly efficient and reports that 3/4 participants strongly agreed it saved time and inspired new ideas, but no quantitative effect size is provided.
findings.measure: Perceived time savings, workflow efficiency, and usefulness of rubric-based feedback; post-survey and interview responses

findings.finding_summary: The paper identifies risks and implementation concerns for LLM-supported CRP tools, including bias, cultural stereotyping, and the possibility of 'routinizing' CRP into a template-like process that could replace teacher judgment. These are qualitative cautions rather than measured harms, and the authors emphasize that LLM suggestions must be adapted with teacher context and training.
findings.measure: Perceived risks and implementation concerns from interviews/discussion

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small exploratory mixed-methods pilot with four teachers and qualitative interview/survey data. It is useful for implementation insights, but it does not provide controlled causal evidence or effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported benefits are promising but are based on self-reported confidence and perceived efficiency in a very small sample, with no effect sizes. The evidence suggests potential practical value, but the magnitude of impact is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Student-Teacher Curriculum Learning via Reinforcement Learning: Predicting Hospital Inpatient Admission Location
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to improve neural network training by using a teacher-student curriculum learning framework, with the immediate application of predicting hospital inpatient admission location from emergency department triage data. The authors frame training as a reinforcement learning problem in which a teacher network learns to select which batch of training data the student network should see next, based on the student’s current state.

The proposed approach uses the student’s network weights as the teacher’s state representation. Training data are first ordered into a curriculum by an entropy-like measure: for tabular clinical data, Mahalanobis distance after autoencoder encoding; for CIFAR-10, cosine similarity. The teacher then chooses the center and width of each batch, with reward defined by the student’s improvement in accuracy on both training and validation sets, which is intended to reduce overfitting and steer the student through easier-to-harder or otherwise task-appropriate curricula.

The empirical context includes hospital electronic health record data from an Oxford hospital trust (ward admission prediction), MIMIC-III ICU data (mortality prediction), and CIFAR-10 as a non-medical benchmark. The paper reports that the reinforcement-learning-based teacher-student method outperforms simpler batchwise and fixed curriculum baselines, and is competitive with or better than several tabular and image-classification methods. The learned policies often exhibit structured behaviors such as entropy spiking, gradual entropy progression, and transfer across related tasks, suggesting that the teacher can learn stable and task-sensitive curricula from the student’s evolving state.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: A teacher-student curriculum learning framework in which a higher-level teacher agent selects training data batches for a student model based on the student’s state and reward feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a reinforcement-learning-based curriculum learning method for training predictive neural networks, not as a K-12 instructional product.

findings.finding_summary: The proposed student-teacher curriculum learning method improved classification performance over batchwise training, vanilla curriculum training, and prior student-teacher curriculum learning baselines on the ward admission task. On the ward admission dataset, the DDPG student-teacher achieved 0.62 (SD 0.02) accuracy versus 0.45 (0.01) for batchwise training and 0.48 (0.02) for curriculum training (n=14,324 total patients; 8,589 training patients).
findings.measure: Classification accuracy on ward admission prediction

findings.finding_summary: On the MIMIC-III mortality prediction task, the DDPG student-teacher achieved 0.70 (SD 0.01) accuracy, outperforming batchwise training (0.63, SD 0.01), vanilla curriculum training (0.63, SD 0.02), and the DQN student-teacher baseline (0.66, SD 0.02). The study reports the dataset contained 8,806 patients and used a train/validation/test split of 60/20/20.
findings.measure: Classification accuracy on MIMIC-III mortality prediction

findings.finding_summary: On CIFAR-10, the DDPG student-teacher reached 0.90 (SD 0.01) on sample 1 and 0.90 (SD 0.01) on sample 2, exceeding batchwise training (0.65, SD 0.02) and vanilla curriculum training (0.68, SD 0.01) as well as the DQN student-teacher (0.86, SD 0.04; 0.88, SD 0.02). The paper evaluates three sampled CIFAR-10 test sets and reports competitive performance relative to image-classification baselines.
findings.measure: Classification accuracy on CIFAR-10
findings.sample_size: n=12,000 training images sampled; n=3,000 test images sampled per run

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is not an empirical K-12 education study and does not evaluate an instructional AI tool in classrooms. It is a machine learning methods paper about reinforcement-learning-based curriculum training for hospital prediction and image classification.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct K-12 instructional or coaching impact, and no evidence about teacher support, lesson feedback, or student learning in education settings. Its reported effects are limited to classification accuracy in non-educational tasks.

paper_profiles.title: Novobo: Supporting Teachers’ Peer Learning of Instructional Gestures by Teaching a Mentee AI-Agent Together
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to support teachers’ professional learning of instructional gestures, which are embodied, tacit teaching skills that are difficult to learn through text-based instruction or prescriptive feedback. The authors argue that existing approaches to gesture training are often time-consuming, overly simplified, or socially awkward when based on peer critique alone. They therefore investigate whether a teachable AI agent positioned as a mentee can stimulate collaborative reflection and peer learning among teachers.

The intervention is Novobo, a generative AI system designed as a novice teacher that teachers mentor together. Novobo uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), prompt engineering, and a multi-agent workflow to suggest instructional gestures for a scenario, explain the theoretical basis for its suggestions, and invite collective teacher ratings, comments, bodily demonstrations, and explanations. Its knowledge base combines literature on gesture types and instructional intentions with annotated gesture examples from classroom videos. The interface includes a four-step loop: posing a teaching scenario, commenting on AI-generated gestures, demonstrating gestures using a skeletal mirror view, and explaining the rationale for the demonstrated gesture.

The study was conducted with 30 teachers from seven primary schools in China, organized into 10 collaborative study groups. The evaluation combined vignette analysis of interaction videos with thematic analysis of focus-group discussions. Teachers used the system to externalize tacit knowledge, compare gesture choices, and co-construct shared understanding of how gestures should vary by grade level, subject, and classroom context.

The authors conclude that framing AI as a learnable mentee can reduce social pressure, encourage richer peer discussion, and support collaborative knowledge exchange around embodied instructional practices. They also highlight design implications for teacher-facing generative AI, especially the value of traceable knowledge sources, embodied interaction, and mentor-mentee framing. The paper is primarily a design-and-evaluation study rather than a causal effectiveness trial.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-family large language models used for retrieval-augmented generation, gesture description generation, dialogue management, and instructional-intention analysis within a multi-agent teachable agent system.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the model backbone for Novobo: GPT-4-turbo handled instructional-intention analysis and gesture generation, GPT-3.5-turbo handled conversation, and OpenAI embeddings powered RAG over a knowledge base of gesture theory and teacher-annotated examples.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative user study with 30 teachers in 10 collaborative sessions, Novobo supported peer learning by prompting teachers to externalize, exchange, and co-construct knowledge about instructional gestures. Teachers used the agent’s generated gestures, retrieved sources, and discussion prompts to share tacit practice-based knowledge and reported that the mentor-mentee framing reduced peer pressure and criticism concerns.
findings.measure: Observed knowledge exchange, collaborative discussion, and teacher experiences in user study sessions/focus groups

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods empirical study with 30 teachers, not a controlled effectiveness trial. The paper provides rich design and interaction evidence, but no causal estimates or standardized outcome measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful but unquantified improvements in collaboration and knowledge sharing. Because no effect size is reported, the magnitude of impact on teacher learning remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring K-12 Physical Education Teachers’ Perspectives on Opportunities and Challenges of AI Integration Through Ideation Workshops
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 physical education (PE) teachers perceive the opportunities and challenges of integrating AI into their classes. The authors focus on a context that is relatively underexplored in AI-in-education research: PE, where instruction takes place in large open spaces, involves physical activity and safety concerns, and requires teachers to manage heterogeneous student abilities while also delivering feedback and assessments.

Rather than evaluating a deployed AI system, the study used ideation workshops to elicit teachers’ views on what AI could do in PE. Seventeen in-service secondary school PE teachers in South Korea participated in focus-group workshops that included brief AI literacy instruction, individual sketching of ideas, group storyboarding, and role-play. Participants imagined AI in four supportive roles: operational assistant, personal trainer, group coach, and evaluator. Their ideas included environment and safety monitoring, automated attendance and health checks, personalized movement feedback, balanced team formation, and multidimensional assessment.

The paper concludes that teachers see meaningful potential for AI to reduce workload and support instruction, but only if AI remains a supporting tool rather than replacing teacher judgment. They also emphasize major barriers and risks, including limited infrastructure in PE settings, uneven teacher technology readiness, misalignment with PE’s educational goals, overreliance on AI, and student privacy and autonomy concerns. The study offers design implications for developers and policymakers, especially the need for AI systems that are pedagogically grounded, usable in physical activity settings, and sensitive to ethics and implementation constraints.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / AI system concept, including AI-enabled perception, NLP, automation/optimization, and reasoning/prediction capabilities discussed at a conceptual level rather than as a specific product.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as an ideation target in focus-group workshops with 17 in-service secondary PE teachers, who imagined AI as an operational assistant, personal trainer, group coach, and evaluator for K-12 physical education.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative ideation/workshop paper with no empirical evaluation of a specific AI system, no intervention, and no outcomes measured for student or teacher performance. The study elicits perceptions and design ideas rather than testing effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful design directions for K-12 PE, but it reports no measured effect sizes or demonstrated outcomes. Impact is therefore speculative and not yet evidenced in practice.

paper_profiles.title: To what extent is ChatGPT useful for language teacher lesson plan creation?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how ChatGPT can support foreign language teachers in creating lesson plans. The central question is not about student learning outcomes, but about the quality, consistency, and pedagogical alignment of AI-generated lesson plans when prompted in different ways. The authors focus on practical prompt-engineering issues relevant to teachers: how much specificity is needed, whether more detailed prompts improve output, and whether the same prompt produces consistent results.

The study uses ChatGPT-4.0 with five zero-shot prompts that increase in specificity across iterations. The prompts were designed around a high school novice Spanish lesson on a Costa Rican restaurant and aligned to ACTFL proficiency guidelines, ACTFL world-readiness standards, and an edTPA-style lesson template and checklist. Each prompt was entered into 10 separate new chats, producing 50 lesson plans total. The outputs were scored against 25 rubric criteria derived from best practices and the licensure-oriented template, and the authors analyzed score variation, word counts, and output similarity using statistical and clustering methods.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT can generate generally useful lesson plans for language teaching, but that added prompt specificity does not reliably improve quality in a linear way. Including a checklist of required criteria produced the strongest outputs, while adding a lesson-plan template sometimes reduced quality by encouraging formulaic or teacher-centered sections. The same prompt often produced highly variable outputs, sometimes including outdated or anachronistic pedagogical practices such as audiolingual-style activities or weak cultural integration. The authors argue that teachers should use ChatGPT with critical review, explicit criteria, and revision, and that AI literacy should include checking for bias and pedagogical misalignment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's ChatGPT is a conversational large language model for generating and revising text and other content from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate foreign language teacher lesson plans via five zero-shot prompts of increasing specificity, each run 10 times, with outputs scored against a lesson-plan rubric aligned to ACTFL/edTPA criteria.

findings.finding_summary: Using ChatGPT 4.0, the authors generated 50 lesson plans (5 prompts � 10 iterations) and scored them against a 25-point rubric. Increasing prompt specificity did not lead to a linear improvement in quality: mean scores were 21.2 (P2), 19.8 (P3), 19.6 (P4), and 21.6 (P5), with only a marginal overall group difference (p=0.0442) and no significant pairwise differences after correction.
findings.measure: Lesson-plan rubric score (25 criteria)

findings.finding_summary: The study found that adding specificity reduced variance in some cases and changed output length, but it did not reliably produce more complete or better-aligned plans. The paper argues ChatGPT can streamline lesson planning, but outputs still required human evaluation and revision because identical prompts often produced divergent results.
findings.measure: Word count; output consistency / Jaccard distance; presence/absence of rubric criteria

findings.finding_summary: Qualitative inspection showed some outputs reflected outdated pedagogical practices, including teacher-centered warm-ups, limited cultural connections, and occasional audio-lingual-style activities. The authors warn that ChatGPT may reproduce historic biases from its training data and that human attention is needed to correct these weaknesses.
findings.measure: Presence/absence of culturally responsive and contemporary pedagogical features in generated lesson plans

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single mixed-methods/quantitative study using rubric scoring and multivariate comparisons, not an RCT or meta-analysis. The methods are clear and replicable, but evidence is limited to one content area and one model version.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports statistically detectable but modest and inconsistent effects of prompt specificity on lesson-plan quality, with mixed practical implications. The impact is clearer for workflow guidance than for large measurable gains in educational outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Three Pivotal Concepts in K-12 Science State Standards and Maps of Conceptual Growth to Research in Physics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how K-12 science standards align with core physics concepts and why some of those concepts are especially difficult for learners to master. The authors ask whether there are a small number of physics ideas that are both foundational to later science learning, consistently present in state standards, and known from research to be persistently misunderstood by students. To answer this, they analyze concept maps from Project 2061 and examine science standards from four U.S. states with different styles and grade-band organizations.

The paper focuses on three topics that emerge as pivotal across these analyses: Newton’s laws/force and motion, conservation of energy, and geometrical optics. Rather than testing a new intervention empirically, the article synthesizes prior physics education research to explain common student misconceptions and to describe instructional approaches that have shown some success, such as prediction-based demonstrations, conceptual explorations with air tracks and motion sensors, and guided discussion of free-body diagrams and energy reasoning. The intended users are teachers, teacher educators, curriculum developers, and professional development providers working in K-12 science.

The main conclusion is that these three concepts are central to the K-12 science curriculum and should receive sustained instructional attention because they function as conceptual building blocks for many other science ideas.
