The authors argue that standard coverage alone is not enough; effective teaching must explicitly address students’ naïve conceptions, help them focus on deep structural features of problems, and connect standards to research-based strategies. The paper also highlights that state standards vary substantially in how explicitly they name and quantify these ideas, which has implications for teaching, curriculum design, and teacher professional development.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Computer-assisted instruction or concept-based instructional support systems used to guide learning through structured activities, prompts, and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper does not study an AI product. It discusses research-based instructional approaches and assessment tools for teaching Newtonian force and motion and conservation of energy in K-12 and introductory physics, not generative AI or coaching software.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/disciplinary education paper about physics standards and student misconceptions, not an empirical evaluation of an AI system. No AI tool, generative model, or coaching platform is studied.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Because no AI intervention or measured AI-related outcomes are reported, there is no tool impact to assess. The paper’s influence is theoretical and curricular rather than an AI effectiveness result.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT/GPT-3-like systems, for education. The authors focus on how these models could support learning and teaching through content generation, personalized feedback, lesson planning, assessment support, and educational dialogue, while also identifying major risks such as bias, hallucinations/unverified output, overreliance by learners and teachers, copyright/plagiarism issues, privacy and security concerns, and sustainability costs.

The paper is not an empirical intervention study; instead, it synthesizes existing literature and proposes a conceptual view of how large language models may be integrated into educational settings. It discusses applications across learners and teachers in primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional development contexts, and briefly references use cases such as quiz generation, feedback generation, adaptive tutoring, and teacher support for lesson design and grading.

The main conclusion is that large language models can be valuable educational tools, but only if they are used with human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, clear governance, and strong privacy and ethical safeguards. The authors argue that educational systems need training, policies, and responsible design approaches to prevent misuse, protect student data, reduce bias, and ensure that the technology complements rather than replaces human instruction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot and large language model system for dialogue, text generation, and assistance across tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as a general-purpose large language model for education, including teacher lesson planning, personalized feedback, assessment, and professional development; no empirical evaluation in this paper.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper and literature discussion, not an empirical evaluation of a tool. It provides conceptual opportunities and risks rather than a study with a clear methodology or measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct effect sizes, samples, or outcome measurements are reported for an intervention. The paper identifies possible benefits and harms, but does not demonstrate impact empirically.

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how Artificial Intelligence, especially generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, is changing education and what skills are needed to use it responsibly. The central question is not whether AI should be adopted, but how students and educators can avoid common problems such as hallucinations, overreliance, misalignment, unfair use, and weak critical evaluation while still benefiting from AI’s capabilities.

The paper is a conceptual discussion grounded in the author’s experience at a Swiss University of Applied Sciences, combined with a narrative literature review. It focuses on higher education, though the author notes that the ideas may also be useful in K-12 contexts. The paper describes the institution’s internal response to AI adoption, including AI-use guidelines that require transparency, documentation, and critical evaluation of AI outputs. It also reviews practical classroom uses of AI such as experiments, case construction, curriculum support, gamification, and immersive technologies.

The main conclusion is that effective AI use in education depends on building an AI culture supported by AI literacy, prompt engineering skills, and critical thinking. The paper argues for workshops, formal courses, updated guidelines, dedicated staff support, and ongoing institutional engagement rather than relying only on policy documents. It frames AI as a sparring partner rather than a tutor or ghostwriter and emphasizes that responsible adoption requires both technical understanding and ethical awareness.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbots used for text and other content generation, instructional support, brainstorming, and conversational interaction.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generative AI in education broadly, with examples including ChatGPT and other LLMs, focusing on how students and teachers might use them for writing, classroom activities, and prompt engineering. It is a conceptual discussion and narrative review rather than an empirical study of a single product.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual discussion and narrative literature review with a single institutional case description, not a controlled empirical evaluation of an AI tool. No outcome data, effect sizes, or comparative analysis are reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report measured impacts on learning, coaching, or feedback outcomes. It offers recommendations and cautions, but no empirical evidence of positive, null, or negative effects.

paper_profiles.title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory paper examines how ChatGPT responds to prompts related to science education, and whether it can be useful for educators designing science teaching materials. The paper asks three questions: how ChatGPT answers science-education questions, how educators might use it in science pedagogy, and what reflections arise from using ChatGPT as a research tool. The study is positioned as a self-study exploration rather than an evaluation of learning outcomes.

The paper is not an intervention study with participants. Instead, the author interacts directly with ChatGPT through a series of prompts about effective science teaching, pedagogical choices, student failure in science, and the creation of a Year 7 unit, rubric, and quiz on renewable and non-renewable energy sources. These outputs are compared with relevant science education literature to judge alignment, usefulness, and pedagogical quality. The context discussed is science education broadly, with examples framed for Year 7 classrooms, early-career teachers, and pre-service teachers, but no actual students or teachers are studied.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT can generate plausible and often pedagogically aligned ideas, especially for lesson design, rubrics, and quizzes, but its responses may be generic and require substantial teacher judgment and contextual adaptation. The paper also emphasizes important concerns: ChatGPT may present itself with unwarranted authority, lacks evidence grounding, may produce false or misleading references, and raises ethical issues including bias, privacy-adjacent concerns, environmental impact, and copyright. Overall, the paper argues that generative AI may be a useful support tool for educators and researchers, but it does not replace professional expertise and should be used critically and transparently.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model system that generates human-like text responses and can be used for conversational assistance, drafting, summarization, and other language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a self-study exploratory paper to answer science-education prompts and to generate teaching resources such as a 5Es unit, a rubric, and a quiz; also used as a research/writing aid for editing and clarifying prose.

findings.finding_summary: This paper is an exploratory self-study rather than an effectiveness trial. The author reports that ChatGPT's answers often aligned with key science-education themes and could be helpful for drafting units, rubrics, quizzes, and for editing prose, but also warns that it lacks evidence grounding and may position itself as an epistemic authority without sufficient qualifications. No sample size or effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Quality/alignment of ChatGPT-generated responses with science-education themes; usefulness for generating teaching materials and editing text; ethical/epistemic concerns

findings.finding_summary: The author highlights risks including fake citations, bias, Western skew, environmental impact, content moderation concerns, copyright infringement, and the possibility that students may use ChatGPT as an essay hack rather than as a learning aid. The paper argues that educators should critically evaluate outputs and that ChatGPT does not replace teacher expertise.
findings.measure: Observed/argued risks and ethical concerns associated with ChatGPT use in education and research

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative exploratory self-study with no controlled comparison, randomization, or quantified outcome analysis. It provides reflective evidence and illustrative outputs, but not high-causality evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports potential usefulness for drafting and editing, but also substantial concerns and no measured learning gains. Overall impact is unclear and largely contextual rather than demonstrated with effect sizes.

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a review article that surveys the emerging literature on artificial intelligence in education, with particular emphasis on chatbots and ChatGPT. Rather than testing an intervention, the authors synthesize prior work to explain what AI technologies are, how chatbots function, and how generative AI may be used in educational settings. The paper is framed around both the opportunities and the risks of using ChatGPT-like systems in teaching and learning.

The article discusses potential applications such as personalized instruction, instant feedback, automated assessment, student support, and administrative workload reduction for teachers. It also highlights major concerns including bias, privacy, deception, unreliable or inaccurate outputs, weak links to pedagogical theory, and over-reliance on AI. The discussion repeatedly emphasizes that AI tools should not be adopted uncritically and that teacher preparation, responsible use, and alignment with educational goals are essential.

Because the paper is a literature-based overview, it does not report a participant sample, a specific school level, or an empirical implementation in a classroom. Its main conclusion is that AI and ChatGPT may have transformative potential in education, but their effective use depends on ethical safeguards, sufficient training and support for educators, and further research on benefits, risks, and pedagogical integration.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot and large language model system that produces human-like text responses from natural language prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a review focused on ChatGPT and related chatbots in education, discussing their potential uses, benefits, and ethical/practical challenges rather than evaluating a single classroom intervention.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI/chatbot systems used for text generation, question answering, feedback, and related educational support functions.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper broadly reviews generative AI and chatbot use in education, including teacher support, feedback, personalized learning, and instructional applications, without reporting an empirical study of a specific generic system.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a review/article synthesis with no original empirical evaluation of an AI tool in K-12 instruction or coaching. It primarily discusses potential benefits and risks, so it does not meet criteria for higher-evidence tiers.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report measurable effect sizes or outcome data, so direct impact is unclear. However, it identifies important risks and implementation concerns that are relevant to practice, which supports a cautious non-red impact classification.

paper_profiles.title: The Potential of AI Chatbots in Enhancing Lesson Planning in K-12 Education - Insights from Practicum-Experienced Teaching Graduate Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This thesis examines whether and how generative AI chatbots support lesson planning for teacher candidates preparing to teach in K-12 settings. The paper asks three main questions: the extent to which preservice teachers use AI chatbots during practicum, the benefits and challenges they experience, and their views on school-age students using these tools. The motivation is to understand a rapidly emerging educational use case for generative AI, particularly for instructional planning, curriculum development, feedback, and related preparation tasks.

The study uses a mixed-methods design combining an anonymous survey and semi-structured interviews. The survey was distributed to Master of Teaching program students and yielded 103 valid responses; four respondents were also interviewed. Participants were graduate-level teacher candidates with practicum experience in K-12 classrooms in Ontario, Canada. Most reported using AI chatbots, especially ChatGPT, for generating lesson ideas, creating activities, and drafting feedback, with use occurring occasionally to about half the time for many respondents.

The main conclusion is that teacher candidates generally perceived AI chatbots as useful for increasing efficiency and improving lesson quality, but they also identified important concerns. Reported issues included technical problems, over-reliance on AI, privacy and data security, intellectual property concerns, potential bias, and alignment with curriculum standards. The thesis argues that AI can be a helpful instructional support, but only if used critically and with ethical oversight, professional guidance, and clear boundaries to avoid harmful dependence or pedagogical misalignment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI generative AI chatbot/large language model used for text-based conversational assistance, content generation, and response drafting.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as one of the AI chatbots used by practicum-experienced K-12 teacher candidates for lesson planning, generating lesson ideas, creating activities, and providing feedback on student work during practicum.

findings.finding_summary: Among 103 valid survey responses, 78% reported using AI chatbots for lesson planning during practicum, and ChatGPT was the most commonly used tool (79% of chatbot users). Participants reported that it helped them generate lesson content ideas, classroom discussion prompts, lesson materials, and feedback on student work, and many perceived it as improving efficiency and lesson quality.
findings.measure: Survey-reported use of AI chatbots for lesson planning and perceived benefits of ChatGPT in lesson preparation

findings.finding_summary: Some participants raised concerns about over-reliance on AI, technical issues, privacy and data security, intellectual theft, bias/fairness, and alignment with curriculum standards. The thesis also notes risks of diminished critical thinking and pedagogical misalignment when chatbots are used uncritically.
findings.measure: Survey and interview reports of concerns and challenges associated with AI chatbot use

identified_tools.name: Magic School AI
identified_tools.description: An education-focused generative AI platform designed to support teachers with lesson-planning and classroom materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Included as one of the AI chatbots reportedly used by practicum-experienced K-12 teacher candidates for lesson planning, though at a much lower rate than ChatGPT.

findings.finding_summary: The survey reported that 9% of participants who used AI chatbots indicated using Magic School AI. The paper groups it with other chatbots that were used to generate lesson ideas, activities, and teaching materials to save time and support lesson planning.
findings.measure: Self-reported chatbot usage in lesson planning

identified_tools.name: Eduaide.AI
identified_tools.description: An education-focused AI platform for generating lesson plans, presentations, quizzes, and other instructional materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Reported as one of the chatbot tools used by K-12 practicum teacher candidates for lesson planning and curriculum support.

findings.finding_summary: The survey reported that 5% of participants who used AI chatbots indicated using Eduaide.AI. It was used in the broader set of tools for creating lesson ideas, materials, and feedback supports, which participants perceived as efficient and helpful for teaching preparation.
findings.measure: Self-reported chatbot usage in lesson planning

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI chatbots/large language model systems used for conversational assistance, content generation, and instructional support without a single named product focus.
identified_tools.use_case: The thesis frames the study broadly around generative AI chatbots in K-12 lesson planning, especially when discussing benefits, challenges, ethics, and teacher candidates' experiences with multiple tools.

findings.finding_summary: Across 103 valid survey responses, 78% reported using AI chatbots for lesson planning during practicum, and 25.33% used them about half the time while 18.67% used them most of the time and 2.67% always. Participants commonly used chatbots to generate lesson content ideas (46%), facilitate classroom discussions (20%), provide feedback on student work (10%), and assist with homework (14%).
findings.measure: Self-reported frequency and applications of generative AI chatbot use for lesson planning

findings.finding_summary: Participants reported concerns about over-reliance on AI, diminished critical thinking, privacy and data security, intellectual theft, bias and fairness, and alignment with curriculum standards. The paper also notes that some nonusers avoided the tools because of skepticism, budget constraints, lack of knowledge, or concerns about effectiveness and poor-quality AI-generated answers.
findings.measure: Survey and interview reports of challenges, non-use reasons, and ethical concerns

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods thesis with survey and interview data, which provides useful primary evidence but not experimental causal identification. The evidence is qualitative/observational and based on self-report, so it fits a yellow tier rather than higher-evidence categories.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear perceived benefits and substantial adoption, but it does not provide effect sizes or objective outcome gains. It also reports meaningful concerns and mixed/negative issues such as over-reliance, privacy, and poor-quality answers, so overall impact is unclear rather than clearly large or modest.

paper_profiles.title: Speculative Futures on ChatGPT and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Collective Reflection from the Educational Landscape
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the promises and pitfalls of ChatGPT and generative AI in education through a speculative, future-oriented lens rather than an empirical intervention study. The authors aim to surface emerging themes, including potential benefits such as personalized learning, language support, accessibility, faster feedback, and time savings, alongside harms and risks such as bias, privacy concerns, weakened academic integrity, reduced creativity, over-reliance, teacher replacement, and unequal access.

The approach is a collective writing exercise in which a large international group of education scholars wrote fictional narratives imagining positive and negative AI futures. The paper includes multiple speculative stories set across educational contexts, including school-age learners, university students, and educators, but it does not evaluate a real-world deployment of ChatGPT in a controlled study. Instead, it reflects on how AI might reshape learning, teaching, assessment, and academic work.

The main conclusion is that generative AI can support educational tasks but should not be adopted uncritically. The authors argue that education must remain human-centered, that educators should retain the leading role, and that AI use should be ethical, intentional, and context-sensitive. They emphasize the need for AI literacy, new assessment practices, and safeguards around equity, privacy, and bias before large-scale adoption.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational generative AI / large language model chatbot used for text generation, question answering, summarization, and other language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses ChatGPT as the central example of generative AI in education and includes a fictional narrative generated by ChatGPT; it is not an empirical evaluation of a teacher-coaching or lesson-feedback intervention.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a speculative, conceptual paper using fictional narratives and collective reflection rather than a systematic or empirical study design. It does not report measurable outcomes, sample sizes, or effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No causal or quantitative impact on K–12 coaching, lesson feedback, or teacher practice is reported. The paper identifies possible risks and opportunities only at a narrative level.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a PRISMA-based systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education (HE) research published from 2016 through 2022. The authors sought to update earlier reviews and describe how the field has evolved, including where studies were conducted, which academic departments produced the research, which student populations were studied, and what AI was used for in HE settings. They also aimed to identify trends and gaps in the literature to inform future work.

The review screened 371 records and included 138 peer-reviewed journal articles. The studies covered 31 countries across six continents, with the largest share from Asia, especially China and Taiwan, and a substantial number from North America and Europe. Most studies focused on undergraduate students, though graduate students were also represented. First authors were most often affiliated with colleges of education, followed by computer science. The paper notes a strong increase in publications in 2021 and 2022, suggesting rapid growth in the field.

Using grounded coding, the authors found five main uses of AI in HE: assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. Across the review, AI was used for tasks such as automated assessment and feedback, performance and dropout prediction, chatbot or virtual-agent support, adaptive tutoring, and learning analytics for instructional decision-making. The authors conclude that AI is increasingly being used in traditional efficiency-enhancing ways, while more exploratory and pedagogically transformative uses remain underdeveloped. They call for more research in underrepresented regions, more work at the graduate level, more attention to instructors and managers, and exploration of newer tools such as ChatGPT.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / AI assistant used for educational tasks such as answering questions, providing feedback, generating questions, and supporting instruction; the paper does not identify one specific commercial product.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education from 2016-2022. It includes studies of AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment/evaluation tools, predicting applications, and learning analytics, but does not isolate a single named generative AI product such as ChatGPT.

findings.finding_summary: Across 138 higher-education studies, the review found that AI was used mainly for assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. The paper does not report a single quantified effect for a named GenAI product; instead it synthesizes heterogeneous uses and notes that much of the evidence reflects traditional efficiency-oriented applications rather than unexplored affordances.
findings.measure: Systematic review synthesis of 138 peer-reviewed journal articles (AI use categories in higher education)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review with transparent PRISMA methods, but it synthesizes heterogeneous studies rather than testing one AI tool directly. The evidence is therefore descriptive and review-based, not a single high-causal-design intervention study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports broad field trends and categories of AI use, but no direct effect sizes for a specific tool. Because no single intervention outcome is quantified, impact is unclear rather than demonstrably large or small.

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines the opportunities and risks of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for human learning. Rather than reporting a primary empirical study, it synthesizes emerging research from learning sciences, educational technology, and human-computer interaction to argue that GenAI could reshape learning support, resource creation, feedback, and assessment.

The paper discusses how GenAI can personalize tutoring, generate diverse instructional materials, provide timely feedback, and support more authentic assessments. It also highlights major concerns, including hallucinations, lack of transparency, privacy risks, inequality in access, bias, overreliance, and the possibility that AI-generated outputs can undermine valid assessment. Examples are drawn from prior studies and products such as ChatGPT and Khanmigo, but the paper itself does not test an intervention on a participant sample.

The authors conclude that GenAI should be used in a human-centred way, with strong AI literacy, evidence-based decision-making, and rigorous research standards. They argue that educators, researchers, policymakers, and technology providers must work together to ensure GenAI augments rather than replaces human learning and instruction.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI systems, including large language models and diffusion models, that create text, images, video, audio, or autonomous agent outputs for educational use.
identified_tools.use_case: This perspective paper discusses GenAI as a broad class of tools for learning support, learning resource creation, learning feedback, and learning assessment; it does not evaluate a single system empirically.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/theoretical paper rather than an empirical evaluation. It synthesizes prior work and raises concerns and research needs, but does not present primary data, controlled comparisons, or pooled estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct impact estimate is reported because the paper does not measure outcomes for a specific tool or intervention. Its value is conceptual, not evidentiary for effect size or causal impact.

paper_profiles.title: War of the chatbots: Bard, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, Ernie and beyond. The new AI gold rush and its impact on higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the rapid rise of large language model chatbots—especially ChatGPT, Bing Chat, Bard, and Baidu’s Ernie—and their implications for higher education. The central problem is that generative AI is advancing quickly enough to affect teaching, assessment, academic integrity, and institutional policy, while also creating risks such as hallucinations, misinformation, privacy concerns, and deceptive or biased outputs.

Rather than presenting a primary experiment on learners, the article offers a comparative, critical review of major chatbot systems and a synthesis of the emerging English- and Chinese-language literature on chatbots in higher education. The authors describe the corporate background of major systems, summarize their capabilities and shortcomings, and discuss how these tools are being used or considered by students and instructors in higher education contexts. They also note the limits and risks of current systems, including inaccurate answers, hallucinations, lack of reliable sourcing, jailbreakability, and censorship-related constraints in China.

The paper’s conclusions are largely precautionary. It argues that current chatbots are powerful but still fall short of the sensational claims made about them, and that higher education should respond through assessment redesign, careful teaching practices, student guidance, and institutional policy changes. The article does not report a K–12 intervention or empirical study of coaching or lesson-plan feedback; instead, it is a theoretical and review-oriented discussion centered on higher education.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI chatbot/LLM system used for generating, summarizing, and answering text prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper reviews and compares ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) as one of several major LLM-based chatbots relevant to higher education, discussing its capabilities, limitations, and risks.

findings.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes prior literature and notes that ChatGPT has substantial potential for higher-education uses, but also major weaknesses including hallucinations, outdated knowledge, unreliable reasoning, and ease of jailbreaking. It cites claims that GPT-4 outperforms GPT-3.5 on tests such as the UBE and AP exams, while also emphasizing concerns about misinformation and academic integrity.
findings.measure: Narrative review of reported capabilities, limitations, and test-performance claims in prior studies

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/article rather than an empirical evaluation, and the paper itself does not report original outcome data for ChatGPT. The evidence presented is secondary and descriptive.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper describes potentially substantial effects on assessment and teaching, but without primary effect estimates from this article. Because the synthesis highlights both benefits and serious harms/limitations, the net impact is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: A large-scale comparison of human-written versus ChatGPT-generated essays
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether ChatGPT can produce argumentative essays that are comparable to, or better than, essays written by students. The authors focus on a practical education-related concern: if generative AI can write high-quality essays, then traditional homework and essay grading may need to change. They also examine whether AI-generated writing has distinctive linguistic properties compared with human student writing.

The study compares 90 human-written argumentative essays from an essay-feedback forum used by German high-school students with essays generated by ChatGPT-3 and ChatGPT-4 using a simple zero-shot prompt asking for an essay of about 200 words on the same topic. Teachers at secondary schools participated as expert raters after a short online training session; they evaluated anonymized essays on seven criteria including topic completeness, logic, expressiveness, language mastery, complexity, vocabulary/text linking, and language constructs. The authors also conducted a computational linguistic analysis of lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, nominalization, modality, epistemic markers, and discourse markers.

The results show that both ChatGPT versions were rated higher than the human-written essays on all major essay-quality criteria, with ChatGPT-4 outperforming ChatGPT-3. The AI texts were structurally more rigid and differed linguistically from student writing: they used more nominalizations and more complex sentence structures, while students used more modals and epistemic markers. The authors conclude that generative AI can already perform strongly on this kind of school writing task and argue that educators should adapt homework and writing instruction accordingly. They also note that hallucinations were not a major issue for this argumentative-essay task, though they caution that subtle errors may have been missed and that the models are fast-changing targets.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational large language model chatbot interface based on GPT-family models, used to generate and interact with text.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate argumentative student essays from 90 topics via zero-shot prompts, compared against human-written essays and across ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 outputs for essay quality and linguistic characteristics.

findings.finding_summary: In a large-scale essay evaluation with 111 teachers and 658 ratings across 270 essays, ChatGPT-generated essays were rated significantly higher than human-written essays on all seven rubric criteria. Mean overall ratings were 4.36 for ChatGPT-3 and 4.68 for ChatGPT-4 versus 3.69 for human essays; reported effects for human vs. ChatGPT-3 ranged from d=0.52 to 1.15 and for human vs. ChatGPT-4 from d=0.88 to 1.43.
findings.measure: Teacher-rated essay quality on seven criteria (topic/completeness, logic/composition, expressiveness/comprehensiveness, language mastery, complexity, vocabulary/text linking, language constructs) and overall score
findings.sample_size: n=270 essays rated by 111 teachers; 658 ratings

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT essays showed distinct linguistic patterns relative to human essays: they had higher sentence complexity and nominalizations, but also differed in modal use, epistemic markers, and discourse markers. The paper reports significant differences in most linguistic markers, with no significant difference for sentence complexity (depth) between humans and ChatGPT-3, and no significant difference for discourse markers between humans and ChatGPT-3.
findings.measure: Computational linguistic markers (lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, nominalizations, modals, epistemic markers, discourse markers)

findings.finding_summary: The authors report that hallucinations were not a major problem in this argumentative essay setting because the tasks relied on general argumentation rather than factual correctness. They also caution that subtle hallucinations may have been missed and note some low ratings for criteria related to factual correctness.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings plus qualitative discussion of factual correctness/hallucination risk

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single observational comparative study with teacher ratings and computational linguistic analysis, not an RCT or meta-analysis. The design is systematic and statistically rigorous, but it remains correlational/benchmark-style evidence rather than intervention evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported differences are large in magnitude for essay quality (many effects well above d=0.20, often medium-to-large or larger). The paper suggests substantial educational implications for homework and writing instruction, indicating high potential impact.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can function as an automated teacher coach by scoring classroom instruction and generating useful pedagogical feedback. The authors frame the problem around a real shortage of consistent, high-quality instructional coaching and test whether a generative AI system can complement human feedback in K–12 teacher development.

The study evaluates ChatGPT in three zero-shot tasks using elementary mathematics classroom transcripts from the NCTE dataset: (A) predicting scores on selected CLASS and MQI observation items, (B) identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and (C) generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student reasoning. For the qualitative tasks, two experienced math teachers rate model outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty. The quantitative task compares model predictions with expert human ratings using Spearman correlation.

The context is U.S. 4th- and 5th-grade math classrooms drawn from 317 teachers across four school districts serving largely historically marginalized students. The findings show that ChatGPT performs poorly at rubric scoring, often overpredicting scores and showing low correlation with human ratings. For feedback generation, teachers judge many outputs as irrelevant, uninsightful, or unfaithful, and the model frequently repeats what the teacher already does in the transcript. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has some promise for scalable feedback, but current outputs are too limited and too error-prone to replace expert coaching, and they highlight privacy and hallucination concerns as important barriers.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative chatbot based on GPT models, used for conversational text generation, scoring, and feedback generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used zero-shot to score classroom transcript segments, identify highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generate actionable suggestions for eliciting student mathematical reasoning from K-12 elementary math classroom transcripts.

findings.finding_summary: On transcript scoring (Task A), ChatGPT showed low correspondence with human ratings across CLASS and MQI observation items. Reported Spearman correlations were near zero or negative for most dimensions (e.g., CLPC DA=0.00, CLBM DA=0.35, CLINSTD DA=-0.01; EXPL DA=0.02, REMED DA=0.05, LANGIMP DA=0.00, SMQR DA=0.17), and adding rubric descriptions or reasoning did not improve performance.
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between model-predicted observation scores and human ratings on CLASS and MQI items
findings.effect_size: see reported correlations: CLPC 0.00, CLBM 0.35, CLINSTD -0.01; EXPL 0.02, REMED 0.05, LANGIMP 0.00, SMQR 0.17

findings.finding_summary: For identifying highlights and missed opportunities (Task B), teachers generally judged model responses as not insightful or relevant, and 20-30% of outputs were rated unfaithful to the transcript. Performance was worse on MQI than CLASS, with 'No' ratings increasing from CLASS to MQI for faithfulness (22% to 29%), relevance (35% to 55%), and insightfulness (51% to 71%).
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for generated feedback examples

findings.finding_summary: For actionable suggestions to elicit student reasoning (Task C), teachers rated most outputs as faithful, relevant, and actionable, but novelty was poor: ChatGPT repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript 82% of the time. The paper characterizes this as redundant rather than novel suggestion generation.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, actionability, and novelty of suggestions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-sample empirical evaluation with human ratings and correlational analysis, but not a randomized or controlled outcome study. The evidence is informative yet limited by sample size, qualitative judgments, and task-specific setup.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports mostly low or negative performance on scoring and feedback quality, with one mixed finding on suggestions that were often actionable but highly redundant. Overall impact is unclear and limited by near-zero correlations and substantial hallucination/redundancy concerns.

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-service elementary science teachers incorporated ChatGPT into lesson planning and what they thought about its usefulness and risks. The authors address a gap in empirical research on generative AI in education by moving beyond general claims about ChatGPT’s promise and looking at concrete lesson-plan evidence, including both quantitative rubric scores and qualitative survey responses.

The intervention/context involved a brief professional-learning sequence in a university course: 29 pre-service elementary teachers in Korea received four 2-hour sessions introducing ChatGPT, discussing possible uses in science teaching, reviewing instructional methods, and learning how to write lesson plans. Participants then created a 45-minute elementary science lesson plan that had to include ChatGPT and attach a simulated chat transcript. The lesson plans were evaluated with a modified TPACK-based rubric, and open-ended survey responses were analyzed for perceived benefits and concerns.

Results suggested that participants imagined many uses for ChatGPT across science domains and instructional methods, especially for questioning, individualized support, formative feedback, and supporting cooperative learning or analogy activities. On average, lesson plans scored relatively high on the rubric, but participants were less adept at choosing appropriate ChatGPT functions than at aligning ChatGPT with content goals and instructional strategies. They also expressed concerns about inaccurate or misleading outputs, possible hallucinations, and student overdependence. The paper concludes that ChatGPT has promise for science lesson planning, but teacher education should emphasize critical evaluation of outputs, digital/AI literacy, and classroom structures that reduce overreliance and pedagogical misalignment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on GPT large language models, designed for conversational text generation and interactive assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by pre-service elementary science teachers to design and revise lesson plans, generate role-play scripts, support questioning, provide individualized learning support, and offer formative feedback in science lessons.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative/mixed-methods study of 29 pre-service elementary science teachers, lesson plans integrating ChatGPT scored moderately high on a modified TPACK-based rubric (M = 3.29/4, SD = .91). The strongest area was instructional strategies & ChatGPT (M = 3.48), while ChatGPT function selection(s) was lower (M = 3.00), reflecting both appropriate and inappropriate use cases in lesson planning.
findings.measure: Modified TPACK-based lesson plan rubric (TIAR-derived scores)

findings.finding_summary: Participants reported concerns about ChatGPT accuracy and reliability (11/29) and over-dependence by students (13/29). The paper also documented incorrect or non-existent outputs, including non-existent YouTube links and unsuitable use for visual information and experiment design, indicating hallucination and pedagogical misalignment risks.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported concerns and qualitative examples of inappropriate ChatGPT use

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods pre-service teacher study, not an experimental evaluation, so evidence quality is limited for causal claims. The paper does, however, provide direct empirical analysis of lesson plans and participant concerns.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes are reported, so impact cannot be quantified. The evidence suggests mixed utility: some promising integration potential, but also clear concerns about hallucinations, overreliance, and misfit with certain science tasks.

paper_profiles.title: LessonPlanner: Assisting Novice Teachers to Prepare Pedagogy-Driven Lesson Plans with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: UIST ’24 (The 37th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge novice teachers face when preparing lesson plans: identifying effective pedagogical strategies, finding suitable materials, and organizing content into a coherent instructional flow. The authors argue that while large language models (LLMs) can generate useful teaching content, using them through a generic chat interface often produces fragmented, hard-to-manage outputs and requires substantial prompting skill and iterative refinement.

To address this, they develop LessonPlanner, a web-based interactive system powered by GPT-4 that structures lesson-plan creation around Bloom’s Taxonomy and Gagne’s Nine Events of Instruction. The system provides a goal-setting page, a block-based outline editor, preset prompts for common instructional activities, sidebar-based LLM assistance, and flexible editing/regeneration tools. The design was informed by a formative study with six novice teachers and teaching assistants.

The evaluation included a within-subjects study with 12 university students who acted as teachers and prepared lesson plans for familiar data-structures topics, plus expert interviews with six teachers from university, elementary, and high-school contexts. Compared with a baseline ChatGPT interface, LessonPlanner improved the rated quality of lesson plans and reduced workload. Interview findings also suggest that participants valued the pedagogy-driven structure and the more organized interaction model, but they raised concerns about the accuracy, subject-specific usefulness, and cognitive burden of prompting LLMs. The paper concludes with design implications for supporting teaching activities with LLMs.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI generative AI chatbot/LLM system used for conversational content generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the baseline web app for lesson-plan preparation; also referenced by participants as an existing tool they had used to generate lesson-plan-related content such as answers to student questions.

findings.finding_summary: In the formative interviews, three participants reported prior use of ChatGPT for lesson preparation, but five participants expressed distrust of its outputs. Concerns included needing to double-check detailed content, inability to produce course-appropriate questions/materials, and a tendency for outputs to be useful only as a rough outline rather than directly usable lesson content.
findings.measure: Interview-reported perceptions of usefulness, accuracy, and subject-specific suitability of ChatGPT-generated lesson-plan content
findings.sample_size: n=6 (formative study); n=12 (within-subjects study participants had baseline access to ChatGPT)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The paper uses mixed methods: a formative interview/co-design study plus a within-subjects comparison, but the reported finding here is primarily qualitative and does not provide inferential effect estimates for ChatGPT itself. This supports a yellow tier rather than a higher-evidence tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The evidence for ChatGPT in this paper is mostly about user distrust and concerns rather than a measured positive or negative performance effect. Because no effect size is reported and the findings are mixed/qualitative, the impact is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: To what extent is ChatGPT useful for language teacher lesson plan creation?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can be useful for foreign language teachers creating lesson plans, and whether more specific prompts produce better and more consistent outputs. The authors focus on zero-shot prompting with ChatGPT 4.0, examining how lesson-plan quality changes as prompts become increasingly detailed and as the same prompt is repeated across multiple independent chats.

The intervention was not a classroom implementation but an evaluation of AI-generated lesson plans. Five prompts of increasing specificity were developed around a 45-minute high school Level I Spanish lesson on a Costa Rican restaurant theme. Each prompt was entered into ChatGPT ten times, producing 50 lesson plans total. Outputs were scored against a 25-item rubric based on ACTFL world-readiness standards and edTPA-aligned lesson-plan criteria used in a university foreign-language teacher preparation program in the United States.

The study found that ChatGPT could produce generally high-quality lesson plans, but more detailed prompts did not reliably improve quality in a linear way. Adding a lesson-plan template sometimes reduced scores, while adding explicit scoring criteria improved them most. Outputs were highly variable even for identical prompts, with some responses missing many rubric elements and others scoring near perfectly. The authors also identified recurrent weaknesses, including weak cultural integration and occasional generation of outdated, behaviorist, or communicative misalignments with contemporary language-teaching practice. They conclude that teachers can use ChatGPT as a planning aid, but outputs require careful human review and revision, and AI literacy training should emphasize prompt design as well as critical evaluation of model outputs.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on GPT models, used for conversational text generation and prompt-based content creation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate foreign-language lesson plans from five zero-shot prompts of increasing specificity, with each prompt run in 10 separate chats to examine output quality and variability.

findings.finding_summary: Across 50 ChatGPT-generated lesson plans (5 prompts �d7 10 iterations), increasing prompt specificity produced a marginal difference in overall rubric scores (p=0.0442; F=2.668; DF=4) and a significant difference in word count (p=0.0047; F=4.338; DF=4), but score gains were not linear. Mean scores ranged from 19.6 to 21.6 out of 25, with the checklist-based prompt (P.5) performing best on average.
findings.measure: Lesson-plan rubric score and word count

findings.finding_summary: The same prompt often yielded highly variable lesson plans. For example, scores for P.1 ranged from 16/25 to 23/25, and P.5 ranged from 20/25 to 25/25; outputs generated from identical prompts varied by at least five rubric elements. The authors conclude that more specific prompts did not always produce predictable or deterministic outputs.
findings.measure: Within-prompt variability in rubric scores and presence/absence of lesson-plan criteria

findings.finding_summary: Qualitative scoring showed several strengths and weaknesses in lesson-plan design. Meaningful context, teacher input aligned to objectives, and activities appropriate to student proficiency appeared in all outputs, but cultural connections, ACTFL standards integration, and student interaction were inconsistently present, often only around 50% of the time in some prompt groups.
findings.measure: Presence/absence of 25 lesson-plan rubric criteria

findings.finding_summary: The authors identify repeated evidence of pedagogical misalignment and possible historic bias, including outputs reflecting 20th-century instructional practices such as audio-lingual-style repetition, scripted role play, and teacher-centered warm-ups. They caution that ChatGPT can reproduce research-rebuked practices and may require human review to avoid reintroducing outdated methods.
findings.measure: Qualitative analysis of generated lesson-plan content

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical single-study paper using a structured scoring rubric and repeated prompt trials, but it is not a controlled educational outcome study and has no randomized comparison group. The evidence is best classified as mixed-methods/observational evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports modest positive utility alongside substantial variability and several negative concerns, but it does not report a clear effect size for educational outcomes. Overall impact is unclear because findings concern lesson-plan quality rather than student achievement.

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether K-12 educators prefer lesson plans generated by generative AI models or by human curriculum designers, and which lesson-plan components are strongest or weakest for AI. The authors frame the problem as an emerging need for evidence on GenAI’s usefulness in lesson planning, especially given concerns about pedagogical alignment, factual accuracy, and contextual appropriateness.

The study compares three sources of math lesson plans: a customized prompt-based GPT-4 model, a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model, and human curriculum designer-created plans. Educators rated paired lesson plans across four dimensions: warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality. The design combined quantitative preference comparisons with qualitative comment analysis using thematic coding and topic modeling, making it a mixed-methods comparison of AI-generated versus human-authored instructional materials.

Participants were 20 experienced K-12 mathematics educators spanning elementary, middle, and high school levels in the United States. Each educator reviewed 20 lesson-plan pairs over several weeks, with weekly check-ins and an online web-based evaluation interface. Four participants withdrew before completion, leaving 16 educators and 529 complete pairwise comparisons.

The main finding is that human-authored lesson plans were generally preferred, especially for elementary grades, warm-ups, main tasks, and overall quality. GenAI plans, however, were more competitive for cool-down sections and in higher grades, with GPT-4 and especially fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b sometimes outperforming human plans in high school contexts. The authors conclude that GenAI is better positioned as an assistive, collaborative tool for lesson planning rather than a replacement for educator expertise, while noting persistent needs for better scaffolding, discourse support, differentiation, and developmental appropriateness.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used for generating and optimizing lesson plans via prompt engineering.
identified_tools.use_case: Compared customized prompt-based GPT-4 lesson plans against fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b and human-created K-12 math lesson plans; educators rated preferences across lesson-plan components and overall quality.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-method preference study with 20 experienced K-12 mathematics educators, customized GPT-4 was preferred over fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b FT in raw pairwise comparisons by 57.7% to 42.3%. Human-created lesson plans were still preferred over customized GPT-4 overall (58.7% vs. 41.3%), but GPT-4 was preferred for cool-down activities (59.7% vs. 40.3%) and in the bootstrapped aggregate analysis of cool-down measures (38% vs. 35.0% for human-created plans).
findings.measure: Binary educator preference for warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall lesson quality; bootstrapped aggregate preference by measure
findings.confidence_interval: 95% confidence intervals reported for bootstrapping, exact values not provided in text
findings.sample_size: n=20 educators; 529 lesson-plan pairs; 2,116 total evaluations

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta LLaMA-family large language model fine-tuned for lesson-plan generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Compared fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b lesson plans against customized GPT-4 and human-created K-12 math lesson plans; educators rated preferences across lesson-plan components and overall quality.

findings.finding_summary: In pairwise comparisons with K-12 mathematics educators, fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b was preferred over human-created lesson plans 46.4% to 53.6% overall, indicating competitive but slightly lower performance. LLaMA-2-13b outperformed human-created plans in cool-down activities (57.9% vs. 42.1%) and was especially strong at the high-school level, where it was preferred over human-created plans 59.2% to 40.8%; however, it was below customized GPT-4 in direct comparisons (42.3% vs. 57.7%).
findings.measure: Binary educator preference for warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall lesson quality; grade-level-disaggregated preference
findings.confidence_interval: 95% confidence intervals reported for bootstrapping, exact values not provided in text
findings.sample_size: n=20 educators; 529 lesson-plan pairs; 2,116 total evaluations

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-method comparative user study with educator preferences, not an RCT or meta-analysis. It provides useful evidence but includes subjective judgments and some dataset imbalance, so overall certainty is moderate-to-lower.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports preference differences rather than a quantified learning effect size. Findings suggest meaningful use-case-specific advantages for GenAI in cool-down tasks and higher-grade lesson planning, but overall impact on outcomes is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: New Curriculum, New Chance – Retrieval Augmented Generation for Lesson Planning in Ugandan Secondary Schools. Prototype Quality Evaluation.
paper_profiles.venue: Ndejje University Second Annual Research Dissemination Symposium 2024
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of low-quality or absent lesson planning in Ugandan secondary schools, especially in the context of a new competency-based curriculum that has made existing lesson plans obsolete. The authors ask whether a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system can generate lesson plans that meet necessary technical standards for classroom use.

The intervention is a prototype lesson-plan generator built with Cohere LLM, sentence embeddings, and LangChain. It retrieves information from government-accredited secondary school textbooks and generates lesson plans in the Ugandan lesson-plan format. The prototype was made available on a public website and tested on three Secondary 1 textbooks: ICT, Mathematics, and History (including Political Education).

The study context is Ugandan secondary schools, with the intended users being teachers. The prototype produced 24 lesson plans, which were evaluated by three independent raters using an adapted Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP). The authors report average scores of about 75-80%, with none below 65%, suggesting that the generated plans were technically strong and comparable to or better than human-created lesson plans in prior East African studies.

The paper also identifies important risks and limitations, especially hallucination: one generated plan addressed the wrong topic when the source textbook had insufficient material. The authors note that the system may still require teacher judgment and future safeguards such as confidence indicators or plausibility checks. Overall, they conclude that RAG has promise for supporting lesson planning in Ugandan classrooms, while cautioning that content accuracy and ethical considerations still need further work.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI lesson-plan system built with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), using a large language model, sentence embeddings, and LangChain to generate customized lesson plans from government-approved textbooks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper developed and evaluated the NDU Lesson Plan Generator (NLPG) prototype for generating lesson plans for Ugandan secondary school teachers aligned to the new curriculum.

findings.finding_summary: Across 24 generated lesson plans, three independent raters using the Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP) reported average quality scores of 75-80%, which the authors describe as 'very good lesson plan' quality. None of the plans scored below 65%, although one plan (History07.pdf) addressed the wrong topic due to insufficient source content.
findings.measure: LPAP-based technical quality of generated lesson plans

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a prototype evaluation working paper with a quasi-random generation protocol and expert ratings, but it is not a controlled trial and evaluates only technical quality. The evidence is informative but limited and therefore fits a yellow tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported lesson-plan quality is high, but no standardized effect size is reported and the study does not test classroom learning outcomes. Impact is therefore promising but unclear at the level required for higher tiers.

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how an LLM-based lesson planning system, Shiksha Copilot, was used by teachers and curators in low-resource government schools in Karnataka, India. The central problem is whether generative AI can help teachers create curriculum-aligned, context-sensitive lesson plans while reducing workload, and what challenges arise when such tools are introduced into multilingual, administratively burdened school environments.

Shiksha Copilot combined retrieval-augmented generation, bilingual English-Kannada support, and human-in-the-loop curation. Curators first reviewed and refined AI-generated learning objectives and lesson plans, and teachers then customized the curated plans for classroom use. The system also included optional features such as lesson-specific chat, general educational chat, and question generation. The deployment involved 1,043 field teachers across Karnataka and 23 curators, with data collected through interviews, surveys, and platform logs.

The study found that the tool reduced lesson-planning time, eased bureaucratic record-keeping, and lowered teacher stress, while supporting a shift toward more activity-based pedagogy. English lesson plans were generally high quality with relatively minor edits, but Kannada translations required extensive linguistic revision, showing that language and localization were major challenges. Teachers often adapted plans off-platform using their own expertise and peer networks, indicating that AI outputs were useful but not sufficient on their own. Overall, the paper concludes that teacher-AI collaboration can be effective in low-resource settings, but only when human oversight, localization, and curriculum alignment are built into the system.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI / large language model–based lesson-planning and teacher-support system that drafts, translates, and customizes instructional materials with human-in-the-loop curation.
identified_tools.use_case: Shiksha Copilot was deployed in Karnataka government schools to generate, curate, translate, and customize bilingual lesson plans for grades 5–10, with optional lesson-specific and general educational chat features for teachers.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that Shiksha Copilot reduced bureaucratic workload, lesson-planning time, and teaching-related stress. The paper reports that teachers used the AI-generated lesson plans for both classroom instruction and record-keeping, and that the system enabled access to curriculum-aligned plans; however, it does not report a causal effect size for these outcomes.
findings.measure: Lesson-planning time, administrative workload, and teacher stress (Teacher Stress Scale and custom survey items)
findings.sample_size: n=406 (matched survey responses); n=22 interviews; 5,544 teacher-created lesson plans in logs

findings.finding_summary: The tool was associated with a shift toward activity-based pedagogy, but systemic constraints such as staffing shortages and administrative demands limited broader pedagogical change. The paper frames this as a partial positive shift rather than a fully realized instructional transformation, with no numerical effect size reported.
findings.measure: Reported shifts in teaching practices and pedagogical orientation from interviews and thematic analysis
findings.sample_size: n=22 teacher interviews; n=17 curator interviews; n=4 mentor interviews

findings.finding_summary: The study found high reliability in English lesson plans but substantial post-processing burden for Kannada translations. Curators edited only 4.1% of English content blocks (314/7,744), while 94.4% of Kannada content blocks were edited, indicating that the system was efficient for English but much less so for Kannada due to translation quality problems.
findings.measure: Curator edits to AI-generated lesson-plan content blocks by language medium
findings.sample_size: n=991 curated lesson plans (965 English, 26 Kannada)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods field deployment with interviews, surveys, and log analysis rather than a controlled impact evaluation. The evidence is credible and rich, but causal attribution is limited and many outcomes are descriptive.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported benefits are meaningful but mostly qualitative or process-based, with no effect sizes for the main outcomes. The study shows clear workload reduction, but the pedagogical impact is partial and constrained by context and language quality issues.

paper_profiles.title: Understanding Teacher Revisions of Large Language Model-Generated Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how teachers revise large language model (LLM)-generated formative feedback before it is delivered to students. The authors focus on a practical but under-studied question in AI-supported education: when AI feedback is produced for classroom use, do teachers accept it, edit it, or rewrite it, and what does that reveal about the fit between model output and instructional needs? The study is especially relevant to concerns about pedagogical misalignment, overexplanatory feedback, and the degree to which teachers actually mediate AI output in practice.

The intervention/approach studied is a co-creation workflow in the Tutoria platform, where an LLM drafts feedback on short open-ended student responses and teachers can accept, edit, or fully rewrite the feedback. The analysis uses 1,349 feedback instances from 117 teachers, drawing from Brazilian high school chemistry contexts, introductory computer science in higher education, and related extracurricular classroom deployments. The researchers quantify textual changes, predict which drafts will be revised using text-only machine learning models, and qualitatively code how pedagogical feedback types shift from AI draft to final teacher message.

Results show that teachers accepted AI feedback unchanged in about 78%–80% of cases, and many teachers rarely edited at all; however, a small subset revised frequently. When revisions occurred, teachers usually shortened the feedback while preserving most of its meaning, suggesting compression rather than wholesale correction. Teachers also often shifted feedback away from more explanatory high-information forms toward more concise corrective forms, indicating that verbosity and pedagogical framing can trigger intervention. Overall, the paper concludes that default AI behavior is instructionally consequential because most drafts are delivered unchanged, and that AI feedback tools should better align with teacher priorities while reducing unnecessary editing effort.

identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies AI-generated formative feedback drafts produced by LLMs in the Tutoria platform and how teachers revise, accept, shorten, or rewrite those drafts before delivery to students.

findings.finding_summary: Across 1,349 feedback instances from 117 teachers, teachers accepted AI feedback without modification in 77.8% of cases (1050/1349). Revised feedback was only modestly longer than unedited feedback (48.3 vs. 41.9 words within-teacher difference = 6.4 words, p=.024), suggesting most teacher edits were limited rather than full rewrites.

When AI feedback was revised, high-information feedback decreased from 59.9% in the initial messages to 48.0% in the final teacher explanations, while corrective feedback increased from 40.1% to 43.5%; the change was statistically significant (Cram�e9r�e2s V=0.12).

findings.finding_summary: Text-only models could predict which AI feedback would be revised above chance, but only modestly. Holdout ROC AUC ranged from 0.698 to 0.746 across models, with overlapping confidence intervals and close-to-modest Cohen's ba values.
