paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods observational study using retrospective log data, descriptive statistics, predictive modeling, and qualitative coding rather than an experimental design. It provides useful evidence on teacher mediation of LLM feedback, but causal claims are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The most concrete effect is operational: teachers accepted most AI feedback unchanged, and revisions were usually small. The reported behavioral shifts are modest in magnitude (e.g., Cram�e9r�e2s V=0.12), so the practical impact appears limited but real.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the effectiveness of ChatGPT-based feedback compared with teacher feedback and self-feedback: Evidence from Chinese to English translation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether ChatGPT-based feedback can improve translation performance as effectively as teacher feedback and self-feedback. The authors focus on a gap in the literature around the real effectiveness of ChatGPT as a feedback tool for language learning, especially when compared directly with human-provided feedback and self-revision.

The intervention is a three-condition comparison of revised Chinese-to-English translations: ChatGPT-based feedback, teacher feedback, and self-feedback. Participants were 45 advanced Master of Translation and Interpreting students at a top Chinese university. Each student translated the same Chinese press release into English and then revised their draft under each feedback condition, with two-week intervals between conditions to reduce carry-over effects. The authors evaluated outputs using BLEU for overall translation quality and Coh-Metrix/CFA/SEM analyses for lexical, syntactic, and cohesion-related features.

The main finding was that teacher feedback and self-feedback outperformed ChatGPT-based feedback on overall translation quality, while ChatGPT showed strengths in lexical enhancement and referential cohesion. Teacher feedback was better for syntax, especially verb phrase use and passive voice, and none of the three conditions significantly improved deep cohesion. The paper concludes that ChatGPT has promise as a supplementary tool, but it is not yet a replacement for teacher-led feedback in translation practice, particularly for advanced learners and syntax-sensitive tasks.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot used to generate feedback and responses from user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate feedback on students' Chinese-to-English translation drafts and compare its feedback effects against teacher feedback and self-feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In a sample of 45 advanced Chinese MTI students (135 revised translation texts across three feedback types), ChatGPT-based feedback produced the lowest overall translation quality by BLEU score (M=0.472) compared with teacher feedback (M=0.501) and self-feedback (M=0.485). The paper notes that an increase of 0.02 in BLEU is widely considered meaningful, so ChatGPT-based feedback lagged behind the other two conditions on this overall measure.
findings.measure: BLEU score for overall translation quality

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT-based feedback yielded the highest lexical scores among the three conditions, outperforming both self-feedback and teacher feedback on the lexicon latent factor. At the indicator level, it produced longer average word length and more specific verbs, with significant main effects reported for DESWLlt (F(2,132)=16.181, p<.001, ηp2=.197) and WRDHYPv (F(2,132)=12.269, p<.001, ηp2=.157).
findings.measure: Lexicon latent factor; word length (DESWLlt); verb specificity/hypernymy (WRDHYPv)

findings.finding_summary: For syntax, ChatGPT-based feedback was less effective than teacher feedback and self-feedback. The paper reports that teacher feedback scored higher than ChatGPT-based feedback on the syntax latent factor, and on specific indicators teacher feedback led to denser verb phrases and more agentless passive voice than ChatGPT-based feedback (e.g., DRVP: F(2,132)=3.405, p<.05, ηp2=.049; DRPVAL: F(2,132)=9.686, p<.001, ηp2=.128).
findings.measure: Syntax latent factor; verb phrase density (DRVP); agentless passive voice (DRPVAL)

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT-based feedback did not significantly improve cohesion overall relative to teacher feedback or self-feedback. The authors report no significant main effect for cohesion across the three feedback types (F(2,132)=2.368, p>.05), and no significant effect on deep cohesion (PCDCz: F(2,132)=.618, p=.54), although referential cohesion was higher under ChatGPT than the other conditions (PCREFp: F(2,132)=4.401, p<.05, ηp2=.063).
findings.measure: Cohesion latent factor; referential cohesion (PCREFp); deep cohesion (PCDCz)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical comparative study with a modest sample and no randomized classroom intervention design described in the excerpt. It provides quantitative evidence, but the design and reporting do not rise to the level of high-causality experimental evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows a meaningful negative effect on overall translation quality for ChatGPT-based feedback and a positive effect on lexicon, with reported effect sizes that are modest to medium (e.g., ηp2=.157-.197). Overall impact is mixed rather than uniformly large.

paper_profiles.title: DRESS: Instructing Large Vision-Language Models to Align and Interact with Humans via Natural Language Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to improve large vision-language models (LVLMs) so they better align with human preferences and can refine their responses during multi-turn interaction. The authors argue that existing LVLMs can still produce unhelpful, hallucinated, or harmful outputs, and that their multi-turn dialogue capabilities are limited because they do not effectively use prior feedback.

To address this, the paper introduces DRESS, a training framework that uses natural-language feedback (NLF) generated by GPT-4. The feedback is split into two categories: critique, which summarizes strengths and weaknesses of a response, and refinement, which gives concrete suggestions for improvement. The model is trained with generalized conditional reinforcement learning to condition on scores and feedback, and then tested on helpfulness, honesty, harmlessness, and multi-turn interaction.

The work is evaluated on standard vision-language benchmarks such as LLaVA-Eval, LLaVA-Bench, COCO-based captioning for hallucination control, adversarial prompting via a VLSafe dataset, and multi-turn refinement settings. Results show improved helpfulness, lower hallucination rates, stronger resistance to harmful prompts, and better ability to incorporate feedback across turns, while largely preserving core visual question-answering performance. The study is about LVLMs rather than K–12 education, so no student or educator population is reported.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language models used here as an LLM feedback provider and evaluator, and also as a source of natural-language feedback for training and assessment.
identified_tools.use_case: GPT-4 is used to generate natural language feedback (including critique and refinement) for LVLM outputs, and GPT-3.5-Turbo is used for some evaluation and multi-turn feedback-provider experiments.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that GPT-4 was used to generate feedback on model outputs and that, with sufficient contextual information and instructions, it could produce natural-language feedback on par with human annotation. No quantitative effect size for this claim is reported.
findings.measure: Quality of LLM-generated natural-language feedback compared with human annotation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical systems paper with comparative evaluations, but it is not a K-12 education study and does not use a randomized educational design. The evidence is therefore best treated as mixed-methods/engineering evidence rather than high-rigor causal evidence for schooling.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported improvements are moderate in the model domain, but they do not map directly to learner outcomes in K-12 settings. The paper does not provide a clear educational impact estimate for teacher coaching or lesson-plan feedback.

paper_profiles.title: Common Problems and Effects of Feedback on Fun When Programming Ozobots in Primary School
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 17th Workshop in Primary and Secondary Computing Education (WiPSCE ’22)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines what kinds of problems primary school children encounter when programming Ozobot Evo robots and how different forms of teacher/supervisor feedback affect students’ fun during the activity. The authors are motivated by the challenge that primary school teachers often lack deep computer science subject knowledge and may struggle to provide effective, encouraging feedback while helping students debug programming tasks.

The intervention studied is a sequence of seven Ozobot Evo workshops with programming activities in two modes: pen-and-paper color-code programming and one block-based digital activity using OzoBlockly. The study recorded students’ problems and the feedback given by supervisors, then linked these observations with children’s self-reported fun using the Fun Toolkit (Smileyometer and Again Again Table). Participants were 116 primary school children in third and fourth grade, working mostly in pairs in a classroom workshop setting in Germany.

The paper identifies eight common problem categories, including task misunderstanding, wrong color codes, robot-specific issues, reading directions, U-turns, directional errors, app-related issues, and miscellaneous technical/organizational problems. It finds that feedback can reduce fun when problems are urgent or threaten self-efficacy, and that direct instruction is associated with worse fun ratings, whereas hints are associated with better fun ratings. Overall, the workshops were rated very positively and did not show meaningful gender differences, leading the authors to recommend prepared hints and supportive materials rather than relying heavily on direct instruction.

identified_tools.name: Ozobot Evo
identified_tools.description: A programmable educational robot that can be controlled via color codes in pen-and-paper mode or via the OzoBlockly block-based programming interface.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in seven primary-school workshops to study common programming problems, the kinds of corrective feedback teachers/supervisors gave, and how that feedback related to students’ reported fun.

findings.finding_summary: Across 116 primary school children (41 third grade, 75 fourth grade), fun ratings were generally high (Again Again table mean=1.9; Smileyometer mean=3.72). The paper reports that corrective feedback could lower fun when the problem was urgent or potentially self-efficacy threatening, and that direct instruction significantly reduced Smileyometer ratings while hints had a positive effect.
findings.measure: Fun ratings via the Again Again table and Smileyometer after Ozobot Evo activities; associations between specific problem/feedback types and fun
findings.effect_size: r_pb values ranged from -0.17 to 0.18 depending on problem/feedback type; direct instruction on Smileyometer r_pb=0.13, hints r_pb=-0.17; task understanding p=.001, app p=.022

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods workshop study with qualitative coding and correlational analysis, not a controlled intervention. The evidence is useful but observational, with no random assignment or causal identification.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects on fun are small to modest and inconsistent across measures, with mixed directions depending on the problem and feedback type. The paper’s strongest result is a negative effect of direct instruction on likeability, but overall impact is limited and context-specific.

paper_profiles.title: An Evaluation of the Pedagogical Soundness and Usability of AI-Generated Lesson Plans Across Different Models and Prompt Frameworks in High-School Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-generated lesson plans are pedagogically sound and usable for high-school physics instruction, with a focus on whether different large language models and prompt frameworks produce stronger or weaker educational outputs. The study is motivated by concerns that generative AI lesson plans may be convenient but can suffer from weak curricular alignment, hallucinated or missing content, and low cognitive demand in objectives.

The author generated 15 lesson plans for a single topic, The Electromagnetic Spectrum, using five LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Grok) and three prompt frameworks (TAG, RACE, and COSTAR). The outputs were evaluated automatically on readability, factual accuracy/hallucination, standards alignment with NGSS, and Bloom’s taxonomy cognitive level. The context was a mixed-ability Grade 9–12 physics classroom, and the lesson plans were intended to be 60-minute classroom lessons.

The findings suggest that model choice mainly determines readability, while prompt framework has a stronger influence on factual completeness and incidental curriculum alignment. RACE generally produced the lowest hallucination index and strongest standards resemblance, while DeepSeek produced the most readable plans and Claude produced the densest language. Across all models and frameworks, learning objectives were concentrated at the Remember and Understand levels, indicating limited higher-order thinking. The paper concludes that AI lesson planning can be useful, but only when paired with explicit pedagogical constraints, standards references, and teacher oversight.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based large language model chatbot used to generate and refine text outputs, including lesson plans and code assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate lesson plans alongside Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Grok, and also to refine Python code snippets for readability indices, verb extraction, and similarity analysis.

findings.finding_summary: Across the fifteen AI-generated lesson plans, ChatGPT's outputs showed intermediate readability and factual reliability relative to the other models. Its mean Flesch Reading Ease was 41.73, mean Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level was 10.86, mean Gunning Fog Index was 14.04, mean Hallucination Index was 2.50, and mean NGSS similarity was 0.063; cognitive demand was concentrated at lower Bloom levels (CDI=2.294).

identified_tools.description: Anthropic's Claude family of large language model chatbot systems used for text generation and instructional content creation.

findings.finding_summary: Claude produced the densest and most complex lesson-plan language among the compared models, with mean Flesch Reading Ease of 9.89, mean Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level of 19.89, and mean Gunning Fog Index of 23.29. It also had the highest mean NGSS similarity (0.110) and a mean Hallucination Index of 2.67; cognitive demand remained low overall (CDI=2.262).
findings.measure: Automated readability, hallucination, curriculum alignment, and Bloom taxonomy metrics

Its mean Hallucination Index was 2.33, mean NGSS similarity was 0.061, and cognitive demand remained concentrated at low Bloom levels (CDI=1.578).

However, it had the highest mean Hallucination Index (2.83) among the models, while mean NGSS similarity was 0.061 and CDI was 2.193.

identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies generative AI lesson-plan generation more broadly via structured prompts and multi-model comparison, but the empirical models named are ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Grok.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-study automated comparison of five LLMs on one physics topic, so it is empirical but not an RCT or meta-analysis. The design is structured, but the evidence is limited by small sample size and single-topic scope.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports descriptive model differences, not experimental effect sizes or a causal estimate of impact. Findings are useful for tool selection and prompt design, but the practical impact is mixed and modest, with clear tradeoffs across models.

paper_profiles.title: Interactive authoring of outcome-oriented lesson plans for immersive Virtual Reality training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the difficulty subject matter experts and educators face when authoring effective lesson plans for immersive virtual reality (iVR) training, especially when creating instruction that is aligned to desired learning outcomes. The authors propose FlowTrainer, an LLM-assisted interactive workflow that applies Backward design so that users define learning outcomes first and then generate objectives, skills, assessment criteria, and learning activities to form a lesson plan.

The system combines a web-based editor with a graph-based interface and a library of reusable learning activities. Users can iteratively author, edit, and verify iVR lesson plans, with the current study implemented for a welding training use case. The intended users are subject matter experts and educators who may not have strong VR development expertise but need to create training scenarios for manufacturing instruction.

The paper reports a user study with 8 experienced welders who also had varying levels of VR and teaching experience. Compared with a baseline non-LLM version of the editor, FlowTrainer reduced perceived workload and time for authoring, and generally improved usability, particularly for more complex authoring tasks. The main conclusion is that the LLM-supported, backward-design workflow can make iVR lesson-plan authoring more flexible and cognitively accessible, supporting broader adoption of iVR training content creation.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: An LLM-supported lesson-planning and instructional-design assistant that helps users generate and revise lesson plans, objectives, skills, assessment criteria, and learning activities.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in FlowTrainer, a web-based editor for authorsing outcome-oriented lesson plans for immersive VR training. The system generated lesson-plan components from user-provided learning outcomes and supported iterative editing of the instructional flow.

findings.finding_summary: In a user study with 8 experienced welders, the LLM-supported SystemB reduced the time and technical expertise required for authoring compared with the non-LLM baseline. The paper reports higher usability and lower perceived mental workload for SystemB in later sessions, along with shorter completion times for complex tasks, but does not report a formal between-system effect size.
findings.measure: System Usability Scale (SUS), NASA-TLX workload ratings, task completion time, subjective user feedback

findings.finding_summary: Sequence length increased with task complexity in both systems, indicating that users were able to author more detailed plans over time. The paper reports significant Friedman-test effects of task complexity on sequence length for SystemA (χ2 = 10.57, p = 0.0051) and SystemB (χ2 = 6.07, p = 0.0482), but no significant difference between systems in how complexity affected sequence length.
findings.measure: Sequence length distribution of authored lesson plans

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small user study with mixed quantitative and qualitative measures rather than a large controlled trial or meta-analysis. The methodology is clear, but the evidence base is limited by n=8 and the absence of effect sizes for the main comparisons.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports practical improvements in usability and reduced workload/time for the LLM-supported system, but the magnitude of impact is not quantified in effect-size terms. The evidence suggests modest-to-clear operational benefit, yet the limited sample keeps the impact assessment cautious.

paper_profiles.title: Quantum feedback: theory, experiments, and applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad review of quantum feedback control rather than a study of educational intervention or any human-participant experiment. It asks how feedback can be formulated, analyzed, and implemented for quantum systems, with emphasis on the distinction between measurement-based feedback and coherent feedback.

The paper surveys the theoretical foundations of continuous quantum measurement, quantum filtering, quantum trajectories, Markovian feedback, Bayesian feedback, and coherent-feedback networks. It also discusses how feedback can be used for tasks such as noise reduction, state stabilization, squeezing, quantum error correction, entanglement control, and parameter estimation. The discussion is framed in control-theoretic terms and develops the relevant stochastic and input-output formalisms.

The contexts covered are physical laboratory systems such as quantum optics, trapped atoms and ions, superconducting circuits, optomechanical systems, and quantum dots. Because the article is a review, it synthesizes prior results and experimental demonstrations rather than reporting a single new dataset. Its main conclusion is that quantum feedback is a powerful control paradigm, with coherent feedback often offering advantages over measurement-based feedback in some settings, while measurement-based approaches remain important for direct state estimation and control.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / chatbot system using large language models to generate or transform text.
identified_tools.use_case: Not studied in this paper. The provided text is a review of quantum feedback control in physics, not an education or generative-AI-in-teaching paper.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/review paper about quantum feedback control, not an empirical education study. It does not evaluate an AI tutoring or coaching tool in K–12 settings.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention, outcome measure, or learner/teacher impact is reported. The paper has no direct relevance to K–12 instructional coaching or lesson-plan feedback outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Using Transformers to Provide Teachers with Personalized Feedback on their Classroom Discourse: The TalkMoves Application
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of scaling feedback on K-12 mathematics classroom discourse so that teachers can reflect on and improve their instructional practices more efficiently than through manual observation and coding. The authors focus on “talk moves,” a set of discourse strategies associated with productive classroom discussion, equitable participation, and student learning.

The intervention is the TalkMoves application, an end-to-end system that uses automated speech recognition and transformer-based natural language processing to analyze classroom recordings and classify teacher utterances into six accountable-talk categories plus a none class. The system then generates personalized feedback dashboards for teachers, including talk-move frequencies, teacher-versus-student talk, wait time, and changes over time. The paper reports model development experiments comparing BiLSTM, attention, and transformer variants, with RoBERTa-large performing best on the test set.

The population context is K-12 mathematics classrooms in the United States. The deployed pilot version was used by 21 teachers across grades 3–12 in two midwestern school districts during the 2019–2020 academic year, with teachers recording lessons, viewing feedback, and participating in surveys and interviews. The paper concludes that transformer-based models can provide feedback approaching human reliability for this task, but it also notes important technical challenges, especially errors from automatic speech recognition on children’s speech, and the need for continued refinement of the system.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI/NLP-based automated feedback system for analyzing classroom discourse from teacher and student speech/transcripts and producing personalized instructional feedback for K-12 teachers.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies the TalkMoves application, which uses transformer-based models and automated speech recognition to classify accountable talk moves in K-12 mathematics lessons and generate feedback dashboards for teachers.

findings.finding_summary: The system automated classroom discourse analysis and feedback generation that would otherwise require highly trained human observers and hand coding of transcripts. The paper emphasizes scalability and reduced burden, but does not report a formal comparison of labor time or cost.
findings.measure: Automation/scalability of transcript coding and feedback generation
findings.sample_size: n=21 teachers (pilot use of the application); 501 transcripts for model development

findings.finding_summary: Model performance for classifying talk moves improved to F1=79.33% with ROBERTA-LARGE on the test set, compared with 65% for the prior base model and 72.26% for the BiLSTM baseline. The paper reports MCC=0.7779 for the best model, but does not report a learner outcome effect.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports technical limitations that affect system performance, including severe underestimation of student talk by Amazon Transcribe and classification errors arising from noisy classroom speech and varying talk move types. It also notes that some talk-move classes had lower individual F1 scores, including 75%, 73%, and 69%.
findings.measure: Error analysis; ASR and classification limitations

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary system-development paper with a clear empirical model evaluation and pilot deployment, but not a randomized or quasi-experimental study of teacher or student outcomes. The evidence is mostly technical/mixed-methods rather than causal educational impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows moderate-to-strong technical performance for discourse classification (F1 up to 79.33%), but it does not report measurable gains in teacher practice or student learning. Reported limitations and ASR errors make the practical instructional impact unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Fine-Tuning Large Language Models for Educational Support: Leveraging Gagné’s Nine Events of Instruction for Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.venue: Conference Proceedings of the 28th Global Chinese Conference on Computers in Education (GCCCE 2024)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how large language models (LLMs) can be adapted to support teachers in lesson planning and classroom dialogue generation in educational settings. The authors focus on aligning LLM outputs with Gagné’s Nine Events of Instruction, a well-known instructional design framework, to make generated teaching content more pedagogically structured and curriculum-aligned.

The paper describes two approaches: prompt tuning using Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompts with ChatGPT, and model tuning using LoRA-based fine-tuning of open-source models such as ChatGLM and Llama2. The dataset is built from math curriculum standards, definitions/examples of Gagné’s events, and teacher dialogue collected from real classrooms, with GPT-4 used to generate additional examples that were then manually reviewed and corrected by educators and subject matter experts. The context is compulsory education mathematics in East China Normal University–affiliated work, with a focus on classroom dialogue analysis and lesson-plan generation rather than student-facing instruction.

The paper reports that the proposed pipeline can generate and analyze teacher dialogue in ways that better match instructional principles and curriculum standards. However, the work is primarily a framework and system description: it presents the dataset construction, prompting strategy, fine-tuning process, and planned human evaluation, but does not report completed experimental outcomes with participants or learning impact. The authors conclude that the approach has promise for curriculum development, instructional evaluation, and AI-assisted teaching design.

identified_tools.use_case: Fine-tuned as an open-source baseline model for generating teacher dialogue aligned with instructional events.

identified_tools.use_case: Included as an open-access baseline model for fine-tuning and evaluation in the educational dialogue generation pipeline.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a framework / methods paper describing dataset construction, prompt tuning, and model fine-tuning rather than reporting a completed empirical study with outcome data. No quantitative results, sample sizes for outcomes, or causal evidence of effects are provided.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper proposes a potentially useful instructional workflow, but it does not report measured impact on learners or teachers. Because there are no outcome effect sizes, the practical impact remains unclear rather than demonstrably positive or negative.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether an analytical AI platform can improve lesson-plan quality in teacher education, and whether using such a system influences students’ AI literacy, attitudes toward AI, digital competences, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and motivation. The authors frame the work around a practical problem in university teacher education: providing frequent, detailed, individualized feedback on lesson plans is difficult for instructors, especially in complex domains such as vocational business education.

The intervention used EDDA, an analytical AI platform that analyzes uploaded lesson plans and provides expert-level feedback across ten main categories and 57 subcategories related to didactic planning principles such as sustainability, action orientation, process orientation, problem orientation, individualization, digitalization, learner activation, and lesson structure. Unlike generative chatbots, EDDA classifies lesson-plan text using a trained BERT-based model and returns reproducible feedback linked to pre-produced recommendations. In the experimental condition, master’s students received AI feedback throughout the semester and could also consult their university teacher; the control group received human feedback only. The study was conducted across two winter-semester cycles in Germany with 103 master’s students in business education working in small groups on 90-minute lesson plans.

Results suggest that AI feedback can match or surpass human feedback on some planning dimensions. The experimental group showed higher ratings for some sustainability-related competences and for dimensions such as social competences and reflexivity, while prior performance often predicted less growth over time. However, the use of the AI platform did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, or motivation. The authors conclude that analytical AI can effectively supplement traditional feedback, but only as part of a broader pedagogical framework and not as a standalone solution.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model systems that generate text and feedback, but no specific commercial or research chatbot product is named in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as the broader comparator and risk context for AI feedback in lesson planning; the paper contrasts generative AI with the analytical AI platform EDDA and cites limitations such as lack of reproducibility, bias, privacy, and weak domain specificity.

findings.finding_summary: The paper cites prior literature indicating that generative AI can support feedback but also carries risks for educational use, including lack of reproducibility, untransparent training data, bias reproduction, and data-protection/ethics concerns. It also notes claims that generative tools may reduce critical thinking skills and that they can be weak in understanding complex specialized contexts.
findings.measure: Narrative discussion of prior studies on generative AI risks and suitability for feedback

identified_tools.name: EDDA
identified_tools.description: EDDA (electronic didactic assistance for lesson planning) is an analytical AI platform that analyzes uploaded lesson plans and materials and returns individualized expert feedback via a graphical interface using a trained BERT-based classifier.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the experimental intervention for semester-long lesson-planning feedback in vocational teacher education; students in the experimental group received EDDA feedback and then could request human clarification.

findings.finding_summary: In a longitudinal intervention with N=103 student teachers (n=55 experimental, n=48 control), EDDA matched or surpassed human feedback on some lesson-planning dimensions. The paper reports significant positive effects for some planning outcomes, including social competences for sustainable development (p<0.05) and reflexivity (p<0.10), while the system also underestimated some plans because of unbalanced training data, which the authors note could have demotivating effects.
findings.measure: Ratings of lesson plans on didactic/planning dimensions and sustainability-related competences

findings.finding_summary: For the meta-dimensions measured across the semester, the paper reports that the mere use of EDDA did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, motivation, or self-efficacy. The authors state that these meta-dimensions did not show the expected broad positive development attributable to the AI platform.
findings.measure: AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competences, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and motivation questionnaires

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal intervention study with a comparison group and repeated measures, which is stronger than correlational evidence, but it is not randomized in a traditional sense and includes several measurement/model limitations noted by the authors. The study also relies partly on self-report meta-dimensions and small group-based samples.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports some positive effects on specific lesson-planning outcomes, but many effects are small, selective, or null for broader outcomes like AI literacy and motivation. The overall impact is modest and mixed rather than large or consistently transformative.

paper_profiles.title: Teachers and AI: Understanding the factors influencing AI integration in K–12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the psychological and pedagogical factors that shape K–12 teachers’ readiness to integrate artificial intelligence into instruction. The study asks what helps or hinders teachers’ adoption of AI, with particular attention to efficiency, student engagement, curriculum alignment, ethics, and cultural fit.

The researchers used an exploratory qualitative design in a professional development context at a private school in Türkiye. Sixty-six teachers from 11 disciplines participated in a 14-week AI-in-education course within a Digital Learning Academy. Data came from online discussion forums and AI-supported learning-activity design tasks, and were analyzed inductively using thematic analysis.

Findings showed that teachers viewed AI positively for saving time, supporting lesson planning, enabling differentiated instruction, and increasing interactivity and personalization. ChatGPT and MagicSchool were frequently mentioned as useful tools. At the same time, teachers identified barriers including technical problems, limited devices, workload, curriculum misalignment, language and cultural mismatch, privacy/security concerns, risks of plagiarism, and worries that students could become less creative or overly reliant on AI. The authors conclude that AI can support teaching, but successful integration requires better infrastructure, targeted teacher support, and stronger ethical and curricular alignment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM tool that produces human-like text responses and supports content generation, drafting, and interactive prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by teachers in AI-supported lesson/activity design and referenced as a commonly used classroom AI tool for lesson planning, quiz/story creation, and other instructional tasks.

identified_tools.name: MagicSchool
identified_tools.description: A teacher-facing generative AI platform offering multiple tools for lesson planning, content creation, student support, and classroom productivity.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by teachers as an AI tool in designed activities and discussed as a preferred tool for lesson planning, content generation, adaptation, and support.

identified_tools.name: Canva
identified_tools.description: A design and content-creation platform used for generating visual materials, presentations, and learning resources.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned as an AI-supported tool used in designed learning activities, especially for visual design and differentiated instruction.

identified_tools.name: Gamma
identified_tools.description: An AI-powered presentation/content generation tool used to quickly create slide decks and other instructional materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by teachers for presentation creation in lesson activities and cited as a preferred tool for quickly preparing presentation files.

identified_tools.name: Character.ai
identified_tools.description: A generative AI character-chat platform that enables users to create and interact with AI personas for conversation and learning tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in classroom activities for creating characters, discussions, and reflective or creative learning tasks.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's generative AI chatbot/model family for conversational text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Referenced in the literature review as part of the broader evolution of LLMs; also appears in the paper's discussion of AI tools by way of Google's Bard/Gemini family normalization.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory qualitative study with 66 teachers from one private school, so the evidence is descriptive and context-specific rather than causal. It provides useful implementation insight but no experimental effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceived benefits and barriers, including concerns about curriculum mismatch, privacy, creativity loss, and inaccurate content, but does not measure impact on learning outcomes. Any positive impact is reported only as teacher perception, so overall impact remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Primary school students’ perceptions of artificial intelligence – for good or bad
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Technology and Design Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This case study asks how primary school students perceive artificial intelligence (AI), both cognitively and affectively, and whether they already use AI tools in everyday or school-related tasks. It also explores how students understand AI after a short instructional project on AI literacy and related classroom activities.

The intervention was a school-based AI project in a Swedish compulsory primary school. Grade 5–6 students (ages 11–12) took part in ten 40-minute lessons over several weeks, taught by their science and technology teachers using lesson plans on AI. Activities included introductory discussions of AI examples, algorithms and machine learning, ethical dilemmas, and later student use of ChatGPT for test practice; at a university visit, students also used ChatGPT and DALL-E to create stories and hear a short AI lecture. Data came from a pre-test, focus group interviews with 12 students, and 30 short written evaluation reports.

Findings show that students viewed AI as both a machine and a humanlike or brain-like system, often associating it with robots, computers, phones, Google, Snapchat, Tesla, and self-driving cars. Their attitudes were mixed: they appreciated AI’s usefulness for studying and practical tasks, but were also worried about rapid development, job loss, privacy invasion, cheating, and potential harm. Students reported some prior use of AI and, after the project, emphasized the need for regulation and slower, more careful development. The study concludes that even young students already have meaningful AI perceptions and concerns, and that AI literacy education should address both use and ethics.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot for conversational text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by primary school students during lessons about AI and for creating practice questions before tests; also discussed as an AI tool students had used or heard about.

findings.finding_summary: This qualitative case study reports that students used ChatGPT for generating practice questions before tests and viewed it as helpful for studies, but also raised concerns about cheating, rapid development, privacy invasion, and potential harm. The paper does not report an experimental effect size for ChatGPT; evidence is based on pre-test responses, focus groups (n=12), and evaluation reports (n=30) from a total sample of 60 students.
findings.measure: Student-reported use, perceived usefulness, and concerns about ChatGPT and other AI tools

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods case study rather than an experimental evaluation, so it provides descriptive evidence but no causal estimate. The study is useful for documenting student perceptions and concerns, but not for strong efficacy claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows practical uptake and perceived usefulness of ChatGPT, but the evidence is not quantitative and includes notable concerns and potential harms. No effect size is reported, so impact is unclear rather than demonstrably positive or negative.

paper_profiles.title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can be used effectively as an automated writing evaluation tool in English as a new language (ENL) writing instruction, and whether students prefer AI-generated feedback to feedback from a human tutor. The authors focus on GPT-4/ChatGPT-generated feedback on student writing, motivated by broader concerns about how generative AI may affect instructional practice, feedback quality, and student learning in education.

The study combines two related investigations conducted over a six-week period at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region. In Study 1, 48 ENL university students were split into an experimental group that received GPT-4 feedback and a control group that received feedback from a human tutor; writing outcomes were measured using pre/post tests and weekly writing tasks. In Study 2, a separate group of 43 ENL students received both AI and human feedback on weekly assignments and completed repeated preference surveys plus open-ended responses about the two feedback modes.

Results from Study 1 showed no significant difference in writing gains between the AI-feedback group and the human-tutor group, suggesting that GPT-4 feedback did not outperform human feedback but also did not harm learning outcomes. Results from Study 2 showed a near-even split in student preference, with some students valuing the clarity, specificity, and consistency of AI feedback, while others preferred human interaction, engagement, and the ability to ask follow-up questions. The authors conclude that AI-generated feedback may be used in ENL writing instruction without reducing learning outcomes, but they recommend a blended model that combines the strengths of both AI and human tutoring.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based chatbot interface for interacting with large language models, capable of generating and revising natural-language text, including feedback on writing.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate individualized corrective feedback on ENL students' weekly writing assignments (GPT-4 via ChatGPT) and to compare AI-generated feedback with human tutor feedback over six weeks.

findings.finding_summary: In Study 1 (n=48; analyzable n=48 minus 1 posttest-only case excluded), ENL students who received GPT-4-generated feedback showed no significant difference in writing gains compared with students who received human tutor feedback. The mixed 2�d72 RM-ANOVA found no significant group �d7 time interaction (F=3.094, p=0.085, b7p2=0.063) and no significant between-group effect (F=0.241, p=0.626, b7p2=0.005).
findings.measure: Pretest/posttest writing scores on an analytic rubric (content, coherence, language use, sources and evidence; max score 40)

findings.finding_summary: In Study 2 (n=43; weekly survey responses varying from 32 to 41), student preferences for GPT-4 feedback versus human tutor feedback were roughly split. The six-week average preference counts were 18 for human tutor feedback and 19.667 for AI-generated feedback, with questionnaire means slightly favoring human feedback on satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and overall preference but all means remaining above 4 in most weeks.
findings.measure: Weekly Likert-scale preference/satisfaction survey and open-ended responses

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental longitudinal study with repeated measures and a separate preference survey, but it is not a randomized controlled trial. The mixed-methods design and modest sample sizes support moderate confidence, though causal inference is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main efficacy finding is null: GPT-4 feedback did not outperform human tutor feedback, and the reported effect sizes are small. Student preference was mixed rather than strongly positive or negative, indicating limited demonstrated impact.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an analytical AI platform can support lesson planning in teacher education by providing individualized feedback on lesson plans. The authors focus on a practical problem in vocational teacher education: university instructors often cannot provide frequent, detailed, expert-level feedback on complex lesson plans, especially when students must incorporate multiple didactic principles and planning dimensions.

The intervention used an analytical AI system called EDDA, which classifies uploaded lesson plans and materials into a coding framework and returns expert-like feedback. Unlike generative AI chatbots, EDDA is designed for reproducible, criteria-based feedback grounded in pre-trained categories. In the study, students in a master's-level vocational business education course worked on lesson plans across a semester and received AI feedback, with optional human follow-up discussion. A control group in a comparable course received human feedback only. The study also tracked several meta-dimensions, including AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competences, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and motivation.

The participants were master’s students in business education in Germany, organized into small groups, with data collected across two winter semesters. The paper reports that the AI-supported group often matched or exceeded the control group in some lesson-plan dimensions, especially certain sustainability-related and didactic aspects such as action orientation, relatedness, technology use, lesson structure, and learner engagement. However, the authors also found that simply using AI did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, or motivation. They conclude that analytical AI can effectively supplement traditional feedback, but it should be embedded in a broader pedagogical framework and used cautiously because the system tended to underestimate performance in some categories.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI/LLM chatbot or assistant used for producing or providing feedback, without a specific named product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reviews prior generative-AI feedback research in teacher education and contrasts generative AI feedback risks with the analytical AI platform EDDA; no specific named generative product was studied in the intervention.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal intervention study, but the AI system evaluated is an analytical AI platform (EDDA), not a generative AI product. Because the user’s topic is specifically generative AI evidence, the paper is only indirectly relevant and does not provide direct named-product evidence of GenAI use.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports a substantive intervention effect for the analytical platform on some lesson-planning dimensions, with one significant positive effect on SDG 15 and other positive effects on social competences and reflexivity. However, the findings are not about generative AI, so the impact for the requested GenAI evidence base is limited and indirect.

paper_profiles.title: How should we change teaching and assessment in response to increasingly powerful generative Artificial Intelligence? Outcomes of the ChatGPT teacher survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how educators believe teaching and assessment should change in response to the rise of generative AI such as ChatGPT, and what motivates those changes. The authors frame the study as a baseline snapshot taken soon after ChatGPT’s release, intended to capture teacher beliefs before practices and attitudes evolve further over time.

The study used a mixed-methods survey of 318 educators from multiple countries, teaching levels, disciplines, and experience levels. Participants reported perceived impacts of generative AI on teaching and assessment using Likert-scale items, and also answered open-ended questions about how curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, and teacher practice should change. The sample included primary, secondary, and university educators, with responses gathered online via social media and professional listservs during early 2023.

Findings show that most teachers expected ChatGPT and similar tools to have a major or profound impact on both teaching and assessment, though a meaningful minority expected little or no impact. Greater AI awareness was associated with stronger perceived impact, suggesting an 'ignorance effect.' Qualitative results emphasized teaching AI literacy, critical thinking, ethics, and process-oriented learning, while assessment should shift toward higher-order thinking, authentic and supervised tasks, and more oral or in-person evaluation. Teachers were mainly motivated by performance expectancy, especially concern for student learning and fairness, but also expressed concern about plagiarism and the need to adapt to an AI-saturated future.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/large language model system for conversational text generation and task assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers' perceptions of how ChatGPT and similar generative AI tools may affect teaching, assessment, and teacher practice; no direct intervention or implementation study was conducted.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods survey of 318 educators, 93% of respondents rated the impact of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT on teaching as minor/major/profound, with only 7% selecting 'none' (mean=2.7/4). For assessment, 93% rated impact as minor/major/profound and only 7% selected 'none' (mean=2.8/4).
findings.measure: Perceived impact ratings on teaching content and assessment (4-point Likert scales)

findings.finding_summary: Higher awareness of ChatGPT/generative AI predicted higher perceived impact on teaching and assessment. For teaching, high-awareness respondents averaged 2.7 versus 2.4 and 2.3 for medium/low awareness (Cohen's d=0.45). For assessment, high-awareness respondents averaged 3.0 versus 2.6 and 2.8 (Cohen's d=0.35).
findings.measure: Perceived impact by prior awareness of generative AI

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported substantial intended changes to curriculum and pedagogy in response to ChatGPT, especially teaching students how AI works, how to use AI, critical thinking, ethics, and altered assessment design. However, 31 respondents said they would not change their teaching, and 36 said ChatGPT would have minimal or no impact on assessment.
findings.measure: Open-ended survey responses on intended teaching and assessment changes

findings.finding_summary: Teachers frequently said ChatGPT could improve workflow and assessment efficiency, including helping create resources, gather ideas for lessons, and assist with feedback or plagiarism checks. These were perceptions and motivations rather than measured performance outcomes; no causal effect on teacher efficiency was tested.
findings.measure: Reported motivations and anticipated usefulness for teaching/assessment work

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods survey study with correlational and qualitative evidence, not an experimental evaluation of ChatGPT. It provides useful descriptive evidence but does not establish causal effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong perceived impact and intended practice changes, but these are beliefs and self-reports rather than measured learning gains or harms. Reported effect sizes for awareness-to-perception are modest to moderate, while no direct negative or positive outcome was experimentally tested.

paper_profiles.title: AI prediction leads people to forgo guaranteed rewards
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether merely believing that an AI system can predict one’s behavior changes the choices people make. The authors build on Newcomb’s paradox and investigate whether AI prediction can shift decision-making toward forgoing a guaranteed reward, even when no recommendation is given and the AI’s actual predictive accuracy is not revealed. They frame this as a psychological mechanism they call “predictive binding,” in which people treat a prediction as if it partly determines what they will do.

The paper reports four preregistered online experiments with 1,305 adult participants recruited through Prolific. Study 1 compared an AI predictor with a random picker wheel in a one-shot monetary choice task. Study 2 tested robustness across interactive and non-interactive interfaces, including an LLM-based chatbot (GPT-4.1) in the AI condition. Study 3 generalized the effect to vignette scenarios about job interviews, mobile data plans, and freelancing task selection, comparing AI prediction, human-expert prediction, and no-prediction controls. Study 4 examined repeated interaction over five rounds, with the AI consistently predicting either one-boxing or two-boxing.

Across studies, participants were more likely to choose the lower-payoff option when it was framed as predicted by AI, thereby foregoing a guaranteed reward. The effect persisted across interfaces, decision contexts, and repeated exposure, even after repeated prediction failures. The authors conclude that perceived predictive authority can reshape decisions, not just forecast them, and that this influence may be self-reinforcing over time. Because the work is about general decision behavior rather than education, it does not directly address K–12 instructional coaching or lesson-plan feedback.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based large language model chatbot/assistant.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in Study 2 to support the interactive AI condition as the LLM-based chatbot. The authors state that the interactive AI condition was powered by OpenAI’s GPT-4.1 API, and ChatGPT was also used to refine the system prompt for the chatbot.

findings.finding_summary: This paper did not evaluate ChatGPT as a pedagogical tutoring or feedback tool; it used a GPT-based chatbot as a predictor in a behavioral decision task. In Study 2, the interactive AI condition used an LLM-based chatbot powered by OpenAI’s GPT-4.1 API, but the paper reports no educational outcome for ChatGPT itself. The broader finding was that AI prediction increased one-boxing relative to random framing, but that effect was about predictive authority rather than instructional coaching.
findings.measure: Choice in a Newcomb-style one-boxing task and perceived predictiveness
findings.sample_size: n=801 across Studies 1 and 2; Study 2 n=601

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The paper is a preregistered multi-study experiment with randomized conditions and a fixed-effect meta-analysis across Studies 1 and 2, which supports strong internal validity. However, the tool use is not an educational intervention and the GPT-based system is only incidental to the study's main behavioral task.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effect on one-boxing is statistically meaningful and the odds ratio is large, but it concerns a non-educational decision task rather than K–12 instructional coaching or lesson-plan feedback. Because there is no direct evidence of educational benefit or harm, the impact on the requested topic is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: LLM Performance Predictors: Learning When to Escalate in Hybrid Human-AI Moderation Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a general systems problem in human-AI content moderation: when an LLM’s output should be trusted and when it should be escalated for human review. The authors argue that existing uncertainty metrics for LLMs are insufficient for production moderation workflows, especially when decisions have asymmetric costs and require reliable routing between automation and human oversight.

To tackle this, the paper proposes LLM Performance Predictors (LPPs), a supervised meta-model that uses gray-box and black-box signals from LLM outputs, including token probabilities, entropy, verbalized confidence, and uncertainty-attribution indicators. The framework then applies a cost-aware thresholding policy to decide whether to trust the LLM or defer to humans. The method is evaluated on text and multimodal content-moderation datasets across several proprietary and open-source LLMs.

The study is not about education or teacher-facing generative AI use; it is a content-moderation systems paper. It reports that the proposed meta-model generally improves error prediction and reduces expected cost relative to standard uncertainty baselines, but performance varies across models and datasets, especially under multimodal distribution shift. The paper also notes that chain-of-thought prompting inflated confidence and harmed calibration in this setting.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s Gemini family of large language models used for automated content classification and moderation, including uncertainty estimation and selective escalation in human-AI workflows.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated Gemini variants (e.g., Gemini Flash Lite models) as base LLMs in content moderation tasks, then learned when to trust versus escalate their outputs using LLM Performance Predictors.

findings.finding_summary: On the OpenAI Moderation Dataset, the meta-model reduced expected cost relative to the best baseline for Gemini models. For gemini-2.5-flash-lite, expected cost decreased from $122 to $77 and escalations decreased from 315 to 227; for gemini-2.0-flash-lite, expected cost decreased from $74 to $41 and escalations from 248 to 162.
findings.measure: Expected cost ($) and escalation count under cost-aware selective escalation
findings.sample_size: n=1,680 text samples (OpenAI Moderation dataset) and n=1,500 videos (Multimodal Moderation dataset); model-specific evaluation counts not separately reported

findings.finding_summary: On the Multimodal Moderation Dataset, the meta-model also lowered cost for some Gemini models. For gemini-2.5-flash-lite, expected cost decreased from $51 to $40 and escalations from 90 to 20; for gemini-2.0-flash-lite, the meta-model improved F1 from 69.85% to 85.47% and Macro-F1 from 52.67% to 61.09%.
findings.measure: Expected cost ($), escalation count, F1, and Macro-F1

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT family of large language models used for automated classification, moderation, and confidence estimation in human-in-the-loop workflows.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated GPT-family models (e.g., gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o, gpt-4.1-mini) as base models for content moderation and studied whether LPP-based routing could predict their errors and reduce review costs.

findings.finding_summary: For GPT-family models, the meta-model consistently improved error-prediction performance on the OpenAI Moderation Dataset. For gpt-4o-mini, F1 increased from 81.27% to 94.14%, AUC-ROC from 83.55% to 93.46%, and Macro-F1 from 64.96% to 82.31%; for gpt-4o, F1 increased from 84.41% to 91.35%.
findings.measure: Error prediction performance (F1, AUC-ROC, Macro-F1)

identified_tools.name: Qwen
identified_tools.description: Alibaba’s Qwen family of large language models used as base models for moderation and uncertainty-aware selective escalation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated Qwen models as base LLMs in moderation tasks and compared baseline uncertainty heuristics against an LPP-based meta-model for predicting correctness and routing to human review.

findings.finding_summary: Results for Qwen were mixed. On the OpenAI Moderation Dataset, QWEN3-14B had lower expected cost with the meta-model than with always-trust ($56 vs. $127) but only modest improvement over baselines; on the Multimodal Moderation Dataset, QWEN3-14B was matched or outperformed by baseline methods on several metrics, and QWEN3-32B showed no reported cost results on the text dataset due to evaluation limits.
findings.measure: Expected cost ($), escalation count, F1, AUC-ROC, Macro-F1
findings.sample_size: n=1,680 text samples and n=1,500 videos

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta’s LLaMA family of large language models used as base models for moderation and uncertainty prediction.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated LLaMA models as base LLMs in moderation workflows, including error prediction and escalation decisions.

findings.finding_summary: For LLAMA32-11B on the Multimodal Moderation Dataset, the meta-model did not provide a clear operational advantage over baseline uncertainty methods, with expected cost remaining comparable to the Top-2 Margin baseline. The text reports that some LLaMA results were omitted or not reliably evaluated on the OpenAI Moderation Dataset.
findings.measure: Expected cost ($), escalation ratio, and predictive performance under selective escalation
findings.sample_size: n=1,500 videos; text-dataset results partially omitted/not reported

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical systems paper, but not a K–12 education study and not a randomized or educational intervention study. The evidence is observational/benchmark-based and focused on moderation workflows rather than instructional coaching.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not study K–12 teaching, lesson feedback, or student learning outcomes. Its impact is therefore not directly relevant to the requested educational use case, despite reporting operational effects in another domain.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI and Information Asymmetry: Impacts on Adverse Selection and Moral Hazard
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can reduce information asymmetry in principal-agent settings by producing more precise signals about hidden agent type and effort. The core problem is classical adverse selection and moral hazard: principals have limited information about agents’ quality and actions, which leads to inefficient contracts, information rents, and welfare loss.

The authors propose a theoretical principal-agent framework in which generative AI generates noisy signals about an agent’s latent type and effort. They analyze how increasing signal precision affects contract design, incentive compatibility, screening, and monitoring. They also extend the model to multi-period contracting, multi-agent settings, and different market structures such as competition, oligopoly, and monopoly. The paper includes simulation experiments in online labor-platform contexts to illustrate the theoretical claims, but these are stylized and not framed as a study of educational users or K–12 settings.

Overall, the paper concludes that more accurate generative AI signals can reduce adverse selection and moral hazard, lower information rents, and improve social welfare, especially in competitive markets. It also notes risks and boundary conditions, including manipulation, privacy, transparency, and uneven benefits under monopolistic market structures. The article is primarily a theoretical and simulation-based economics paper, not an empirical study of educational intervention.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI / large language model systems used to generate or synthesize signals from data and assist with text-related tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in this paper as AI-generated signals in a principal-agent model and in simulations to improve observation of agent type and effort; also noted in acknowledgements as assisting literature retrieval and text polishing.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports theoretical and simulation evidence that generative AI signals reduce adverse selection and moral hazard by improving type and effort observation. In the single-period simulation, high-ability agents' average effort increased from 0.7525 to 0.9990, and the improvements analysis reported welfare = 1.5126.
findings.measure: Agent effort, adverse selection/selection rates, and social welfare in a single-period simulation

findings.finding_summary: In the multi-period, multi-agent simulation, generative AI improved adverse selection, effort, and welfare in competitive and oligopolistic settings, but the effects were limited or negative in monopoly settings. Reported outcomes include improvements in adverse selection such as High_Ability = 0.0269** in competitive markets and negative changes such as High_Ability = -0.0073 in monopoly markets, alongside effort and welfare gains in competitive markets and declines for some monopoly groups.
findings.measure: Adverse selection, effort, and social welfare by market structure
findings.effect_size: Competitive: High_Ability 0.0269**, High_Effort 7.15%**, High welfare 1.8578**; Monopoly: High_Ability -0.0073, High_Effort -1.44%**, High welfare -0.5461**

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/mechanism-design paper with simulations rather than a clearly described empirical education study or controlled trial. The paper does not provide a standard study design, sample size, or validated causal inference framework for K-12 coaching or lesson feedback.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported simulation effects are sometimes positive and of moderate size, but the paper is not about K-12 teacher coaching and includes no direct educational intervention evidence. Impact is therefore indirect and only moderately informative for the requested topic.

paper_profiles.title: ‘Studies for’: A Human-AI Co-Creative Sound Artwork Using a Real-time Multi-channel Sound Generation Model
paper_profiles.venue: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025) Creative AI Track
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a case study of a collaborative AI-assisted sound artwork, Studies for, created with sound artist Evala. The work is motivated by the difficulty of archiving site-specific and performative sound art, where the original experience depends on time, place, and spatialized audio conditions that are difficult to preserve in conventional archives. The authors propose a “new form of archive” in which an AI model trained on an artist’s prior works can continue generating new outputs that remain stylistically faithful while still introducing novelty.

The intervention is a real-time, multi-channel generative sound system based on SpecMaskGIT. The model was trained exclusively on approximately 200 hours of Evala’s past sound artworks and conditioned using both audio and text prompts derived from the artist’s prior work. The system was optimized for fast, continuous eight-channel generation at 48 kHz so it could run throughout a three-month exhibition in Tokyo. Artist feedback was incorporated iteratively to preserve the artist’s identity in the outputs and avoid outputs that were merely collages of prior pieces.

The paper is not an educational study and does not involve students or teachers. Instead, it reports an art-and-technology deployment in an exhibition setting with an adult public audience. The authors conclude that lightweight, fast generative models can support iterative human-AI co-creation, preserve artistic style, and enable continuous generation over long periods. They also argue that multi-modal conditioning can help produce outputs that are both faithful to the artist and sufficiently surprising to be creatively useful.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI / text-to-audio model used for real-time generative synthesis rather than a specific named consumer product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies SpecMaskGIT, a lightweight text-to-audio generative model, as the core AI system for co-creating and continuously generating sound in the artwork Studies for.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a creative AI system paper describing the design and implementation of a generative sound installation, not an empirical education study. It does not evaluate instructional coaching, lesson-plan feedback, or K–12 outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention outcomes are reported, and there is no measured impact on learners or teachers. The paper focuses on artistic workflow and system design rather than instructional effectiveness or harm.

paper_profiles.title: Consensus Sampling for Safer Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of making generative AI safer when individual model outputs may contain risks that are difficult or impossible to detect by inspection alone. The authors focus on threats such as steganography, hidden security vulnerabilities in code, and other misalignment risks, arguing that output-only inspection cannot reliably remove or identify such harms.

The proposed approach is consensus sampling: given multiple generative models, the algorithm samples from the mixture of their outputs and only accepts outputs where enough models assign sufficiently similar probability. If agreement is insufficient, the algorithm abstains. The method is architecture-agnostic and uses access to model probabilities rather than model internals.

No human participants, students, teachers, or classroom context are involved. The paper is theoretical and develops formal guarantees showing that the algorithm’s risk is bounded relative to the safest subset of models, while abstention decreases as overlap among safe models increases. The authors also show that the method can limit information leakage and is robust to certain adversarial settings, but they emphasize important limitations, including the need for multiple safe models, possible abstention, and accumulation of risk over repeated use.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / language model system that samples outputs from multiple models and aggregates them via consensus sampling to improve safety and reduce leakage risk.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and analyzes a black-box consensus sampling procedure for aggregating multiple generative models; it is a theoretical safety framework rather than an empirical study of classroom use.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical / algorithmic paper with proofs, not an empirical education study. It does not evaluate a K–12 instructional coaching or lesson-feedback intervention, so there is no experimental evidence tier to rate beyond red.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No K–12 outcome was measured and no effect size is reported. The paper addresses safety properties of model aggregation in general, not instructional impact, so educational impact is not demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: AI Conversational Tutors in Foreign Language Learning: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation Study
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings 14th Panhellenic Conference iCT in Education, Rhodes, October 2025
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the design and quality of AI conversational tutors for foreign language learning, with a focus on how well they support conversational practice, contextual feedback, and learner interaction. The author frames the work around three questions: identifying common design patterns in AI tutors, comparing specialized language-learning tutors with general-purpose voice-enabled AI models, and proposing a framework to evaluate tutor quality from chat transcripts.

The study uses a mixed-methods approach. In the first phase, the author manually explored four specialized language-learning applications (talkio, talkpal, univerbal, and langua) by creating a Spanish learner profile and engaging in short free-chat sessions. In the second phase, the author compared two general-purpose conversational AI systems, ChatGPT and Gemini, used in voice mode for Spanish conversation practice. In the final phase, transcript-based quality evaluation was performed using a 10-dimensional rubric and five LLM-based evaluators, scoring six tutors in total.

The context is foreign language learning rather than K–12 schooling. The paper emphasizes learner-facing conversational use, including speaking practice, correction, turn-taking, and feedback. Across the systems, the study finds that many tools provide supportive and interactive experiences, but they vary substantially in handling breakdowns, contextual correction, and transcript completeness. The author also identifies privacy concerns, noting that voice data are stored without clear consent or warning in some tools. Overall, the paper concludes that conversation representation, contextual error handling, and feedback integrated into the flow of interaction are key design requirements, and that even general-purpose tools can sometimes provide strong conversational quality, though specialized tools may offer better targeted feedback.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI system used for text and voice chat, generation, and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a general-purpose voice conversational tutor for Spanish language practice (o4-mini) and as one of the artificial expert evaluators (GPT-4-turbo) for transcript-based quality scoring.

findings.finding_summary: In the voice tutoring comparison, ChatGPT followed the instruction to provide feedback on learner mistakes and produced longer, more verbose exchanges than Gemini. The paper reports that the total voice interaction time was 10.45 minutes, average tutor turns were 130 words, and average learner turns were 61 words, but no learning outcome or effect estimate was reported.
findings.measure: Voice interaction behavior; transcript completeness; feedback presence

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that the transcript shown after voice interaction was incomplete for ChatGPT, with parts of the conversation missing from the script. The author had to use speech-to-text to obtain a full record for later analysis, indicating a limitation in record keeping rather than a measured learning effect.
findings.measure: Completeness of transcript after voice interaction

findings.finding_summary: In transcript-based quality evaluation by five LLM judges, ChatGPT scored highly on feedback, vocabulary, and supportive style relative to the other tools. No numeric score, confidence interval, or learner outcome effect was reported in the paper text provided.
findings.measure: Transcript quality ratings on ten-dimensional framework

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's Gemini family of conversational AI models used for text and voice chat and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a general-purpose voice conversational tutor for Spanish language practice (Gemini 2.5 flash) and as one of the artificial expert evaluators (Gemini 2.5 Pro Preview 05-06) for transcript-based quality scoring.

findings.finding_summary: In the voice tutoring comparison, Gemini did not follow the instruction to provide feedback on learner mistakes, although the interaction itself was described as fluid. The total voice interaction time was 6.47 minutes and average tutor turns were 32 words, but no learning outcome or effect estimate was reported.
findings.measure: Voice interaction behavior; feedback presence

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that the transcript shown after voice interaction was incomplete for Gemini, with missing parts of the conversation in the script. A separate speech-to-text service was required to recover a full record for analysis.
findings.measure: Completeness of transcript after voice interaction

findings.finding_summary: In the transcript-based quality evaluation, Gemini lacked clarity and timely feedback relative to the better-performing tutors. The paper does not report a numeric score or effect size for this specific model beyond the qualitative ranking.
findings.measure: Transcript quality ratings on ten-dimensional framework

identified_tools.name: DeepSeek
identified_tools.description: DeepSeek's large language model family used here as an artificial expert evaluator.
