identified_tools.use_case: Used only as one of five LLM-based expert raters to score anonymized tutor transcripts on a ten-dimensional quality framework.

findings.finding_summary: DeepSeek-V3 was used as an automated evaluator of tutor transcripts. The paper reports inter-rater reliability across the six tutors for the ten dimensions, with overall alpha values ranging from approximately 0.754 to 0.911, but does not isolate DeepSeek-specific outcomes or effects.
findings.measure: Automated transcript evaluation scores

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods empirical study with transcript-based evaluation and expert judgment, not an RCT or meta-analysis. It provides useful descriptive evidence but no randomized causal estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports qualitative strengths and limitations of several tutors, but no effect sizes for learner outcomes and no clear evidence of meaningful academic impact. The findings are informative for design and privacy concerns, yet impact on learning is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether K-12 educators prefer lesson plans created by generative AI models or by human curriculum designers, and which lesson-plan components are strongest or weakest for each source. The study is motivated by growing use of GenAI for lesson planning, alongside concerns that AI-generated content may be pedagogically weak, contextually inappropriate, or inaccurate. The authors focus on a practical adoption question: whether GenAI can support teachers in planning without replacing human expertise.

The intervention or comparison involved pairwise evaluations of lesson plans produced by customized GPT-4, a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model, and human-authored open-source curriculum materials. Educators rated plans on warm-up, main task, cool-down, and overall quality, and also wrote comments explaining their choices. The sample consisted of 20 experienced K-12 mathematics educators, with comparisons spanning elementary, middle, and high school lesson plans. Data collection occurred over several weeks, with participants completing practice rounds, weekly check-ins, and approximately 10 hours of evaluations each.

Results show that human-authored lesson plans were generally preferred overall, especially for elementary instruction and for components requiring student engagement, scaffolding, discourse, and inclusive supports. GenAI plans were more competitive in higher-grade contexts and were especially favored for cool-down sections and structured summaries. GPT-4 tended to outperform the fine-tuned LLaMA model in several comparisons, while the fine-tuned model was stronger in some high-school contexts. The authors conclude that GenAI has promise as an assistive tool for lesson planning, but human pedagogical judgment remains essential, particularly for younger learners and for instructional design requiring nuanced differentiation and classroom interaction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-based generative language model used to generate instructional text and lesson plans.
identified_tools.use_case: Compared customized GPT-4-generated K-12 mathematics lesson plans against human curriculum designer-authored plans and fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b plans.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods comparative preference study with 16 educators evaluating 529 lesson-plan pairs, customized GPT-4 was preferred over fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b in raw pairwise comparisons 57.7% vs. 42.3% overall. However, human curriculum designer lesson plans were still preferred over GPT-4 58.7% vs. 41.3% overall, and GPT-4 was especially preferred for cool-down tasks 59.7% vs. 40.3% over human-created plans.
findings.measure: Educator pairwise preference for lesson-plan sections and overall quality
findings.effect_size: Preference margins reported as percentages; overall GPT-4 vs LLaMA-2-13b: 15.4 percentage-point margin
findings.confidence_interval: 95% CIs reported for bootstrapped aggregated analyses, but not specified for the pairwise percentages
findings.sample_size: n=16 educators; 529 lesson plan pairs; 2116 evaluations

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta LLaMA-family large language model fine-tuned for generating K-12 lesson plans.
identified_tools.use_case: Fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b was evaluated against customized GPT-4 and human curriculum designer-authored lesson plans for K-12 mathematics.

findings.finding_summary: In the comparative preference study, fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b was preferred less often than customized GPT-4 overall (42.3% vs. 57.7%), but it was still competitive with human curriculum designer lesson plans, which were preferred 53.6% vs. 46.4% overall. LLaMA-2-13b performed particularly well in cool-down activities, where it outperformed human-created lesson plans 57.9% vs. 42.1%.
findings.measure: Educator pairwise preference for lesson-plan sections and overall quality
findings.effect_size: Preference margins reported as percentages; HCD vs LLaMA-2-13b overall margin 7.2 percentage points
findings.confidence_interval: 95% CIs reported for bootstrapped aggregated analyses, but not specified for the pairwise percentages
findings.sample_size: n=16 educators; 529 lesson plan pairs; 2116 evaluations

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods comparative preference study with human ratings, not a randomized impact trial. It provides useful empirical evidence, but the outcomes are subjective preferences rather than direct student-learning effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports percentage preference differences rather than standardized effect sizes, and the practical impact is mixed. Human-authored plans were often preferred overall, while GenAI showed strength mainly in cool-down tasks and some higher-grade contexts.

paper_profiles.title: AI and the EU Digital Markets Act: Addressing the Risks of Bigness in Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 202, 2023
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the regulatory risks posed by the rapid growth and concentration of generative AI markets. The authors argue that existing competition and platform regulations in the European Union, especially the Digital Markets Act (DMA), do not adequately cover generative AI systems that may become dominant gateways for AI-based services.

Rather than presenting an empirical study or educational intervention, the paper develops a policy and legal framework for classifying certain generative AI services as "core platform services" and certain providers as "gatekeepers" under the DMA. It discusses how generative AI can be delivered as a platform through products like ChatGPT-style services and APIs, and it identifies sources of gatekeeping power such as compute resources, early-mover advantages, data accumulation, and integration with other services.

The paper is set in the European Union regulatory context and focuses on market structure and governance, not on a human participant population. Its main conclusion is that the DMA should be amended or interpreted to explicitly include generative AI services in order to preserve contestability, fairness, diversity, and innovation, and to prevent a few large firms from becoming entrenched gatekeepers in the generative AI ecosystem.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI systems such as large language model chatbots and related foundation-model services used for text, image, and other content generation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a theoretical/policy analysis of generative AI as a market and platform layer under the EU Digital Markets Act, not an empirical evaluation in education.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual and policy analysis paper, not an empirical study of an AI tool in K-12 education. It does not present a study design, sample, or outcome evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational outcomes, effect sizes, or measured impacts are reported. The paper discusses regulatory risks and market structure rather than instructional effectiveness or harm in classrooms.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an analytical AI platform can improve lesson-planning feedback in teacher education, compared with conventional human feedback. The authors focus on a core problem in teacher preparation: providing frequent, detailed, and individualized feedback on lesson plans is difficult for university instructors because it is time-consuming and hard to scale.

The intervention was EDDA, an analytical AI system built with unsupervised machine learning and a BERT-based classifier. EDDA analyzed student-teachers’ lesson plans and materials and returned expert-level feedback on didactic planning dimensions such as action orientation, process orientation, problem orientation, motivation, digitalization, sustainability, and basic lesson-structure features. In the experimental condition, students first received AI feedback and then could request human feedback to clarify or discuss the results; the control group received human feedback only. The study was conducted across two university cohorts in Germany and Austria, but the data collection reported here was in Germany, with student teachers in a master’s-level business education program working on lesson plans throughout a semester.

The results suggest that the AI-supported condition matched or exceeded human feedback on some planning dimensions, especially certain sustainability-related competences, social competences, reflexivity, and some aspects of lesson structure and technology use. However, the paper also reports that simply using the AI platform did not automatically improve students’ AI literacy, AI attitudes, motivation, or digital self-efficacy. The authors conclude that analytical AI can effectively supplement traditional feedback, but only as part of a broader pedagogical framework and with human guidance when the system’s outputs are uncertain or potentially misleading.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI / large language model chatbot or feedback assistant with no specific commercial or research product named.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generative AI generally in the literature review as a feedback medium for lesson planning, including risks and limitations, but the empirical intervention itself used a different analytical AI platform (EDDA), not a generative chatbot.

identified_tools.name: Adaptive Feedback System (General)
identified_tools.description: An analytical AI feedback platform that classifies uploaded lesson plans against predefined criteria and returns individualized expert feedback rather than generating free-form text.
identified_tools.use_case: EDDA was used as a longitudinal feedback tool for vocational teacher education lesson planning; students in the experimental group received EDDA feedback across a semester and compared it with human feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In a longitudinal intervention with N=103 vocational business education students (n=55 experimental, n=48 control), AI feedback on lesson plans matched or surpassed human feedback in some planning dimensions. The paper reports significant positive effects for the experimental group on certain sustainability-related planning outcomes, including social competences for sustainable development (p<0.05) and reflexivity (p<0.10), while some other dimensions were not significantly different.
findings.measure: Content analysis ratings of lesson plans on sustainability-related planning dimensions and competences

findings.finding_summary: For several measured planning dimensions and meta-dimensions, the paper reports no significant intervention effect. For example, the authors state that the mere use of AI did not automatically enhance AI literacy, change attitudes, or improve motivation, and many planning categories showed no group difference.
findings.measure: AI literacy, AI attitudes, motivation, and selected lesson-plan planning dimensions

findings.finding_summary: The platform’s own training-data limitations led to systematic underestimation of planning performance in some cases, which the authors note could have demotivating effects because it may mask competence development. The paper also flags that some categories had insufficient reliability, increasing the potential for error in the feedback.
findings.measure: Observed limitations in EDDA feedback accuracy and reliability across categories

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal intervention study with a comparison group and repeated use of AI feedback across a semester, which is stronger than a one-shot correlational design. However, the non-randomized assignment and some measurement/reliability concerns keep it below the highest evidence tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports some positive planning effects, but they are selective and not consistently large; many outcomes were null. The most concrete negative signal is the platform’s tendency to underestimate performance, which may demotivate users, but effect sizes are not reported.

paper_profiles.title: A cross-sectional look at teacher reactions, worries, and professional development needs related to generative AI in an urban school district
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers in a large urban school district reacted to generative AI, especially chatbot tools such as ChatGPT, shortly after their widespread emergence. The study asks what factors shape teacher willingness to allow student use of generative AI for different academic tasks, what concerns and benefits teachers associate with AI for themselves versus students, and what professional development needs teachers identify. The motivation is to understand early teacher perceptions and implementation barriers in a context where schools are rapidly forming policies but empirical evidence remains limited.

The authors used a district-wide survey embedded in the annual employee survey for certificated educators. Responses from 1,454 teachers were analyzed using a mixed-methods design that combined logistic regression on closed-ended items with thematic coding of open-ended responses. Teachers reported whether they had used chatbots recently, whether they allowed student use for specific tasks, and what concerns, benefits, and training needs they had. The sample came from one large West Coast urban district serving elementary, middle, and high school levels.

Findings show that willingness to allow generative AI decreased as grade level increased: high school teachers were generally more restrictive than elementary teachers, and more experienced teachers were also more likely to disallow use. Teachers were especially concerned about overreliance, plagiarism, and misinformation, with these concerns differing between teacher use and student use. Teachers also saw different benefits for themselves and students, and reported grade-specific professional development needs: elementary and middle school teachers wanted foundational AI literacy, while high school teachers emphasized how to manage student use and detect AI-generated work. Overall, the paper concludes that teachers are cautious about generative AI, and that policy and professional development should be tailored by grade level and instructional context.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI chatbot technology used for text generation, concept explanation, and related academic assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed K-12 teachers’ reactions, concerns, benefits, and professional development needs related to generative AI chatbots in schools, with examples explicitly including ChatGPT as an instance of the category.

findings.finding_summary: In a cross-sectional survey of 1,454 teachers in a large urban district, teachers were less willing to allow generative AI use as grade level increased. The probability of allowing AI chatbot use decreased from elementary to middle/high school across idea generation, paper editing, full-paper writing, concept explanation, and code generation, with the largest disallowance for editing/completing a paper.
findings.measure: Teacher allowability/policy toward student use of AI chatbots for five academic tasks
findings.effect_size: dy/dx ranging from -0.117 to -0.150 for grade level; elementary more-experienced teacher dy/dx = -0.489, -0.502, -0.587 for idea generation, editing, and full-paper writing
findings.confidence_interval: grade-level models: [0.025, 0.975] ranges reported in tables; e.g. -0.126 to -0.116, -0.125 to -0.108, -0.138 to -0.132, -0.133 to -0.117, -0.156 to -0.144; exact CIs vary by outcome
findings.sample_size: n=1,454; outcome-specific N ranges from 24 to 254 depending on task/model

findings.finding_summary: Teachers’ qualitative concerns emphasized overreliance, misinformation, and plagiarism/misuse. Overreliance was the most frequently named concern for both teachers and students, and teachers especially associated student AI use with plagiarism/misuse and overreliance.
findings.measure: Open-ended concern coding from teacher survey responses
findings.sample_size: n=668 for teachers’ concerns; n=669 for students’ concerns

findings.finding_summary: Teachers saw different benefits for teachers versus students. For teachers, commonly cited benefits included preparing lesson plans/materials (21.41%) and increased efficiency (13.62%); for students, the most common benefit was information retrieval/searching (20.33%).
findings.measure: Open-ended benefit coding from teacher survey responses
findings.sample_size: n=626 for teachers’ benefits; n=630 for students’ benefits

findings.finding_summary: Professional development needs varied significantly by grade level but not by subject or experience. Teachers most often wanted guidance on appropriately using AI for pedagogical purposes, while high school teachers especially wanted help with instructing/managing student AI use and detecting AI-generated work.
findings.measure: Open-ended professional development needs and chi-square comparisons across grade levels/subjects/experience
findings.sample_size: n=1,454 overall; qualitative need proportions reported for grade-level subsamples

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional mixed-methods survey study with descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and logistic regression, but no experimental or longitudinal design. Evidence is useful for documenting teacher perceptions and concerns, yet it cannot establish causal effects of generative AI use.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial attitudinal differences and clear concerns, but not effect sizes for learning outcomes or direct harm from the tool itself. Findings indicate important adoption barriers and cautionary perceptions rather than demonstrated positive or negative achievement impact.

paper_profiles.title: A comprehensive AI policy education framework for university teaching and learning
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for an institutional policy framework for generative AI in university teaching and learning, prompted by the rapid emergence of tools such as ChatGPT and concerns about academic misconduct, overreliance, privacy, transparency, and assessment integrity. The author argues that existing AI-in-education policies are too generic and often do not reflect the realities of text-generative AI, so a more practical policy model is needed.

The study uses a mixed-methods survey design with both closed- and open-ended questions. Data were collected online from 457 students and 180 teachers/staff across multiple disciplines at universities in Hong Kong. Participants reported on their current use of generative AI, perceptions of its benefits and risks, and recommendations for institutional policy. Quantitative analysis was descriptive, and qualitative responses were thematically analyzed.

Findings showed generally low current experience with generative AI, but substantial openness to future use and a strong belief that universities should have plans to manage associated risks. Participants saw benefits such as time saving, personalized feedback, and possible gains in digital competence, but also raised concerns about cheating, overreliance, weakened social interaction, reduced generic skills, and data privacy/security. The paper concludes by proposing an AI Ecological Education Policy Framework with pedagogical, governance, and operational dimensions, emphasizing training, ethical use, transparent governance, and balanced adoption rather than replacement of human teaching.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model system for text generation and conversational assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studied stakeholders’ perceptions, concerns, and intended uses of ChatGPT and similar generative AI technologies in university teaching and learning, including feedback, support, and policy implications.

findings.finding_summary: In this survey of 457 students and 180 teachers/staff in Hong Kong universities, respondents generally viewed ChatGPT-like tools as potentially beneficial for teaching and learning. Students (mean=4.0, SD=0.891) and teachers (mean=3.87, SD=1.32) agreed that integration of generative AI would have a positive long-run impact, and they also endorsed institutional planning for risk management (students mean=4.5; teachers mean=4.54).
findings.measure: Survey ratings of perceived long-run impact of generative AI and need for institutional AI planning

findings.finding_summary: Respondents saw some efficiency-related benefits, including time savings (students mean=4.23, teachers mean=4.06), 24/7 availability (students mean=4.16, teachers mean=3.81), and personalized/immediate feedback (students mean=3.75, teachers mean=3.86). At the same time, they expressed concern about over-reliance (students mean=3.11, teachers mean=4.24) and possible limits on social interaction and transferable-skill development.
findings.measure: Survey ratings on time savings, immediate feedback, over-reliance, and social/skill impacts

findings.finding_summary: The paper does not report an intervention effect, but it documents substantial institutional concerns around academic misconduct, privacy, transparency, accountability, security, equity of access, and the need for AI policy, training, and assessment redesign. These were derived from open-ended responses and indicate perceived governance risks rather than measured outcomes.
findings.measure: Open-ended survey themes on policy, governance, privacy, equity, and assessment

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods survey study with descriptive and thematic analysis, not an experimental or longitudinal field evaluation. It provides useful stakeholder perceptions but no causal estimate of AI effectiveness or harm.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no quantified effect size or outcome improvement/decline; impacts are indirect and perception-based. It is most informative for governance and adoption concerns rather than demonstrated educational impact.

paper_profiles.title: The AI generation gap: Are Gen Z students more interested in adopting generative AI such as ChatGPT in teaching and learning than their Gen X and millennial generation teachers?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Gen Z students and Gen X/Gen Y teachers in higher education perceive and intend to use generative AI tools such as ChatGPT. The study is motivated by the rapid rise of GenAI in education and the need to understand both perceived benefits and risks, including overreliance, misinformation, bias, privacy, and pedagogical concerns. The authors frame the work as a response to the lack of evidence-based guidance for responsible GenAI adoption in teaching and learning.

The study used a mixed-method online survey with 583 participants: 399 undergraduate students and 184 teachers recruited through convenience sampling. The survey included closed-ended Likert items and open-ended questions, and the analysis combined descriptive statistics, t-tests, and thematic coding of qualitative responses. The context was higher education, with most participants located in Hong Kong and some in other regions; the teachers were assumed to be mainly Gen X and Gen Y based on their role.

Findings showed that students were more frequent users of GenAI and were generally more optimistic about its future educational value, especially for saving time, improving writing, and providing personalized support. Teachers were more cautious and expressed stronger concerns about factual inaccuracy, bias, manipulation, social isolation, and overreliance. Both groups recognized the need for fact-checking, institutional guidelines, and digital/AI literacy, and both saw GenAI as something to be used alongside, not in place of, human teaching. The paper concludes that responsible integration should emphasize policies, critical evaluation, and human oversight, while acknowledging that current AI detection tools are unreliable and that GenAI is not a substitute for teachers.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model chatbot system such as ChatGPT used for text generation, question answering, summarization, feedback, and other instructional support tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed teachers’ and students’ current experiences, perceptions, knowledge, concerns, and intentions regarding use of generative AI in higher education; the paper explicitly mentions ChatGPT as an example but does not evaluate a specific product in a field intervention.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods survey of 583 participants (399 students, 184 teachers), students reported higher current use of GenAI than teachers (M=2.27 vs 2.03, p=.023) and more optimistic views of its future impact on teaching and learning (M=3.90 vs 3.58, p<.001). However, teachers expressed stronger concern about risks such as inaccurate outputs (M=4.27 vs 4.08, p=.011), bias (M=4.20 vs 3.91, p<.001), and over-reliance (M=4.12 vs 2.87, p<.001).
findings.measure: Self-reported usage, perceptions, knowledge, and concerns about GenAI in higher education

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods survey study rather than an experimental evaluation, so causal effects are not identified. The evidence is useful for perceptions, concerns, and intended use, but it does not test a specific intervention or measure learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear attitude differences and substantial concern about risks, but no learning-effect estimate or practical implementation effect size is provided. Its impact for instructional coaching or lesson feedback is therefore suggestive rather than demonstrably positive or negative.

paper_profiles.title: How should we change teaching and assessment in response to increasingly powerful generative Artificial Intelligence? Outcomes of the ChatGPT teacher survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how educators believe teaching and assessment should change in response to the rapid emergence of generative AI such as ChatGPT, and what motivates those changes. The study frames generative AI as a disruptive educational technology and argues that teacher beliefs and motivations are important baseline evidence for understanding future adoption and pedagogical change.

The authors used a mixed-methods survey design with 318 educators from a diverse set of teaching levels, regions, experience levels, and discipline areas. Participants were recruited online through social media and professional teaching networks. The survey measured perceived impact of generative AI on teaching and assessment, as well as open-ended views on what should change in curriculum, pedagogy, and assessment, and why educators felt motivated to change.

Overall, most respondents expected ChatGPT-like tools to have a major or profound impact on teaching and assessment, though a substantial minority predicted little or no impact. Greater prior awareness of generative AI predicted higher perceived impact. Qualitative responses suggested that teachers wanted more emphasis on learning about AI, critical thinking, ethics, process-oriented and authentic tasks, face-to-face or supervised assessment, and using AI as an aid for lesson design and exemplars. The authors conclude that generative AI is likely to drive pedagogical and assessment redesign, but their findings reflect teacher perceptions rather than evidence that these changes are effective.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot and large language model system for natural-language text generation and interaction.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers were surveyed about how ChatGPT and similar generative AI tools might affect teaching and assessment, and about how they might use ChatGPT in curriculum, pedagogy, and assessment design.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed-methods survey of educators (n=318), 93% of respondents said ChatGPT/generative AI would have at least a minor impact on teaching, with 73% rating the impact as major or profound and only 7% selecting none. Mean perceived impact on teaching was 2.7/4, and on assessment was 2.8/4; higher AI awareness predicted higher perceived impact.
findings.measure: Perceived impact of ChatGPT/generative AI on teaching and on assessment (4-point Likert scale: none to profound)
findings.effect_size: teaching: Cohen's d=0.45 for high vs low/medium awareness; assessment: Cohen's d=0.35 for high vs low/medium awareness

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported multiple intended changes to teaching in response to ChatGPT, including teaching students how AI works (n=40), critical thinking/evaluating AI responses (n=38), ethical and responsible use of AI (n=26), and using ChatGPT as exemplars/models (n=17). A subset reported no planned change to teaching (n=31), and only three respondents said they would discourage AI use.
findings.measure: Open-ended teacher-reported intended changes to teaching practice

findings.finding_summary: For assessment, teachers suggested changes such as spoken tasks (n=29), examinations (n=21), higher-order thinking tasks (n=71), authentic tasks (n=65), process-focused assessment (n=50), and more supervision/invigilated assessment (n=69). Some also proposed embedding AI into assessment tasks (n=54), while 36 respondents said ChatGPT would have minimal or no impact on assessment tasks.
findings.measure: Open-ended teacher-reported intended changes to assessment practice

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional mixed-methods survey rather than an experimental or longitudinal study. It provides useful educator perceptions at scale, but it does not test actual repeated use, coaching outcomes, or causal effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports mostly perceived impact and intended practice changes, not measured student or teacher outcome effects. Findings suggest substantial anticipated influence of ChatGPT, but no direct evidence of harm, attrition, or sustained-use performance effects.

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT in the digital era: Perspectives on chatbot implementation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how educators and students perceive the use of ChatGPT in education during the digital era. The authors focus on perceived benefits and risks, including immediate feedback, reduced workload for educators, support for students’ learning, concerns about answer accuracy, loss of personal interaction, and privacy and data-security issues.

The study uses a qualitative design with in-depth interviews and content analysis, supplemented by NVivo. Participants were 25 Thai higher-education stakeholders in Krabi, Thailand: ten educators and 15 students. The paper frames ChatGPT as a tool for academic support and classroom assistance rather than as a formal instructional intervention, and it includes suggested classroom uses such as brainstorming, answering routine questions, summarising texts, and language support.

Overall, the findings are broadly positive but cautious. Respondents saw ChatGPT as useful for efficiency and support, but they emphasised that it should complement, not replace, human teaching. The main concerns were inaccurate or biased outputs, reduced teacher-student interaction, and privacy/security risks. The study concludes that educators and policymakers should provide guidance and training for responsible use, while future research should examine longer-term effects and broader implementation contexts.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model interface that generates human-like text responses and can assist with answering questions, generating ideas, summarizing text, and providing feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a chatbot implementation in education through qualitative interviews with educators and students in Krabi, Thailand, focusing on perceived benefits, concerns, and classroom use.

findings.finding_summary: In interviews with 10 educators and 15 students, participants generally held positive perceptions of ChatGPT for education, especially for providing immediate feedback, answering questions, and reducing educator workload. However, they also raised concerns about information accuracy, loss of personal interaction, and privacy/data security. No quantitative effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Perceptions of educational use, workload reduction, immediate feedback, accuracy concerns, personal interaction, and data privacy concerns

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative interview study, so it provides useful contextual evidence but not causal or quantitative estimates. The sample is small and limited to one setting in Thailand.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceived benefits and concerns rather than measured learning impact. The evidence suggests usefulness for routine feedback and workload reduction, but impact is unclear and no effect size is reported.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in physics education: A pilot study on easy-to-implement activities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper explores how ChatGPT can be used in secondary physics education to support critical thinking and classroom discussion. The author argues that large language models have educational potential, but also notable risks and limitations, including biased or incorrect outputs and the need for students to critically evaluate AI-generated text.

The paper presents two easy-to-implement classroom activities centered on quantum physics. In the first, students generate ChatGPT responses about photons, critique their scientific accuracy and clarity, compare answers across prompts, and revise the text using additional sources. In the second, students use ChatGPT to create a short conceptual survey on wave-particle duality, check the items for validity, and discuss the results with peers. The activities are framed as tools for fostering student reflection on both the benefits and pitfalls of ChatGPT.

A pilot field study tested the approach in two 12th-grade physics classes at a German Gymnasium. The intervention consisted of two 45-minute lessons taught by an instructed teacher during regular physics instruction. Using a one-group pretest-posttest design and a questionnaire on students’ perceptions of AI and ChatGPT, the study found generally more favorable post-intervention views of ChatGPT, including stronger agreement that it should be incorporated into daily life and can be useful for learning tasks. The author concludes that the activities may positively shape student perceptions of ChatGPT, while emphasizing that more research is needed on long-term effects and on how ChatGPT can be integrated into classroom practice.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative pre-trained transformer chatbot for conversational text generation and other natural-language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in two easy-to-implement classroom activities for secondary physics: students generated and critically analyzed ChatGPT outputs, and students used ChatGPT to create a three-item conceptual survey on quantum physics for peer discussion. The paper also reports a pilot field implementation of these activities in two 12th-grade physics classes.

findings.finding_summary: In a one-group pretest-posttest pilot with two 12th-grade physics classes (n=53), students' perceptions of ChatGPT improved after a two-lesson intervention. Agreement increased for several ChatGPT items, including belief that it should be incorporated into daily life (M=3.53 to 4.60), that benefits outweigh harms (M=3.13 to 4.45), and that it helps accomplish tasks more quickly (M=3.42 to 4.38).
findings.measure: Students' perceptions of the importance/benefits of ChatGPT on a 9-item 5-point questionnaire

findings.finding_summary: One ChatGPT-related item moved in the opposite direction: agreement with the statement that students can use ChatGPT even if they do not understand how it works decreased from M=3.32 (SD=1.32) to M=2.66 (SD=0.95). The authors interpret this as possible increased awareness that outputs should not be consumed uncritically, but they do not report statistical significance.
findings.measure: Agreement with the statement that ChatGPT can be used without understanding how it works

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small one-group pretest-posttest pilot study with no control group and no inferential statistics reported, so internal validity is limited. It still provides direct classroom field evidence on repeated use of ChatGPT by students and a teacher-led implementation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported changes are modest to positive in student perceptions, but no effect sizes are given and the design does not support strong causal claims. The study does include a potentially informative negative/critical-awareness signal on one item, but not evidence of harm or no effect.

paper_profiles.title: LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL-POWERED CHATBOTS FOR INTERNATIONALIZING STUDENT SUPPORT IN HIGHER EDUCATION
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language model (LLM)-powered chatbots can be used to improve student support and internationalization in higher education. The authors frame the problem as helping international and Moroccan students access timely, relevant information and interact more easily with university services in a digitally transformed educational environment.

The intervention is a chatbot built with GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4-Turbo, LangChain, OpenAI embeddings, and Chroma Vector Store. The system uses a retrieval-augmented design: official university webpages are manually collected, embedded into a local vector store, and used to ground responses. A second GPT-4-Turbo step acts as a verifier to reduce hallucinations and align responses with the source data. The chatbot also includes summary memory to support ongoing conversations and multilingual response capability.

The study population is Al Akhawayn University students, with survey evaluation conducted on 11 final evaluators (10 Moroccan and 1 international) who rated chatbot responses on quality, relevance, correctness, formality, and human-likeness. The paper reports generally strong evaluation scores and concludes that the chatbot can provide rich, relevant, and generally accurate support for international student inquiries. It also notes that hallucinations can still occur in unsupported areas and recommends larger-scale evaluation and broader datasets in future work.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-based large language model chatbot system used for conversational response generation, with prompting, memory, vector retrieval, and post-generation verification.
identified_tools.use_case: Built and evaluated as a chatbot for international student support in higher education, using GPT-3.5-Turbo for initial responses and GPT-4-Turbo as a verifier/fact-checker.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that the chatbot was capable of providing comprehensive responses, with a low error rate, real-time engagement, memory capabilities, and critical data access. It was described as effective for student support and information retrieval, though no controlled comparison or effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Survey ratings of chatbot response quality, relevance, correctness, formality, and human-likeness; qualitative testing of provocation-proofness and information retrieval

findings.finding_summary: The authors state that the chatbot could improve student engagement, information access, and support in higher education internationalization, and suggest it may be relatively low cost and easy to implement across universities. This is a claim based on the described prototype and survey feedback rather than a causal field study.
findings.measure: Student survey feedback and author interpretation of implementation implications

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical prototype evaluation with survey-based testing, but it is not a controlled study, RCT, or field experiment. The evidence is qualitative/mixed-methods with limited participants and no causal design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported ratings are generally high, but no standardized effect size is provided and the study lacks a comparison group. The impact appears favorable but remains unclear and modest in evidentiary strength.

paper_profiles.title: AI-based response assessment and prediction in longitudinal imaging for brain metastases treated with stereotactic radiosurgery
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of analyzing and predicting treatment response in longitudinal MRI for brain metastases treated with stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS). The authors note that follow-up imaging creates a substantial clinical workload and is often assessed only by visual observation, motivating automated methods for curation, clustering, and response prediction.

The study develops an automated pipeline to extract, register, resegment, and track longitudinal lesion data from routine clinical PACS records at Lausanne University Hospital. Using 896 brain metastases from 177 patients with follow-up over about a year, the authors cluster lesion volume trajectories and train both classical machine learning models and graph machine learning models to predict one-year lesion-level response from early follow-up MRI and clinical/radiomic features.

The paper finds five dominant growth trajectories, including patterns consistent with complete response, pseudoprogression, and progressive disease. Predictive performance improves when longitudinal information is included, with robust results after the first follow-up scan and the best performance with more time points. The authors conclude that automated longitudinal analysis may support clinical decision-making and personalized care, while also noting that their graph models did not consistently outperform classical approaches.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general AI/ML-based automated pipeline for longitudinal medical image curation, lesion tracking, clustering, and response prediction; no named generative AI product is studied.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to automatically curate longitudinal brain metastasis imaging data, propagate segmentations, track lesions over time, cluster growth trajectories, and predict 1-year response after stereotactic radiosurgery.

findings.finding_summary: Using longitudinal imaging features, the models achieved robust response prediction for brain metastases after SRS. For CR vs non-CR, the best ROC AUC reached 0.90 (95% CI 0.88-0.92) using pre-treatment and first follow-up MRI; for responding vs non-responding, the best ROC AUC reached 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.98) when using the full follow-up period.
findings.measure: ROC AUC for lesion-level one-year response prediction

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that the semi-automatic pipeline made curation of a large longitudinal imaging dataset feasible where manual processing would be unfeasible. The authors note rare quality-control issues (about 16% partial segmentation and other failures; about 1% misaligned image pairs) and that automated rejection of outliers reduced manual cleaning to a minimal level.
findings.measure: Manual processing burden / quality-control of automated curation pipeline
findings.sample_size: random subset of 66 lesion time series for quality control

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a technical medical imaging/ML paper rather than an education study, and it does not evaluate an educational AI tool. The evidence is empirical but not relevant to K-12 instructional coaching or lesson-plan feedback.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No K-12 teaching, coaching, or lesson-feedback outcome is studied, so there is no direct educational impact to assess. Any reported performance is for medical prediction, not classroom use.

paper_profiles.title: Semi-Disentangled Spatiotemporal Implicit Neural Representations of Longitudinal Neuroimaging Data for Trajectory Classification
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of representing and classifying longitudinal neuroimaging trajectories when scan times and sampling density vary across subjects. The authors argue that conventional deep learning methods struggle with irregularly sampled longitudinal MRI because they operate on discrete inputs and do not directly capture continuous developmental or disease-related change over time.

To address this, the paper proposes a semi-disentangled spatiotemporal implicit neural representation (INR) that models each subject’s brain-aging trajectory as a continuous function over space and time. The architecture separates spatial, temporal, and combined parameter streams, and a downstream encoder/classifier operates directly on INR parameters to classify trajectories as healthy versus AD-like. The method is evaluated in a fully synthetic proof-of-concept setting using simulated longitudinal 3D T1-weighted MRI data generated from a conditional diffusion model and then altered with an ODE-based deviation process to create healthy and accelerated-aging trajectories.

The simulated cohort contains 450 artificial subjects with regular and irregular sampling schemes. Results show that the proposed INR approach reconstructs longitudinal scans reasonably well and that temporal INR parameters, especially the temporal stream alone, perform best for trajectory classification under irregular sampling, outperforming the SFCN baseline in that setting. The authors conclude that the approach is promising for irregular longitudinal neuroimaging analysis, but they emphasize that real-data validation is still needed.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: A general category of intelligent tutoring systems or learning analytics models. In this paper, the term is not applicable to an educational tool; no educational AI system is studied.
identified_tools.use_case: Not studied; the paper is about longitudinal neuroimaging trajectory classification with implicit neural representations, not education AI.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a computer vision / neuroimaging methods paper with no educational intervention, no teachers, and no instructional coaching or lesson-feedback study. It does not evaluate any K-12 AI tool, so there is no education evidence to rate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no K-12 educational outcome, no instructional practice outcome, and no AI tutoring/coaching system evaluated. Accordingly, there is no educational impact evidence in this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Longitudinal Linear Mixed Models End-To-End: A Reproducible Case Study in Mouse Body-Weight Growth
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a reproducible teaching case study on longitudinal linear mixed models using mouse body-weight data. The core problem is pedagogical: many learners encounter mixed models as fragmented theory or software output, so the author aims to provide a coherent end-to-end workflow that links raw data, exploratory plots, model specification, estimation, diagnostics, and interpretation.

The approach uses a preclinical mouse experiment in which 31 mice from three groups were weighed weekly over 12 weeks: wild-type controls, pair-fed ob/ob mice, and unrestricted ob/ob mice. The dataset is reshaped from wide to long format and analyzed with random-intercept linear mixed models in R. Three candidate mean structures are compared by maximum likelihood, and linear contrasts are used to estimate group differences in weekly weight trajectories and 12-week gain.

The paper is aimed at advanced undergraduate and graduate students in biostatistics, epidemiology, applied statistics, and public health methods. It reports that the unrestricted ob/ob group has a much steeper growth trajectory than the other groups, while wild-type and pair-fed mice have similar slopes. The author concludes that the case study is a useful reusable teaching module for demonstrating transparent longitudinal modeling and reproducible statistical practice.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI chatbots or large language model systems in general.
identified_tools.use_case: Not studied. The paper is a statistical teaching case study about longitudinal linear mixed models for mouse body-weight data and does not evaluate any AI tool.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper does not present an empirical evaluation of an AI tool; it is a methods/teaching case study about linear mixed models. No AI intervention, dataset, or outcome attributable to an AI system is reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured educational or operational impact from an AI tool in this paper, so impact cannot be assessed. The paper is unrelated to generative AI use in K–12 coaching or feedback.

paper_profiles.title: A Longitudinal Measurement of Privacy Policy Evolution for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how privacy policies for mainstream large language model (LLM) providers evolve over time, with a focus on what kinds of data practices are disclosed and how those disclosures respond to product launches and regulatory pressure. The authors argue that LLM privacy policies are underexplored despite the sensitive and extensive personal data collected through prompts, uploads, feedback, and agentic tool use.

The study uses a longitudinal document-analysis approach rather than a participant-based intervention. The authors curate 74 historical privacy-policy versions and 115 supplemental privacy documents from 11 LLM providers across 5 countries, then extract and code 3,463 sentence-level edits between consecutive policy versions. They also compare these policies with older general-software privacy policies and propose a new taxonomy tailored to LLM-specific data practices.

The paper finds that LLM privacy policies are substantially longer, more complex, and more vague than traditional software policies. They increasingly disclose first-party collection of chat transcripts, AI outputs, and feedback; third-party interactions via plugins and downstream apps; model-training uses of user data; and more explicit rights and controls. The longitudinal analysis suggests that policy changes are often driven by product releases and, with some delay, by regulatory actions such as GDPR-related enforcement. The overall conclusion is that LLM privacy policies are evolving quickly but remain difficult to read, fragmented across supplemental documents, and still highly ambiguous.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Large language model services and chatbots used for general-purpose conversational and agentic interaction, with associated data collection and privacy-policy disclosures.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies privacy policies and policy evolution of mainstream LLM providers and their LLM services, including general references to chatbots and agentic systems, rather than evaluating a classroom-specific AI tool.

findings.finding_summary: In a longitudinal empirical study of 11 mainstream LLM providers, the authors collected 74 historical privacy policies and 115 supplemental documents and extracted 3,463 sentence-level edits. They found that LLM privacy policies are substantially longer than traditional software policies, require upper-college to graduate-level reading ability (median FKGL 14.77 in 2023, 15.66 in 2024, 15.74 in 2025), remain highly vague, and often expand disclosures about model training, third-party integrations, and user rights over time.
findings.measure: Privacy policy length, readability (Flesch-Kincaid grade level), vagueness, and longitudinal policy edits across LLM providers
findings.effect_size: Policies were around 53.6% longer than the 2019 general-software baseline
findings.sample_size: n=11 providers; 74 historical policies; 115 supplemental documents

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal empirical document-analysis study, but it does not evaluate instructional outcomes or classroom use. The evidence is observational and descriptive rather than experimental.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows meaningful policy evolution and privacy burden in LLM services, but it does not demonstrate direct educational impact or harm in K–12 instructional coaching or lesson feedback.

paper_profiles.title: Demystifying Instruction Mixing for Fine-tuning Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how mixing different instruction-tuning datasets affects large language model performance. The authors ask whether combining general-purpose chat instructions, NLP downstream-task instructions, and coding instructions produces uniform gains or whether some mixtures help specific capabilities while hurting others.

The study fine-tunes LLaMA-2 7B and 13B on combinations of three public instruction datasets: Alpaca (general chat), P3 (NLP task reformulations), and CodeAlpaca (code generation). The evaluation is entirely computational and uses standard NLP benchmarks, HumanEval for code generation, and FLASK/GPT-4 based alignment-skill scoring. No human learners, teachers, or schools are involved.

The main finding is that specialized instruction data improves performance in its own domain, but mixed datasets do not always improve all outcomes. In particular, P3-style NLP instructions can reduce alignment/chat ability, while code instructions can improve both coding and alignment when combined with general instructions. The paper also reports that performance depends on model size and instruction ratio, with larger models benefiting more from diverse mixtures.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta's LLaMA family of large language models for general-purpose language understanding and generation, including instruction-tuned variants.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper fine-tunes LLaMA-2 7B and 13B models with different instruction mixtures (Alpaca, CodeAlpaca, P3) and evaluates NLP, code, and alignment performance.

findings.finding_summary: Across zero-shot NLP and code benchmarks, specialized instruction datasets improved performance on their respective task areas, but combining all instruction types did not uniformly improve all tasks. For example, P3 improved NLP averages and CodeAlpaca improved HumanEval pass rates, while some mixtures performed best depending on model size (7B vs 13B).
findings.measure: NLP benchmarks (ARC, Winogrande, PIQA, MMLU, RACE, HellaSwag) and HumanEval pass@1/pass@10

findings.finding_summary: Mixing P3 data caused a drop in alignment skills of -2.8 points for LLaMA-2-7B and -3.6 points for LLaMA-2-13B on the FLASK-based GPT-4 alignment evaluation. The authors conclude that P3 has a negative impact on fine-tuning chatbot LLMs.
findings.measure: FLASK alignment skill scores averaged over eight dimensions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled experimental study that systematically compares multiple fine-tuning mixtures and evaluates them with benchmark tasks and a GPT-4-based alignment rubric. It is not an RCT in the education sense, but the methodology is clear and reproducible.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful performance changes, including negative alignment effects from P3 mixing, but the effects are reported as benchmark-score differences rather than standardized effect sizes. The educational relevance is indirect because the study is on general LLM fine-tuning, not K-12 teacher coaching.

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using generative AI to personalize K–12 mathematics instruction. The central question is how teachers interact with ChatGPT when adapting existing curriculum tasks to students’ interests, and whether that process is efficient, pedagogically sound, and appealing to students.

The study involved 7 middle school mathematics teachers in the United States who used GPT-4o / ChatGPT to modify problems from the Illustrative Mathematics curriculum. Teachers personalized problems for popular-culture interest areas, iteratively prompting the model during recorded Zoom sessions and then assigning the resulting problems to 521 seventh-grade students via ASSISTments. Teachers received a 2-hour training session before implementation, and the same procedure was repeated in two different units so the researchers could examine changes over time.

Results show that teachers commonly used prompts to adjust the specificity of interests, realism, numerical appropriateness, readability, and age-appropriateness. Students generally preferred finer-grained, more specific references, while teachers often worked to repair shallow or unrealistic AI output. Personalizing one problem took about 4 minutes on average, and this did not become clearly more efficient across iterations; in fact, teachers used more prompts and more time in the second unit, though student ratings also improved. The paper concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can improve instructional quality and provide professional learning, but it is still time-consuming and may not align well with students’ desire for more individualized, fine-grained personalization.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s generative AI chatbot/LLM system used to generate and revise text-based outputs through prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Seven middle school mathematics teachers used ChatGPT (with underlying model GPT-4o) to personalize existing Illustrative Mathematics problems for students’ interests and to iteratively revise the problems over two units.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers spent an average of 246 seconds (about 4 minutes) to pose each of 143 personalized problems, using 558 prompts in total (average 3.2 prompts per problem). Efficiency did not clearly improve over time: from Unit 4 to Unit 6, teachers used significantly more prompts and more time per problem, although student ratings of interestingness and closeness also increased.
findings.measure: Teacher time per problem; number of prompts per problem; student ratings of interestingness and closeness
findings.effect_size: B=1.26 (prompts per problem from Unit 4 to Unit 6); B=70.4 seconds (time per problem from Unit 4 to Unit 6); B=0.33 for student ratings increase from Unit 4 to Unit 6; B=0.240 for 3-5 prompts vs other prompt counts
findings.sample_size: teachers n=7; students n=521; problems n=143

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods study with direct teacher use in authentic classrooms, but it is not an experimental comparison and has no control group for learning outcomes. Evidence is informative but largely observational and exploratory.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports small-to-modest differences in student ratings and mixed efficiency findings, but it does not demonstrate a clear positive or negative instructional impact on achievement. The most salient result is that teacher-in-the-loop personalization remained time-consuming and did not become more efficient over time.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Toolkit - A Framework for Increasing the Quality of LLM-Based Applications over Their Whole Life Cycle
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes the Generative AI Toolkit, a framework intended to improve the quality and reliability of LLM-based applications across their full development and operational life cycle. The authors frame the core problem as the manual, trial-and-error nature of current LLM application development, testing, deployment, and monitoring, especially given prompt sensitivity, hallucinations, and the need to maintain quality after release.

The toolkit is presented as an automation layer for DevOps-style workflows: it supports bootstrapping agents, defining custom metrics, creating repeatable evaluation cases, comparing model/prompt permutations, integrating testing into CI/CD pipelines, and logging/monitoring interactions at scale. The paper illustrates these features through example use cases such as a text-to-SQL agent, a restaurant menu RAG agent, an in-car assistant, and a model-comparison scenario. These are development examples rather than human-subject studies.

No K–12 population, teachers, or instructional coaches are studied. The main conclusion is that the toolkit can reduce cycle time, increase test coverage, and help surface quality problems such as hallucination, lack of tool use, or poor response quality, thereby improving development and deployment practices for LLM-based systems.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model / generative AI application used to generate and evaluate text, prompts, and agent behaviors.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper presents a framework for developing, testing, deploying, and monitoring LLM-based applications and agents; the named examples are internal use cases and model comparisons rather than a specific educational product.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a framework/preprint about DevOps tooling for LLM-based applications, not an empirical study of an education AI tool. It does not report a controlled evaluation with participant outcomes relevant to K–12 teachers or coaches.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact outcome is measured. The paper discusses software-engineering benefits such as quality improvement and reduced cycle time, but provides no direct evidence of harm, null effect, or sustained teacher use in K–12 settings.

paper_profiles.title: Making Physical Objects with Generative AI and Robotic Assembly: Considering Fabrication Constraints, Sustainability, Time, Functionality and Accessibility
paper_profiles.venue: GenAICHI: CHI 2025 Workshop on Generative AI and HCI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This workshop paper examines how generative AI for 3D object creation should be paired with fabrication methods that can handle the constraints of the physical world. The authors argue that producing a digital 3D model quickly is not enough; the downstream fabrication process must also be fast, sustainable, functional, and accessible.

As a case study, the paper presents a system that combines text-to-3D generative AI with discrete robotic assembly. A user speaks or prompts for an object, the AI generates a 3D mesh, and the system discretizes that geometry into modular components for assembly by a UR10 robotic arm. The paper discusses the need for overhang detection, connectivity analysis, and reachability checks to make assembly feasible.

The paper is not a study of teachers, students, or schools. It is a technical workshop paper focused on fabrication workflows, using MIT-based prototyping and demonstrations of several assembled objects. The main conclusions are that discrete robotic assembly can partially address fabrication constraints, reduce time compared with slower manufacturing methods, and support reuse of parts for sustainability, but accessibility remains limited by the cost and hardware requirements of robotic systems.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI system used to create 3D models from text or image inputs.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses 3D generative AI as part of a prompt-to-physical-object workflow, and uses Meshy.AI as the example text-to-3D generator within a robotic assembly system.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a workshop case study / framework paper focused on fabrication and robotic assembly, not an empirical K–12 education study. It does not evaluate teacher coaching, lesson-plan feedback, or instructional outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational or K–12 instructional impact is measured. The paper reports engineering/design observations about 3D generative AI and physical fabrication, so there is no relevant evidence of positive or negative impact on teachers or students.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an analytical AI platform can support lesson planning in teacher education by providing individualized, expert-level feedback on lesson plans. The authors focus on a practical problem in higher education: university instructors often cannot give frequent, detailed feedback on complex lesson plans, especially in vocational business education, where planning must account for multiple didactic dimensions such as sustainability, process orientation, problem orientation, action orientation, individualization, and digitalization.

The intervention used EDDA, an analytical AI system built on unsupervised machine learning and a BERT-based classifier. Over a semester, the experimental group used EDDA to receive feedback on lesson plans and then could discuss the AI output with a university teacher; the control group received human feedback only. The study involved 103 master’s-level student teachers in business education in Germany, with lesson plans produced in small groups and collected at the beginning and end of the semester. The authors also tracked meta-dimensions such as AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competences, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and motivation using questionnaires.

Results suggest that AI feedback can match or sometimes surpass human feedback on several planning dimensions, especially some sustainability-related criteria and aspects of learner engagement, lesson structure, and technology use. However, the authors also report that simply using AI did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, motivation, or self-efficacy. They conclude that analytical AI can supplement traditional feedback, but it should be embedded in a broader instructional framework and accompanied by human support, especially because EDDA tended to underestimate performance in some categories due to uneven training data.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI/LLM chatbot used for producing or delivering feedback, text generation, or related instructional support, without a specific commercial product named.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generative AI in the introduction and motivation for the study, contrasting it with the analytical AI platform EDDA. It does not report an empirical evaluation of a named generative AI product.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The paper is a longitudinal intervention study with a clear comparison group and repeated measurement, which is strong empirical evidence. However, the AI system studied is analytical rather than generative, and the generative AI discussion is only contextual.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Because the paper does not evaluate a generative AI tool, there is no direct impact estimate for the requested topic. The reported effects pertain to an analytical feedback platform, so impact for generative AI specifically is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Mapping the emerging research landscape on applications of ChatGPT in Language teacher education: a systematic narrative literature review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emerging empirical literature on ChatGPT in language teacher education, with a focus on how English language teachers use generative AI for instructional support, reflection, professional learning, and student-facing activities. The review was motivated by the rapid uptake of ChatGPT in education and the need to understand both its benefits and its risks, including overreliance, ethical concerns, cultural misalignment, and possible erosion of teacher judgment.

The authors conducted a systematic narrative literature review of 13 peer-reviewed empirical studies published between January 2023 and March 2025. The included studies covered pre-service and in-service English language teachers across a range of contexts, including Türkiye, Iran, Saudi Arabia, South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, the United States, and international samples. Study designs included qualitative case studies, phenomenology, mixed-method interventions, and experimental studies. The review synthesized how teachers used ChatGPT for lesson planning, feedback, reflective practice, professional development, and classroom support.

Overall, the review concludes that teachers generally perceive ChatGPT as a useful pedagogical assistant and reflective partner that can reduce workload, support creativity, and improve self-efficacy when used intentionally and with appropriate training. At the same time, the literature consistently warns that the tool can produce repetitive, culturally inappropriate, or inaccurate outputs and may encourage overreliance if used uncritically. The paper argues that ChatGPT should be treated as a mediational tool that augments rather than replaces teacher expertise, and it calls for stronger AI literacy, ethical guidance, and future longitudinal classroom-based research.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model system used for dialogue, text generation, and assistance with instructional and feedback tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: This systematic narrative review examined empirical studies of English language teachers using ChatGPT for lesson planning, reflective practice, professional development, student feedback, and related instructional support contexts.

findings.finding_summary: Across 13 empirical studies (2023-2025), ChatGPT was generally perceived as helpful for lesson planning, feedback, reflection, and professional development, but the review also identified recurring concerns about overreliance, cultural insensitivity, ethical risks, hallucination/accuracy problems, and contextual misalignment. The review notes that sustained or structured use could improve teacher self-efficacy and instructional competence, but most included studies were short-term and not longitudinal.
findings.measure: Teacher perceptions, instructional use, reflective practice, self-efficacy, and reported pedagogical/ethical concerns across included studies

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic narrative review synthesizing heterogeneous qualitative, mixed-method, and experimental studies rather than a single rigorous trial or meta-analysis. The evidence is useful but indirect for the specific question of negative/null/sustained-use effects, and most included studies were short-term.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review reports important practical concerns (overreliance, hallucination, privacy, cultural misalignment) and some positive instructional uses, but it does not provide a single quantified effect size for harm or benefit. Overall impact is plausible but unclear and context-dependent.

paper_profiles.title: E-EVAL: A Comprehensive Chinese K-12 Education Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2024)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of a dedicated benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) in Chinese K-12 education. The authors argue that existing general-purpose benchmarks and Chinese language benchmarks do not sufficiently capture the subject-specific, grade-specific, and culturally specific knowledge needed to assess LLM performance in primary, middle, and high school contexts.

To address this gap, the paper introduces E-EVAL, a comprehensive multiple-choice benchmark with 4,351 questions spanning 23 K-12 subjects, divided into arts and science domains. The items were collected from regional homework, practice questions, and mock exams sourced from schools and educational institutions, with manual processing to standardize formulas and verify answers. The study evaluates 15 open-source and commercial LLMs using zero-shot, few-shot-answer-only, and few-shot-chain-of-thought prompting.

The benchmark is not a teacher intervention or classroom deployment study; it is an evaluation paper focused on model capability rather than human participants. The results show that Chinese-dominant models generally outperform English-dominant models on Chinese K-12 questions, but all models perform better on arts than science, and many struggle with mathematics. The paper also finds that few-shot prompting usually helps modestly, while chain-of-thought prompting often lowers overall performance, though it can help on more structured science problems. The authors conclude that E-EVAL can support more rigorous assessment of LLMs for Chinese K-12 educational applications.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational large language model system used for general-purpose question answering and generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of 15 LLMs on the E-EVAL Chinese K-12 benchmark under zero-shot, five-shot answer-only, and five-shot chain-of-thought prompting.

findings.finding_summary: On the full E-EVAL benchmark, ChatGPT achieved 54.6% average accuracy overall (Table 3/8), below multiple Chinese-dominant models and only modestly above random (25.0%). Under prompt variations, it improved from 54.5% zero-shot to 56.9% five-shot answer-only, but dropped to 52.3% with five-shot CoT, indicating limited and unstable gains from prompting.
findings.measure: Accuracy on E-EVAL multiple-choice benchmark

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General large language model category / generic generative AI used for educational question answering and reasoning.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper benchmarks multiple general-purpose LLMs in Chinese K-12 education and analyzes their strengths and limitations as a class, including effects of few-shot prompting and chain-of-thought prompting.

findings.finding_summary: Across 15 evaluated models, performance was generally higher in arts than science and higher in middle school than primary school for top models. The paper also reports that few-shot prompting usually helped slightly, while chain-of-thought prompting had a negative impact on overall performance but helped complex science subjects such as mathematics.
findings.measure: Benchmark accuracy patterns across subject categories and prompt types

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark evaluation paper rather than a field or intervention study, so causal evidence about teacher coaching or lesson-plan feedback is absent. The methodology is systematic and transparent, but the evidence is limited to model benchmark accuracy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports moderate-to-high benchmark performance differences, but these are not direct educational outcome effects and do not demonstrate classroom impact. The overall findings are informative for model capability assessment, yet they do not show clear positive or negative impact on teachers or students.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether an analytical AI feedback platform can support lesson planning in vocational teacher education, and whether it can do so as well as or better than conventional human feedback. The authors focus on a practical problem in teacher education: university instructors often cannot provide detailed, individualized feedback on lesson plans at scale, especially when students are working on complex didactic planning tasks.

The intervention was EDDA, an analytical AI system based on a BERT model trained on coded lesson plans and teaching materials. EDDA analyzed students’ uploaded lesson plans and returned structured expert feedback on didactic and planning dimensions such as sustainability, process orientation, problem orientation, action orientation, individualization, digitalization, learner activation, lesson structure, and cross-linked learning. In the experimental condition, students first received AI feedback and then could request human clarification; the control group received human feedback only. The study ran longitudinally across a semester in two cycles and included 103 master’s students in vocational business education in Germany, working on lesson plans in small groups.
