The main findings suggest that AI feedback can match or sometimes surpass human feedback on some planning dimensions, particularly some sustainability-related aspects, social competences, reflexivity, action-oriented planning, and elements of lesson structure and technology use. However, the study also found that simply using AI did not automatically improve broader meta-dimensions such as AI literacy, attitudes toward AI, motivation, or self-efficacy with digital technologies. The authors conclude that analytical AI platforms can be a useful supplement to traditional feedback, but only when embedded in a broader instructional framework and used with human support.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / AI feedback system, here discussed as a class of LLM-based tools that can generate or evaluate feedback for educational tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reviews prior generative AI feedback literature in teacher education and contrasts it with the analytical AI platform used in the study. It is not the focus of the empirical intervention itself, which uses EDDA instead.

identified_tools.name: Adaptive Feedback System (General)
identified_tools.description: A general analytical AI feedback platform that classifies uploaded lesson plans against a predefined coding scheme and returns individualized expert feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: EDDA (electronic didactic assistance for lesson planning) was used longitudinally across a semester to provide feedback on vocational teacher education lesson plans, compared with human feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In a longitudinal intervention with N=103 vocational teacher education students, the AI-feedback group (n=55) received higher ratings than the human-feedback control group (n=48) on some planning dimensions. The paper reports significant positive intervention effects for sustainability-related social competences and reflexivity, and for SDG 15 (life on land), while some sustainability dimensions were also affected by prior knowledge and attitudes.
findings.measure: Content-analytic ratings of lesson plans on sustainability-related planning dimensions, including SDGs and competences for sustainable change agents

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that the AI feedback did not significantly improve all planning dimensions; several outcomes showed no significant group effect, and some were instead associated with starting level, sustainability knowledge, or sustainability attitudes. The authors also state that the model tended to underestimate planning performance, which could have demotivating effects, but this was discussed as a limitation rather than directly tested as an outcome.
findings.measure: Content-analytic ratings of lesson plans across multiple didactic/planning dimensions

findings.finding_summary: The study did not report direct efficiency outcomes such as time saved, attrition, or repeated adoption behavior by teachers; it instead describes the AI system as a supplement to human feedback and notes that human feedback was still used in the experimental group when needed. No direct measures of overreliance, hallucinations, or privacy harm were reported in the results.
findings.measure: Not directly measured; study design and author discussion only

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal intervention study with a comparison group and repeated use over a semester, which is stronger than a cross-sectional design. However, assignment was not randomized in a traditional sense and the paper reports complex model adjustments and some measurement limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports some positive effects on specific planning dimensions, but many outcomes are null or mixed and effect sizes are not reported in the excerpt. Overall impact appears modest and domain-specific rather than large or consistent across outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI-assisted feedback and EFL writing: a study on proficiency, revision frequency and writing quality
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether AI-assisted writing feedback can improve EFL learners’ academic writing compared with traditional teacher feedback. The paper addresses a practical instructional question: whether a widely available AI writing assistant can support better writing outcomes, more revision activity, and stronger student engagement, while also probing concerns about overreliance and the limits of tool-generated feedback.

The intervention used Grammarly Premium as an AI-assisted feedback system. Sixty postgraduate EFL students in a mandatory English for Academic Purposes writing course were randomly assigned to an experimental group using Grammarly or a control group receiving traditional written teacher feedback. The intervention lasted 6 weeks within an 8-week course, and the same instructor taught both groups with standardized lesson plans. Students in the experimental group received a short training session on using Grammarly critically and were instructed to revise drafts using the tool’s feedback; the control group received delayed written feedback from the instructor.

The study found that the Grammarly group scored significantly higher on the post-test overall writing measure, with especially strong gains in language use and organization, but not in content. Within the experimental group, greater use of AI features and more revisions were positively associated with higher post-test performance. Interview data suggested that students perceived the tool as increasing efficiency, confidence, and grammar awareness, while also emphasizing the need for critical judgment and noting that the tool was weaker for broader language support such as fluency and style.

Overall, the paper concludes that AI-assisted feedback can improve certain dimensions of EFL writing when used thoughtfully, but it does not replace teacher support for higher-order writing concerns. The authors also caution that students should not rely passively on AI suggestions and that the tool’s benefits are concentrated in surface-level correction and revision support rather than content development.

identified_tools.name: Grammarly
identified_tools.description: An AI-powered writing assistant that provides automated feedback on grammar, spelling, punctuation, style, clarity, vocabulary, and limited rewrite suggestions, with plagiarism detection.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by the experimental group as Grammarly Premium for automated feedback and revision support on EFL writing tasks over a 6-week intervention, compared against traditional teacher feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test study with 60 postgraduate EFL students (n=30 Grammarly, n=30 control), the Grammarly group scored significantly higher on the total post-test writing score than the control group. Reported means were 54.37 (SD=5.54) vs 45.50 (SD=5.32), Welch's t(47.35)=10.89, p<0.001; Mann-Whitney U=16.50, z=6.42, p<0.001.
findings.measure: Total post-test academic writing score

findings.finding_summary: For the Content sub-score, the Grammarly group did not differ significantly from the control group. Means were 17.05 (SD=2.15) vs 16.10 (SD=2.30), t(58)=1.68, p=0.098.
findings.measure: Content sub-score of post-test writing rubric

findings.finding_summary: The Grammarly group outperformed the control group on Organization. Means were 18.12 (SD=1.95) vs 15.65 (SD=2.55), Welch's t(51.88)=4.31, p<0.001.
findings.measure: Organization sub-score of post-test writing rubric

findings.finding_summary: The Grammarly group outperformed the control group on Language Use. Means were 19.20 (SD=1.40) vs 13.75 (SD=2.80), Welch's t(40.15)=9.55, p<0.001, indicating a large advantage for the AI-assisted feedback condition on language/mechanics-related writing quality.
findings.measure: Language Use sub-score of post-test writing rubric

findings.finding_summary: Within the Grammarly group (n=30), higher frequency of using Grammarly features and higher revision counts were positively correlated with total post-test score. Significant correlations included generative AI feature use (practice r=0.346, assignment r=0.373), grammar/vocabulary feature use (practice r=0.374, assignment r=0.348), and total revisions (practice r=0.359, assignment r=0.375).
findings.measure: Correlations between feature use / revision frequency and total post-test score

findings.finding_summary: Within the Grammarly group (n=30), use of generative AI features was positively correlated with total revisions during both practice and assignment activities (practice r=0.421, assignment r=0.398), suggesting repeated use was associated with more revision activity.
findings.measure: Correlation between generative AI feature use and total revisions

findings.finding_summary: In hierarchical regression within the Grammarly group (n=30), assignment score explained 16.2% of variance in post-test scores, and adding generative AI usage increased explained variance by 11.3% (R2 from 0.162 to 0.275). Revision frequency did not significantly add explanatory power. The final model reported assignment score (β=0.38) and generative AI usage (β=0.34) as significant unique predictors.
findings.measure: Hierarchical multiple regression predicting post-test score

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single quasi-experimental mixed-methods study rather than a randomized field trial, and some outcomes rely on self-reported usage plus post-hoc correlations. The design is informative but has moderate risk of bias and limited generalizability.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports large, statistically significant gains on total writing and especially language use, with the strongest effects well above the 0.20 threshold. Even the null content result is offset by substantial positive outcomes on the main writing measures.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an analytical AI platform can support lesson-planning feedback in teacher education and whether such support performs as well as or better than human feedback. The authors focus on a practical problem in university-based teacher preparation: instructors often cannot provide frequent, detailed, individualized feedback on lengthy lesson plans, especially when student numbers are large. They also note concerns often associated with AI in education, including transparency, bias, reproducibility, and data protection, and position their system as an alternative to generative AI by using analytical rather than text-generating methods.

The intervention is EDDA, an analytical AI platform that classifies uploaded lesson plans and materials using a BERT-based model and returns expert-level feedback across 10 main categories and 57 subcategories. In the study, one group of master’s-level vocational business education students received AI feedback during a semester and could then discuss the output with a university teacher; a control group received human feedback only. The study was longitudinal, with lesson plans collected at the beginning and end of the semester, and with repeated survey measures of AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competences, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and motivation.

The sample consisted of 103 students in master’s programs for business education in Germany, working in small groups. The study found that AI feedback can match or surpass human feedback on some lesson-planning dimensions, especially several sustainability-related and pedagogical criteria such as social competences, reflexivity, action orientation, lesson structure, learner engagement, and some technology-related aspects. However, the authors also found that simply using AI did not automatically improve AI literacy, motivation, or attitudes, and they emphasize that the platform works best as part of a holistic, teacher-supported framework. They additionally report that some categories in the training data were weaker, which could lead the system to underestimate planning quality and potentially discourage users.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model-based chatbot or AI feedback system with no specific commercial product named.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generative AI generally as a comparator and as a source of potential risks for feedback, but the empirical intervention used EDDA, an analytical AI platform rather than a generative chatbot.

identified_tools.name: Adaptive Feedback System (General)
identified_tools.description: A general analytical AI feedback platform that classifies uploaded lesson plans against predefined criteria and returns individualized expert feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper’s empirical intervention was EDDA (electronic didactic assistance for lesson planning), an analytical AI platform used throughout a longitudinal semester intervention to provide feedback on lesson plans in vocational teacher education.

findings.finding_summary: In a longitudinal intervention with N=103 vocational business education master’s students, EDDA feedback improved some lesson-plan dimensions relative to human feedback, including sustainability-related planning aspects. The paper reports significant positive effects for SDG 15 (life on land; p<0.10), social competences for sustainable development (p<0.05), and reflexivity (p<0.10), while other sustainability dimensions showed no significant intervention effect.
findings.measure: Content analysis ratings of lesson plans for SDGs and competences for sustainable change agents

findings.finding_summary: The study reports that EDDA can supplement traditional feedback because it provides reproducible, individualized expert feedback on lesson plans, but it also tends to underestimate planning performance. The authors explicitly note that this could potentially have demotivating effects because it may mask competence development, and they identify low reliability in some categories as a limitation that increases the potential for error in recommendations.
findings.measure: Expert feedback quality / reliability of automated lesson-plan feedback

findings.finding_summary: For the meta-dimensions, the mere use of the AI platform did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, or motivation. The abstract states that results show the mere use of AI does not automatically enhance AI literacy, change attitudes, or improve motivation; the control and experimental groups did not show clear intervention-driven gains on these broad measures over the semester.
findings.measure: Self-reported AI literacy, AI attitudes, motivation, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and digital competences

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal intervention study with a comparison group and repeated use across a semester, which is stronger than a simple cross-sectional design. However, it is not randomized in the traditional sense and the sample is relatively small, with some measures and categories showing reliability limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention shows modest positive effects on some lesson-plan dimensions, but the paper also reports null effects for broader AI literacy, attitudes, and motivation, plus a potential negative downside from underestimation that could demotivate users. Overall impact appears mixed and generally modest rather than large.

paper_profiles.title: A review on enhancing education with AI: exploring the potential of ChatGPT, Bard, and generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a review of the role of generative AI in education, focusing on ChatGPT, Bard, and similar large language model-based tools. It asks what benefits these systems may offer to teaching and learning, and what challenges arise when they are introduced into educational settings. The review emphasizes both the promise of generative AI and the need to account for ethical, pedagogical, privacy, and implementation concerns.

The paper does not report a single empirical intervention. Instead, it synthesizes 33 recent peer-reviewed articles selected from 2020–2024, drawn from educational and related journals. The review covers uses such as personalized learning, virtual tutoring, content generation, automated grading, administrative support, and accessibility enhancement. It also discusses concerns including academic integrity, content accuracy, bias, transparency, data privacy, teacher training, equity of access, overreliance on AI, and the need for ongoing adaptation.

The context is broad and international rather than tied to one school level, country, or institution. The article frames generative AI as relevant to students, teachers, curriculum developers, policymakers, and school leaders. Its main conclusion is that generative AI may support education, but responsible adoption requires strong human oversight, professional development, ethical guidelines, privacy protections, and quality assurance mechanisms. The paper is largely conceptual and review-based, so it does not provide direct evidence from classroom implementation or longitudinal use.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's generative AI chatbot/model family for conversational text generation and assistance; Bard is a prior name in this family.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reviews Bard alongside ChatGPT and other generative AI tools in education, discussing potential uses such as personalized learning, content creation, virtual tutoring, and feedback.

findings.finding_summary: This review synthesizes claims and concerns about Bard and similar generative AI in education rather than reporting original empirical results. It highlights potential benefits such as personalized learning, content generation, and automated feedback, but also emphasizes privacy, ethical, pedagogical, and overreliance concerns; no effect sizes or sample sizes are reported.
findings.measure: Narrative review of opportunities and challenges in education

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI system used for text generation, question answering, tutoring, and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reviews ChatGPT as a generative AI tool in education, focusing on its potential roles in personalized learning, virtual tutoring, lesson-plan/content generation, and feedback, along with associated risks.

findings.finding_summary: This review does not present a direct field study of ChatGPT with teachers or instructional coaches. It synthesizes perceived benefits (personalized learning, tutoring, lesson creation, administrative support) and risks including privacy concerns, inaccurate generated content, bias, teacher training needs, and overreliance; no quantitative effect estimates are reported.
findings.measure: Narrative review of opportunities and challenges in education

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review article, not a primary empirical study or meta-analysis. It summarizes general claims about generative AI in education without original outcome data, effect sizes, or a teacher/coaching field study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper discusses potentially important system-level implications for education, including privacy, overreliance, and pedagogical concerns, but it provides no measurable impact estimates. Because there is no empirical effect to assess, the impact is best treated as unclear rather than positive or negative.

paper_profiles.title: Transforming learning or creating dependency? Teachers’ perspectives and barriers to AI integration in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines teachers’ perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) integration in education, with a particular focus on whether AI can transform learning or instead create dependency. The study is motivated by growing enthusiasm for generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and DALL-E alongside concerns about overreliance, misinformation, plagiarism, privacy, and the erosion of critical thinking and teacher roles.

The authors conducted a qualitative phenomenological study using a single focus group discussion with 127 teachers from five districts in South Kalimantan, Indonesia. Participants were teachers in rural Madrasah Aliyah (Islamic senior high schools), and the discussion centered on perceptions of AI, anticipated impacts, barriers to implementation, and suggested solutions. Teachers generally saw AI as useful for tailored information, brainstorming, immediate feedback, and creative support, but they also warned that students—especially low-motivation and low-literacy learners—could become overly dependent on AI, use it as a shortcut, or accept hallucinated or biased outputs uncritically.

The study concludes that AI integration in these rural schools is constrained by low student motivation, weak digital and AI literacy, limited teacher readiness, administrative burden, smartphone restrictions, and broader infrastructure and policy barriers. Teachers recommended project-based learning, personalized curricula, greater openness to controlled device use, and targeted professional development. Overall, the paper argues that AI should be treated as a support tool rather than a replacement for human teaching, and that successful adoption requires parallel investments in literacy, teacher capacity, and ethical guidance.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM used for conversational text generation, question answering, and related language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers discussed ChatGPT as an AI tool for information provision, lesson support, brainstorming, translation, feedback-like assistance, and classroom learning support; the paper did not evaluate a specific deployment but reported teacher perceptions of its use in education.

findings.finding_summary: In focus group discussions with 127 teachers, ChatGPT was viewed as useful for tailored responses, synthesis of complex information, brainstorming, and immediate assistance, but teachers also reported concerns about over-dependence, reduced critical thinking, misinformation/hallucinations, plagiarism, and privacy. The study is qualitative and reports perceptions rather than measured effects.
findings.measure: Teachers' perceptions in focus group discussions

identified_tools.name: DALL-E
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative image model for creating illustrations and visual content from text prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers referenced DALL-E as an AI tool that could generate illustrations meeting specific learning needs.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers described DALL-E as useful for generating illustrations for creative and visual learning. No outcome data were measured; this was a perception-based qualitative study.
findings.measure: Teachers' perceptions in focus group discussions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative focus-group study with 127 teachers, so it provides contextual evidence about perceived benefits and risks but no causal or longitudinal effectiveness estimates. The methodology supports insight into barriers and concerns, not efficacy claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful concerns and some perceived usefulness, but there are no quantitative effects, no intervention outcomes, and no direct evidence of impact on teacher coaching or lesson-plan feedback.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can serve as an automated teacher coach by generating classroom-observation scores and pedagogically useful feedback from classroom transcripts. The authors focus on three teacher-coaching tasks for generative AI: scoring transcript segments using classroom observation rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study evaluates gpt-3.5-turbo (ChatGPT) in zero-shot mode using the National Center for Teacher Effectiveness (NCTE) transcript dataset. The transcripts come from 1,660 elementary mathematics classroom observations collected from 317 teachers across four U.S. school districts serving largely historically marginalized students. For the qualitative tasks, the researchers recruited two experienced math teachers, including one instructional coach, to rate model outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty. For the scoring task, they compared model predictions with existing expert ratings on CLASS and MQI observation items.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT shows promise as a scalable feedback tool but performs poorly relative to human expert judgments. It has low correlations with human scores on observation items, often produces generic or redundant suggestions, and generates a nontrivial amount of unfaithful or hallucinated feedback. The paper argues that current generative AI should complement, not replace, human coaching, and highlights privacy, hallucination, and alignment concerns when using classroom transcripts for automated feedback.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational language model used for zero-shot text generation and prediction.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated zero-shot on three teacher-coaching tasks: scoring classroom transcript segments, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: On transcript scoring, ChatGPT showed low Spearman correlation with human ratings across CLASS and MQI dimensions (e.g., CLPC 0.00/0.04/-0.06; CLBM 0.35/0.23/0.07; CLINSTD -0.01/0.07/-0.05; EXPL 0.02/0.12/-0.11; REMED 0.05/0.06/-0.06; LANGIMP 0.00/0.02/0.04; SMQR 0.17/0.17/0.06 across DA/DA+/RA prompts). The paper concludes the model performed poorly at scoring classroom transcripts and that added rubric descriptions or reasoning did not improve performance.
findings.measure: Spearman correlation between model-predicted and human-rated observation scores

findings.finding_summary: For identifying highlights and missed opportunities, teachers generally did not find ChatGPT's responses insightful or relevant. The paper reports that 20-30% of responses were judged unfaithful, with model performance worse on MQI than CLASS; low scores on faithful increased from 22% to 29%, relevant from 35% to 55%, and insightful from 51% to 71% when moving from CLASS to MQI.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for generated feedback
findings.sample_size: n=504 evaluated items total (216 CLASS + 288 MQI)

findings.finding_summary: For actionable suggestions to elicit student reasoning, 82% of ChatGPT's suggestions were redundant, meaning they repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript. The authors note that although many suggestions were actionable and faithful, the strong redundancy indicates limited novelty and substantial overreliance on transcript restatement.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of faithfulness, relevance, actionability, and novelty/redundancy of suggestions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single paper with qualitative and correlational evaluation of ChatGPT rather than a randomized or causal field study. The methodology is clear, but the evidence is limited to a small sample of teacher raters and transcript segments.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main findings are negative or null for teacher-coaching performance: low score correlation, unfaithful or non-insightful feedback, and 82% redundant suggestions. Reported effects are not framed as beneficial classroom impact and there are no positive outcome effect sizes to support meaningful impact.

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service elementary science teachers incorporated ChatGPT into lesson planning and what they believed the tool could and could not do in science instruction. The study was motivated by a gap between optimistic claims about generative AI in education and the limited empirical evidence showing how it is actually used in classroom-oriented planning.

The intervention/context consisted of a short professional-learning experience on ChatGPT followed by an assignment in which 29 pre-service teachers at a Korean teachers' university created elementary science lesson plans that used ChatGPT. Participants also attached simulated ChatGPT conversations and completed open-ended survey questions about their reasoning, anticipated benefits, and concerns. The authors evaluated the plans with a modified TPACK-based technology-integration rubric and analyzed the survey responses qualitatively.

The pre-service teachers envisioned ChatGPT supporting a wide range of science topics and instructional approaches, especially cooperative learning, POE, the learning cycle, analogy generation, and concept mapping. Overall lesson-plan quality was moderately high, but participants were weaker at selecting the most appropriate ChatGPT functions than at aligning ChatGPT with goals and instructional strategies. They saw potential for questioning, individualized support, and formative feedback, but also worried about inaccurate or misleading outputs, hallucinated or non-existent resources, and student overreliance. The paper concludes that AI literacy, critical checking, and structured classroom interactions are necessary to mitigate these risks and that future research should test ChatGPT in real science classrooms rather than only in lesson plans.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's LLM-based conversational AI chatbot for generating and refining text, answering questions, and supporting interactive dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: Pre-service elementary science teachers used ChatGPT in lesson-plan design for science instruction, including content expansion, role-play scripting, individualized support, formative feedback, and simulated teacher/student interactions.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative/mixed-methods study of 29 pre-service elementary science teachers, lesson plans integrating ChatGPT received an average modified TPACK-based TIAR score of M=3.29 (SD=.91) on a 4-point scale. Scores were higher for curriculum goals & ChatGPT (M=3.44, SD=.87) and instructional strategies & ChatGPT (M=3.48, SD=.99) than for ChatGPT function selection(s) (M=3.00, SD=.93); the difference between items 2 and 3 was significant, t(28)=2.3173, p=.0280.
findings.measure: Modified TPACK-based lesson-plan rubric (TIAR) scores

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that some uses of ChatGPT were appropriate, such as supporting extended questioning, role-play organization, and concise summarization, but others were inappropriate or unreliable, including nonexistent YouTube links, inaccurate or non-existent materials, and use in visually oriented tasks where ChatGPT was poorly matched. The authors also note risks of overdependence, hallucination, and pedagogical misalignment in lesson planning.
findings.measure: Qualitative analysis of lesson plans and survey responses

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods preprint focused on lesson plans and perceptions rather than a controlled effectiveness study. It provides useful empirical evidence about how ChatGPT was planned for instructional use and about concerns such as hallucinations and overreliance, but causal evidence is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports mixed practical implications rather than outcome gains or harms on student achievement, and no effect size is provided. Its main impact is descriptive: it surfaces both promising uses and clear risks in teacher planning with ChatGPT.

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study examines how K-12 math educators evaluate lesson plans generated by generative AI systems versus human curriculum designers. The paper addresses a practical question in educational AI: whether GenAI-produced lesson plans are perceived as pedagogically comparable to human-authored plans, and which lesson-plan components benefit most from AI assistance.

The intervention/approach compared three sources of lesson plans: a customized prompt-engineered GPT-4 model, a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model trained on lesson-plan data, and human-created lesson plans retrieved from an open-source repository. Twenty experienced K-12 mathematics educators, all with more than 10 years of teaching experience, reviewed paired lesson plans online over several weeks and selected their preferred plan across four dimensions: warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality. Participants also left written comments explaining their choices, which were analyzed thematically alongside the quantitative preference data.

The study found that human-created lesson plans were generally preferred overall, especially for elementary grades and for instructional elements requiring scaffolding, differentiation, student discourse, and structured collaboration. GenAI plans were more competitive in cool-down/lesson-wrap-up sections, and performance tended to improve in higher grade levels, particularly for the fine-tuned LLaMA model in high school contexts. The authors conclude that GenAI is better suited as an assistive planning tool than a replacement for educators, with human expertise still needed for pedagogical nuance and inclusive instruction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used to generate instructional text and lesson plans.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a customized prompt-based GPT-4 model to generate K-12 mathematics lesson plans for comparison with human curriculum designer lesson plans and a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model.

findings.finding_summary: In pairwise educator preference ratings across 529 lesson-plan pairs (16 educators; 2,116 total evaluations), customized GPT-4 was preferred over fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b in 57.7% of comparisons, but was less preferred than human curriculum designer plans overall (human plans preferred 58.7% vs. GPT-4 41.3%). GPT-4 was especially favored for cool-down sections (59.7% over human plans), while human-authored plans were favored for warm-up, main tasks, and overall quality.
findings.measure: Binary educator preference for warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall lesson quality

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta large language model used to generate instructional text and lesson plans.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model trained on expert-designed K-12 lesson plans to generate mathematics lesson plans for comparison with customized GPT-4 and human curriculum designer plans.

findings.finding_summary: In pairwise educator preference ratings across 529 lesson-plan pairs, fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b was preferred less often than customized GPT-4 (42.3% vs. 57.7%) and slightly less often than human curriculum designer plans overall (human plans preferred 53.6% vs. LLaMA-2-13b FT 46.4%). LLaMA-2-13b performed comparatively better in cool-down sections (57.9% over human plans) and was particularly competitive at the high-school level, where it was preferred over human-created plans in 59.2% of comparisons.
findings.measure: Binary educator preference for warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall lesson quality

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods comparative user study with direct educator preferences, but it is not a randomized field trial and reports no causal learning outcome estimates. Evidence quality is therefore moderate-to-lower for inference about instructional effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports preference differences rather than effect sizes on student or teacher outcomes, and no impact estimates are provided. The practical signal is mixed: AI was sometimes preferred in cool-downs, but human-authored plans were generally favored overall.

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a generative AI-based lesson-planning system, Shiksha Copilot, was used by teachers in low-resource government schools. The paper is motivated by a practical problem common in under-resourced K–12 settings: teachers face heavy administrative demands, limited preparation time, multilingual classroom needs, and pressure to produce curriculum-aligned lesson plans for documentation and instruction. The authors ask how teachers collaborate with AI, what challenges arise when deploying LLM-generated lesson plans in non-English-medium classrooms, and how the tool affects teachers’ work practices.

Shiksha Copilot combined LLM generation, retrieval-augmented generation, human curation, and bilingual English-Kannada support. Lesson plans were first drafted by AI, then reviewed by expert curators, and finally customized by teachers for their own classrooms. The deployment involved 1,043 teachers across 757 government schools in Karnataka, India, plus 23 curators and 4 mentors. Teachers received training before deployment and then used the web-based system to access curated lesson plans, customize them, and optionally use chat and question-generation features. The study used a mixed-methods design with interviews, surveys, and platform log analysis.

The findings suggest that the system was useful for reducing lesson-planning time, easing bureaucratic documentation work, and lowering teacher stress. Teachers often used the plans as a starting point and adapted them using their own expertise and peer resources. The paper reports high reliability for English lesson plans, but substantial linguistic problems in Kannada translations, which required extensive human editing. More broadly, the authors conclude that AI can support teacher work in low-resource settings when paired with human oversight, but that multilingual quality, pedagogical alignment, and classroom context remain major challenges.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI / LLM-based lesson-planning and teacher-support system used to draft, translate, curate, and customize curriculum-aligned lesson plans, plus related chat and question-generation features.
identified_tools.use_case: Shiksha Copilot was deployed in Karnataka government schools to support teacher lesson planning, bilingual English-Kannada content generation, curation, customization, and lesson-specific/general educational Q&A.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed-methods deployment with 1,043 teachers and 23 curators, the system reduced lesson-planning time and eased bureaucratic workload. Teachers reported lower record-keeping burden and lower teaching-related stress; the paper also states that 85 of 5,542 teacher-created lesson plans (1.53%) and 19 of 1,480 Kannada-medium plans (1.28%) were modified on-platform, while most customization happened off-platform.
findings.measure: Lesson-planning time, administrative workload/record-keeping burden, and teacher stress (Teacher Stress Scale); platform log counts of edited lesson plans
findings.sample_size: n=1043 teachers; n=23 curators; survey analyses on n=406 matched responses

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods field deployment with surveys, interviews, and log analysis rather than an experimental impact study. It provides useful real-world evidence, but causal attribution is limited and key outcomes are reported without effect sizes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful practical benefits such as reduced lesson-planning time and stress, but no effect sizes are provided and the evidence is not from a controlled design. The low on-platform edit rates suggest adoption, but they do not quantify impact magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: Augmenting Coaching with GenAI: Insights into Use, Effectiveness, and Future Potential
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how professional coaches are currently using generative AI tools and what shapes their adoption, with particular attention to perceived benefits, limitations, ethical concerns, and expectations for future use. The study is motivated by the rapid spread of large language models in professional workflows and by the lack of empirical evidence on real-world GenAI use in coaching. Rather than testing a classroom intervention, the paper asks how coaches already using GenAI integrate it into their practice and how they evaluate its usefulness and risks.

The study used an online survey of 205 active coaching professionals recruited through Prolific in January 2025. Participants were mostly health and fitness, business, career, and life coaches based in the United States, the United Kingdom, and other European countries. They reported on their use of text-based GenAI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude across coaching tasks including research, content creation, administrative work, analysis, and relational support. The survey also measured AI literacy, positive and negative attitudes toward AI, ethical considerations such as transparency and privacy, perceived effectiveness, and expectations for future AI use.

Findings show that GenAI is already widely adopted for efficiency-oriented tasks, especially research, brainstorming, content generation, and administration, but is used less for relational and interpretive work. Higher AI literacy, positive AI attitudes, and stronger perceived impact of AI were associated with greater use. By contrast, negative attitudes, concerns about replacement, and ethical concerns did not significantly reduce current use. Frequent users reported greater awareness of ethical issues, especially transparency and privacy, and many respondents emphasized the need for stronger safeguards and coaching-specific tools. The paper concludes that GenAI functions mainly as an augmentation tool in coaching rather than a substitute for human coaches, while calling for better AI literacy training, ethical guidelines, and longitudinal research on how use evolves over time.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based generative AI chatbot / assistant for text generation, analysis, and conversational support.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as one of the text-based GenAI tools used by coaching professionals in their coaching practice; the paper reports ChatGPT 4.0 as the most frequently preferred primary tool.

findings.finding_summary: Among 205 coaching professionals, ChatGPT 4.0 was the most frequently preferred tool (65.4%). Nearly half of participants (49.8%) had used their preferred tool for more than one year, and 36.1% used it daily with another 36.1% using it multiple times per day. Coaches reported high perceived usefulness for research, automation, and content generation, while use was more limited for deeply interpersonal and interpretive tasks.
findings.measure: Self-reported tool preference, duration of use, frequency of use, and perceived effectiveness/role in coaching tasks

findings.finding_summary: In a multiple regression predicting GenAI use, perceived current AI impact, AI literacy, and positive AI attitudes were significant positive predictors, but negative AI attitudes, ethical considerations, expected future AI use, belief in AI as a substitute, and concerns about AI replacing coaching were not significant. The overall model explained 50.6% of the variance in GenAI use (R2=0.506, Adjusted R2=0.488, F(8,196)=25.343, p<.001).
findings.measure: Regression model predicting GenAI use

findings.finding_summary: The paper identifies privacy and confidentiality as a key ethical concern in coaches' use of ChatGPT-based tools, noting that almost 94% of respondents reported using a version of ChatGPT as their primary GenAI tool and that these tools are not set up for secure handling of personal, sensitive data. This is presented as an ethical limitation rather than an outcome effect.
findings.measure: Self-reported ethical considerations and discussion of data security/privacy risks

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey with self-report measures from coaches already using GenAI, so it provides useful descriptive and associative evidence but not causal or field-experimental evidence. The study is methodologically clear, but it is not a direct K–12 teacher coaching intervention study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported associations are substantial in size for adoption behavior (e.g., R2=0.506), but they describe use, attitudes, and ethics rather than learning or instructional outcomes. The paper suggests meaningful operational impact for coaching workflows, yet it does not demonstrate educational harm or benefit in K–12 teacher coaching specifically.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring K-12 Physical Education Teachers’ Perspectives on Opportunities and Challenges of AI Integration Through Ideation Workshops
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 physical education (PE) teachers perceive the opportunities and challenges of integrating artificial intelligence into their classes. The authors note that while AI has been widely discussed in education, PE remains underexplored despite its distinctive instructional demands, such as large open spaces, safety monitoring, individualized feedback, and multi-dimensional assessment.

To explore these issues, the study conducted in-person focus group ideation workshops with 17 in-service secondary school PE teachers in South Korea. Participants first discussed their classroom challenges, then received short instructional introductions to basic AI capabilities and ideated potential AI-supported solutions through sketching, storyboarding, and role-playing. The workshop format was designed to surface both envisioned uses of AI and the concerns teachers had about adoption and implementation.

Teachers envisioned AI in four broad supportive roles: operational assistant, personal trainer, group coach, and evaluator. Across these roles, they imagined AI helping with class management, personalized feedback, balanced team formation, and assessment automation. At the same time, participants raised concerns about institutional support, infrastructure, teacher technology readiness, pedagogical misalignment, overuse and overreliance, and student data privacy. The paper concludes that AI should support rather than replace teachers and that successful integration in PE requires alignment with pedagogical goals, robust infrastructure, and careful attention to ethical and practical constraints.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI / AI chatbot or AI system concept used for instructional support, feedback, class management, and evaluation; no specific commercial product is named in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is an ideation-workshop study in which 17 in-service K-12 secondary physical education teachers envisioned possible AI roles in PE classes (operational assistant, personal trainer, group coach, evaluator) and discussed benefits and concerns.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative ideation/workshop study with 17 teachers, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool. It provides useful user-perspective evidence but no outcome testing or causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report measured effects on student or teacher outcomes, so there is no demonstrated positive or negative impact. It does surface important implementation concerns such as overreliance, privacy, and pedagogical misalignment, but these are anticipatory rather than observed impacts.

paper_profiles.title: PIR Over Wireless Channels: Achieving Privacy With Public Responses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a communications-theory problem: private information retrieval (PIR) over a public additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel, where server responses are visible to other servers and may leak the identity of the requested message. The authors focus on the privacy risk introduced by a wireless/shared-medium setting, which is not covered by earlier PIR work that assumed servers could not overhear each other’s responses.

To solve this, the paper proposes a joint PIR-channel coding scheme based on nested lattice codes and wiretap coset coding. The scheme is developed for both a two-server case and a general N-server case, including a block-fading AWGN multiple-access channel. The user sends carefully structured queries, servers encode linear combinations of messages, and the public transmissions are designed so the intended receiver can decode while a curious server cannot infer the desired index from overheard signals.

The paper is purely theoretical and does not study human participants, teachers, students, classrooms, or any educational intervention. Its main results are achievable PIR rate expressions showing that positive PIR rates remain possible even under public responses and, in the fading case, even when the malicious server’s channel can be stronger than the user’s. The authors also discuss secrecy and decoding conditions, along with scaling behavior as the number of servers increases.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system: an AI-driven instructional system that provides adaptive guidance, practice, or feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Not studied in this paper. The paper is about private information retrieval over wireless channels in information theory, not an educational AI tool.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is not an education study and does not evaluate an AI tool in a K–12 setting. It is a theoretical information theory paper on private information retrieval over AWGN/MAC channels.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured educational impact, no teacher or student sample, and no instructional coaching or lesson-feedback intervention reported.

paper_profiles.title: Generalized Planning with Deep Reinforcement Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of generalized planning: learning a policy from small planning instances that can be reused to solve much larger instances in the same domain. The authors argue that a good generalized planner should discover principles that extend beyond the training distribution, rather than memorizing instance-specific solutions.

The proposed approach combines graph neural networks with deep reinforcement learning. Planning states are represented as graphs derived from PDDL predicates, and candidate actions are represented through their effects. A policy and value function are trained with PPO on sparse binary rewards, using randomly generated instances from five classical planning domains: Blocksworld, Satellite, Logistics, Gripper, and Ferry. During inference, the learned policy is optionally embedded in a GBFS-style search procedure (GBFS-GNN) to improve performance on harder instances.

The paper evaluates whether policies trained on small instances can generalize to much larger ones. The main findings are that the approach generalizes well on four of the five domains and can outperform or match a strong classical planner on several metrics, but it fails to generalize well in Logistics. The work is methodological and does not involve teachers, students, or educational settings; it is included here only because it relates to generative/AI methods, not because it studies instructional coaching or lesson feedback.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring / automated planning or decision-support system archetype that learns policies to choose actions in sequential decision problems.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies generalized planning policies learned with deep reinforcement learning and graph neural networks for classical planning domains, not an educational product or teacher-facing tool.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/algorithmic machine learning paper on generalized planning in classical AI domains, with no educational intervention, no teacher sample, and no empirical study of a K-12 instructional coaching tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There are no reported education outcomes, no effect sizes, and no evidence of impact on teachers, coaching, or lesson-plan feedback in K–12 settings.

paper_profiles.title: Privacy Games
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies how privacy concerns change strategic behavior in a simple Bayesian signaling game. The authors ask whether the behavior of a self-interested, utility-maximizing agent with explicit privacy costs can be modeled using differential privacy ideas, and how that behavior differs depending on how privacy loss is operationalized. The central question is not about educational technology or AI, but about the game-theoretic behavior of agents when one player tries to infer another player’s hidden type.

The paper introduces a family of “coupon games” in which agent B has a secret binary type and sends a signal to agent A, who then takes an action and/or makes a prediction. The authors analyze three payment structures: symmetric proper scoring rules, identity-matrix payments, and a variant with an opt-out option. For each game they derive Bayesian Nash equilibria and compare them to a benchmark game without signaling. The analysis is theoretical and mathematical, with no human participants, experiments, schools, teachers, or instructional setting.

The main conclusion is that small changes in how privacy costs are modeled can lead to very different equilibrium behavior. In some settings B randomizes in a way related to randomized response; in others at least one type behaves deterministically; and in some parameter regimes the receiver’s posterior becomes symmetric or otherwise threshold-based. The paper also shows that whether an information-disclosure game is worthwhile for the receiver depends on the payment rule and parameter values, but it does not address education, coaching, lesson feedback, or generative AI use.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: No AI tool or generative model is studied in this paper. The paper is a theoretical game-theory/privacy paper about privacy-aware agents and coupon-game equilibria, not an empirical evaluation of an educational AI product.
identified_tools.use_case: Not applicable; the paper does not study teacher coaching, lesson-plan feedback, or any generative AI system in education.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/game-theoretic paper with no empirical study, no educational setting, and no evaluation of an AI tool. It does not provide evidence about K–12 teacher coaching or lesson-plan feedback.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured educational or operational outcome and no direct AI intervention, so there is no impact to assess.

paper_profiles.title: Novobo: Supporting Teachers’ Peer Learning of Instructional Gestures by Teaching a Mentee AI-Agent Together
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI and teachable-agent designs might support teachers’ professional learning around instructional gestures, a form of embodied pedagogical skill that is difficult to teach through text alone. The authors argue that existing approaches to gesture training are often time-consuming, overly prescriptive, or insufficiently reflective of context, and propose a teacher-facing AI mentee that can stimulate peer learning rather than simply deliver feedback.

The intervention, Novobo, is a generative AI teachable agent built around retrieval-augmented generation and a multi-agent architecture. Teachers pose classroom scenarios, review AI-generated gesture suggestions with literature references, rate and comment on them, demonstrate their own gestures using a skeletal webcam mirror, and then explain the pedagogical rationale for their choices. This design intentionally frames the AI as a novice mentee so that teachers can mentor it together, externalize tacit knowledge, and discuss gesture use in a low-pressure collaborative setting.

The study involved 30 teachers from seven local primary schools, including two special education schools, in collaborative study-group sessions. The evaluation combined vignette analysis of interaction behavior with thematic analysis of focus-group reflections, yielding evidence that the system helped teachers share, compare, and refine embodied knowledge through discussion and demonstration. Teachers also valued cited sources and the mentor-mentee framing, which reduced skepticism and social pressure. The paper concludes that teachable agents can support collaborative professional development for teachers, but the reported evidence is exploratory rather than outcome-comparative, and the system was not evaluated for long-term learning gains or classroom impact.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-based large language model system used to generate instructional-gesture descriptions, analyze instructional intentions, and support conversational interaction in a teachable-agent workflow.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the underlying LLM family for Novobo’s multi-agent architecture, including gesture generation, intention analysis, and conversation management via GPT-4-turbo and GPT-3.5-turbo.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative/mixed-methods field evaluation with 30 teachers across 10 collaborative sessions, Novobo’s GPT-based design supported teachers’ peer learning of instructional gestures. The paper reports that teachers externalized tacit knowledge, exchanged ideas, and co-constructed understanding while interacting with the agent; no quantitative effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Teacher peer-learning processes, knowledge exchange, and responses in field evaluation and focus groups

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical field evaluation with teachers, but it is qualitative/mixed-methods rather than a controlled trial. The evidence is useful for design insight but does not establish causal impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive interaction and collaborative-learning effects, but no quantitative effect size or causal estimate is provided. Impact is therefore suggestive but unclear in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: LLM Performance Predictors: Learning When to Escalate in Hybrid Human-AI Moderation Systems
paper_profiles.venue: Proc. of the 25th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems (AAMAS 2026)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of when to trust a large language model’s output versus when to escalate to a human reviewer in hybrid human-AI content moderation systems. The authors frame this as an uncertainty quantification and selective classification problem: a system should automate easy cases and defer risky ones to human review. They propose a new meta-model based on LLM Performance Predictors (LPPs) derived from model outputs, including token probabilities, entropy, verbalized confidence, and explicit uncertainty-attribution indicators.

The approach is evaluated on two moderation benchmarks: the OpenAI Moderation dataset and a multimodal moderation dataset spanning text, video, transcripts, thumbnails, and multiple languages. The experiments compare several proprietary and open-source LLMs and show that the proposed meta-model often improves error prediction and reduces expected moderation cost relative to baseline uncertainty heuristics such as maximum softmax probability, entropy, and top-2 margin. In some cases, however, performance is mixed under distribution shift, and the paper notes model-dependent limitations.

The paper is not a K–12 education study and does not involve teachers, students, classrooms, or instructional coaching. It is a technical systems paper about human-AI moderation workflows. Its main conclusion is that uncertainty-aware routing can improve operational efficiency and explainability in moderation, but the authors also note limitations such as the need for labeled data, the possibility of calibration issues, and mixed generalization across model families and datasets.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: A Google family of large language models used here as a base model for content-moderation classification and uncertainty estimation in a hybrid human-AI workflow.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of several LLMs whose outputs were used to predict correctness and decide whether to trust the model or escalate cases to human reviewers in content moderation tasks.

findings.finding_summary: Across the OpenAI Moderation dataset, Gemini-family models showed lower expected cost under the proposed meta-model than under baseline uncertainty heuristics. For example, gemini-2.5-flash-lite decreased from $122 to $77 expected cost with escalations falling from 315 to 227, and gemini-2.0-flash-lite decreased from $74 to $41 with escalations falling from 248 to 162.

paper_profiles.title: Late-Time Observations of Type Ia Supernova SN 2014J with the Hubble Space Telescope Wide Field Camera 3
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper does not address education or generative AI. It presents late-time astronomical observations of Type Ia supernova SN 2014J using the Hubble Space Telescope Wide Field Camera 3. The study was motivated by questions about late-time supernova light-curve behavior, light-echo contamination, and whether late-time decline rates can be compared directly across supernovae to test proposed correlations with intrinsic luminosity.

The intervention or approach is complementary HST photometry in three filters (F438W, F555W, and F814W) taken between roughly 365 and 1296 days after peak B-band light. The author performs aperture photometry, checks for contamination from resolved and unresolved light echoes, and compares the resulting light curves to those of other well-studied Type Ia supernovae observed in similar bands. The analysis also includes linear fits to estimate decline rates over late-time intervals.

The paper concludes that SN 2014J’s late-time photometry is not contaminated by an unresolved light echo and that the new WFC3 measurements are consistent with previous ACS measurements in the overlapping green bandpass. It also finds that the observed late-time decline rates in F438W and F555W remain consistent with the previously reported trend that more luminous Type Ia supernovae decline more slowly at late times, though the author notes that the sample remains small and additional supernovae are needed for a definitive test.

paper_profiles.title: An Evaluation of the Pedagogical Soundness and Usability of AI-Generated Lesson Plans Across Different Models and Prompt Frameworks in High-School Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-generated lesson plans are pedagogically sound and usable for classroom instruction, with a focus on high-school physics. The central question is not student learning impact, but how lesson-plan quality varies across large language models and structured prompting approaches, especially in terms of readability, factual accuracy, curriculum alignment, and cognitive demand.

The study generated fifteen lesson plans for a single topic, The Electromagnetic Spectrum, using five LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Grok) crossed with three prompt frameworks (TAG, RACE, and COSTAR). The plans were created for mixed-ability Grades 9–12 classrooms and then evaluated with automated metrics measuring readability, hallucination/factual errors, NGSS alignment, and Bloom’s taxonomy level. No human participants were involved as intervention recipients; the paper evaluates model outputs rather than classroom implementation.

The findings suggest that model choice most strongly affected readability, while prompt framework structure mattered more for factual completeness and incidental standards alignment. RACE generally produced the best factual and curricular results, while DeepSeek produced the most accessible language. Across all models and prompts, objectives clustered at lower Bloom’s levels, with few higher-order objectives. The paper concludes that effective lesson planning with generative AI requires careful model selection, structured prompts, and explicit instructional checklists to improve completeness and pedagogical quality.

identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational large language model/chatbot used for generating text outputs such as lesson plans.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate AI lesson plans for the high-school physics topic The Electromagnetic Spectrum under TAG, RACE, and COSTAR prompts; also used to refine Python code snippets.

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT-generated lesson plans showed moderate readability (mean FKGL=10.86; mean FRE=41.73) and moderate incidental NGSS alignment (mean 0.063). run_graph_section:
## Research Architecture & Open Questions

### Field Anchors

The citation structure points to two pre-2023 works as the clearest foundations for the present literature on teachers’ use of generative AI for coaching-like support and lesson-plan feedback. The first, “Characterization of Models for Identifying Physical and Cognitive” (2020), appears to function as a methodological anchor for later education-facing reviews and design papers, especially those concerned with how AI systems are characterized, interpreted, or positioned for instructional use [17], [21], [27]. In practice, later work seems to depend on it less for teacher coaching specifically than for a broader framework for thinking about model capabilities and educational applicability. The second anchor, “Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code” (2021), appears to establish an evaluation logic for large language model performance that is then taken up in work on code generation and broader generative AI surveys [25], [30]. For the teacher-feedback topic, its importance is indirect but still consequential: it underwrites expectations that model outputs can be assessed systematically and compared across tasks before being embedded in educational support workflows.

More immediate domain-specific grounding comes from adjacent literatures rather than from a mature teacher-coaching lineage. Peer feedback and observation research provides a non-AI baseline for instructional improvement [22]. Reviews of AI in higher education, ChatGPT in education, K–12 use, and teacher professional development establish the surrounding conceptual and implementation landscape into which teacher-facing generative AI feedback studies now fit [17], [15], [16], [20], [21], [9].

### Intellectual Lineage

| Foundational Paper | Year | What It Established | Extended By (papers from this run that build on it) |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Characterization of Models for Identifying Physical and Cognitive | 2020 | A general framework for characterizing AI models that later education papers draw on when discussing model use, capability, and educational deployment. | [17], [21], [27] |
| Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code | 2021 | An evaluation-oriented precedent for judging large language model outputs, especially in task-based settings. | [25], [30] |

### Research Gaps

The clearest gap is evidentiary rather than conceptual. The network identifies an active subfield with substantial momentum but no randomized controlled trial evidence. That matters directly for teacher coaching and lesson-plan feedback, where many recent papers are reviews, mappings, or exploratory studies rather than causal tests of effectiveness [4], [5], [6], [9], [15], [20]. There is some emerging work on AI-supported lesson planning in vocational teacher education [28], [29] and on pre-service teachers’ perceptions of AI versus expert or peer feedback [19], but modern extensions remain thin for in-service K–12 teachers, especially in school-based coaching contexts. English language learner contexts are also flagged as underrepresented in the hypothesis surface, and current extensions appear more concentrated on student writing and language-learning applications than on teachers as feedback recipients [10], [14], [27]. Outcome coverage is similarly narrow: the literature appears stronger on perceptions, revisions, and use cases than on observed instructional quality, transfer into classroom practice, or sustained professional learning gains.

### Hypothesis Surfaces

One testable hypothesis is that in-service K–12 teachers who receive generative AI lesson-plan feedback will produce higher-quality lesson plans than teachers receiving business-as-usual self-revision alone. The population would be in-service K–12 teachers, the intervention would be structured LLM-based feedback on lesson plans, the primary outcome would be rubric-scored lesson-plan quality, and the appropriate design would be a randomized controlled trial.

A second hypothesis is that pre-service teachers receiving generative AI feedback plus human coaching will outperform those receiving AI-only feedback on both revision quality and later instructional enactment. The population would be pre-service teachers, the intervention would be hybrid AI-plus-coach feedback, the outcomes would be lesson-plan revision quality and observation-based teaching performance, and the design should be a multi-arm randomized trial including AI-only, human-only, and hybrid conditions [19], [22].

A third hypothesis is that K–12 teachers serving English language learners will benefit more from domain-tailored generative AI coaching prompts than from general-purpose prompts. The intervention would be specialized AI feedback for ELL-responsive planning, the outcome would be rubric-based measures of instructional responsiveness and plan quality, and the design should be a comparative randomized trial.
